But on being a conclusion to its predecessors, it became too much of a movie about Corey, and didn't even fulfill its purpose of being a Corey movie. It's like towards the end they suddenly remembered that it's a Halloween movie about Laurie and Michael, and then wrote that movie instead.

Name: Palthu Janwar
Review: Rather than a full fledged movie, Palthu Janwar felt like watching bits and pieces of a bigger story, like this could be a series and this is just the first 3 episodes. So the movie alternates between being a character driven piece about the main character Prasoon and the plotline related to Davis and the other villagers. While Palthu Janwar felt a bit "incomplete" on the whole, it was still a nice watch. The movie is made well, the performances are great, the characters are likable and the movie has heart. Impressive special effects too.

Name: Awakenings
Review:
This was a deeply moving film. Both De Niro and Williams were amazing, especially De Niro. It made me smile a lot and it made my eyes wet and my chest heavy. Randy Newman's score kicked in at the perfect places. The writing is so good and so on point. The drama is effective, the characters are easy to connect to, and the supporting cast is great too. 

This is one of the few movies where you'd just wish that they'd let it end with one of those cheesy "movie" endings, but it chose to stick to the reality, and that hurt.

Name: Rosaline
Review:
Shakespeare might be the writer with the least toxic fanbase. His stuff has been adapted in all shapes and forms with different settings, swapped genders, swapped races, swapped genres and swapped time periods, and yk, people are mostly cool with it and a lot of them adapt the material in quite interesting ways. Maqbool, Joji and Denzel's Macbeth can exist in harmony. Hamlet, Haider and The Lion King can exist in harmony.

"Rosaline" is the newest Shakespeare adaptation that outright begins with making fun of Shakespeare's poetic language. It's a comedy that focuses on Rosaline, who's Juliet's cousin and Romeo's ex girlfriend. The characters talk like millennial people, modern music is used both in the background and within the movie, so basically this is more of a parody than a "faithful" adaptation.

I was more interested to see how they'd deal with the tragic ending of Romeo and Juliet with the whole silly vibe the movie has. But that turned out to be the most fun part of this movie. Kaitlyn Dever is awesome as Rosaline.

The movie has no big surprises and is exactly what we'd expect at the beginning. It's a charming and delightful watch.

Name: Aaranya Kaandam
Review: Aaranya Kaandam is the perfect blend of style, substance, humor, great performances and great cinema. Some of the cinematic choices have aged in 2022, but still, it's still very impressive, the writing is brilliant and the narrative is brilliant.

Name: CODA
Review: All the scenes involving the family were so wholesome, whether it's the writing or the performances or the direction or the editing. They just let the actors do their thing and convey those emotions beautifully, we really feel their love and connection. A lot of important scenes don't even have any background score and that silence works beautifully in the film. Yes, some of the narrative choices are along the safe feel-good territory of things. But there are so many beautiful, well crafted and tender moments in the film that filled up my heart and even made me year up. So since the amount of great scenes and the overall heart of the movie over weighed the generic stuff, I don't care about the generic stuff.

Name: Black Adam
Review:
The announcement that Dwayne Johnson was going to play DC's villain/anti-hero Black Adam came 15 years ago. It took Dwayne Johnson 15 years to get this movie made too. He has talked about how he has argued with studio executives for years to get to play the comic book character that he wanted to play the way he wanted to play it. We finally have the end product that's more than a decade in its making and it did remind me of superhero movies that I've watched a decade ago. And no, that's not because Black Adam isn't "woke", on the contrary it is very woke. The political stand the movie takes against western invaders in the middle east is pretty clear. But rather it has "stuff" that I've seen before, be it faceless CGI soldiers, a one dimensional villain, scenes designed in a certain way that so many superhero movies have done before and of course the fudging sky beam! But regardless of it all, I still kinda enjoyed the movie and had fun.

Black Adam does have the unique aspect of having a central superpowered character with a shady sense of morality. Black Adam doesn't mind killing people and he finds gruesome ways to do it too (within PG-13 constraints). And yet, the movie doesn't sell the "anti-hero" thing too hard. Black Adam is basically your average superhero, who's also played by The Rock, with a taste for murder.

Just like superhero movies having a formula they stick to, Dwayne Johnson movies have their own formula. Make no mistake, this is a movie star, and there's "movie starness" in this movie. So when the superhero formula and The Rock formula joined hands, we can see elements of both here. I don't think the Black Adam theme music sounding similar to The Rock's WWE entrance music is a coincidence. This really is him fulfilling his fantasy of being this particular character. On a scale from Baywatch to Jumanji 2, this is pretty close to the Jumanji 2 side of things.

The action doesn't have any stakes because our dude is Invincible, we know how the action beats are going and it's mostly mash-blast-pummel-fry-repeat. The action is big and cool to look at though. There are attempts at Zack Snyder-ish slo-mo sequences, some of them looked cool, some of them looked unnecessary, some looked silly.

Lorne Balfe's score is cool, especially the main theme, the characters range from cool to interesting to paper-thin. The Rock, Aldis Hodge and Piece Brosnan get the most to do with their characters. There are characters worth expanding in the future here too.

Last year's DC outing The Suicide Squad put an interesting spin on the whole faceless soldiers and CGI villain thing, it also had main characters who were proper anti-heroes. The action had stakes and team members were dying even before we saw the opening credits. Then it had the series "Peacemaker" as a follow up, which again followed an anti-hero who was seen as a villain by everyone who saw its predecessor. While maintaining him as an anti-hero, it also did a similar "faceless soldiers" storyline, but with a different twist. So, what I mean to say is, DC already did the whole "anti-hero" thing pretty well before Black Adam even got released. So while the movie does establish his murderous rage and places him as a "threat", dude is still more hero than anti. The Rock still wants kids to like him and buy his action figure.

On the post credits scene : Cool hairstyle.

Name: Terrifier 2
Review:
Last week I watched Halloween Ends. A concluding chapter of the new big budget follow up to John Carpenter's iconic low budget original. The movie wasn't what the promotional material made me believe it was at all. Now, this week I watched Terrifier 2, a low-budget crowd funded slasher, which is everything its promotional material makes us believe and more.

Damien Leone's Terrifier was one of those movies I randomly discovered from a random movie list. It had this psychotic and sadistic killer clown, played to perfection by David Howard Thornton with the great makeup adding to the overall creepiness. The movie just throws us into Art being creepy asf and just killing people. There was little to no plot and it was all mayhem. With effective music, old fashioned practical visual effects, makeup and a whole 80s grindhouse slasher vibe going for it, Terrifier was impressive, though it also ruined my mood for the whole day.

Coming to the sequel, it's a bigger movie than the original in every way, even duration wise. This time we do get some plot, setup and character back stories. Though some of the stuff is left vague, I felt that's intentional. The kills are all gory and disgusting, with lots of blood, guts and practical special effects mayhem. The sound effects really sell the violence too. It's unabashedly over-the-top and gratuitous. Art doesn't just kill his victims, he plays with them, mutilated them. With Thornton having creepy-funny-scary vibes throughout and the way some of the kills are too over the top with victims staying alive way more than they should, Leone pulling off these sequences is kinda impressive. We could clearly see the low budget special effects at play, but the sequences just work, seem gross, sell the creepiness and that's indeed impressive filmmaking. 

The music was good and Lauren Lavera had great retro final girl vibes as the lead. The writing has a lot of 80s slasher sensibilities, it's not a movie that's too worried about its story, we can clearly see that the focus here is the creepy clown and the violence. With the grainy look, practical effects, retro music and the way it's shot, someone could indeed mistake this for a grindhouse slasher from the 80s.

There's some dreamy/surreal/fantasy stuff in the movie that didn't really make sense to me. But like I said, I felt that was intentional.

Name: Julie & Julia
Review: Meryl Streep, Amy Adams, cool parallel storytelling, cool music and the food. Yum!

Name: Don't Worry Darling
Review:
Don't Worry Darling isn't as bad as I expected it to be. It takes a Black Mirror-ish concept and stretches it out way more than it needed to be. There are various plotholes and conveniences. Harry Styles' performance looked over the top and cartoonish at times. But still, I couldn't completely hate this movie. Florence Pugh looked gorgeous throughout and was brilliant here, her conviction towards the character kind of made me forget the writing issues at times. I also liked the background music, cinematography, costumes and the sets. 

This would've worked better as a Black Mirror episode with smarter writing. It is a concept we've seen before, there's something interesting deep in there. It spent too much time on filler and too little time on more important stuff. Like I said above, despite acknowledging its issues, I'm not able to hate don't worry darling completely.

Name: Barbarian
Review: The only thing I knew about this movie was a cool promo they released in Youtube titled "Justin Long's New Movie". That instantly made me want to watch this. I went into Barbarian not knowing anything about what it's about, and I think that's the best way to watch this movie. It's shot well, edited well, the music is great, the performances are great, the creepy atmosphere and the scares are effective and on the whole this is a really cool proper horror movie.

Name: Pearl
Review:
Pearl immediately looks like a very different movie than its predecessor X. The music is different, the colors are different and the entire visual language is different. X was along the lines of a traditional slasher, but here the movie follows the title character Pearl for the most part, telling the story of where exactly she snapped and started being murderous. There are also the numerous cinema callbacks that are used for dark humour as well as to give us the creeps. Mia Goth gets a lot more to do here as just Pearl than she got to do in her brilliant performance as both Pearl and Maxxine in X. There are scenes which entirely rely on just her performance, and she is so brilliant throughout. We feel Pearl's sadness and her troubles but we also see just how sadistic and creepy she can be. I think Mia Goth's performance creeped me out the most in Pearl than the gore or the violence. The movie even ends with an eerie smile from her that's just hard to forget. She plays the character with so many layers of emotions while also being a horror icon at the same time.

Well, a shotgun recoil later, we're getting Maxxxine next in the Mia Goth Slasherverse, this set of movies may turn out to be iconic on the whole.

Name: Jaya Jaya Jaya Jaya Hey
Review:
Jaya Jaya Jaya Jaya Hey starts off by introducing us to the protagonist Jaya, how she's in a world where everything in her life is dictated by the men around her. Her brother is the only relatively good man in her life. There are flashes of humor poking fun at patriarchy while the movie builds up to Jaya's marriage to the abusive Rajesh. 

There's familiar territory being covered here in terms of the subject matter, but the movie then builds upto a literal punch! (that erupted the entire cinema hall BTW) There's a sudden shift and now it becomes a full-fledged comedy. There's also a shift in POV as we now follow Rajesh more than Jaya. Basil Joseph, who was great as the abusive husband till then gets to show off his physical comedy skills and plays a role that's out of his "zone" really well and makes it his own. Darshana Rajendran as Jaya is great too, but what I loved more is the physical performance by her here, there's a particular kind of physicality involved in Jaya that I wish to see more in Malayalam cinema.

There were multiple memorable sequences that were hilarious and executed well. The performances were great. Even when I felt like the movie was losing focus (especially around the middle part of the second half), something funny or entertaining happened that put me right back in. While handling a universal and sensitive topic like domestic abuse, the movie doesn't get too preachy about it and mostly uses humor to convey its ideas. While I could see where the story was heading towards at times, it was more interesting to see how that journey was made to be hilarious.

Name: The Batman
Review: I can watch this movie again and again and still appreciate how it looks and feels. Definitely one of the best looking movies of the year.

Name: Decision to Leave
Review:
In the version that I watched, the subtitles were weird (ie, bad) and as someone who doesn't understand Korean, I could also feel that I'm losing a lot of the context, especially in the conversations involving the Chinese main character.

I could see that it's a beautiful looking movie with great music and awesome editing. But I don't think I can have a proper opinion without having a proper viewing experience.

Name: Appan
Review:
Appan gets many things right despite its flaws. It's set around the same house and its surroundings, there's only a handful of characters and it all revolves around one despicable person. It's a darkly humorous, sad portrait of a family who has to suffer because the titular father was an absolute villain. Through various character interactions and reveals and by the man himself, we see just how evil this man is. The atmosphere the movie sets is great and the more we get to know about the character Itty (The titular father) the more we hate him and feel bad for those around him.

The performances are great, the use of the location is great, the character development and gradual reveals were nice too.

Name: See How They Run
Review:
I really loved the Wes Anderson-ish style and the quirkyness of this movie. Saorise Ronan and Sam Rockwell were great as the leads, their scenes were great and their "tired drunk veteran - enthusiastic rookie" chemistry was entertaining to watch. They could even turn this into a fun buddy cop series with the two of them.

There were hilarious and fun moments and great energy throughout the movie. The cinematography, editing, music, art and costumes were great. But where it felt lacking was in the central whodunit department. Though there's a great cast playing characters who seemed interesting at first, as the movie moved forward I hardly cared about most of them and like I said above was more interested in the lead cops. So when the killer was finally revealed, it didn't feel like the unraveling of a great mystery the way something like Knives Out made me feel.

So while it felt short on the whodunit for me, this was a fun and entertaining experience nevertheless.

Name: Causeway
Review:
The posters give off a vibe that Jennifer Lawrence's Causeway is a sad and dark movie. Though themes like trauma, loss, guilt and mental health are explored, this is more about moving on and recovering. So it's not essentially a "sad" movie, it's more on the feel-good territory.

Causeway is about a soldier played by Jennifer Lawrence recovering from an injury trying to adjust with life back home. Her interactions with the character James played by Brian Tyree Henry are my favorite parts of this movie. Both of them are wonderful and have great chemistry together. Even though the movie follows only Lawrence's character, I wished if Brian had more screentime too.

I loved the music and cinematography. The character dynamics and their individual flaws were also explored in an interesting way.

Name: Weird: The Al Yankovic Story
Review:
Weird is a self aware parody of both musical biopics in general and of Weird Al himself. Which is indeed the best and most accurate way to do a Weird Al biopic. The movie doesn't take itself seriously at any point and the jokes keep coming constantly. Even the casting of Daniel Radcliffe itself is a joke. There are always stuff happening or people looking or acting a certain way that made me laugh. There's the hilarious way they made use of "Real" Al Yankovic's cameo. They even had a Harry Potter joke in there.

The jokes don't stop after the movie ends either. The consistency that Weird had for being sillier and, well, weird was something that I really loved. The cast was great, most of the jokes made me laugh and I almost stopped the movie before the end credits, and I'm glad I didn't. You're indeed a legend Al.

Name: Enola Holmes
Review: Enola Holmes works better as a fun adventure comedy than as a mystery. I liked the performances, the characters, their chemistry, the style, the look and feel of the movie and the music. It was so energetic from the start and there was no dull moment. As a "detective" story, the fact that the mystery and sleuthing didn't feel all that sleuthy is indeed a flaw, but I had so much fun watching the movie that it was forgivable.

Name: Kooman
Review:
Kooman is partly character driven and partly an investigative thriller. It follows the main character Giri, a police constable with his own insecurities and issues. Giri has a particular way of dealing with people looking down on him and his own negative emotions. The rest of the movie explores its consequences while he faces another unexpected set of events in between.

I loved the characterization of Giri and the way he was brilliantly portrayed by Asif Ali. A lot of the movie relies on us connecting with what Giri is going through and it worked. Even in the way Giri carries himself in the initial scenes, we can sense that this is not the kind of "mass police hero" that Indian cinema is regularly accustomed to, we can sense the weight of his insecurities. The initial half of the movie had a lot of thrilling moments where I could see director Jeethu Joseph doing the things he did best in Drishyam (The first one) again.

Like I mentioned in the first sentence, towards the middle, the movie shifts towards an investigative thriller route. While I enjoyed the latter half and felt that it was thrilling, if l had to choose, my favorite parts of Kooman are the stuff related to Giri himself than the investigation. That whole part can be expanded into its own movie. I loved the background score, which had an eerie vibe to it. A lot of scenes felt creepier due to the score and the whole "owl" theme in the music was also cool. 

For me, Kooman is right up there with Drishyam (The first one).

Name: Enola Holmes 2
Review:
I liked Enola Holmes 2 better than the sequel. The central case was more intriguing, the style and the deduction sequences seemed more fun, the humor worked, the chemistry between the characters were great and Henry Cavill's Sherlock having more screentime than the first movie was also nice. 

I really hope they keep this series going.

Name: Mukundan Unni Associates™
Review: A great anti-hero is a rare find nowadays. Mukundan Unni Associates follows the narcissistic and evil Mukundan Unni, who'd do anything to become the "great" version of himself he believes to be. He has no redeeming qualities and we're not given anything that makes us want to empathise with him. But we do see how much of a vile human being he can be at multiple points. The movie is almost entirely through his perspective, with his deadpan narration driving the whole thing. Everything from the aspect ratio to the precise editing to the use of sound and the overall style gave off the sense of something really unique. Vineeth Sreenivasan was absolutely brilliant both on screen and in his constant darkly humorous narration. Mukundan Unni being as despicable as he is depended on that performance too.

Name: Black Panther: Wakanda Forever
Review: This was beautiful. It's an emotional tribute as well as a passing of the torch. The way it tackles themes like grief and vengeance was so heartfelt. My eyes watered up multiple times throughout the movie. I did feel that Namor's arc wasn't as well defined as Killmonger's. This film also doesn't have the 3rd act CGI issue that the original had. The end credits animation was also beautiful and pretty much sums up the entire movie. Letitia Wright is a star.

Name: Monica, O My Darling
Review: The dope retro soundtrack, the awesome performances, the quirky style, the use of colors, the cinematography, the editing, the structure, the soundtrack (again, the soundtrack!), I could praise each of them forever. While not as brilliant as something like Andhadhun, it comes pretty close.

Name: Smile
Review: There were some cool scares and some effective and creepy looking vfx, designs and music. But on the whole, it felt like the movie was stretching a very thin premise way too much. So by the time it reached its predictable conclusion, the only takeaway was how cool it looked.

Name: Spirited
Review:
Spirited is a nice shake-up of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol that does seem unique among other adaptations of the same material. It's a musical comedy with plenty of meta jokes and the kind of humor that Ryan Reynolds has been doing since Deadpool. Will Ferrel is joyful as he brings the sort of innocence into his character (The ghost of Christmas present) that he did in Elf. Ryan Reynolds is the "Scrooge" here, and he's exactly what we'd expect from Ryan Reynolds acting in a Scrooge musical, he's Ryan Reynolds. The character is meant to be an annoying wise-ass, so I don't know if it was intentional or if the "Reynolds charm" was wearing off on me, but at times he was just a little bit too annoying.

There are interesting angles at the beginning of the movie like a satiric one that's based on social media toxicity, but it's left unexplored afterwards as the movie becomes more about the two protagonists. Spirited tries to be a parallel story that deals with both of its protagonists, sometimes it works, sometimes Reynolds' character just got on my nerves.

The jokes are there in plenty, and there's a lot of funny ones. The only ones that got too old is where Reynolds' character always questions the "Christmas Carol format" and is self aware of the situation, like, you know, WE GET IT DUDE, YOU WERE DEADPOOL!

The songs were really cool, I loved the dance numbers too, all the actors were great during those sequences. The movie does have heart, I liked the way it ended. Though it is a bit stuffy and could've been a lot better with the idea it had, it still made me smile at the ending reprise song, so that's a win. 

Apologies if my opinion on the movie became too much of a rant on Ryan Reynolds. (Please do that Deadpool movie soon and vent out the Deadpoolness, Ryan).

Name: 1744 White Alto
Review:
I liked what this film was trying to do. The criminal duo consisting of a bigger silent guy and a smaller talkative guy obviously screamed FARGO from the beginning. The whole movie does have a Coen tribute-ish vibe. Combine that with the use of color palette, music, quirky editing, and the way the rural setting is showed with a weird visual sense, the world and the quirky characters seemed pretty cool. The background jokes were a nice touch too. 

While I do think that the pacing could've used some work, 1744 White Alto was pretty fun.

Name: Kumari
Review:
Kumari is such a waste of a good premise, moody music and great looking visuals. A folklore based tale with good intentions that's pulled down by lackluster writing, hilariously over the top acting and bad dialogues. The movie also had early 2000s malayalam Yakshi movie sensibilities, which I didn't mind, including the "village girl" introduction song, that I thought went extinct.

 The opening minutes showed promise and the movie does look great. The special effects and makeup effects hold up too, I don't think I've seen a Malayalam movie that looks this good in this genre. Malayalam folklore still has a lot of promise, so I do wish we get other attempts, Kumari does get some things right, but it got some important bits wrong, so that's why it felt like wasted potential.

Name: TÁR
Review:
The final touch in Todd Field's TÁR is quite ingenious and darkly comedic. After 160 minutes of spending time in a world that's centered around classical music, orchestras and a conductor, the soundtrack choice for the end credits felt poetic and made me appreciate the film even more.

The film is about the titular Lydia Tár, a renowned classical music conductor. Lydia is in every scene of the film, with Cate Blanchett brilliantly portraying the wide range of emotions she goes through perfectly, the portrayal does justice to the brilliant writing and enhances it. Talking about the writing, this is one of those films that takes its audience seriously. As in it actually asks quite a bit from us. When the initial half of the movie is filled with classical music jargon, it needs us to understand that we need to look past the jargon and the music and see that those scenes are meant to make us understand Lydia. This is not a movie like The Big Short where the movie does expect us to understand its jargons and tries to explain them. The movie also expects us to understand several subtle nuances that are not really spoonfed to us. 

This here is a character piece. The film, which is centered around the music world, barely has a background score except for the track in the end credits. Rest of the music is all things we hear within the film itself. It even takes the movie an hour or so before we even see Lydia conducting an orchestra, but even by then, the writing is so precise and Blanchett is so brilliant that we have already bought into the fact that she's a great conductor.

As the film gets deeper in, the musical jargon fades, it becomes all about Lydia and her sins than about the music, the movie gets political too, and when the movie eventually builds to an ingenious climax, that buildup is also masterfully paced and written, with the end credits soundtrack being the final cherry on top.

Name: The Wonder
Review: The visuals, the atmosphere, the performances and the music are brilliant. I do think that this particular story could've been a more intense movie. It was a very satisfying watch anyway.

Name: Kantara
Review:
While it sticks to the cliches of the genre with dated elements older than the setting, with plenty of problematic elements too, Rishab Shetty does occasionally impress, especially when it comes to action sequences. The movie loses steam towards the second half while its building upto a twist that we could see from the very beginning. But the action in the climatic sequence was pretty great with Rishab transforming into that particular entity pretty convincingly.

Didn't find any blatant right wing propaganda in the movie though, no idea why Indian savarna right wingers were celebrating this movie. Lol.

Name: The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special
Review: Simple and sweet, but still retains James Gunn touches.

Name: The Addams Family
Review: The jokes in this movie are timeless and the characters are so awesome. Though the core plot related to Fester is underdeveloped, the movie is consistently entertaining and funny.

Name: Gold
Review:
Gold (except for the epilogue) had everything I expect from an Alphonse Puthren movie. It shares its good and bad with Puthren's previous body of work (again, not counting the epilogue).

This is unapologetically a style over substance movie, the characters are caricatures, even the main character Joshiy. Joshiy's mom begins as a loving mother, who transitions into a stereotype, who then transitions into an ironic running joke. Likewise every situation and every character is a visual gag. Some work, some don't. It mostly worked for me and I was having a great time. I understand that the style can be a bit too much at times. There are shots that seem like Alphonse Puthren forgot editing while he was "editing", where you don't need to be a professional editor to sense that he objectively didn't cut at the right time. There are moments that are meant to build up tension that fall flat because of the way its edited together too. And there are insert shots and sequences that occasionally look out of place. But when the style and the editing does work, it was a joy to watch. Gold is not entirely a lost cause, there are several moments where I did get to see the Alphonse Puthren flair that I expected. There's a phone call scene between Lalu Alex and Shammy Thilakan that was so childish that it was hilarious.

Then there are scenes that confused me on whether the humor I felt was intentional or unintentional. Remember the scene from Premam where George gets flashbacks of the moments he spent with Malar as they part ways forever? There is a similar scene in Gold, but instead of showing flashbacks of the characters spending time together and having a connection, we get flashbacks of snacks being offered and being eaten. There's sad background music, but it just made me crack up and get confused if this was indeed a "funny" scene.

The epilogue was where Gold completely became something else. Till then it was a silly Mish-mash of caricaturish characters and situational humor. In the epilogue, it's either trying to be one of those Tamil message movies or is crossing over with Prithviraj's own Jana Gana Mana. The ending is so confusing and doesn't fit in with the rest of the movie at all. I was honestly waiting for a punchline by the end of it, but there wasn't one. So, it left a sour aftertaste. It was immediately followed by the song "Thanne Thanne" and some bloopers, so I got reminded of the movie that ran before the epilogue again.

Gold ends with Alphonse Puthren saying that he missed us for 7 years. Since I watched this movie after knowing the general audience reaction, that ending text felt bittersweet. Gold is definitely not the worst movie of the year, it isn't even the worst Prithviraj movie of the year (grrrrrrr).

Name: Addams Family Values
Review: It's darker and funnier than the previous part. Though the villain is easily defeated and is weak, this was a more satisfying movie. They take it up a notch in every way. I wish I could see more of Angelica Huston as Morticia though.

Name: Freddy
Review:
"Lonely, shy, introvert turns into a killer", is not that much of a fresh premise, even for Indian movies. We have a lot of villain origin stories with the same template. "Freddy" initially seemed like it was going along the route of something like Joker, where a sympathetic but troubled person would be pushed to the point of being a psychopath. As the movie progressed and we see Freddy being a genuine creep, as an introvert myself, I was getting ready to get offended by the movie. But as it turns out, it should be the bullies who should be offended by Freddy more.

Freddy wants to be a "descent to madness" movie and a generic revenge movie at the same time. The movie expects us to sympathise towards Freddy even though he doesn't give us a lot of reasons to do so. So it makes the villains even shittier. They talk and act like they're from another universe. There are stereotypes here that went extinct years ago, or at least in the last Luv Ranjan movie Karthik Aaryan did. Freddy ends up being lifeless, devoid of logic and convoluted with a lot of cavities.

 I watched Freddy out of my love for stories involving anti-heroes. But not even the movie itself can decide whether Freddy is an anti-hero. It is an achievement that the movie depicts both introverts and extroverts in a shitty manner though.

(They had a dentist as the main character but have no idea how a mouth looks without teeth in it?)

Name: Jackie Brown
Review: Even the least violent Tarantino movie still reminds us that it's a Tarantino movie. Jackie Brown is groovy and well made. Everyone from Pam Grier to Sam Jackson to De Niro is awesome. The soundtrack is awesome, the dialogues are awesome, the staging is awesome. I know this is an adaptation, still, the ending lacked the usual Tarantino touch, but still, the movie is undeniably awesome.

Name: Love Today
Review:
The movie is pretty problematic in its portrayal of "modern" relationships. A lot of serious and disgusting actions by characters are casually brushed over while the movie makes a big deal out of some others. The shitty things the male lead and his friends do in the movie were too shitty to be redeemed by a marathon of emotional monologues and sad background score. When the movie ends, it doesn't earn that particular conclusion at all. At the beginning I expected the movie to be a satire or dark comedy that would subvert the usual toxic tropes in south Indian romance movies. But the movie turned out to be about trust, if "trust" was loving your [male] partner even if he's a pervert, part of a cyber crime gang or is generally a toxic dude (but he's caring tho). 

But I can't deny that the arc involving Yogi Babu's character was great. It was like a culmination of all the characters he has done where his physical traits were the joke. I was genuinely moved by that scene and the way he delivered it. But ironically the rest of the movie doesn't do justice to that arc.

Name: Monster
Review:
Is it bad? It's horrendous.

Is it ironically funny and entertaining? Yup.

Monster is so shitty that the shittiness becomes the best thing about it. The attempt to be "progressive" is so ironic that it made me laugh.

Name: Troll
Review:
It's Norwegian Godzilla, with a few king Kong elements thrown in (and they're not hiding that fact at all). Everything follows the kaiju movie template. The visual effects looked great though this is not as big as Hollywood monster movie productions. A really cool helicopter action scene looked pretty much like a similar sequence in Kong : Skull Island, but it was fun anyway. The backstory was also nice, though it's kind of the exact same as Kong.

Anyway, it was fun, though derivative.

Name: Prince
Review: As dumb as it is, there was a lot of genuine fun and laughs here. It doesn't take itself too seriously especially towards the climax where the usual "hero speech" scene in Tamil movies is played for laughs. Compared to something as shitty as Don, Prince was pretty nice enough for me to forget its flaws.

Name: Joyland
Review:
Joyland is an interesting take on the concept of Joy. Its characters are people who are actually restricted from experiencing joy. Either by the traditions they have to follow, or by peer pressure or just by society in general. There's people who keep their love, sexuality, passions and identity repressed because they've been trapped in certain roles. The one main character who does try to be what she wishes to be is Biba, but even then, we get to see how hard it is for her and how she's constantly judged for trying to have "joy" in life.

The film is beautifully shot and staged. There's a great warmth to the scenes, the characters felt real and it was easy to connect with their emotions, even when the movie does minimal hand-holding through a lot of key moments. The pacing was very calculated, with scenes getting set up beautifully, with emotions pouring in at just the right amounts at the right moments. Combine that with the great performances by the cast and the camn and poignant mood set by the music, the editing and the cinematography, Joyland is indeed beautiful, though it also covers some sad and ugly sides of life.

Name: Aftersun
Review:
Aftersun is a film that explores a father-daughter relationship in a quite beautiful and sensitive way. As we watch Calum and his daughter Sophie get started on their vacation and bonding, slowly we sense the sadness in the air. Something is pulling Calum down, he tries his best to seem happy, but Charlotte Wells uses silence and long continuous shots in several key moments to show us another layer of the man. As the scenes progress, we get an incomplete version of him, through the eyes of his daughter.

Aftersun has beautiful instances of subtle writing, performance and symbolism. We just see the father and daughter enjoying a vacation through most of it, but embedded in it is a layer of profound cinematic storytelling that's just as beautiful as it is sad. The film plays out like we're inside the mind of a person who's holding onto precious memories from her past, at an age where she couldn't process a lot of the stuff her father was experiencing. As they danced to "Under Pressure" together with the lyrics perfectly matching the situation, and Calum finally "walked out the door" with that beautiful score playing in the background, it was such a beautiful and heartfelt ending and it made me tear up.

Name: Yashoda
Review:
While it's cool that a proper female-led "mass" action movie exists, from telugu of all places is kind of cool, Yashoda also has the baggage that a lot of Telugu action movies have. Clichés after clichés play out on screen, with twists that have appeared in almost every masala movie for the last few decades. Though the initial setup gave off Squid Game vibes, the film immediately jumps into predictable masala movie territory with predictable and often hilarious twists, tacky visual effects, terrible dialogue and hilarious vfx.

But among all that, there's Samantha being an absolute badass during the action sequences and in places where she has to have the action hero presence. The action is well choreographed and thankfully doesn't resort to the telugu movie formula of goons just flying around in slow-motion. So like I said, Yashoda just existing is kinda cool, though it's far from a good action movie.

Name: Avatar: The Way of Water
Review:
A "singular vision" might be one of the things Hollywood blockbusters started losing after the whole superhero trend caught on. In the early 2000s, if you compare two movies like True Lies and Bad Boys, it's pretty easy to distinguish between the Michael Bay one and the James Cameron one. But with the last decade, "The Blockbuster" started to look and feel like the same movie. There are exceptions, of course, but big movies after 2010 that feel very unique to a filmmaker in terms of the look, the style, and the narrative are pretty rare. Even this year's biggest non-superhero movie hit, Top Gun: Maverick, isn't the singular vision of its director, Joseph Kosinski. It follows the original Top Gun director Tony Scott's style most of the time, and it follows the recent nostalgic "legacy sequel" trend too. The movie also has obvious contributions from Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie.

Avatar 2 felt entirely like James Cameron's vision. Other than listening to algorithms, data, or executives, it's the kind of old-school, huge spectacle that Cameron has been making for decades. While the technological innovations and visual grandeur on display are advanced, the writing didn't exactly get updated as much as the visuals did. Avatar (2009) was pretty much like this too in terms of writing, with lines and situations that seemed like they belonged in an 80s or 90s movie (the script was actually written in the 90s too, I think). I didn't really mind the old-school writing or Cameron's teenagers still talking like John Conner from Terminator 2. Flaws aside, when the writing does tap into the basics, in this movie's case family, it really hits the right places. The setpieces are brilliantly staged too, especially the climatic one, which is a pretty cool callback to one of Cameron's iconic films.

The first film had a lot of sequences that were just about letting us see the beauty of Pandora. The sequel has more of this stuff. This might either be a showcase of the cutting-edge technology and the gorgeous visuals, or it's just Cameron's love for nature and especially the ocean being shown on screen in digital glory. It might be tiresome to some, as there are enough Pandora beauty shots here that a nature documentary could be edited together from them. For me, getting to spend more time in Pandora and basking in those visual details in 3D was a wholesome experience.

The film's message still leans on protecting the environment, like its predecessor. Cameron's love nature and his anti-colonisation views are pretty evident in the film. 

As a spectacle and a cinematic experience, Avatar: Way of the Water is glorious when it wants to be. My jaw was on the floor multiple times, as these were some of the most gorgeous and unique images that I've seen on a cinema screen. The setpieces were exhilarating, with Cameron doing what he does best in the third act. I couldn’t stop admiring even the tiniest object for looking so perfect, or the water interactions that looked amazing. I could see how advancements in performance capture technology showed us more of the nuances in the actors' performances than the first film.

Avatar: The Way of Water isn't flawless, but it delivered on everything that I had hoped from it.

Name: The Banshees of Inisherin
Review:
Martin McDonagh's The Banshees of Inisherin is set on an Irish island in the 1920s, with the Irish Civil War happening in the background. But the story being told here is pretty universal, at least at its core, though the movie proceeds to get darker and weirder. The movie starts off with Colm (Brendan Gleeson), who decides to cut ties with his best friend. This is a sudden decision from him, and his now-former best friend Pádraic (Colin Farrel) is unable to even process this big change in his routine. The sudden rejection and self-doubt that Pádraic feels are instantly relatable to anyone who has been abruptly ghosted by their close friends.

The movie isn't a straightforward, relatable comedy-drama about friendship though, and neither is it of the "feel-good" variety. The emotions are relatable, but the events aren't. The storyline becomes pretty dark moving forward, but the film is still fueled by the lost friendship. We never see flashbacks, and we never see how these two people used to be when they were best friends, but in their current situation, they're far from it, though we could see flashes of what they used to be. The interactions between the leads are written and shot brilliantly, with amazing performances by Gleeson and Farrel.

With such a seemingly simple conflict, The Banshees of Inisherin constantly keeps things interesting and doesn't get tiresome or repetitive, though this is the kind of storyline that could've easily gone that route. The Irish dialogues are sharp and witty, and that's where a lot of the humour comes from. The witty dialogue and the amazing performances keep the film constantly alive. There's also the background score, which comes at the perfect moments to convey a sense of eeriness, and the cinematography, which captures the Irish landscapes beautifully and also accentuates the drama.

The Banshees of Inisherin is focused on a single conflict from beginning to end and ties everything up beautifully, making the events seem weird and the emotions seem relatable at the same time.

Name: The Fabelmans
Review: I could just feel how personal this film was for Spielberg. When I saw Sammy Fableman's love for cinema, his passion and his wonder, that's just Steven Spielberg communicating his audience directly. It's shot and actred beautifully with a lot of beautiful visual storytelling. The score was beautiful and I just love the warmth it had throughout. This is a film with classic Hollywood sensibilities and yet, there are aspects of it which are timeless too. The drama and the character relationships are developed beautifully, with a lot of standout scenes. Loved the meta moment at the end too.

Name: Bones and All
Review: Great cinematography, beautiful music, great performances by an amazing cast, but all for a film that takes itself way too seriously with writing that's more fit for an 80s slasher. The characters didn't feel all that interesting, it felt very detached, I guess this would've worked better as a season of American Horror Story.

Name: Knives Out
Review: Knives Out is the rare kind of whodunit that's so fun to watch even after you know the twists and turns. The writing, the direction, the editing, the cinematography, the music, the performances and that Benoit Blanc accent, everything is awesome. It was nice to catch up on it again before watching the sequel.

Name: Glass Onion
Review: Glass Onion has all the things that made its predecessor great with a great new mystery in a different format. Craig and the accent is still so much fun to watch, with a lot of interesting new characters. Some of them are caricatures of real-life people and that kind of satire is one of the things that makes Glass Onion different from Knives Out. The humour and the suspense were always on point and I kept being impressed by both. Add to that the various visual and aural cues that add to the world with cool cinematography, music and editing, this was a pretty gripping and entertaining movie.

Name: Kajillionaire
Review: Weird, funny and emotional, at just the right amounts.

Name: Violent Night
Review: This felt like it was written a kid friendly family movie at first, which was then converted to a violent foul mouthed R Rated action movie. Because the moments of extreme violence and cursing is surrounded by the cheesiest Christmas movie plot ever, that too in a movie that's not meant for kids. All the "good" characters including our main dude Santa perform acts of extreme violence in several occasions, only to behave like your usual family movie sunshine people in the very next scene. Confusing tone and bad writing aside, I did have fun while watching this movie, there are cheesy asf one-liners by Santa and the main antagonist Mr. Scrooge that made me Crack up every single time. The action sequences are pretty good, though they tend to get repetitive after a while. There's instances of enjoyable dark humor, with even an R-Rated throwback to Home Alone. While some of these work as standalone moments, the movie that's wrapped around them is still confused about what it is.

Name: White Noise
Review:
White Noise is Noah Baumbach going bigger and weirder than his usual style of slice-of-life, relatable, "real people" movies (including Madagascar 3). It's a bit messy and incoherent, throwing in a lot of satirical ideas and humour, which doesn't always gel together well as a singular narrative. And yet, there are things I loved about the movie. There are scenes that made me chuckle and conversation scenes that had the rhythm and chaotic brilliance that Baumbach is so good at. Adam Driver was brilliant and hilarious as Jack, and I wish Greta Gerwig's Babette had more screentime and that they had more scenes together. Their husband-wife chemistry was amazing. 


The interesting blended family is not explored as much as I thought it would be in the film. The film is divided up into chapters, but I felt disconnected from the characters and the situations at several moments, though this might be intentional. This is not like the previous Noah Baumbach-Greta Gerwig movies, which were about actually getting to know characters and following their interesting quirks and emotions. In short, even though White Noise felt messy and I expected more from Baumbach, I still loved parts of it.

Name: The Menu
Review:
The "rich pretentious assholes" genre has seen several entries in 2022. White Lotus S02, The Triangle of Sadness, Bodied Bodies Bodies and Glass Onion are the others that immediately come to mind. The Menu is directed by Mark Mylod, who has directed several episodes of Succession, another acclaimed "rich assholes" piece. The Menu also has the same spirit as that of Succession. It has a cynical tone, a pitch-dark sense of humor, and a similar depiction of capitalism and pretentious delights. The difference is that it isn't focused on diving deep into its characters or their relationships. The Menu works more as a satirical horror comedy that gets progressively weirder and darker as it progresses.

As the pretentious weirdness of the chef, played to perfection by Ralph Fiennes, transformed into more violent spaces, I loved the way the movie incorporated humor into the chaos. Nicholas Hoult plays a food enthusiast with the most punchable face, and there's a scene in the kitchen with him that's both hilarious and brilliant. Anya Taylor-Joy plays the "odd one out" in this group of rich assholes, which is also the kind of character we're familiar with, having already seen similar characters in films like Knives Out and Ready or Not. Is this a pattern?

The Menu is original and hilarious while also being familiar, especially when it comes to Anya Taylor-Joy's character. As I can't resist making a food reference, the movie felt delicious and is exactly the kind of dark comedy that I love.

Name: The Elephant Whisperers
Review:
This is just the cutest. Raghu and Ammu are love. Wholesome feels throughout and I had tears towards the end.

Edit : My thoughts on this doc have changed since I saw the news about the subjects of the doc facing disrespect from the filmmakers. Still, retaining the rating for the people and animals that I saw on screen, not the filmmakers.

Name: Just Like Heaven
Review:
Is the sudden urge to watch cheesy romantic comedies from early and mid 2000s a sign that I'm getting old?

Ruffalo is so cool in romantic movies though. Plus the movie is pretty funny (sometimes unintentionally). The cheesiness and mid 2000s vibe is so entertaining.

Name: 13 Going on 30
Review: Yet another deliciously cheesy watch in my  recent cheesathon. Jennifer Garner as a teenager is both weird, funny and cute at the same time. Rufalo is super cool yet again. The movie is yet another lighthearted slice that's watchable just for the vibes.

Name: Darbar
Review:
Murugadoss' attempts at recreating Petta are so sad and laughable in Darbar, with all the "Thalaivar tribute" references spectacularly falling flat. Anirudh overuses the Annamalai theme too much on the score and the whole sad affair just reminded me just how awesome Petta was. Surrounding it is a police movie that plays out more like a Hari movie than a Murugadoss movie. More than the predictability and formulaic nature, the whole thing just felt lazy and half-assed, which is seasoned with shitty Ram Laxman fight scenes that's just dumb gravity defying flying, bouncing and sleeping by the stuntmen and slo-mo posing by Rajini (which is usually how all Ram Laxman stunt sequences are).

Rajini doing Rajini stuff is fun to watch, Anirudh's music is cool too, just that his music makes the sad attempts to be another Petta even sadder.

Name: Maharshi
Review:
The trend in Hollywood is "eat the rich" right now, whereas in Telugu cinema, the trend has been "Lick the rich" for decades. In a "Lick the rich" movie a rich dude will incarnate into a random village to save all the common people from the bad guys and preach some social messages and/or motivational quotes.

Maharshi is yet another "rich dude saves poor people" story, which also is stretched more to add a college flashback. The college flashback reminded me of 3 idiots, well, 3 idiot minus the charm and humor. Mahesh Babu plays the most perfect dude in the universe, every single thing is based on existing formula, and sometimes hilarious.

I had a lot of unintentional fun though. Mahesh Babu's character seemed to be inspired by Elon Musk a bit, and watching the movie now makes that even more hilarious.

Name: Arab Blues
Review: Golshifteh Farahani is so charming and likable in this movie. Watching the performance itself was my favorite part in Arab Blues. It's a simple film, with some quirky moments and occasional laughs. Satisfying.

Name: Chungking Express
Review: Gorgeous and brilliant.

Name: RRR
Review: "It's so dumb" "Oh, It's so dumb it's brilliant!" "NO!! IT'S JUST DUMB!!" - Glass Onion (2022)

Name: Nanpakal Nerathu Mayakkam
Review: There's a lot to appreciate here. From the wide static frames that make the scenes look like a stage play set at times and sometimes like paintings, to the rare use of close-ups that bring about a lot of meaning, the soundscape that's given life by TVs and radios in the background, a stellar cast led by a brilliant Mammootty completely disappearing into the character, and LJP once again stepping into a lighter magical realism territory after the much more aggressive Churuli, It was such a meditative experience, and after stepping out of the cinema, it's still inside my head.

Name: Kaapa
Review:
I couldn't even watch 10 minutes of "Kaduva." So compared to that, Shaji Kailas' Kaappa is an upgrade, though it falls flat. The issue with Kaappa is that, while Kaduva had a hollow mass masala screenplay that was shot like a hollow mass masala movie, Kaappa has a screenplay that warrants a gritty, dark, and realistic crime drama rather than a "commercial" potboiler. The slo-mo, "hero" close-ups, and flying goons don't really mix into Indugopan's screenplay, which is a grounded and serious affair otherwise. The writing here isn't as deep as something like Vada Chennai, but still, Kaappa would've been a way better movie if it lost its Shaji Kailasness. So many potentially great themes and character nuances are wasted because of the movie's attempts to be "commercial."

Njan Steve Lopez supremacy.

Name: M3GAN
Review:
It's weird to call M3GAN "modern Child's Play" when Child's Play itself had a reboot that swapped the "doll possessed by a serial killer" plot for an AI-controlled personal assistant doll turning into a killer plot. So premise-wise, M3GAN covers familiar territory. But there are enough unique tweaks made to the formula that the movie entertains and feels refreshing without seeming repetitive. The trailer basically had the whole plot in it, and even if I hadn't seen the trailer, I would've guessed where the movie was going the moment I saw the doll.

The best thing about this movie is, indeed, the title character. The way they chose to portray her is also interesting. M3GAN is neither entirely a puppet nor entirely CGI, but an actual actress' performance enhanced by makeup and visual effects, and this does add to both the weirdness of the character and her personality, so to speak. Both the actresses who did the voice work and the physical performance for M3GAN have done a great job here. The way M3GAN is written is also fun, with enough touches that make her different from other murderous robots or toys. There were parts where it felt more like an evil Toy Story than a Child's Play homage. The amazing visual effects convincingly sell the illusion of what M3GAN is. The touches of dark humour and the effective scares helped to keep me engaged, too.

With such a predictable and formulaic premise, it's kind of impressive that M3GAN was able to be as awesome as it is.

Name: Pathaan
Review:
The "YRF Spy Universe" films are like a blend between the newer Fast and Furious movies and the pre-Craig Bond movies. They're over-the-top, excessive, and loud spectacles that move from locations to set pieces to dance numbers. Pathaan also repeats the same formula, but does so with the ever-charming SRK at its front and center. SRK is in fine form here, and it's his charisma that makes the movie fun even when it's just moving from set piece to set piece with very thin writing.

This is the kind of movie that has good-looking leads and makes sure we see how good-looking they are; all three leads get their "model" moments in the film. Deepika's femme fatale is not just eye candy; she gets to be an absolute badass too besides looking gorgeous. Still, only in present-day India would the audience cheer for the colour of a bikini. What a world! John Abraham is playing a generic, one-dimensional villain here; he's pretty nice in the fight scenes, though. I also liked Dimple Kapadia's performance. 

I liked how the movie acknowledges the size and strength differences between the protagonist and the antagonist, though it's operating on an unrealistic terrain. The action setpieces range from cool to flat. Some of the attempts at going "big" seemed more cartoonish than thrilling, though this approach did work in the train action sequence that reminded me of a level from the game Uncharted 2 (the cameo was better than I expected). The best ones were the ones with the least amount of CG, or green screen, of course.

The self-referential humour at times was a nice touch too. But about the Spy Universe itself, I wish they'd prioritise doing practical stunts and action moving forward rather than CG/green screen fests. You know, be more like Mission Impossible or The Craig Bond movies than Fast and the Furious. Overall, Pathaan was fun!

Name: Thankam
Review: Thankam is a straightforward procedural drama that I really loved. The performances were great with Biju Menon, Vineeth Sreenivasan, Vineeth Thattil and Gireesh Kulkarni being the standouts. The humor worked without slowing down the seriousness of the investigation, with the score and the cinematography setting the mood perfectly. The buildup felt great, the score was effective, Vineeth Sreenivasan's Kannan was a very interesting character, and as a procedural, Thankam worked for me.

Name: Carnal Knowledge
Review: Carnal Knowledge is an interesting character study about lust and misogyny with such great writing and brilliantly staged scenes. Jack Nicholson and the rest of the cast are brilliant, with the film itself being such a timeless portrayal of toxic masculinity.

Name: An Action Hero
Review:
An Action Hero is a satirical action comedy that takes existing action movie clichés and breaks them (or follows them) in hilariously self-aware ways. Aayushman Khurrana steps out of his usual territory (except for Andhadhun) to play a pretty grey superstar action hero, and he's pretty solid in the action sequences and fight scenes, truly seeming like an action hero. While casting someone like Tiger Shroff in the role might've made the movie more meta, when it comes to handling dark humor and delivering a great performance, Aayushman feels like the right person for the job.

The movie blends several action movie templates together while wrapping them up with a layer of satire. The constant news footage montages become a character of their own and make fun of the whole "Boycott Bollywood" circus by just basically showing reenactments of actual footage (I don't think the dude who played the Arnab equivalent in this movie was even half as over-the-top as the actual Arnab, lol). The humor, action, and satire blend so well. Jaideep Ahlawat is also awesome at pulling off dark humor. The action is well choreographed, well performed, and well shot, except for some weird wire work in the final fight scene (Was that intentional though?) 

I'm a bit disappointed that this movie didn't do well at the box office, though. It's sad when movies like this or Mard Ko Dard Nahi Hota don't really make an impact, but films with horrendous-looking action scenes do become huge hits as "action entertainers" (I'm not talking about Pathaan; I liked Pathaan).

Name: You People
Review: While Eddie Murphy and Julia Louis-Dreyfus are in fine form here, and the movie did make me laugh at various points, something still felt missing.

Name: Tiger Zinda Hai
Review: Bhai doesn't even need a Spy Universe, he is the universe. Jokes aside, Tiger Zinda Hai is the most straightforward spy thriller in the "YRF Spy Universe", with the majority of the runtime spent on the action and the main mission (which is based on the same incident as the Malayalam movie Take Off, just with Bhai). The action looked really cool, with a lot of it impressively being done practically. That one City Council scene with Katrina Kaif was badass and it's kinda disappointing that she never got to do a full on solo action movie. Bhai does Bhai stuff, but just like Ek Tha Tiger, it's a much more toned down Bhai. There are plenty of action movie clichés and deshbhakthi movie clichés in the film. Still, seeing as how India is presently and how the latest installment of the franchise Pathaan was censored, some of the India - Pak stuff that was in this movie and was not censored was surprising. Tiger Zinda Hai is big dumb derivative fun, bhai style, it's a more straightforward action thriller than the other spy universe movies, and the Tiger movies are definitely the best in the franchise.

Name: Babylon
Review: So, the critically panned film that was called "the worst film by Damien Chazelle" is actually one of the best films I've watched recently. Pure, glorious cinema—unfiltered, unapologetic, and just crazy. So many brilliant scenes, gorgeous to look at, great performances, amazing music, and at even 3 hours and 10 minutes long, I wish this masterpiece was longer. I'd definitely revisit it.

Name: Sardar
Review:
I actually liked the plotline involving the Influencer police officer at the beginning than the main plot involving espionage and the water conspiracy that followed. While the movie has enough Whatsapp University-ish bullshit just like P S Mithran's previous movie Hero, and old man makeup on Karthi that doesn't seem convincing at all, there are some good fight scenes and build ups here. I especially liked the parts where the scenes intercut between the son and the father (both Karthi) and how the shots were matched up.

So, Sardar is dumb, but not just movie dumb, whatsapp uncle dumb. It's pretty generic and formulaic, but still, enjoyable in parts.

Name: Romancham
Review:
Jithu Madhavan's Romancham starts off with the kind of bachelor housemate setting that the Malayalam audience is familiar with. The characters and the house itself are set up pretty quickly, and the situational comedy begins from the moment we meet them. The production design and art are great, with the house looking like a real, lived-in place, with things like the toilet bowls, rats, the rat graveyard, the poster on the wall, and the various religious symbols adding in details that are constantly part of various running jokes. This consistency is present in the characters too, with their various quirks and unique problems being a part of the situational humour from beginning to end. Setting up and detailing the location this way gives the humour so much life that, by the second half, even certain looks by the characters cracked me up. The characters and some of the events are clearly inspired by real-life situations, and that's pretty evident. 

When Romancham starts to transition into horror territory too, it does so in a way that the consistency of the layer of humour is maintained. It doesn't take itself too seriously, and yet the scares and the creepiness somehow feel effective. Sushin Shyam's score, Sanu Thahir's cinematography, and Kiran Das' editing give so much life to these sequences, especially towards the end. This is the kind of comedy that does rely on its performers and their comedic timing and prowess to land the jokes. Soubin Shahir is back to doing what he does best (finally), Arjun Ashokan is hilarious and creepy at the same time whenever he appears on screen with that smile of his, and everyone in the main cast, including Sajin Gopu, Afsal P. H., Abin Bino, Siju Sunny, Jagadeesh Kumar and Anandaraman, get their fair share of laughs. 

There's a disclaimer at the beginning of the movie that the animals used are dummies or CGI, so if those rats weren't real, that's so impressive and some of the best special effects I've seen. This is the kind of movie that's perfect for community viewing in the cinemas, with consistent laughter and fun. 

While watching the movie, I wanted it to be expanded into a series since the setting and characters were so much fun. I do wish that would happen.

Name: Iratta
Review:
Iratta is a police procedural that drops us immediately into its central crime. Then the investigation happens within the closed space that the crime has happened in, a police station. Then, through multiple perspectives, the portrait of a person is painted. This is the kind of character study that leaves us with many questions. Are these accounts reliable? Is such a terrible person worthy of redemption? Was he actually terrible? These questions are answered in a final act that just left me speechless. 

Even after the credits rolled, I kept going back to the story and that haunting conclusion. Joju George is excellent as the twin main characters, especially as Vinod, with both of them having enough differences in body language and mannerisms that we never doubt who's who, and that pays off in key dramatic moments.

Name: Indian
Review: I'm not going to nitpick Indian, because yeah, clearly parts of it haven't aged well. But it is still epic, large scale event cinema and a lot of fun.

Name: Spadikam
Review:
Two things to say after watching the remastered version of Spadikam on the big screen:

Number one, the movie itself is a reminder that "mass" in Malayalam cinema in the past wasn't about replicating the larger-than-life hero worship of masala movies from other Indian languages. They were about flawed protagonists, human conflicts, and actual drama. The action and the catchphrases were just a part of the larger storytelling, and even the action was grounded, had stakes, and made us feel the violence rather than just being rubber humans in photoshoot slow-mo.

Number two, while a filmmaker is the final authority on what to do with his own work, as an audience member, I just couldn't agree with a lot of the choices made here to "upgrade" Spadikam. The film itself begins with a shot of a badly animated CGI vulture, when nothing was wrong with the shot of the actual vulture in the original. Then there are several pieces of newly shot footage randomly inserted that don't really add anything to the movie. The editing is also different, as the transitions between some scenes felt jarring. But while the new shots are just momentary hiccups, what really made me feel disappointed was how the sound effects (most importantly, the punches and kicks) and original score have been replaced by "upgraded" versions, with everything including Aadu Thoma's theme music sounding like an inferior cover of the original. There are even "modern" soundtrack additions that stick out like a sore thumb. I also think that I heard a background score track from the God of War video games during the climax. This is not an insult to God of War; it's an insult to Spadikam. So even though I'm no authority to talk about remastering a pop culture phenomenon, I'm pretty sure that when releasing it in a new form, the main concern has to be preserving the things that made it a pop culture phenomenon and not "upgrading" them away. I'd rather not say anything about the Facebook post-credits scene. 

If I ever feel like revisiting Spadikam, I'd rather watch the original version with the original score and sound effects, even if it's not in 4K or Atmos, than the upgraded one.

Name: Mahaveeryar
Review: They did have an interesting idea. There were occasional laughs. But the movie is just bland, incoherent, and tone-deaf on the whole. The insensitivity towards the end is pretty extreme to be balanced by saying it's satire or an allegory.

Name: Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania
Review:
While I didn't feel that Quantumania was as bland and forgettable as the previous Ant-Man and the Wasp movie, it's still QuantuMEHnia. It's still the same old recycled formula with tropes we've been seeing for ages. I could go on and list all the clichés present, but that would just be me describing the entire movie. It's basically a micro version of things we've seen done better, ranging from a rebellion to a father-daughter bond to an alternate world. The "quantum realm" falls flat, and it just seems like yet another alien planet from the previous Marvel movies, just with another label stuck on it. With all the buildup given to the realm, it's just another green screen set with CGI characters and people wearing prosthetics. This is not the kind of movie that's interested in doing any kind of world-building.

As for Kang the Conqueror, he's definitely a great villain, with Jonathan Majors delivering a performance that's both hammy and self-aware while still seeming like a formidable threat. Kang is definitely better than the villains from the previous Ant-Man and the Wasp movie and is interesting. But still, this movie doesn't really add anything more to Kang than the 30 minutes in Loki already did. Or was this like a reintroduction to Kang for people who don't care about the TV shows? Anyway, the amount of buildup that Kang receives here didn't really require the padding of a feature-length movie.

The Cassie-Scott relationship is supposed to be the main core of this movie, but it wasn't all that well developed. The rest of the Ant-family is also just there, doing stuff to keep the plot moving. Paul Rudd is still charming as ever, and the occasional self-aware Paul Rudd quip kept things from being entirely bland. The whole MODOK arc is so badly written that the acronym and the face end up being the things least dumb about him.

When Loki introduced Jonathan Majors as "He who remains" into the MCU, people expected his full-length introduction in this movie to be something bigger. While this movie is bigger CGI-wise, it really doesn't deliver on the buildup given to Kang or the Quantum Realm that much. Meh.

Name: Malikappuram
Review:
The people who compared Malikapuram to Lijo Jose Pellissery's Amen deserve a special place in hell.

Malikapuram is about a girl who's not just a devotee to Ayyappan; she's obsessed with him, to a dangerous level. She wakes up to Ayyappan, walks around with a mini Ayyappan statue, draws Ayyappan while in class, only wants to hear stories about Ayyappan, and only talks about Ayyappan. And if that wasn't enough, the movie itself mentions Ayyappan every 2 seconds through dialogue or music. The movie is so Ayyappan that it Ayyappans until the end credits.

After watching the movie, I was surprised that the Disney+ logo still says Disney+ and not Ayyappan+.

I hope to reach the same level of innocence as the people who say this movie doesn't have any right-wing messaging.

Name: The Whale
Review:
Fraser, Hong Chau, and Sadie Sink were amazing, with Fraser's performance and innocence being the only thing that made me feel empathy towards a character who was just there as a placeholder to show misery. Even though the CG and makeup looked weird at times, Fraser was so good that it didn't matter that much to me. The background score was beautiful too.

About the movie, it felt like it was more interested in showing a morbidly obese person suffering than its story and characters. There is a Father-Daughter arc at the center, but it didn't have any of the nuance or depth that I felt in Aronofsky's own The Wrestler.

I miss the Aronofsky who did Requiem for a Dream.

Name: Varisu
Review: It's indeed cringe and terrible. The constant preaching and family value lessons are hilarious. Vijay's attempts at comedy range from effective to unintentional laughs for the wrong reasons. The sets are so bad, the green screen is so bad, and the fight scenes are bad. And still, I had a lot of fun watching this. This is just the kind of shitty movie that's just fun in a way that makes me not regret watching it.

Name: Knock at the Cabin
Review:
It's not as bad as Old, I guess. But still, apart from Shyamalan's cool framing and use of camera moves, the movie is just monotonous and drags on for too long, even though it's just under 100 minutes. 10 Cloverfield Lane did it better.

Dave Bautista has great potential as a dramatic actor though.

Name: Veera Simha Reddy
Review:
Even though I started watching Veera Simha Reddy for ironic purposes, I ended up enjoying it way more than I expected. Firstly, it didn't have the religious propaganda and religious murder justification angle that Akhanda had, so that was a win. We do get to see 62-year-old Balakrishna, with no de-aging or deep-faking involved, play the 25-year-old son of Honey Rose, which is the kind of phase that other stars were starting to move on from once they passed a certain age. Thankfully, the older Dad Balayya has more screen time than the mid-20s Balayya. Balayya makes SUVs fly with just a kick; he makes multiple people fly with single hits, and it feels like watching anime. It's still got flying and slow-motion photoshoot fight scenes, but with a lead actor who just makes excess seem subtle, even in his dialogue, it's more fun. Though the movie is so terribly dated in parts, I get the appeal. Thaman's music was also cool here. Where was this Thaman in Varisu? 

Plus there's a pre-interval portion where the dude is really good, as in unironically good, where I felt the emotions, though it's an extremely over the top Thankachi Paasam sequence in Hell. 

The movie is not a theme park; it's a theme planet.

Name: Women Talking
Review:
Powerful, moving, and brilliant cinema. I loved the ensemble cast, the music, the visuals, the writing, the dialogue, and the way it handled its themes. 

To the uninitiated viewer, the setting of the film may seem like some dystopian world, but the fact that this actually happened and how the perspective given in the narrative adds that sense of surrealism make the film more brilliant.

Name: Waltair Veerayya
Review: So, in addition to being in the remake to Mohanlal's Lucifer, Chiranjeevi also did a movie similar to Mohanlal's Aarattu.

Name: A Man Called Otto
Review: A Tom Hanks movie with music by Thomas Newman is something I expected to be wholesome no matter what the reviews were. I haven't watched the original, but the movie itself is of a familiar format. Though the emotional core and the themes of grief and depression could've benefited from more depth, I still liked the movie, I loved the performances, the music, the whole vibe it had and its heart. It's like one of those feel-good dramas with grumpy characters turning soft that I used to love.

Name: The Legend
Review:
Alright, so a rich businessman wanted to be Rajnikanth in Sivaji: The Boss, and this is basically that movie, without the Rajinikanth and without Shankar, and a decade too late. In addition to being a fantasy fulfilment for Legend Saravana Stores owner "Legend" Saravanan, this is also a feature-length ad for his business and for himself, to be marketed as, you guessed it, the "Legend."

It's got the same villain and even the same sidekick as Sivaji, with this being one of the late Vivek's final performances. He passed away before recording his lines, so the raw audio being used for his dialogue is really weird. Plus, he's doing the kind of cringey scenes that were dated even at the time Sivaji came out, and then he just randomly disappears from the movie. Suman stars as Tony Stark and gets to say terrible lines, get mercilessly roasted by the legend, and then get the shit beat out of him.

Both the female leads are weird in their scenes, but with the legend being so bad at acting himself, he chews the scenery and makes sure all the attention goes to him. Veteran actors like Prabhu and Nasser are also there; Yogi Babu is there; music by Harris Jayaraj is there; and everything is made to make this look like a legit Tamil superstar movie production. But yk, even if we replace the legend with a Vijay or Rajini, this is still a shitty movie with shitty writing, shitty editing, shitty direction and shitty dialogue. Credit where credit is due, Legend Saravanan is pretty good in some of the fight scenes.

The incredibly specific look and energy of the legend himself have kind of reminded me of Tommy Wiseau a bit.

Name: History of the World: Part I
Review: There's a lot of dated jokes, and jokes that I'm sure didn't work that well in the 80s too, but still, there's some fun stuff here.

Name: Missing
Review: The screen recording format has its own restrictions on storytelling, and yet searching was very gripping and thrilling. With Missing, whatever it was that made searching so cool is repeated yet again, and though the movie is formulaic and has some logical issues, it is thrilling and engaging enough that I was fully engaged in the mystery. The twists and turns were handled very nicely, as was the use of screens to tell the story.

Name: Thuramukham
Review:
Sure, it sounds cool when filmmakers and writers talk about how too much exposition is bad and how cinema should reveal information creatively. One of the main issues I have with Thuramukham is that a person unaware of the actual events might completely get lost in the core issues and struggles depicted. There's little to no world-building, and we're left with just understanding the bare minimum that the workers are being mistreated, but that's not enough for a compelling narrative, is it?

While some of the themes here are similar to Rajeev Ravi's more "commercialized" Kammattipadam, I didn't care about Thuramukham's characters the way I did for Kammattipadam's characters. Nivin Pauly's performance ranged from being amazing at times to falling flat at others.  His arc seemed messy and incoherent. While using a background score that sounds like ship horns for a movie set within a port seems like a great idea on paper, the background score actually needed to add something to the scenes rather than sounding like random ship horns, didn't it? Then there are the repetitive action scenes that started to get, well, repetitive. 

This could have been so much more.

Name: Luther: The Fallen Sun
Review:
Watching Idris Elba be John Luther again was the only good thing about this movie mostly. The case involving Andy Serkis' villain was pretty plain; things are fairly easy for Luther even though the circumstances seem so difficult at first. The movie is also apparently tweaked to be a stand-alone thing, as there's no mention of Alice or the stuff that happened in the show all that much. The prison riot was pretty cool though. 

Just like The Many Saints of Newark, this movie also ends with the theme to the TV show, so even though the movie before it was dull, the theme reminds me of the show that I loved as the movie ends.

Name: Cocaine Bear
Review: This movie had exactly what I expected from a movie titled Cocaine Bear.
