It's an extremely simple premise, which is obvious from the title itself, and all the fun lies in the titular Cocaine Bear meeting a set of silly, over-the-top characters and either ripping them apart or scaring the life out of them. The kills were fun, and the whole silly vibe the movie had going for it was nice, though the ending felt a little "normal" compared to how over-the-top and silly the rest of the setpieces were.

Name: Mufti
Review:
There are interesting ideas in Mufti (2017). I initially thought this was going to be like The Departed, where it's an undercover cop struggling to keep sane while being in the middle of a ruthless and violent environment, with a South Indian masala movie skin on it. Then the movie goes a different route after the introduction of Shiva Rajkumar's gangster character. Then I thought, this is still interesting; maybe this will be about the cop's moral conflicts on being on two sides of the law, or it will be about exploring that grey area that asks if the gangster's combination of philanthropy and murder is right or wrong. But instead the movie just becomes a sappy melodramatic piece, where the dude who was built up to be a ruthless gangster is somehow a softie with a heart of gold, and it's about solving decade-long family issues with emotional monologues, disregarding all the innocent people who were killed by this dude, and just spreading joy and goodness all around. Sri Murali's permanent anger face doesn't really flesh out his character much other than looking angry, even during romance scenes. Shiva Rajkumar was nice, though, even when the character was confusing tonally. The less I say about the utter crap romance track and comedy track, the better. 

It starts off as "The Departed," but ends up being Ted Lasso. I wonder if the Simbu remake has made any changes to the absolute tonal confusion here.

Name: Shazam! Fury of the Gods
Review:
Well, I did have a lot more fun watching this movie than I did for Ant-Man 3 or Black Adam. There are occasional moments of the charming kids movie energy and humor that were in the first Shazam. But this time the problem is that there's a way smaller amount of it. There's just a lot of generic superhero material here, with unimaginative and plain action sequences that just seem like a tired routine now. The only thing that makes Shazam unique and charming is the humor and innocence I mentioned, and other than that, it's indistinguishable from any other generic "theme park." The editing seemed a bit off at times; I don't know if bits were cut off or if they were unnecessarily tacked on. There was a bit of a dramatic highpoint towards the end, which was ruined by one of the worst fan service cameos I've seen, which makes no sense and just seems like such an unimaginative way to both do the cameo and build to that conclusion. In comparison, the Peacemaker finale episode did the cameo thing a lot better.

Superhero movies seriously have to retire the sky beam and the CGI monster soldiers. It's the worst thing Joss Whedon has contributed to comic book movies after Moustache Superman.

Name: Purusha Pretham
Review: Loved the humor, the style, the cinematography, the editing, the music, the writing, the social commentary, the blend of realism with the cinematic and the performances. This movie is a gem.

Name: John Wick: Chapter 4
Review:
It's amazing that John Wick has stretched such a thin premise into a 4 film saga, but at the same time, it's not that much surprising either.  The amount of creativity that goes into the action setpieces and the style are the winners here, not the thin plot; it never was. The choreography, the way the action is shot and edited, the cinematography and the use of colours and locations are still a treat to behold 4 films in.  While Keanu is kicking ass as he always does, Donnie Yen also joins this time around with his own unique style, and the choreography done for him is also beautiful. The setpieces keep feeling new and exciting, even though most of them involve face shooting. I completely bought into the action, the world and the beautiful choreography. Hats off to all the stunt performers involved. 

A lot of films of the similar style came after the first John Wick, but this movie further cements that the OG is the OG.

Name: Guillermo del Toro's Pinocchio
Review:
Beautiful art that's powerful, touching, and heartfelt In addition to the achievements made in artistry and animation, this is also a well-written movie with great voice acting and beautiful music. The themes of war, loss, grief, and identity are beautifully woven in while maintaining the film's status as an animated film that's appropriate for children. Words are not enough to describe the craft behind the puppets, the locations, and the animation. 

Cinema!

Name: Amigos
Review: They could've just remade John Woo's Face/Off scene by scene instead of this weird mishmash of the evil lookalike plot. The villain was definitely scary at times, but it felt like a wasted opportunity to play with identity theft. The romance arc might be one of the worst I've seen, where they actually placed the duet song at a moment where the bad guy is perving over the good guy's fiancé while pretending to be the good guy.. I mean.. The lead up to the romance involving "tasks" is also hilariously terrible. I knew this movie would not be that good, but I still gave it a chance because of an interest towards stories involving lookalikes.

Name: Tetris
Review: The movie presents a story about acquiring the rights to a video game like an espionage thriller. It's consistently engaging, the video game references were charming, the music was cool, and the film was satisfying. It was easy to root for the main characters; I don't know how much they changed the actual story around to make it a thriller like this, but the movie was fun, and Taron Egerton was great.

Name: Inside
Review: Dafoe is awesome in this solo performance but the movie just felt flat (hihi). There's an Indian movie called "Trapped" which did the "trapped in an apartment" thing a lot better.

Name: Pranaya Vilasam
Review: The central love story involving the flashback and its connection to the present was nice, and it hit the right feels. That plot is wrapped around a weaker version of Anuraga Karikkin Vellam, with a few instances of cringe, cliches, and an insignificant romance arc for the son. But on the whole, the movie made me feel things, so I liked it. The music by Shaan Rahman was nice, and the performances were nice.

Name: Evil Dead Rise
Review:
Evil Dead Rise faithfully follows the Evil Dead formula and has everything to be expected from an Evil Dead movie—well, more along the lines of the ones that went light on the comedy and heavy on the horror and gore. So this is no Army of Darkness.

What's different this time around is the setting. The 2013 film also had the cabin in the woods as its main location, but this time most of the action happens inside an apartment building. The corridor, the elevator, the basement, and the apartment itself are set up brilliantly in the beginning, and once the carnage starts, these locations are used masterfully for scares. Apart from the amazing production design, the makeup, practical special effects, CGI, and cinematography do wonders in maintaining the mood. The music is effectively creepy, and there are so many great sequences, including one involving a door peep hole. The performances are great, and the movie has constant momentum.

Evil Dead Rise is successful in what it sets out to do. Groovy!

Name: Ghosted
Review:
Though this movie is streaming on Apple TV, it's more along the lines of those other big budget action movies that are on Netflix that have huge stars, flashy locations, great costumes and shitty writing.

This movie sort of reminded me of True Lies, in that it also has a civilian paired with a spy. In True Lies, even with Schwarzenegger's limitations as an actor and similarly generic and cheesy writing, Cameron made up with great action setpieces, constant momentum and great chemistry between the actors. Here, the chemistry is laughable and I face-palmed hard when the characters were suddenly in love after being through situations that didn't drive them towards that point at all. There are some good ideas here for the action, but they kinda end up looking plain and generic than exciting. Some of the sets look like those old sitcom sets. Ana De Armas and Chris Evans have their moments, but the performances and their chemistry just look so plain. 

Even though I didn't like Ghosted, it isn't unbearably shitty, I mean yk, it's an easy watch, and not something that pissed me off. Though yeah, it's bad. I wish the writers were Ghosted when they pitched this.

Name: Scream VI
Review:
I'm a fan of Scream's whole self-aware style and the whole whodunit mystery within a slasher thing. It also gives the writers a "parody" pass for actual clichés within the movie too, but it's always been a good time for me; I've loved even the ones that are termed "the worst" in the series.

Scream 6 has a new setting, and it does use that setting for new set-pieces and kills that range from exciting to a repetition of the same-old. The vibe of the originals is captured accurately here, including the unrealistic stabbing tolerance that characters can have. Still, Ghostface is a purist who just stabs, unlike that dude from Terrifier, who'd do weird shit to people who just refuse to die.

I enjoyed the meta/parody elements and the whodunit elements in Scream 6 too. The kills and the moments of tension were effective and visceral. The final confrontation wasn't as exciting as the ones in previous Scream movies that I've loved, but Melissa Barerra's performance made up for it. Even in my opinion for the previous movie, I ranted about the whole "daughter of a serial killer" thingy being used as a way to show her as some natural stabber who'd just instantly become Ghostface just because "it's in her blood". I mean, that's so dumb, and they do downplay it a bit here, though it's still present. And if there are future installments, the whole "serial killer inside of her" thing is going to be the main thing they'd be exploring too. So idk.

Name: Pachuvum Athbhuthavilakkum
Review:
Pachuvum Albhuthavilakkum by Akhil Sathyan fits right in with the two Fahadh Faasil movies his father Sathyan Anthikad had done, i.e., Oru Indian Pranayakadha and Njan Prakashan, where a quirky and self-centred Fahadh Faasil protagonist becomes a part of some other character's story, and helping them eventually makes him a better person. The movie follows this formula pretty faithfully, though I'd argue that apart from a few awkward melodramatic scenes towards the end, this film has more of the stuff that worked in those two movies and less of the stuff that didn't.

Fahadh Faasil is on fine form here, and it's his comedic timing and charm that carry this almost 3-hour movie. He got laughs for both the great jokes and the cheesy recycled ones; it was just pure charm. The rest of the cast does a great job too, with Justin Prabhakaran's songs and score also adding to the mood of the movie.

Apart from some of the dramatic portions during the third act seeming awkward to me, Pachuvum Albhuthavilakkum was a lot of fun, with a good amount of laughs and FaFa wholesomeness.

Name: Kalaga Thalaivan
Review: The villain and his team were legit terrifying and ruthless in this movie, there are some interesting stuff happening plot-wise, and it's thrilling in parts. But at the same time, there are long stretches of an awful romance arc that just develops in a way that's so dumb that it becomes hard to take the movie seriously when it's trying to be smart. Even the climatic showdown has some nice touches, on how it handles the protagonist going against 14 people at the same time. So this movie is great stuff diluted by the shitty stuff.

Name: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3
Review:
Vol. 3 has a lot of heart, and I could tell that a lot of love has gone into it. Sure, there are common tropes and formulas of the genre being used, but just like its predecessors, this one too is character-driven, and it's in those moments that it shines. After the Yondu sent-off set to Cat Stevens from Vol. 2, this one too made me teary-eyed in multiple instances.

James Gunn's Guardians have always been their own thing, disconnected from their version in the comics and even the rest of the MCU in a lot of ways. And after two Avengers movies, ditching Thor for his standalone movie with a cameo, and a wholesome Christmas special, they're back in their home territory. Though this is the final entry in Gunn's trilogy, it is also the one that gives Star-Lord the least focus, and it works. He has his own arc and is a constant presence throughout the film, but this time, the story branches more throughout the Guardians than making them his supporting cast. This is more or less Rocket's movie, but told in a way where the rest of the Guardians are more involved in it too. That delicate balance in handling the characters is done really well, even better than the Avengers movies handling the characters as a "team", I'd say.

Dave Bautista and Pom Klementieff maintain the chemistry and heart they had from the Christmas special, with Drax being more wholesome and fleshed out than before. Pratt, Zaldana, Gillan, and newcomer Will Poulter are delightful. Sean Gunn and Bradley Cooper together bring the most fleshed-out version of Rocket to life, and the film does amazing things with the character. Just like the last two Guardians movies, this one too has a thinly written villain that the movie doesn't care all that much about. Chukwudi Iwuji does what he can to make him menacing.

The jokes and fan service land most of the time, the playlist is epic this time too, and the action was fun and kinetic, especially that stand-out hallway fight scene made to look like a single shot, which does things with the camera and the action that can only be done in such a movie that blends live-action and animation together, with actors and animated characters blending perfectly together with exaggerated camera moves that's not achievable with an actual camera.

Beyond the spectacle and the jokes and the "popcorn", Gunn really cares about his characters, and that love is seen throughout this movie. Since the whole thing is packaged in a way that it works as a stand-alone trilogy (plus the two Avengers movies), I'd definitely revisit Gunn's Guardians in the future.

Those few kinetic shots of Adam Warlock flying make me feel hopeful about James Gunn's Superman.

The 2018 Kerala floods are something most Malayalis who watched this movie have lived through, whether they were safe during the disaster or not. So what this cinematic retelling of those events succeeds in, even though it takes a lot of liberties—and I mean A LOT, is letting us relive those days, but not as misery porn, but with hope as the main focus, as all the dark stuff is just touched over and overshadowed by the good stuff. 

I don't know how much this movie would resonate with those audiences for whom the Kerala floods weren't that intimate an event. Yeah, the movie is pretty clichéd; there's lots of cringey dialogue and formulaic setups, but the "real" helps to forgive the "reel", especially because of how effectively Jude Anthany and his team recreate the floods and those few days, even with a modest budget. From the production design to the VFX to the sound, everything felt immersive (no pun intended). The movie is pretty well made and edited, with multiple thrilling sequences and effective use of the background score. The performances by the cast are great too, and all of this helps to mostly mask the flawed writing and janky character arcs, in addition to the core audience's personal connection to the material.

There was a Ron Howard movie last year with a similar premise called Thirteen Lives, also based on real incidents. That film was laser-focused on the rescue mission being recreated and didn't spend too much time on giving individual arcs to the characters, and it only benefited by making them feel like real people. So, maybe such an approach would've been better here instead of having uneven character arcs that sometimes just boil down to "disasters magically solving issues". I mean, again, we lived through the floods; it wasn't THIS magical. It's a flood, not a marriage counselor. 

Also, the film severely underplays the role of the state government and political organisations during the flood. Underplays as in they really don't do anything in the film, while they did a LOT in real life. Also, according to the movie, a church did more towards helping the state during the floods, than its government. Hmm.. 

Hats off to the people behind this movie for releasing it right beside blatant propaganda against Kerala, though. That might be the best coincidence ever.

Name: Renfield
Review:
Nic Cage as Dracula is the best thing about this movie. Every scene with him is a delight, with the Cage rage in full effect. Even the prosthetic makeup on him is impressive, while the other special effects in the movie are uneven. The action does this thing where blood looks like Sci-fi goo most of the time, and is not that remarkable. Nicholas Hoult is great in his scenes with Cagecula, but the movie kinda falls apart whenever Cage is not present, which is a lot. There's an unnecessary subplot with Awkwafina's character which is so badly written. Her character is all over the place and is more rushed than smokey Dracula.

That being said, I'm all in for a sequel if it's a stand-alone movie with The Cage.

Name: Corona Papers
Review:
The movie looks great, and there are instances of great filmmaking, but there's also instances of hilarious dialogue where I was confused whether the humor was intentional, as this is a thriller otherwise. Shine and Siddhique are great, whereas Shine Tom is just Shine Tom, who's also TR. It did not bore me though, the entire thing was fun enough and the unintentional (?) humor was also fun.

I have no idea why they titled this movie "The Corona Papers" apart from that scene where the antagonist angrily throws some papers while yelling "Bloody fucking Corona!". I mean, other than being set during the pandemic era, this movie has nothing to do with the pandemic. I haven't seen 8 Thottakal or the Kurasowa movie, so this was a fresh watch.

Name: Vichithram
Review: It could've been the Haunted House version of Kumbalangi Nights, but even at just over 2 hours, the movie seems too long, there's uneven balancing of the characters, as some of them disappear for long stretches of time, plus the over reliance on jumpscares was disappointing. I liked the performances, the music and the visuals. The ending was nice too.

Name: Air
Review:
AIR is a heartfelt, wholesome, charming, and surprisingly funny drama that's based on a business deal that was probably not this entertaining in real life, though the outcome of it was revolutionary. This might be my favourite film directed by Ben Affleck, with such great performances by the actors led by an amazing Matt Damon. Michael Jordan is not technically a character in the film, though the entire movie revolves around him basically, but through archival footage and a body double, it just works.

The soundtrack was also groovy.

Name: Fast X
Review:
The Fast movies are a genre of their own at this point. It may not be based on any comics, and it isn't technically "sci-fi" or fantasy, but from its beginnings as street racing and heists to where it is now, it's definitely mythological. And for better or for worse, the first part of its finale has everything that has defined the Fast and Furious franchise from the 5th movie onwards. So when a sociopathic villain teams up with the good guys and transforms into one of the good guys, it's okay because it's family. When a dead character suddenly resurrects, it's okay because it's family, and the Fast Franchise makes it a point to not let us actually see someone dying, so that anyone who "dies" off-screen can come back. When family members who were not at all mentioned in any previous installment pop up, it's okay because it's... Yk.. And this movie has all of this and more. It makes sure to mention family every two minutes so that we don't forget what it's about.

The action is indeed over the galaxy, and I'll admit there are some cool stunts and cars being totaled in creative ways. There's the expected silly humour and some self-aware digs, but unlike Hobbs and Shaw, the self-awareness is pretty light, and Vin Diesel's Dom Torretto still takes himself too seriously, though his melodramatic lines and one-liners are often hilarious. Still, there's fun to be had, especially with John Cena hitting an Attitude Adjustment (his finisher move in the WWE) on a dude that makes him literally go through the floor, or John Cena (again) lip-syncing to a Marky Mark song, resurrecting the Mark Wahlberg meme. Or how screenshots and scenes from other movies are disguised as surveillance footage while the agency dude gives a YouTube review of the Fast Franchise—like I said, lots of fun.

Then there's Jason Momoa doing the bro-est Joker impression ever, being one of the few cast members who understands how dumb the movie is and hamming it up and embracing the dumbness. The movie is pretty much set up like Avengers: Infinity War, with the team, ahem, family being split up and taken apart and then building up to the eventual big showdown crossover event in the next movie(s). But in this case, instead of 10 years of multiple superhero movies, it's 20 years of ressurected family members, villains turned heroes, any A-List celebrity who Vin Diesel can get to join in, and family members who returned because their future in DC is unsure.

I'd be lying if I said I didn't have fun watching this. I was entertained but just confused about whether a lot of the fun was ironic or not.

Name: Kadina Kadoramee Andakadaham
Review: Firstly they marketed this movie wrong by selling it as a comedy movie, with even a title that makes it seem like a comedy. This is a pretty emotion heavy drama centered around grief, loss and how characters navigate through those feelings while dealing with unfamiliar conflicts set up by the pandemic. While the movie strikes the right emotional chords and depicts grief with the perfect melancholic tone and empathy, the writing can seem a bit weak at times, with the movie seeming too long for this story, though it's only barely 2 hrs. The "plot" itself is minimal and the sony LIV synopsis pretty much spoils the entire movie except the climax, so I don't know if that affected my enjoyment too. Basil Joseph delivers an amazing and multi-layered performance here, further cementing him as a dependable lead actor.

Name: The Super Mario Bros. Movie
Review:
The animation looks gorgeous, the action sequences are great, and the movie is a lot of fun to watch. The game references and the use of music and sound effects from the games were cool. Writing-wise, unlike a video game adaptation like HBO's The Last of Us, the goal here was to get kids to play the video games, though with the use of retro soundtracks and references to the old games, they're aiming at the adults who grew up with these games. Still, the writing lacks the heart that even Illumination's own Despicable Me has and is basically low-effort template writing where it moves from point to point while distracting us with the beautiful visuals and cool music.

Contrary to fan backlash, I thought the choice of having Chris Pratt do a neutral Brooklyn accent instead of the over-the-top Italian accent from the games was a good one. The way the accent is explained within the movie was also nice. But such instances of originality or genuinely chuckle-worthy moments of humour were very few. But still, I had a lot of fun watching this movie, so even though it's an elaborate video game/toy commercial, which is still not as good as a toy commercial like the Lego Movie, I kind of like The Super Mario Bros. Woo hooo..!

Name: Ayalvaashi
Review: I don't think the simplicity of the inciting incident was the issue here, but rather how the rift it causes between the characters and the problems it brings to their lives seem very trivial. Even though Soubin tries earnestly to sell his character's mental turmoil, I just couldn't feel it. Though an investigative movie that's not a murder investigation and just a tiny neighbourhood issue is an ingenious idea and the way it unfurls in the end is also pretty cool. Loved the Chewing Gum scene and its background dancers too.

Name: Bhargavi Nilayam
Review:
Well, it's a classic. Parts of it are dated, because it's a malayalam movie from almost 60 years ago, but other aspects are still brilliant, especially the evergreen soundtrack. This is a product of Malayalam cinema that was slowly building up from the roots in stage dramas. But still, cinematic tools such as lighting, editing, camera moves and scene staging are used brilliantly in certain scenes. All the songs are a treat to the ears and it's also hard to not appreciate the poetry in the lyrics.

I'm about to watch the 2023 version next, pretty sure Tovino can't smoke a cigarette as cool as Madhu did.

Name: Neelavelicham
Review:
As a modernized adaptation of a classic, I loved Neelavelicham. It's not like Gus Van Sant's Psycho, which was merely a shot-by-shot remake in color. Firstly, Neelavelicham is nearly 30 minutes shorter than the original adaptation of Basheer's Neelavelicham, the timeless classic Bhargavi Nilayam. While Neelavelicham strives to preserve most of Basheer's original text, especially the iconic lines, it trims numerous scenes and dialogues, particularly the comedic moments.

Even though the same dialogues are used, the delivery in Neelavelicham is refreshingly modern. However, apart from Shine Tom Chacko, whose overly animated delivery and mannerisms still resemble those of present-day Shine Tom (which does end up being kinda appropriate for the character of Naanukuttan), the rest of the cast doesn't exhibit as much "drama" in their performances as their original counterparts. Tovino Thomas doesn't attempt to emulate Madhu, and Roshan Mathew, in his subtle and charming portrayal of the lover Sasikumar, doesn't try at all to imitate Prem Nazir. This approach is indeed better than coming off as an impersonation, leaving the "Nazirness" to the legend himself.

I have mixed feelings about the depiction of Bhargavi in Neelavelicham. Rima Kallingal looks absolutely gorgeous every time she appears on screen, but I would have preferred the use of old-school cuts and camera illusions to portray Bhargavi's appearances and disappearances, instead of relying on CGI effects and particles. Although the titular "blue light" is meant to be a significant element in this color adaptation, aside from one scene involving the lantern, the effect sometimes feels out of place. Personally, I preferred the glowing Bhargavi from the original.

Neelavelicham excels in great cinematography, great production values, a nice score, and mostly good performances, while maintaining a clear love for the source material. I enjoyed the remixed versions of the original songs too. Another modern choice made in this adaptation was to forgo lip syncing for all the songs, except for two, and instead present them as montages. However, I do wish that "Ekanthathayude Mahatheeram" and "Thamasamenthe Varuvaan" had retained the actors lip syncing to them.

Name: Beau Is Afraid
Review:
Beau is Afraid is the ultimate mommy issues movie. There's a lot to appreciate here, but the film has the kind of absurdity that'd either make one absolutely hate it or absolutely love it. I belong to the second category. While I confess that I didn't understand every single bit of symbolism and weird imagery on screen, there was enough within the chaos that I was able to appreciate. It visualises anxiety in such creative ways and I'm sure just like Ari Aster's previous films there's things and details that I've missed. The central performance by Joaquin Phoenix as the shattered Beau is all sorts of brilliant and surprisingly empathetic, with the movie having so many long shots that's just stuck to his face. There are so many memorable sequences and frames, moments of humor, a lot of interesting visual storytelling and it was a treat in the big screen. This is definitely the weirdest movie I've seen in the cinemas. 

Also, fuck the Indian censor board for censoring key moments from the film.

Name: Bhediya
Review:
Harmless formulaic fun with the expected elements. Just like the case with SS Rajamouli's Eega, though the CGI is not as detailed as big budget Hollywood productions, it's well conceived and executed, meaning the scenes just work and it serves its purpose in the story. The laughs are effective, the performances are good and the characters are likable. The drama is basic but nice.

Though Thumkeshwari is a catchy song, it's placement towards the end of the movie, while it had THAT ending, was weird.

Name: Sulaikha Manzil
Review:
Sulaikha Manzil had the kind of vibe that I generally enjoy. I loved the music, Lukhman, and the rest of the performances. The movie is set mostly around the wedding eve of a quickly put-together arranged marriage and mixes in the wedding celebrations and ceremonies with some confusion between the two people who are actually supposed to get married.

Though I do kinda like the movie to an extent, I don't think it quite explores the potential of the story it has going for it. Now, I didn't expect Sulaikha Manzil to be a critique of the entire system of arranged marriage. That being said, does the movie romanticise the whole thing of two people who barely know each other getting married? I'm honestly confused about that. Because while it does address the fact that the two main characters barely know each other and haven't even interacted enough or even connected on a surface level, it doesn't really address the sadness of the situation, and everyone involved is a wholesome person at the end of the day. So yeah, while it addresses the fact that the main characters who are getting married are literally strangers to each other, if I'm asked if this movie is regressive, I really don't have a clear answer. Because I just really felt bad for the main characters.

Talking about the potential of the story, I wish the character of Haala was more fleshed out and that her motives and intentions were more clear. Anarkali Marakkar doesn't get a lot to work with, writing-wise, though I did like the performance. Haala's conflict felt undercooked, as did the conflict she had with her brother. Though the way it resolved seemed wholesome, with the music and Chemban Vinod Jose's performances doing the work, when thinking about it, it didn't feel like an earned moment. Meanwhile, Lukhman's character, the performance, and everything he felt were easy to connect to, though the way he reaches his conclusion is also a bit..... confusing. But yk, "love is mysterious" I guess.

How dope is that soundtrack, though?

Name: Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse
Review:
They took everything that worked in the first movie and dialled it up like crazy. There's so much creativity being flooded into the writing, the art, the animation, and the filmmaking. The music and the repeat-worthy soundtrack playlist, combined with the amazing voice acting, elevate the visual spectacle on screen a lot. Different types of art styles are blended together beautifully, and the various Easter eggs and cameos feel more earned than just lazy fan service. The humour always hit the mark, as did the comic book-ness of the whole thing. It never loses its focus on the core story despite being flooded with so many Spider-People.

It was definitely spectacular on the big screen. 

Also, hats off to everything they did with Spider-Man: India, they clearly had actual Indians working on that material, and it shows.

Name: Ponniyin Selvan: Part II
Review: Ponniyin Selvan 2 is definitely one of the sequel movies ever made.

Name: Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret.
Review: It's a wholesome movie in every single way. The colors, the performances, the direction, the editing, the humor, the soundtrack, the writing, the dialogues, the story itself, the way it shows a pre-teen girl's perspective, the mother's perspective and their relationship, everything was wholesome.

Name: The Flash
Review:
The Flash was pretty enjoyable. While it treads similar ground to what Spider-Man: No Way Home did and the superior Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse did and has tropes expected from the time-travel subgenre, I found enough original ideas and a connection to the main character that I was satisfied.

The Flashpoint comic storyline, the main inspiration for this movie, was a huge epic event story; this is comparatively a lot "smaller". Even the final "battle" within a small desert area seemed tiny compared to the climatic stretches of Man of Steel, which seemed huge. So while The Flash isn't as huge as its source material or its potential, I don't hate it for it. The CGI was very bad though. Ezra Miller was great as the lead, as were Michael Keaton, Sasha Calle, and even Ben Affleck in his brief appearance. The humour and the heart of the film worked for me. The cameos were all well done, especially the final one. The plot holes here are the kind present in most movies with the same kind of storyline. I loved all the Batman action sequences in this film, and it kind of makes sense that Andy Muschietti is doing a solo Batman movie.

The Flash is not without its share of flaws and didn't expand its full potential at all, but still, I was satisfied.

Name: Extraction 2
Review: Just like in the last movie, I didn't really care about the characters or the drama surrounding the action, but when the action kicked up, it was glorious. They did take a risk by putting their biggest and most impressive action sequence (The Prisoner) as the very first action setpiece, and it was indeed amazing and exhilarating, with great choreography, practical action, impressive feats in staging and cinematography, and great filmmaking overall. But after that, the action never reaches those levels, and the climatic stretch is a lot smaller in comparison. But overall, Sam Hargrave and his team aren't making John Wick clones here, and that's the best part about Extraction; the action and style do have their own identities. Since the movie is packed with impressive action setpieces and the characters are not "super" fleshed out, I did care for Rake and Nik, and Extraction 2 is a satisfying sequel.

Name: Thrishanku
Review: The idea they had was nice. The whole eloping within an eloping thing, which could've been expanded even beyond what they did here. The ending and the resolutions ended up being too simple compared to what was set up. Still, it was fun to watch. I liked the humor, the music and the performances. Nandu and Suresh Krishna were awesome.

Name: Maamannan
Review: Though I didn't particularly like the ending and there's some cringe in the latter half, Vadivelu and Fahadh were amazing, and so was the music by AR Rahman. The first scene in which the three main characters appear together was also awesome.

Name: Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny
Review:
Well, I definitely liked it more than Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. But it's nowhere near the first three movies in terms of action and excitement.

Deepfake young Ford in the opening looked way better than I expected, with him looking like the real deal in a lot of the shots and the immersion breaking only in certain moments where he's in motion. But the technology is certainly evolving to the point where the uncanny valley will disappear.

Mangold sticks to the Indy formula, with an older and more physically restricted Ford still seeming better than how he did in Crystal Skull. The action setpieces were okay; there are no goofy CGI monkeys, awful green screens, or extreme cartoon logic this time around, but still, they don't rival the action in the first three movies at all.

Ford is a treat to watch as Indy, and he's still Indy. Mangold doesn't try any of the reinventing stuff he did for Wolverine (it worked for Wolverine, but it wouldn't have for Indiana Jones). Indy is not the same, but it feels like his changes are appropriate to his age and the emotions he's going through within the film. Phoebe Waller-Bridge was equally cool as Helena, and them together as the veteran mentor and his younger companion make this movie a way better adaptation of the video game Uncharted than the actual Tom Holland Uncharted movie (yeah, I know the games were based on Indiana Jones, but I couldn't resist saying this).

Kingdom of the Crystal Skull also went Sci-fi with its macguffin, and it fell flat hilariously. This, in comparison, felt better, though the idea isn't exactly new.

John Williams' score still feels at home, and hearing the main theme at the end made me tear up.

I would've been harder on this movie if Kingdom of The Crystal Skull wasn't the film that preceded it. Dial of Destiny was a good time, a nice Indy adventure, and it's always a joy to see Ford being Indy. Farewell sir.

Name: Almost Famous
Review: The soundtrack, the performances, the writing, the dialogues, the filmmaking, this movie is just brilliant and special in every way.

Name: BlackBerry
Review:
Even without any knowledge about the people involved or the story, I knew what had happened to Blackberry phones. So as this movie begins, I know it's not an inspirational success story, but a buildup to failure, and they set it up brilliantly. The film is perfectly paced, with the kind of frantic energy that I've seen in something like Uncut Gems from the TV show The Bear. The writing is sharp, the drama is perfect, the humour works, and the performances are great. Glenn Howerton's bald cap was a bit distracting, but I don't know if it's because I've become so familiar with how he looks from seeing him on It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia. The score, the cinematography, and the editing were all serving their purpose. Even when we know the conclusion, the journey there is thrilling, interesting and of course, sad.

I'd even say this is up there with The Social Network.

Name: Witness
Review: Witness begins as a cop thriller and ends as a cop thriller, with a middle part that has Harrison Ford hanging out in an Amish community and connecting with its people. This is Ford's only Oscar nominated performance and he's indeed the highlight of the movie. The chemistry between him and Kelly McGillis was also cool. This isn't a very loud or violent movie, but the occasional instances of violence and terror were brilliantly crafted.

Name: Cool Hand Luke
Review: Prime Paul Newman was something else.

Name: Asteroid City
Review:
The framing device itself is a black and white 4:3 TV show about the production of a fictional play, and we're seeing the color 16:9 cinematic version of that play. So it's Wes Anderson being cheeky with his signature style and quirkiness from the beginning. This isn't a collection of disconnected stories like The French Dispatch, but this is yet another showcase of Anderson going all in with his signature. Every single thing is deliberate; every single thing is Wes. While it tackles themes like grief, it does so from a unique perspective.

Though I love these films where Wes is being more loud with his style and imagination, and I loved Asteroid City and its brilliant cast, I do miss the Wes that did The Royal Tenenbaums and The Darjeeling Limited.

Name: Transformers: Rise of the Beasts
Review:
Half-baked, but still better than the Bay Transformers movies. I do have some nostalgia for the Bay movies, but this seems so much better without blatant product placements, terrible human characters, or the cringe. It does miss the Bayhem and the epicness of the Bay movies, but on the other hand, the action is clearer; when two robots are fighting, we can see who's fighting who and what's going on, rather than chaotic imagery that's too much to process for us.

The human characters are better too; they seem like they actually matter, and they finally do something in the Transformers movies with the humans that I'd wished they did 15 years ago. It's not as good as Bumblebee as an overall package, but it's a huge step above The Last Knight.

Name: Padmini
Review: There were laughs and fun moments, the premise was interesting, but the drama fell flat, some of the characters didn't really work. There was another Kunjiramayanam or Thinkalaazhcha Nishchayam in there though.

Name: Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning
Review:
Cruise-McQuarrie has successfully delivered yet another impressive Mission. The stunt work is amazing, the action is shot and edited brilliantly, and even the setpieces that are light on stunts, like the airport sequence and the party sequence, are amazing at building suspense and tension. The entire climactic setpiece is an amazing cinematic achievement.

Cruise is on fine form here and gets a lot of Cruise moments. But from Ghost Protocol onwards, the MI movies have swayed towards being more ensemble pieces than something that revolves around just the protagonist, and that's being carried forward here too with the rest of the cast, both returning and new, getting their moments. Esai Morales is great as the villain, though not very unique or memorable, even with the connection he's made to have with Hunt, which didn't really add much. Philip Seymour Hoffman is still my favorite MI villain, followed by Henry Cavill from Fallout.

Lorne Balfe's score is great, with a lot of cool variations of the classic MI theme, and the score adds a lot to the thrills and chills. There are also action moments in the film without any background score, where the amazing sound design and the visuals do the work, and they're just as thrilling. These reminded me of McQuarrie's own Jack Reacher, which didn't have a score for any of its action sequences.

Writing-wise, there's not much we haven't already seen in other movies or TV shows, but the writing serves its purpose and provides a coherent narrative, rather than the film purely seeming like a loosely tied collection of action setpieces. Most of all, it succeeds in building up a threat that does seem bigger and more dangerous than anything Hunt has ever faced before. A threat that's truly impossible for him to defeat. As the weak aspects of the writing were covered by brilliant filmmaking and solid performances, I don't have complaints.

What I love about the MI movies is that, seven movies in, they still humanize Ethan Hunt to some extent. He still does many difficult, ahem, impossible things, but he's never Invincible. After all, it's not Mission: Invincible. We never see Ethan Hunt completely dominating anyone in a fist fight. He's rarely in control of the situations he's in, with either dumb luck or his team saving him multiple times. So even in the sequences where he's doing cool over-the-top things, every small thing that contributes to humanizing him works towards making those sequences more thrilling and more believable. Of course, the brilliant practical stunt work also helps. Ethan Hunt comes off more like an extremely skilled agent than as a superhero or a mythical, larger-than-life figure. Which is a lesson I wish other action films would learn from Mission Impossible.

Name: Oppenheimer
Review:
Oppenheimer has all the trademarks of Nolan's more grand body of work. There's the use of music, the non-linear narrative, the editing patterns, the flow of the dialogue, and the entire feel of the film is purely Nolan. But unlike his last two movies, Tenet and Dunkirk, which kept the audience at a distance from their characters and were more about the spectacle, Oppenheimer brings us closer in. This is a deep character study into the psyche of its main character, through two different perspectives (differentiated through the use of color) and through different points in time intercut with each other. While the "main" narrative that starts from Oppenheimer's beginnings unfolds, separate events from the future are also unfolding in parallel, and the results are magnificent. Nolan again impresses with the way he uses nonlinear narratives.

This film has some of the highest-stakes scientific discussions and government hearings I've seen on screen. Something so technical and mundane is converted into huge cinematic setpieces, with some intercut conversations seeming as thrilling as the action sequences Nolan has done. The use of sound here is also absolutely brilliant; Oppenheimer's guilt, horror, and psychological turmoil are conveyed a lot more visually and through sound than through dialogue. Cillian Murphy's career-defining performance makes Oppenheimer say a lot with just his eyes. There's a particular scene involving Oppenheimer delivering a speech where the sound of applause and cheers is made to sound disturbing and terrifying, with close-ups on Murphy's face, camera distortions, and his brilliant performance all culminating in something so powerful that it's the most memorable scene from the movie for me, compared to the hyped-up trinity test sequence, which was also a brilliant sequence and a masterclass in suspense building, but I didn't understand why the audience in the theater I was in cheered when the bomb went off.

The last two Nolan movies were criticized for their sound mixes, but I don't have that complaint with Oppenheimer at all. The way sound is used here is ingenious. Ludwig Goransson's hypnotic score is present in most of the scenes, but the scenes without the score or scenes with silence are also there at the perfect moments. Like the applause sound I mentioned above, there are other sounds, like the wind, that take prominence at times, adding to the drama of a scene.

Oppenheimer could very well be called Christopher Nolan's first horror movie rather than Christopher Nolan's first Biopic, and it's far from being a glorification of the bombings or something remotely resembling jingoism. With brilliant filmmaking, sound work, music, cinematography, visual effects, production design, performances, and writing, Oppenheimer is a cinematic gem.

Name: Barbie
Review:
Barbie is different from anything that Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach have ever done, but it still has their signature. Gerwig's Barbie is the opposite of what something like Transformers was: it's not a narrative built around the toy; here, the narrative is using the toy and the brand as a tool to do its own thing, like how The Lego Movie did. (Both of these movies coincidentally have Will Farrel playing a human that owns the toys.)

The characters are loud and caricaturish, the dialogue is deliberately over-the-top, and the jokes and punchlines keep coming, the film is self-aware, and there are plenty of hilarious meta moments. The laughs are constant, and Barbie was a total win in terms of the fun I had. Even when serious themes like feminism, existentialism, and individuality are addressed, there's a layer of comedy on top of it.

Barbie is for the most part a satire, with characters, situations, and dialogue that are "intelligently" silly. It's hard to believe that this was made by the same creative minds behind Frances Ha and Lady Bird, but I loved the sharp satire, social commentary and energy that I saw. The performances are amazing, with Margot Robbie disappearing into being Barbie. From the "perfect" Barbie to her various transformations, Robbie made me root and feel for the character, and even in points where the movie became emotional, Robbie's performance made the scenes feel deeper than the writing. Then there's Gosling. Gosling is an absolute blast as Ken. He made me laugh in almost every scene he was in. This is the Gosling I've wanted to see more of ever since I saw him do comedy in The Nice Guys. Gosling is effortlessly hilarious and makes the role his own; there's no other Ken, not even the other Hollywood Ryan. The choice to make use of Gosling's singing talents was also perfect.

The ending did seem a bit rushed compared to the rest of the movie. It felt like a feminist satire and a story about a character questioning her own existence were in a bit of conflict with each other. Even when the element of comedy saved the ending from being tiring, it lacked the energy of the rest of the movie a bit.

But on the whole, Barbie is a hilarious, fun, intelligent, self-aware, surprisingly wholesome, and extremely entertaining experience. It never skips a beat, most of the jokes land, the performances are great, the soundtrack is great, the production design is amazing, the visual style is cool, the satire is sharp, and the product placement is done brilliantly (by making fun of the product, addressing criticisms against it, and even making fun of the company that sells them).

I want Greta Gerwig to keep making both kinds of movies: deep and realistic films like Lady Bird and something big and loud like Barbie. She's awesome at doing both.

Name: They Cloned Tyrone
Review: Funny, entertaining, Sci-fi satire with clever twists, conspiracy reveals and badass performances. Loved the music and the visual style too.

Name: Sillunu Oru Kaadhal
Review: There's a better movie in here, where it's about Bhumika's character escaping from a relationship with an absolute psychopath and becoming a baddie.

Name: The Broken Hearts Gallery
Review: This has the same vibe as that of Nora Ephron rom-coms from the late 90s and early 2000s, but with a bit more modern sensibilities, of course. It sticks to that rom-com template but still offers plenty of heart, great performances, humor, cool music (pop songs, of course), and nice visuals. It's a nice watch.

Name: Red Eye
Review: This is a tightly packed thriller that gets straight to the point. At just around 77 minutes or so, Red Eye is only a tiny bit longer than your average streaming series episode. So it's fast-paced, thrilling, and has Craven creating suspense in creative ways during the plane scenes. The ending action sequence does play out like one of Craven's Scream movies, but there too, the location of the house is used effectively. Great performances from Rachel McAdams and Cillian Murphy too. Wheezing Cillian Murphy with a hole in his throat is superior to Ghostface. Fight me.

Name: Caramel
Review: A blissful slice of life film with great performances, beautiful nuances, beautiful music, and wholesome visuals Brilliant.

Name: I Am Not an Easy Man
Review: The detailing and the way in which the inverted society with reverse gender roles is depicted is brilliant. There's a lot in terms of world building (or inverting) that felt ingenious. The ending was also really well done and not what I expected.

Name: Joy Ride
Review: It sticks to the buddy movie template, there are plenty of laughs, awesome performances, likable characters and it's got heart. It's no Bridesmaids, but with a fresh POV on the buddy movie, it's satisfying.

Name: The Beanie Bubble
Review: There was an interesting movie here, but it got diluted by all the generic blandness. Nice performances though. Opening credits sequence was also cool.

Name: Inception
Review: Well it's probably the movie I've rewatched the most. I'm biased. It's a masterpiece. Happy Birthday Chris Nolan.

Name: Tenet
Review: This movie is so much fun if you just switch off and get in for the ride.

Name: Lady Bird
Review: This movie is so beautiful. Everything about it has a lot of heart. The characters, the emotions, the growth, the music, the visuals, the filmmaking, the performances, it's all wholesome.

Name: Training Day
Review: The stars are not entirely for the movie itself or its writing, but for one man, Denzel Washington. Training Day is more like a stylized showcase for Denzel to be awesome than anything else. He just plays a corrupt cop way beyond the dimensions that the writing gave the character. The humanity within the corrupt Alonzo is all Denzel's work. Things like the twist with the cousin were stuff that reminded me that the dude who wrote this also wrote Suicide Squad. The movie would've been basic if Denzel's presence wasn't there, even with Ethan Hawke's great performance. A legend like Denzel just made it something else.

Name: The Equalizer
Review:
Denzel is like 😐
And then he starts being like 💀

The badassery made me forgive the generic stuff.

Name: The Equalizer 2
Review:
I've heard people say that this is not as good as the first one, but to me, it seemed the same, with improvements in some areas. The writing is still meh, just like the first one. A sniper scope is not needed to see the big reveal coming from miles away; some of this movie is just Denzel executing justice in self-contained episodes, kind of like a procedural drama, which I understand is this movie's source material. But I loved everything involving Denzel being an absolute badass, just like the first one. But here, Denzel is more Denzel than the mostly stoic McCall from the first movie. Not just in the hair, McCall seems more emotive and animated this time around, though he does switch to cold and brutal when it matters.

The action still looks cool and brutal, with the kind of choreography that's perfect for what they're going for. I'm not a fan of quick cuts in action, but here it works.

Name: Wild
Review: Beautiful filmmaking, brilliant use of a non linear narrative, great editing, beautiful cinematography and amazing performances from Reese Witherspoon and Laura Dern. Wild is deep and masterful.

Name: Dune
Review: I have newfound appreciation for Dune while watching it again. Though Paul still doesn't feel like a compelling protagonist, I like him more now than my first watch, I was able to appreciate everything else, more than before. Dune is cinema!

Name: The Suicide Squad
Review: This is one of those movies that I'd never get tired of. It's so unique, has little touches that makes it unique, it follows comic book movie conventions and yet has so much else going for it. The action is awesome, the humor is awesome, the visual style is awesome and the performances are awesome. Those gore effects strike the perfect balance between stylised and cartoonish too. The first time I watched it I do remember being unsure about character deaths, while that element is not present in a rewatch, this movie does deliver on the promise of a suicide squad movie, way more than its predecessor.

Name: Brooklyn
Review: Saoirse Ronan supremacy.

Name: No Hard Feelings
Review:
No Hard Feelings is, ahem, surprisingly deep for a movie with a boner joke title. It was sold as a raunchy comedy along the lines of something like American Pie, but the movie sort of takes another route. It's really focused on the two main characters, their insecurities, and their relationship that stems from a really uncomfortable arrangement, and Jennifer Lawrence sells the hell out of the humor and the drama, legend. There are enough laughs, intentional cringe humor, and, within it, a lot of heart. Gene Stupnitsky was a longtime writer and director on The Office, and I could really see that influence being reflected here. Surprisingly wholesome. 

A naked Jen Lawrence straight up German suplexing a dude is something I never expected to see in cinema history.

Name: Jailer
Review:
Jailer is kinda better than a lot of recent "mass" superstar movies and the previous films of both Rajinikanth and Nelson (Annaatthe and Beast). I wouldn't call it a great movie, or even a great Rajini movie. Petta had the Thalaivar kicking asses with nunchucks; now that's cinema.

Jailer does work at times; the buildup given to Rajini's character and the occasional payoffs were nice. Rajini himself shines as the menacing title character, with plenty of Thalaivar moments. Vinayakan's villain was also nice, and he was the character for whom Nelson's dark humor worked the most. He seemed effectively over-the-top psychotic and hilarious throughout, kind of like a darker and unhinged version of Dude from Aadu. The Mohanlal-Shiva Rajkumar cameos were effective, and the cheers were the proof. The movie is pretty violent and gory, but the gore effects were pretty well done, both the CGI stuff and the practical effects. It's rare to see that in South Indian movies, where goofy-looking CGI is what we see the most. Many scenes, such as Mohanlal's intro sequence, which reminded me of a moment from Inglourious Basterds, are pretty hard-hitting (hehe) because of that. Anirudh's score is also dependably effective in elevating the scenes and even does a lot of the heavy lifting during some of the scenes that would've fallen flat otherwise.

Nelson's dark humor does work more effectively than Beast's here, but that does not mean it always works. When it falls flat, it's spectacularly flat. The good stuff I mentioned above is peppered evenly so that the movie jumps a bit when it's just about to become unbearable. The writing is pretty uneven; a lot of plot points don't have proper development, and some characters randomly disappear into the background. The movie then morphs into a Heist movie at random, with none of the finesse Nelson's Doctor had when it did something similar. The attempts at drama also don't work most of the time and are undercut by the attempts at comedy or buildup scenes. Nelson also casts Ramya Krishnan in an insignificant part and gives her nothing to do (ideally she should've left her psychotic husband by the end of the movie), and Tamanna's just there as a badly written plot device and eye candy.

Rajini's Muthuvel does belong to the same league as Nelson's previous mostly cold protagonists, in spite of the occasional Rajinisms, and the movie does have Nelson's unique style and personality, which is pretty evident now more than ever. Being a fan of dark humor, I do enjoy Nelson's efforts at it when it works. Jailer will turn out to be a big win for Nelson box office-wise, but I hope the dude works on his writing and gives us more of the good stuff and discards the significant amount of bad stuff. The jump from Beast to Jailer is pretty big, though.

The bravest creative decision Nelson took might be how he constantly makes fun of bald movie people who wear wigs in this movie, which stars Rajinikanth in a wig.

Name: Oppenheimer
Review: Rewatched it in IMAX. Gorgeous.

Name: Maaveeran
Review:
The veeran had low expectations for this movie. The veeran turned out to love its creativity and sense of humor. The veeran approves. 

Firstly, I was surprised that Leigh Whannell's Upgrade was not on the list of inspirations for this movie, which was shown at the end; even some of the shots were replicated from it. Madonne Ashwin knows his stuff. For me, this movie felt like Will Ferrel's Stranger Than Fiction combined with Upgrade, but according to the list shown at the end, there are other inspirations too. Maaveeran is pretty neatly made, though. The writing has some flaws, but I didn't mind. The action sequences were well choreographed and shot. The comedy worked most of the time. Sivakarthikeyan does something outside of his current zone, reminding me of Sivakarthikeyan during his earlier Ethir Neechal days. SK, Mysskin, Yogi Babu, and most of the cast members do a great job. The music was good, the production design was good, and though the occasional instances of CGI didn't look so realistic, the sequences just worked. Vijay Sethupathi's voice performance was also great.

Name: Lost in Translation
Review: Wholesome, yet sad. Simple, yet complex. Brilliant, in all ways.

Name: Nights and Weekends
Review:
There's no "plot" or a traditional narrative structure. It's a collection of intimate moments between two people, the good, the awkward, and the bad. The conversations and the performances seem so real. Improvised seeming scenes with the actors just behaving than playing characters, with occasional instances of great cinematography and filmmaking, despite the low budget indie aesthetics. I could also see elements in the movie that would appear in Greta's other films. 

Also, Greta Gerwig is love.

Name: Heart of Stone
Review: Well, I didn't hate it as much as Red Notice. Heart of Stone is kind of written like a Mission Impossible movie, just without the, ahem, Heart and the action sequences. Maybe with more awesome looking action, this would've been a better experience, like the Extraction movies. The visual effects and scale were pretty nice in the very few instances where they worked. It was generic upon generic otherwise.

Name: Maggie's Plan
Review: Greta is lovely as always, with Ethan Hawke, Julianne Moore, Bill Hader and the rest of the cart being awesome. Lots of smart writing and humor, wholesome filmmaking and a cool soundtrack.

Name: 1001 Nunakal
Review: The writing is not without flaws, as at times, it felt like there wasn't any actual pressure on the characters to reveal their intimate secrets like this. But the performances were good, the cinematography, editing and direction were nice, and most importantly the film was engaging throughout, which is hard for a dialogue driven chamber drama to achieve.

Name: Along Came Polly
Review:
Is it a good movie no? Is it fun? Yeah. I have a thing for early 2000s romantic comedies and their whole vibe no matter how bad they are. This one has early 2000s written all over it, with the addition of Philip Seymour Hoffman being the only thing that sets it apart. Here we have, an absolute legend, one of the greatest ever, explaining what a shart is. Then he's shooting basketball and missing, he's performing Jesus Christ superstar, and if this movie was at least 90% Hoffman, this would've been a comedic masterpiece.

The movie tries to create an amalgamation of There's Something About Mary with Meet The Parents using Stiller and is nowhere near those two. The Salsa scene made me smile though.

Name: Past Lives
Review:
This movie hit me on a different level. Firstly, the cinematography and the music were just absolutely gorgeous; I could listen to that soundtrack on loop forever. The performances were brilliant, with the characters and their emotions feeling pretty real. Celine Song's filmmaking style also seems unique and personal. I did feel a Wong Kar-Wai vibe at times. 

I don't know whether to call Celine Song's Past Lives a love story or a story about love. Because it's not a traditional romance. It's about the yearning, the longing, the "what could've been" and moving on. It's the kind of beautiful cinema that has a profound effect on me. 

There are lots of instances of brilliant framing and shots with so much life. Loved this.

Name: RDX: Robert Dony Xavier
Review:
As an action film, RDX gets some of the basic things that make a great action movie right, and this is what made me overlook its flaws and just take in the spectacle. These basics that make a great action movie are important because they're things that newer Indian films with the "action" label lack most of the time. Action movies with invincible main characters and repetitive "fight" scenes with goons randomly flying and the hero giving random slow-motion poses to the camera just don't work for me. I'm not talking about realism here; I'm just talking about doing action sequences that actually mean something rather than just being photoshoots for the hero.

In RDX, the main characters are extremely skilled martial artists, but they're not invincible; they get hurt and put in danger, and in each fight, the threat feels more real than like something they can overcome with ease since they're supernaturally awesome. Then there are other touches like giving each character their own fighting style and moments of drama within the action, which all add extra layers to the setpieces, even if they're elevated above realism. Here we feel the impact of the hits, and the pain seems real. Realism doesn't matter for an action film, but internal logic does. Bringing in Anbariv to choreograph the action was a great choice, but I do wish that the fight scenes used a lesser amount of slo-mo like in Lokesh Kanagaraj's movies. Shane Nigam's boat fight scene with no slo-mo is a favorite of mine for the same reason.

All three title characters get their moment to shine on the screen, with the choice of different fight styles for each of them setting them apart during the action. The writing surrounding the action is basic and simple, and it sticks very closely to Malayalam commercial film sensibilities during the 90s and early 2000s. But while the writing is traditional, the choices that make RDX a solid action film make it pretty modern. Sam CS' score also boosts moments that would make the crowd go wild. There are a few instances where the buildups fall flat, but the stuff that worked outweighs the stuff that didn't.

Shane Nigam, Antony Varghese, and Neeraj Madhav successfully pull off seeming like absolute badasses. When the three of them stood together at the closing shot and the audience cheered, they were cheering for Robert, Donny, and Xavier and not for the previous movies these three actors had done. That right there is a win!

Name: Satyaprem Ki Katha
Review: Confusing movie. It does have a sensitive portrayal of a relevant subject matter, but it does so while being surrounded by a good amount of regressiveness too.

Name: You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah
Review:
Adam Sandler produced a good movie after such a long time, and it's for his daughter to be an absolute star. Sunny Sandler carries the movie wonderfully; the teen movie elements are familiar, but the movie does have heart and is very entertaining. The movie belongs to the kids, with Sandler, Menzel, and the other adults mostly taking the backseat. Sandler still manages to get a scene where he's yelling stuff, though. Sunny Sandler and Samantha Lorraine are the true stars of this movie.

Even though it's a teen movie and operates on non-screwball comedy terrain, there are characters like the Rabbi and the DJ and enough farts to place this one into the Sandlerverse. Perhaps Sandler produced this so that his entire family could act in it, but this turned out to be a pretty nice family movie, literally.

Name: Thallumaala
Review:
Some dudes complain that Malayalam cinema doesn't have KGF, Baahubali, Pushpa, and stuff. But, bruh, they can NEVER EVER have a Thallumaala.

Onam rewatch.

Name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem
Review:
This movie has heart, great jokes, great pop culture references that you really don't see in kids movies that much, great music, great art and design, great voice acting, and awesome animation. The drama and emotional stakes could've been better, but on the whole, this was a wholesome experience. It's refreshing to see the Turtles actually be teenagers; this movie's Turtle interactions are kind of like the ones in Superbad, just more kid-friendly. I loved the entire visual style and humor so much. The score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross and the songs being used were groovy.




Cowabunga!

Name: The Last of the Mohicans
Review:
The initial 30 minutes or so of the movie seemed extremely dull, and I couldn't care less about the English-French stuff. Things got mildly interesting after Cora and Hawkeye met, but I didn't feel the romance was well developed. The actors had nice chemistry, though. The music and cinematography were amazing; there are some spectacular action setpieces, like the ambush towards the end. But I was always disconnected from the narrative. I don't know much about the political or historic aspects, but I've definitely seen better films set in the same era.

There is no denying that Michael Mann is a legend and Daniel Day Lewis is the GOAT; just that I didn't feel that this movie is the classic that it's lauded to be.

Name: A Fistful of Dollars
Review: "Get five stars ready." Pew pew..

Name: For a Few Dollars More
Review:
Bravo! 

I mean, I could nitpick about the stuff that hasn't aged well, but given the time this was shot and the budget they had, it's just pure artistry that the film looks and sounds like it does. Yeah, the bullets don't leave any impact on people when they get shot, but still, the shootings and the guns convey the tension and the violence; the use of closeups and the editing are textbook. The frames are art, and the score is magnificent. 

 Pew pew.

Name: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
Review:
Bigger in scale than the last two movies in every single way, a cinematic marvel even in the present day. Leone's craft, Morricone's magnificent score, the three main leads' terrific performances, the editing, the cinematography.. Everything's a blast. There are so many elements that have been borrowed by films, even now, and yet, everything seems unique here. The tension building is excellent. Even moments like how Eastwood dons the poncho and fully becomes the "man with no name" in the climax are eternally awesome. 

 I mean.. Pew pew... It's a masterpiece!

Name: Iruvar
Review:
Brilliant acting, gorgeous visuals, amazingly staged scenes and beautiful music elevate this cinematic experience. While it felt like the decades spanning saga of Friendship and ambitions going in parallel deserved a more in-depth approach, this is still great cinema.

Man, Mohanlal!!!!!

Name: Jawan
Review:
Jawan is closer to the vigilante films by Atlee's mentor Shankar than the three films Atlee made with Vijay. It does have all the elements present in the Atlee-Vijay movies, the good and the bad. Atlee has always borrowed elements from iconic Tamil commercial entertainers in his films, and Jawan is no different. Though the language is Hindi and the star is the King of Bollywood, Jawan is pretty much a Tamil movie. Even when Prabhu Deva and Siddhique did Bollywood films, they didn't feel as South Indian as Jawan does.

Anirudh's music does sound like his South Indian soundtracks, but I thought it fit here. Vijay Sethupathi plays an over-the-top formulaic corporate villain, but towards the second half, he does get some cool scenes and some funny fourth wall-breaking one-liners that made me feel Atlee is indeed aware of the kind of movie he's making. Nayanthara gets more to do than she did in Bigil, including a cool action scene. The rest of the supporting cast was pretty nice too, including the Deepika Padukone cameo, though the characters are not that well-written. The movie does have good production values and VFX work. There's a cool highway action sequence that I loved, and a single-shot-like moment in the climax fight sequence, which was very impressive. There's cool choreography and use of weapons involved, other than dudes randomly flying, and yes, there's slow-mo and posing too; it's Atlee.

One can easily see Thalapathy Vijay in the same movie, and yet the best part about Jawan is that Shah Rukh Khan doesn't feel out of place at all. The dude uses his charisma and his own brand of badassery to make this an SRK movie. From the action to the slow-mo shots to the dancing and comedy, SRK does SRK stuff, but with an Atlee flavor. It made me wonder if several elements that made Theri, Mersal, and Bigil "Vijay Movies", were just stuff that made them Atlee movies. Even the action is a bit less grounded than your average SRK fight scene, where he usually gets beaten up a lot. He still gets action scenes where he's covered in blood, though, in true SRK fashion.

Atlee's "girl power" efforts in Jawan are a lot less cringey than in Bigil. I tend to give a pass for Atlee's cringe in this area since at least the dude is not trying to make the audience cheer for misogyny. Well-intentioned cringe is forgivable cringe. There's political messaging here, nothing radical, and stuff we've seen in other Tamil movies and even Atlee's own films, but considering this is a Hindi-language film starring Shah Rukh Khan releasing now, this is a bold move. Shah Rukh Khan looking at the audience and giving a long monologue about democracy is a pretty new thing to a large audience group.

Is it formulaic? Yes. Is it occasionally cringe and illogical? Yes. Did I have a great time watching it? Absolutely. Did I appreciate the attempts at messaging? Absolutely. Popular movies have been glorifying the wrong stuff for decades, so flawed attempts at conveying the right stuff make me give them a pass.

I dig Thalapathy Khan.

Name: Dead for a Dollar
Review: The lack of a budget was clearly evident, especially in those CGI bullet wounds. The cast was great, but the performances were all over the place. The movie does occasionally shine, but not enough.

Name: Unforgiven
Review: It's a deep, melancholic deconstruction of what made Clint Eastwood the icon he is. The film takes its time to let us know how Eastwood's William Munny is not the man he once was. We hear lines about how scary the old William was, which immediately have me flashbacks more to Eastwood in the iconic Sergio Leone movies than anything else. At the same time, it's also building up Gene Hackman's sheriff as a threat. Munny lives with the weight of his past deeds, and Eastwood's performance perfectly captures the pain and reluctance that he has to go back to his old ways. Even when he does at the end and bullets start flying, it's all about pain, grief, and regret, masked as revenge and aggression. As a director and an actor, Eastwood gave himself the best farewell ever to his western gunslinger era.

Name: Birdman or (The Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance)
Review: This must be my 4th or 5th rewatch. I'm still in awe of this movie. The cinematography, the philosophical themes, the satire, the way Iñárritu crafted the scenes, the performances—everything still feels brilliant. It's funny, it's sad, it's existential, and damn, Keaton deserved that Oscar.

Name: Talk to Me
Review:
The writing and character work aren't revolutionary, but damn, this was an effective horror movie. The Gen-Z aspect was interesting, though they didn't expand it like I thought they would after the initial act. 

The scares and the atmosphere were effective, the sound work and the special effects were on point, and the makeup was flawless. Sophie Wilde's performance was great, but the character, not so much. 

Talk to Me is no Midsommer or Hereditary, but it's a pretty well-made horror movie.

Those head bashes, though. Damn.

Name: Elemental
Review:
The writing isn't up to Pixar standards, as they themselves have handled the same themes in better ways. The world is interesting, but it's not explored as much. The visuals, character design, and animation are innovative and impressive, a true achievement. Thomas Newman's score is also beautiful, with the Indian element being quite surprising.

It's not Pixar enough, but wholesome enough.

Name: Mark Antony
Review:
SJ Suryah SJ Suryaying is fun to watch, but it's more fun when it's got a superior film around it like Maanaadu. Time travel plotholes are easy to forgive because it's such a messy kind of fiction that we can find such confusions in even the most complex and meticulous time travel fiction. Mark Antony is the familiar Tamil gangster movie template with a time travel/butterfly effect wrapper. Vishal was struggling as both characters, but the dad seems better, mostly because most of his face is covered in hair (lessons from Rocky Bhai). The voice was also unintentionally funny in some scenes. Adhik's female characters are not as shitty as his previous movies, but they're not good either (the disrespect shown towards Silk Smitha included), and they don't have much to do. Plus the movie has instances of queerphobic "comedy", as dated as the era it's set in, why da why? The various pop culture references related to the era are also hilarious, in a bad/ironic kind of way. The less I say about the writing the better. I'm also confused about the balance between self-aware parody and actually being bad in the movie. The editing also seemed a bit weird during certain scene transitions. The movie is very fast and rushed, as if the editor and director doesn't trust our attention spans. 

The second half of the movie is literally a loop—not a time loop, just narratively repetitive. SJ Suriyah's performance and GV Prakash's Background Massacres (the movie itself calls its music a massacre; don't ask why) are fun. The Anaconda reference was funny, but did Lokesh Kanagaraj just start a trend that we're going to see in every South Indian movie now?

Name: We Need to Talk About Kevin
Review: Tilda Swinton's performance is brilliant, and she carries the film like a true legend. The dread, helplessness, and horror are conveyed brilliantly. The way the film is structured is very smart, building up to Kevin unleashing what he's capable of in the form of memory flashbacks as his mother is experiencing its aftermath in the present day. Ezra Miller and the two child actors are effective in making Kevin a creepy, cold, and detached person. There are several instances of masterful horror on display, with the violence and its darkness mostly being implied rather than making excessive use of gore. The music is effectively creepy, as is the cinematography and editing. The filmmaking here is very deliberate and unique.

Name: Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani
Review:
I liked it in parts. I didn't like some other parts. I didn't really care about the titular "love story" that much after the halfway point. There's stuff I don't agree with, and there's some cringe and flaws. But there are some nice moments, music, and performances too. I do have some issues with the film's politics, which are progressive on the surface and address several issues, but they're not without flaws. But I wish more mainstream "family" movies and soap operas convey similar ideas, or even better ones than being blatantly regressive.

Alia Bhatt crush intensified.

Name: Bottoms
Review: Bottoms is a hilarious, sharp, and intelligent satire with awesome performances from the cast, cool music, and a director-writer combo who really knows what they're doing with a movie about two queer high school girls starting a fight club. Emma Seligman does something that's so different from her debut, Shiva Baby, with a caricaturish world, over-the-top characters, and exaggerated events. But even through all that—the constant jokes, the crude humor, the satirical digs, and the violence—the movie has heart.

Name: No One Will Save You
Review:
An alien-horror thriller movie with almost no dialogue might initially sound like a quiet place replica, but Brian Duffield's No One Will Save You is far from being one. The lack of dialogue is part of a different creative choice here, than the narrative reasoning A Quiet Place had for it. The movie depends on Kaitlyn Dever's great performance to do a lot of heavy lifting because of this. The great production design, tension building, impressive setpieces and visual effects also add to making this a gripping film. The cinematography, the weirdness, the way themes like trauma, isolation, guilt and grief are handled, and how the movie presents all this without spoken dialogue, is pretty brilliant.

Apparently the writer-director realised the movie doesn't have any dialogue only halfway through writing it. But minimal dialogue can lead to thrillers thrillering better, so win-win.

Name: The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar
Review: "This was awesome", I said.

Name: Kannur Squad
Review:
