Mammootty was love, consistently brilliant, and he seemed a lot less stiff and a lot more realistic than usual in the fight sequences for some reason. The rest of the cast was also cool, notably Azees. Sushin's music was nice, with some groovy tracks.

The movie is basically a police procedural, with a prologue episode that isn't really connected to the rest of the movie and one main case. I did think the crime itself had a lot more screen time than it required. The investigation part was pretty grounded; there's no Sethuramayyar kind of deductions, just police work, including mundane info searches. Though things do enter the "mass" territory occasionally during certain action sequences, Mammootty's physical performance during the action scenes was surprising; there might be doubles being used, but everything looked well put together anyway. The cinematography was nice, and the movie is well made for the most part, apart from some moments of awkward editing that made some scenes fall flat (there's a particular scene towards the end fight scene where it's so apparent).

Also, although almost all Indian cop movies I've grown up with have glorified police violence and made it seem heroic, I expected something different from this film because of the semi-grounded approach but got disappointed. Police violence gets heroic treatment here when they even brutally torture people for information. Sure, the crime they're investigating is pretty gnarly, and one can argue that those dudes "deserve" this. But I don't think the movie really emphasizes that this is an act of vigilantism and not part of the systemic violence normalized by a lot of other movies. I mean, Kishore is a part of the cast here, and the dude was literally in Visaaranai, which was all about looking at police violence from the other side.

Anyway, apart from feeling that the titular squad could've been made more gray based on their methods, I enjoyed Kannur Squad, and though this is a pretty long movie, I never really lost my attention or got bored. The crime flashback is the only part which I thought was a bit too long than it had to be, it was also gratuitous and insensitive, seriously, using insensitive portrayal of SA to justify the main characters' violence is just shitty.

Name: Sapta Sagaradaache Ello – Side A
Review: Damn that was heavy.

Name: The Creator
Review:
The Creator is undoubtedly a visual triumph, even if we don't consider the fact that it was made on a fraction of the budget of major Hollywood big-budget movies. That itself is something Gareth Edwards can be proud of—that the film looks and sounds as great as it does and looks a lot better than a lot of big-budget productions while costing less than half of what they did.

The cinematography, the production design, the visual effects, the sound design, and the music by Hans Zimmer are at the top of their games. Even without reading up about the way this film was made with a relatively smaller budget for something this big, it's an impressive feat of filmmaking. There are lots of awe-inducing visuals and moments of grandeur. There are lots of gorgeous shots of real-life locations enhanced by brilliant visual effects to feast on.

The Creator's writing is not like your average popcorn flick; it is serious in tone for the most part, tonally a lot similar to Edwards' on Rogue One: A Star Wars Story. There are small moments of humor, and the relationship between a child and the man escorting her is the heart of the movie. Yep, yet another Logan, Last of Us kind of situation.

The writing is indeed borrowing from a lot of existing stuff. From Blade Runner to Avatar to a few others. While this can be called derivative, I did read that Edwards has been open about his inspirations. Real-world events, the Vietnam War, and the thing America has for invading other nations are all part of the plot. But it doesn't really explore the concept of AI or a real human vs. a copy of a human concept the way something like Blade Runner did. I expected a film about AI and its philosophical complexities, but I got something that had a different kind of philosophy, one that focused on humanity's own mistakes and the West's invasion of foreign nations. I did love a line in this movie that went like "Do you know what we'll do to the west when we win this war?".

While this technically is an "original" sci-fi film, which in these times just means a movie that's not an existing IP, the concepts are not entirely original. But at the same time, that doesn't make the technical achievements of this film any less impressive. The Creator might not be Blade Runner 2049 in terms of its writing, but as an achievement in filmmaking, it's indeed a triumph.

Name: King of Kotha
Review:
There's a really great action sequence towards the end of King of Kotha, with some first-person perspective stuff, some long takes, some cool camera moves, solid choreography, and visceral and violent action, and Dulquer does seem like a genuine badass in this movie for these few minutes. But what's sad is that everything else is so utterly terrible, with the bad ranging from generic bad to laughably bad to problematically bad to laughably problematically bad.

In terms of trying to replicate KGF, they did have toxic masculinity like KGF, terrible dialogue like KGF and a terrible romance arc like KGF, but failed at becoming another KGF or Pushpa anyway. This one action scene was cool; the kalikal Raju Bhai ozhivaakkaled for that fight scene were worth it.

Name: Blue Beetle
Review:
I wouldn't call Blue Beetle a terrible movie. I'd have even loved it a lot more if it had come out in the early 2010s. It's just that even if they do a straightforward superhero origin story, they have to do something new for it to stick out. The first Shazam! movie did that by being the superhero version of Tom Hanks' Big; the second Shazam! movie was an unfocused generic superhero movie, and it didn't work.

In Blue Beetle, the uniqueness comes in the form of how the main character's family is more directly involved in the action than in a usual superhero film and how the movie incorporates the Mexican-American immigrant perspective. The film does do justice in this regard. The action and the visual effects are a lot better than Shazam 2 and The Flash, too. Though they end up reminding me of the first Iron Man movie at times, Xolo Maridueña is a charming and likable lead, and the rest of the cast delivers great performances too. Someone like Susan Sarandon is reduced to being a generic superhero movie villain, though. The quick backstory given to the character Carapax to give him more depth, after making him a mindless muscle guy for the rest of the movie, could've been done better.

I liked the characters and the humor, and I had some fun. But this is indeed a very generic movie, but with a Pixar movie kind of charm and energy. Even though this film wasn't a hit, I heard the characters would return. So I hope they crack the formula next time.

Name: To Die For
Review: Nicole Kidman was awesome in this movie. Teen Joaquin Phoenix was also brilliant. But this is Kidman's movie.

Name: Nalla Nilavulla Rathri
Review: This movie spends close to 75 minutes setting up nothing. There's random conversations involving each character's motivations, some business shit, some personal issue shit, and it all builds up to, nothing. I guess the intention was to make us guess who the killer is once the murdering starts, but nothing of that sort happens. I will give this movie a bit of appreciation for solid looking gore makeup. But that's it. The CGI is tacky, the shots of the dog biting people look cartoony than scary. The ending is very weird and not the good kind of weird. And then the whole thing ends without tying up anything. If they thought this thing deserves a sequel, their optimism is off the charts. Random plotlines with no purpose include : * Rony's daughter's surgery * Baburaj's kadam * Some shit between Baburaj and Chemban when they were young. * Paul dude is a habitual liar. * Ganapathi's stabbing case * Baburaj's udayipp deal, and Jinu's maru udayipp * Rony and the other dude want to cancel the deal * Binu Pappu And Jinu have trust issues. And the real reason for the slashering in this slasher is that, Chemban randomly kills a dude on the way to the vellamadi, because he felt like eating some pork as touchings. I mean.. Even the reason in Tovino's Kala, which was the dude seeking revenge for Tovino murdering his dog, was way better than this.. Irumban oru kurumban. I should've rather rewatched Kala, if I knew this is just the Irumban version of that. Did Baburaj's character die from a dog biting his leg? How'd Chemban kill the two dudes when he's been cornered? Why is the end text saying it's a war, when these injured and tired dudes can be easily killed by Adaikalam from LCU? Orikkalum utharam kittatha chodyangalum aayi njan keezhadangi. I watched King of Kotha yesterday, which was also a bad movie, but it didn't feel as much as a waste of time as this one did. Raju Bhai thani thankam.

Name: Spiral: From the Book of Saw
Review:
Well, this is the Saw movie with the most star power, but still, Chris Rock and Sam Jackson deliver hammy and over-the-top performances playing badly written characters. They had the budget for gnarly-looking special effects and gore prosthetic makeup but couldn't get decent fake facial hair for Rock and Jackson.

Spiral is a so and so police procedural, with the traps and the saw name being used more as dressing. While some fans might be disappointed by the lesser number of traps and kills, that's not where my disappointment lies. The original Saw was not about the gore and body count either, but there were certain elements that made it brilliant, even when that film too was an amateur project. So a Saw movie can be brilliant even without all the gore and kills that defined it later on. But Spiral isn't that movie.

Name: Njanum Pinnoru Njanum
Review: Creepy asf for all the wrong reasons. Watched it to laugh at a shitty movie, ended up being creeped out, while also simultaneously finding the shittiness funny. Myr.

Name: The Equalizer 3
Review:
The appeal lies in seeing Denzel do Denzel stuff. From being warm and caring to being cold and deadly to bringing his thespian energy to even the most basic of scenes, the man just does justice to the legend he is in this movie too. Equalizer 3 has a lesser amount of action than the previous ones and is in an entirely different mood than those. There are returning elements, but the music and cinematography specifically gave this a different feel.

This entire trilogy's appeal is only Denzel and the way he's presented. And damn, he's badass.

Name: The Nun II
Review: I didn't give a shit about anything that happened in this movie. There are a few cool horror setpieces, but there's too much repetition on their placement and there's too less storytelling involved that I just didn't care. Maybe those would've worked better as self contained shorts or something. The Nun appears so much randomly that, at this point she's not even that scary. James Wan understood scary, despite the indulgence on jump scares. But the people who followed up on what Wan did ended up trying to replicate the weaker aspects of the two Conjuring films by Wan. The Nun worked in Conjuring 2, because Wan understood less is more, and he set a thrilling narrative around it.

Name: Totally Killer
Review: The newest movie in Blumhouse's slasher-comedy series which started with Happy Death Day, and this time it's about time-traveling to the past to face a masked killer, back to the future style. I had a lot of fun watching this movie, and it was pretty open about its inspirations and references. Back to the Future is referenced a bunch of times, as are the Breakfast Club and Halloween, and the main character is named Jamie Hughes. I liked the time travel humor and pop culture references and the whole Gen Z being trapped in the 80s situation. The whodunit aspect is not as great as something like the first Scream, but it still worked. Kiernan Shipka was great as the lead. This is the kind of slasher that's a lot less focused on delivering scares or gruesome kills, and the way they explained or didn't explain time travel plotholes and simplified the convoluted nature of time travel was kinda nice.

Name: Aadukalam
Review: Other than a weird and problematic romance arc and wooden acting from a beginning stage Tapsee Pannu (who has since become an amazing actress), Aadukalam was brilliant cinema. The movie really kicks in during the second half with how character dynamics and their male egos are developed by Vetrimaaran. Amazing acting from the rest of the cast, led by a brilliant Dhanush, too.

Name: Viduthalai: Part I
Review:
Viduthalai is well-crafted, well-written, well-acted, and hard-hitting cinema. There's a lot to appreciate here. There are some brilliantly staged sequences, gorgeous cinematography, and powerful politics.

I am not giving it 5 stars because of the mostly unremarkable and meh Ilaiyaraaja music at times. Vetri's filmmaking is so good that not even the music that doesn't match the mood of the movie could ruin the scenes. Still, I wish this movie had a GV Prakash or Santhosh Narayanan score instead of recycled Ilayaraja stuff that just sounded so out of place in several scenes. (I like the song Kaattumalli and some tracks in the background score, though)

Name: The Rat Catcher
Review: Ralph Fiennes doing Voldemort doing the Ratcatcher dude. Also, hats off for Rupert Friend and Richard Ayoade for nailing the Wes Anderson stares.

Name: Poison
Review: The one that made me laugh the most. Wes should do a full length movie with Dev Patel in the lead.

Name: Khufiya
Review:
Tabu and Wamiqa were awesome in this. There are instances of great filmmaking and writing in Khufiya. The writing isn't perfect, but props to them for showing realistic and grounded spy work, while spy movies in India are moving towards Fast and Furious-ish YRF Spy Universe movies. This movie reminded me a bit of the FX series The Americans. There's also no jingoism or deshbhakthi elements; what a relief! The film has a very clear political stand, which is rarely seen in such movies, especially in India. Even a relatively more "realistic" Indian intelligence depiction like The Family Man had clichés that Khufiya avoided.

Khufiya does have flaws, but I liked what it was trying to do.

Name: Leo
Review:
Leo is flawed, for sure, but it was a lot of fun. There's lots of well-shot, well-choreographed fight sequences and a familiar storyline inspired by A History of Violence that's trying more to be an action movie than the darker, subtler, and toned-down approach that film had. Leo is not subtle, not by a long shot. But it worked for me. Vijay is way less his star persona and way more embodying the character in Leo. When Lokesh said Master was 50% and this was 100%, the math was pretty accurate. Scenes where Vijay is in rage mode were indeed badass. I also liked the way the movie handled the main character's internal conflict and morality. Sanjay Dutt and Arjun as the villains didn't have the impact that Vijay Sethupathi in Master and Vikram had. Trisha's character in Leo had way better writing in terms of being the wife of a violent dude than Ramya Krishnan in Jailer did.

In Kaithi, even with a lower budget, Lokesh pulled off thrilling chase sequences that worked gloriously. When he tried something similar in Master, it didn't really work the same way. It's kind of similar in Leo too; cartoonish-looking CGI and physics take away the sense of danger in Leo's big chase sequence, though the idea of it, the choreography, and the conception of it like a long uninterrupted shot were nice on paper. The CGI Hyena looked pretty good, though; it worked for me.

The rushed flashback scenes were a weak link in the movie, and in a movie with so many amazing hand-to-hand combat scenes, a certain fight scene in the flashback had weird wirework and choreography consisting of goons flying without the impact being felt. But the rest of the action was the kind I love. The hits pack an impact, the weapons feel deadly, and the violence is visceral, Vijay himself gets hurt a lot and feels vulnerable. The Indian censor board made obvious cuts and blurs to the action, but I'm hoping the Netflix release won't have those.

Anirudh does his typical Anirudh thing; there is the expected Anirudh-ish kind of music and a lot of scenes that are made cooler by the score. Anirudh's music is the least subtle thing in this movie, too. There's literally a song called "Shit Scared" when the protagonist is scared, and his theme music literally calls him a badass. There are also other instances of unsubtle music placements that I'll avoid explaining because it's too soon for spoilers. And despite all the action and grittiness, is there also a big dance number by murderous criminals in the movie? Yes, there is.

I liked Leo better than Master, but not as much as Vikram or Kaithi. It's not without its flaws, but when it works, it's BADASS.

Name: Saw X
Review:
After all these years since the third one, they finally made another good Saw. The best choice made in this movie was to put Tobin Bell's John Kramer front and center. I think this is the only Saw movie that's told through John Kramer's perspective for the most part. The people getting "tested" are indeed terrible, and John is more of an anti-hero here than an actual villain, though the sadistic traps and gore are present here too. Tobin Bell delivers his best performance as Jigsaw and gets more material to work with than before.

While some of the previous Saw movies were reduced to having overcomplicated, lackluster narratives only meant to build up to the gore, and the movies ended up being more about the gore, Saw X does mix it up, give room to its characters, and explore the weird moral code that John Kramer has, despite his sadistic nature otherwise. It is not devoid of gore like the original Saw. It's a mixed bag of having stuff that made the original Saw great and also having the gore and creatively sadistic traps that the series then became known for. With only a handful of traps and gory sequences, it doesn't actually enter gratuitous torture porn territory like some of the other Saw films. The non-game parts are not bland like Spiral, either.

The production design, special effects, make-up, and CGI were pretty solid, and all the gore looked and felt horrific. The references and callbacks to the previous Saw films were nice. There are some glaring logical flaws towards the end, but still, the movie stays pretty solid, mostly because Tobin Bell sells the hell out of Jigsaw, even when the man himself is a puzzle.

Name: Love at First Sight
Review: This movie was my kind of cheesy with late 90s - early 2000s romcom vibes. Also, Haley Lu is always love.

Name: The Royal Hotel
Review: The film is well made, and the performances are amazing. The tension keeps building from the moment they step into the bar. Every sexist joke, every display of toxic masculinity, and creepy dudes being creepy get the horror treatment. We feel the discomfort that Hannah feels in that environment. The lack of music also add to the atmosphere. But still, I wish the ending was a bit better. While I understood the idea that's being conveyed, I expected more.

Name: Killers of the Flower Moon
Review:
Killers of the Flower Moon might be the most political Martin Scorsese picture that I've watched. Scorsese shows the Osage county murders of native Americans through the perspective of the white perpetrators themselves. While making sure that we see them for the greedy, cold monsters they are, there's no effort made to make them sympathetic. Scorsese is not new to evil and villainous protagonists, but here, the historical context and politics add an entirely new kind of depth. In doing so, the theme of the film and its examination of greed, exploitation and oppression stay eternally relevant.

The film has all the trademarks of a Scorsese picture. To me, it seemed like a perfect blend of the more subdued Scorsese style from Silence combined with the signature Scorsese montages and cutaways from his crime movies. Thelma Schoonmaker's editing perfectly adapts to the film's changing gears, with the late Robbie Robertson's score also fitting perfectly to individual scenes and never seeming out of place. There's gorgeous cinematography by Rodrigo Prieto, with some amazing use of shadows and closeups. This IS a film meant for the big screen, and I'm glad that the original plan for a limited release was changed to a worldwide release. I was glued to the screen for the entirety of the almost 3.5-hour runtime.

The entire ensemble cast is amazing, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Robert De Niro portraying two different kinds of evil. It was great to see De Niro play a cold and manipulative villain like William Hale after such a long time. DiCaprio's Earnest Burkhart has a kind of innocence and naivety about him, but the kind that doesn't make us sympathize with him as he becomes a part of terrible acts of violence. There's a closeup shot, towards the end, of DiCaprio's face that goes on for quite a while, which was absolutely brilliant. Lily Gladstone's Mollie is indeed the heart of the movie, and though she doesn't have as much screen time as De Niro and DiCaprio, she shines in a performance that's subtle and deep and that stayed with me even after the film ended.

Killers of the Flower Moon is aware that it comes from a white man's perspective. But the story it tells and its larger themes are important. The film is brilliantly crafted, and Scorsese still manages to surprise me with each new film. What a legend!

Name: Boyhood
Review:
I was 17 when I first watched this movie. Watching it in my mid-20s now is even more comforting. Time passing for real in the movie just works on a whole other level, plus the movie just flows from scene to scene without making each phase episodic. Yeah, just like most Linklater films, it's not a traditional drama; there's no traditional plot; it's just like peeking into someone's life, their little moments of happiness, despair, disappointments, trauma, everything. The entire cast is beautiful, and Linklater did capture how "growing up" feels, not just for the kids but for the parents too.

An ever-evolving comfort watch.

Name: A Haunting in Venice
Review: A Haunting in Venice took me by surprise because this is a very different film from the last two Kenneth Branagh Hercule Poirot movies. The last two were huge, over-stylized "Hollywood" productions with loud scores, vibrant colors, and excess. Here, the colors are muted, the score by Hildur Guðnadóttir is minimal and atmospheric, Poirot himself comes across as a different man; he's got less popcorn flick energy now, and Branagh comfortably switches styles both as an actor and a filmmaker. Most of the film takes place indoors at night, lit by candles and lanterns. It keeps it contained, the CGI landscape shots from the last films are almost gone, and even the few instances of visual effects present to show 1947 Venice are of a more realistic kind than the over-stylized stuff from the previous movies. I haven't read any of the books, so I've approached each of these films with a fresh perspective. The mystery was pretty good, with horror elements blended in a way that does not defeat the purpose of this being a whodunit operating on a logical plane. I dig Branagh's Poirot. I do want to see more of them, especially if they build up on the style established here, than the last two movies.

Name: Leo
Review: Watched the version that wasn't butchered by Indian Censor Board. The censor board kinda did a favor to Lokesh by blurring some of the gore which didn't look so great unblurred, though.

Name: Fingernails
Review: This movie has great performances, a great soundtrack, some lines of dialogue that I loved, cool cinematography and a concept with a lot of potential. With the kind of concept they had, they could've done more with this movie. So it felt a bit incomplete like a 50% Love test. Still a pretty nice watch. Riz Ahmed and Jessie Buckley are love. Chef Carmy was a bit underused though.

Name: Nayakan
Review:
Nayakan is a masterpiece. I'm aware that the first two Godfather movies were an inspiration, and there are even scenes that are a direct parallel to The Godfather, but man, The Godfather movies never made me weep like Nayakan did. Firstly, Ilaiyaraja created a beautiful track like Thenpaandi Cheemayile. The film itself has a backdrop of tragedy and melancholy from the very beginning, and the track pops up at the perfect moments to amplify those feelings. Kamal's performance as Velu Naicker through various phases of his life is absolutely brilliant. Pain is a constant in the character's life, and so is questioning his own morality, and Kamal makes sure we feel it. Mani Rathnam's masterful filmmaking and writing fleshes out something that could've been a template gangster story into something deeper, something melancholic.

I'm so glad a better remastered version of the film now exists so that the Ilaiyaraja music and the P. C. Sreeram frames can be appreciated better.

Name: Thalapathi
Review:
It's a bit too melodramatic for my taste, though it does have its moments. Rajini is amazing, with lots of scenes showcasing him more as an actor than as the Super Star he came to be associated with. Mammootty was also great, and their chemistry was awesome, especially in parts like the Kaattu Kuyile song. Though some of the Nanban Paasam lines (which I'm aware are iconic) seemed funny when hearing them now, the movie still has an incredibly effective mother-son relationship arc, with one of the best Amma Paasam theme songs ever (Rajaaa!).

The Mahabharat-Karnan inspired storyline does struggle a bit to strike a balance between the friendship arc and the mother-son arc. I wish Banupriya's character was also fleshed out a bit more. But overall, it does live up to the hype.

Name: Irugapatru
Review: There are three relationships in focus in this movie, with all of them being problematic. While two of them were shit to the level of me hoping the women would leave these dudes in the first half itself, the Vikram Prabhu-Shraddha one was not that toxic... Until Vikram Prabhu had his big monologue about what true love is (spoilers, being a suspicious privacy-invading toxic partner is true love). And I was like, "You too, dude? STFU!". Also, the dudes don't deserve the redemptions at the end at all.

Name: The Killer
Review:
There have been two attempts at adapting the Hitman video game series into live-action films, and both of them have not come close to The Killer in terms of emulating the feel of those games. I don't mean that The Killer is a film that feels like a video game, though. It's far from it. The Hitman games were designed to put the players in the shoes of a professional killer. David Fincher does the same thing for his audience through meticulously crafted cinema.

There's not a lot happening in The Killer in terms of a "plot". It's simple and straightforward, and even the Netflix synopsis describes the entire thing. The Killer is more about the feel of it; it's about following this killer, who continuously says he lacks empathy and that he doesn't "give a fuck", but his actions suggest otherwise. The main character is very meticulous, very careful, very professional, very planned, and very organized. The movie is, too. The attention to detail is amazing, and it's all presented in a slick and stylish manner. There is voice-over narration by Michael Fassbender, but it's not constant. It appears only during moments where the killer is actively pursuing a target. The movie itself is divided into chapters, which are named after the place it's set in and the target (very much like a level in a Hitman game). The killer's persistent motto is "anticipate, don't improvise", as he plans every move, but at unpredictable moments where he does have to improvise, the film's entire visual language shifts. There are two brilliantly staged and choreographed action sequences where this shift happens. I especially loved the indoor hand-to-hand fight scene that's brilliantly choreographed and makes brilliant use of space. It reminded me of a fight scene from the HBO show Barry, which also coincidentally follows a professional killer.

Michael Fassbender is amazing as The Killer, who insists he lacks emotions, but yet we can't fully believe him. His deadpan delivery is perfect, and I even thought "Dude sounds more like Dexter Morgan than Dexter Morgan". Fassbender is in every scene, and the movie never shifts focus from him. The rest of the cast, including Tilda Swinton and Charles Parnell, delivered great performances too.

The cinematography and editing follow the style expected from a David Fincher film. The score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross was very atmospheric and faded to the background most of the time, while the primary "music" in The Killer is a nice compilation of songs by The Smiths. The use of sound and music in this film is brilliant. 

On the whole, I got what I expected from Fincher.

Name: The Marvels
Review:
The Marvels is yet another lighthearted superhero movie that pretty much follows the formula. There is no strong emotional character development here like in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3. Brie Larson's Captain Marvel still remains the same; there's not a lot that's unique about her, and I don't even properly know her exact powers and weaknesses even now, the emotional arc between her and Monica is good, but it needed more time. Even though a lot of the plot points from the first Captain Marvel movie are carried over and this is essentially a sequel to that movie, the true star of this film ends up being Iman Vellani's Ms. Marvel/Kamala Khan. Teyonah Parris' Monica Rambeau's plotline involving her mother could've actually been very compelling, but the film does not give her enough time to breathe and rushes from one scene to the next. But through all that, Kamala Khan is Kamala Khaning. Sam Jackson's Nick Fury becomes the comedic supporting character from Captain Marvel yet again, but he does get some good jokes in. (This is way better than whatever the Secret Invasion show was trying to do, but still not an effective use of Nick Fury or Sam Jackson like Captain America: The Winter Soldier). The three main leads do have good chemistry together and their combination scenes were fun. 

Iman Vellani's charm and comedic timing help keep the film fun throughout. The Marvels does work as a comedy when it's not being a generic superhero movie, with scenes that are weird and crazy even for a superhero film. We have a generic villain with a sympathetic backstory yet again (who could've been better developed if given more time too). There is a sense of warmth in the way character relationships are handled, too, though the film could've spent a bit more time on them. I was not bored by this movie, and it was a positive vibe kind of experience.

I hope Marvel understands Iman Vellani's potential as a star and gives her more stuff to work with!

Name: Jigarthanda DoubleX
Review:
Though it's labeled as the sequel to Jigarthanda, by the end of Jigarthanda DoubleX, it felt like Karthik Subbaraj's attempt to make a better version of what he tried to do with Jagame Thanthiram. Jagame Thanthiram was about a narcissistic criminal who ends up helping a community of refugees. While this transformation was where Jagame Thanthiram fell flat, here, Jigarthanda DoubleX becomes something much more than the film I thought it was once it entered into the more serious storyline involving a tribal community and police brutality.

Karthik Subbaraj takes Jigarthanda's "gangster and director" thing but spins it into something entirely different from the first film. The first film was primarily a dark comedy, but Jigarthanda DoubleX isn't. There are instances of humor, but the film and its themes become much more serious moving forward, and the stakes of the film too are much more complex this time around than the simple nature of the first film. The film is also a lot bigger than the first one in every way. A much more profound tribute is given to cinema as a medium this time around.

Both Raghava Lawrence and SJ Suriyah deliver great performances that are distinct from what's usually expected of them. SJ Suriyah's usual over-the-top antics have been toned down here. There are moments where he's doing the SJ Suriyah thing, but most of the time it's a different kind of performance. In the case of Lawrence, this is a complete overhaul for the man. While his introduction and the action scene that followed made me think he's going to do the same stuff he's been doing since the Kanchana movies, he surprised me till the very end. From the Clint Eastwood references and body language to the humor and emotion-heavy monologues and scenes, Lawrence was amazing. Nimisha Sajayan and Naveen Chandra were the other standouts.

Santhosh Narayanan's soundtrack in Jigarthanda DoubleX wasn't as memorable as his other Karthik Subbaraj collaborations, but the score does have some great tracks that perfectly fit the film. The film also makes effective use of Ennio Morricone's iconic score from For A Few Dollars More. The scenes from that film are also placed in a cool way. All the Clint Eastwood references were really cool throughout.

The various logical flaws and writing issues I felt were forgivable on the whole. The final stretch of the film is great cinema; it gets political, it speaks about oppression, occupation, and exploitation, it becomes emotional, and it did make me tear up. Cinema is powerful, but it might not be as powerful as this film shows it to be, but within this film, we do feel that power, and isn't that because cinema is indeed powerful?

"Idhu thaan da cinema!"

Name: Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory
Review:
I've watched the Tim Burton one on TV as a kid more times than I can count. This one too followed familiar beats to that one and even seemed less weird until the factory door opened and Willy Wonka stepped out. Gene Wilder acting like an unhinged psychopath is what this movie is all about. The man's just being all kinds of crazy here, with the dry humor, the one-liners, the weird body language, and even seeming terrifying at times. I mean, for a kids movie, stuff like the tunnel sequence was pretty terrifying, with Wilder being the scariest thing about it. In the Tim Burton version, there are attempts to make Wonka sympathetic, but here he's pretty much a psychopath, who could indeed actually murder these kids, until he becomes nice and offers Charlie the factory. While the Burton version ties everything up, shows the surviving punished children, and shows Charlie and the family after he gets the factory, here they're just flying in the elevator. Did this dude crash the thing and kill grandpa and Charlie? Are the rest of the kids even alive? I mean, this was basically Saw for kids in the 70s.

Now this version of Wonka is getting a backstory prequel starring Timothee Chalamet. Judging by the trailer, he's charming, but he doesn't have the "could kill ya at any second" vibe that Gene Wilder did.

Name: Haseen Dillruba
Review:
There's a part in this movie where Vikrant Massey's husband tries to kill Taapsee Pannu's wife multiple times and gets turned on by seeing her in pain and almost dying. But the twist here is that, joke's on him, she's into that shit. So, she's turned on by the fact that he's turned on by her almost dying. Him trying to kill her by igniting a gas stove "reignites" their love (fuck me).

What did they mean by this movie?

Name: Kaathal - The Core
Review:
Kaathal is an important film. It sets up important discussions, and I hope it leads to more mainstream stars and production companies telling such stories the way Mammootty and MammoottyKampany have done here. Kaathal addresses its socially relevant topics while its narrative moves through its characters and their internal conflicts.

Mammootty's Matthew Devassy is a man going through internal turmoil through most of the movie. He's mostly quiet; his whole body language says a lot about what he's going through, and he even struggles to make eye contact with people. Matthew is struggling with his own identity and the man he should be perceived as, and placing him in an election scenario amplifies the public eye that's on the man. Jyothika's Omana Philip is also going through the results of making a hard decision that was the right thing to do for her. Both Mathew's and Omana's perspectives are handled empathetically by the film. The other star of the film is Thankan, played by Sudhi Kozhikode, in a performance that becomes the heart of the film at several points, especially in a pre-interval scene where some glances from Thankan and how Mathew reacts to him tell a way bigger story than what flashbacks could. The rest of the supporting cast, consisting of a lot of new faces, also delivered good performances.

Director Jeo Baby and writers Adarsh Sukumaran and Paulson Skaria discuss social themes while sticking to the characters. Even the main conflict is revealed in an interesting way, slowly through several character interactions. The court scenes are the only places where the film gets verbal, and even there, the lawyers talk more than the main characters (which is pretty realistic too). Otherwise, the drama is told through the performances. Even in a scene where I expected Matthew to deliver an emotional monologue to the screen, the film just avoids it. This restraint and subtlety shown by the film to stick to its characters stays throughout. Even Matthews Pulickan's suitably emotional score is used sparingly. This is a film that does rely on its performances and visual storytelling. There's a shot where Thankan sticks a poster on a wall that says a lot about what he's been going through without actually showing it.

Kaathal is a great step towards mainstream cinema telling important stories. It's not a flawless film, but it is an important film. I wish this was the kind of movie that'd set up a trend.

Update : Despite the film having its heart at the right place, the several "compromises" made to keep Mathew and Thankan at a distance, and the lack of acknowledging of what they put Thankan through at the end, seemed weird the more I thought about it, and the explanations given by the writers and the director on the same wasn't that convincing. So, yk.. There's that..

Name: Bhagavanth Kesari
Review:
So, there's a short and cringey romance track in the movie, but there's no duet song or an "item" song. Plus, there's a surprising amount of progressive stuff (it's flawed, and there's cringe, but yk). Anyway. Just like how I'd never understand how Rajinikanth did Kaala, I'd never understand how Balakrishna did this.

What I saw in the end fight scene of this movie is something I've always wanted to see big Indian male stars doing, but I never expected Balakrishna to be one of the dudes who'd do it. It's still the template we've seen in so many movies, with over-the-top Balayyaness, and yet this is so different because it actually tries to subvert the tropes of these hero worship masala movies and be kinda progressive, while also being yet another hero worship masala movie.

In a Telugu movie context and a Balakrishna context, this is a pretty big leap.

I started watching this movie expecting it to be a guilty pleasure cringe watch, but I ended up liking it. Judge me, Ai don't keyar.

Name: Scott Pilgrim Takes Off
Review: This just got crazier and crazier, and I just loved every minute of it.

Name: Christopher
Review:
As it's the Mammootty Renaissance right now, I felt like watching the shitty Mammootty movie that I missed for some reason. And, oh boy, is it shitty. Aarattu, the previous creative collaborative clusterfuck from B. Unnikrishan and Udayakrishna, was at least bad in a fun way. It was shitty, but I could laugh at it. But Christopher is just an insensitive, terrible, and gratuitous trauma-filled bad movie. The only thing I found funny is how Mammootty looks like he's bored and sleepwalking through most of it, even looking like he'd rather be in the sets of a better movie. Even a good Mammootty performance couldn't save this horrible movie, though, so I'm almost glad about that. It's about a vigilante cop who shoots down rapists. But the movie is more focused on showing what the rapists did to their victims than on the act of vigilantism, and what we get is a movie that is a montage of women getting violently attacked or killed, with Mammootty shooting the attackers in between. I won't even say that they "meant well" with this movie; how is this meaning well? If they were allowed to make this movie in a country where censorship laws weren't this strict, I have no idea the extent of violence that their "imagination" would cook up. Almost all the female characters in the movie are abused, raped, killed, or both. That's not how you make a progressive film.

Even Udayakrishna's Monster, the attempted queer representation thriller that turns out to be queerphobic, was bad in a laughable way. But I couldn't laugh at Christopher. It's just horrible in the worst possible ways.

As a fan of Mammootty, I just wish, with the new "renaissance" thing going and all, that even if he does bad movies, he doesn't do something that's problematic on so many levels, like Christopher.

Name: Chithha
Review:
I'm conflicted about Chiththa. Firstly, it's super incoherent. It starts off by establishing the uncle-nephew relationship; there's an insignificant romance track and a song (of course), then the movie briefly becomes about a man being falsely accused of abusing a child. So at that point, I expected the film to go along the route of something like Thomas Vinterberg's The Hunt. But it doesn't; this plot line is quickly resolved, and then it becomes about a missing child who's been kidnapped by a dangerous predator. Then, towards the end, it tries to talk about vigilante justice—how revenge becomes more of a priority for a man when someone close to him is abused than actually caring for the survivor and helping them recover.

The thing is, all these pieces felt incoherently placed together. Nimisha Sajayan gets two great scenes towards the end, where her character raises points that are almost never pointed out in Indian films where a protagonist sets out for revenge (mostly we just make it heroic). But the movie still doesn't go all in on it. While the acknowledgement of how men make it about themselves rather than the survivor is present, the movie just does the vigilante thing anyway. Well, at least it's in a gray area and not seem to look heroic. Towards the end, when there was a revelation that the man who Easwaran wants to kill might not be the abuser, I thought this would connect to the fact that Easwaran himself was falsely accused at the beginning. But it didn't.

Though Nimisha's monologues address the errors of the main character and men in general, the movie itself doesn't give its female characters much to do otherwise. Maybe the screen time given to the false accusation plot and some of the extended scenes with the predator could've been given to the women? At least, Sakthi? Because after the initial song or so, she's pretty much insignificant till the end.

This is a dark and disturbing movie, for sure, and it was a tough watch. But just like the disclaimer at the end, it is reality, unfortunately. But still, it felt incoherent, but there were some great scenes and great points it raised that I loved too. But also, I'm still clueless about whether it handled its themes properly.

Great music and great performances from Siddharth and Nimisha Sajayan too, btw.

I'm confused about what to put, star rating wise.

Name: May December
Review:
The subject of the movie is pretty uncomfortable and complex, and Todd Haynes was pretty aware of that. A lot of the complexities are left open to interpretation brilliantly, with the writing, filmmaking, and performances providing layers upon layers of real but hard-to-digest emotions. The outsider perspective of Natalie Portman's actress, who sees these people as characters and subjects rather than as real humans, Julianne Moore's Gracy, who felt like a mystery throughout, and Charles Melton's Joe, who was like a boy trapped in a man's body, All of them are placed in the aftermath of a very messed-up situation. The movie itself leaves many things open to interpretation, but despite the campyness and ambiguity, it still addresses the trauma involved and does not present the uncomfortable scenario as an ideal one. 

All the scenes involving Natalie Portman and Julianne Moore in front of mirrors were cinema. The acting in this movie was phenomenal throughout. Charles Melton also broke my heart towards the end. Such a breakout performance.

Name: Garudan
Review: If we take out the goofy SG performance, the goofy kerala police dialogues at the end, and lines that sound like SG himself wrote it, retain Biju Menon's performance, and swap some other bad performances, there's a solid thriller in Garudan. I mean, I got a sense of a good thriller in there, and there were good ideas and nice twists and though some of it was predictable, it was solid. But, the Suresh Gopi character, his lines and his performance were so bad, and maybe at the hands of even post-Odiyan Mohanlal, this'd have been a better movie. Because more than the flaws in writing and the filmmaking, the lead character and the performance is the biggest dud. Also, "police mass daa", meh.

Name: Family
Review: The way this movie builds up the creepiness, manipulation and gaslighting is!!!!!!!!

Name: Perfect Days
Review: Comfort in the routine. I felt that. It's about finding joy in the little things, it's about escaping to the routine so that life is more "predictable". And it's about so much more. This might be the movie that stays with me for a long time after the IFFK.

Name: Anatomy of a Fall
Review: I wish there was an Oscar for the best dog.

Name: Monster
Review: Blissfully brilliant. The pacing, the way each perspective adds up to the larger story, is all amazing.

Name: The Teachers' Lounge
Review: I liked the lead actress' performance. Reminded me of Emma Stone.

Name: About Dry Grasses
Review: Might be the most beautiful movie where the main character is an absolute asshole.

Name: Now and Forever
Review: Might be the closest thing to Black Mirror that I've seen in Indian cinema. Though the way the Sci-fi concepts are blended into the relationship drama is not perfect, and the Sci-fi could've been more focused, when it works, it works. Great production design, visual effects, music and performances too.

Name: Kennedy
Review:
"I'm just Ken-nedy"

It's the same old, but there's enough of the new and the cool for me to enjoy.

Name: How to Have Sex
Review: It starts off like one of those early 2000s teen sex party movies, and then becomes something else entirely. The main lead's performance and the way her mental state is visualised while everyone else is partying, was brilliant.

Name: Green Border
Review: Thrilling and powerful.

Name: Afire
Review: It's one of those well-written and well-acted movies that makes me feel like an asshole for finding the main character relatable. The character relationships and arcs were so good, and so was the way the literal fire was used.

Name: Paradise Is Burning
Review: Great performances, vibrant visuals, lovable characters, warmth and wholesome vibes.

Name: Cobweb
Review: I've always loved movies about movies and I'm partially biased towards them. This one works mostly as a comedy, the drama is there too, but the comedy overshadows it. The humour is on point, and though some of the "movie within the movie" scenes were longer than they needed to be, on the whole it worked for me. The ending sequence involving a long shot was also all sorts of brilliant and chaotic. The camerawork at times reminded me of mockumentary sitcoms like The Office too.

Name: The Zone of Interest
Review: Never thought the sight of kids playing could look so disturbing.

Name: Wonka
Review:
Both Chalamet and this film were a *sweet* surprise (cringe intended). Paul King's Wonka has the same energy as that of his Paddington movies. The dark humor and Wonka acting like an unhinged psychopath part of the original Willy Wonka movie are not present here. Instead, Chalamet's Wonka has a charming, innocent, funny, optimistic, and joyful presence. So basically, the child-like Wonka shut off from the world after the events of this movie and became the kids version of the Jigsaw killer from Saw. This Wonka is more Ted Lasso than Jigsaw. And I thought that was a great choice overall. Chalamet is not imitating Gene Wilder's iconic performance, and the character itself is different enough to have that distinction. There are moments where he reminds me of Wilder, mostly the showmanship and sense of humor at times. And he's definitely not Johnny Depp's Michael Jackson Wonka either.

The movie is sweet, fun, and wholesome, with a great soundtrack and dance sequences. The police chief's fat jokes are appropriate for classic Dahl books, I guess, but also so dated and unfunny. Apart from that, this was indeed pure imagination. Also, this might be peak Hugh Grant right here, I wish he had more screen time. Also, multiple Peep Show cast members being a part of the cast was cool.

Name: Leave the World Behind
Review: Being stuck watching episodes of Friends is definitely my worst doomsday scenario.

Name: In the Heights
Review:
I watched this because of my massive Melissa Barrera crush and because I loved Miranda's Hamilton (I watched the recorded movie version, of course). Now, when I say I loved Hamilton, I didn't particularly care about the story, the characters, or American history. I just enjoyed the performances, the humor, the dance numbers, the music, and the rap. But In the Heights is different in that regard, because I cared about the characters, I cared about their individual stories, and I cared about its larger themes. There are so many cool songs and sequences, and I was smiling through most of this movie, with the Abuela song being a tearjerker. And of course, amazing performances from the entire cast, great cinematography, production design, and visual effects.

Emotional monologues are cool, but emotional monologues in the form of rap are infinitely cooler.

Name: Ugramm
Review: Prasanth Neel realised that the Ugramm Veeram song is the coolest part in his first movie, and then devoted his entire career to making feature length Ugramm Veeram music videos.

Name: Neru
Review:
Neru has a lot of great ideas, executed not so effectively. Firstly, seeing Mohanlal in a character-focused performance rather than one purely set around his stardom was refreshing. There are moments where I saw a Mohanlal that I've not seen in quite a while on screen. Also, the film itself gives Anaswara Rajan's survivor character enough prominence that it doesn't entirely turn out to be a savior/heroism romp for Mohanlal's lawyer. The movie does have almost the same setup as the Hindi movie Pink, and just like Pink, the lawyer is not a "star" and is a helping hand for the one seeking justice (the remakes of Pink, especially the Telugu version, made the lawyer the star and the front and center, which changed everything).

The court procedures are depicted realistically, but sometimes they do feel overstretched. After watching the courtroom scenes in Anatomy of a Fall last week, I couldn't help but subconsciously compare the two and feel how Neru was inferior. The music works beautifully in some scenes and is misfit in some other scenes, bringing a soap opera appeal at times. I did like the Drishyam callback and how this essentially becomes reverse Drishyam after a point, though.

I loved Anaswara Rajan's performance in this movie too, and just like Jeethu Joseph's Drishyam 2, Neru has a problem with the performances of a lot of supporting characters feeling weird. The co-writer of the movie herself plays a character whose sole purpose is to explain the plot and provide exposition and data ex-machina. Which is pretty meta when I think about it. While it covers a sensitive topic involving sexual assault, I felt it could've been more sensitive about it.

The biggest takeaway was the joy of seeing a pretty good Mohanlal performance. A10 is Kenough.

Name: Priscilla
Review:
I've read opinions that the Baz Luhrmann Elvis movie and this movie releasing so close to each other is some kind of "Elvis Fatigue." But I believe the opposite: that both of these movies complement each other. Because both of them, though they're set around the same person, use different perspectives and have gaps that are filled by the other film. The Luhrmann film was about Elvis being exploited and manipulated by his manager, Colonel Tom Parker, for the most part, and Elvis trying to maintain some kind of artistic integrity despite having the Colonel and others breathing down his neck, and he himself spirals into addiction. We're made to feel bad for him, but we don't really see Elvis himself as a manipulator and an abuser, which we see in Priscilla. And all the gaps about Elvis that we don't see in Priscilla, since Priscilla presents vignettes of certain moments from their pretty messed-up relationship rather than a proper biography, we see in Elvis. So both movies have a symbiotic relationship that way.

The scene where Priscilla finally leaves a drug-addicted, negligent Elvis is presented as a polar opposite in both films. In Luhrmann's Elvis, the scene is heavy on emotion: Priscilla announces why exactly she's leaving, Elvis has a breakdown, they then have a tender moment together, they share a hug, and he still wants her to stay, but she then leaves. Even though it's acknowledged that Elvis was not a good husband to her, we're made to feel bad for him. But in Priscilla, the interaction is very straightforward, the scene is very short, there's no emotional breakdown from Elvis, and Priscilla just has a beautiful line where she says, "If I stay, I'd never leave.".

It did take some time for me to adjust to Jacob Elordi's Elvis, as Austin Butler still occupied my mind. But moving forward, he really surprised me. Especially in scenes where we see the darker and more abusive side of Elvis, he was appropriately scary, almost making Priscilla a horror movie. Cailee Spaeny's performance as the title character felt a little uneven, though the movie itself has this vignette kind of narrative, so the writing itself presents the character in a certain way. The leads have no romantic chemistry together, and seeing where the movie goes, I guess it was intentional. They do play off each other well, especially in scenes that dive into the toxicity of the relationship. Elordi is taller than both Austin Butler and the actual Elvis, and Spaeny's a lot smaller than him physically. There are scenes where this physicality comes into play in depicting the abuse, so I guess it was intentional too. Spaeny and Elordi's scenes together look pretty, but they're shot in a way that comes off weird.

The movie looks really pretty, and Sofia Coppola's aesthetics are on point as always. The makeup, hair, and costume departments deserve praise too. Also, this opinion is based on what I got from seeing these people as characters in movies, and I am not that informed about the actual Elvis and Priscilla. So no disrespect is intended, thenks.

Name: Salaar: Part 1 - Ceasefire
Review:
Prashanth Neel said in an interview that he actually attempted to flesh out the drama and build the world in Salaar rather than making it a series of buildups like KGF. And he's right; in this repackaged, blown-up version of his own Ugramm, instead of the movie being a compilation of hero worship montages, Neel does try to set up character relationships, an interesting world, and a power struggle. The main character is still larger than life; the hero worship dialogues, montages, and buildups are still present, but this movie is not *just* the buildups. Neel does succeed in setting up the scale of the world; it looks huge, even if stuff like the shots of foreign armies walking in front of the green screen are goofy af (but just like KGF, shots go so fast that we don't get the time to think about it).

The romance arc from Ugramm is completely removed in Salaar; I don't know if they'd develop it further in the sequel, but at present, Shruthi Hassan's character and Prabhas' Deva barely even interact to say they have any chemistry or not. At least both Ugramm's Agastya and Salaar's Deva are not dickheads like Rocky Bhai; they're more like care bhais, protectors, and saviors. The relationship between Deva and his mother was better in Ugramm; here, it's so over the top and even unintentionally funny at times, but when everything is over the top, the more ordinary-seeming mom in Ugramm would not fit in, I guess.

During the first half, some kid characters make fun of Deva by calling him "cut-out," and that's exactly what he is during the initial stretch. The man doesn't show any emotion and is a big, monotonous muscular cutout. But of course it eventually leads to a scene with him kicking ass, and man, Phabhas seems like an absolute beast in the action scenes here. Of course he's a large man, but the choreography itself is used to make him seem like a "dinosaur", as the teaser trailer implied. He carries himself like a man capable of pulling someone's head off with his bare hands too.

After the first half, the movie deviates from the Ugramm baseline and starts establishing the world of Khansaar and the drama. The film spends a considerable amount of time here before we see Deva again. But I do wish this was an area where the film should have spent more time instead of filling the first half with stuff like the plastic knife scene. It's in the second half that the movie really starts to breathe, but I wish that was the case from the beginning itself. Even Deva himself starts feeling more like a character than a cut-out in this flashback, with Prabhas getting a chance to do acting rather than cut-outing. The second time Deva unleashes the beast is my favorite scene in the movie. The bromance between Deva and Prithviraj's Varada was yet another aspect they could've spent more time on. Their interactions had a cool vibe to them (though an "I'm sorry" during a tender moment between them made almost everyone in the theater laugh). The conflicts being set up for the sequel were also very interesting.

I liked Salaar more than I liked KGF. It was fun, both ironically and unironically, even the cringe was fun. The Ugramm part of the first half could've been trimmed further to flesh out the Khansaar portion, and though Deva transitioning from cut-out to character is awesome when it happens, he could've been less of a cut-out like Agastya from Ugramm. Though there's no hint of a romance arc with Shruti Hassan in this movie, I wish Neel would keep it that way; he probably won't. At least Salaar Part 1 doesn't have a shitty, problematic romance arc like KGF Part 1, and Deva is not an asshole like Rocky. Almost every flaw and misfire in this ceasefire are things they can rectify in a sequel. Ravi Barsur's music gave me mixed feelings, there were some cool tracks, but a lot of duds too. KGF definitely has a better soundtrack. 

John Vijay's performance was so bad, though, but I know he's a good actor, so what happened there?

Also, I watched the Malayalam dubbed version of the movie, and it just made me wish I could watch the original Telugu version. There are so many awkward translations and instances of goofy dubbing. (Who tf says "kazhiyukayilla" and all? Even if they're from a fictional crime city?)

Name: Thanksgiving
Review:
Eli Roth's Thanksgiving is an expansion of his own fake trailer that was part of Grindhouse. So I kind of expected this feature length version to be a grindhouse B-movie kind of experience like Death Proof and Planet terror. But it isn't, at least entirely. It's more similar to 90s slashers like Scream than older and "dirtier" ones like the one parodied in Grindhouse. Like Scream, Thanksgiving is a whodunit plus slasher hybrid. Thanksgiving's plot moves in a pretty straight tone, with the over-the-top gore being the area where the movie is at its grindhousiest. The gore is executed brilliantly, with practical prosthetics that look real enough to seem gruesome and goofy enough to seem B-movie-like. Though the movie is a conventional slasher for the most part with conventional slasher characters, stereotypical teen characters and a traditional final girl, this odd mix of grindhouse sensibilities do work. Though it's not as much of a parody as the fake trailer it is based on, Thanksgiving still manages to incorporate most of the scenes from it, and even the line "There'll be no leftovers".

This was a fun slasher though, I had missed fun slashers that just don't give a shit.

Also, that initial Black Friday scene was absolutely brilliant. The way it builds up, the dread in the eventual chaos, and how it becomes the perfect setup for what follows.

Name: The Holdovers
Review: The Holdovers is the best found family movie that I've seen in quite a while. It's philosophical, political, funny, wholesome and most of all it's so warm and empathetic. The writing, the dialogues and and Payne's filmmaking were so on point and I loved everything about this movie. It's got classic film sensibilities, though it's also quite modern. All the performances are amazing and I hope Paul Giamatti gets all the acting awards for this. The music was also beautiful throughout the movie, so was the colors and visuals. Though the movie is set in winter, watching it feels like a warm hug.

Name: Silent Night
Review:
Despite the negative reviews, what sold me on this movie is John Woo and the whole "dialogue-less non-stop action" promise. But most of the movie is just dialogue-less buildup where the lack of dialogue becomes a liability than an advantage. This year there was another movie named No one will save you, which also didn't have any dialogue, but there the lack of dialogue worked beautifully and is even justified.

Even when John Woo made a Mission Impossible film, it was a John Woo film than a Mission Impossible film. But here, it's John Woo trying to do a John Wick during the action scenes. It's less John Woo and more post-John Wick gritty action flick. There are instances of John Woo-ness but they're far less than I expected. The stairway shootout scene was awesome, though oner action scenes are a cliché at this point, I can't get enough of them.

Silent Night would've benefited with more of John Woo's signature style and more action. It takes too much time to get into the action and with the lack of dialogue, it's pretty hard to care about the characters and the buildup. Though it does address things like how the dad is negligent towards his grieving wife, and how after months of training with dummies, the dad struggles greatly when he has to fight an actual person who is trying to kill him. Though at the end, this is indeed a style over substance film, and not something that explores the emotions associated with revenge the way a movie like Blue Ruin does (recommended btw). 

The CGI was very off in this movie too. But this is the dude who has pulled off amazing action scenes without even using CGI. Confusing. 

I need another Face/Off from John Woo if he does American movies again. Time to rewatch Face/Off.

Name: Dream Scenario
Review:
Firstly, the premise of this movie itself is brilliant. A random dude becoming an overnight celebrity just because he pops up in everyone's dreams without any explanation, is like such an ingenious entry point for a movie. The movie then uses it to satirise modern day social media trends, viral sensations and mass hysteria. It brings lots of interesting ideas further in and lots of brilliant, funny and even sad and unsettling sequences. The dream scenes were all brilliantly done. The film's editing is also brilliant in how the cuts become erratic and weird based on the scene. Dream Scenario has a very distinct visual style and feel to it, Kristoffer Borgli shows a lot of promise and his style is just the kind of thing that I love.

Dream Scenario is philosophical and it also works as a satire. And of course, Nic Cage is absolutely brilliant here, with adequate amounts of subtlety, amazing comedic timing and the occasional Cage Rage. It's an engaging and interesting film and the only complaint of mine was that it wasn't long enough. I felt this concept could've been fleshed out and developed even more.

Name: Kho Gaye Hum Kahan
Review:
The initial half of this movie with the friends vibing and their individual arcs was nice. The way the dependence on social media, the constant comparisons with people who seem better than us over there and the need for external validation was shown was also cool. Each character is flawed in their own way, and the main three characters' arcs were going good. The drama between the three friends was also pretty nice. 

The performances of the main leads were good, Ananya, Sidhant and Adarsh were great in depicting their characters' individual arcs and the three of them had great chemistry together. But the smaller characters were really one note, though as always Kalki was love. Also, I didn't really dig the ending that much. It doesn't really address everything properly, and opts for a preachy ending that felt abrupt and rushed. 

The soundtrack was cool though.

Name: Curry & Cyanide: The Jolly Joseph Case
Review: Hollow. So many gaps are there in the case which are not addressed at all.

Name: Face/Off
Review:
Face/Off is fucking epic okay? Every rewatch of it is fun. The signature Woo action and style is firing on all cylinders. Every single cheesy writing choice and filmmaking choice adds so much flavor here. It's the kind of old school formulaic cinema that's got some endearing quality to it. And man, the dramatic (extremely dramatic) scenes and the action are just awesome. I don't care that the stunt doubles' faces are visible during the big action setpieces. Those dude actually did all those stuff for real. They're heroes.

Nic Cage is legendary in Face/Off, Travolta is also unhinged ("Isn't this religious?"), and on the whole the movie gives us a very effective villain in Castor Troy. All the scenes where the two of them, ahem, face off, have such an over-dramatic flair to it that so unique and awesome. Hero-Villain combos that play off of each other like this rarely happen. 

I don't care about the plot holes and how dumb it is, the style is epic, the action is epic, Nic Cage is epic, the music is epic. So Face/Off is epic.

When I die, I want Nic Cage to yell "DIEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE".

Name: Falimy
Review:
3 for the movie, and one more star for Jagadish. What a legend! Jagadish has such an expressive face, and he can convey so much using microexpressions and subtle body language, which is what makes performances like Appukuttan in In Harihar Nagar special. From drama to comedy, he's just amazing, and he's paired with Manju Pillai, who's at the top of her game too. The entire cast is great, and this is one of the few movies where Basil Joseph's limitations as an actor are visible because of who he's sharing the screen with. Though Basil too gets his moments, like in the third act, where there's a dark humor bit surrounding grief, we see Basil do the same thing in two entirely different contexts. Falimy is a Little Miss Sunshine-ish dysfunctional family road movie. Though it doesn't get as deep as that movie, it does have its moments, both funny and wholesome.

Also, the Trivandrum slang was noice! 

Also, Muhsin Parari's lyrics game is!!!!!

Name: 12th Fail
Review:
Vikrant Massey can play such rootable and lovable characters. Even in a movie as fucked up as Haseen Dilruba, where he was acting like an absolute psychopath, I felt sorry for him at multiple instances. 12th Fail with the unrealistically honest and earnest Manoj Sharma is no different (I have no idea about the real person btw). As a movie this was such a joy to watch with a by the books and effective "inspirational movie" template. Manoj's journey is emotional and has heart. Loved the performances of the entire cast, the music and the way Vidhu Vinod Chopra wrote and staged all the dramatic moments, especially the climax.

I don't know if the real Manoj Sharma is as earnest and honest as the one we see on screen, is it possible in this world to be that much of a good person?

Name: Saltburn
Review: Barry Keoghen was amazing in it and provided so much texture to a character that wasn't written with that much depth. Jacob Elordi, Rosamund Pike and the rest of the cast was great too. Writing wise, Saltburn is pretty surface level, but I loved the style and aesthetics of it. The weird and gross scenes were effectively weird and gross, even more so because of Keoghen selling the hell out of them, but they were also weird just for the sake of being weird. "Eat the rich" movies are a regular thing now and this is a different kind of take on that, but I wish the writing was better. The mood, atmosphere and aesthetics were on point though.

Name: The Batman
Review:
The more I watch The Batman, the more I appreciate everything about it. Yes, there are aspects of it that are dumb, but even the Nolan movies had those, so give it a break. The entire movie looks so gorgeous! I mean, even stuff like Batman beating up dudes through gun muzzle flashes looks so awesome. Then there's the constant rain, and how both visually and sound design-wise, the rain takes on a personality of its own. Pattinson plays probably the most vulnerable and sensitive version of Batman in live action; in this film, he realizes that just being a dude who beats up criminals won't bring about the change he wishes to see in the city. Also, the way his grief and social anxiety are shown is also on point. I think this is also the live-action Batman movie where he spends the most amount of time in costume as Batman than as Bruce Wayne, and we can clearly see how he's different as both, how he's more reserved and quiet as Bruce, and even how his posture is different as he becomes Batman. Zoe Kravitz's Selina Kyle needs her own spin-off; Colin Farrel is already getting one, and I'm glad that I'm getting more of this particular version of Gotham because this is such a unique and yet familiar take on the place. The score, Nirvana's Something in the way being used as the base for the main theme, Ave Maria being used for The Riddler's theme, the detective vibes, the way the mystery reveals itself—it's all stuff I love. The Riddler is the villain here, so the pun-filled riddles and deductions are sort of justified.

More Detective Batman, more Noir Gotham, please!

Protect Matt Reeves' Batman at all costs!

Name: Parking
Review: The way the initial conflict built up gave me flashbacks of a screaming match between my own father and our neighbor that happened because of eerily similar circumstances. The way the conflict builds up, though it may seem simple, was perfect. Then it escalates and escalates into over-the-top circumstances. MS Bhaskar was brilliant in this, and even when his character becomes psychotic by the end, he sells it perfectly. The Harish Kalyan character Easwer, on the other hand, is one the movie tries to establish as the "better" person. He also does his fair share of shitty things, but at the end of the day, the MS Bhaskar character is the "villain." Also, Easwer even gets a Tamil movie hero-ish fight scene and stuff. Anyway, all this would've been ignorable if the movie had an ending that justified the madness, but it doesn't. The ending kind of gives too easy of a pass for all the crazy stuff these two did to each other, and it's almost funny to see things this extreme being brushed over as just an "ego" issue. The women around both of these men had to deal with all their psychotic behavior, and they're just expected to be so forgiving, like it's just some normal neighborly quarrel, when things took a turn for much worse in the movie by then. For the tone it was going for, the ending should've been darker, or at least neutral, than the one we got here. Props to the effective tension building at multiple moments, though.

Name: The Great Dictator
Review:
Some of the comedic bits didn't really land for me, and felt like Chaplin just inserting them in there to make it a "Charles Chaplin Picture" while the actual intend is much more political. It is incoherent as a movie and doesn't work in a way something like Modern Times does as individual sketches stitched together.

The satire does work at times, and the speech towards the end where he breaks the 4th wall was also all sorts of brilliant. Neither Chaplin or the people who laughed at this movie at that time knew the extend of Hitler's cruelty, and that's the grim part about this film's ending.

Name: Joe
Review:
When Nic Cage listed this movie as one of his favorite Nic Cage movies in a Colbert interview, I just knew I had to watch this. Joe is a slow burner, but not as slow and melancholic as something like Cage's own Pig. But the setting is unique, and though the plot beats are familiar, the setting, the characters and the atmosphere make Joe pretty unique. Nic Cage is of course amazing, he adds so much to the character of Joe. Joe has a former life that he can never go back to, he has violent tendencies that he can't quite control, but also there's empathy in him and an inherent sadness, and Nic Cage communicates all of that brilliantly. The chemistry between Tye Sheridan and Cage was great and I wish we got to see more of them just hanging out, like the scene when they look for the dog.

I agree with Nic Cage that this is also one of my favorite Nic Cage movies too.

Name: Hi Nanna
Review: It reminded me of those bollywood romantic dramas from the early 2000s with pretty people, pretty locations, pretty costumes, filled with melodrama and emotionally emotional music that we don't really see that much anymore. The last one I remember from Hindi is Yash Chopra's Jab Tak Hai Jaan, and the last one from Telugu I remember is Mrunal Thakur's own Sita Ramam. I liked the leads' performances, but I didn't feel any kind of chemistry between them. There are a few twists which are revealed nicely though they're nothing novel. The entire thing is pretty clichéd and some of the drama do feel flat. But as a lover of everything cheesy, and since I have a crush on Mrunal Thakur, this was a pretty good watch for me.

Name: Aattam
Review: Anand Ekarshi's Aattam is one of those films where the writing, filmmaking, performances, and every creative decision come together in harmony to serve a narrative, with everything complementing each other. In a dialogue-heavy drama like Aattam, which is mostly set in a single location, there's no shortcut for maintaining audience engagement. This is where the film excels. Except for a few familiar faces, the majority of the cast were people I was seeing on screen for the first time, and yet the film establishes those characters and their dynamics quickly, and each of them is unique, and the performances are unique. This is also one of those films where every buildup serves a purpose. Anjali, played by Zarin Shihab, is the heart of the film, and the film starts and ends with her. Even the middle stretch where she's absent is there in the film so that when she reappears, all that was established so far is unraveled in quick succession. Beautiful cinema and character work are at play as a situation where Anjali should be the one receiving empathy transforms into a situation where a group of men are exhibiting various shades of misogyny and selfishness. I felt the movie itself treated Anjali with such empathy, though. The conversations and arguments have such a rhythm to them, and I don't know if that's why there's no background score when people are talking in the film. The score is only used in places without dialogue, and with the conversations constantly shifting tones and varying in emotions, it was the right choice to let the performances and the dialogue do the heavy lifting. Zarin Shihab, Vinay Forrt, Kalabhavan Shajohn, and the rest of the cast were great, and Aattam, with its unique setting and great sound design, is fit for the big screen experience, and it's also an important film that addresses toxic masculinity brilliantly.

Name: Gaganachari
Review:
I had fun watching this movie, especially with an audience for its preview. I dig the mockumentary format since I'm a fan of The Office, What We Do in the Shadows, and a lot of other comedies of the format. Gaganachari is a post-apocalyptic sci-fi mockumentary comedy, that goes back and forth between being a mockumentary and a "movie". The writing, the VFX and the production design do succeed in setting up a weird dystopian world with a lot of funny twists of present day scenarios and some satirical elements. The satire and world-building aren't super deep, I felt the film was more focused on the laughs. There are lots of pop culture references and Malayalam movie references. When we read the synopsis and watch the trailer and the film's distinctive look, we expect a dystopian, funny version of E. T., but this is more Kilukkam than E. T. Despite a lower budget, the CGI and production design are on point and serve the setting well. The humor and the characters themselves are very rooted in Malayalam cinema, while the setting couldn't be any different from ones seen in Malayalam cinema. The visual style and visual humor were great too. The performances were fun, including the two voice-only performances that were spitting punchlines constantly. The music was also cool. 

Funnn!!

Name: Scrapper
Review: It's like a wholesome and funny companion piece to Aftersun. 🥹❤️

Name: Tiger 3
Review: Movie makes a strong case that Katrina Kaif should be the actual lead of these movies.

Name: Abraham Ozler
Review:
It's unfair to compare Abraham Ozler with Midhun Manuel Thomas' previous thriller, Anchaam Paathira. Though this is also a murder investigation procedural, it lacks the mood and atmosphere that Anchaam Paathira set, for which cinematographer Shyju Khalid was a big reason. Ozler, on the other hand, lacks that atmosphere and is more of a straightforward investigation procedural during the initial half. The police officer with a tragic half is a tired trope, but I liked Jayaram in this. He was convincing as the title character, and other than an awkward pre-interval fight scene where the film didn't know whether it should be a classy thriller or a "mass" movie, he was good. It certainly didn't make me cringe and laugh like Suresh Gopi in Garudan did; now that was a terrible performance that killed the movie. Jayaram's performance, on the other hand, even makes some of the dumb and awkward dialogues seem better than they are.

The writing is all over the place. The writer of the movie is a doctor, and the doctoring is all over the screenplay. I haven't seen medical dramas like House and Grey's Anatomy that much, but I doubt even they have the amount of medical jargon that Ozler has.
