I guess the intention was medical accuracy and authenticity; I didn't know what most of the stuff meant, so idk. But even if the film were medically accurate, the investigation thriller part wasn't all that well written. The dialogue felt awkward constantly; even some of the acting by smaller artists did. The flashback was longer than it needed to be, and after being a police procedural for a period of time, it just becomes another movie entirely.

Abraham Ozler ends by setting up a sequel. Though I liked Jayaram's performance, there isn't enough distinctiveness about Ozler that sets him apart from the zillion traumatized cop characters I've seen. Ozler, the movie, was unsure if it wanted to be a character piece, a procedural, or be about an entirely different character. And that confusion shows. Even Ozler's insomnia and hallucinations which are established early on, has no relevance once the case starts. 

As an Ikka fan, I'd be lying if I said the Mammootty intro didn't give me goosebumps. But that was kind of the highest point of the film too. The buildup to him and his presence was cinema. He wasn't really needed for this character, but it's awesome that he's there.

Also, Midhun Mukundan's score was nice, but not on par with Sushin Shyam's work in Anchaam Paathira or his own work in Rorschach in delivering that creepiness.

Movie has logical flaws, conveniences, bad lines and hilarious dumbness, but I can't hate it completely.

Name: Captain Miller
Review:
Something I really disliked about RRR as an anti-colonial film, along with how it panders to the right-wing hindutva narrative, was how it completely disregards the caste angle, though the storyline revolves around a tribal community. Even Bheem's subservient body language towards Ramaraju is to be seen as something brotherly and innocent. This is fixed in Captain Miller. Captain Miller revolves around a community that is under threat from two different forces. There's the British colonizers, who of course want to occupy their land and plunder their wealth, and their own local rulers, who won't let them enter their own temple that their ancestors built, and who also want to take over their land. There's even a line of dialogue that compares both the oppression due to caste and the oppression due to race that they have to endure together. Having two different kinds of oppressors as the villains itself is pretty brilliant, though the film doesn't develop or explore it that deeply. There's a Hindu angle towards the end of Capitain Miller too, and though I thought it was unnecessary, the context here is a lot better than the one in RRR.

 

Dhanush is amazing as the title character. The transformations he goes through are pretty familiar for this kind of story, but I wish they were better developed. The film rushes through a lot of changes that happen to Miller, even with how he transforms into a bandit, but spends too much time on some others. Like, there's a flashback for something that was already established through dialogue, possibly because they needed somewhere to put the one song and dance sequence in. But even with the rushed and underdeveloped characterization, it's Dhanush who succeeds in selling Miller as the killer he is. The intensity, rage and body language were perfect throughout. GV Prakash Kumar's score is the other heavy lifter, giving the film that epic atmosphere that it definitely needed. Some of the tracks are similar to ones I've heard in some Hollywood movies, but who cares, they're awesome!

 

Arun Matheshwaran is definitely a style-over-substance dude. And he IS one of those filmmakers who do have their own signature style. But with something like Captain Miller, which handles some heavy themes, some more substance would've helped. There are amazing sequences in the film where the staging, the cinematography, the editing, and the music all just sing together gloriously. But some of the choices in between are uneven. A lot of the action is just continuous shooting, and Arun and his team do find ways to keep things interesting.

 

Just like a lot of films set in pre-independence India with white villains, the British characters here are pretty one-dimensional and just "evil" too. I don't remember any other Indian movie than Sardhar Uddham that had British characters who were more than one-note dudes who shouted their lines. But the entire setting involving facing two different kinds of oppression together was nice, and though underwritten, Captain Miller himself was a badass main character. The supporting cast was also good, and I was glad that Priyanka Mohan's character was not just another love interest who added nothing to the plot.

Captain Miller does have flaws, and it could've been a lot better. I don't know if a longer cut exists that develops everything better than rushing through it, but as a theater watch, it was awesome.

A major reveal towards the end of the film was spoiled months ago by the film's promotions. Why,  though?

Name: A Murder at the End of the World
Review:
The show loses some steam towards the middle; I didn't particularly care about the extended Darby and Bill flashbacks, though their relationship and their whole dynamic do matter to the main present-day murder mystery and Darby as a character. Darby Hart, played wonderfully by Emma Corrin, is our detective in this mystery, and she's a very interesting character who does have the potential to appear in future installments if they're doing it. Corrin's entire demeanor as Darby and the way they approached the character are very unique, and Darby is an easy protagonist to root for. Not all of the supporting cast was memorable, except for the main players like Lee, Bill, and Andy, though each of them, if not all, did serve a purpose. The mystery in the flashbacks is no mystery, as its conclusion is revealed in the first episode itself. The flashbacks are more about fleshing out the Bill-Darby relationship and what happened to them, and though these were my least favorite part, as the show wrapped up, I realized that they did serve a purpose.

The main mystery weaves sci-fi into it brilliantly, with the futuristic hotel, all the sci-fi tech, and the cold Iceland location providing a unique atmosphere. This is almost like Agatha Christie meets Black Mirror with a dash of Mr. Robot once the actual mystery kicks in, and the way it all wraps up was also pretty brilliant. Not a lot of whodunits have engrossed me and surprised me this way.

Like I said, I do hope to see more of Darby Hart.

Name: Merry Christmas
Review:
Merry Christmas is a crime thriller with a lot of quirky and brilliant details and layers that fit together like a beautiful jigsaw puzzle, but at the same time, it's also a love story. The crime complements the romance, and the romance compliments the crime, and it's all blended together perfectly in a way that's very unique to Sriram Raghavan. Other than one flashback, the entire film occurs on Christmas Eve and the following morning. From the first split-screen shot itself, everything on screen serves a purpose, and every object serves a purpose. Even when the two main characters, Vijay Sethupathi and Katrina Kaif, break out into dance, it's not your typical Bollywood dance number that's there so that the film would have some "color." It's not even choreographed like one, and this is indeed a brilliantly choreographed sequence where both the actors are amazing. The use of music in the film is also brilliant, both in the original score and when classic pieces of music are used. The Christmas theme is reflected in the music too, in quirky and even hilarious ways.

This might be the best Katrina Kaif performance that I've seen, as she fits into Sriram Raghavan's world perfectly and makes the character her own. For Vijay Sethupathi, it was a joy seeing him back in a dark comedy again after so long, after having been a fan of him in dark comedy films like Soodhu Kaavvum. His comedic timing and charisma are still there, and the two leads have great chemistry together during the initial meet-cute romance and after things take a different turn.

It's hard to talk about the brilliance of a film like Merry Christmas without spoiling anything, but this is brilliant cinema. Madhu Neelakandan's cinematography, Pooja Ladha Surti's editing, the music, the sound design (even the sound of a dosa pan heating is used to create tension here), the writing, the dialogues, the retro vibes—everything blends together so well. Must watch!

Name: Three of Us
Review: Serene, bittersweet, warm and melancholic.

Name: Self Reliance
Review:
The premise here is very interesting. Such a storyline where a person is part of a game where a group of people is trying to kill them is generally the setup for an action movie. But Self-Reliance is not an action movie. It takes that survival premise and makes it about the main character's loneliness. So basically, he has to be in close proximity to another person to avoid getting murdered, and the fact that he has a pretty lonely existence detached from anyone doesn't help. While the premise is interesting, it doesn't explore the whole crazy and weird set-up as much as it should. There's even confusion at a point about whether the game is even real, but that too is not developed that much. This could've been the funny and sad lonely dude version of David Fincher's The Game, but after a solid start, the final act was kind of underwhelming. It was still a nice watch, though. Jake Johnson does have it in him to make good, better movies.

Also, I can't resist looking at Emily Hampshire's reactions in every shot she's in. She's so cool.

Name: The General
Review: This is one of those films where, the older it gets, the more impressive the filmmaking and stuntwork on screen is. The spectacle is truly amazing, though, the confederates being the good guys in this, not so much.

Name: Fallen Leaves
Review: This movie is a joy. The deadpan style, the colors, the music, the cinematography, the performances, the production design, the weird chemistry between the leads and how the quirky romantic comedy is embedded into their mundane everyday life, loved everything. Bliss!

Name: The Curse
Review:
I'm fresh out of watching the finale of The Curse, and my feelings are all over the place. The show is good, as in great, as in brilliant, if you have the stomach for cringe humor and lots of deliberately and painfully uncomfortable character interactions. Again, just like how the Safdie Brothers induce anxiety and panic in their movies, here Benny Safdie, one half of the Safdies, along with Nathan Fielder, are playing with a different kind of uncomfortable emotion. It is a comedy, it is a satire, and it is a character piece, but not in the conventional sense. The show is shot in a very specific way, as if we're spying on these people, with lots of weird camera angles and editing that lingers on that uncomfortable space the characters are in a lot. The cringe here is so constructed and well designed; there's nothing unintentional in this show; they're aware if a particular scene is funny because of the cringe or plain uncomfortable because of the cringe, and the performances and the filmmaking enhance it in so many ways.

 

When I say uncomfortable, I don't mean there's something dark or disturbing happening on screen. The show is basically about a white couple making a reality show where they're "developing" a neighborhood with eco-friendly homes and branded stores. They want to come off as well-meaning and holistic, but in reality, they just want to look like white saviors while they're actually saving no one. So The Curse also works as a satire that mocks white saviors who lack awareness and earnesty, and a lot of the episodes involve scenes set around their hypocrisy and how various problems arise to which they have the worst responses. Emma Stone leads the cast, along with the show's own co-creators, and this might be the best Emma Stone performance that I've seen so far (I haven't seen Poor Things yet). Almost every character interaction in the show is weird or uncomfortable, and just being this weird constantly, with a lot of nuance, takes skill. Even with Fielder, his character is putting on an act most of the time; he never comes off as a real person, and so even though he's not an actor like Stone, the gaps in the performance just make sense.

 

Most of this opinion has been about the first nine episodes of the show. Because it becomes something entirely different in the final episode. The less I say about it, the better, and it's even hard for me to put into words how I feel about it. I expected a straightforward satirical conclusion, but what I got was... Phew... Anyway, long story short, The Curse is truly unique, and it's brilliant and intelligent. It might not be for everyone, though, but I'd say it is must-watch TV.

Name: Yavanika
Review: I watched the new 4K remaster available on YouTube. What a gem! Certain aspects of it do show their age, but the writing, the filmmaking, and the performances are still top-tier. Gopi plays the despicable drunk to perfection. Then there's Mammootty's investigating officer, who's a joy to watch in every interrogation scene. His whole attitude and the way he tries to lead the witnesses are even kind of hilarious; the Mammootty scenes have my favorite character interactions in this film. The flashbacks that are each character's perspective of the same shitty person all add up brilliantly, making this more of a character piece than a whodunit. I also loved the way the stage play was integrated into it.

Name: Malaikottai Vaaliban
Review:
Firstly, Mohanlal was perfect as the title character. His body language, his presence, his look, and his physique were perfect for the larger-than-life mythic warrior Malaikottai Vaaliban, who seems like he could be a part of folklore or Amar Chitra Kadha's. But I don't think the writing and filmmaking did justice to the actor or the character. Vaaliban is supposed to be the stuff of legends, and within the movie he does do epic and unbelievable feats, but it just comes off as very flat during a lot of key moments. Even during the action scenes, the movie makes the choice of using realistic sound effects for fight scenes that are choreographed to be over-the-top. This is a weird mix, and it just lessens the impact of those moves, which are supposed to feel extremely powerful. Except for a second half stretch, Vaaliban never came off as the stuff of legends that he is, though Mohanlal was being the same himself, which is sad. I loved the performance so much, and he's in control the entire time. There are emotional highs that work just because of his earnest effort, which rises above the writing and filmmaking. There are only a handful of shots where Vaaliban actually seems larger-than-life, and those were even cherrypicked for the film's promotions.

The music was cool at times and mundane at others. I liked the main theme, which had Dollars Trilogy vibes. The cinematography was beautiful, and there's a lot of gorgeous frames that feel like paintings, but once again, this is a film and not a photography exhibit. I don't have a problem with episodic narratives or even a slower pace; I actually even miss big movies that are calmer and that take time to develop the drama over here. Even if this was just Valiban going from place to place and having different adventures while an emotional throughline develops in the background, it would've worked. But instead, this feels more disjointed than episodic. Events are just randomly thrown at our faces. It's like the movie is trying to be all three movies of the Dollars Trilogy at the same time and be an entirely different fantasy drama by the end. Except for Vaaliban himself, I didn't care about the other characters and was very detached a lot of times, though the movie wanted me to care, and the emotional narrative towards the end was very lazily written, and it was something that could've been introduced a lot earlier in the film.

The production design and costumes looked great; even the use of the crowd towards the end was nice. But when everything surrounding it is so disjointed and half-baked, I don't know. And why did Rajeev Pillai's armor look like he belonged in the Perunnal float from Amen?

The effort put into creating a unique, timeless folklore world and the care given to the aesthetics are appreciative. But I wish LJP and his team had also tried to make a coherent film. Never have I seen a multi-part film that has too much for one film and too little for one film at the same time. The film also has some problematic elements in it, but that's a different rant. 


I haven't seen Yojimbo, but I've watched its unofficial western remake, A Fistful of Dollars. Clint Eastwood was not even a big star when that movie was released, and even then, when he says, "Get three coffins ready" and quick-guns those dudes, we get the idea that this dude means business. Here, when Vaaliban is introduced, though there's dialogue that boasts his legend, with Mohanlal himself being the star he is, it's lacking. And for a character like this, I think the presentation is very important.

Like I said at the beginning, both Mohanlal's great and earnest performance and the character deserved better.

Not giving it less than 3 stars since A10 was way too good in this.

Name: Sapta Sagaradaache Ello - Side B
Review: The first movie focused on both characters, while this is about Manu and his obsession with Priya after the events of the first movie. Manu's love is as innocent as it gets, but his actions are very shady. Still, his motivations somehow justify them. So the movie does a great job of walking that thin line of morality where Manu's guilt and love are driving him to do all these dark things. I expected Side B to be a revenge story, but it's still about love, though not in the way Side A was. As a love story, side A was better, though it did drag towards the middle. Side B is a story about love, and though things are way too easy for Manu at times when he decides to strike back against those who wronged him, the emotional core makes it forgivable. The music was gorgeous, just like on side A, and so were the performances of the cast. The cinematography and the use of colors and light were also things that I loved. I loved the old-boy-inspired fight scene towards the end too. Side B is a pretty satisfying and emotional conclusion; the plot holes and conveniences are forgivable. I actually cared about the characters, and the music is still playing inside my head. That's all that matters. Rukmini Vasanth's eyebrow acting game is strong!

Name: Animal
Review:
Sandeep Andi Vaan.. Ahem.. Sandeep Reddy Vanga's Animal is the most penis movie of 2023. Barry Keoghan literally shows his dick in Saltburn, and even that movie is not as penis as Animal. I believe the only reason we don't see Ranbir Kapoor's dick in Animal is the Indian Censor Board.

About the misogyny in the movie. I mean, it's not even misogyny that comes as a part of character development or something that comes naturally. The misogyny in Animal comes from someone who was triggered by his last film's misogyny being criticized. So parts of the movie seem like they were written while the writer was jerking off to Andrew Tate podcasts, because "how dare they say my movie was misogynistic?!!!". So it's regressive just for the sake of being regressive, which is sad and absolutely hilarious at the same time. You're not a provocateur, dude; you're just whiny and funny.

Then there's other stuff, like how the Swastik steel logo looks more like a Nazi Swasthika than a Hindu Swasthika, complete with a Nazi salute-like scene (if it wasn't obvious, there's a church scene that makes it obvious), "aathmanirbhar bharat", drinking cow urine, and how the movie portrays Muslims.

Yes, Ranbir is good even with such colossally awful writing; he made me laugh a lot, but if I wanted to see Ranbir Kapoor as a rich man-child with Daddy issues, I'd rather watch him in Wake Up Sid or Tamasha than as this penis cancer in human form. The movie tries so hard to make us feel for him as a "sympathetic anti-hero", but the only feeling I got was that this dude should've been locked up while he was a teenager itself. Dude's more of a hilarious cartoon than an anti-hero, and the jokes keep on coming (the scenes are supposed to be serious for the most part, though). Also, Vanga should realize that saying the word "Papa" every five seconds is not how you show an "intense", fucked up and dysfunctional father-son relationship. Showing one intense confrontation towards the end with both Ranbir and Anil Kapoor at the top of their game doesn't help when it comes after more than three hours of shit. The scene just looks like it belongs in a different movie that actually cares about a dysfunctional father-son relationship.

I won't elaborate on the "romantic" side of Animal, because calling that hilarious fuckupedness romance is an insult to romance, apart from the actors having zero chemistry together. The only genuine chemistry I felt in this movie was when the "villain" Abrar, played by Bobby Deol, and our anti-zero Rannvijay locked eyes with each other for the first time, but that's supposed to be Alpha male rage eye contact and not romantic eye contact, apparently. The hilarious fight scene afterwards might, unironically, be the most tender and romantic moment in the movie. Saying that Vanga's idea of intimacy is fucked up is an understatement. I'm not elaborating further on the awfully written female characters either. (The men are awfully written too, but on a different level of awful. Equality, yay!)

 

I do agree that the movie has great music, as did Arjun Reddy, but I'm just sad that it doesn't belong in a good movie. The same goes for some of the great action sequences that I saw here. The editing is cool in some places; things like the transition from Rannvijay to Abraar look cool in isolation, but the movie is still a turd. I won't say the movie has great editing since this thing didn't need to be 3.5 hours at all. Scenes go on for way too long; a lot of the plot points and dialogue are so awkward, weird, and hilarious, and I don't think it came from a deliberate creative decision to make them weird and funny. On the conquest to trigger people who criticize his misogyny, Vanga actually forgets what his second (third?) movie is supposed to be about. And the answer is not dick. There are more references to dick in this movie than there are to Papa. There's even a reference to Papa's dick. That's how deep Vanga's fascination with dick goes. 

 

I did have ironic fun and laughs watching this testicular hit comedy film. If this was intended as satire, then it'd have been brilliant, but the thing is, it's supposed to be a serious and intense drama, which makes it even funnier. Animal is more insulting and offensive to men than it is to women, with its cartoonish protagonist, hilarious dialogues, and stupidity. Even an intentional satire like Barbie was way nicer and kinder to men. Men should be more triggered by this movie than women, honestly.

 

Those who have the opinion that this film does not glorify toxic masculinity and abusive relationships are actually insulting its creator. Because this is deliberate glorification to trigger people, denying its existence is the bigger insult to the creator, and for that, Sandeep Reddy Vanga's penis deserves an apology.

 

Animal, starring "Super Star" Penis, ft. Ranbir Kapoor.

Name: Bheeshma Parvam
Review:
Five stars because it cured me of The Sandeep Reddy Vanga disease named Animal. 

Thanks for gifting us with Ikka as Anjootti Michael, Amal Neerad.

Name: The Beekeeper
Review:
Once every while I'll come across an action movie poster, it'd have Jason Statham or Liam Neeson looking all serious, and it'd have the most random noun as its title. So when I saw a poster with Statham looking all serious with the title "The Beekeeper," I was pretty sure that this movie was not some drama set around Beekeeping. Without even seeing the trailer, I guessed that Jason Statham is an ex-military/spy type who's keeping bees in the present day and springs back into action because of some revenge/justice-like situation. And I was almost correct. Just that the beekeeping itself was a part of his killing machine persona for some unexplained reason that leads to some hilarious dialogue and not some throwaway disguise. Directed by David Ayer, The Beekeeper is like a re(bee)packaged version of what Antoine Fuqua did with the Equilizer movies (fun trivia: Ayer wrote Fuqua's Training Day). The character of the Beekeeper has an almost similar demeanor to that of Denzel's Robert McCaal, the Beequalizer, if you will. He's an almost mythical badass; he has a strong moral code where he makes sure that only those who deserve it die by his hands. He's in control in almost every situation and is calm and composed most of the time. Now, Statham's Beekeeper also has some deadpan sense of humor and is kind of the only character who is almost self-aware of how dumb the movie is.
"You're just a man." "I know."
So the novelty of this movie lies in the beekeeper character and the action sequences. I especially loved the brutal one-on-one fight scene towards the end. Otherwise, the writing is all kinds of dumb, with laughworthy bee trivia and bee puns thrown in because it's indeed the "beekeeper." The word bee is repeated constantly, to an annoying degree. Despite being the titular Beekeeper, Statham might be the one who says the word bee the least in this movie. Everything is cartoonish. I guess the intention was to create a unique version of the underworld like the one seen in the John Wick movies, but the results are unintentionally funny. Like, why do assassins have to care so much about Bees to kill people anyway? But for some cool-looking action and some laughs (mostly unintentional, sometimes intentional), The Beekeeper is a fun watch.

Name: Mr. & Mrs. Smith
Review:
Simon Kinberg's writing here is very dumb and formulaic, but what makes up for it is Brad and Angelina being all kinds of sexy and Doug Liman's direction. The chemistry is amazing to watch, whether they're in love with each other or trying to kill each other while being in love with each other. The movie starts up very generically and picks up once they both learn about the other spouse being a competing assassin. Then it's fun af. The writing is dumb, and the ending is confusing, but the lead pair's hotness and Doug Liman's skill at pulling off great action make this a fun watch. The way Liman plays with the tension in their initial confrontations after the identity reveals is such great filmmaking, which builds up into probably the sexiest fight scene ever inside the house. The chase sequence afterwards was also awesome. The movie also has some great looking practical explosions. 

The late 90s and early 2000s were the peak Angelina Jolie era, wasn't it?

Time to watch the Donald Glover-Maya Erskine show.

Name: BEEF
Review:
These kinds of storylines where two characters are fueled by ego and put against one another have a high possibility of running dry and getting repetitive. It has happened for shorter feature-length movies a lot, so I was curious as to how Beef would develop this conflict between two people that starts with just a honk and a middle finger without losing stream over 10 episodes. And it delivers big time. Both the characters, Danny and Amy, have well-defined arcs and personalities. They have great supporting characters on both sides, with each individual arc and relationship feeling so fleshed out. So beef never feels repetitive. The writing is so intelligent, and the filmmaking is so precise in how it builds up conflicts and how these two lives intersect with each other, with a deep and meditative finale episode that gives a beautiful closure to the two of them. Plus amazing performances from the whole cast, especially the two leads, Ali Wong and Steven Yeun. 

Must watch!

"Maybe normal people are just delusional fucked up people"

Name: The Seven Year Itch
Review: Marilyn Monroe deserved much better.

Name: American Fiction
Review: With an amazing leading performance by Jeffrey Wright, American Fiction is all kinds of brilliant. It's sharp and direct in its satire and even has the best ending possible for such a storyline, with even the brilliant and hilarious ending proving the film's point.

Name: Shortcomings
Review:
The title itself gives away what kind of movie this is. We are following Ben; he's got his share of issues, and yet there's something real about him. Even through his rants, hypocrisy, and "honesty" which mostly boils down to being insensitive, he didn't come off like an irredeemable asshole. He's just a person, flawed, growing, evolving, and trying to navigate through life. It even subverts the way movies like these usually play out for protagonists like Ben, with a chair bit towards the end that made me laugh out loud. I liked how much the movie leans into his girlfriend Miko's point of view, although it follows Ben in every scene. Movies like this rarely do that (looking at you, 500 days of summer).

All of the performances were great, the dialogues were witty, smart, and interesting, and Randall Park as a director really sets the perfect mood for something like this. The cinematography and music fit perfectly, and I loved the way the editing and style changed during the big argument between Ben and Miko.

I wouldn't mind this being a longer movie or even a series, though. It was surprisingly funny, sweet and wholesome, for a movie with a not so likable protagonist.

Name: Premalu
Review:
TL;DR of Premalu is that it's a hilarious and wholesome romantic comedy that gave me a lot of fun and laughs.

Just like the previous two movies directed by Girish A. D., in Premalu too, there's care gone into adding several nuances that add depth to several scenes and the characters; a better word than "depth" would be "color." We have Sachin, played by Naslen, going through early-20s angst and confusion after graduating from college. Then there's Reenu, played by Mamitha, just starting out her first job in a new place, comfortable with where she is at the moment. While the characters and the meet-cute and love story that unfold are familiar, Girish and co-writer Kiran Josey add so much texture to these characters and the world around them. The 20s angst, how it feels to live away from home—it's all peppered throughout. The jokes and visual humor keep on coming, and the writing, filmmaking, and performances succeed big time in making the comedy work. For every joke that didn't land for me, something laugh-out-loud hilarious followed in quick succession. Sometimes it's not the jokes themselves; it's the delivery, the reactions, and the direction that pull off the laughs. Along with that, Vishnu Vijay's score and songs work wonders for the mood the film is trying to set.

Premalu is a light and fun movie on paper, but it's pretty smart too. It breaks enough clichés, makes fun of cringey "feel-good" tropes, even subverts some of them, and stays fun and hilarious while it's doing it. It also knows when to make use of classic comedic tropes in an effective and updated manner. The lead pair had great chemistry together; the romance and tender moments do work when they have to work, though the film is primarily a comedy, and other than just Reenu, Sachin also had great chemistry with his friend Amal Davis (Sangeeth Pratap, the senior dude from Hridayam, now being awesome in anti-Hridayam) and his nemesis Aadhi (Shyam Mohan, very effectively playing a type of dude we've all seen in our classes or at work, unless you're him yourselves). Several confrontations between Aadhi and Sachin and the constant exchanges between Amal and Sachin were so much fun. The occasional social media references were a cool detail, except for that CBSE-state stereotype troll joke (yeah, I was CBSE, hehe.).

In short, Premalu delivers on the fun, and Naslen and Mamitha are stars!

Name: Guntur Kaaram
Review:
The novelty of Guntur Kaaram is that Mahesh Babu isn't playing a rich NRI who saves poor Telugu people. It's sad that this actually could've been a better movie. The caste angle and family drama towards the end had the potential to be so much better than Trivikram's Ala Vaikuntapurramlo, which had a terrible drama plot at the center. Here, at least it was redeemable, but it focuses on all the wrong stuff.

Mahesh is not playing his usual kind of dude, but that doesn't mean he's that interesting either; the character is bland af. Then there's the terrible romance arc; at least this time he's constantly perving over her figure rather than just her thighs like in Ala Vaikundapurramlo. Yay, full-body creeping! Mahesh Babu looks young for a man who is almost fifty, but even then, Sreeleela looked too young to be his romantic interest (The movie itself wasn't sure about Ramana's age either, or was it wrong Netflix subtitles? Because it alternates between him being in his early 20s and early 30s, MB definitely doesn't look like an early 20s dude). The romance storyline is utter shit, with the occasional Sreeleela dance scene and the chair-folding song being the only things worth watching.

The action didn't make me feel anything. There are gimmicks, of course, like using long shots, the robotic camera, and of course the usual telugu movie slo-mo posing, but everything falls flat. TBH, I think the action in Trivikram's Ala Vaikuntapurramlo was shit too. So there's that. Even if Ramana is the usual Telugu movie invincible badass, he shouldn't have been this bland. And what's with all the dated misogyny? Some women beat up Mahesh, then he beats up the dudes over there and tells the women to go back to the kitchen. Is that Trivikram's version of woke? Like how Udayakrishna's version of woke here in Malayalam was Lalettan beating up a lesbian couple?

Thaman, as usual, delivers a very Thaman score, and Mahesh will probably go back to NRI saving poor people mode. Oh wait, his next movie is the international Rajamouli project, so he'd be an NRI saving poor people in that movie, I guess.

If you want to watch a great movie about a partially blind badass with Mommy issues, watch the Ikka-Anwar Rasheed iconic padam that is Rajamanikyam.

Name: Anweshippin Kandethum
Review:
It's like watching two episodes of a straightforward police procedural. Episodic police procedural movies are not new to Malayalam cinema, but this one felt especially like an episodic drama (in a good way) with two self-contained investigations split right in the middle. The movie is set in the 90s, and it has the spirit of classic Malayalam police procedurals of that era.

Tovino Thomas was great as the lead. The first case had aspects like how his seniors are unfair to him and block him from conducting a proper investigation, and how they then try to frame someone just to wrap it up. I expected that thread to be better developed than how it eventually wrapped up quickly. But even then, the movie continuously puts an emphasis on the fact that our lead investigation team doesn't resort to violent methods or torture to get information (something that I didn't like in Kannur Squad), except for the occasional threat of violence. Did such ethical cops exist in the Kerala Police? I don't know, it's not like they are peace loving cops who don't beat up anyone, but at least police violence is not shown in a heroic light too much. Intentional or not, it was a good decision to make the investigation actually about gathering clues and making deductions rather than resorting to violence, while putting an emphasis on how the bad cops in the movie are all those who unnecessarily beat up suspects.

Santhosh Narayanan's score blends into the movie, and it's not like the stuff he does for Karthik Subbaraj or Pa. Ranjith movies; the opening credits song was metal, though.

The amount of exposition in the movie can be too much at times. I wish a lot of the information was visual or that the explanations were shorter, but as a fan of investigation fiction, this was pretty satisfying on the whole.

Name: Ayalaan
Review:
After seeing all those terrible reviews, I was prepared to hate this film and consider it a cringe watch. But I couldn't, to an extent. Firstly, the CGI is pretty impressive. Yeah, it's a bit uneven too, but when it works, it looks great. And this is relatively a lower-budget movie than your average SS Rajamouli, Shankar, and YRF Spy Universe movie, so the CGI fidelity they achieve here is a great achievement, and so I feel bad for actually being rude about this movie. This was how I felt about SRK's Zero too, a film with some of the best VFX work in the world, with everything else being a dumpster fire. And I think the basic problem that Ayalaan and Zero had is the same: the filmmakers and the team were so concerned about creating these impressive effects and pulling off this technical achievement that they probably considered the writing and everything else secondary.

 

Ayalaan, in both character design and plot, reminded me of the 2011 movie Paul, where Seth Rogen voiced a foul-mouthed CGI alien who hangs out with two friends played by Simon Pegg and Nick Frost. Paul had a very simple premise of a buddy road trip movie, with two agents chasing the alien, and it was a lot of fun. Ayalaan felt like it's more Paul than ET/Koi Mil Gaya, with the parts where the alien hangs out with the group of dudes being the most fun scenes in the movie.

 

That was supposed to be the film's USP—how it feels to have an alien be a roommate to some middle-class Tamil dudes barely surviving in a city. Instead, Ayalaan, in its second half, tries to be a superhero movie, and that's where things fall flat. Sivakarthikeyan's protagonist is a template good guy who lacks personality, and even the alien himself is no different. It was painfully obvious that the Sidharth voiceover was added at the last minute, and so the alien doesn't have a definite personality, like how the alien in Paul felt like CGI Seth Rogen.

 

Sivakarthikeyan's last film, Maaveeran, brilliantly incorporated social themes with a superhero plot, with a rootable protagonist and everything, but in Ayaalan, the serious scenes and the drama are all flat, even for a kids movie. A lot of it is hilariously stupid, and if this just stayed a silly buddy movie, it wouldn't have mattered. But the second half stretch is where I lost interest in Ayalaan with bland action and bland drama. AR Rahman's music was lackluster.

 

I can't totally hate on Ayalaan because there is some impressive CGI work and some heart in it. But the movie is also dated and badly written. Maaveeran should be the blueprint.

Name: Team America: World Police
Review:
It's from the South Park dudes, so the excess was expected. But still, it doesn't go as hard as South Park usually does. There are jokes that I couldn't digest, but the whole thing is intentionally extreme anyway. Through all that, this puppet movie might be one of the most honest portrayals of the US military of all time. Even the opening scene has them destroy the entirety of Paris to stop some terrorists from blowing up a single street. That right there is cinema.

Team America is constantly hilarious with all kinds of extreme gags, from the dick-pussy-asshole pep talk to the Pearl Harbour song (which should've gotten all the awards that ever existed), it's just all-in. All the foreign characters are portrayed to be over-the-top racist stereotypes, but also, most "serious" US military movies that boost patriotism aren't any better, right? And in a movie with a theme song that has lyrics like "America, Fuck Yeah! Slavery, Fuck yeah!" The way they're making fun of America and its foreign policies is not just on your face; it's in your mouth.

I also loved how all the action literally felt like some kids having fun blowing up and playing with some toys. 

Even with the ironic satire thing going on, I did feel some of the gags were too much, but still, this just made me want to see a Team India film about the Right Wing sanghis here.

Name: Anyone But You
Review:
Silly, cheesy, formulaic goofy fun with hot people being hot, beautiful locations, and a pop music soundtrack. I got exactly what I expected. No complaints.

I didn't realize that I missed unapologetically cheesy movies so much. Yeah, it's neither deep nor real, but for me, that's a part of the appeal.

Name: Deadpool
Review:
Deadpool is also a case of clever production. I mean, the way they got the movie made is in itself a badass move. Then, with a budget that's technically big but nowhere near that of a conventional superhero movie, they pulled off making this look like a "big" movie, though it only has two big action setpieces. The origin story bits are still the dullest parts of the movie, but they were aware of that and placed them in between that big highway action sequence where Wade is still Deadpool. This is clever in two ways. The movie begins with this big action scene with Deadpool doing Deadpool stuff, and then the dull flashbacks give his generic origins. Cutting back and forth means it gives the illusion of the highway setpiece seeming longer than it is and keeps the origin story from boring us too much. As generic as this movie is, it is intelligent af, both from a writing and producing perspective.

The humor still works, and the parts that made me chuckle then still make me chuckle now. Though Ryan Reynolds started putting up this persona for everything he did afterwards to the point it became annoying, when he's actually Wade Fucking Wilson, he's awesome. All the meta-jokes and 4th wall breaks are still love, and so is that soundtrack.

What I also appreciated here is Tim Miller's over-the-top style. There's a stylistic flair in the first movie that the second movie doesn't have. David Leitch can make cool looking movie action, but Tim Miller's action has more of a comicy feel to it than that of an action movie.

Anyway, like the great Alphonse Puthren said, Poda Swimming Poolu, Deadpoolu.

Name: Bramayugam
Review:
One thing I can definitely say about Rahul Sadasivan is that he knows how to do atmospheric horror. In Boothakalam, all the creepy stuff happened in a very normal middle-class home. It was not just fear of the paranormal either; the psychological trauma of a dysfunctional family builds up gradually, and it adds up to the creepiness. Coming to Bramayugam, here too, the horror works in different layers, but in a different context. In Bramayugam, the horror comes from oppression and control, from the feeling of losing one's freedom without even realizing it, and the other layers complement this psychological dread.

The black-and-white aesthetics are not a gimmick here at all. They add so much to the tone and atmosphere the film is trying to set. Most of Bramayugam takes place within the confines of a single mansion, or Mana, to be accurate. The Mana is a paradoxical structure, from the moment we set eyes on it. It's decaying; parts of it have been taken over by nature; other parts are dusty, dirty, and twisted in all kinds of ways. What the monochrome does is that, though greenery is present all around the Mana, the lack of green gives the impression that nature is not a part of this place. It separates the Mana and its surroundings from the rest of the world, where legends from folklore might be lurking around. The production design and cinematography work together brilliantly to set the perfect atmosphere for the madness to unfold. The Mana hence feels like a labyrinth where time and space seem distorted, and enter Mammootty as Kodumon Potty.

The introduction to Kodumon Potty felt like such great filmmaking. Of course, Mammootty is a star, and he's had many intro sequences that were tailor-made for making the audience cheer. But here, the buildup is also meant to add to the larger horrors and madness. The kind of madness where one person is inferior to the other person just because of some non-existent labels, and the madness of all the crazy things that's about to happen to our POV character Thevan, played by Arjun Ashokan. Potty is revealed to us as Thevan is reacting to his presence. It's not a star introduction; it's Thevan's uncertainty and fear we're seeing through his eyes. Afterwards, we get more information about the Mana and its mysteries through the cook played by Sidharth Bharathan. And it's these three brilliant performances, along with the Mana itself being a character, that drive the madness forward.

Kodumon Potty is built up to be a creepy presence from his introduction itself. And it only escalates from there, with Mammootty nailing the oppressive monster, and the character is presented so effectively that even the sound made by his wooden sandals seems scary. Bramayugam also makes brilliant use of sound. The dead silences inside the Mana are broken by the sound of chains or Potty's sandals and all kinds of creepy noises; even the rain sounds eerie. Christo Xavier's score also effectively elevates the horror, and this is the kind of horror film that makes effective use of silence too. Even a minor character like the yakshi, played by Amalda Liz, has such thought gone into it. The costume and the way she carries herself fit the "beautiful yet scary" descriptions perfectly. 

Bramayugam effectively blends folklore legends with the very real madness that is how oppression works and presents a very immersive experience that had me glued to its paradoxical monochrome world from beginning to end. Rahul Sadasivan gets horror.

Name: The Iron Claw
Review:
I used to think that Zac Effron was just another Hollywood pretty boy. But I was wrong. Zac Effron in The Iron Claw is what Casey Affleck was in Manchester By The Sea. A man drowning in grief and sadness, barely holding onto himself, and we can constantly see how tired and shattered he is underneath that big, strong physique.

The movie destroyed me, BTW. It was a tough watch. I couldn't do it in one go and took breaks in between. I meant that in a good way; it's not because I didn't like what was happening on screen; it's a well-made and brilliantly acted film, and the sadness and grief just felt overwhelming at times. I just wanted to reach inside and give these dudes some hugs.

I'm going to watch Deadpool 2 to recover.

Name: Deadpool 2
Review:
In terms of the humor, the meta jokes, and the fourth wall breaks, this is a step above the first movie. But the writing otherwise is indeed lazy, and being self-aware about it doesn't help. The few moments of emotional storytelling do work, like the death at the end, how it blends in with the comedy, and yet feels emotional (though yk, they could've removed the collar then and there too, which is still so dumb). The scene afterwards with Vanessa was also great; Reynolds peaks when he's being Deadpool for some reason.

In terms of action, Tim Miller had an over-the-top and cartoony flair in the first movie, which seems to be missing here. The attempts at replicating it only work during the Domino sequences. Otherwise, the action just felt generic action movie-ish. David Leitch is great at doing action; even Bullet Train had some great stylized fight scenes, but for something like Deadpool, a way more over-the-top and comic booky style like what Miller did fits more. The VFX also looked weirdly inconsistent here. 

Anyway, it was fun and escapy enough to help recover from being destroyed by The Iron Claw.

Name: Varathan
Review:
I still remember when I first watched Varathan. PUBG had just become a thing, and the dudes in the theater were more excited to see Fafa use a pan as a weapon than the moment where he turns on the red light. Fafa looks so damn good in this though. Like, dude can play an absolute badass to perfection if he wants to.

Would I watch Four Brothers again? No. Would I watch Big B again? Fuck yes.

Would I watch Straw Dogs again? No. Would I watch Varathan again? Fuuuuckkk yesssss.

Name: Theater Camp
Review:
The movie does have heart, and there were moments that made me laugh. It especially picked up from the halfway point, and I really loved the ending. The whole School of Rock vibe it had was great. There's also a great argument scene between the main characters, Amos and Rebecca, that's done so well.

It's supposed to be a mockumentary, but it actually isn't. The style of cinematography and editing fits a mockumentary, but in addition to the lack of talking heads, the characters don't really acknowledge the presence of the camera. Idk if it's because I've watched all these mockumentary sitcoms, but I was expecting the characters to look at the camera or acknowledge it in some way, but it doesn't happen.

But anyway, apart from the confusing choice of presenting it as a documentary, when it doesn't commit to the mockumentary style, this was pretty fun.

Name: Fair Play
Review: The buildup and the exploration of power dynamics and male ego was really great and both the lead actors were amazing. Though I do wish the ending was a bit more of a gut-punch than what we got here.

Name: Mean Girls
Review:
When I watched the first Mean Girls, I was still at school and younger than the characters. Now, I'm older than the characters in the new Mean Girls, but the movie is still kind of the same. I know that this is the movie adaptation of the stage musical adaptation of Mean Girls (phew), but as it began, though the characters use smartphones and there's the obligatory existence of social media, the characters, the stereotypes, the story beats and the way they talk and behave are still very early 2000s. Even the occasional social media montages feel more like an afterthought than something that's actually a part of the narrative.

That's not to say I didn't have fun watching this, though. It felt like watching a Bollywood remake of the original Mean Girls at times, with the songs, dance numbers, vibrant costumes, and overdose of color. Some of the songs were meh and forgettable, but there were some fun ones with some visual flair and great choreography. Some of the performances were good while some felt weird. 

There are occasional moments of genuine "updated" content in between, like the occasional meta jokes and self-referential digs, that reminded me that Tina Fey did make something brilliant and funny like 30 Rock in between the two mean girls movies.

Almost near the halfway point, I was able to just enjoy the jokes and songs and have fun. Still, when "updating" something for a newer audience, what the new Mr. and Mrs. Smith TV show did seems like a better option than redoing the early 2000s movies like an early 2000s movie with a 2020s movie filter on it.

Name: Manjummel Boys
Review:
I just loved how straightforward Manjummel Boys was in telling a story of friendship, bravery, and compassion. There's nothing "extra" in here. It's to the point. Subhash is established as an atheist early on in the film, but is Manjummel Boys about the spiritual awakening of an atheist? No. Subhash sees the light from above, but it's not part of religion; it's human and real.

I loved the way Chidambaram played with contrasting emotions between a birthday celebration and a funeral in Jan-e-Man; in Manjummel Boys too, there's a nicely executed sudden tonal shift. When a playful trip turns into something dreadful in an instant, I, as a spectator, also felt the way the mood shifted for the main characters. The same place they were having fun a while before suddenly seemed dark. The film makes the choice of not really showing the cave as a dangerous place before Subhash falls in; there's no long dreadful buildup; it just happens.

Sushin Shyam's score, the amazing sound design, Shyju Khalid's cinematography, Ajayan Chalisseri's production design, Vivek Harshan's editing, the costumes, the cast—it's like Chidambaram got the best crew possible to pull this off. The rescue setpiece was so brilliantly executed, and it was the place where Soubin Shahir shined as Kuttettan. It's thrilling and emotional cinema, regardless of knowing the real story behind it. And like I said at the beginning, it does so while sticking to the basic emotions and not doing anything "extra".

Like the dude who acted in Gunaa said, Anbe Sivam. ❤️

Name: Apocalypse Now
Review: This is basically how every single war movie should be made. By acknowledging the violence, the horror, by acknowledging that it's indeed murder and there's nothing heroic about it.

Name: Poor Things
Review:
I obviously don't have the insight or knowledge to talk about the portrayal of womanhood or female sexuality here. But still, I'm conflicted about Poor Things being as progressive and feminist as some opinions said it was.

But what I can definitely say is that there aren't enough superlatives in all the human languages to describe Emma Stone's performance in this. The character is constantly evolving, and she just embodies the weirdness and dark sense of humor of each phase in the best way possible; nobody else can be Bella. This is like an ascension movie in that sense, where Emma Stone sets in Stone (hehe) that she's one of the greats. This is the best lead performance of the year for me (Male and Female combined). 

It's also a joy to see Mark Ruffalo playing an absolutely hilarious asshole rather than a nice dude. All the Stone-Ruffalo combination scenes were brilliant. Where Yorgos Lanthimos shines is in his unique and trippy style, aesthetic choices, dark humor, and overall weirdness. Lots of scenes made me laugh out loud or be in awe of the visuals or the Emma Stone craziness. (That dance, OMFG!)

Anyway, I'd give this 5 stars or more just because of how epic Emma Stone is in this movie. But the confusing themes made me take a star off. (I have no idea how to rate stuff, so my stars don't mean anything anyway).

Name: Volver
Review: The filmmaking and writing here is very brilliant, but it's brilliant in a very sneaky and unassuming way. I loved that. And also, Penélope Cruz. Gorgeous.

Name: Dune
Review:
The more I watch Dune, the more I appreciate everything great about it.

Part two preparation rewatch.

Name: Dune: Part Two
Review:
The one complaint I had about the first Dune was that, though the entire film was just buildup and world-building, Paul as a protagonist felt lifeless. But one of the main things that Part 2 improves upon is this. There's so many layers added to Paul. It also helps that, unlike the first film, which switched between characters frequently, part two focuses only on Paul for most of its initial half. Paul's journey is the white savior/Messiah trope promised by the first film, but at the same time, it is a subversion of that trope too. Dune brilliantly subverts the idea of a Messiah here and really makes an effort to show us that religion, religious propaganda, fundamentalism and a "holy war" aren't something that's all divine and heroic. Even Paul's journey of becoming the "chosen one" is not so "good vs. evil." He aims to do good, but his transformation from someone who just wants to assist the fremen to their prophet is treated more like corruption here than as an ascension, where a revolution for freedom from imperialists warps into a religious war that'd bring more death and destruction. Yeah, even with an entire part dedicated to buildup, some of the big changes still feel sudden since the source material is still very dense, even for two films. But still, I have no complaints, since as a film, I could view this grand spectacle on an IMAX screen, being transported into that world, rather than as an episodic TV series at home.

Zimmer's music, Fraser's cinematography, the grandeur, the visual effects, the technical milestones, and the amazing production design all carry over from the first Dune. Even performance-wise, Chalamet's Paul seemed better, and Austin Butler as the very effective villain didn't show any signs of Elvis. Phew. Zendaya and Rebecca Ferguson were great, and though others like Florence Pugh, Léa Seydoux, and Anya Taylor-Joy have only a tiny bit of screen time, there's always the third movie. I loved Javier Bardem and how he made me laugh at the most unexpected moments with his "hail the Messiah" attitude. I didn't expect him to be funny like this when he appeared in the first movie at all.

The audio-visual spectacle of Dune is impressive af, with Villeneuve really shining at moments of drama, grand buildups, and payoffs. But more than part one, the deeper themes connected with me more in part two. Oppenheimer and Dune 2 are the only two movies I've seen in IMAX so far, and Dune 2 easily is my favorite watch in that format. I'd even revisit it if I could've (budgetary constraints, you see).

To having back-to-back Dunathons in the future, and also to being excited for Dune: Messiah.

Name: Spaceman
Review: There's great acting by Sandler and great voice acting work from Paul Dano, some great music, production design and visuals. But apart from that, I couldn't connect with the relationship at its core, and even at just 100 minutes, the movie felt like it was dragging.

Name: Petite Maman
Review: Warm, cute, sad, deep and surreal all at the same time. That too while being "Petite" as a film too. Cinema!

Name: Ricky Stanicky
Review: I've always had a love for those R-rated comedies with over-the-top gags and simplistic plots that the Farrelly brothers and Jay Roach made. Even as the reviews for them started getting worse, I've enjoyed these movies. Now, at a time when such movies are seen as outdated relics from the past, here comes Ricky Stanicky, like it belongs right alongside those late 90s and early 2000s comedies. It's light on the stuff that made movies like Dumb and Dumber a riot, though, but there's still stuff like a baby sucking on a man nipple, a duck fighting a dog, baby dick jokes, and an entire bit involving air-dicking. Good fun. Cena is a tremendous comedic performer and can make even the worst joke seem funnier than it is. Do I think this is a good movie? No. Did I enjoy it? Yes!

Name: Little Women
Review: I just want to talk about the brilliant way Gerwig structured this non-linear adaptation of the linear source material, which was a pretty big risk but done with such a deep understanding of the characters and their emotions. I'm not exaggerating when I say this is one of the best screenplays in cinema. Each time Little Women cuts back and forth between the present and the past, it's with such intent. It doesn't confuse the viewer at any point, it's not a gimmick, it only takes us deeper into these characters. As a result, we see the romance Teddy has with both Jo and Amy and how it eventually ends on a bittersweet note, going in parallel in a way that treats both these women and Teddy himself with empathy. Beth's loss is much more heartbreaking when the happiest moment they had together as a family cuts back to her death. Likewise, each back-and-forth timeline shift is so well designed and so elegantly put together, with the editing finding the perfect balance between modern and traditional. This is carried on till the very end, very consistently. Even the subversion in the ending is brilliant and quirky. ("I suppose marriage has always been an economic proposition, even in fiction"). Greta Gerwig's brilliance is often underrated. Could she have adapted a straightforward version of Little Women? Yes. But she didn't; she made it entirely her own while also respecting the source material just enough. Even when she made a toy movie, she could've made one like Transformers, a formulaic and cash-grabbing toy commercial in all its glory. But instead, she used the toy to make a satire on misogyny and existentialism. I mean, it would've been way easier for them to make a Disney-ish movie, but they didn't. She doesn't get enough credit for taking these big swings, just because she does it so well that they don't even seem so big.

Name: Napoleon
Review:
There's some really cool looking battles, good performances from Phoenix and Kirby, great visuals, production design and costumes. But the writing just felt so dull. There's historical and political stuff happening that I didn't give a shit about at all, but I guess they also give the year and name of each event, for a detailed history lesson perhaps? The Napoleon - Josephine relationship is supposed to be a central point here, I didn't give a shit about that either. Both the actors are great, but I didn't feel any chemistry between them. Everything just felt so monotonous and boring. I'd blame it mostly on the writing than on Scott. Scott's flair is seen in some of the impressive ways the film captures violence and even on some of the surprising comedic bits. But unlike The Last Duel, which had far more superior writing, this was a tough one to sit through. 

I've heard that a longer cut exists, maybe that one doesn't look like a mundane and underdeveloped collection of historic events?

Name: Midsommar
Review:
I had forgotten enough about Midsommar that I was able to experience the director's cut as an entirely new thing. I don't even know what the differences between this and the movie I saw in 2019 are. Anyway, this was the first Florence Pugh movie that I had watched, and still to this day, this IS the best Florence Pugh performance. From that long closeup right at the beginning when she calls Christian to that smile at the final shot, even after she's been in all these huge movies, working with a lot of big names, this is peak Pugh for now.

Ari Aster feeds so much beauty into something that's actually very sad and grim. The tone and pace here are so perfect, and the way he visualizes each scene is so unique and brilliant. There are so many details and deep thematic storytelling going on, I don't think I even caught all of them. The look of it, the feel, the music, the cinematography, the editing—it's just the kind of dark horror movie that I can't take my eyes off, despite all the weird and dark stuff happening. 

The ending is this big cinematic operatic spectacle, and I have no idea why that final closeup on Pugh made me cry this time. I seriously can't explain it.

Name: Barbie
Review:
Barbie is not the first product placement movie or even the first toy brand movie. Even something like Toy Story eventually led to Disney selling actual toys with the characters (some of them were existing toys there too, including Barbie and Ken themselves). So, what I mean is that it feels reductive to cancel out a movie like this as just a toy commercial. What Michael Bay did with the Transformers movies qualifies as just a toy commercial, with on-your-face product placement and very formulaic and lazy writing (the Bayhem is always cool to watch ngl). But films like The Lego Movie and Barbie, though they are also there to sell toys, have so much thought and creativity fed into them, and I love these movies and can't cancel them out as toy ads; they're cinema. Don't you think it'd have been easier for Gerwig to make something more generic for a toy commercial than the weird meta-satire that we got here that looks and feels different than your typical Hollywood blockbuster? 

My rewatch of Barbie didn't really make me like it any less. I was still smiling or laughing through most of the movie. I still think the ending is rushed and that the movie was a bit confused on how to conclude the parallel threads involving Barbie's existential crisis and the patriarchy satire involving the Kens, with the Ken arc feeling a bit more complete as a result. But this time, I did notice another thing. The mother-daughter relationship between Sasha and her mom is very underwritten and surface-level. The movie was already being a meta-satire and a self-discovery movie at the same time, and developing the Sasha-Mom arc would've affected the pacing and length for sure, but also, after beautifully exploring such a relationship in Lady Bird, it was surprising to see Greta being so basic with it. (Yes, this is louder and weirder than something like Lady Bird, but yk)

Other than that, Barbie is still sweet, hilarious, self-aware, and intelligent in what it wants to be. SUBLIMEEEEEEEE!

Name: La La Land
Review:
I'm in love with how La La Land uses music and how it separates between fantasy and reality. I thought about it more after realizing that there's an entire stretch of La La Land where it just STOPS being a musical. It ditches the fantastical style it had so far and the musical numbers. This happens after we see Mia and Seb in their most comfortable state, singing City of Stars together. Afterwards, Seb gets too involved with the band and neglects the person and the music he had loved the most. A song is still there during this stretch, but it's John Legend's "Start a Fire", a song that doesn't fit in with the rest of the La La Land soundtrack, which is also not shot with the flair of fantasy and magic that the rest of the songs have. Mia and Sebastian hold anger, resentment, doubt, and insecurities in their minds during this whole stretch, and La La Land doesn't give songs to any of these darker emotions, only the good stuff, even if it's bittersweet sadness.

 

Every Mia-Seb argument or interaction during this stretch is not accompanied by music; they feel more realistic in style. Their meet-cute was musical, their romance was musical, but their arguments aren't. The movie shifts back into a musical again only when Mia starts giving her audition. This time too, the emotion is love, but it's her love for art. And then La La Land becomes musical one final time for that epilogue, where it shows the "What could've been?" of Mia and Seb. We feel the love, the longing, the yearning, and the bittersweet melancholy. Afterwards, Mia and Seb share a glance. There's complete silence. The music starts building up once they start smiling at each other, conveying beautifully that though they couldn't be happy together, they're happy for each other. Cinema, my friends!
This is one sweet heartbreak that I'd revisit over and over and never get tired of. 

I love you Damien Chazelle 
I love you Emma Stone
I love you Ryan Gosling
I love you Justin Hurwitz

Name: The Place Beyond the Pines
Review: The film is a tragedy that spans multiple generations, and yet it doesn't feel like something sad and sombre, and I mean this as a compliment. It's shot and crafted gorgeously, the acting is amazing, and the music is beautiful. Derek Cianfrance has structured the whole thing beautifully. The film does this thing where the perspective switches from one character to another and becomes their own story until another switch happens. The way that shift happens is brilliant. Even though I've had the Ryan Gosling storyline spoiled to me years ago, watching it with the knowledge of what happens affected me much more. Even as the film ended, what I felt was a feeling of warmth and a hope that the ripples created by the mistakes these men made would finally end.

Name: Blue Valentine
Review:
"How do you trust your feelings when they can just disappear like that?" "I think the only way you can find out is to have the feeling."
Blue Valentine broke my heart. With the kind of non-linear structure and dialogue it sets at the beginning, it's pretty obvious where it's headed, and the fact that it's obvious makes it even more heartbreaking. Blue Valentine ends up being Memento for sad people by the end. The editing and cinematography are so brilliant, the writing, directing and performances are amazing and the music is beautiful. And that beautiful end credits sequence with the fireworks and beautiful pictures of them together is like putting salt on a would. I mean.. You already had me crying bro 😭

Name: Drive-Away Dolls
Review: Turned out to be a nothing movie by the end. It did have a lot of potential to be an absurd lesbian buddy movie. But it turns out to be a lot of great ideas executed not so effectively. And the Coens were always about great execution. Loved the cast, the occasional subversions and I did chuckle at times. The movie didn't bore me either.

Name: Anchakkallakokkan
Review:
Anchakkallakokkan was a fun theater watch. Both the action setpieces were awesome; the music was cool, the acting was good, the cinematography looked gorgeous, and I was digging the unique style of it all. The writing had room for improvement, and some narrative choices could've been handled better. But anyway, it was stylish and fun. 

To put the coolness of the movie into perspective, there's a dude who dances while he's fighting multiple dudes. While that's something we've all seen before in some form, this is a pretty gritty and nasty fight, and this dude continues to dance even as he's getting beaten up. He's in pain, but he's grooving with psy-trance music in the background. Genuine badass. Both the action setpieces made great use of the space (or arena) they're set in, with some well-executed violence and gore and great choreography. Great action sequences are always a joy to watch.

Name: Road House
Review:
Jake Gyllenhaal is the kind of actor who'd look cool in almost anything; even if it's just a one-dimensional Marvel villain, I can never get tired of seeing a Jake Gyllenhaal performance. I'm biased about Road house that way too.

I haven't seen the Patrick Swayze original, but the premise here isn't something revolutionary. It's the same old badass drifter hero becoming the savior of a small town story (or a small town bar and book store in this case). Road house reminded me more of South Indian action movies than 80s American action movies. The sensibilities and the buildups all belong right in a movie someone like Lokesh Kanagaraj would make. I mean this in a positive way. Road house doesn't pretend to be serious, gritty, or layered. It's a formulaic action movie that's aware of what it's supposed to do and just unapologetically does it.

The way Gyllenhaal's character was presented was really cool. He's like Ted Lasso, if Ted Lasso broke bones and gave concussions. He explains the injuries he's about to inflict or has already inflicted; he's very chill, soft-spoken, and gentle, like his entire demeanor is the opposite of how such tough guys and action heroes in movies usually are. And it works. He has a very basic flashback, but the movie is smart enough to not give him any more depth or backstory than he actually needs for a movie like this. Except in the flashback, Dalton, the main character, doesn't even raise his voice in the movie, even when he has a big transformation towards the end and snaps. I dig it. And like I said, it's always fun to watch Jake Gyllenhaal Jake Gyllenhaaling. 

Gyllenhaal has put in a lot of effort to look and move like a UFC fighter here, though. But occasionally the movie does do him dirty, as the CGI used to make the impacts seem real occasionally looks janky and weird. Road house can't quite pull off the kinetic style that the Kingsman movies had with similar action scenes at times. That made me feel like they should've just avoided putting in that extra effort to show punches making contact and done it the old-fashioned way, which would've, ironically, maybe even made the fights look more real. There are several moments where the action choreography, stunt performance, CGI, cinematography, and style come together great, and the effort put in to show the impacts does work, but I just wish it was consistent.

Conor McGregor is a limited actor, but they kind of understood that and made his character as weird as possible. So everything he does just adds to the weirdness. He's obviously great during the action sequences since he's an actual UFC fighter, and he comes off as a formidable threat against the main character.

Anyway, this was a fun watch; it felt more like watching a fun Tamil or Malayalam action movie than a Hollywood movie.

Name: You'll Never Find Me
Review: The idea here is brilliant, the sound design, the acting and the filmmaking does everything to build up the tension and creepiness. The payoff to the entire thing is brilliant too, but still, even at just 1.5 hours, it felt 30 minutes too long. Some of the ramblings by the main character go on for way too long, and though those rants have some information that becomes important later, there's too much of them. Still though, with a single location and just two actors, the people behind this film do pull off creating effective psychological horror thrills to an extend.

Name: The Goat Life
Review:
I haven't read the original Aadujeevitham novel. The film itself is not without its flaws, but it did make me feel things. The film effectively conveys Najeeb's isolation, his helplessness, and everything he goes through because of Blessy's skill at portraying emotionally heavy moments and a brilliant performance from Prithviraj.

I wouldn't call Aadujeevitham a fast-paced film, but it did feel rushed at times. Things that should've been given more time to develop are often rushed, and in contrast to the desert narrative that seemed grounded, the flashbacks set in Kerala felt very "pretty". As in, Blessy is someone who has beautifully portrayed both a rural Malayali family in Kaazcha and an urban Malayali family in Thanmathra, so it was surprising that Najeeb's village and family seemed, idk, "foreign" and distant. The flashbacks looked like they belonged to another movie; even Amala Paul's character did. But I did get the parallels the movie was trying to make through them with the desert-water transitions. And there's always the possibility that these flashbacks look so pretty and filmy from the Najeeb we see in the desert because it's his dream version of what his life at home was like as he gets trapped into being a goat herder.

Prithviraj was brilliant throughout and did wonders in carrying the film and conveying everything Najeeb goes through. Whether it's the scene where he sees his face after a long time or when he struggles to get words out of his mouth because he hasn't had a proper conversation with a human being for a long time, there were several moments where the movie made me tear up. The physical and mental exhaustion, how he gives up hope several times and yet pushes on, and how he eventually survives—the journey is riveting, and the desert survival portion is my favorite part of the movie, though towards the end, Aadujeevitham seemed to be in a hurry to wrap everything up.

The makeup, prosthetics, and production design looked great. There are several shots of Najeeb's foot that are still stuck in my head. The CGI was inconsistent at times, especially in two instances involving vultures and a sandstorm. The cinematography succeeds in making the desert look gorgeous and terrifying. A. R. Rahman's score started kicking in for me more towards the second half desert episode.

Anyway, Blessy's Aadujeevitham did succeed in delivering a heart-tugging story of a person put through the unimaginable, with an amazing lead performance that does complete justice to the heaviness of the material. It did feel a bit rushed at times, and I'd like to believe that the village portions are not a part of this film (I'll buy the "Those were dreams" theory).

Name: Godzilla × Kong: The New Empire
Review:
Except for Gareth Edwards' first Godzilla movie and the campy Kong: Skull Island, all the other films in the MonsterVerse franchise have followed the same basic formula of having a bare minimum basic plot that the audience could care less about and then filling it up with plenty of CGI monster mayhem. So I go into these movies expecting the big monke and the big lizard to destroy stuff and fight other creatures, and that's what's delivered. Godzilla x Kong : The New Empire, in that way, really understands that the human characters are the least important parts of these movies and might be the film with the least amount of screentime for the humans.

The film is self-aware, though. I always feel that a self-aware dumb movie is better than a dumb movie that pretends to be serious and deep. It's aware of what the audience wants from it, does exactly that, and embraces its campiness way more than its predecessor. Dan Stevens even says something like "While we're randomly throwing shit at the wall" in the middle of an exposition dump. Stevens is a great addition to the cast, though, with his Jeff Goldblum from Jurassic Park energy. Both he and Brian Tyree Henry are dependable charismatic comedic reliefs, though they don't get much screentime to shine (look at me, complaining about the lesser amount of human screentime in a monster movie). Rebecca Hall, an amazing actress, is once again restricted to just being there to deliver expositional dialogue. Kaylee Hottle, too, doesn't have much to do than being your typical "chosen one" character. 

Like I said, this time, the human plot is extremely thin, both in screentime and otherwise. Even the main cast is way smaller than previous MonsterVerse films, though focusing on just a group of four characters going through a jungle adventure, has more of a campy adventure movie vibe than some of the other MonsterVerse films and the previous Godzilla vs. Kong, which took themselves too seriously at times. This one is closer to Kong: Skull Island in terms of embracing the silliness that way. Kong emotes a lot this time too, with even some well-placed smiles and smirks. Godzilla doesn't emote, though, which is a good decision. But this movie does show Godzilla diving from a mountain into the ocean like it's a swimming pool. Yeah, it's dumb, but it looks cool (which is basically the whole movie, lol). The final battle was a lot of fun, and Wingard does throw in twists like anti-gravity and various weapons and powers so that it looks vibrant and fun rather than just mindless, monotonous monster bashing. There's enough campy humor, and it's very fun. It's cool to look at, and the music too does its job well. 

Anyway, if you want a Big Monke and Big Lizard action movie that doesn't take itself seriously, this is exactly that. Also, the CGI animals in this movie still have more personality than Sandeep Reddy Vanga's protagonists.

Name: Lover
Review:
Lover is comparatively better than other movies in the "shitty men redeeming themselves" series of movies, which includes Love Today, Irugapatru, and the entire penile filmography of Sandeep Reddy Vanga. Lover is based around a toxic relationship where the man is constantly putting the woman through emotional abuse, controlling her, and manipulating her until she has had enough. 

The film begins brilliantly, with a flashback montage depicting their initial meet-cute and romance, immediately followed by the boyfriend, Arun, being at his absolute worst. The film does show Arun's POV more than the female protagonist Divya's. Arun is insecure; he's an underachiever; he comes from a broken home and is struggling to get his life in order. Compared to that, Divya is better settled and happier in life. But that doesn't excuse Arun's abusive behavior, though, as he channels his insecurities to make Divya's life hell. Every time Arun lets out the asshole in him, the film takes Divya's side. There's no attempt to justify or balance his abuse (like Love Today did), though the film doesn't show him as an absolute villain either.
