This is where this becomes a better written film, and a film like Animal feels like it was written using a penis. 

Manikantan and Sri Gouri Priya were brilliant as the leads, carrying the movie well. The supporting performances felt a bit uneven. The third act Gokarna stretch felt like it should have been shorter. There's even a genre shift at a point where, briefly, the film becomes a comedy where the asshole boyfriend is being roasted. 

Then there's the confusing ending. Though Lover doesn't end with the kind of redemption arc for the men that the other movies I mentioned above do and is still comparatively better, it is still way too kind to the dude and lets him off easy. I wish the ending had made it more absolutely clear that the movie is still on Divya's side. Because apparently there are people who, after seeing Arun being an absolute piece of shit for 140 minutes, still think he's a paavam and justify him. Deii.

Name: The Nice Guys
Review: Gosling peaked here and he's still peaking.

Name: Sometimes I Think About Dying
Review: While it doesn't reach the heights of something like Paul Thomas Anderson's Punch, Drunk, Love, which was also about a loner finding love, this movie did work for me for the most part. Set around the mundaneness and loneliness of an office job and an empty and lonely existence with only fantasies of dying in between, Daisy Ridley was amazing as the main character Fran, conveying her social anxiety and self-imposed isolation beautifully. This is a slow movie, deliberately so, because it wants us to feel how Fran experiences her days. I do admit I was a bit disconnected at times, but by the end it left a smile on my face. The scene where Fran finally decides to let people in, and really struggles to do so, was so fucking real. By the final shot I had a big wide smile on my face. Also, beautiful cinematography and music too.

Name: Teri Baaton Mein Aisa Uljha Jiya
Review: It's disappointing to watch a bad movie that could've been a great movie. TBMAUJ (I'm not even going to try to type the full title) is a human-robot love story with a really great concept that self-destructs by not getting its own point. Because it's not supposed to be a love story. The film so badly wants us to care about its protagonist, who's actually the villain of the story, and treats his red flags as mere "imperfections." The movie lacks the emotional and philosophical depth that something like Spike Jonze's her or even HBO's Westworld series had, so it's hard to buy the "love" here. The protagonist, Aryan, is basically a privileged man-child who looks down upon every woman he comes across because they're not up to his standards; this even includes his maid (don't ask if he himself is perfect, okay?). But the movie doesn't want us to hate this asshole and is a redemption story for him without addressing any of his privileged podcast bro traits. Eventually he meets and falls for Sifra the robot, played by Kriti Sanon, who not only looks absolutely gorgeous throughout the movie but also delivers a very convincing performance as a robot, finding that fine balance in just "seeming" human, making me think she'd fit right in with the cast of Westworld. The problem with Aryan's "love" is that, in something like Spike Jonze's her, Theodore and the AI Samantha actually connect with each other, have conversations, and form an emotional bond. We feel that the relationship is real, even though Samantha doesn't even have a body. But here, Aryan basically falls in "love" with Sifra only because she's hot and obeys all his commands perfectly. Even after supposedly falling in love, this dude still makes her his Siri and commands her to do stuff that she's programmed to never say no to. So he basically just wanted a gorgeous-looking girl who'd obey all of his commands, would never question him, and would attend to his personal and sexual needs without him having to provide anything in return except the electricity needed to keep her charged? Not a great look. Sifra is basically the kind of project that someone like Andrew Tate would invest in. The in-world logic of how Sifra works is pretty vague, so the movie always alternates between what kind of fictional AI she is—is she emotionless and task driven like The Terminator or does she have emotions like Chitti the Robo? Anyway, this would've been a far superior movie, or even the robot version of Barbie, if they had made Sifra the actual protagonist and Aryan the villain and addressed this toxic relationship properly and made it a satire. Instead, even as we see how fucked up everything Aryan does is, the movie still wants us to sympathize with him and his "emotions." Yes, towards the end, the movie spoonfeeds the message that an imperfect human is a better partner than a perfect robot who's programmed (or does it?). But also, it does this by never holding Aryan accountable for his actions; dude even delivers a monologue about love towards the end. What you had was never love, you deranged fuck! Kriti Sanon as Sifra deserved a way better movie. Her and the songs are the only saving graces here. Ironically, I'd still watch the sequel that's teased at the end just for her 🙈. Shahid Kapoor has been hell-bent on playing shitty men since encountering His Dickness Sandeep Reddy Vanga, I guess. There's a cameo towards the end when Shahid Kapoor actually connects with a real human girl (run, girl, run!) And as the shot cuts back from her to Kriti Sanon playing a robot, the difference between a bad actress and a great actress is so evident. (The stars are ONLY for Kriti and the music, btw.) Update: I just watched Companion and that's the movie that this one should've been.

Name: Aavesham
Review:
Both Aavesham and Jithu Madhavan's previous movie Romancham feel like heightened versions of real-life incidents that a dude will narrate in casual gatherings. Romancham without the actual existence of the supernatural felt like a compilation of lived-in experiences. Aavesham, too, seems like something that could've actually happened if we took out the larger-than-life gangster at the center. But the gangster Ranga, played to wacky and intimidating perfection by FaFaa, is where all the fun is.

There's a 2008 film named Drillbit Taylor, starring Owen Wilson, where some bullied high school kids hire an adult bodyguard to fight their bully. Aavesham's promotional material reminded me a lot of that film. But Aavesham doesn't quite go the same way, though there are a few similarities. The film still follows the perspective of three college students for the most part, and we see the gangster Ranga through their eyes. When Ranga is a clown to them, he's a clown; when Ranga makes them scared, he's terrifying and intimidating; and it's a joy to watch FaFaa do his thing, making Ranga seem like a goofy dude who could also murder you at any moment.

The film just lights up the moment Fahadh or Sajin Gopu as Ambaan come to the screen, with all kinds of jokes and fun sequences. Even when the film enters serious or emotional territories, or even, like Romancham, into horror, it doesn't stop being fun. An unexpected joke, one liner, or a moment of visual humor will still pop up, and the handling of tone that way is perfect in Aavesham. Ranga with his Kannada-Malayalam accent and mommy issues is a badass, a scary villain, a sad soul, and a goofy and cute idiot simultaneously. So the comparisons between Ranga and Mammootty's iconic Raajamanikyam are on point. Then there's Sushin Shyam's score and songs that are dependably cool in elevating the movie, Sameer Thahir's cinematography, Vivek Harshan's editing, and the great fight choreography. I just loved the way the fight scenes were shot and edited here, with a final setpiece that could belong right in a Lokesh Kanagaraj film.

In short, Aavesham gave me Romancham. Eda Mwoney FaFaa puliyaanu ketta!

With the Rajamanikyam parallels and that great Chotta Mumbai reference, Aavesham is a cool tribute to peak Anwar Rasheed in that way too.

Name: Varshangalkku Shesham
Review:
There are two types of cringe, according to my friend and me. There's good cringe and bad cringe. I won't try to explain that theory, but basically, Hridayam was entirely bad cringe for me, and Varshangalkk Shesham was more good cringe than bad cringe. The things that I hate about Hridayam are present in VS too: the hilariously bad instances of dialogue, flat drama, character transformations that are weird and sudden, over-simplification for feel-good purposes, plot conveniences because the movie has to movie and, of course, the cringe. But the thing is, while Hridayam was a marathon of bad cringe, VS has instances of genuine fun peppered throughout and a pair of likable protagonists whose friendship and chemistry just work, though it's not that deep when we think about it.

Pranav Mohanlal didn't make me believe for a second that he's a middle-class musician from a village or that he's a man in his early 70s; he still talks and behaves like the rich kid with an urban accent that we saw in Hridayam. But still, he's cute, charming, and likable, and he looked way better and more comfortable on screen than in Hridayam, like it's a way better performance than I expected, with even some opportunities to show off some comedic ability. Dhyan Sreenivasan was better at seeming like a village person and as an older man, though he too wasn't entirely consistent in playing the older person (the makeup and hair styling were excellent and did a lot of work, though). Then there's a huge ensemble of actors and cameos, with even some scenes that felt like they were written just so that a particular person could be included in this movie, and of course the Nivin Pauly cameo.

My favorite version of Vineeth Sreenivasan is the one that wrote the first half of Oru Vadakkan Selfie. It was like he himself wrote a spoof of Hridayam before he even made Hridayam. There's a quirky sense of humor there that I've missed a lot, and flashes of it are peppered throughout the second half of VS. There's a lot of self-awareness, meta jokes, and 4th wall breaks, and this would've been a way better film if it were entirely satire, because there are still serious scenes in this film that could belong in a spoof too. Anyway, the self-awareness and the various digs at film people, media, and influencers were fun, with Nivin Pauly as Nitin Molly doing what he does best, playing himself like if Umesh from Oru Vadakkan Selfie became a film star, with a hilarious scene that makes fun of the real life incident when fans cheered at a popular influencer abusing them in public (a lot of these references rely on how much context the viewer has of mallu social media too, though). Nitin Molly being a creep is an angle this movie could've avoided though. It's not funny and it just makes the character more confusing than a satire. 

Unlike Hridayam, which used the 15 beautiful songs to camouflage the cringe, here the songs are not that prominent. It does have a great background score, which, like other Vineeth Sreenivasan movies, makes a scene seem emotional no matter how superficial it is (except for the Veena tracks during the scenes with Kalyani Priyadarsan, which just made the cringe seem funnier). Anyway, VS is so much fun in a good cringe kind of way when it's self-aware and when it doesn't take itself seriously, and it ventures into bad cringe when it does.

In a world where Sandeep Reddy Vanga makes films about penises, I don't want to be too harsh towards some harmless, fun krinj.

Name: Sasneham Suhra
Review: Cute little moviee. Warm feels.

Name: Philip's
Review:
Your typical uchayoonu padam with pleasing aesthetics, peaceful music and some good performances (not all). There's a sitcomy comfort watch quality during the first half with the urban middle class single parent daily routine stuff, which is lost as the film enters melodramatic territory, which felt like it went on forever, though it's a pretty short movie. The drama felt weak and I couldn't connect with it the way the earlier portions felt. 

Hats off to Kalabhavan Joshiy's dubbing for the late Innocent which complimented the performance without feeling out of place, while watching Innocent on screen. The tribute at the end was also sweet.

Name: Civil War
Review:
I don't know what to think of Alex Garland's Civil War. On one hand, there's a lot of brilliant imagery, stellar direction, amazing cinematography, brilliant use of music and sound, and great performances. A lot of the sequences are thrilling and haunting, especially that chilling scene with Jesse Plemons.

It's about journalists putting themselves through dangerous situations to tell their stories during a fictional civil war in America and then asking, "At what cost?". Because they're spectators, they're helpless and powerless and can do nothing else than watch as people get murdered right in front of their eyes (and their cameras). We don't see why this war happened, and we don't know who's at fault. There's no good vs. bad. We just see how people at the ground level lose their lives and are put through trauma because somewhere someone had a conflict that they decided to "solve" with violence.

So, what is this movie about? Is it about the US getting a taste of their own medicine for what they've done to other countries? Or is it about just war in general, just placed in the US, just that war, whomever it's between, is just darkness and violence that never should happen in the first place? The Jesse Plemons scene does imply that the movie sees scary racist rednecks as evil, but also, as an Indian, I lack context about American politics. But I do know that if this movie was set in India and the right-wing Hindu Nationalists were not explicitly blamed for fucking up the country, and if that movie had the "everyone's bad" interpretation as a possibility, I'd hate that movie.

Name: Immaculate
Review:
It's another one of those "good for her" movies where the main character has to survive a traumatic situation, but blasphemy style! It's kinda implied that the movie is set in the early 2000s or so, but Sydney Sweeney still sounds too Gen Z. But she has less dialogue during the second half of the film, and it's mostly face-acting and screaming; she's brilliant in that area. I wasn't invested in Immaculate for the initial 30 minutes or so, but then it started getting fun. The fun I had was more of a pulpy kind than atmospheric horror. Because the film tries to generate some suspense and creepiness, I wasn't really immersed in the beginning. But once Sweeney's Cecilia is put through the central event of the film, then it gets more interesting. Alvaro Morte was also fun to watch as the evil version of what Andrew Scott was in Fleabag.

The finale is all kinds of violent, gory, pulpy fun. The gore looks great, the CGI, makeup and practical special effects in that area are perfect for the tone this film is going for. The finale in The Catacombs has some great horror filmmaking. But does the main character have it easy for her, despite her physically being in a condition where she can never outpower these people? Yup. But it was cool, and they actually went there! Those weapon choices though, amen!

Name: Late Night with the Devil
Review:
Whoa. Just when I thought The Conjuring movies and their spin-offs had milked demonic possession horror movies to the maximum, I got to see this unique gem of a horror film. Now, plotwise, it's a generic affair, but as a film, it's anything but. The whole thing is framed as a late-night TV show and its behind-the-scenes footage, and everything just makes sense, and the movie plays around with this format a lot, especially towards the end. The presentation format is not just a gimmick here; that's what makes it unique and sets it apart from other horror films with similar themes and even the same plot. The multi-camera TV show aesthetics and editing add a lot, and as things become weirder and scarier, the film also changes accordingly. The lower budget occasionally sticks out when CGI is involved, but the excellent filmmaking makes up for it. The production design, costumes, and atmospheric horror are excellent otherwise. David Dastmalchian is impressive in his first outing as a solo lead, with a great mix of showmanship and moral ambiguity. The rest of the cast was excellent too. This is not just a creepy and atmospheric movie; it's also pretty funny occasionally, and it's a satire on the media. 

Demonic possession movies are a hard sell these days because of the sheer amount of repeated content, but this small gem satire horror movie just managed to out-devil them all through sheer imagination and commitment to its vision.

Name: Monkey Man
Review:
Monkey Man is a revenge action film with a political backdrop. The politics is not as well integrated into the action narrative as something like Monkey Man's producer Jordan Peele's Get Out did. I also don't know how much of the film's anti-caste, anti-Islamophobia, and basically anti-Sangh politics was toned down to make the movie "safer", because during a key scene, saffron flags and banners are so clearly edited to be red, while some other scenes do have saffron flags and banners. It's kinda funny. There's a lot of Hindu mythology references too, a lot of references to Hanuman of course and Ramayana, but since the villains of the movie are, you know who, the way Hanuman is placed here becomes a lot different from how Ram was placed in RRR. If you think the villains were too over the top here, just listen to one of Narendra Modi's speeches from the 2024 election campaign.

Anyway, like I said, this is primarily a revenge action movie that tries to mix in some serious political themes with mixed results. But even with that, this film didn't get an Indian theatrical release (were they scared or what?). And now as the elections are happening in India, the film is available on digital.

The action is well choreographed and shot, with Dev Patel taking style cues from what Gareth Evans did in the Raid movies. The action and the violence are visceral; there's blood, biting, mutilation, effective use of crunch sound effects, and a real sense of pain. Patel's fictional Indian city of Yatana works like a John Wick-ish hub world with its own logic and culture rather than seeming like any real-life Indian city. The music choices are really great, as were the overall aesthetic choices in the film. Patel carries the film confidently as an actor too, though his character is as thinly written as he's ferocious. The main character is defined only by his goal of getting revenge, and he's not alone. Almost every character in Monkey Man can be defined by a single line. But the main character is an oppressed person getting revenge against his oppressor, so there's that. 

Monkey Man didn't get an Indian release, though I felt it played safer with its politics than I thought it would. It's still a good watch, though. I don't know if such films would be allowed to exist in India again, so hat tip to the British-Indian dude for that.

Name: Stockholm
Review: Lots of fun visual humor with some heart. It has a short and simple storyline that made me both smile and laugh.

Name: Love Lies Bleeding
Review: It's sexy stuff. The style, the use of colors, the way it's edited, the performances, the music, the occasional surrealism—it was all awesome. Plus, this might be the first time that I've seen muscle-body horror. I've seen the Hulk transformations in Marvel movies, but this is something else. One of the main characters, Jackie's muscles, do some weird things in this movie, and the visual effects and the sound design are effectively in body horror territory. The way the movie handles violence is also very interesting. The sound design makes every hit seem gruesome, and when Jackie bashes someone open with her bare hands, we feel the impact. There's also a great moment involving a silenced gunshot. But as much as muscles and blood are involved, love is too. Because this is essentially a love story between Lou and Jackie, wrapped in a crime drama. Kristen Stewart as Lou is amazing here, and she carries this movie the most. Tbh, I did disconnect a bit during the third act; the arc involving Ed Harris' dad character didn't really get the payoff that it was set up to have. But even then, the leads had great chemistry, I was digging the whole style of it that Rose Glass was going for, and this was a jacked movie.

Name: Aavesham
Review:
This is not an opinion on the film. This is just an appreciation for Rangannan being a 10/10. Characters like Rangan happen very rarely, and he's more special than we realize. He's a lot more than just a spoof character, because Ranga has so much more dimensions and vibrancy than a one-note mommy-issues gangster character like Rocky Bhai. Ranga is a mix of a wide range of quirky characteristics and character beats, which the film could turn into dramatic character development instantly.

Take, for instance, Ranga's own mommy issues. When Ambaan narrates the story of Ranga's mom leaving him and then later tells the story of how Ranga stopped hitting people when his mother died, the tone there is goofy. It's not presented in the same melodramatic register as the mommy issues in something like KGF or Raajamanikyam; even the boys don't feel any sympathy for Ranga and dismiss it as one of Ambaan's "thallu". We see a glimpse of Ranga's vulnerable mommy-issues side when Bibi's mom calls afterwards (with that KGF mommy-issues ringtone for added effect), but it's only towards the end that we see him break down and express his remorse about losing his mother and disappointing her. It kind of kills Ranga that these three boys saw this side of his, but his mother never did. But the fun here is that even as this vulnerable side of Ranga, which we never saw till then, is revealed, Ranga is still funny, the tone is still that of a comedy, and Aavesham manages to get laughs out of Ranga's vulnerability too.

We see Ranga through the boys' eyes, and that's why Ranga works too. Because Ranga doesn't really change much over the course of the film, only the boys' perception of him does. This is an entirely different film through Ranga's eyes. The boys don't take Ranga seriously at first, or at least they feel safe around him. They don't take Ambaan's stories seriously, and though they're aware that Ranga is a gangster, they choose to be ignorant about the extent of his violence. Ranga himself is goofy enough to make things easier. Ranga has many whimsical qualities, be it the way he claps and cheers like a child, the way he gives a "tataa", the way he gets very animated and jumps around when he's frustrated, his Instagram reels. He makes it tough for the boys as outsiders to take him seriously, and the audience has the same perspective too. The shift happens after Ranga does what the boys expected him to do, that is, beat up their senior bullies and the boys get a reality check about their college education. Now Ranga is a liability to them; to add to that, he puts their lives in danger during the mall action sequence and then gives them a "tataaa" like they just went to a theme park.

When the boys' perception of Ranga changes, Ranga becomes scarier; in the Dumb Charades scene, the boys realize he could be a threat to their own lives too, and then afterwards, they fear for their lives more and just want to escape. But Ranga had always been the same guy, and that's the fun part of the character creation. The boys already knew Ranga had slashed Ambaan during Dumb Charades; they already knew Ranga and his gang walk around with deadly weapons; they just chose to only see him as this goofy guy they could exploit into getting free booze and protection from their college seniors. For Ranga, this itself was the appeal; the boys didn't see him with the fear and respect that the others around him did.

Ranga has a very lonely existence that way, where he's unsure if these people would be around him if he didn't have the money and power. It takes the movie just a few minutes to establish this fact, and everything becomes clear then. Ranga just wanted friends who hung out with him because they thought he was cool, not because he's "Rangannan". To Ranga, the boys were just that, until they weren't. When Bibi tells Ranga that they too only needed Rangannan the gangster and not Ranga the friend, and that they never considered him a friend and even wanted him dead, Ranga unravels. And as darkly humorous as this scene is, I'm not completely sure if Ranga wouldn't have killed the boys, but this sad and dark situation is shown with a brilliant touch of dark humor. Then Bibi's mom calls once again. It's established pretty early on that Bibi's mom talks to everyone the same way, she tells them that Bibi has talked about them to her, and she asks them if they're happy. When she interacts the same way with Shaanthan initially, Shaanthan is just confused. But with Ranga, the lack of warm or positive affirmation—"Are you happy?"—in his life is pretty evident. It's the most genuine, unconditional, and loving thing he's heard, and he really believes that he's a brother to Bibi. He even started asking the boys if they were happy after that first call with Bibi's mom. There's a great conflict happening within Ranga at this point because just a few scenes ago, the boys saw him about to kill his north Indian fighters for trying to escape (though we later learn that Ranga forgave them too), and he just killed his own mentor a while ago. Ranga generally operates on this plane of aggression and violence as far as the boys know and not the one that involves love and empathy. So by the film's end, Ranga learns to forgive and become an absurd guardian angel to the kids instead of a terrible influence, just because Bibi's mom talked to him like she does with every random dude her son interacts with, just because Ranga lacked love and genuine connections in his life, though he doesn't also realize that Ambaan loves him differently than the rest of his goons, which is pretty evident when Ambaan stays frozen when Ranga says he has no one.

Ranga is an amazing character creation, and the more I think about him, everything about him makes sense. He's a darkly humorous anti-hero that we can laugh at and sympathize with. He can come off as a badass and a psychopath. So saying Ranga is a spoof of a one-note inferior character like Rocky Bhai is an insult to Ranga. Rocky never knew the sorrow of not getting likes on Instagram. And Rocky's idapazhakal with women wasn't as good as Rangannan.

Name: Argylle
Review:
Unlike other generic streaming service action movies like Red Notice, Ghosted, and that whole bunch, Argyle actually had a solid and unique premise, a great plot, and plenty of fun twists and turns. So I imagine that the source material novel is a great fun read, but this isn't a great adaptation of its potential. With someone like Matthew Vaughn at the helm, such an interesting storyline, and an all-star cast, the fact that this turned out to be a disappointment is a big surprise. 

There are instances of Vaugh's stylistic flair in the film, in some scene transitions, the way fiction blends with reality in the train scene, and the overall energy the film had. But the action wasn't as memorable as the ones in the Kingsman movies. It's not just a case of Vaughn not doing R-rated violence, though, because he had done great PG-13 violence in X-Men First Class. Here, the action and the visual effects ruin a lot of moments that could've been a lot more exhilarating, including the CGI cat. The train sequence and the oil skating sequence are the only ones that are memorable. The performances are great, with Howard and Rockwell having great chemistry with each other. 

But this cast and this source material deserved a way better movie. If this was executed as well as Kingsman, the source material here was way better than Kingsman, with a lot of playful subversions of spy movie tropes. There are fun ideas peppered throughout that I wish were part of a superior film. I don't know if the sequels are still happening, but there's enough potential here that I still believe Vaughn can make gold out of this world and this material.

Name: Malayalee from India
Review:
**സ്‌പോയിലർ ഭയമുള്ള മലയാളികൾ ഇംഗ്ലീഷിലുള്ളത് വായിക്കാതിരിക്കുക, മലയാളികൾക്ക് മാത്രം വേണ്ടിയുള്ള സ്‌പോയിലർ അലേർട്ട്**

Sharis Muhammed and Dijo Jose Antony return with yet another collab that treats serious and sensitive socio-political themes with the weight, depth, and strength of a kaachiya pappadam. Paavam Nivin does a lot of heavy lifting here with his cuteness, comedic timing, and charisma, but even that's killed by the fact that his character is a sanghi. It's a Sanghi redemption tale that's so half-assed. A well-intentioned satire to promote secularism while the country is more divided than ever before is something that I'd accept with my whole heart. But I just can't here. They can't even show hinduthva terror with conviction when they always balance it out with the Muslim side doing something shitty and balancing it out with "both are the same, bro." Which is such a huge oversimplification of the current communal scenario in India that I'd rather call the movie Erappali From India.

The second half is the redemption part of our sanghi, and here I could actually appreciate Nivin's cuteness and charm because apparently he's no longer a sanghi like before. The chemistry with the Pakistani character was alright. But whenever the movie got serious, it fell hard into cringe territory again. Yeah, Gopi predictably bonds with the Pakistani, understands humanity is above religion, and becomes a new, responsible man. But is he still a Sanghi? Does he fully renounce what the Sangh stands for? His Hindutva terrorist friend is all cute and funny in the second half, and he's still his friend. Despite being a "political" movie that promotes secularism, all these things are left hanging, while Muslim terror is questioned seriously till the very end. The way the situation in the village is resolved is also hilarious (in a bad way). A lot of dialogue and scenes are hilariously bad, and even funnier than the intended comedy scenes. And that Malayali in ISIS representation and how it's placed, dude, this is how you wanted to showcase the pride of being a malayali? In 2024? The film becomes a lot less about Hindutva terror by the end, as the Hindutva terrorists become cute and silly buffoons. And to top it off, by the end, this was a Malala origin story where Malala praises the former(?) sanghi from God's Own Country for inspiring her to fight for the right to education for girls in Pakistan. Phew.

Anyway, enough ranting. I don't know why the movie devoted a considerable amount of screentime to Gopi creeping on a girl half his age. So I randomly threw that here, just like the movie did.

One star, because there's only one star here, that's Nivin. Ottaykk vazhi vettiyavane pattikkunnoda!

Name: Nadikar
Review:
I've always felt that showing art within art is pretty risky. Because when you show a "great" movie, a "great" song, or a "great" performance within the context of the film, those have to seem great or at least some degree of "good" to the audience as well, otherwise, the disconnect would be massive for the audience. In Imtiaz Ali's Rockstar, A. R. Rahman's album is as important as the writing and filmmaking to sell the fact that Janardhan becomes Jordan the Rockstar, the illusion is lost if the songs fall flat. In The Marvellous Mrs. Maisel, every time Midge Maisel gets on stage and delivers a hilarious stand-up act that the audience loves and everyone thinks is brilliant, they've managed to have Rachel Brosnahan perform these amazing stand-up sets as the character that always sells the fact that she's an amazing comic. They pull this off for the entirety of the show, which is something I think is an amazing achievement. On the other hand, we have something like Udayanaanu Thaaram, where the climax works not because the audience thinks Udayabhanu's film within a film that we're watching is a brilliant work of art, or because the film sells that Saroj Kumar's performance on screen is brilliant (it isn't); the ending works because we've seen the protagonist Udayabhanu lose for 90% of the movie, and this is his big win after all that buildup, so in this case, this payoff is enough for us to forgive the fact that "Annu Peytha Mazhayil" doesn't look like a great movie.

Nadikar suffers from an art within art issue. There's one more plug I wish to include, and it's the HBO series Barry. In Barry, there's a scene where the contract killer protagonist, who's also an acting student, acts out a scene. He has been a wooden and terrible actor up to this point, but for this particular scene, he's made to channel his past trauma and darkness to deliver it, and it results in him having a breakdown on stage and then getting applause afterwards. This scene works perfectly, not just because of Bill Hader's amazing performance but also because of the great buildup and filmmaking. The fact that Barry is a bad actor is established well, and when he channels into his personal trauma and then transforms, it just works.

Nadikar is about superstar David Padikkal, who, after a few hits, fails to maintain his career momentum, and it's further revealed to him that he might not be that good an actor, though he doesn't want to believe it himself. So the film basically becomes about David discovering his craft and learning to stay grounded as a person rather than as a privileged dickhead. It's a solid premise, ripe for a character study or a coming-of-age film, that sabotages itself by trying to be too many things at once. Either this could've been a longer series with all of these subplots included, or it could've just focused on the important stuff.

Tovino does a great job as David, and I felt the reason why David's transformation from a meh actor to a great actor as the film progresses wasn't that well registered because we didn't see enough of David being a bad actor or a wooden actor. Or the things we did see were too subtle for an audience member to recognize as bad performances. There are moments like the scene where David calls his ex and vents out his frustrations and insecurities where we see glimpses of what Nadikar could've been. It could've been more about this lonely and insecure man trying to mask his fragility while the fragile career he built is about to become dust. Instead, the film wanders around at times, unsure about what it is. Even the relationship between David and his acting coach, Bala, played by Soubin, could've been more interesting than what we saw on screen. Even David's eventual redemption seemed rushed and sudden, and while the part where David mixes his personal trauma and art together was nice as an idea, the results were mixed. 

There are also some satirical elements and references to Malayalam cinema pop culture. I've never thought I'd live to see the day when I'd hear director Ranjith say, "Manjinte Andi!". Lots of actors, cinema people, and Manjummel Boys are packed in here too in tiny cameos and supporting roles, including three former Bigg Boss Malayalam contestants, out of whom the dude who played David's watchman is clearly a terrible actor. I mean, seriously, why tf is that social pest in this movie? Did he blackmail someone or something? Or was his inclusion some meta joke that I didn't understand? The dialogue has lots of modern Malayalam slang words and even some modern slurs. Out of which, the casteist/classist slur that David calls Bala was at least used in the right context, but I thought I heard David's assistant Lenin (Balu Varghese) say a homophobic slur word very casually during a scene too (I'm not sure though), and it's not really addressed in the movie (it was not funny as a joke either). The dialogues sounded inconsistent at times and were occasionally not legible; idk if that was a recording issue or something.

Anyway, Nadikar is an artist's coming-of-age tale with a super cool soundtrack, great costumes, pretty visuals, a great lead performance, some fun scenes, a lot of potential, and writing and filmmaking that didn't do justice to that potential. Still, I didn't feel it was as bad as I thought it'd be after seeing the initial negative reception. Nadikar had all the potential to become Malayalam's Bojack Horseman. But nope. 

Also, just like how Hollywood films are allowed a single "fuck" and retain a PG-13 age rating, Malayalam movies can now have a single "myr/myre" and retain a U or U/A rating? Both the new Malayalam releases that I saw this week are single myr movies.

Name: Amar Singh Chamkila
Review:
Amar Singh Chamkila is a terrific example of getting creative with a biopic. The way it's structured is brilliant. It begins by showing its subject getting killed. The rest of the film unfolds as flashbacks as people discuss Chamkila, his life, his career, his love, and what eventually led to his demise. Rather than unfolding as a traditional biopic, this structure allows Imtiaz Ali to unleash his creative force in interesting ways. The characters are not just reciting Chamkila's story here; they have interesting commentary and opinions about the man and the events too. The film alternates through different perspectives this way, and there are also other stylistic flourishes like the cool montages, the use of animation, art, and graphics, the changing aspect ratios, the use of split screens, showing archive footage, and pictures of the real Chamkila. The film is filled with such touches that it kept me glued to the screen. So many sequences are so brilliantly executed. 

Diljit Dosanjh carried the film with so much grace and energy. As I mentioned above, the film is more like people remembering what they know about Chamkila than us seeing an intimate or in-depth version of Chamkila. But even then, the performance is amazing, and the writing does a great job at balancing between the myth and the person. Chamkila's songs had dirty lyrics and sexual innuendo, and he was killed by people who were apparently "preserving culture". The politics of censorship and intolerance are pretty relevant even now, when people are abused verbally and physically for not adhering to the "culture" in India. More violence and inhumane cruelty happen in the name of this culture than in defiance of it.

Chamkila's lyrics deserved criticism, not violence. And he was not the only artist who wrote such songs; he just didn't exist in a place of privilege. I've read criticisms that the film doesn't properly address the caste POV in Chamkila's story. But I don't have enough insight or know enough about the actual person to talk about that. But even today, people like Sandeep Reddy Vanga are actually praised and celebrated for spewing misogyny by the elite themselves too, so there's that. 

A. R. Rahman's soundtrack and the way this movie was edited also have all of my love.

Name: Godzilla Minus One
Review:
It's been a long time since I've seen a monster movie where the humans matter more than the CGI monster. Godzilla Minus One, despite what the posters look like, is a story about people rather than the monster. Godzilla is just a threat here, and it's a huge, terrifying threat too. This film works more like a war movie, with the real-life point of view of a war-torn Japan mixed in. It's about people trying to survive after the trauma of the second world war and then facing the new threat in the form of this colossal monster.

Godzilla looks, moves, and operates like a force of pure destruction here. It's scary, even in its smaller form in the first scene. There are several touches, like how its atomic breath charges up, how its body burns afterwards, and the way it regards humans as mere bugs, that just add to the terror. The slow lead up to the atomic breath works perfectly to build drama in the film. Godzilla's only in four scenes or something in this film, but less is better in this case because this film really wants us to care about the humans, their relationships, their emotions, and their character journeys, especially that of the protagonist Shikishima, than wait for the next time Godzilla would appear. And it does work. The emotional arcs and payoffs are familiar, but they're executed effectively and with heart. We really do feel like rooting for these characters; their trauma, desperation, and eventual courage are portrayed well. The climatic setpiece was also nicely executed, with director Takashi Yamazaki pulling off the emotional beats and dramatic payoffs beautifully. The ending here is large-scale filmmaking at its best, and even there, the humans do the cool stuff and not the monster.

The amazing visual effects and music have all my love too. The classic Godzilla theme music pops up at the perfect moments in this film. The visual effects were very cool throughout and are even more impressive when considering the fact that this had a way lower budget than your average Hollywood blockbuster. The shots of Godzilla on water were very cool. The creature design was on point, too!

Name: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
Review:
On revisiting Rise after watching the entire Trilogy, it feels like Rise set a solid foundation for its successors to build upon. The visual effects still holds up after all these years, though both Dawn and War then took it to new heights of photorealism. What I love the most about the Apes Trilogy is that they're not spectacle driven or event driven, they're character driven. This is true in the case of Rise too. I remember that this film was marketed by leaning heavily on the big climatic stand-off. But the film is anything but an action spectacle. It's still focused on Caesar and telling his story. Being the shortest entry in the Trilogy, Rise is still a bit rushed, but even then it works both as a great setup to Caesar's bigger character journey and as a stand-alone prequel to the original Planet of the Apes. 

In Rise, Andy Serkis only gets a few moments to shine as Caesar, because Rise doesn't really lean into his performance that much the way Dawn and War do later. But they made the right call in making Caesar front and center in the later movies and really focusing on Andy Serkis to pull of the drama. Because, as much as I love Rise, the human characters in Rise were.. Yk..

Name: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
Review:
For me Dawn is perfection. Caesar begins as a pet, then he's put in a cage, and then he becomes a revolutionary, becomes the people's leader, and then eventually becomes their Messiah. It's one of the most compelling character arcs in cinema. And Dawn is the first film where I've felt that the actor that drives the CGI character deserves an Oscar or all the acting awards that exists. Sure, a character like Caesar is a combination of the artistry of both Andy Serkis and the animators, but still, you can clearly feel that there's an actor that belongs with the greats who's driving the performance. The way Caesar carries himself and the way he communicates and acts is so different from the Caesar we saw in Rise, Caesar has Don Corleone energy now, and yet, we can see that he's still the same ape from before too. The leap in the visual effects is also evident in Dawn as it achieves photorealism most of the time and Matt Reeves is able to pull off these amazing close up shots. 

That's the other thing about Dawn that's different from Rise. There are far more closeups of Apes, and this is a more Ape driven film than a human driven film. Even then the human characters in Dawn are better than the humans in Rise. The human - ape conflict is well developed, with the arc of a vengeful Koba being carried over from Rise. Koba himself is a great villain, who has every reason to hate humans and be afraid of them. Toby Kebbel does a great job as Koba here too. 

Dawn is also a character driven drama, though we also get a monkey riding a horse with a machine gun along with it too. The film looks absolutely beautiful, the cinematography is gorgeous, Matt Reeves stages these amazing cinematic moments, and Michael Giacchino's score is also great. And that final shot of Caesar being embraced by his people that zooms into his eyes is!!!!!!!!!!!!!

Name: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
Review:
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes is a worthy successor to the Caesar Trilogy and lays enough groundwork for interesting stories in the future. It doesn't pack the punch that the previous trilogy had, and I felt Proximus Caesar as a villain was underused, though he was great in the few scenes he did get.

Firstly, the visual effects. Wow. Each time I think an Apes film has reached absolute photorealism, the team at Weta Digital goes ahead and proves me wrong. It's hard to explain how this looks superior to War for the Planet of the Apes, which itself was stunning, but here, the fur, the skin, the teeth, and even the saliva look real. During some wide shots, they just seem like real apes or people in costumes, like in the old-school ape films. There's also all kinds of stunning water effects being showcased, a step forward from the amazing water visual effects Weta already innovated for Avatar: Way of the Water.

Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes is stunning to look at; the cinematography and visual sensibilities carry over from what Matt Reeves did with Dawn and War. Kingdom also uses a lot of closeup shots of the apes, and the improved photorealism makes these closeups even more impressive. Wes Ball's post-apocalyptic ape planet does feel like a natural extension of what came before, with a lot of interesting detailing.

Noa is our protagonist this time around, and I liked that even though Noa is a chimp who looks similar to Caesar in appearance, they have made him a lot different from Caesar. Noa is not a Caesar rehash; his personality, goals, and the way he operates are different. But still, Kingdom is less of a character-driven piece than the previous Apes Trilogy, and hence, Noa does lack the depth that Caesar had. Sometimes he just feels like a traditional "good guy" hero character, but this can be fixed in future installments. The human played by Freya Allan is also plain as a character, though her performance is great. The intention here was to make the human seem mysterious, but the result ends up being a character that lacks personality. Proximus Caesar didn't have as much screen time as I thought he would, and it seemed like a missed opportunity to pull off another Koba or even the dude Tim Roth played in the Tim Burton movie (yeah, I don't hate Tim Burton's Planet of the Apes that much).

Cast performances were great though; Owen Teague as Noa could indeed carry the franchise forward, and like I said above, Kevin Durand as Proximus felt underutilized. That one scene where he hypes up the other apes with Caesar propaganda was amazing.

Caesar wished for peace; he just wished for apes to live and prosper independently. So of course, generations later, when he's seen as a Messiah, there are other apes who twist his words and use them to oppress and divide others. At least religion works the same for both apes and humans, which is something I wish Wes Ball's new trilogy would explore further. I am interested to see how they develop this storyline in future installments, though.

Name: Abigail
Review:
I just wish they promoted Abigail like how Jordan Peele promotes his movies, so that I could've watched it fresh. Because it seems to be made that way to be watched with a fresh mind. But since everyone knows from the posters and promos that this is a ballerina kid vampire movie, the initial 50 minutes of buildup to that reveal loses some of its effectiveness. As formulaic and traditional as it is, Abigail still managed to surprise me in multiple instances. 

Firstly, the cast was fun, and their banter was good. The characters are unique and quirky enough, and though Melissa Barrerra's character is not that much different from Sam Carpenter in the scream movies, she's still a dependable final girl and does it well. Dan Stevens was the standout, though, in a performance that embraces the campy nature of the material. It's a hilariously over-the-top performance, just what a film like this needed. Alisha Weir, as the title character, was also effectively creepy and menacing. The creepy ballet dancing stuff was a great touch. Even though the setup is pretty long here, the characters, atmosphere and performances were cool enough that I didn't mind, the mansion was a great setting too. Kevin Durand as the stereotypically dumb and gullible big dude was also fun to watch.

This film is closer to the director duo's Ready or Not than their Scream films, and just like Ready or Not, this too is primarily set in a single big mansion. Abigail also has a dark and bloody sense of humor that really starts getting fun after the big reveal. This movie is anything but monotonous. The gore and blood effects are pretty well done, and there are plenty to go around. Just like their previous work, it does hit that sweet spot of being scary, gory and violent while maintaining that campiness and sense of humor. Abigail never gets too serious; it doesn't try to explain anything too much (there's even restraint to even say the word "Dracula,"  though they do say Nosferatu).

Abigail starts off as Vampire Home Alone, and it's fun how the film flips the script on the home invasion format by making the kid a truly powerful menace. It then uses a lot of fun twists, scares and setpieces and humor to keep things moving. There's some impressive stunt work towards the end too. The stunt team did a phenomenal job towards the end.

Anyway, like I said, I'd have loved Abigail a lot more if they hid their hand while promoting it. But still, this was so much funnnnnn.

Name: Guruvayoor Ambalanadayil
Review:
Everything written by Deepu Pradeep so far has arranged Hindu weddings and the theppukaari stereotype as recurring elements. I'm not a big fan of the way his stuff is innocently regressive, though, out of all the theppukaari scripts he's written, Guruvayoor Ambala Nadayil at least tries to subvert the trope to an extent. Kunjiramayanam, written by Deepu Pradeep, has Basil Joseph's directorial flair to thank for it being as fun as it was, despite these issues being a part of it too. In Guruvayoor Ambalanadayil, Vipin Das does make some interesting style choices that make the film more fun than it should be, but sometimes it's not enough.

The film revolves entirely around a wedding, and it focuses on the groom and the brother-in-law the most. Their over-the-top chemistry and goofy energy were a lot of fun to watch, and both Basil and Prithviraj were great together, whether it was the phone calls or when they finally met. The core conflict was introduced in a very fun way, and I expected a lot from this setup. But the payoff wasn't that satisfying. There were lots of interesting ways they could've played around with this, like how Priyadarsan or Rafi-Mecartin did with similar themes, but the way it develops is kind of basic. But still, the setups in the first half leading to the chaos in the second half were interesting as an idea.

After making Nikhila Vimal stand around confused and silent for the entirety of Perilloor Premier League, Deepu Pradeep makes Nikhila Vimal stand around confused and silent for the entirety of Guruvayoor Ambalanadayil too. Nikhila is someone who has already proven her comedic ability and timing (even in this film's own promotional interviews), and she's wasted here too, though with much less screen time than PPL. Anaswara Rajan plays the bride, and she too doesn't get enough screen time to shine, though in almost every scene she's in, including that initial bedroom phone call scene with Vinu, she lights up the screen.

The buildup to the big wedding sequence is LONG and often repetitive, and that length is really felt when the comedy falls flat. And the big climatic sequence is very simplistic in resolving everything and is less chaotic than it builds up to be. Core conflicts are resolved in single lines of dialogue, and some of the serious lines here are more corny than the corny lines the film parodied earlier. The Nandanam callback was cute and funny, though. The action, too, looked basic and wasn't as cool as the martial arts stuff from Jaya Jaya Jaya Jaya Hey. While I appreciate the crew's effort to recreate the exterior of Guruvayoor temple and the way the crowd was used to look like it's the real thing, I was still disappointed that even after setting up all these pieces for a chaotic climax, the end result was pretty meh.

I had mixed feelings about the music and the background score and felt it got too loud, especially towards the climax. The film does look beautiful, though, and the costumes for everyone looked great. I also liked the way the film was edited and structured and how parallel events were shown together. I wish the second half had more of the Aliyan-Aliyan chemistry between Basil and Prithviraj, because that's what I enjoyed the most in this film. Prithviraj being all kinds of hammy and over-the-top was also fun.

Spoilers

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

.

I don't usually have a problem with movies being dumb; I don't really dig around for logic. I don't mind that in this day and age, it's hard to believe that Vinu and Parvathy didn't see photos of each other when they're a part of such an alliance. I don't mind that the heavy government security around Guruvayoor temple let Anandettan be mass. Me mostly sad with the movie for not doing more with such a fun premise and cast.

Name: Challengers
Review:
It's sexy stuff. And I don't just mean all the brilliantly shot sexy intimate moments or Zendaya looking and carrying herself like an absolute dream. The way the film's non-linear narrative is structured is amazing, and Challengers has some of the best editing I've seen lately in cinema, Marco Costa is a god. Whether it's the shifting between timelines or the conversations or the intimate scenes or the kinetic tennis matches, the editing here is always to the point, and the rhythm of the film feels like a symphony. The music by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross is amazing, and I've already started listening to the OST, the cinematography by Sayombhu Mukdeeprom is amazing, and the performances by the three leads Zendaya, Josh O'Connor and Mike Faist are great.

This might be the best sports film that's not actually about sports that I've seen since Raging Bull. It's a triangular tennis love story, and yet the film is as much about tennis as it's about love. The central tennis match here between Art and Patrick begins in the first frame of the film itself, even before the studio logo is shown. We're essentially just watching this single tennis match, with the history that led to this match developing along with it. Past and sport intertwine with each other in brilliant ways, with some of the best dramatic sweating that I've seen, and it leads to an amazing finale that's foreshadowed by Zendaya's character Tasha pretty early on, and the way the scene is shot does full justice to what she described. From the use of slow-mo, to close-ups, pov shots, wide shots, bird's-eye views, and even the camera becoming the ball, and the great use of VFX, Challengers just about covers every way a game of tennis can be shot and edited cinematically.

Luca Guadagnino stages certain scenes beautifully; the tension, whether it's romantic, erotic or spiteful, is really felt, and the visuals convey a lot of information and life. And though we don't really know much about the characters beyond this two-way relationship, it just works. There's an initial kissing scene between the trio, and the entire film essentially becomes an extension of that. I did get a feeling that Challengers was occasionally longer than it had to be, but still, I never took my eyes off the screen because, yk, it's sexy.

Name: Turbo
Review:
Midhun Manuel Thomas' strong suit seems to be writing lighthearted stuff like Om Shanthi Oshanaa or Ann Maria, or something that's silly and goofy like Aadu. Because when a goofy scene that would belong in Aadu perfectly pops up in something that the audience is supposed to take seriously, it's not a great look. But compared to something like Abraham Ozler, Turbo is not a movie that's tonally supposed to be serious, so the damage is slightly lesser, but I wish it was a bit lighter than it ended up to be. 

Turbo is not the first time that Vysakh has been tasked with elevating bad writing, though. Pulimurugan had awful writing, but what that script had was enough gaps where Vysakh could deliver on over-the-top action and a larger-than-life presentation of its star Mohanlal. In Turbo, these gaps are smaller in number, and Turbo really charges up towards its third act because there is less plot and more action, which is where Vysakh is able to do his thing. Mammootty himself, as Jose, feels agile and powerful in the action scenes. I don't know what kind of code Ikka, the filmmakers and the stunt team have cracked here, and I am aware stunt doubles and cinema magic are used (which is nothing to be ashamed about; watch Ryan Gosling's Fall Guy), but for some reason, Mammootty just seems more agile in the action scenes in both Kannur Squad and Turbo. It also helps that Jose gets tired and hurt during the final setpiece; he's sweating, bleeding and he's fighting for his life, so even when the film is operating on unrealistic terrain, it's grounded enough to make the action exciting. The action choreography is not just Jose randomly making goons fly, and they do try to execute a lot of creative ideas, action-wise. The stunt team did impressive work for the big chase sequence too. 

Credit where it's due; I did like the way Jose Ettayi as a character was created and presented. Sure, it's not the kind of character that Mammootty has never played before, but in a movie where everything else feels like an over-the-top mass padam, Jose Ettayi is presented as a prakrithi ettayi. The line delivery here feels like Jose Ettayi is a Pothettan character in a Shaji Kailas world. Even when he's delivering an emotional monologue about his childhood trauma (which doesn't affect the rest of the movie in any way), Mammootty doesn't deliver it like an over-the-top masala movie protagonist usually does. Jose is grounded in surprising ways, and he doesn't even have traditional punch dialogues. Jose Ettayi even quips occasionally, just like his Ammachi's favorite Tony Stark does. I loved the quip he made when he saw the ninjas. That was the tone that I wish Turbo had more of, where it embraced its campiness rather than trying to seem more serious than it should be. But yeah, it was weird to see Ikka play an immature son character at his present age. 

Raj B. Shetty as Vetrivel Shanmukha Sundaram, on the other hand, is having fun playing an over-the-top villain as over-the-top as he can, occasionally while he gives his review on the Turbo screenplay to the point where him saying "What a cliché?" becomes a cliché. Still, like Jose Ettayi, Vetrivel Shanmukha Sundaram was also a fresh way to look at an over-the-top masala movie villain being performed this way. Bindu Panicker's mom character wasn't that well written, but she does get some cool one-liners, and she finished the entire MCU Infinity Saga way faster than I ever did. You go, Ammachi! Anjana Jayaprakash's Indulekha was also not just a throwaway character, and I liked her performance too. 

Christo Xavier's score had its moments, but the loud EDM music occasionally just sounded the same. Idk if KGF started the whole trend of the background score being mixed in so loud for action scenes in our movies, or if it's just that I've gotten too old. 

Anyways, like full-name addict Vetrivel Shanmukha Sundaram said, What a cliché, mahn? But regardless, I liked Mammootty as Jose Ettayi, how he was presented by Vysakh, the occasional moments of lighthearted fun and I liked the action sequences. Everything else is, ahem, not that good and occasionally bland, but I didn't mind. (Fan bias thanne) 

Also, hats off to Vetrivel Shanmukha Sundaram for being the kind of psychopath who only murders his victims and doesn't engage in sexual assault. Yeah, I know it's a weird hats off, but I've just been so fed up with the whole trope of using cruel scenes of sexual violence towards women in films lately, which even Kannur Squad did. Turbo is not regressive or misogynystic like Vysakh's previous films, so there's that too.

Name: Mad Max: Fury Road
Review:
When George Miller does a 2 hour long chase sequence, it's cinema. The way this movie was conceived, shot and edited still blows my mind. This might be my fifth time watching it, and it's epic every single time. Plus that epic score by Junkie XL that pumps up a movie that's already visually so pumped up. 

The action is so!!!
The music is so!!! 
Miller is so!!!

Name: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga
Review:
George Miller's Mad Max movies are not known for being character studies. They were always more about Miller's version of a post-apocalyptic wasteland, its absurdities, and, of course, glorious, glorious action. Even in Mad Max: Fury Road, the title character spoke less; we didn't know anything about him other than what we knew from the first Mel Gibson Mad Max film, and in Fury Road, it was like Max was a supporting character in a story where Furiosa was the lead. And now it's Furiosa's turn to get a backstory.

Furiosa didn't feel like a character study either, and yet it's not a continuous action spectacle like how Fury Road was a continuous chase sequence that was very light on plotting. Here, Furiosa herself speaks very little, maybe even less than she did in Fury Road. The only time I heard her utter more than a single line of dialogue was during the final confrontation. Furiosa, too, is more about exploring the wasteland and its absurdities, and Miller does the title character gag on us again because, for almost half of the movie, we follow Dementus, played by Chris Hemsworth, rather than Furiosa herself. Yeah, eventually Furiosa does become front and center, but Dementus gets a considerable amount of screentime by then. And it's a brilliant performance from Chris Hemsworth. He's funny, cruel, and even weirdly sympathetic. The guy didn't wish to be a savage warlord, and that whole side is conveyed beautifully by Hemsworth, though the writing doesn't dive deep into it. Anya Taylor-Joy's Furiosa is not channeling Charlize Theron by any means. This is a very different Furiosa, who's mostly silent and emotes mostly through her eyes. Though somehow, by the end, it just blends into the person we saw on Fury Road. 

Like I said, though it's not a deep character study, this is still a plot-driven movie with more drama than in Fury Road. The action too lacks the punch that Fury Road had mostly, except for two big setpieces after the initial hour where the vehicular combat was epic in Miller's signature style. But compared to Fury Road, where the CGI and the practical stunt work seamlessly blended together, Furiosa did have moments where the CGI and digital backgrounds looked more obvious. Still, the final confrontation between Furiosa and Dementus is where the film surprised me. It's where both the protagonist and antagonist play off each other brilliantly, with both Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Hemsworth at their best in this film.

Anyway, though this is essentially a companion piece to Fury Road that fits perfectly with it, this is a different kind of movie altogether. We don't get a deep character study on Furiosa, but rather how she fit into this whole world and how she eventually became who she is when Max comes in contact with her. Junkie XL's score, the production design, and Miller's world-building and signature style are all intact here too.

Name: Thalavan
Review:
Thalavan felt like a solid murder mystery, with great lead performances by Biju Menon and Asif Ali. But just like the case with Jeethu Joseph thriller movies, the performances for the smaller characters were not so great. Was Jis Joy being too faithful to Jeethu Joseph's style by inheriting his flaws too or something? Idk. Anyway, despite the flaws and a prison fight scene that doesn't really belong in an otherwise grounded film, as a fan of investigative thrillers, I was engaged and satisfied. It's devoid of any kind of Jis Joy style preaching too, and it's pretty straightforward as a police procedural. Deepak Dev's score was nice. 

I do wish the film explored the ego angle between the two characters and the gray sides of Biju Menon's character a bit more as the case progressed, though.

Name: The Fall Guy
Review:
Fall Guy is some wholesome, big cinematic fun that I wish I got to see on the big screen. David Leitch, himself a former stuntman, has a clear love for the stunt community, and this is the movie where he goes all in on that love. I'm not that aware of the original TV show, but what I did read about it makes this a very loose adaptation of it. Fall Guy follows stuntman Colt Severs, who wants his life outside stunts to be a romantic comedy, but gets put in an action movie because of the actor he's the stunt double for. What we get is lots of jokes, lots of fun, clearly improvised fun interactions between the actors, big practical stunts, impressive stuntwork that's shot like they want to show off the impressiveness of the stunt work in the best way possible, lots of meta-jokes, self-aware cheesiness that works because of the performances and the earnestness, a pretty solid thriller plot, and good old cinematic fun.

Gosling's Colt Seavers has shades of his character Holland March from The Nice Guys, though Colt can handle himself in a fight better than March and is an overall badass. Whether it's the comedy, action, or cheesy romantic plot, Gosling is a very dependable leading man. Emily Blunt as Jodie too has a lot more to do in this film than just being a love interest, and all the scenes where Gosling and Blunt played off each other were a lot of fun. Aaron Taylor-Johnson as the dickhead movie star Tom Ryder was also over-the-top in the best way possible.

Fall Guy has a very cool soundtrack. The meta-jokes and the digs at cinema were fun. Leitch was clearly channeling a lot from his personal experience as a stunt artist here, but it's packaged in a way that even someone who's not into the technicalities of moviemaking can join in on the fun. There are lots of funny callbacks to stuff that was previously mentioned, a literal Chekhov's gun, a reference to this film's own script that's disguised as a reference to the film within a film's script, a fun scene involving split-screen, and also pop-culture references galore.

Fall Guy also tries to incorporate almost every kind of stunt possible. There's fist fights, there's a gun fight, there's a car chase, a fist fight on a moving truck, a car jump, a car flip, and so on, and a lot of falls. If a fun, cheesy, old-school movie that's also a love letter to the stunt community was the intention here, I'd say mission accomplished.

The film also ends by showing behind-the-scenes footage of Gosling, Gosling's stunt doubles, and the other stunt artists who worked in the film. Actors like Tom Ryder do exist in real life who claim to do their own stunts and don't acknowledge all the hard work done by their stunt doubles, and there's also audience members who make fun of an actor or see them as inferior for using stunt doubles. There's such an obvious reason why such trained professionals exist; they're an integral part of any great action movie, and they do deserve to be acknowledged for what they do.

Name: War for the Planet of the Apes
Review:
Even with the word war in the title, the Caesar Trilogy chose to end by still being a character piece. It's such a gorgeous movie, and the unbelievable achievements in visual effects still hold up. Certain close-ups of Bad Ape and Caesar with those bloodshot eyes are just unbelievable. All these years later, big films that reach up to these levels of photorealism are still rare, because it's not just the tech and the money; it's also the artistry and the vision.

War for the Planet of the Apes has a deliberately bleak aesthetic because it is mostly set in a snow-covered prison. It's more about Caesar's personal journey of vengeance and how this post-apocalyptic world pushes both humans and apes towards violence and hate, and not at all about delivering spectacle. After the big opening battle, there's no big action setpiece till the very end. Even with a title like War from the Planet of the Apes, this might be the film with the least amount of action in the trilogy. Everything is servicing the drama and the character development here; all the apes are well fleshed out and brilliantly performed, led by, of course, Andy Serkis as Ceasar, in an amazing performance that completes Ceasar's journey with the glory it deserves. Caesar goes into dark and desperate places here, and along with Serkis, the VFX and animation team at Weta make him look so good. Like I said above, I couldn't help but appreciate how detailed and photorealistic an injured Caesar with bloodshot eyes looked. Though, as much as I paused to appreciate the technical wizardry, Matt Reeves still pulled me back into the intense drama.

We rarely get big-budget movies that focus on drama over spectacle, like the Apes Trilogy. Since I rewatched War after I had watched the newer installment Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes, I felt that even Kingdom favored delivering spectacle and thrills and operated more like a typical big-budget event film, while War was an intense character piece through and through, with the technical wizardry being there to service the drama.

Michael Giacchino's score was also very beautiful and deserves more praise. His Caesar theme from Dawn and War was used in the beginning of Kingdom too, and that's kind of the only piece of music that I remember from that film now.

Name: The Omen
Review:
Parts of The Omen are sillier than I remember, I still hate the morphine-high priest for being as dumb and unnecessarily cryptic he was, but still, the aspect of The Omen that remains timeless and sounds creepy even in isolation is Jerry Goldsmith's iconic score. The music is legendary in this movie. Also, the film itself picks up pace after Gregory Peck starts to investigate about the boy, the cemetery scene with the dogs and the climax confrontation has some great horror thriller filmmaking from Richard Donner, though the gore and special effects occasionally show their age, it's well directed enough to convey the intended effect. Also, though the rest of the cast is all kinds of over-the-top, and the film itself becomes campy after a while, Gregory Peck plays it dead serious, it's endearing.

Also, Damien is an effective creepy kid. That final shot will always be iconic and creepy, though it's just a cute kid smiling at the camera. Cinema!

Name: The First Omen
Review:
The First Omen is such a well-written prequel. It's so well integrated into The Omen that it doesn't feel like this movie was an afterthought that happened after decades, especially after watching them back-to-back. We already know about Damien Thorn's origins from The Omen itself, as almost half of that movie was about Robert Thorn uncovering that himself. So I went into this expecting a generic horror movie that'd just end with Damien's birth in the end. The First Omen feels like just that at the beginning too, there's an over-the-top gory kill that has the balance between shock and silliness that the Omen had, but after a while, we get much more revealed to us about the conspiracy behind creating the anti-christ. For me, the film became much more interesting after this piece of exposition from Father Brennan, who, unlike the Morphine-high vague and cryptic version from the original, is pretty direct and clear about revealing twists to our protagonist.

The film is a tribute to the original in having over-the-top kills and much of it being about investigating a big conspiracy. But I'd argue that this is a way darker film, and of course, as a modern production, there's modern touches in the filmmaking and the production values, but still, this one has more sinister stuff happening and more gruesome imagery. The visual effects, makeup, and gore are pretty well executed; stuff like the hand coming out of you-know-where was gnarly. The First Omen is able to build upon The Omen instead of just riding on its legacy. The fact that we know this would eventually end with the birth of the anti-christ only increases the dread as the film builds up to that inevitable conclusion.

It's quite a weird coincidence how Immaculate and The First Omen were released so close to each other and how similar both of these movies are. But Immaculate was a standalone affair, and this is a legacy prequel, and yet, The First Omen remains the superior film. Arkasha Stevenson and her team create something that actually adds texture to the original. Stevenson is successful in maintaining a dark atmosphere throughout; the creepiness of the whole thing is effective, and the scares are effective. It also doesn't rely too much on jump scares. Yes, there are formulaic elements and some campiness that The Omen also had, but it's forgivable and didn't make me face-palm like something like The Nun did. Nell Tiger Free's lead performance was also great, and this is a horror movie where having a well-acted protagonist does help. She was also pretty convincing in feeling like a nun from the 70s, unlike Sydney Sweeney, who sounded so Gen-Z in immaculate whenever she talked.

Anyway, the film does have an okay horror movie score that does its job in building up the eerie atmosphere and the dread, but still, the only piece of music that remained with me is the original Omen theme by Jerry Goldsmith that pops up at just the perfect moment. The original film hasn't aged well, but that score is still a masterpiece. 

They actually leave room open for future storylines towards the end of this film, and I do want to find out the interesting ways in which they'd take this forward. So in the end, The First Omen didn't feel like a generic legacy movie that was just riding on nostalgia; it succeeded in becoming its own thing, leaving room open to continue its own storyline in its own world.

Name: O.Baby
Review:
Dileesh Pothan's performance is great in this, but this plot, with this kind of drama, deserved a different kind of approach. The attempts at subtlety and realism just end up falling flat a lot of times, with an ending that makes the whole thing look almost like a comedy. The supporting cast performances didn't help either. 

If you want to watch a great dark drama centered on the fucked-up dynamics of an elite Christian family, which is set at their big family compound during the COVID lockdown, with great filmmaking, amazing acting, great writing, and better use of myr in the dialogue, just watch the movie directed by this movie's lead actor that got released in 2021.

Name: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga
Review: Rewatched it because the first time there was some glitch in the projector that created these annoying red flickers that took me out of the movie a lot. On the rewatch I could appreciate the action and the drama a lot more. But still, the film is not without its flaws. But it's still cinema! I'll witness anything George Miller creates.

Name: Hit Man
Review:
Hit Man reminded me so much of similar dark comedies the Coens have made and even the Fargo TV show. But make no mistake, this is nowhere near as violent as those films, but there's still dashes of well-executed dark humor there. The character interaction scenes are where Richard Linklater shows his signature flair. He has done comedy and crime movies in the past, and this one too feels like a Linklater film in ways I can't quite explain. I can listen to Linklater characters talk and go through daily life forever. All the sting operations and arrest montages were very fun. Glenn Powell carries the film so well; he's there in every scene, and he's a very likeable, funny, and dependable lead. He makes a lot of the wacky scenes and comedy work. Adria Arjona was also great, but I wish her character's moral ambiguity was better explored by the film. But still, the main character, Gary, was pretty well-written and brilliantly performed by Powell. I absolutely loved the style of this movie, it's dark sense of humor and the themes it handled, though I do wish it had more fun with the moral ambiguity and the complexity in the relationship between the two characters by the end.

Glenn Powell is Ryan Gosling at home at this point. He's cool.

Name: Maharaja
Review:
Maharaja is not without its flaws, but in terms of the way this film is structured and the way its story unfolds, it's brilliant. The film's structure is deceptive, and it keeps us guessing. What it reminded me of is Christopher Nolan's way of using non-linearity in films like Memento and The Prestige, where the twists and shocks are all an end product of the structure in an otherwise straightforward storyline.

Vijay Sethupathi is great as the protagonist, a barber who doesn't talk or smile much and comes off as a bit weird. We also get glimpses of his inner violence and brute strength, even before an actual fight scene happens. And yet, despite the darkness of the setting and the character, Vijay Sethupathi succeeds in making the character funny when he needs to be too, without diluting the darker shades. I have mixed feelings about the way comedy is integrated into an otherwise dark storyline, though. But even when it doesn't work, the film quickly switches to something more interesting. Anurag Kashyap as the villain does his usual psychopath routine, but like all his Tamil movie appearances, his lack of lip-syncing to the Tamil dialogues is a bit distracting for me.

There are flaws and issues, but like I said, it kept me engaged and guessing throughout, and the way everything connected together was great, though the storyline itself is generic and a part of a trope and problematic depiction of graphic sexual violence that I've grown tired of. The film also felt a bit overscored and too melodramatic at times. 

Also, I loved that brutal pre-interval fight scene.

Name: The Strangers
Review: I liked the idea here, that we don't know anything about the criminals and we only see what the victims see. But the execution left me with mixed feelings.

Name: Beverly Hills Cop
Review:
It's a cheesy and formulaic 80s cop comedy with all the traditional elements mixed in pretty well (well it's also the movie that defined some of these elements). Eddie Murphy shines here, and his charisma, charm and sense of humor is the secret sauce of Beverly Hills Cop, in addition to that iconic soundtrack by Harold Faltermeyer (I've thought that this theme was from the Crazy Frog music video for a long time though, kill me 😭), and I didn't mind how many times the theme got repeated, I was waiting for it to pop up again. Judge Reinhold as the silly and cute sidekick character was also an 80s movie kinda addition I was glad this movie had.
