It's also surprising that despite having all the formulaic elements, Axel's relationship with the female lead remains platonic. Murphy balances the fine line of balancing his larger than life comedic persona and making Axel feel like a competent police officer. The action is no Die Hard, but it serves its purpose, I wish the action had some more comedy mixed into it, like that opening sequence. 

Murphy carried the film well, and the parts of this film that I loved certainly involve his performance, though Martin Brest deserves credit here for the movie being as fun as it is. I wish Gigli never happened and we got more Martin Brest movies.

Name: Beverly Hills Cop II
Review:
It's a Tony Scott movie and it definitely looks and feels like a Tony Scott movie. There's fun here, but it's still inferior to the original. Scenes play out in a way that makes the other characters seem dumb than Axel feeling smart. Eddie Murphy is still a dependable lead, along with Billy and Taggart, and they're a cool trio to watch with great chemistry, but even with familiar beats and scenes to the original, it was lacking at times. The jokes don't always land, some are outdated, and even the action isn't as impressive as other Tony Scott flicks. The first movie was cheesy and formulaic too, but it had some novelty, it was also simpler and the elements were better mixed in. Here the crime plot is too complicated with too many players, and like I said, most attempts at showing Axel doing random smart stuff comes off like him getting away just because the other characters are too dumb. 

The music and Murphy's energy maintain the charm.

Name: Ullozhukku
Review:
At a time when most movies are tailored to compensate for our diminishing attention spans, Ullozhukku is a drama that takes its time to let its characters, the drama, and the emotions sink in. The writing and the pacing here are beautiful; every single scene adds details and texture to these characters, their inner conflicts, and their eventual unraveling. Christo Tomy's approach to drama is more visual than verbal, with the imagery, the setting, and the performances conveying so much.

The promotional material for this film gave the impression of a sad and dark film. Yes, this film deals with emotionally heavy material, but there's so much warmth, love, and empathy here, and the way the emotional arcs of the two lead characters are developed is so beautiful. The film is so character-focused; even Sushin Shyam's effectively beautiful score blends into the drama just at the right moments, and the sounds of rain are just as important as the music.

I loved the performances of both Parvathy and Urvashi as the main characters, but Urvashi in particular was just something else. Urvashi as Leelamma is the kind of performance that dives deep into the character. She's a grieving mother going through a big emotional journey over the span of just a few days, and every single emotion is portrayed brilliantly. Like I said, the filmmaking and the editing give the performances enough time to shine, including several long shots that stay on these characters while they're being vulnerable. So much is told through their gestures, eyes, and body language. Parvathy's Anju is also in constant dilemma and internal conflict, and it's interesting how the film treats both of these characters with empathy, telling both their sides and their own justifications. Both of them are driven by loneliness and a yearning for love, and both of them are women who had to let go of their own needs and desires because of the patriarchal households they were a part of. In a film that doesn't rely too much on dialogue to convey emotions, the performances matter a lot.

Anyway, I was crying by the end, and that theme music by Sushin Shyam pops up at the perfect moment, with a beautiful final shot. For me, this was an effective drama, and Urvashi made me cry.

Name: Beverly Hills Cop III
Review:
This one didn't even feel like a Beverly Hills Cop movie, the second one by Tony Scott at least felt like it was trying to emulate the energy of the first one though it was inferior to the original. Here, everything just feels so off. John Landis has made Coming to America and Trading Places with Murphy, so it's not like he's oblivious on making a funny Eddie Murphy movie. It's just that the film had way less instances where Murphy even attempted to be funny, it again took the crime plot too seriously, it was too generic with less amount of fun. Not having Harold Faltermeyer to do the score meant nothing except the reused stuff from him felt like Beverly Hills Cop music.

Idk, the entire movie just felt off, it didn't even feel like Murphy was playing Axel Foley here. 

Let's see how the 2024 movie handles the nostalgia ig.

Name: Bad Boys
Review: This is such a fun watch; the chemistry between Smith and Lawrence is great, Téa Leoni is gorgeous and fun, and it's cool to see Michael Bay doing all his signature Michael Bay style flourishes even in his first movie. The low-angle shots, the sweeping camera moves, the slow motion, the epic score, the way his style makes everything seem bigger and more dramatic—it's all here. The action and the explosions still look great; the comedy works because of the lead performances; the plot and the villains are generic, but I didn't care. The end setpiece is still awesome. Yeah, some of it can feel dated in 2024, but yeah, Bad Boys is cool.

Name: Bad Boys II
Review: Bad Boys 2 is longer than it had to be, Bay goes overboard with the style but it's still pretty fun, mostly because of Smith and Lawrence. Lawrence and Smith are still a great leading pair, though there's a clear change in the dynamic after the first one, since by this movie Smith had become the bigger star. The action and violence are bigger and better, and the parts where Mike and Marcus are riffing off each other and being generally hilarious are still the best thing about the Bad Boys. With the product placements, general aesthetic choices, objectified women, and over indulgence, this is closer to being a "Michael Bay movie" than the first one. I liked the style choices in the first one better, because here, a lot of times the style didn't really add anything, and even felt like a burden on the film.

Name: Falling Down
Review:
This is a straightforward thriller about your average psychotic, passive, aggressive asshole deciding one day that he's going to be direct about his aggression and violence, but there's a lot to unpack since the social themes of this film have created big discussions. I mean, I did read that this film is racist and that it glorifies the wrong things, but for me, the main character was a villain from the moment he attacked the store clerk, and it didn't feel like the movie itself was being racist. We enter this movie at the exact same time this guy snaps; he doesn't get a big sympathetic arc like Todd Philips' Joker does; he isn't a vigilante with the delusion of justice like Travis Bickle; he's just angry, angry at everything from simple everyday things to the system, at his own delusions, and at his own failed marriage. He's basically hurting other people because of the weight of his own existence. I don't know how much people fantasize about snapping one day and unleashing their inner violence on everything they hate. A lot of people do have that in them; they just aren't snapping like this dude does, and that thought is disturbing.

Anyway, such a great performance from Michael Douglas. A main reason why the psychopath feels more real and we feel the sadness in him is the performance. Robert Duvall was also great, especially in that final confrontation. I loved the music, too.

I'm not informed enough to talk about the bigger social themes here, but I saw this film as a portrayal of someone's inner rage and frustrations with their very "normal" and insignificant daily life and their failings in life transforming into something sinister. It touched a nerve in me because, if you asked me if I have had violent fantasies regarding people or situations I hate, I'd say yes. It's weird when you feel that connection to a psychotic villain. It's kinda more disturbing when the psychopath villain isn't someone with a dark, traumatic past. It's just a dude who had a white-collar job who just snapped one day, and he doesn't even realise that he's the bad guy, he feels he's entitled to express his aggression like this. 

Still, I could see how this movie could be interpreted in a bad way by the wrong crowd too (though the only person the dude directly kills in the movie is, of course, a racist, homophobic, misogynistic neo-Nazi).

Name: Crew
Review:
The three leads were great together, and their banter and chemistry were fun, plus, again, they're gorgeous women who looked great throughout the movie (Also, me a Tabu Stan). I also liked the fact that this movie is about middle-class people fucking over rich folk. Since most Bollywood movies have an elite, rich POV, it was fresh to see a heist movie with this POV. The movie was a fun light-watch and all, but the heist part is too poorly written. It'd have done this movie such a favor if the heist itself had been more smartly handled. It had a great premise and a great cast, but I wish this premise got an Ocean's Eleven treatment, or at least an Ocean's Eight treatment; this is just too dumbed down and simplistic. 

Also, the product placements in this movie are sneakier than all the smuggling and heisting in the movie. Diljith Dosanjh literally plays the good-looking love interest who has nothing much to do. It's funny because it's like the perfect gender reversal of what the female love interest does in similar Bollywood films when they're male-led (minus the objectification). 

Anyway, it was a fun, cheesy watch that I could relax to.

Name: Bad Boys for Life
Review:
This is definitely my favorite Bad Boys movie and one of my favorites in the revival/legacy sequel trend. Firstly, Adil & Bilall don't try to imitate Michael Bay's style, which is great. They try to make this its own thing, but with certain nods and tributes given to the original and Bay's style, like the general aesthetics of it and things like the iconic low-angle shot to show the Bad Boys fail, and the fact that this one too ends with a big explosion. I'm also glad that this is taking style cues from the first Bad Boys (even having an opening that parallels that film) rather than the second one, where I felt Bay was overindulgent with the style and the campiness.

The banter between Marcus and Mike is fun, and I could never get tired of it. Smith and Lawrence fit back into these characters and their chemistry with ease, and the new supporting cast was fun too. This one also has some great drama going for it, be it Marcus considering retirement or the villain arc this time, which is pretty personal to Mike. This is the only Bad Boys movie where the villains had so much more going for them than just being generic criminals, so that was good. It was also good to see the theme music from the first movie returning and being used in multiple areas. Lorne Balfe does a great job updating these theme songs in general. This might also be the Bad Boys movie where they refer to themselves as the Bad Boys the most (I haven't seen Ride or Die yet). Even the song is used in a fun way. The action also looked great; there's some well choreographed fight scenes this time around too. Also, yeah, the women have more to do this time too. 

This one has great laughs, great action, surprisingly great drama, character arcs, and music while staying true to the spirit of the OG Bad Boys and the leading pair's chemistry, which is what I loved here. The formulaic-ness of it just fit too. Staying basic is good for a movie like this. It's pretty much a great way to revive an old franchise.

Name: Kalki 2898-AD
Review:
Kalki [I don't want to memorize the year] A. D. is a true masala sci-fi movie. As in, it's a cocktail that mixes elements of various Hollywood movies and TV shows as well as Indian movies. The evil empire, the rebel alliance, the prophecy, the chosen one, the Marvel-style one-liners—it's all here. So maybe George Lucas, Peter Jackson, James Cameron, J.K. Rowling, George Miller, and Kevin Feige, among others, deserve more credit for providing inspiration than Hindu mythology and the Mahabharath. I'm not complaining though; it's a pretty fun cocktail, something that uses Hindu mythology the way DC and Marvel have used Biblical, Greek, and Norse mythology, which is something I've always wanted to see. I mean, The Empire vs. Ashwathama from Mahabharath, Kamal Haasan as Emperor Palpetine, meta-jokes—there's so much fun here. But yeah, it is derivative, with the drama lacking punch and depth, but in terms of the fun world-building, it's still interesting.

Sri Prabhas is playing Bhairavaa, the Star-Lord type, who himself was the Han Solo type, with even the rocket boots included. He's a selfish bounty hunter, and it's inevitable that this dude will become the hero, but I liked the way this movie played around with his arc and that character development that the audience would expect from the beginning itself. Also, this is a Telugu movie where the world doesn't revolve around the star. Even in something like Baahubali, the entire film and the world still revolved around the two Prabhas characters. But the world of Kalki and its plotlines don't revolve around him; he's just one part of the bigger narrative. Sure, he gets his Telugu star-style intro, with even a fun way to show the title "Rebel Star" and plenty of hero worship moments, and yet, Nag Aswin pulls off the Marvel thing where the big star seems like one piece of the bigger world. So this is an entirely different kind of masala movie in that regard and can't quite be compared to what SS Rajamouli does, where the films do revolve around star power and hero worship. Tbh, I enjoyed the quirky, cheesy, and quippy Prabhas here; dude understood the assignment and was great during several action setpieces too. I also felt like I missed out on some of the Prabhasness because I watched the Malayalam dub rather than the original Telugu version.

Sri Amitabh Bachchan plays Obi-Wan Gandalf the Maav. The other character in the film who is presented as a larger-than-life figure. Both the performance and the presentation succeed in making this person seem like the mythical figure that he is, and even in action scenes, he's got this anime character energy, so we'd always get the sense of this immortal badass rather than a mere mortal in his 80s.

Sri Kamal Haasan plays the Emperor Palpatine type, who resembles Supreme Leader Snoake from the new Star Wars movies. It's clear why Kamal Haasan would love to do something like this (no, not just the money); he gets to play an over-the-top, larger-than-life villain who's got both sci-fi powers and mythical powers, and an army; he gets to wear prosthetics; and also, he himself has tried the whole mythology/sci-fi blend in Dasavatharam, so it feels like it's a world he'd actually be interested in. Also, the prosthetics and CGI on Kamal look great here.

Deepika Padukone and Disha Patani are the two top-billed cast members who don't get the Sri/Smt treatment in the opening credits, and their characters too are reduced to two basic Telugu movie stereotypes. Disha Patani plays the eye candy, who doesn't add much to the story and is not even mentioned after a while. I don't know if her character gets some kind of prominence in the future, but for now, looking hot seemed to be the only assignment. Deepika Padukone, on the other hand, plays the human Macguffin/damsel in distress here. She gets one cool-looking Khaleesi moment but is otherwise just a plot device. Only the baby inside her matters to the other characters, and she herself lacks any kind of identity unlike the similar Sarah Connor from The Terminator. Which, again, can be solved in sequels. Other female characters, such as Anna Ben's Kyra and Shobhana's Mariam, get their moments, but I was disappointed in the way those characters were handled eventually. Also, Bujji, the AI voiced by Keerthy Suresh, was fun in a cringey kinda way and one of the few characters in the Malayalam dub whose dialogue didn't sound, yk, "dubbed". Then there's a big ensemble of cameos and the kind of supporting characters you'd expect in a movie like this, with Sri Brahmanandam as the insignificant comic relief also getting a Sri in the opening credits. Seriously, though, what's the criteria for the Sri? If it's because they're senior citizens, then why does Prabhas get a Sri?

The VFX work was solid and did wonders for making the movie work. The visuals of the battle of Kurukshethra looked appropriately epic. It's not photorealism, but there's enough vision and imagination poured in here, and the tone of the film itself is so over-the-top and comics-ish that it fits in. The only downside was the deaging done on Amithabh Bachchan, which can't even be called uncanny valley; he ends up looking creepier than the Kamal Haasan character, who's deliberately made to look creepy. Anyway, during the action setpieces and the portrayal of the dystopia below and the paradise above, the visuals were great. The action sequences looked like your average Telugu movie action scenes initially, especially in Bhairava's introduction fight. There is the in-world justification that Bhairava wears booster gloves that give him the ability to make goons fly, but at the end of the day, it just looks like your average Telugu movie fight scene with goons flying and obvious wirework. But afterwards, when Bachchan's The Maav gets into the action, things get interesting. Then the fight scenes are more along the lines of anime style than Telugu movie style, and those scenes were a lot of fun. The techniques used to make Amithabh Bachchan seem bigger and those used for the Kamal Haasan character's appearance were soild. The production design and the overall production quality were nice. There's a lot of Star Wars, but it's nice.

I really liked Santhosh Narayanan's music here; there are tracks that have his signature, especially one that reminded me of the theme from Jigarthanda, and it's nice to hear his music in a movie like this. Whether the mode of the movie is sci-fi or mythology, the score also changes appropriately.

Anyway, it's not a flawless movie; there are issues, it is derivative, and it does cram too much stuff into one movie that results in it lacking depth. It then ends with a cliffhanger anyway, but there are things to be appreciated here. I did like the world building here, and the way mythology has been mixed with dystopian sci-fi is interesting. The purpose here is to bring us into this world, and I do want to know how this story progresses and how this world will be further developed. Prabhas is just "a" hero here and not "the" hero, and so is The Maav, and yk, building a world that way feels impressive. When I was a kid, I've always thought about Mahabharath and Ramayana looking like Marvel movies and Star Wars, and this ended up being literally that. Also, they show Krishna as being an actual dark-skinned person rather than being light-skinned or blue, points for Krishna accuracy!

Name: The Naked Gun: From the Files of Police Squad!
Review: They just throw joke after joke every 10 seconds no matter how silly it is. It's awesome. Leslie Nielsen is so dead serious in his performance that it makes it even more funny.

Name: The Strangers: Prey at Night
Review: Well, it's not a great horror movie, but compared to the first one, this was more fun. It's more similar to your average formulaic slasher that follows the template set by Halloween. The first one was trying to be like Texas Chainsaw Massacre, and this is the Halloween version of the Strangers. It doesn't drag on like the first one, it's more gory and slashery, there are cool moments of camp like that Shotgun scene, and the score was also cool. It does lack the novelty and tragic nature of the first one, but anyway, it was a fun afternoon watch.

Name: Beverly Hills Cop: Axel F
Review:
Well, this legacy sequel is a better follow-up to the original Beverly Hills Cop than the two other sequels that it got. It gets the tone right, it gets the formula right, it gets the comedy and charm right, it gets Axel Foley right, and it gets the music right, plus there's enough callbacks and references to the first movie with quirky little changes and updations instead of redoing that movie with an older Axel. This film also has more action, and the action is also better executed.

Eddie Murphy is back in form as Axel F, after whomever the person was that he played in Beverly Hills Cop 3. The charm, the comedic timing, the fast talking, the skills—it's all here, and it does feel more like an older Axel F than an older Murphy trying to play Axel like he did in his 20s. He had great chemistry with the other cast members, both Taylour Paige as his daughter Jane and Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Detective Abbot. Though Taggart and Billy are both in this movie, we don't actually get the original trio that much here. And not enough Billy being silly either. Well, but the entire movie happens just because Billy chooses to keep a video file on an SD card instead of uploading it to the cloud or just simply sending it to Jane or the authorities. So that's a significant amount of silly from Billy.

Lorne Balfe's score makes great use of Harold Faltermeyer's original themes, and the updates are really cool. The original tracks also maintain the same vibe. The Axel F theme is not used as much as the original movie; the lead-up to the theme plays occasionally, but the entire theme only pops up a handful of times, two of which is the new Lil Nas X song, which was an interesting choice.

Just like the first movie, the crime plot is also simple and straightforward, and Kevin Bacon's villain is also an appropriate 80s callback villain. Though I do wish the whole angle where he's an evil Axel Foley who ends up using his smarts to be a criminal was better explored. The one thing this movie does differently from the old ones is that it's got more action, and it's also bigger. The helicopter chase through the road and the snowplow setpiece from the beginning were especially cool. The finale is, of course, straight from the original movie, but with better choreography.

Anyway, this was a fun movie to watch, and I liked it as much as I liked the original. It had fun, it had action, it had Eddie Murphy in form, it was appropriately cheesy and simple, and all the formula elements were mixed in pretty well. Yes, it's dumb, but it's the good kind of dumb. It pays homage to the original, but it still does plenty of things on its own too.

Name: In a Violent Nature
Review:
When this movie first caught my attention, I only saw the poster and the synopsis and thought it's just yet another low-budget Friday the 13th clone and didn't try to watch it. Then I saw a clip of one of the kills from this movie on Instagram, and that didn't look like any other slasher kill that I've seen, so that made me curious to check this out. 

Make no mistake, this is still a Friday the 13th clone, with the exact same plot of a supernaturally strong, silent, disfigured, ressurected killer brutalizing some campers. The events that happen in this movie and the characters it's filled with all belong in a Friday the 13th movie from the 80s. But there's a significant change in approach and perspective here that makes it seem like an entirely new thing. The cinematography and editing are very calm; there are lots of long shots; the pacing of the movie is also peaceful and smooth; it's in no hurry. Even the first shot of the killer resurrecting doesn't have any over-the-top dramatic flair. He just gets up from the underground and walks on. The movie doesn't have any background score, and all we hear mostly are peaceful nature sounds, lots of back shots of the killer walking too, btw, because this movie also puts us in the killer's perspective mostly, which again makes each kill and encounter seem so different. It's also interesting to see an unstoppable killing machine hunting his prey through himself rather than his victims. Just like Jason Voorhees, he makes no visible effort to stay hidden; he doesn't run when his victims try to run away from him, and despite that, he still manages to kill them. It's hilarious when we think about it, but the movie still manages to make him look scary, and the kills seem brutal. 

There's a lot of well-executed 80s-style gore and special effects here. And though the gore is over-the-top, the movie still maintains that same pace and vibe even during the kills, making each kill seem unique in one way or another. I can really see what Chris Nash was going for here, and I find it cool. The characters are indeed one-dimensional, but yk, so were the characters in the slasher movies this movie is trying to emulate. It's just all about seeing those movies from a different perspective, directed, edited, and shot in a different way, with everything else being the same as those movies. There's even some well-executed dark humor here too, either by the killer doing absurd acts of violence or by the characters being dumb. Seriously, it's not that hard for them to escape a dude who never even runs, but still, they don't and do the stupidest stuff to get killed. But there are some memorable kills, like when one of them just accepts their faith to get their head stretched out in an ultra-gory way, and when the killer takes one of them to a wood chopper and kills the person as if he's just routinely slowly and patiently chopping some wood. The lack of slashery filmmaking and the slowness just add a layer of absurd dark humor here. There's also the final kill that made me laugh out loud at how stupid that character was. 

There's a change in perspective towards the end, and it's then that I realized the effectiveness of this movie yet again. After following the killer for so long, following this other character adds a layer of tension that wasn't present for the killer because, yk, he was unstoppable and he was the predator. But this character is shot like the camera itself is chasing her, and we're not even sure if it's the camera or the killer, and that whole building of tension is brilliantly done. 

Anyway, as a fan of slashers, this was a very unique perspective to look at a slasher, and I liked that it only changed the perspective and narrative style of the old cheesy slashers and everything else pretty much remained the same, except for the victims being Gen-Z, of course. Lots of moments of beautiful cinematography too, though most of those shots have this killing machine walking in them, changing up the context. 

That yoga kill tho. Yikes. 

It would've been cool if Johnny's last name was Walker, or if there was a "Here's Johnny!" reference.

Name: Aalavandhan
Review:
So the new remastered version that I watched has almost 50 minutes of absurdities cut out and stuff like the awful opening military mission scene intact. This is truly a unique film, though, especially for Tamil cinema in the early 2000s. It's so weird and absurd, with a lot of big swings in weirdness and absurdities during the first half. This is also a big production, and there was also the use of new technologies involved. Idek if they actually cared if the audience would accept this amount of weirdness back then; maybe the constant product placements and ads throughout the movie covered for the big production cost too.

Yes, it borrows elements from Cape Fear, but this is way crazier than Cape Fear, with Kamal having so much fun playing the villain Nandu rather than the far more bland Vijay. This might be one of the reasons why he agreed to do Kalki too—to be a mythological sci-fi Nandu, a Kadavul-Mirugam in the literal sense.

Also, headless Riyaz Khan is the real Thala from 2001, not the dude who was in Dheena.

Name: 28 Days Later
Review:
I can see how stuff like The Last of Us and The Walking Dead have taken inspiration from this. In terms of setting the atmosphere and the world, this is an amazing achievement in filmmaking. The infected themselves are depicted so differently from your average zombie, not just because they can run; they just seem so animalistic, aggressive, and dangerous, even if it's just a single one. Also, the way the zombie encounters are shot and edited also gives them a frantic and visceral energy that just works every single time. That initial scene of Cillian Murphy walking through an empty London is indeed iconic, and the character relationships and bonding are done really well, with great performances from the entire cast. It really gets us to care about these characters, so the dark events afterwards hit even harder. The music was amazing throughout, too. 

Still, Cillian Murphy's delivery guy with hardly any combat experience suddenly becoming Rambo at the end was a little hard to buy, especially since the rest of the movie had been so grounded. Unless he was really an MI6 agent and lied about being a delivery guy xD.

Name: Indian 2: Zero Tolerance
Review:
Indian 2 is a follow-up to Indian (1996) and a parody of that original movie at the same time. Now, I'm not saying that the original Indian wasn't a goofy film. It was. Most of that movie was Senapathy killing corrupt officers and doing the whole vigilante thing on one side, and Chandru, the other Kamal Haasan character, had his own triangle love story plot and the whole set of dated Gaundamani-Senthil comedy scenes. Senapathy's Varma Kalai skills and superior physical ability were superhuman even in that film, but it had a balance where we could still buy him as an old man, and though exaggerated, his antics were still grounded to an extent, and Kamal Haasan played him dead serious, giving the murderous vigilante an identity of his own.

Indian 2's main issue is this: it basically overexaggerates an already exaggerated Senapathy. The goofy and dated elements of the first movie get a pass now because it's from the 90s. But the same cannot be said for the sequel. This version of Senapathy would've been a weird follow-up to Indian even if it released in the 90s, with a Senapathy in his 70s, and here we have Senapathy in his 100s, and he's like Benjamin Button Senapathy here since he acts and seems younger than the person we saw in the last movie. Varma Kalai, which seemed like a mythical martial art technique that gave an older and slower man an upper hand physically, now seems like it made this old man into Chitti the Robo. I mean, there's literally a scene where he scans some buff dudes' nerve points and transforms his own body to be buff. I mean, that's something that's totally a scene that'd work for Chitti the Robo, but for Senapathy, there's a limit to exaggerating "martial art." Senapathy only immobilized his foes with varma kalai in the first movie. And it completely made sense, because this person was so old that he couldn't probably take a younger person in a straightforward fight. So he uses this skill of his to have the upper hand. And then here's the Senapathy of Indian 2, the same man 28 years later, doing all kinds of crazy stuff. Also, Varma Kalai transforms people into horses, makes them sing to death, and drains the water from their bodies. Why? Why couldn't it just stay as a thing he did to incapacitate people? Why does it have to be this mythical? The creative decisions made here to present an "upgraded" Senapathy are so absurd. An ideal Senapathy in his 100s would've at least been presented in a way that does address his advanced age in some way. Yeah, apparently there are real-life martial artists who can do stuff past the age of 100 too, but yk, there's a limit to exaggerating a 105- or something-year-old dude doing all this stuff with no fantasy or sci-fi involved, right?

Anyway, the sad part of Indian 2 is that Shankar did actually have the perfect followup to the first movie in here, just that it got buried by the other bad decisions around it. Because pretty late into the movie, Senapathy's brand of vigilante justice is questioned, and these are the few scenes where I took the film seriously rather than as a guilty pleasure watch that I was laughing at. Because the first film portrayed him as a virtuous hero and didn't really question his whole thing of straight-up murdering people in the name of justice. He kills even his own son, but when he asks other citizens to have the same kind of approach towards justice, is that perfect? Though Indian 2 does still lean into Senapathy being right and him being a hero, questioning his brand of justice was the perfect plot for a follow-up. There's even a villain teased who knows Varma Kalai the same as Senapathy, which is also the best foe for a character who is so superior to others otherwise.

Anyway, there's lots of scenes of corrupt people doing corrupt stuff, and how the "barking dogs" gang, our group of younger protagonists, reacts to them, and how they react to Senapathy's message for youngsters. These scenes often feel repetitive, as they're the same template that Shankar always uses but lack the dramatic punch his previous movies had, except for the one involving Sidharth's character towards the end. Even in Indian, things only get interesting once the vigilante thing becomes personal for Senapathy. He is pushed towards this path because of his daughter, and eventually it leads to him murdering his own son. And that drama and Kamal Haasan's performance during those scenes were indeed great. But here, Senapathy just lacks depth, and his actions don't make sense. Varma Kalai being more powerful than the force from Star Wars also doesn't help.

There are moments in the film where the prosthetics on Senapathy looked amazing—even better than the prosthetics in the original—and seemed like actual skin. But there were also moments where it looked way worse than the old guy makeup from the 90s. It is my understanding that a combination of prosthetics and CGI was used for Senapathy, but when your main character is the one who wears prosthetic makeup in almost every scene he's in, consistency matters. There are some nice moments of action, though the scene where Senapathy transforms into a bodybuilder by scanning some bodybuilders is ridiculous all the way through. And like I said, the first movie acknowledged the 70ish-year-old Senapathy's age during the action scenes in ways this film doesn't when he's 100ish, so that's a major hit to our suspension of disbelief when seeing the action. Anirudh's score is actually good; some of the themes don't fit Senapathy from the last movie, and Senapathy himself is not behaving like that version either anyway. The songs were catchy. A. R. Rahman's songs and score were a huge part of uplifting the original film, even making the horrible romance subplot watchable because of the songs being iconic. But in defense of Anirudh, even delivering the most iconic soundtrack couldn't save this sequel from its ridiculousness. The CGI work was also great; even the deepfake faces for late actors Nedumudi Venu and Vivek weren't too distracting, though they did occasionally have weird distortions that gave away that it wasn't them.

There were two great ideas here: Senapathy appealing to youngsters and them realizing his method of vigilante justice is flawed, and Senapathy confronting a foe who has mastered the same martial art that he has. Developing these in a way that pays tribute to 90s cheesiness by staying modern instead of seeming more dated than the 90s version would've made this a great sequel. Like, even after laughing at the movie for almost two hours, when that conflict finally showed up towards the end, I took it seriously. Though the angry tweeting was funny, Shankar's understanding of social media is pretty boomer-coded.

I did have fun watching Indian 2, and I'd not say this was a waste of my time. It's just so ridiculous and funny. I had no idea if Shankar's intention was to genuinely make a parody movie at times because of how goofy and cartoonish it occasionally is. Look at what Indian Thaatha does when he wants to appeal to the youth in India. He posts a bad low-angle selfie and goes live on Facebook. It's a very accurate thing for a Thaatha to do, but it's so funny. Even the live itself, with Senapathy even fixing the phone stand inside his pants (?) at a point. In the original, Senapathy hitting a person's nerves had a weird slow motion effect and a whooshing sound effect; here, it's a CG shot of the person's nerves, heart, and brain being affected by the hit, followed by the person doing something ridiculous, and Senapathy marmamsplaining to us what he just did. This got old too fast (no pun intended). The attempts to "upgrade" Senapathy don't feel like a natural continuation of the character in the original, but it's still hilarious in how ridiculous these big swings are. The original had multiple intense and dramatic scenes for Kamal Haasan to shine, but it's lacking here, so I would blame the writing for the weaker Senapathy and not the actor. Though Senapathy mostly kills only the elitest of the elite this time around than your average government officer, which was cool. He kills one during his kid's ultra-grand wedding (Hehe, Ambani), then the Vijay Mallya type, and then there's even a dude who's killed because of a scam that's pretty similar to the recent NEET, NET scam irl. Senapathy killing just the elite is the kind of vigilante justice that I'd have cheered for, but yk, instead I laughed at most of it.

Though the film is mostly big swings to "upgrade" Senapathy that only degrade him, I still had fun watching this. For me, Indian 2 fits right in the "so bad it's good" kind of cinema. And yeah, if they do release Indian 3, I'd still watch it.

Name: Kill
Review:
Kill is a pretty effective version of the Die Hard format, where a trained soldier has to survive against a group of bandits inside a train, and the film is also very fast in building up to this situation. It literally doesn't waste a moment, as the main intention here is to deliver on the action. While the narrative itself has familiar beats and clichés, the film makes up for it with its approach to action, violence and how everything just seems gritty and grounded. Yes, our protagonist is a trained killer, and he's basically superior to almost all of the bandits in terms of skills, but he's not superhuman (well, maybe in terms of pain and injury tolerance), and he can get hurt. He gets hurt, the goons do occasionally overpower him, and he has to get up and push through, yeah it's pretty dumb of the goons to keep him alive at times in positions where he could overpower them, the film has some justifications for the goons making those choices, but yk, it doesn't make sense too, but who cares when the action is so cool and the events are so thrilling?

The entire thing happens inside an Indian train and the narrow spaces inside. The fights are very convincing and they use great use of that narrow environment and it's restrictions. The cinematography is great, with the action never feeling bland or repetitive. Frankly, the only far-fetched thing here was that the protagonist and his girlfriend could be all cute and romantic inside the train's toilet, which is impossible in an actual Indian Train's smelly af toilets. Anyway, the CGI and the gore effects were really well done, and the performances too were mostly nice. Lakshya as the main guy Amrit effectively looked and sold the part of a rage filled badass and was efficient in the action sequences, but his limited acting skills kinda show in some other moments. There's a particular Batman to Punisher transformation here that was so awesome. The soundtrack was also appropriate for the film. 

For me, this is the way an action movie should be made, the main character is skilled, but can get hurt, it adds a layer of tension and thrills that won't exist when they're just invincible superheros, which is what a lot of big Indian action movies get wrong. The way the violence is depicted is also interesting. Yes, Amrit is essentially protecting his fellow passengers from the bandits, but the violence he inflicts on them is shown as barbaric, it's coming from a dark place, there's not much heroic about it. Also, the bandits are not mere fodder for Amrit to cut down. There's texture, personality and motives given to them. They even grieve for their dead ones. This humanizes even the goons, and there are ones among them who never wanted to be a part of the killing and just wanted to steal some stuff and get off, but as the killings start, nobody's safe. Though the film is just focused on thrills and setpieces, I also wish the bandits' POV was better addressed, because yk, they're clearly underprivileged while Amrit, his lover and her family clearly come from a place of privilege, and these bandits are getting murdered, and they too have families. Yeah, they're bandits who murder too, but yk, why are they bandits? And does Amrit deserve a hero moment for brutalising them? How's he different from them? 

Instead of being a video game-ish piece where Amrit just kills goons back to back, there are interesting twists and turns at every point, making the situations more tight and thrilling. Like, despite being set in the same train compartments, and the whole film essentially being one big fight scene, it still doesn't feel repetitive or like it's too long. Still though, I couldn't keep up with the train compartment positions and what's happening where and all. But still, the action was actioning. The writing does have issues, but the pacing and action made me forget about them.

Name: Twister
Review:
Good old fashioned 90s fun with lovable characters, a basic but cute love story at the center (poor Melissa though), great performances from the cast, cool music, and great 28 year old visual effects that still mostly hold up. 

When this movie really gets going, it's very exhilarating and thrilling. Also, young Philip Seymour Hoffman was the broest of bros. And I had the biggest crush on Helen Hunt when I watched this movie on TV when I was a kid, now too.

Name: Twisters
Review:
Well, this was also cheesy fun like the original, and this time it's bigger, with the advancements in technology clearly making an impact. But still, the tornadoes were scarier in the original, despite the more primitive visual effects. Because of the primitive visual effects, the makers of the original had to get around it using practical methods and clever filmmaking, so in an age where anything that can be imagined can be rendered on screen, some of the things that grounded the first movie are lost. This is very apparent when we compare the drive-in scene from the first movie to the rodeo scene in the sequel. The drive-in scene seemed more visceral and dangerous, whereas even with that cool single-shot moment, the rodeo scene doesn't quite deliver the same feelings. The only time the tornadoes did seem scary in the sequel in a way that mirrored how I felt watching the first movie was during the final setpiece. There, it was brilliantly portrayed, intercutting between people affected by it and the destruction on its path.

Daisy Edgar Jones and Glen Powell are dependable leads. The first movie was mainly about Bill Paxton and Helen Hunt as exes bonding over chasing tornadoes, set in a single day, and very simple and straightforward. This one has a lot more going for it and more characters. But it's mostly set around Edgar Jones' Kate. Glen Powell delivers the charm and is still successful at being the other Gosling (put Ryan and Glen in a movie together already!).

Lee Isaac Chung still wants the movie to have the cheesy 90s energy from the original, and it shows. The tornado sequences are well made, and the visual spectacle is indeed impressive. The characters are likable and charming, and it's a good time.

Also, the soon-to-be Superman saying "I DON'T CARE ABOUT PEOPLE!", made me laugh out loud in a way that confused a lot of other people who were in the cinema hall.

Name: Sunshine
Review:
A space mission to bomb the sun to save the world sounds like the sequel to Michael Bay's Armageddon, but this is not your average popcorn sci-fi flick, this is serious and dark. The premise had a lot of potential, but yeah the film just becomes a slasher movie by the end and doesn't quite explore its sci-fi potential. But still, it's so well-made that I can't complain. It's baffling that this film is not mentioned along the likes of Gravity, Interstellar or 2001.

There are so many beautiful shots, the visual effects look gorgeous, and just like the zombies in 28 days later, whenever the villain appears, the filmmaking and editing just transform into something else entirely. I do wish the villain was better developed though. 

Also, such a beautiful soundtrack too. They absolutely nailed how getting sunlighted to death would look, and for that, I applaud.

Also, I think Sunshine might be the superior movie where Cillian Murphy has to blow up a bomb.

Name: X-Men
Review: This was THE early 2000s superhero movie, that set the template for many that followed. The action and visual effects still look great all these years later, with only the occasional Storm lightning or Cyclops laser looking weird. Also, this movie aged more gracefully than Sam Raimi's Spider-Man and all, plus the Magneto - Professor X conflict and the Mutant - Human conflict is set up pretty well. So is each character and their interactions and relationships, and all under almost 95 minutes. It's a pretty impressive movie tbh. And I didn't know that Solid Snake wrote it.

Name: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
Review:
Much has been said about this movie's bad writing, sewed-pool, how it didn't even have an actual script because its production was during a writer's strike. But what confuses me the most is the hideous CGI in this movie. When I first watched this movie, it was the leaked workprint, with unfinished visual effects, but I had no idea that even the finished visual effects looked so bad. Even something that's so basic and essential in a Wolverine movie like Logan's claws look so hideous here. Like, that's something which looked perfect even in the very first X-men movie.

But still, this is a fun watch in so many ways, sometimes because of how bad it looks, like, there are times when it looks cheaper than a fan film. And other times it is genuinely cool. There are moments of badass action that's done well, like all the explosions (especially the helicopter explosion) and some of the fight scenes. Jackman looks like an absolute beast, and rather than the good movies where he's played Logan, a bad movie where he doesn't even need a proper script to make Logan look so cool, is a testament to the legend he is. Seeing Liev Schriber hamming it up instead of his usual suble deadpan routine also is fun.

Then there's sewed pool. Though Reynolds himself hates the direction in which this film took Deadpool, with that post credits scene, I've felt the intention was for him to grow into the comic accurate Deadpool anyway. But yk, he got a different origin story anyway and now a proper crossover with Logan, so win-win.

Name: Deadpool & Wolverine
Review:
Deadpool and Wolverine is the biggest Deadpool movie, and it might even be the best-written Deadpool movie, though that bar was not that high. The assignment here was to deliver a crossover that the fans have been wanting for a long time, and with things like the Fox-Disney merger and the MCU multiverse saga mishmash, there was plenty of material for a 4th wall-breaking comedy to make meta jokes out of. Even then, the film tries to set up an emotional arc for both Deadpool and Wolverine, and though the writing and development of it lacks depth, it does provide enough of a reason for the fan service, cameos, and meta-jokes to exist; it does do respect to both the characters, and both Reynolds and Jackman are a delight together. We never feel like it's the first time these characters are interacting with each other; the chemistry, whether it's them bringing in the cute bromance, playing off of each other with the crazy yapper and strong silent type combination, or when they're genuinely trying to rip each other apart, the duo carries the movie so well.

If I've said it once, I've said it a million times. Just when we think we've seen the maximum amount of range Hugh Jackman can do with Wolverine, now, 24 years later, he just plays a version of Logan that we've never seen. Yes, his arc involving him being the "worst Wolverine" and his reason to be all pathetic and brooding is not written that well, but whether it's James Mangold's well-written dramatic arc in Logan, or the lazily written one here, or even the script-less X-Men Origins: Wolverine, this dude can act the hell out of it. Bringing in the badassery, the deadpan humor, and the more tender moments in a way that makes us forget about the shortcomings in the writing. Towards the end, we care about his redemption and his growth, only because Hugh Jackman is THAT good.

Coming to Ryan Reynolds, unlike Jackman, he isn't covering any new terrain here, and it's the kind of humor and performance he's already done. And even the dynamic between him and Wolverine isn't all that different from what he had with Cable in Deadpool 2. But still, even here, Jackman being the person opposite to him makes all the difference (I'm sorry, I can't resist fanboying over Jackman), and makes this a better combo than Deadpool and Cable (well yk, Deadpool and Wolverine also get more screentime together than Deadpool and Cable did). The best moments in the film all involve scenes that have the two of them together, whether it's the comedic ones, the action scenes, or the few moments of drama. And like I've always felt, Ryan Reynolds is annoying when he plays other characters like they're Deadpool, but he's awesome when he's actually playing Wade Fucking Wilson.

Shawn Levy's approach to action here is a mix between Tim Miller's stylized and cartoonish approach of the first movie and the more martial arts movie-ish approach from David Leitch in the second movie—well, more of the first than the second, and it is fun. I still think Tim Miller was the best at doing Deadpool-style gory action, though he got to do only like two action scenes, but Levy does deliver on multiple occasions, as action scenes from this movie are still more memorable than the ones from DP2. I especially love the long oner towards the end, with so much stuff happening, lots of cool slomo and gore.

Anyway, this movie succeeds in what it set out to do and then some. The soundtrack was cool, and the style of humor here is the kind of thing that I enjoy. It creates comedy material out of superhero movies, pop culture, and the MCU itself; the fan service is so well integrated; and there's just enough of a loose narrative that it doesn't feel like a series of comedy sketches stitched together. Yes, the narrative lacks depth, and Emma Corrin is wasted as a one-dimensional villain, but it makes up for it with FUN. It's also a pretty respectful tribute to the era of early 2000s Marvel films that I grew up with and made me weirdly emotional.

Name: Devadoothan
Review:
Devadoothan was pretty novel at the time it came out, and that's probably one of the reasons why it bombed at the box office too, and also one of the reasons why it maintained a cult appeal(plus, of course, that amazing soundtrack). Horror movies in Malayalam at that time were of the Yakshi/vampire, white saree, sorcery variety, so I do remember when I watched this as a kid, the expectation was Mohanlal vs. Evil Ghost, or something along the lines of what Malayalam horror movies were around that time. But Devadoothan's supernatural entity wasn't a physical presence; it just left signs, opened windows, some pigeons here and there, barking dogs, influencing the protagonist's mind, the skeleton, and so on. There are several jump scares and stuff, but yk, it was pretty different from what the audience would expect, both from a horror movie and from a Mohanlal movie at that time. This was essentially just a spirit using the protagonist as his messenger to convey something to his lover. Why'd the spirit choose A10? Idk. Why does the Sneha girl follow A10 around? Idk. 

Anyway, I've only seen the entire movie as a kid, so I don't remember enough of the original release to talk about what's been trimmed in the remastered version, but the trimming doesn't really "enhance" the movie much because some events just happen abruptly, and we could just tell something was supposed to happen in the middle. Jagathy Sreekumar's entire character has been cut out, and tbh, I didn't even remember he was in this movie till I saw people saying he was completely removed from this new cut. Sibi Malayil is being the inverse Zack Snyder here, cutting out his movie to make it closer to his "true vision.". 

Anyway, yeah, Devadoothan is not as scary as I remember; the skeleton was the stuff of my nightmares then, but now it makes me chuckle many times. There are many such serious scenes that look goofy when I watch it now, but I have no complaints though; I had fun. But still, despite that, it does maintain some atmosphere, mystery, and that yearning of lost love that still holds up. The remastered version looks gorgeous though. The cinematography is beautiful, and the film looks so vibrant, I loved the use of colors, whether it's the costumes or the locations and sets. 

Plus, no matter how dated the movie might become, Vidyasagar's score and soundtrack would be eternally magical and brilliant. Also, despite having the worst seats in the hall, I had the best company to watch this movie, and that definitely helped.

Name: Longlegs
Review:
I get the tone they were going for here. It's a mix of what David Fincher did with Seven and Mindhunter, with a seasoning of Silence of the Lambs and a major caffeine shot of Twin Peaks. The end result is definitely a well-shot movie with some great atmosphere building, effective creepiness, one of the best horror film scores ever, disturbing depiction of violence, great cinematography, and epic Nic Cage. But yeah, it does end up being too dark to be campy and too campy to be dark. 

With a premise like this, it's indeed hard to maintain that balance, though even after the major reveal, there are still some chilling sequences. Maika Monroe is an effective horror movie protagonist, and the supporting cast is also great.

During the initial chapter, the film takes the Mindhunter approach, where we don't see much violence and it's all just descriptions. Nic Cage as the title character is never fully shown either; we just see parts of his face and quick shots of it. And it's so effective in building up this menacing and creepy dude, and the threat of him lurking around is persistently teased. Then, of course, it does start getting gory; we see the violence directly, and we do see Nic Cage in all his glory. Yeah, he's only in this movie for like 10-15 minutes or less, but he steals the scenery in every single shot he's in. He's so effortlessly creepy; Nic Cage probably didn't even need those prosthetics to be creepy, but the makeup and the entire presentation of his character were amazing.

I do have mixed feelings about the direction this movie takes towards the end. It was a nice dark twist if it was executed better, but yeah, it ends up being campy writing being shot and acted very seriously. Like, that kind of thing could work; it did work in Twin Peaks, but here, idk. Anyway, they do this thing where Nic Cage addresses the camera directly several times. And man, he's the real deal. I'd give this five stars just for the 10-15 minutes of Cagelicious Cage Rage.

Again, the whole dark atmosphere was maintained really well. I just wish the writing did more to compliment that atmosphere.

Name: Con Air
Review: At one point, Nic Cage is like, "I'm going to show you God does exist," and that awesome electric guitar theme kicks in, and Nic Cage plows through the villain dudes; one of them shoots him on the arm, and he doesn't even flinch. Nic Cage becomes the terminator. It's so badass. Con Air is so badass. It has Nic Cage running in slo-mo in the middle of explosions, with the electric guitar blazing. Nic Cage does that awesome wink, and it's shown TWICE. Nic Cage says, "You don't treat women that way" while beating the shit out of Danny Trejo. It has a car being pulled by a plane that destroys an air tower. It has Dave Chappelle dropping from the sky; it has Steve Buscemi playing a serial killer for no reason whatsoever and ending up surviving the movie. It has John Malkovich playing The Cyrusest of Viruses with so many quotable lines, and he threatens to shoot a stuffed bunny. Con Air rules. Nic Cage is god.

Name: A Quiet Place: Day One
Review:
What Michael Sarnoski does right here is not that different from what he did with Pig. Pig had a premise that made it sound like a John Wick clone; I even remember seeing posts about it saying it's Nic Cage's John Wick with a Pig instead of a dog. But what we got was no action movie; it was something intimate and sad. Coming to A Quiet Place: Day One, its marketing also made it seem like a big Alien Invasion movie, where we'd be put into Day One of the invasion, that too in a big city like New York (we did actually get a glimpse of how Day One looked like in the Abbot's small town in Part Two). But this one too works more like a more intimate drama that focuses on two people and a cat than the sci-fi horror movie we expected. That's not to say this movie doesn't have any scary aliens or horror setpieces; it does. Just that, rather than "expanding" the world or showing the full-scale carnage as the creatures attack New York, the movie is laser focused on the characters and their perspective. 

We're following Lupita Nyong'o as Samira and Joe Quinn as Eric the whole time. Their dynamic and chemistry just instantly work, and with them is the most peaceful cat in the world. I mean, the aliens are CGI, but I'm pretty sure the cat wasn't for most of the movie. That cat was excellent; not only does the cat add so much tension during so many scenes, but putting something so innocent into a post-apocalyptic world is just genius (yeah I understand that when a small meow means death, them keeping the cat around doesn't make sense, but I'm willing to give it a pass, I mean c'mon!). It's those tender moments between the characters, their bonding, and their companionship that work beautifully here.

There are many memorable horror setpieces too, like the one involving the big crowd, where the tension builds and builds until the worst happens. The aliens are still scary, and like the previous installments, their absence is scarier than their presence. When the sound design puts an emphasis on each and every little sound and the tension builds up, that's the best part of these movies. Still though, the creature design and their quick and erratic movements are scary too. The final setpiece did feel a bit underwhelming though, but it didn't bother me because the character drama there was so on point. Both the leads and the cat are brilliant throughout the movie. 

Also, the score and the use of silence were pretty great. It does stay unique from Krasinski's films while belonging to that world. And whatever it is that gave Pig the heart it had, some of it is present in this movie too. It ended up being surprisingly more tender than I expected it to be.

Name: The Guest
Review:
I've always wondered what the action movie badass would look like as a horror villain, and this is exactly that. Dan Stevens basically plays the character Jason Statham usually plays: a handsome, soft-spoken, cool-seeming dude who has an incredible appetite for violence and is an unstoppable killing machine.

Usually, the kind of super soldier Stevens plays here is the hero, the bringer of justice; give him a shield and a suit, and he's Captain America. But he's not the good guy here, and that change in context is what makes this movie great. Even during an initial bar fight with teenage bullies, it's usually the kind of thing that'd make us root for the person punishing these bullies, but here, there's a very specific way of showcasing the violence that visually makes it known that Stevens' David is violent in a way that's not exactly admirable. And things only keep escalating from there.

Stevens is indeed the star here, in how he seems menacing and at the same time bringing in the energy of your typical action movie hero as the villain. Maika Monroe and Lance Riddick were also great. Riddick gives a John Wick style buildup for Stevens at a point, when Stevens is just a killing machine that lacks empathy than the "avenging angel" that Wick was, and Riddick being in both of these movies made me compare how both movies approach scenes where the main character stylishly kills his way through characters.

Anyway, this is a well-made horror movie with an action movie twist. There's some well-crafted action sequences here, and I really do hope Adam Wingard does more of these movies instead of the CGI monster fight stuff.

Name: Nosferatu
Review:
This movie is a 102 years old. And yeah it has aged (obviously, it's a fuckin antique), but no matter how many centuries pass, Max Schreck as Count Orlok will forever be so effectively creepy. The way he looks, the way he moves unlike any human being, his overall stiffness and body language add so much towards selling the "terror" of this movie. Orlok is an eerie presence from the first time we lay eyes on him, and it's baffling that our human protagonist Hutter doesn't run for his life then and there. Nosferatu has brilliant horror filmmaking, that still works, whenever Orlok comes on screen or his presence is felt. Like, the movie absolutely has no jump scares (idk if jump scares were a thing then), all of Orlok's appearances have him slowly slithering onto the screen, or just staying still in the creepiest pose possible, and it definitely creeped me out. The music was effective in conveying the mood too. Yes there are goofy Orlok scenes too, like when he strolls around town carrying a coffin. But yk, on the whole, Orlok is still, a century later, an effective movie monster. 

I can't wait to see what Robert Eggers does with this.

Name: Shadow of the Vampire
Review:
Just like how Max Schreck sold the original Nosferatu, Willem Dafoe is the MVP of this movie. This is not an accurate retelling about the production of Nosferatu, but it's like fan fiction of the urban legend that Max Schreck was an actual vampire (the dude was that good in the original). And though the movie is appropriately silly initially, it does take it seriously too, especially towards the end. It's like a mix of silly metahumor with straight horror elements, and it worked for me.

Dafoe isn't just emulating Schreck's original performance here, which he does so wonderfully; several of the iconic shots from the original are recreated using Dafoe. But also, his count is a very different character and a very unique vampire. The original Count Orlok and even Count Dracula were mostly menacing and creepy. Dafoe's count is also old, tired, and sad. He's not really a bloodthirsty monster; he's been alive for so long that he has forgotten how to be human. So all his weird body language and stiffness are because he has basically been all alone for centuries. Yes, he needs to feed on blood to survive, but it's more of a curse for this person. Dafoe really elevates this role, which is so silly on paper, because after all, it is basically a vampire pretending to be a person pretending to be a vampire for a film.

Malkovich as the narcissistic director was also great, especially during the climax, which is where the film became a true horror movie, and I did feel that the atmosphere and presentation of the count were somewhat similar to the original. The score was also great.

The film does show great respect to the original Nosferatu, the film, but I don't know if portraying the people behind it like this is disrespectful towards them or not. It is essentially "alternate history" meta-cinema and not meant to represent the actual people though, but yk.

Name: Mom and Dad
Review: It's a very dark premise presented in ridiculous fashion. Though it doesn't show kids and babies being murdered directly, there are many off-screen murders. But parents randomly trying to murder their kids, and it being related to all the repressed anger parents do have for their kids, than being a full on zombie virus or something, was an interesting idea. But this movie isn't that interested in philosophy or depth. It builds up the premise for almost half of the movie, and it takes half of the movie till we see Nic Cage snap. This is a short movie of about only 80 minutes, but some of the initial buildup did seem unnecessary, as the film then became an extended action scene set in a single house after the halfway point. Nic Cage acting insane is always fun to watch, even in the terrible movies he's been in. But here, it does actually work for the absurd dark territory the movie covers. There's a particular scene involving three generations of the same family, that made me laugh out loud. It's an insane movie, with an insane premise. And yeah, Nic Cage sells the ridiculousness of it perfectly. Selma Blair was great too in being menacing. I had fun.

Name: Arcadian
Review: There was way less Nic Cage in this movie than I thought it would have, and he doesn't even have much to do, except for a really cool moment towards the end. Everything else just felt like an inferior version of A Quiet Place. Even the monster design and CGI was weird than terrifying. It does have some great music and cinematography though.

Name: MaXXXine
Review:
X worked as a straight conventional slasher that paid tribute to retro slashers, and I was all for it. The dark atmosphere, the campiness, the throwback special effects and gore, Pearl's character, and the creepiness of the whole thing. Then came Pearl; it had gory kills too, but it was more of your "descent into madness" arc movie than a slasher. And it was my favorite movie of this trilogy. All three movies have a great leading performance from Mia Goth, but Pearl was where she shined the most. It was tragic, dark, campy, and the bright, vibrant aesthetics similar to old-timey musicals for dark story material just worked.

Now, X and Pearl were drastically different movies from each other, except for the fact that they shared a main character and had kills and gore. Maxxxine too is different from the other two, with still having the kills and the throwback style practical gore. But Maxxxine lacks a certain edge the other two had, the "X Factor" (hehe). That's why I felt like talking about them first before I talked about Maxxxine. Mia Goth and the cast are fantastic; I loved the soundtrack, the aesthetics, and the style choices. The production design and the costumes were great too. This is a pretty high-quality production and a lot bigger than the two predecessors. But the two smaller movies still had a great atmosphere and vibe that this one just lacked.

I did like the final twist, but the finale otherwise just fell flat. It just felt like this generic movie, but the previous movies felt like something new that's built on top of paying tribute to older generic movies. This just didn't have that novelty. It's campy and kinda fun, but it felt like a tiny packet of chips, while something like Pearl felt like a full meal.

Name: The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent
Review:
The weakest part of this movie is when it transitions into an action comedy towards the final act. The action sequences aren't that remarkable, and the action lacks stakes. That wouldn't normally be a problem for a comedy movie, but this one stars Nic Fuckiiiiiiiiinnnnnnnggggg Cage, he's been in multiple iconic action movies, so the action part is my only disappointment in this movie. Other than that, this is the perfect movie, so the five stars I gave will stay intact. 

This movie is ingenious on multiple levels. It takes the perceived public persona of Nic Cage, the myth of Nic Cage to be exact, and constructs this unique and ridiculous character named Nick Cage, a once big star, now looking for a comeback (not that he went anywhere), having insecurities, and his delusions of grandeur split personality literally looking like a young version of himself. Whenever this movie pokes fun of the actual Nic Cage or his career, it's so awesome. Not many established stars would do what Nic Cage did here, and this isn't like an SNL sketch or something either; the character actually has an arc and stuff. Nick Cage here is a full-fledged character and not just a one-off parody. Then there's the effortless chemistry he has with Javi, played by Pedro Pascal. The scenes with Pascal and Cage are the best parts of this movie. Pascal would always throw some random Nic Cage trivia, even in the middle of a shootout, and it's so fucking cool. This movie is a great time, especially for someone like me who grew up watching Nic Cage movies on TV. Nouveau Shamanic foreva! 


"Tell em Nick Cage smooches good"
"Paddington 2 made me want to be a better man"
"100 plus years of rich cinema, you can't just reduce it to one"

Name: Brokeback Mountain
Review:
This film is so beautiful. Like, it feels like poetry. The pacing here flows like the steam of water in the titular mountains. It starts from the initial meeting of the main characters, Ennis and Jack. We follow their daily lives as sheep herders at the titular brokeback mountain for a bit, and we see them bonding organically, growing closer, becoming comfortable with each other, till eventually they fall for each other. They couldn't live together as a gay couple during that time in America, so they go on their separate ways, trying to live the "acceptable" life that a man should, while holding back this love inside them. There's an air of melancholy to the proceedings because what these two men have is something deep and emotional, and not just sexual. But circumstances force them to spend time together as if they're committing adultery, but in reality the heterosexual marriages they're a part of are the adultery, while the small amount of time they spend together is the real relationship.

The physical intimacy is portrayed brilliantly here, and both Gyllenhaal and Ledger are amazing and have great chemistry together. Every nuance and change in body language convey the internal conflict of the characters and their relationship. They're always in conflict between the men they "should be" and the men they actually are. When Ennis and Jack meet again after a gap of 4 years, the physical embrace feels so real; we see how Ennis initially hesitates and looks around to see if anybody's watching and then just gives into the love. There are several time jumps in the movie, but it never feels jarring. The direction and editing are masterful, and the film just flows at this beautiful pace. Every bit of emotion in their journey is felt—every conflict, every confusion, the feeling of insecurity, the helplessness, the yearning for love—like, yeah, people were understandably right for being pissed off that cinema like this didn't win the best picture Oscar that year.

The beautiful cinematography, the editing, Gustavo Santaolalla's beautiful melancholic score that's still looping in my head, Ang Lee's direction that made me cry without the movie ever feeling overly melodramatic, and the amazing acting. This movie is a gem.

Name: Golam
Review:
The crime part was pretty interesting, and though there are gaps in logic, watching the crime unravel was cool. Though how the crime gets "solved" is pretty stupid, our police officer dude just randomly stumbles on clues that lead him to an exposition machine person who provides all necessary exposition like they're crime movie ChatGPT. We never feel like the case was solved with wits and intelligence, because everything that led to the conclusion was pure luck, and because someone existed who'd just blurt everything out without putting much pressure.

But like I said, the crime itself and the motive behind it were all pretty cool. The movie is conveniently designed to hide the limited acting range of its leading man. There's two things he maintains well: the first is his impressive physique, which the movie makes sure we don't miss; he removes his shirt the very first time he's on screen; and there's a scene where he's doing shirtless pull-ups right before getting some exposition; the second is the monotony of his character. A stoic cop character isn't something new, but he just came off as bland rather than stoic. There's nothing interesting about the character in the writing itself, so I wouldn't blame just Ranjith Sajeev. The ensemble cast moves the film forward more than the leading man. As far as a nepo movie starring a rich kid from a business fam, produced by their family goes, at least this is a better approach than whatever Legend Saravanan did with "The Legend". So I don't feel like being so rude on the guy. Maybe a Vineeth Sreenivasan movie could fix him. xD

The bigger ensemble cast was mostly okay. I wouldn't call them all great performances, but they served the purpose. The production design looked cool. The music was pretty much what we'd expect in a movie like this, sometimes it was a bit overscored too. And I'm pretty sure a track towards the end was lifted from the Now You See Me soundtrack. 


Anyway, I also hated the sequel baiting in the end. It felt like the movie was already over, but then it just goes on, till we realize it's sequel bait. The movie also does this weird thing where it shows us each individual character's reaction during a scene, like how soap operas do it. And there's like 10-12 characters here. It felt funny.

Also, I even protect my cringey photos on my phone more carefully than how incriminating digital evidence is left open for anyone to find in this movie.

Also, Sunny Wayne randomly appears in the movie. Like how he randomly appeared at the end of this movie opinion on Letterboxd.

Name: Phir Aayi Hasseen Dillruba
Review:
I absolutely hated the first movie and tbh, the only reason I watched this one is because Tapsee looks so gorgeous in those sarees. It also helps that this one doesn't focus too much on romanticising the fucked up and abusive aspects of the Rishu-Rani couple. It doesn't really question them for it either, but at this point, we're just supposed to accept that they're a fucked up couple, and the movie is more focused on how they'd evade the authorities. Sunny Kaushal was a good new addition to the cast, and contrary to the first movie I could appreciate the cheesy pulpiness here. But still, towards the end the movie got rather tedious and dumb, "plans" relied on just dumb luck, and them having olympic athlete level swimming ability. But still yeah, more dumb fun than the first one. 

Also, Pandit Ji is Nic Cage from the movie Next at this point. Is the dude writing novels or prophetic murder manuals? There's a Pandit Ji book for every crime available? Well, in the first part, committing a crime inspired by a Pandit Ji book was okay. But this one takes it to whole other (worse) levels.

Name: The Instigators
Review: I have no idea why this movie got all those negative reviews, because to me it was a very fun watch. It's about two dudes, who are in no way professional criminals, put in the middle of a high-profile heist, where they now have the burden of navigating through a situation involving powerful people while neither having the smarts nor resources for it. It was constantly funny; the banter between Damon, Affleck, and Hong Chau was great; yes, they joke a lot during serious situations, but it just seemed right. Like, yk, I've missed these kinds of movies, the Pineapple Express and Soodhu Kaavum style of crime comedy cinema. Yes, these dudes would never practically survive a situation like this, and that's what makes it fun—their being able to act like master criminals while not being master criminals. Also, Hong Chau is so good in this movie, and it made me wish there was more screentime for her. Yes they could've played around with the situation more, because it was ripe for all kinds of crazy twists and turns, but it worked for me anyway. This was a fun watch; remind me to never trust negative reviews.

Name: The Bikeriders
Review:
Benny and Johnny relationship here reminded me a bit of Christopher and Tony from The Sopranos. Kathy played by the always dependable Jodie Comer is our narrator and POV character. I loved the style of the movie, the performances were great, the soundtrack was great, and there are moments of drama executed really well. Also, Norman Reedus in a biker movie, it's like the movie summoned him into it or something.

Though I liked the movie, I think it could've been further fleshed out in a long form format, like The Sopranos. (I haven't seen sons of anarchy, and how a biker gang story is treated in the longer form there)

Name: Thangalaan
Review:
It's another Pa. Ranjith film about standing up against oppression, and as long as oppression exists in one form or another, the politics here are important. Thangalaan specifically shows multiple forms of oppression. There's the Indian caste system and savarna oppressor who doesn't let the villagers own their farmland, or the crop that they themselves farm, and the foreign British colonizer who promises them riches and gold and better living conditions than their previous oppressor. They even forget their own identity, working for the oppressors, only to realize that the label might change, the hierarchy might change, and the local oppressor might be obedient to the colonizer, but towards them, all these oppressors only have one purpose, which is exploitation.

Anyway, Thangalaan is about the hunt for the gold reserve in Kolar, and it's pretty engaging for the most part. Vikram is amazing as the lead, and the supporting cast does a great job too; I especially loved Parvathy. The movie is not without its flaws. I do believe this was supposed to be a longer film because there's a lot of rushed portions, jarring editing, and abrupt transitions. The surreal shift effects during the fight scenes were nice as an idea (there's already a well-executed version of the same in Everything Everywhere All At Once), but here the shifts and the transition effects didn't feel so seamless. The CGI animals don't look photorealistic, but moments like the snake attacks and the panther attack are well conceived enough that the lesser fidelity of the CGI can be excused.

The production design, costumes, and makeup were great. Everyone felt like the characters they were playing—only Malavika Mohanan perhaps seemed a bit out of place, but since her character itself is written and presented a certain way, and since her appearance is supposed to give the feeling of a mythical being from folklore, it works. Her character doesn't get much depth other than just being this mythical figure either.
