The film's blend of folklore fantasy elements and history to tell a tale about oppression and exploitation is quite nice. Though the execution of it is flawed, there is cinema here. GV Prakash Kumar's score is effective in conveying the epic folk fantasy atmosphere (but yeah, occasionally a bit too loud, but idk if it's the music or the mixing, or the speakers in the cinema hall), and I loved the cinematography too.

Captain Miller earlier this year had a similar theme that dealt with villagers having to face both the white oppressor and their savarna Indian oppressor, but yk, it also had a religious angle about a temple and all, while Thangalaan is about land, resources, and wealth being stolen from their rightful owners by these oppressors. So, of course Thangalaan does it better. I'd place this Pa. Ranjith movie right below how much I loved Kaala and Sarpatta. If a longer cut exists, I want to watch it. Also yeah, like I've already mentioned, the action is well choreographed and well performed, but needed better editing and conceiving to pull off the surreal shift effect.

Name: Bram Stoker's Dracula
Review:
This movie absolutely terrified me as a kid, and some of the imagery from it was the thing of my nightmares. Also, certain shots from this movie were also inserted into a popular Malayalam horror TV show at that time named Kadamattathu Kathanaar, the candle that bleeds, Dracula in werewolf form, and Dracula in the Man-Bat form; all these were imagery that scared me the most as a kid. This film made me so fascinated in the character that I even got the novel from a library and then abandoned trying to read it because at that time the whole "found documents" format of the novel confused the hell out of me.

Enough nostalgic yapping; now about the movie. This movie still holds up pretty well; it won't haunt me like it did when I was a child, but Gary Oldman's performance is still fantastic. The prosthetics, visual effects, use of blood, and the way he plays Dracula are what make this movie work big time, in addition to the big dramatic flair and stylistic choices in the film. As a kid, Dracula's presence in this film only evoked fear in me, but now I could understand the tragedy of the character. Oldman is so convincing in portraying Dracula's yearning for his lost love, how he actually sees his immortality as a curse, and how he even hesitates to turn Mina into a vampire.

Yes, things are a bit rushed; it's not as dense as the source material, and things like the Mina-Dracula/Prince Vlad relationship and its complexities could've been fleshed out. Keanu Reeves and his accent are the most criticized and memed part of this movie, but tbh, I didn't really mind. In most of his scenes, peak thespians like Gary Oldman or Anthony Hopkins would also be there, and I was more focused on them. Oldman is so great as old Dracula at the beginning; the way he says the name Dracula is almost ASMR.

Then there's all the style choices in the movie, the use of red light, surreal imagery, weird and creative editing choices, and camera work, moments like when Dracula's red eyes stare at Jonathan from the weird looking sky when he reads Dracula's letter, it's got such an indie movie vibe for a big studio production at times because a lot of the choices in this movie were not so conventional, and the filmmaking is still so unique. Also, I've always had the image of Van Helsing as a heroic vampire hunter and didn't realize that Hopkins' version here is so weird and crazy.

Name: Manichitrathazhu
Review:
I have only faint memories of watching the entirety of Manichithrathazhu as a child, and apart from the iconic moments from the movie that have popped up in TV or my feed over the years, watching it again in a single stretch was like having a new experience. The movie still holds up pretty well, and it was a great experience on the big screen. Seeing a vintage cute A10 on screen again almost made me cry, tbh. Shobhana's iconic performance too was great to revisit in this format. 

The restoration looks gorgeous visually, and everything from the performances to the costumes and the locations was a treat to the eyes. I do have mixed emotions about the way they have updated the score to fit Dolby Atmos. I don't care if Manichithrathazhu had thundering bass or not; I wish they retained as much of the original tracks as they could. Maybe it's just a me problem.

Anyway, Manichithrathazhu is still a well-made mystery drama; a lot of the fun, the atmosphere, and the great parts of it still hold up. I watched the Devadoothan re-release a few weeks ago, and Manichithrathazhu doesn't even seem as dated as Devadoothan. I don't mean that it doesn't show its age; it does, but the retro cheesiness is more cute than cringe-inducing. Like, in what other 90s Malayalam movie would the dude who came to perform a hocus pocus exorcism ritual suddenly see a psychiatrist and then switch to talk about parapsychology and the stages of psychosis? I don't know about the scientific accuracy of the portrayal of mental health here, but yeah, it is good cinema, always. Stuff like A10 breaking into singing Pazhamthamizh Paattizhayum after a big emotional scene is not something we'd see in a modern movie, but it's so awesome!

The big twist in Manichithrathazhu is the Malayali version of "I am your father" from Star Wars. It's so embedded into our pop culture that most people already know it even before watching the movie (the promotions for the re-release don't even try to hide it). But I do wish to know how it felt to watch it without knowing the fact. Because the way it balances the supernatural with the logical is pretty interesting. There are even some interesting details here and there.

There is still impressive filmmaking here, and the stuff that made the movie iconic stays iconic, especially the cast, the performances, and the music (though the updates to the music in the newer version irked me).

Name: Alien
Review:
This movie is a masterclass of building atmosphere and tension, and it does so brilliantly from beginning to end, always taking its time, always being creative with its scares and the buildups to them. The film even begins with this introduction of the USCSS Nostromo; the camera moves slowly through the interiors of the ship, not only flexing the impressive production design but also setting up this environment where most of the film will be set. We don't know anything about these characters or their lives outside of being crew members of this ship; even our leading lady, Ellen Ripley, isn't treated like the protagonist of the movie until the movie reaches its conclusion. Because the atmosphere is the star here, even more than the titular Alien.

The production design, sound design and special effects are something else in this movie. And it's not just the retro sci-fi stuff; the organic alien parts and gore look so impressive and disgusting too. The Alien is just a man in a suit in this movie, and some creative use of puppetry, but Ridley Scott uses lighting and film magic to maintain the illusion. These are old filmmaking techniques, but since all of them are practical and on camera, almost everything has aged well. But yeah, they do try in making the alien/Xenomorph seem more like a creature than a man in future installments. But this version, who pops up only a handful of times and kills someone instantly almost every time, builds up that terror so much as it eventually sets its sights on Ripley.

There's lots of brilliant buildup. Like how Brett stops to let some water fall on him (as if he's missing the rain) and then looks for the cat, only for the Alien to appear behind him; it's not the silence and jumpscare kind of slow buildup at all, and yet it builds up the terror. Every kill is so brilliantly designed. Like, there's even a fake out towards the end, where we think Ripley is going to be taken out, because she goes out on her own, looking for the cat like Brett, and I'm sure people who were not aware of Ripley being the sole survivor at the end felt like she's going to get Aliened next. But she and the cat survives of course. Cat - 1, Alien - 0.

Sigourney Weaver is just a member of the crew for most of this movie, so Ripley as a badass is something we'd only get to see in its full glory in James Cameron's Aliens, which is what I'm going to watch next, of course.

Name: Aliens
Review:
James Cameron's Aliens is a clearly different film from Ridley Scott's Alien, and yet, it's not still absolutely devoid of horror elements. Just like the first film, Aliens too takes a good amount of time before a Xenomorph appears on screen, but yeah, the buildup is shorter than the first movie. The slow and gradual building of atmosphere in Alien is replaced by faster-paced thriller elements here. Tension and atmosphere are still present, but it's using things like the movement locator, the amount of ammo left, and the threat of the Xenomorphs closing in. The Xenomorphs are still a scary threat, though there are more than one here, and they're easier to kill than in the first movie thanks to all the military weapons. The moody and creepy score from the first movie is replaced by James Horner's thundering thriller music, with even the cling sounds similar to the Terminator soundtrack (one track even reminded me of a track from the Avatar Score).

Ripley is a proper protagonist this time around, and at the end she tapes a flamethrower and rifle together and gets to be a badass. The aliens seem more like a group of bug-like creatures with cockroach-ish bodies here, even when we can see them in better lighting, as the first movie does make us feel like it's a person in a leather suit at times and used lighting and clever filmmaking to make it seem like a creature, but here they just seemed like huge bugs more effectively. The production design, sound design and visual effects are impressive in this film too, but also, the Nostromo from the first movie was an incredible feat in set design; the facility shown in this movie doesn't come near it. 

Anyway, James Cameron pretty much followed the same philosophy from Terminator here. It's an action movie with horror elements, with emotional beats that we can easily connect with, in this case the Ripley-Newt bonding, with great action, thrilling setpieces, cool one-liners, and opportunities for Sigourney Weaver to be an absolute badass; it's a departure from the original, but an awesome one!

With Ripley being the sole survivor in the first one and the only person who assessed the situation correctly while her male crewmates took her for granted, and her being a brave badass in this one, I can't help but wonder if incels would've cried about "forced woke and forced feminism" if Alien and Aliens had released now.

Name: Alien³
Review:
So, David Fincher's Alien 3 is a film that David Fincher himself loathes because the studio didn’t actually let him make it as David Fincher's Alien 3. I did watch the Assembly Cut, which is closer to his vision, though he wasn't involved in creating this cut. 

This is indeed a downgrade from the first movie, and the writing issues are very apparent even without knowing about all the behind-the-scenes drama. It begins by making the very satisfying conclusion of Aliens seem pointless, of course, which does have shock value and make Ripley seem even more hopeless and tortured, but yeah, I understand how it could piss off someone who loved Aliens. The film is aimless for the most part, other than having a few ideas like Ripley carrying the queen, going back to the basics of being a horror film with just one Xenomorph, making the alien seem more like an animal, and of course, the addition of more blood and gore. I realized that both the previous movies didn't have as much blood and gore as this one, and a Xenomorph covered in blood is indeed effective imagery. The creature looks great, and the practical visual effects are good for the most part. Still, the composting hasn't aged well for some of the scenes involving the Xenomorph in motion, but still, this movie has the most fluid-looking Xenomorph.

After going cluelessly and even boring me to an extent, this movie does have a pretty solid third act. Also, despite being directed by a very restricted David Fincher, this movie does occasionally have the Fincher signature filmmaking flair here and there. 

The alien trap sequence and the ending were great; Ripley gets a great emotional send-off, with Weyland-Yutani so comically evil corporationing at this point. Sigourney Weaver was amazing as Ripley here too, though. Not even bad writing can affect her performance. 

Farewell, Ripley, till Ripley was "resurrected," of course.

Name: Alien Resurrection
Review:
I think Alien: Resurrection is underrated. Firstly, it "resurrects" Ripley pretty respectably; the real Ripley is still dead, so her sacrifice isn't meaningless; the one in this film is the 8th version of the Ripley cloning experiment. And of course, all the previous movies played with the plot point of the corporation wanting to use the Xenomorphs for developing bioweapons. So this time they actually get to do that and then fuck up by underestimating these creatures, so that was a great direction for the series to go in. In terms of making the great ending from the previous movie seeming pointless, the off-screen killings at the beginning of Alien 3 is the one that still bugs me. 

This one ditches the darker tone from Alien 3 for a more cheesy, action movie tone similar to Aliens. Well, it ends up being a lot similar to something like Guardians of the Galaxy or your average goofy Marvel movie than Aliens, with quips even after serious scenes. Like when Ripley has to painfully burn down previous versions of the cloning experiment, with one disfigured clone even begging her to kill her, and then the sexist Ron Perlman character is like, "Women something, What a waste of Ammo!". Lol. Well, this was written by Joss Whedon after all, so that tracks. There are also quips that just seem confusing, like Ripley saying, "Who do I have to fuck to get off this boat?" 

Ripley's arc is uneven and all over the place, and the movie is not sure whether to let Sigourney Weaver play this weird disconnected clone with Xenomorph powers or to just be Ellen Ripley. But she does succeed in seeming like an absolute badass. Ron Perlman's character seemed like he was trying to emulate Bill Paxton's Hudson from Aliens. Winona Ryder plays a template good person, though there's a pretty solid reason in the movie for her being that way.

Anyway, this one was fun enough; it's a more coherent movie than Alien 3, has enough goofy charm, and is even pretty short. The blood and gore during the kills were pretty great. Also, this one has better-looking CGI aliens in motion than Alien 3. The puppets and animatronics during closeups are always great in these movies, of course. The final monster involving a human-Xeno abomination was great as an idea, and its birthing sequence looked effectively gnarly (great disgusting alien stuff production design, btw), but its design involving the sad skull face looked goofy. There are some great action sequences, like the two Alien ambushes. 

I've heard this one being called the worst Alien movie, but no, Alien and Aliens are top tier; this one is some good old cheesy fun, and yk, even David Fincher himself hates Alien 3, so I'd say Alien 3 is my least favorite Ripley era movie.

Name: Prometheus
Review:
I actually like Prometheus despite its unevenness in writing, that muddled third act, and the famous running in straight lines to the doom scene. What this movie brought back to the Alien franchise was Ridley Scott's skill at building atmosphere. In Prometheus, the threat is not a single Xenomorph, and we're always on the lookout for what's about to go wrong. The first two acts of this movie are actually amazing. It's all great till they actually decide to go and wake up the engineer. There are many memorable scenes, like the facehugger abortion sequence and the snake-facehugger hybrid attack.

Still though, it has great ideas even in the third act. Like how the Xenomorphs themselves are actually bio weapons developed by the Engineers, the creators of human life, to exterminate humans. Then in the future, the humans of the Weyland-Yutani corporation would want to use the Xenomorphs for the exact same purpose, to kill humans. It's even darkly funny. 

Michael Fassbender as David is the most impressive visual effect in this movie; all the other technological leaps from the original Alien stay second. He brings the coldness and the machine-like body language so much finesse. The entire cast is STACKED with so much talent. Noomi Rapace, Charlize Theron, Idris Elba, Guy Pearce, phew. 

Still though, a creative choice I found confusing in Prometheus is how, despite being a prequel that's set decades before the original Alien and centuries before Alien: Resurrection, the future tech shown in this film looks more futuristic than any of those movies. There are holograms, touchscreens, surgery bots, and all kinds of very advanced future tech and interfaces that we never saw in the other movies. So people just randomly decided to switch to retro-future tech at one point? Because the tech, the sets, and the costumes more represent a version of the future from a 2010s perspective than the version of the future from the 70s perspective that the original Alien had.

Anyway, is Prometheus amazing? No. But did it still offer great atmosphere buildup, sci-fi creature horror, and fun lore into the alien world? That it did.

Name: Alien: Covenant
Review:
Ridley Scott is still so great at building tension and atmosphere. This is structurally more similar to the original Alien than Prometheus. It takes a sweet time to build up to the first creature's appearance. Fassbender as David/Walter is still the best part about this movie, more than the traditional Alien appearing. The Xenomorph doesn't appear until the end of the movie, and Scott makes the choice of making it seem more humanoid, like how the actor in the suit looked like in the original (Aliens and the rest of the sequels made it more like an insect or an animal). Still though, the practical visual effects and animatronics still seem superior in depicting these creatures, though CGI adds more movement fluidity and stuff. There are instances where a practical facehugger, chestburster, and Xenomorph are used, but it's mostly CGI.

 

There are some cool kills, like the one in the Shower, which was very slashery, but also, in a lot of places the use of CGI for some reason didn't make the creature horror seem as scary as the older film. Anyway, more than the creatures, David was more interesting for me. His arc involving being made to serve and then eventually trying to play god himself was very intriguing. Plus the fact that the Xenomorphs we see in all the other movies were a product of David's experiment to kill humans; David was also a product made by the corporation, while the corporation then tries to get the Xenomorphs for themselves to use as weapons in the future. That circular arc is kind of brilliant. Like more than seeing more Xenomorph stuff, I wanted to see how the David arc would be further developed and how it'd connect to the first Alien movie. But that seems unsure at this point, though.

Despite being not as great as the original, I still like the two Ridley Scott follow-ups. Katherine Waterson's Daniels is no Ripley, but they do try to establish character relationships, her grief and all, but it's underdeveloped. This wouldn't have been a problem if the attempt to give more depth was not present and the emotional beats were just more simple, like surviving and saving a cat, like in the original. She was good otherwise. 

Also, at this point, after watching all the Alien movies back to back, a sequel invalidating the previous movie's ending doesn't bother me much. The off-screen kills at the beginning of Alien 3 are still more frustrating than the one in Covenant.

Name: Alien: Romulus
Review:
The premise of Alien:Romulus is nothing new; we once again have the corporation try to play god using the Xenomorphs, and it goes spectacularly wrong. It's not so different from the setup in Aliens, and our main characters walk into this aftermath. But this one is set entirely in outer space, and the tone and atmosphere here are very faithful to the first Alien movie. I even felt some resemblance with the video game Alien: Isolation, which was also set in a space station in the aftermath of a Xenomorph attack. Fede Álvarez takes this premise and uses it to create a very effective horror thriller with so many impressive setpieces, tension building, atmosphere, and just a whole lot of fun. It manages to pay homage to Ridley Scott's original, and towards the end even has a reference to a one-liner from Aliens that put a smile on my face.

Firstly, retro-future tech is back, after the tech and aesthetics in Prometheus and Covenant looked more futuristic than any other Alien movie. The opening credits itself had the same font as the first alien movie; even the score had the same mood, though they don't go all the way and have the title text slowly appear while the credits are being shown. Anyway, the production design, costumes, and look closely follow the original Alien, and it fits in with that movie perfectly, more so than Ridley Scott's own Prometheus and Covenant. For the creatures too, a combination of old-school special effects, puppets, and CGI is used. I don't know how to describe it, but the CGI looks way better here than in Alien: Covenent; the CGI creatures and the practical ones blend in perfectly, and tbh, I couldn't even tell the difference most of the time. Maybe lighting plays a role too, because I think Covenant is the first time we see a Xenomorph in daylight, while all others include this one has them indoors or in dark and dimly lit areas. 

The Xenomorphs behave more like the humanoid version in Ridley Scott's Alien, and overall this is one of the best and scariest depictions of these things. They're a terrifying threat; their acid blood is scary; the damage they inflict is gruesome; the kills are gory, and Álvarez finds new and creative ways to create thrilling horror setpieces with them. The production design is brilliant, and everything in the space station that is setup at the beginning has a payoff. None of the buildups are filler, and that's the sign of great writing and filmmaking. The sound design was also great, and in the cinemas I could feel the tension and ambience of that abandoned space station a lot more. The music too had nostalgia-inducing cues and tracks that fit the film's tone. While this movie follows the tone of the first Alien, it's more fast-paced and is more of a thriller. There's more action, but it doesn't become a full-on action movie like Aliens, though that DNA is also there. It even manages to make connections to Prometheus and Covenent despite seeming more like it actually takes place in the original Alien franchise world than those movies. But the Aliens callback line, cheesy as it is, was still my favorite throwback moment.

The cast and the characters were great. Cailee Spaeny's Rain is a great lead, and she's written to be her own character rather than a "successor" to Ripley. She gets to be both a badass and the survivor on the run. The bond between her and Andy, played by David Jonsson, is at the core of the movie, and the way that relationship plays out in the movie is very interesting. It doesn't feel like filler drama. Jonsson is the next performance here that I loved a lot. Andy is a pretty complex character to pull off, and he does it so well. The rest of the cast too is great. There's also a legacy actor making an appearance (idk if it's a spoiler to say who it is), but unlike a lot of legacy sequel cameos, this one is not just fan service; the character actually fits into the narrative and is just so much more than just nostalgia bait.



Anyway, Alien: Romulus is a very effective horror thriller that's well-crafted, pays respect to its predecessors with an appropriate amount of nostalgia, and modernizes the Alien formula while having one foot on the old-fashioned way too. Towards the end, there's also a better executed design of an idea previously seen in another Alien sequel. The design reminded me of the necromorphs from the Dead Space video games (which itself were inspired by the original Alien) and was also a very effective creature threat.

Name: Beetlejuice
Review:
As a kid while watching horror movies, I've always wondered what an inverse haunted house movie would look like, where the humans are the villains and the ghosts are the protagonists who want to get rid of the evil humans who invade their home. Then I stumble upon Beetlejuice, which is literally that movie. Tbh, I remember watching this because Michael Keaton in the posters reminded me of Jim Carrey from The Mask, and that was the kind of movie that I expected. So it was a surprise that Beetlejuice himself is a secondary character here and that the Maitlands, played by Alec Baldwin and Geena Davis, with Lydia, played by Winona Ryder, were the actual leads.

Keaton is great as the pervy "bio-exorcist" with the over-the-top cartoonish energy and absurdity. But I have the feeling that Beetlejuice is the kind of character who'd only work in short bursts. We don't need to "like" him; he's a creep and a malignant entity, so the amount of Beetlejuice here was appropriate; if the sequel decides to have too much of the juice in it, it'd probably turn out to be a bad decision.

Another thing I love about this movie is the crazy Tim Burton energy and dark humor of it, of course. It's in the music, it's in the cinematography, it's in the overall style and design. The art, production design, and character designs are amazing. The stop-motion animation and the cartoony visual effects and tone are all so well done. It's a PG-13 movie with one F-word, lots of dark comedy and a pervert ghost for a title character, so it's not exactly a kids movie, and yet there's a weird child's fantasy zing to it.

Name: Raayan
Review:
Raayan just made me appreciate Vetrimaaran as a filmmaker a lot more. Because this is like a 144p Vetrimaaran movie. While it was obvious that Dhanush lacked the political perspective Vetrimaaran has for telling working-class stories (January 22, ahem, Sanghi, ahem), Dhanush also lacks the writing and filmmaking chops to pull off a gritty and intense drama. Dhanush has given amazing performances in Vetrimaaran movies; he acts well in this one too, but again, he's no Vetrimaaran. 

There are no socio-political themes here like a Vetrimaaran movie; it's a story about four siblings, and Dhanush plays the eldest brother. The initial setting up of the sibling dynamics and the way the story began were kind of interesting. But after they grow up and we see them as adults, right from the beginning everything just looked so plastic. We see slums, we see their modest households, the street where they have their fast food shop, and everything just lacks any kind of life in them. Most of the sets look like movie sets; we don't feel like these characters are part of this world because there is no world. It just seems so vacant. Even when the movie gets violent, the violence rarely has any weight to it. 

Anyway, then there's a gangster conflict, set up by the ever-dependable Tamil movie police briefing exposition scene, and the police officer played by Prakash Raj is playing mind games to clean up crime because he has a personal vendetta. This character is so poorly written, and he doesn't even feel that relevant. The outline of the core conflict and the drama are interesting, but the way it is developed and the way it is directed is so laughable. There's a big betrayal scene at a point; it's a betrayal of Shakespearean scale; it's supposed to be intense; it's something the movie has been building up to. But it just comes off as so dumb, not because it's a dumb twist, but because of the dumb writing and filmmaking of a great twist. The acting in that scene too is goofy; Dhanush (the director himself) is taking the scene seriously and giving the appropriate response, while the other dudes sharing the scene are doing soap opera acting. It's supposed to be a tragic and heartbreaking scene, but it made me laugh. Aadukalam had such a betrayal at the core of that movie, but there, the way it unfolded was brilliant. 

This betrayal is something that could branch into all kinds of interesting drama, but what followed was bland, dumb, and hollow. The characters act so cluelessly, random stuff just happens, there's an abrupt dance number, a big action scene, and the movie just ends. Compare this to how every betrayal and character beat in Vada Chennai felt, and you'd get how this is just a mere lifeless copy of something like that. There's so much information provided in the name of world-building; that doesn't actually mean anything. 

Dhanush and Dushara Vijayan's performances are great, SJ Suriyah does his reliable villain preset acting, and Selvaraghavan, Dhanush's real-life brother and director of several great Dhanush movies, is reduced to praising the Dhanush character at whatever opportunity he got. But I get it though: if I write and direct a movie and make my older brother act in it, I'd definitely make him say I'm a badass at regular intervals. The two actors that played the brothers were laughably bad; they couldn't save the bad filmmaking with their performance, like the director himself did. The writing was bad and the acting was bad, and they made several moments of drama seem funny.

A. R. Rahman's soundtrack was great and is way too good for this movie. Ideally, this deserved the treatment Anirudh gave to Indian 2. Also, there's some cool action scenes here. Dhanush is bad at directing drama, but he can do action well, I guess. I especially loved a scene in a hospital, which doesn't even involve Dhanush's character. The cinematography looked pretty too. 

I didn't feel like this was a good movie. But still, with that soundtrack, I don't want to rate it too low.

Name: Trap
Review:
Trap has an amazing premise and such a great setup, but just like many M. Night films, this one too falters towards the third act and has bad dialogue, though not as much as his worst films. The whole thing is like a crossover between a Dexter episode and a level from the Hitman games, where we have this huge concert happening in the background, which is a trap set to catch a serial killer, and the killer himself trying to get out of the trap without letting his daughter know about his true nature.

Josh Hartnett is brilliant as Cooper AKA "The Butcher" here and carries the movie so well, even as the writing loses its grip. As the cool and supportive dad who tries to be his daughter's BFF by learning Gen Alpha lingo to the cold and calculated psychopath who'd do anything and hurt or manipulate anyone to get out of the trap he's in, Hartnett is the true star of the movie. The way he convincingly makes up lies on the fly, each change in body language when he's trying to hide what he is, and even a short burst of his violent nature seeping in, was portrayed really well. The movie doesn't have any slasher movie-ish scenes of Hartnett as a serial killer, but whenever he switches from Zaddy to Baddie, it's so convincing. There's an especially scary moment when a character mentions his mother and he suddenly gets up from a couch; that was some really great acting and filmmaking.

Still though, when I said this film reminded me of a level from a hitman game, I should also add that it feels like a level from a hitman game on the easy difficulty. Because as great as the setup is and how the killer is in a tight trap where he also has to maintain the facade of being a concert dad, he gets away with doing a lot of things so easily. People believe him so easily; he could move around in restricted areas easily, and even when he's surrounded by witnesses, nobody really notices him being sus. He even stands conveniently at the right places at the right time to overhear exposition. 

I did like the way the film always stuck to his point of view in the first two acts. Even when we see Saleka Night Shyamalan's Lady Raven, initially we only ever see her from a distance, and on the big LED screens, we always see everything from Cooper's POV. Even the idea of following the killer for 75% of the movie and then shifting the perspectives was great, but the third act seemed so confused about where it needed to go, with only Hartnett's performance maintaining the same momentum, with some great moments for him to shine.

Saleka Night Shyamalan was good as the popstar Lady Raven as long as she stayed as the background presence who we only saw from a distance. Because the moment she becomes a more prominent character, the flaws in her performance start to stick out. Despite her acting needing a bit more work, she does pull off the popstar part of the performance; her soundtrack and stage performances were all cool, and the entire thing does feel like a proper concert, being attended by a big crowd, which is a pretty impressive feat.

M. Night Shyamalan too has a cameo here, and he ironically plays the dumbest, most gullible character in the movie. Like, it's the kind of writing where we just know that Cooper is getting his way only because of plot convenience and not because of him being so intelligent. Despite Josh Hartnett nailing the manipulative psychopath performance-wise.

Anyway, Trap had really great ideas, and unlike something like Knock at the Cabin, this one had the potential to be known among the best of M Night's work had it been better written and the ideas were better realized. I liked the setting, I liked how the movie almost makes us root for the villain before switching perspectives, and Josh Hartnett was awesome.

Name: Saripodhaa Sanivaaram
Review:
My theory is that Vivek Athreya listened to Elton John's "Saturday Night's Alright for Fighting" and took it too literally. But as absurd and dumb as this premise is, it's pretty interesting too, and the film makes use of it in many fun ways. When the writing is dumb, but it's like the fun kind of dumb, I have no complaints. Our main character is basically the Saturday Batman, as in, he fights against injustice, but only on Saturdays based on a lesson his mother was trying to teach him but never got to complete. He switches off the vigilante mode even if it's the same Saturday night and it's past 12 in the midnight, because then it's Sunday. It sounds like the premise for a comedy, and yeah, it's used for comedic effect at times too, but the film also takes it seriously, and it somehow works.

Nani is great as the lead and sells the whole thing really well, and SJ Suriyah is unleashed as an unhinged psychopath, and when he's given enough material to play the unhinged, darkly humorous psycho, no matter how many times I've seen it, I love it. This movie excels in those over the top buildups and "mass" setups and the moments of comedy. Everything is scaled up to seem epic and dramatic. When the hero and villain confront each other, it's presented like this epic event is about to happen. The Saturday gimmick could've easily tumbled this movie, but it ends up being its strength, and I can't quite explain how. SJ Suriyah's character's interactions with his brother were hilarious too. 

The action is pretty generic, from your average telugu movie fight scenes involving randomly flying goons to one that uses shaky cam and quick cuts very inefficiently. But I did love the final climatic action scene. It was very chaotic, very well shot, and effective. Jakes Bejoy's music and score were also very effective in giving the movie the scale it was trying to convey. Overall, it felt like watching a really great Shankar movie from the early 2000s (while the actual Shankar is now making stuff like Indian 2, weep).

The only other Vivek Athreya movie I've watched so far is Ante Suntarantiki, which didn't need to be a 3-hour movie at all and felt stretched out. This one too is almost 3 hours, but it didn't feel like it dragged on that much, except for occasional scenes like when the main character's dad gives an extended KGF-style overhype buildup for his son towards the end. The editing was nice during some sequences and montages, though. There are dumb scenes, but it's so competently made that I was INTO it. 

The romance subplot and how it connected to the main conflict were all okay. But they didn't need to do the cousin angle at all. They could've easily been neighbors or something. I know it's still a normal custom over here in south India to romance and marry cousins, but yk. It really doesn't add much to the movie too and will weird out people who don't understand the context and custom.

Name: Kinds of Kindness
Review:
The first short involving the absurdly over-the-top micromanaging boss-employee relationship was my favorite of the three. I don't know to deeply dissect it, but yk, it works as the depiction of a fucked up corporate employer-employee situation too. It was cool how there were so many parallels in between the first one with the corporate setting and the third one with the cult setting. 

This movie felt like absurd Yorgos ideas that he couldn't develop into a feature-length film like The Lobster or Dogtooth, so he chose to make them this tryptic collection of shorts instead, with some common themes and loose connections. It has all of Yorgos' trademark flair, dark humor and weirdness, though the style more resembles his earlier works than the one seen in The Favorite and Poor Things. I especially didn't notice those camera pans and the curvy lens distortion stuff (I don't know the exact technical term, apologies). The cinematography and special effects were great, and the music was effectively eerie. 

Anyway, Emma Stone, Jesse Plemons, Margaret Qualley, Hong Chau, and the entire cast were great, whether it's to convey the deadpan absurdity and humor or the absurdity when they actually do emote and it's something so disturbing and over-the-top. My least favorite short would be the second one. 

I know I said the word absurd too much in this opinion, but no other word best describes this movie. The weirdness is its best part. It's dark, it's weird, it's funny, it's disturbing, it's Yorgos Lanthrimos.

Also, I'd give five stars just for the greatest shot in cinema history that has Emma Stone dancing to Brand New Bitch.

Name: Pudhupettai
Review:
Pudhupettai is a gem. It stands unique among the vast majority of early 2000s Tamil movies and even Selvaraghavan's own films. Selvaraghavan himself tried to replicate a Pudhupettai with NGK and failed. Pudhupettai is like the Thamizhan Goodfellas. It's a gangster story without holding back any punches or slashes. Kids like Sandeep Reddy Vanga think a teen fantasy with blood, profanity, misogyny, and shouting is what an "unhinged" anti-hero film looks like. But no, when someone who understands the craft and someone who knows cinema presents an anti-hero, we get Pudhupettai.

 

Kokki Kumar isn't a virtuous hero by any means; he has no moral issue with dealing drugs, murdering strangers, or ruining someone else's life as long as he gets what he wants. The film basically doesn't have a sense of morality holding it down; terrible people do terrible things, but they thrive anyway. Kumar could've led a normal life, but tragedy leads him to a life of crime, and by the time he has a choice to not actually be a criminal, it's too late, he's too into it, the power consumes him. Kokki Kumar was Heisenberg before Heisenberg. Kumar opposes prostitution, but only to save HIS girlfriend; he exacts revenge on some rapists, but only because HIS boss told him to. There are moments where we're supposed to feel bad for Kumar, but nowhere is he portrayed to be a good person. An older lady gives him a lecture at one point about how greed corrupts, and just when I thought Pudhupettai is yet another movie that ends with a "message", it surprised me yet again.

 

There are so many great sequences; Selvaraghavan finds new ways to show the action every time; there's the night fight scene with muted colors where the only bright color is the blood on Kumar's shirt and sword; there's the confrontation with the rapists where Kumar casually tutors his henchman to improve his neck slashing technique; and so many more. Kumar wasn't the kind of gangster who did crime to help the poor; he does lose things, but does he become a better person even when he has a choice? Fuck no. I could go on and on about Kokki Kumar and Selvaraghavan's style choices and filmmaking here. It even has a lesser amount of background score usage than most Tamil films; the shots are usually long, unless it's the montages or key action sequences. The editing is great, and Yuvan's score is still a banger. The city is and the world is shown to be so lively and sprawling, and Pudhupettai does seem like this big crime epic, even now. Of course there's even a scene that mirrors the iconic baptism scene from The Godfather, but Pudhupettai on the whole felt more like Scorsese than Coppola.

Name: The Greatest of All Time
Review:
"Dei boomeru, summa Cringah pesathey."

 

The James Bond movies and Mission: Impossible movies begin with putting us right in the middle of a big action setpiece most of the time. When it's something very impressive as the hanging from the plane stunt at the beginning of Mission: Impossible—Rogue Nation, it easily builds up excitement over the rest of the movie. Now GOAT has a similar setup right at the beginning, very Mission:Impossible, but the problem here is that it's such a poorly made sequence, which only made me question Venkat Prabhu for even approving these shots for the final out. Firstly, and most importantly, the deepfake of the late Vijayakanth used looks hideous; it's so ugly, and it's so badly done that it ends up looking more like an insult to the man than a tribute. Honestly, showing a still photo of him at the beginning would've been enough of a tribute than sticking the same photo onto Vijay's face. The opening fight scene has some cool choreography and gun-based martial arts; Vijay shows off some cool moves, but during most of it, his face is covered by the hideous deepfake that'd haunt my dreams, so I couldn't really appreciate the action. Then, after some CGI train stuff, we get the Thalapathy Vijay title card, which everyone in the cinemas was so excited about that they shot the whole thing on their phone, like it's a tourist attraction and not a film on the screen.

Anyway, afterwards we get a so-and-so story about an espionage man with a double life, a less fun version of Amazon Prime's Family Man. But still, Venkat Prabhu does this thing while doing a spy story that Indian spy movies rarely do, even the above-mentioned Family Man. There's no jingoism in GOAT, nor are any of the terrorists Muslims. And also, Venkat Prabhu movies will always have a law enforcement person who's a corrupt piece of shit, and GOAT maintains even that. But the thing is, the movie just seemed so dull, with occasional instances of bad CGI, and things got interesting only once the younger Vijay character got introduced.

The portrayal of the younger character Jeevan and even our main character Gandhi during the 2008 scenes was pretty solid a lot of the time. For Jeevan, they're doing something similar to what was done to Shah Rukh Khan in FAN, where his body proportions, face shape, and features are slightly altered, and he's made to look younger. Jeevan looks really great in some scenes, but the visual effects don't maintain consistency, and there are plenty of instances where he looks weird too. But on the whole, the visual effects done on top of Vijay's face, like Jeevan and younger Gandhi, are better than any of the deepfakes used. Still though, the 8-year-old FAN still has a better use of deageing and distortion vfx than GOAT. There's also Vijay's own teen face deepfaked onto a teenager that looks hideous. The visual effects in the movie on the whole range from "okay" to "wtf is that?".

Vijay's performance is great as both the characters, and he tries his best to carry the film, so he really is The GOAT on that behalf, though there's nothing about the presentation of the character Gandhi that makes us feel he's a GOAT. The goat title is purely just a reference to Vijay himself. There's a lot of references to Vijay, his trademark gestures, his iconic films, and at one point Yogi Babu even mentions both Ghilli and Mahesh Babu's Okkadu within the same scene. Anyway, Vijay succeeds in making both the characters seem like different people, and his performance helps in selling the Jeevan character more than the makeup and visual effects.

Anyway, a lot of the latter half of the film worked as a pretty enjoyable thriller, with only the occasional instance of Bad vfx and a very badly placed duet song ruining the flow. Even the big climax is very VFX heavy, and the VFX looked so unfinished. Still, there are many scenes featuring both the characters together, and for the most part the movie does succeed in making them seem like different people. Yuvan's songs were underwhelming except for the two that I really liked, and the background score too was disappointing at times except for the occasional cool themes for the Vijay characters.

There are lots of twists, betrayals, betrayals within betrayals, weird and absurd ideas being thrown, meta-jokes, and pop culture references going on. Some work, some don't. Now I didn't think GOAT was as terrible as I expected; there was fun to be had, and Vijay's double act was great. But the bad parts of it are so bad that they leave such a bad taste. Even the attempts to create catchphrases, such as "Father of the Nation Da," "Dei Boomeru, summa Cringah pesathey," and all just felt ironically funny (well, the boomer line was intended to be darkly funny, but yk). There's some cool fight scenes and fight choreography, and Vijay shows off martial arts moves, but sometimes the bad VFX comes in between them.

Anyway, Venkat Prabhu had openly stated that Gemini Man starring Will Smith was a big inspiration for this film, and it shows. But it also pretty much got inspired from another recent Will Smith movie, which I won't name. GOAT was fun for me, but for others, it might depend on how much bad stuff you're willing to look past, and that includes two nightmarish hideous deepfake faces.

Venkat Prabhu teases a sequel at the end, while Vijay will retire from films after one more movie, and the final Vijay film was never going to be GOAT 2 regardless of this movie becoming a hit or not. So we're being teased a sequel that'd never happen, why?

Name: iSmart Shankar
Review:
Pokiri is almost two decades old, and this movie feels more dated than even Pokiri, and Puri's sensibilities haven't really grown since then either. Our main character is Ustaad iSmart Shankar, as he keeps reminding us every 5 seconds, till the very end. He's the first dual SIM Apple product. As Steve Jobs said, the iPhone was a mobile phone, an iPod, and a computer combined, and iSmart Shankar here is a criminal, a dickhead, a pervert, and a terrible punchline generator combined with a CBI officer's memory uploaded into him. At one point, he even threatens some cops, "Go home and sleep with your wives; if you sleep with me, I'll not let you sleep till sunrise!". I mean..

Anyway, Shankar has a romance, which is mostly sexual harassment. The girl basically says she loves him when his sexual harassment turns into a sexual assault attempt. I'm not exaggerating anything here; cops even come to arrest him for rape before she says, "It's okay, I like him!". This "true love" is at the center of the movie, as it's what drives Shankar, apparently.

Did I forget to say this is a sci-fi flick too? Yeah, it basically reskins the old spirit possession plotline from Indian movies into sci-fi memory transfer mumbo jumbo. Where a dead CBI officer's memories are transferred to Shankar, he has to live with two sets of personalities and memories in him. This doesn't really matter, though, because Ram Pothineni still acts like your typical Telugu movie hero here, with only switching accents to differentiate between the two characters. It doesn't add any significant layer of drama or thrills, except for Ram Pothineni getting to do dance number songs and beach duet songs with the girlfriends of both the dudes. Both the women are continuously objectified of course. Songs even pop up in the weirdest of places in this movie, like Shankar will break into song just because he sees his girlfriend's photo and all. Everything else about this movie is very typical telugu masala vibes; the sci-fi thing is just a fad. But it did make money. Tik Tok is listed as a social media partner at the beginning, and the movie is literally edited like a Tik Tok video at times. 

Anyway, Amazon Prime was showing the ad for its sequel "Double iSmart" so much, and that's why I decided to check this one out too. This movie is shit, but I'm still watching the sequel next. Don't ask me why; I have issues.

Thank you for reading this rant about a Puri Jagannath movie.

Name: Double iSmart
Review:
Double iSmart does stay true to being the new version of an Apple phone, because it's new on the surface level, but it's so dated, and it has ancient features that other phones have moved on from a decade ago. Ram Pothineni returns as Ustaad iSmart Shankar who still reminds us every 10 seconds that he's Ustaad iSmart Shankar, though this Shankar dude basically died at the end of the last movie when his consciousness was entirely taken over by the CBI dude Arun. But in this movie he's back to being Shankar, with the dual SIM memory port from the last movie intact. I honestly have no idea if this is a stand-alone sequel or a continuation, but I don't think even Puri Jagannath did.

Puri Jagannath basically remakes the first movie, under the guise of it being a sequel. In the first movie, a good guy's memory is uploaded to Shankar, but in this movie, a bad guy's memory is. Don't be mistaken that it will shake up the formula and lead to exciting sci-fi thrills; it doesn't. Shankar has a romance yet again, and neither of the women from the first movie are referenced. Shankar's way into a woman's heart is once again sexual harassment. We're meant to believe that the romantic interest played by Kavya Thapar this time is different and is a "strong female character,"  but nope, she's there to be objectified. A strong female character in a Puri Jagannath movie is the same objectified woman who's perved on by the main character and the camera, just that she'll get to do a fight scene or two. But of course, sexual harassment works wonders for Shankar, and these two become inseparable true lovers.

There is new shitty stuff here, different from the first movie. And if the first movie was bad, this makes it worse. South Indian movies have moved on from having parallel "comedy" tracks for a long time. But Double iShmart brings it back (fuck my life). Ali is there in the movie as an offensive tribal stereotype, a primitive man from the Amazon jungles. It's so wrong on so many levels; the scenes are not even funny, and they don't matter to the rest of the movie in any way. Yeah, Pokiri had that too with the Brahmanandam scenes, but it's been like 18 years yo! Another laughably bad thing this movie does is that it tries to be "political". The big bad (whose name is big bull) has this elaborate plan to divide North India and South India and cause a civil war. He makes Dravidian protests a part of his plans to destroy India. I'm not going to elaborate on this. I don't want to.

Sanjay Dutt's villain here makes me forgive his human sacrifice villain in Leo a lot more. People who thought that the Leo flashback was bad have no idea how much worse the real bad can be. The action scenes are bad, the sci-fi twist doesn't really matter, and the ending even copy pastes the first movie's ending in a way that doesn't even make sense (I guess people liked that ending?). And I'm not kidding, after a point, a random lady with the same name as Shankar's mom stalks him around, hangs on his SUV like Tom Cruise, and walks around a big shootout without getting shot, just to remind Shankar of his mom so that he'd switch from the bad guy to the good guy.

Also, hats off to Ram Pothineni for not even attempting to copy Sanjay Dutt's mannerisms when his consciousness switches from Shankar to Big Bull. Ranbir Kapoor, who? Ustaad iShmart Shankar Raaa!

I survived watching the iShmart duology. iDumb now.

Name: A.R.M - Ajayante Randam Moshanam
Review:
Ajayante Randaam Moshanam, which was later abbreviated to A. R. M. to sound like RRR, has the entire gist of what the movie is in that title change itself. Because this is basically a very small and grounded story set in a village, about a protagonist who lives with the weight of his grandfather being a legendary thief that shook the village, who's in love with a feudal lord's daughter, and then he has to face a conflict related to the stealing of a very important religious idol to the village. Sound familiar? Because that's just Meesa Madhavan with a few tweaks. But the thing is, A. R. M. doesn't feel like a Meesa Madhavan-ish movie. This small plotline is presented like an epic folk tale here; the legendary thief is a mythical badass, and the idol, instead of being a diety or channeling its power from religion, is a space rock, basically making this sci-fi.

 

So ARM felt like a mixed bag; there's some occasional fun and laughs thanks to Basil Joseph's character and one scene featuring an otherwise underutilized Bijukuttan. The flashback sequences have some great visuals and cool action sequences, but the main plot line involving the title character Ajayan, played by Tovino Thomas, felt flat at times. Among the flashback storylines, the one involving Ajayan's grandfather Maniyan was the more prominent one, and its mix of folklore vibes and the larger-than-life presentation of Maniyan was interesting. Plus, Tovino Thomas was great to watch as Maniyan, seeming different than any other character that he's ever played. Tovino was great in the movie on the whole, and impressive during the action sequences as well. The flashbacks don't seem inconsequential; everything does connect together well; it's just that the main plotline of Ajayan in the present day loses some of its focus, though that's where the film spends the most time. 

 

The 3D ranged from gorgeous visual spectacle and showcase of depth, like a very memorable shot where Ajayan walks into a cave, to very obvious gimmicks like fire embers, sparks, particles, and stuff clearly added at the last minute to make the movie look "3D.". The movie occasionally forgets its supposed to be a 3D presentation, and when it suddenly remembers, we get some theepporis to our face. Kriti Shetty was surprisingly good as Ajayan's love interest and even clearly made an effort to properly lip sync to the Malayalam dialogue (Anurag Kashyap kandu padikk). But the person who impressed me the most was Surabhi, as Maniyan's partner, who had the best chemistry with Tovino, and I wish she had more scenes in the movie. Aishwarya Rajesh is barely in the movie, just for two scenes, and is basically just a cameo. 

 

The music and action also pulled me into the film at times, and sometimes they were a bit too much that they pulled me out. That's my feeling about the movie as a whole. It has some great ideas, where a plotline that's familiar to the Malayalam audience is presented in an epic scale with fantasy and folklore elements, but it needed some more tweaking to reach its full potential. The storyline here is very Assassin's Creed, and just like an Assassin's Creed game, the flashback ends up seeming more interesting than the present-day storyline. 

 

The movie also attempts at showing caste discrimination, which connects to both Ajayan's love story and the plotline involving the idol, but it isn't an effective mix of such a theme with folklore like how something like Pa. Ranjith's Thangalaan was. Plus, though Ajayan is constantly seen as inferior and untouchable by the Savarna characters because of his caste, the movie also does this while letting the audience know that Ajayan is actually a half-upper caste person. Which doesn't really matter to the movie at all. Or was the intention to show that the people the Savarna people see as inferior now might be from their own caste too? Nah. And the brownface, bruh.

Name: Kishkindha Kaandam
Review:
I watched Kishkindha Kaandam without even watching its trailer. I've only seen the posters, and I feel like that's the best way to walk into this movie, so I'm not going to talk about the plot here either (apologies to the two people who read my opinions).

Long story short, this was a brilliant movie. It's so well-written, with layers upon layers of drama and interesting character beats. The way the movie reveals each piece of information gradually till we get the whole picture is amazing, and then we'd actually look back at the rest of the movie and see it in an entirely different light after getting the full picture. This is one of those movies where the first watch and the rewatch would feel like watching two entirely different films.

The film is set primarily in a single household, with Vijayaraghavan as the elderly Appu Pillai, Asif Ali as his son Ajayachandran, and Aparna Balamurali as Ajayachandran's newlywed wife Aparna. Aparna is essentially the audience's POV character; she's the new member of the family, and we get to know the rest of this world through her. That's about the most I could reveal about this movie, as the rest is to watch and experience. All three leads are brilliant, and Vijayaraghavan even reminded me of old grumpy retired military men that I've seen irl. It's such a layered portrayal of a brilliantly written character who'd stay in my mind for a long time. Asif Ali too gets several moments where the emotional weight of the film rests on him, and it's such a joy to watch him perform when he gets the right material. The father-son relationship was very interesting and the emotional beats were on point. 

It's a well-written, well-directed, well-shot, and well-edited film; whether it's the quieter scenes or the several montages, the pacing and narrative flow of the movie are on point. I loved the background score too. The house, the surrounding greenery, the monkeys, and the whole area the film is set in also provide a very calm yet eerie atmosphere. It just feels like being transported to someplace else as the narrative pulls me in. Hats off to Dinjith Ayyathan, Bahul Ramesh, Sooraj E. S., Mujeeb Majeed, and everyone involved!

Name: First Blood
Review:
I've never actually watched any of the First Blood movies; I've seen clips of some action scenes, and I'm aware of the general idea of who Rambo is in pop culture, but this first movie took me by surprise. Rambo here is not the badass that pop culture describes him to be in First Blood. This movie doesn't make the violence seem badass or make Rambo seem heroic. I mean, after an introduction like this, making this same character into a heroic badass in the sequel sounds like a very bad creative decision (though, ig, the character's popularity was the reason).

John Rambo is basically a fucked-up war veteran suffering from PTSD. None of his army teammates are still alive; he hasn't recovered from the psychological toll of the violence he inflicted and the violence that he had to see and endure. He's even frustrated about the fact that after going through all that and being a murderer for his country, people don't really see him as a hero (well, none of the Americans involved in the Vietnam War were heroes anyway). The inciting incident then is very interesting; there's no terrorists, mercenaries, or enemy soldiers; there's just some local cops. A sheriff takes one good look at Rambo and decides that he doesn't want this drifter around in his town (as iconic as Sly Stallone is in the role, I couldn't help but think that Rambo being a person of color would've added an entirely new dimension to the sheriff's behavior). Rambo himself came back to America expecting respect and hero treatment, so being disrespected doesn't really sit with him. And the more and more he's pushed, the more he finally snaps. American law enforcement being the first enemies in a film franchise in which foreign dudes are going to be binge murdered by the protagonist in the sequels is pretty ironic. Other than the one accidental death, Rambo doesn't really kill anyone in First Blood, but I know the sequels then turn into kill fests.

Rambo does get a great amount of buildup that makes him an unstoppable killing machine. Even as he first snaps towards the cops, they're no match for him as he fights them off with ease and retreats to the forest. Rambo is always under the control of the situation, with just a hunting knife in his arsenal. Then his mentor comes and further says lines like "I'm not here to save him from you; I'm here to save you from him,"  which makes him the stuff of legends. Yes, Rambo is extremely skilled and superior to every single cop thrown at him. He could take down hundreds of enemies with ease. All that buildup and the display of his survival skills and tactical prowess are on point. He seems as intimidating as The Terminator while still being human. Sly Stallone being so good in the action scenes and his body language also sells this. But still, Rambo is no hero. He's fucked up; the way he escalates the situation to turn a small town into a warzone is fucked up. Sure, the cops were assholes and they push him a lot when he just wants to leave in peace, but towards the end we have him blowing up stuff without even checking if there are any civilians around. The movie ends with him having a mental breakdown over what he just did and what the war had made him into. He's struggling to fit into society, and what did it lead to? Another war. It's a pretty tragic conclusion. 

This isn't a hero vs. villain story. So it's baffling that Sly Stallone then made the sequels all about Rambo being a full-on action hero badass. It kinda defeats the purpose of what First Blood was all about.

Name: Cuckoo
Review:
The cast was great, the film looks great visually, though it didn't really bring me into its atmosphere and weird setting the way something like Midsommar or Get Out did. Once it's revealed what's actually going on, it just becomes very basic. The grief-horror combo has become a cliché at this point, and this movie too doesn't really add anything to it. I did like the climax sequence though. Hunter Schafer is a dependable lead and Dan Stevens is a dependable bad guy. It's the performances and aesthetics that make this movie seem less generic than it is.

It was a fun watch, but they could've done more with the absurd concept and setting they had going on here.

Name: The Batman
Review:
And for the fourth time, The Batman receives a 3 hour standing ovation from me from my room. Matt Reeves and Greig Fraser gave us the best looking Batman movie ever made, fuck, it might be the best looking comic book movie ever made, and it's definitely one of the best looking films I've ever seen. It doesn't just look gorgeous, it sounds gorgeous too. The score is amazing, and adds so much to the atmosphere. The Nirvana song is used twice, and it's used in a meaningful way both times, The Boys can make fun of it all it wants, but the use of the song and how the song's guitar riff is essentially the base for the Batman's own theme is brilliant. The same goes for how The Riddler's theme is based off of Ave Maria, and even Catwoman has her own musical cues. But it's not just the music, the sound design is amazing too. The rain is a constant presence in the movie, and it's so cool how the rain in the background is used in adding to the atmosphere and drama. The production design, the use of colors and the costumes are so well placed together. The action looks great and unique, and gives us plenty of cool moments that are memorable. 

The movie is structured like a proper noir detective film, and yeah, the writing has flaws and dumb conveniences, but the pros outweigh the cons, if people can forgive the flaws in the Nolan Trilogy and call them masterpieces, then The Batman is a masterpiece too. Reeves also gives us the most interesting live-action take on Batman/Bruce Wayne here. Firstly, he spends most of the movie in costume as Batman, and whenever he's Bruce Wayne, we can just see how exposed and vulnerable he is, even without any exposition. It's not just the voice, his entire persona and body language changes when he's Bruce. He carries the grief and loneliness with him, and the relationship between Bruce and Alfred being set up here is something I want the sequels to explore further.

Then there's Colin Farrel as Oz Cobb, with that amazing flawless prosthetic makeup, that should've definitely won the Oscar that year instead of The Whale, and seeing more of him in the new HBO series solidifies that. Yeah, the work in the whale was good, but it did look like an actor wearing prosthetics that got enhanced by CGI, but Oz Cobb here looks like a legit person. 

Anyway, I can always go on and on about how amazing this movie is. It even goes as far as to call out Bruce Wayne as a privileged white man who doesn't really have an idea about how to save the city. It's this big journey where he realises that just beating up criminals won't solve the underlying issues, he even inspires the riddler to be a murderous vigilante in a way he didn't expect. We see him as a detective, as a violent vigilante, and at the end, as someone willing to sacrifice himself for others.

Patronize me all you want, but I'll not stop calling this movie a gorgeous masterpiece. Matt Reeves!!!!!!

Name: Sector 36
Review: Felt more like wasted potential. This could've been something similar to Paatal Lok, I don't necessarily mean this should've been expanded to a series, but the film spends too much time lingering on unnecessary stuff that when the important stuff comes, its impact is lessened. Yes, this is a disturbing film, but the film being inspired by an actual serial killing case, and the disturbing details of that crime itself are the reasons for that, instead of the film itself, because I imagine reading about this case on Wikipedia would be just as disturbing or even more. Deepak Dobrial and Vikrant Massey were great, and that interrogation scene towards the end is where this movie peaked. I wish they did lean more into how the system protects the powerful and how it doesn't care about the underprivileged. Yes, those themes are predominant in the film, but I wish it was more intensely explored.

Name: Blink Twice
Review:
Firstly, I loved the way this movie showed its title in a flash with a camera shutter click. I wish Indian movies showed their titles like this just to troll people who take photos of movie titles inside the theater. 

I felt the initial buildup in this film was excellent. Zoë Kravitz's debut is pretty strong, and her directorial career does look promising. There are familiar elements here that we've been seeing in similar films for the past few years, but that initial buildup and how it eventually leads to the very disturbing reveal were brilliant. Even after the reveal, the way the tension was maintained and the anticipation of what would happen had me glued to the screen. But still, considering the excellent setup, the third act seemed a bit safe. There are several twists, darkly humorous ideas, and stuff during the third act too, but it didn't feel like it had the energy the film initially had. 

During the initial setup, the weird and surreal energy, plus the way it conveyed that something very fucked up is happening to these women without even showing us anything, was very effective. The way the men behave is the same before and after the reveal, but afterwards, the context of what's actually going on makes every advance seem disturbing. Channing Tatum as Slater King was a great performance to watch, especially after his true nature is revealed. Both Naomi Ackie and Adria Arjona were so great after a shift happens to their characters towards the halfway point of the movie. 

The film essentially felt like it was trying to be a Jordan Peele-ish take on women who are manipulated and abused by men with power, and I felt like with a better third act, this could've been as good as something like Get Out.

Name: Vaazha
Review:
Vaazha: biopic of a billion boys, felt like watching an Instagram reels compilation, but unlike scrolling through Instagram where I can swipe up on the videos I'm not interested in, this is supposed to be a film, so I have to watch everything. It's basically about the underachievers, the "good-for-nothing" burden to the house dudes. Typically movies with such characters would be about them eventually finding success and maturing from "boys" to "men," but Vaazha doesn't follow that formula and is sorta realistic about how such Vaazhas lives turn out to be most of the time, which is about the only good thing I have to say about it on the whole.

There were fun moments and jokes that made me laugh, but the fun and laughs weren't consistent. The actual fun I had while I watched this film would also be only as long as an Instagram video. The film tries hard to be relatable, but even then, though it's not all fun and jokes and there is plenty of melodrama, the characters felt so thin, they lacked any identity as individuals, and the only thing that defined them was that they were lazy, irresponsible, immature, and impulsive, which defines them as a collective unit or stereotype, but not as individuals. Popular Instagram content creator Hashir and his gang basically play the version of themselves they play in their Instagram videos, pop in and out for some scenes, and then just leave till that sequel bait at the end. They do get some fun moments, but their inclusion too feels like an afterthought (though the movie was heavily promoted using Hashir and Co).

The problem with Vaazha isn't that it felt episodic. Premam was episodic, and yet there's a character journey there, and I could see how the main character and those around him grow and evolve over time. I didn't get that here; it's just one disjointed scene after another, ten jokes that fall flat and one joke that works, melodrama in between, followed by more jokes, followed by more melodrama. Some of the melodramatic scenes were funnier than the comedic scenes, and a lot of the time I felt second-hand embarrassment than caring about the characters. Like, the main characters are so unlikable, though the film's deal is that we should also empathize with the fact that they're so despised and looked down upon by everyone around them. There was a catchphrase attempt at the beginning with the "athaanathinte beauty," but thankfully the movie forgets about it and drops it entirely as it started to get on my nerves.

Ever since Girish AD started doing movies with characters in their teens and 20s, with actors who are actually of that age, seeing grown ass men playing teenage boys looks unintentionally funny to me. There's a comedy series named PEN15 where two women in their 30s play teens intentionally to be funny, and the parts of this movie where we're supposed to think that these men were playing young boys reminded me of that. And then, after they reach their mid-20s, one dude is like already married with a kid and going through a divorce. Are you trying to give other mid- and late-20s folk an existential crisis, a biopic of a billion boys?

I was also confused about the point the film was trying to make. Is it about toxic parenting? Is it about accepting your kids and letting them be who they want to be? But the movie doesn't really make the boys accountable for their actions, and they don't even grow, and a lot of the stuff that happens to them is their own fault. But that's okay; like I said above, not every movie needs the protagonists to grow, evolve, and succeed, but then, why does it still preach about parenthood? Why doesn't that philosophy extend to the parents? Kids can be flawed, but parents can't? Also, the dude who does study well and was more responsible about his life than our Vaazha gang too ends up being sad and shattered because of his parents anyway. What was the point of the girl with short hair and that bit involving how she styles herself and wants to live her life? Was it supposed to be progressive? Because it didn't seem progressive. There is even an instance of domestic violence that the movie quickly forgets and never mentions. What do you want to say to me, movie???

The climax also felt like a proper reel compilation, with cutting back and forth between scenes that seem like the senti reels that pop up on my Instagram feed. There's even a big psychotic breakdown that reminded me of famous ram for some reason. The performances range from good to amateurish for the boys. Azees Nedumangad and Jagadeesh were great, and I also liked the Basil Joseph cameo and every bit of screentime he was in. I was confused if the editing of the film is a stylistic choice or compensating for small attention spans by making scenes seem like reels, and yet the movie felt so long, though it's only like 2 hours. The music and cinematography were cool, tho.

Name: Devara: Part 1
Review:
I've not particularly enjoyed Koratala Siva's filmography, and the promotional material for Devara didn't really make me expect something great, so all things considered, the movie made me cringe less than I expected, and there are parts of it that I really did like and enjoy. Devara has a frame story similar to KGF where an outsider is listening to the legendary story of the region the film is set in, and the story itself is that of a badass of the seas named Devara (NTR), who's seen as a thing of legends and myths. Though the KGF thing where the narrator (Prakash Raj once again) constantly praises and builds up the protagonist is very less here, it's present, but we see Devara do badass stuff way more than characters verbally throwing all kinds of poetic puns about what kind of a badass he is. But the few lines that do praise him that way are hilariously cringe (idk if it's because I watched the Malayalam dub, so I'll give the bad dialogues a pass for now).

Devara's story spans two timelines, the one where he's a smuggler who has a change of heart and the drama that creates, and one set twelve years later, where Devara has become almost a myth than a person, and we follow his son (also played by NTR) and the rest of the characters. I did actually care about the drama here; yes, it's formulaic Telugu masala and there are stereotypic characters, but there's stuff happening that pulled me in, mostly because of NTR. The man doesn't half-ass a performance, no matter how bad the material is. The character and the performance were fun to watch, whether he's dancing, being a badass, or in the melodramatic bits, unlike the eco-friendly asshole that NTR played in Janata Garage, the previous Siva movie he was in. The action too wasn't that Telugu-cinema-coded. Rather than having goons randomly flying and the hero giving slo-mo poses (which is how Koratala Siva's movies usually do action), the action here is pretty well choreographed and shot well. It's far from realistic, but there's clearly more effort put into the action here. But still, in between the really cool-looking action, there are certain moments where Siva makes the movie look like the kind of movies he did make before, like the scene where Devara pushes two containers with his bare hands and when he picks up a spear with a kebabed dude attached to it and throws him like he's nothing. But on the whole, the visual effects and the action looked pretty solid, fuck, even him riding that shark looked kinda cool, that's the kind of stuff only Telugu cinema would do, and I did like the blue moonlight aesthetics they use for the nighttime action sequences. Anirudh's score and songs were a good fit for the movie, and the theme music makes NTR look badass no matter how goofy the scene is (including the Sura-coded intro scene). 

RRR did fool some Americans into thinking that it's some progressive and woke movie, as many non-Indians won't understand the way caste and religious symbols were used in that movie and how it distorted real-life facts. But at least RRR wasn't as blatantly misogynistic as Devara, so NTR and co. partnering with Letterboxd and all and trying to sell this movie too to the western market might be a road to get canceled. Because Janhvi Kapoor is only in this movie to get objectified. Her arc—sorry, I won't even call it an arc—her character's excuse to have the duet song with NTR is that she wants to marry a hot warrior. That's it; that's her entire personality. Then she has a fantasy duet song with NTR where the camera pervs all over her body, while her character and NTR's Vara barely have interacted outside of that. Afterwards, the movie completely forgets about her existence, unless the sequel can rectify this and actually flesh her out into a character. She also looked more like a rich urban Gen Z girl who came to vacation in a village with retro aesthetics than like someone who belonged there. Even Saif Ali Khan, the other Bollywood member of the cast, kinda fit in with that world. Saif was pretty good; it's the same Scar-Mufasa story arc between him and Devara, and he picks up that Telugu movie vibe in his performance effortlessly. The rest of the women are there in this movie either to be plot devices or to be murdered. I don't think the West will miss out on the regressiveness this time. Our mallu boy Shine Tom Chacko acts as Shine Tom Chacko in a big Telugu movie too. 

This movie will obviously be compared a lot with Baahubali, because this too has an identical father and son, and the bad guy used to be a brotherly ally to the dad, and it does have the familiar Lion King/Hamlet narrative beats. But I felt Devara did do certain stuff better than Baahubali. Devara and Vara felt like actual characters, and NTR gives a certain amount of depth and humanity to them than the writing does, while Prabhas, as both Baahubalis, was just a big buff video game character; he just had to look at the part; Rajamouli did the rest, but here NTR is like even compensating for Siva's shortcomings. Anyway, the Father-Son arc in Devara felt more interesting, with some fun changes to the existing formula. But does this movie need two parts? Idk, Baahubali itself didn't need two parts as the Lion King told the same story within 80 minutes, and it even had more songs! What this movie did blatantly rip off of Baahubali, however, is the cliffhanger ending, the whole "Why did ___ kill ___?" hype gimmick.

Devara is a mishmash of trends that both Rajamouli and Prasanth Neel have brought to these big "pan-Indian" movies.
