It even has the loud af sound mixing, which is when I take the opportunity to buy chips at the cinemas because I'm afraid of being a pest to others if I eat chips during quieter movies. Anyways, Devara is derivative; there's plenty of cringe, but I did have fun. The action especially looks great, and I wish more Telugu movies would take cues and do action this way, with actual choreography and moves and stuff instead of million ways to make goons fly. The one Telugu movie trope Devara couldn't grow out of is the misogyny and the objectification of its female love interest. Especially if NTR intends to use the RRR clout and market this in the west, this is something they should work on.

Name: Rosemary's Baby
Review:
I remember seeing reviews that The Omen was an inferior rip-off of Rosemary's Baby, and after actually watching Rosemary's Baby, I can see why they thought so. The buildup here is excellent. The entire film is locked onto just Rosemary's perspective, with Mia Farrow giving a brilliant performance. We have no idea what's going on in the background just like Rosemary, we only know what she knows. The film starts with her daily routine, and even we as an audience don't realize how the cult has inserted into her life until it's too late. Even then, the film maintains a version of these events where everything is just her own paranoia till that reveal at the end. The creepy music is used only sparingly here, and yet the way Rosemary's paranoia builds up, all the red flags the people around her give, and the way she's framed and shot in a way that amplifies the paranoia—everything is effective. Even the final reveal is done so masterfully. The dream sequences are surreal and chilling even now, but Rosemary being so casual about being raped while she was asleep was weird though.

Anyway, talking about brilliant Polanski movies is difficult for me because his Wikipedia page and the details of his sexual abuse case and its aftermath are a more disturbing read than his films, and Hollywood always seems like a cult like the one shown in this film for protecting him like they did.

Name: Wolfs
Review:
Jon Watts had done a movie called Cop Car before he stepped into the Spider-Man movies, and Wolfs reminded me of that film. Just like Cop Car, Wolfs also only focuses on a handful of characters, and though there's a crime plot happening in the background, we don't necessarily need to follow that, as the actual focus here is on the characters and how they react to being put in this situation. But this movie is a lot funnier. 

Clooney and Pitt play two fixers who get called to clean up the same problem. The rest of the movie is about them having to work together reluctantly. Unlike the usual buddy comedy format of the funny one and the serious one or the young hotshot and the old and wise one, here both these dudes are identical, almost like they're clones of the same person. The fact that they're so similar is what makes how they play off of each other funny. The chemistry and banter between the two leads is pure gold, and after the initial buildup, as they both see each other for the first time, the film sticks to them till the very end, and I never got tired of them. All their little quirks, similarities, the tendency to show off to the other one, and how the film almost adorably parodies depictions of such fixers in cinema (especially the very obvious "The Wolf" from Pup Fiction) is fun. The film made me laugh a lot. 

Despite being a crime comedy, there's a surprising about of heart and wholesomeness to Wolfs; the characters bond over the course of the film, and the very basic yet effective emotional beats were able to make me care about them. The cinematography looked gorgeous with all those great night shots. I loved the background score too. The whole style of the film too is the kind of stuff that I enjoy.

Name: The Adamant Girl
Review:
Usually movies would set up the characters and their relationships and the conflict before stepping into it, but not Kottukkaali; it just steps right into this fucked up family going on this trip. It's a road movie that weirdly reminded me of Little Miss Sunshine, but unlike Little Miss Sunshine, the family is not going on this trip out of any love for this girl; they don't care about her as a person, and over the trip, there's no family bonding or warmth. The more we get to know them, the more depressing the position the girl is in becomes, and the more we feel her pain and suffocation. The girl Meena is played by Anna Ben, who has only one line of dialogue in the movie, and the rest of her performance is all physical. She's the titular "Adamant Girl," but really, she just wants to make her own decisions; the abusive casteist patriarchal men in her family and the women who are forced to support these men despite receiving inhumane treatment from them are the actual adamant ones. 

There's no background score in the film, even when the production company logo or credits are shown. It puts us right in the middle of the trip; there's even the bit involving the autorickshaw not starting properly and the driver needing to pull a rope each time to start it. We see the slow routine of it every time, but it's not supposed to be a cute and funny bonding moment like when they push the van together in Little Miss Sunshine. The film moves at a slow pace; whenever they do something tedious, we see the tediousness of it; along the way they have chitchat about other people in the village or about themselves; it's all normal, routine-like, and along the way we get bits and pieces of information about what's really going on here. Then music hits the film for the first time, but it's not a background score or a song, but them passing through a puberty ceremony where music is played. Meena opens her mouth for the first time to lip sync to a song, and then what follows is our first look into the reality of the situation. Soori as Paandi is amazing here, as he's in full-force as an entitled maniac. 

The film has many moments of dark humor; the setting here is very sad, but there are bits and pieces of the mundane routine and character quirks and symbolic representation of their toxic masculinity and casteism that seem comedic. The film has cool symbolism and visual imagery throughout, including of course the rooster. There's also gorgeous visuals of rural Tamil Nadu that we rarely see in films. It really feels like taking a trip with these characters, just that the setting is far from being wholesome like how family road movies usually go. The abrupt ending followed by the silent end credits too left me feeling confused and shook, but yeah, the entire situation is very confusing and weird anyway, and it's not even fictional; it still happens irl. So....

P. S. Vinothraj is a gem.

Name: Apartment 7A
Review: Julia Garner was great in this movie and during the initial stretch this did seem intriguing. Then after she moves into the Apartment, it just becomes the same plot as Rosemary's Baby, but shot more like a generic horror film. This is Rosemary's Baby if it was shot like The Omen, gone is the sneaky way the cult and the satanic themes sneak up on you, and the feeling of paranoia and helplessness. The film still sticks to Terry's POV like the original did with Rosemary, but it never goes beyond being something generic. Garner is still amazing as Terry though and I love how Terry goes out on her own terms here, which is not what Rosemary's Baby implied about her fate. So at least the ending was better than I expected.

Name: Joker
Review:
Firstly, this movie being 5 years old makes me feel old in a way that I don't like. And yeah, on the rewatch, it didn't feel as impressive as that first watch felt; the flaws in the writing were more apparent, but still, this was a pretty focused movie. Phoenix's performance, Hildur Guðnadóttir's score, Lawrence Sher's cinematography, and the use of colors in the movie and the whole aesthetic still hold up. Coming back to the movie being focused, it has issues, but this was a tight movie; it focused solely on Arthur Fleck, and I think apart from that cutaway to Bruce Wayne's parents getting murdered, every scene features Arthur, and everything's either something he sees or imagines (which means even the Wayne murders can be a part of Arthur's imagination, though it's canon in the comics). Anyway, the sole focus on Arthur and the ambiguity on whether it's all in his head was a good way to tell the story, and it's a pretty respectable reinterpretation of The Killing Joke flashback.

 

I am writing this after watching the sequel, though I rewatched the first one before watching Joker: Folie à Deux. Watching them back to back, I kinda understand where the sequel disappointed me too, and it was the tiny thing of lacking the focus that the first one had.

Name: Joker: Folie à Deux
Review:
Todd Phillips wasn't lying when he said that he doesn't see much future for his version of The Joker. And when they did announce the sequel, he said that it came as a result of several ideas and discussions with his writing partner Scott Silver and Phoenix about where they could take Arthur after the first film. And that's exactly what Folie à Deux feels like; it's just a bunch of ideas being thrown at a wall, with none of those ideas being fully developed enough to really stick. Now these would've worked as separate episodes of a TV series, or even as an anthology collection of short films or something, but this is a single film, trying to do so much, and yet does too little, and ends up being incoherent.

The sad part is, these ideas are actually good on their own. It's just that their execution deserved more finesse, and the film does everything at once. Like, exploring the duality of Arthur and the joker, whether the joker is just a persona or just the same person, is a great idea. Addressing the real-world reactions and criticisms to the first Joker film by using a TV movie based on Arthur's life within the movie and how people got negatively influenced by that film is a great idea. The Joker being more of a conduit of anarchy and anti-social behavior than a single individual was a great idea. And lastly, the addition of Harley Quinn and flipping the original dynamic of the Joker being the abusive manipulator and Harley being the victim to Harley being the one in control and the joker being the one being manipulated was also a great idea. And though the ending is receiving a lot of backlash, it seemed like an appropriate conclusion for Arthur Fleck, though it also removes the ambiguity and multiple interpretations that the first movie allowed.

Yeah, I listed all the great ideas above, but it'd require more words and spoilers to explain how the movie failed to properly execute them. Firstly, Lady Gaga is pretty much wasted, though she does give it her all with the material that she got. The film was heavily marketed as something that would focus on both Arthur and Lee; even the title refers to a shared delusion, but this is still pretty much an Arthur Fleck story. Lee's inclusion is as trivial as Zazie Beetz's neighbor in the first movie, merely being a plot device and the film's excuse to have someone with amazing vocals to do duets with Arthur. Now, having a love interest just for the sake of doing fantasy duet songs is not new for us Indian audience; that's basically every Indian masala movie, but I'm not sure how audiences in other parts of the world would feel when these fantasy song sequences pop out of nowhere in the film, not adding much to the narrative, though they look gorgeous. What this needed to be was a fucked-up La La Land, but it's almost like the musical bits were added as an afterthought. Though Arthur's musical side and dancing were explored in the first movie too, that fit in better.

Parallel to this is this film being a courtroom drama, which is being telecast live because of the sensational nature of the Joker's case, that critiques people who glorify the Joker persona and Arthur's own actions in the last movie. It's also a prison movie, with Arthur being abused and mistreated in Arkham. All these pieces of the film have interesting tidbits that would've worked really well for a follow-up to the first film, but they never really fit in, and so this just feels like an extended epilogue to the first movie where nothing significant happens. This film just lacks focus on anything. Even from Arthur himself. The perspective shifts from Arthur more times than the last movie; there's even shots of the Gotham skyline that the first movie never had. There is a long oner of chaos towards the end that I liked though. 

There are scenes that showcase Phoenix and Gaga's great performances. Brendan Gleeson as the "friendly in a scary way" guard was also a performance that I loved (there's a head smack from him, which was funny and scary at the same time). Hildur Guðnadóttir's score is still great, the cinematography, colors, and aesthetics are great, and I did enjoy the cover songs and sequences as a stand-alone thing, though they're essentially filler in the movie itself.

But yeah, on the whole, I was disappointed by this movie, but it could've been a LOT better.

Name: Speak No Evil
Review:
This was a pretty thrilling movie; the buildup is long, but it's excellent; the pacing is tight and precise; the background score is pretty minimal and sparingly used; and the film manages to let the dark implications of the situation creep in regardless of that. McAvoy is excellent as Paddy, and the film features solid acting from the rest of the cast too, even the children. I did love the tension buildup and how it escalates from small instances of awkward behavior to being absolutely deranged. Still though, the ending felt safe; yes, it was still tense, and the action was very well done, but it just seemed too safe.

Then I was curious about how the original version ended (which I haven't seen) and checked its plot on Wiki, and oh boy, that thing had a way darker version of this situation and an ending that shook me just by reading it. So yeah, the original ending packs a certain punch, though the remake has the ending that I'd wish for the characters. Maybe the remake's intention was to subvert the expectations of those who've seen the original since it's not that old a movie? Now I think my decision to not watch the original was wrong. 😒

Name: Strange Darling
Review:
I just love it when films play around with the form of a narrative and find new ways to explore cinema as a visual medium. Because there are certain things that only cinema can do, so films that make use of those audio-visual tools in new and crazy ways always have my love. Strange Darling has a very simple premise; the events happen around the span of a few hours, and it's small-scale and straightforward. JT Mollner establishes his unique style from the very beginning, even before the credits start rolling. And even the credit sequence is very Tarantino-coded. Yes, there are Tarantino-ish elements here like the credit sequence, the various chapters, and the non-linear narrative, but this film does pretty much have its own style and unique cinematic high going for it. It's tense, it's thrilling and it kept me guessing. 

I won't talk much about how the film's crazy narrative swings work and how exactly the film specifically impressed me, because this is the kind of film that's most enjoyable while watching it with a fresh mind. Willa Fitzgerald is amazing as the lead, and there are several fun scenes here, whether it's conversations, character interactions, or downright tense and gnarly stuff. Kyle Gallner's performance was also great here, and the two of them together provide so much personality to the movie; great acting does benefit even slasher flicks, folks!

Anyway, whether it's the writing, filmmaking, editing, soundtrack, special effects, or acting, this film is pretty impressive. It's small-scale cinema with a big impact.

Edit: Read some alternate readings about this movie's problematic side and how it might be misogynystic. I didn't feel like it was making some regressive statement about gender politics or generalising female victims to appeal to the incel crowd or something when I watched it. Like yeah, it subverts our assumptions, but it felt like a subversion of slasher movie conventions than something that's supposed to be serious and connected to the real world. But yeah, in the process of trying to subvert genre tropes it might've ended up being regressive, but it still isn't comparable to something so intentionally incel-coded like Sandeep Reddy Vanga's Animal. But I do remember that the scene involving the male and female police officers made me cringe. Anyways, I'm kinda confused about this movie now, so reduced my rating a lil bit. Also, TIL that Sneaky Pete was the 30mm camera guy on this.

Name: CTRL
Review:
It's a Black Mirror-ish plot, presented as a screencast movie similar to Searching, Missing, c u soon and all. I liked Ananya Pandey's performance, she actually keeps getting better, and people still seem to be too harsh on her. Nepo Kid Ranbir Kapoor can play a human penis and get praise, but Nepo Kid Ananya Pandey playing an urban Gen-Z girl is the death of the craft? Anyway, the movie itself did have things I appreciated. There's a lot of detail gone into the UI, the screens, and how actual company names or brand names of products and software are never used, and yet it seems familiar. All the influencer videos and meme stuff seem authentic, and the excuse to make us see the actors' faces during the scenes was more plausible than, say, c u soon where Fahadh just leaves his webcam always on for some reason. Still though, do people really do video calls this much? This is not a question about ctrl; this is about all these screengrab movies.

Anyway, then the movie gets into its Black Mirror-ish concept involving digital surveillance, private data mining, AI, and how an AI can, ahem, "ctrl" our lives. The movie HER from Hell basically, because the AI is Aparshakti Khurana with shitty pickup lines than Scarlett Johansson's voice with romantic and sexy flirting. But it felt like the AI paranoia concept was not fully realized to the extent a black mirror episode usually would. Though the creepy AI head, the way there's a loading spinner thingy before every response, and that cringey idle animation were all nice touches.


In films like Searching, the characters go through digital evidence to get to the bottom of something, and it was cool to see a mystery getting solved through a screen in real time, making us feel involved in understanding what's going on bit by bit. But in ctrl's case, Nella, our main character, just gets handed in exposition with ease. It's just exposition after exposition till she finds a video that explains the entire conspiracy and the big reveal that we could see from a mile away, which is even in Netflix's synopsis for this movie ffs. Anyway, the exposition video itself did remind me of Bhavesh Joshi, though; it was where it got reminded to me that this was a Motwane movie.

There are interesting ideas here for sure, and even a fun way to incorporate celebrity appearances towards the end, and the ending too felt suitably Black Mirror-ish than like a Bollywood movie. The format of the film switches towards the end, and I wish there was a clearer thematic connection about how we're "out of the screen" now.

But this needed to only be as long as a Black Mirror episode too; this is still a short movie, but yk, it could've used some trimming here and there. Anyway, the portrayal of Gen-Z, influencer culture, meme culture, and the social commentary it's trying to make are all on point. Motwane is not out of touch about this stuff like Shankar, who wrote "Chitra Aravindan, Social Media." But still, the packaging needed to be a bit better.

And no, I didn't mean Ananya Pandey and Ranbir Kapoor are on the same level acting wise (she could surprise us in future though), but still, stop hating on her so much Internet! She's trying!

Name: It's What's Inside
Review:
This is yet another fun and intriguing movie that took me by surprise. The promos for this made it seem like the kind of mid Netflix movies with a young cast that they regularly churn out, but nope, this is very original, very well made, funny, engaging, with a distinct style and a unique voice. It even does some fun social commentary in between. I loved the way the movie was edited and the entire style of it that had a very Edgar Wright-ish quirkyness to it. It's set around a party and a party game; I won't spoil what specifically happens in the party game itself, because this too is a movie that's best experienced going in with a fresh mind.

The characters are all vibrant and distinct, but yeah, some of them get more of a personality than others, but still, when the craziness ensures, it does work. Just when the movie starts to feel like it's going to repeat itself, they'd throw in a new twist and conflict, making the entire thing more interesting again. I also loveddd that ending; it was perfect.

The cast was great, the music was great, the comedy worked, the filmmaking style and editing were love, and it makes great use of a familiar concept and takes it to crazier heights.

Name: The Platform
Review:
It's a not so subtle allegory of capitalism and an inferior version of Snowpiercer. Snowpiercer was better okay? There wasn't enough happening in the film with this concept that would make it work as a proper film. More like they wanted the absurd concept to carry the whole thing, than doing anything narratively with it. Would've worked better as a short or something. 

But I did love the part where, when the protagonist talks about equal division of food so that everyone gets a share, the cellmate is like "Are you a communist?". Brah.

Name: Beetlejuice Beetlejuice
Review:
This was fun, and Michael Keaton is just as great as the juice as he was the last time he did it decades ago, it's as if the juice never left him. It was also cool to see Tim Burton returning to the stop-motion visual effects, practical puppets, real sets and the kind of aesthetics he didn't really do that much since the 2000s. The movie looks great, the sets, costumes, makeup and hair styling is on point, it has got a great cast and Danny Elfman's score also captures the spirit of the original.

But still, the movie does lose focus. There are so many subplots, and everything does come together at the end, but the movie moves so fast and everything just gets resolved too fast. The first movie focused on a singular plotline involving the Maitlands and Lydia, Beetlejuice was just a supporting player there, but this time each character gets their own subplot and not enough time for it to develop. The juice gets more screentime in this movie than the first one, but he's still pretty much a supporting player while the main focus is on Winona Ryder's Lydia and her daughter played by Jenna Ortega.

In this day and age, it was the right idea to remove the sexual harassment from Beetlejuice's personality. He's still a menace and a pest, but not an absolute pervert like in the first movie. The production design and visual effects are so on point, with Burton getting away with showing a lot of gruesome imagery and gore, just because they aesthetically look cartoonish, just like in the first movie.

Overall this was a fun watch and it did make me laugh. But the writing lacked focus, which really pulled the movie down, though the visuals and gags keep it afloat (The "soul" train having everyone dancing to soul music will never get old). The cast was great, but Monica Bellucci and Willem Dafoe are wasted in the tiny parts they got.

Name: Vettaiyan
Review:
I appreciate Vettaiyan for not being the kind of film that glorifies police encounter killings and extrajudicial justice, because we've already gotten enough of them, and there's even an entire copaganda "cinematic universe" based around it. Vettaiyan even begins by presenting our protagonist, police officer Athiyan IPS, played by Rajinikanth, as a badass while he executes criminals instead of arresting them. While this can be called "compromising" for stardom, it's actually quite an effective use of the stardom and the way similar police violence by cop characters portrayed by star actors has been celebrated on screen. Because the movie then turns the tables on us and then asks us what we just celebrated. Though TJ Gnanavel is presenting Athiyan as a well-meaning heroic officer till the very end and not really demonizing him (this is more of a redemption arc storyline), the movie still makes a strong point that Athiyan's brand of justice is not how the police should ever operate. Like, the movie glorifies police violence for a bit, only to make us feel bad for celebrating it, which is where Gnanavel impressed me the most.

We can clearly distinguish between the parts of the film where Rajinikanth is being the character Athiyan and when he's being Super Star Rajinikanth, not just because Anirudh would always sing "Hey Super Star-u daa" in the background whenever the movie switches to that mode, but also because, just like Jai Bhim, a lot of this film doesn't really revolve around the star in the lead role. The main focus of the film is on the social issues at hand, whether it's the morality of encounter killings or the conflict involving the tutoring scam by BYJ...ahem, NAT Academy. But Vettaiyan does carry over the trend where insensitively shot graphic violence towards women is used as a plot device and for emotional manipulation. I mean, it's already bad that the scene was shot the way it was, and then Gnanavel also goes as far as to replay that scene over and over again till the very end. Gratuitous doesn't even begin to describe it.

Rajini brings in his trademark style and charm; his physical limitations are apparent, but he still uses the style to maintain the cool, whether it's the clip-on glasses or the Samsung Galaxy Flip product placement (the idea of the modern flip phone being used by Rajini in his style was genius though); it's all Rajinism. And still, through that, Athiyan does feel like a proper character, and there are moments where he's just being Athiyan. And yk, whenever he's being Rajini, we'd hear the "Hey Super Star-u daa" anyway.

Among the supporting characters, Manju Warrier is barely in the film, though she does carry the Manasilayo song. But she does get one badass scene. Amithabh Bachchan plays the kind of character you'd never see in Rohit Shetty's cop universe, as he tries to talk sense into the characters in the film and the audience, but his character doesn't really evolve more rather than giving these speeches and lessons. Fahadh Faasil's previous film role was Rangannan, so it's only fitting that here he's playing Rajinikanth's Ambaan, like, he's to Rajini what Vivek was to Rajini in Sivaji, though unlike Vivek, he too gets one single moment to be a badass himself, and he was fun to watch. Ritika Singh as a cop in Athiyan's team is the woman character who did have a bit more to do than being a plot device or a background player, and Dushara Vijayan plays a plot device. Rana plays the template evil corporate villain. The movie does have the thin supporting characters problem.

Anirudh's score is catchy, and the songs are already on my playlist, but yk, in a movie that deals with such heavy themes and social issues, the occasional "Hey Super Star-u daa" whenever Athiyan has to look cool makes it seem like a different movie and reminds me that this is Super Star on screen. Well yeah, Rajini's Super Star persona is an important part of the film, as the subversion of glorifying police violence on film happens through that projection of Rajinikanth as the Super Star. But again, Rajini's intro sequence is through the inside of a cigar, so "Hey Super Star-u da" does fit the tone of the film at times too.

There are dumb parts in the movie; it gets very preachy, and Rajini does look stiff during fight scenes, but still, I'd give it a pass, because this is a better one among Indian cop movies that explicitly states that cops don't get to murder suspects. It also addresses the cops' biases, how the underprivileged is always the target of such encounters while the rich and powerful remain untouched (the Indian censor board mutes some words while Rajini talks about how the police's bias towards certain groups of people hurts investigations, though). It also makes very obvious parallels to the crappy practices of a corporate tutoring firm that exploited and scammed parents. Yeah, both Rajini and Amitabh were background dancers in the Ambani wedding, but it doesn't hurt that in cinema they're bringing justice towards evil corporate exploitation xD. The insensitive portrayal of sexual violence, though, is something that I wish Indian cinema could move on from. Like, the rest of the movie could've remained mostly the same even if that was not there; it just had to write that character better.

Name: Stree 2
Review:
It's effective formulaic fun; the jokes and fun are consistent, like, even if some jokes fall flat, the others hold the movie up, and that tone never changes. Even the high-stakes moments would have a joke attached to them; in that way, the Streeverse is the closest thing in India to watching a Marvel movie. They even do an Avengers-style pose towards the end.

Just like in the first one, jokes that connect the horror-comedy scenario to real-world gender dynamics (specifically Indian) were fun. The cast is reliably great, with everyone getting a chance to get some great jokes in. Shraddha Kapoor doesn't contribute towards the comedy, but she was good as the hair braid lightsaber jedi. Also, the movie has lots of wordplay humor, which I love. 

These movies don't have visual effects that look as detailed as bigger budget productions, but still, the stuff that they do have is so well-conceived and executed that within the movie it just works, despite looking like the most obvious CGI ever. Towards the end, there's even shots that only have fully CGI characters in them, and it somehow blends in with everything. The scares here are just jump scares; there's no attempt to create genuine terror, as most tense moments are undercut by jokes too. But yet, the villain does seem like a legitimate threat, and the mythos and backstory are pretty solid. It's all formulaic stuff, but the formula is well adjusted to be a satisfying meal.

Hollywood movies have the post credits scene, but Bollywood movies have the post credits song to show music videos that don't really fit in with the rest of the movie, and there are two post credits songs here. Still though, this is a lot better than having these songs in the middle of the movie itself, except when this franchise's own Bhediya did the thing where a colorful End Credits dance number followed that movie's tragic ending.

Name: Bharathanatyam
Review:
It's sad that crappy stuff like Vaazha become big hits while something unique like this becomes a flop, yeah I'm the thantha vibe person whining about brainrot. 

I don't know if the Balettan meme trend in fb inspired this movie, but the whole thing takes the conflict from Balettan and creates a fun little scenario. Saikumar, Saiju Kurup and Kalaranjini were so great. There were lots of moments that made me laugh, whether it's the dialogues or the running gags. Only when the movie started going down the melodramatic path that it had been subverting so far towards the third act that it felt jarring. Even then, there's enough good stuff here that this should've been a hit!

Anyway, there were great ideas here.

Name: The Substance
Review:
It was hard for me to sit through The Substance, but not because I hated it, because of how effective it was in doing what it set out to do. The movie gets gory, yeah, but it started making me feel weird and uneasy even before all the gory stuff. There's a lot of visual storytelling and stylistic flair here, and this is a film that's less about the dialogue and conversation scenes and more about the visuals, the sounds, and how they work together; the story itself is about appearance anyway.

Like, right off the bat, it begins with the main character Elisabeth Sparkle's Hollywood Walk of Fame star; we see a time-lapse of the star, which brilliantly conveys Elisabeth's fading celebrity status visually. Then we meet Elisabeth, played by Demi Moore, who's way too gorgeous to be someone who should be worried about the way that she looks. But the lack of relevance, how the media "industry" sees a gorgeous middle-aged woman as a "fossil", the insecurities about aging fueled by unrealistic beauty standards eventually get to her, and instead of doing existing cosmetic procedures or botox like actual celebrities (which is what's being satirized here, of course), Elisabeth opts for the fictional "Substance", which gives birth to (quite literally), Sue, played by Margaret Qualley. Things go horribly bad, of course, and the rest of the movie is just that; it reminds us of cautionary tales, it reminds us of addiction, it reminds us about how addictive validation is, and also, it's about celebrity culture and the media industry as a whole.

Like I said, there's a lot of effectively creepy scenes in this movie, even before things really get gory. There's some very effective food horror here, starting from an initial scene where Dennis Quaid is absolutely devouring some shrimps. Like, it's not even an unclean environment; he's doing it in a fine dining restaurant; everything's clean, and yet, the scene looks so violent, it made me feel sick. The closeups on Dennis Quaid's character are also filmed in a way to make him an over-the-top and weird presence, his performance adds to that too of course. Similarly, later on there's a scene where it's just Demi Moore putting on and taking off makeup. Again, it's the filmmaking and Moore's performance that convey how disturbing that scenario is. And when the gore does pop up, the prosthetic makeup and visual effects (both digital and practical) were so amazing that I was never taken out of the disgusting imagery on screen. I felt each gnarly absurdity with flesh and body parts that the movie did. The production design, costumes and the cinematography give a very specific look to the film, and it does look gorgeous, even as it gets progressively more disturbing. Along with the visuals, the sound too, with all kinds of squishy flesh squelch sounds, makes for some very effective body horror.

Demi Moore is obviously too hot to be insecure about her looks, but it seemed like that was the point here. Unlike, say, the Nutty Professor, where the obese Sherman Klump drinks a formula to become the thin Buddy Love (not an apt comparison, but stay with me here), Elisabeth Sparkles is indeed a conventionally attractive woman, but just that according to the "standards" she's too old. Dennis Quaid as the TV executive Harvey represents the men who do set these standards. All the men in this movie are intentionally caricatures and one-dimensional. They're either perving over Sue like maniacs, or are the boy toys that Sue takes home, or the faceless voice on the phone that talks to Elisabeth about the Substance, the dude who pervs over Elisabeth, and the dude who introduces Elisabeth to The Substance. Elisabeth has a lonely existence here. We don't know anything about who she is outside of this; does she have a family? Does she have an ex? We don't know. None of the women other than Elisabeth and Sue are proper characters here either; they're all just there in the background.

So yeah, with the whole absurdist setup and characters and people who are far detached from the reality we live in, the film is more about the social commentary. But it makes its point way before the halfway mark, and we get where this is heading to, but still, it just keeps us in and keeps going. The situation becomes more and more disturbing, the gore escalates, the filmmaking is visceral, and it culminates into a very surreal and violent finale.

The film is shot and edited very well. Like, I could complain that perhaps the movie lingers too much on the disgusting bits, but I think that was pretty much the intention—to associate/burn in the disgusting imagery with what these beauty standards stand for. The cinematography is amazing, the production design is amazing, the music is great, and the performances are great, especially Moore and Qualley, and of course Dennis Quaid as the capitalist misogynyst.

During the first act, this was a 10/10 film in my head, but I'm taking a star off since, idk, it did feel a bit redundant at times, like there were great ideas for some brilliantly filmed gnarly horror sequences and visual effects/makeup wizardry but the writing being a bit more better in connecting everything could've made this even greater. The way it sets up the rules of the substance and the lead up to how everything goes spectacularly wrong were all very effective horror film writing though.

Name: Baakki Vannavar
Review:
A film like Vaazha has a more sanitized version of a quarter-life crisis and how it feels to be a working-class underachiever; it's like a compilation of insta reels on what unemployment and the struggle to find a place in the world feel like for a 20-something middle-class person. Baakki Vannavar, however, feels like a collection of memories of the sad bits of working-class 20s.

The movie introduces its protagonist with a job interview. It's a pretty great opening scene and even a pretty close recreation of how an actual shitty job interview would go. Afterwards, the movie follows the main character's daily life as he works as a food delivery boy, barely making ends meet; he's in debt; he's trying to find opportunities for getting a better income and to get settled, but nothing seems to work out. He still tries to have one foot in the past, where he goes to hang out with his friends in a college hostel, though he has not been a student there for a long time, and this also sets up some interesting scenes.

Yes, the movie occasionally gets too verbal about the working class politics it represents, but the thing is, I've seen or heard actual experiences about almost every scenario depicted here, whether it's the white collar employees ranting and cursing about their corporate job on their smoke break or the struggles of being a food delivery person. Remember in Premalu, when Sachin's big solution to his 20s woes is going to the UK, but he has no idea if the UK will actually solve everything for him? But the UK has been sold to him as the ultimate success fantasy. The whole abroad migration angle is also touched upon in this movie, whether it's the fact that not everyone has the privilege and capital for such a migration or about the whole argument regarding whether one should migrate itself. When two characters have a big argument regarding migrating to the UK, it reminded me of a similar argument that I too had with a friend, well, with lesser profanity xD.

Baakki Vannavar is a very small indie production, but the acting is mostly solid; a lot of the conversations felt so real; even the profanity did. Even in the abovementioned argument, the protagonist occasionally tries to contribute to the discussion, only to be completely ignored, and I felt that. There are lots of long shots here, and most of the people involved make the scenes feel so lived-in. The cinematography captures the city so well, and the editing too flows between the long shots and the montages involving the protagonist's daily life really well; there's even a very well done panicky situation towards the end. The music and sound design is pretty nice too. I expected the ending to turn out the way it did, but it was still a gut punch.

Name: Bougainvillea
Review:
I did have some fun watching Bougainvillea, and Jyothirmayi is awesome in this movie, and I loved Sushin's score, but yeah, I have to yap about the stuff I disliked too, which is going to be hard without spoiling anything, but I'll try. (There still might be mild spoilers though.) 

Firstly, yes, this is a mystery movie ig, that's the impression that the trailer gives, but as we get into the actual film, we realize there's not that much of a mystery going on here. The gist of what's going on is so obvious that I even felt that it was intentional for them to make it so obvious. Like, there's no alternate routes for the sus here. So even when the direct reveal happens later in the movie, it's not a big "gotcha" moment; it's just casually revealed, like the audience had known this information already. I haven't read the source material novel Ruthinte Lokam (I won't call it "Roothinte" Lokam), but a friend told me that the reveal was very obvious in that book too. And yeah, Fahadh does play a useless cop, his monologue towards the end especially came off as funny because he's talking about not being able to realize the very obvious solution to the mystery that has been staring at the audience since the beginning of the movie xD. 

The movie does look very pretty (Anend C Chandran, yay). The locations, the way people are shot, and the aesthetic game are on point, like all Amal Neerad movies. Sometimes it's funny too; we see Kunchacko Boban's Royce take a Beatles record out of his shelf, and he's apparently playing it, but the music is Vivaldi violin music or something instead of The Beatles. Either poor Royce was conned into buying royalty-free classical music that had a Beatles cover or the film team realized Beatles music rights were expensive af too late. Then there's stuff like a criminal psychologist discussing a case with a book titled "Criminal Psychology" placed on the table in front of her. There's also a moment involving a syringe during the climax that was soo dumb too. I don't mind such stuff while I watch movies, though. If we try to dissect all the goofs and plot holes here, this is going to be a long rant, so I'll keep it short.

Anyway, there's also an unnecessary flashback sequence, with a folk song being looped in the background for far too long. It just felt gratuitous and confusing. The rest of the film would've remained pretty much the same without that whole slice. It's pretty short and shallow, but it could've been shorter; ideally, it shouldn't have even existed.

Yes, Amal Neerad is a style over substance guy, but this is the kind of material that did need a balance of both. Jyothirmayi was great as the Amnesiac Reethu, barely having a grasp of reality as she gets put in the middle of a bigger mystery. I love twisty movies that use memory loss as a plot device, and this could've been taken to lots of interesting places too, and it did show promise initially. But sometimes moments serve just the purpose of looking cool rather than serving the narrative, like, yk, in Amal Neerad movies most characters get the cool slow-mo shots, but when the context is very dark and sadistic and we're seeing deranged shit, does the deranged shit need to look as cool as Bilalikka did?

Though I haven't read it, I've heard that the things that are dumb about this movie are mirrored in its source material novel too, and the novel's author is a co-writer on this movie. Dumbness and the bad flashback apart, I did kinda like the slasher-ish climax sequence. It's where Amal Neerad gets to show off the cool slow-mo stuff. Sometimes the wrong person is made to look cool, but when it works, it works. It's your average slasher movie climatic showdown, which foreign movies have been doing since the 70s, and it even reminded me of movies like Death Proof that paid homage to said 70s movies, so it's hilarious that it's being called "forced woke" and women empowerment and stuff.

Fahadh Faasil and Sharafudeen playing normal supporting roles doesn't bother me as much though. Jyothirmayi is the real star of this thing, and it's cool that the male co-stars, whether it's Kunchacko Boban or Fahadh, are not made to overshadow her and make this seem like every other Malayalam movie that revolves around the dudes.

Name: Woman of the Hour
Review:
Hats off to Anna Kendrick for directing a dark serial killer thriller as her directorial debut when it's not a genre that's associated with her body of work in acting at all. And she does a great job here, both as director and star.

The film is based around the killing spree of real-life serial killer Rodney Alcala. This serial rapist and murderer really did appear in a dating game show on national television, irl, while he was in the middle of his spree. The promotional material and even the title make it seem like the film entirely revolves around Rodney's Dating Game appearance, but the film does have a non-linear narrative where it shifts between different timelines through the perspective of some of Rodney's victims. Anna Kendrick plays Sheryl, based on Cheryl Bradshaw, an aspiring actress who was the Bachelorette in the Dating game.

The Sheryl plotline has satirical elements where it shows Sheryl encounter various forms of sexism, starting from her audition and her appearance in the dating game itself. This portion stands out because it's not just about the killer; it's also about how connected the "casual and fun" misogyny within the show and the deranged violence in someone like Rodney can be, and how he can convincingly pretend to be the lesser red flag. The rest of the plotlines are far darker and show how Rodney actually manipulates his victims into seeming safe, only to show his true nature when it's too late. The true details of the things Rodney actually did are far more disturbing than anything shown in this film, and I'm kind of glad it doesn't go the route of focusing too much on the killer's violence.

There's also a great restaurant scene between Sheryl and Rodney where Kendrick showcases some really great filmmaking to convey a normal date slowly transforming into a creepy and uncomfortable interaction. The sound design is very effective here as the background becomes dead silent, and we really feel the bad vibes creeping in. The movie has many such scenes of effective tension building and suspense, and since it shows Rodney's MO right at the beginning, the fear of that happening is always looming.

Anyway, the narrative structure and the tonal shifts here does seem wobbly at times, when it cuts away from one timeline right as it gets interesting, and toward the end, the movie feels like it's still going on even after seeming like it had ended. It's still a good attempt at storytelling, though. Since I didn't know the details of the real case it was based on, it did offer me plenty of suspense. Even while knowing the details, the suspense might be pretty effective. 

Anyways, it's a pretty impressive debut. Anna Kendrick knows her stuff.

Name: Humanist Vampire Seeking Consenting Suicidal Person
Review:
I can see this as an episode of What We Do in the Shadows, but yet, this is not as slapsticky and irreverent as something like that. This is also like those Disney movies where the main character is so different from the rest of their family, but this is a bit darker, and we have a vampire named Sasha who doesn't want to murder humans like her family does. She needs blood to survive, but she's unable to kill a living being herself to get the blood. Enter Paul, the suicidal teenager who's willing to get killed by Sasha so that his suicide would at least help someone.

Though the subject matter involving teen suicide is heavy, the film treats it pretty lightly (not in an insensitive way). The deadpan humor and dialogue delivery are on point, and yk, this is a rom-com where two people bond over suicide. Over the course of the movie, we just realize that Paul was just lonely, as was Sasha. Both of them have trouble fitting into their respective worlds; both of them contemplate suicide, and then they find each other. It's not that deep, but it's funny enough, and it's got its heart in the right place. There are several cool moments, and the leads had great chemistry together.

Name: Venom: The Last Dance
Review:
The first Venom movie itself was not a great film. The writing sucked, the action sucked, and the visual effects were serviceable, but what held the movie together and made it fun to watch was Tom Hardy's double act as Eddie Brock and the voice of Venom. Now this was a film that had other great actors in the cast like Michelle Williams and Riz Ahmed, but when all of them were restrained to playing one-dimensional comic book movie cutouts, Hardy had the freedom to go beyond the generic writing, do improv, and make the whole thing seem like a body-horror film fused with a buddy comedy whenever it played with the Eddie-Venom dynamics, which has nothing to do with how Venom is portrayed in the source material otherwise. Anyway, the first movie also had a very underrated score from Ludwig Göransson, with themes that were perfect even for a faithful scarier adaptation of Venom. Like the theme music in the first movie was amazing, so it's baffling that both sequels didn't reuse it.

Anyway, the reason why I talked so much about the first movie is that the sequels, including the Last Dance, were merely attempts at repeating the first film's formula without making much attempts to improve or build upon it. When they realized the parts that worked the best were when Tom Hardy was let loose in the first, he became a part of the writing process too, but I'm assuming it's just for the parts involving the Eddie-Venom dynamics, because the sequels too are dumb, generic, and bland versions of the comic book movie formula otherwise. Minus the very cool Ludwig Göransson score.

The Last Dance almost feels like a creatively exhausted film. Tom Hardy himself looks like he's "too tired of this shit", like, he already signed to do three of these things, so he's just getting it done, is the energy he gives. And yet, him physically as Eddie and through voiceover as Venom carries the whole movie, and at least doesn't let it become another Morbius. The film teases the big bad Knull... by making him do an expository narration right at the beginning of the movie. It gives a character's important backstory... by making us see her having a nightmare of that backstory. The movie is so lazy at giving exposition that, for a lot of the film, almost every conversation except the Eddie-Venom banter is just characters throwing exposition at the wall. So the movie gets very tiring whenever Tom Hardy is not in a scene. This time too, there's a great supporting cast, including Juno Temple and Chiwetel Ejiofor, who don't get to do anything. Chiwetel Ejiofor and Rhys Ifans were probably cast for marketing gimmick purposes too. Sony sure loves to do that. They marketed Let There Be Carnage with that post-credits scene showing Tom Holland's photo, which then meant nothing. They marketed Morbius using the Michael Keaton cameo, which meant nothing. They marketed this movie using actors who were in other Marvel stuff or Spider-Man stuff, and also by making the Knull portals resemble the Doctor Strange portals. The thing is, they'd do the same kind of gimmick for the next Kraven movie's marketing too, and people will still believe it'll have some genuine Spiderman connection. Heh.

The bromance/romance between the real Tom Hardy and the CGI Tom Hardy is still fun, and the final setpiece is the largest this franchise has gone in terms of scale (though I assume the US government is much more powerful than the handful of soldiers we see here). But still, the final setpiece had its moments because the enemies were not just CGI goo people whom you could barely tell apart. Well, the enemies were still soulless CGI creatures, but they did seem scarier; the victims' blood spraying out of their backs when they ate them like they were some alien juicer was a nice touch. Anyway, the emotional beats involving Eddie and Venom at the end were also kinda effective, thanks to Tom Hardy's acting, but, as the movie ends, we see a montage of clips from all three movies, which is so bad that it just destroys any emotional resonance the ending made. Like, if it was a last-minute attempt to milk some emotion out of the viewer, it fails spectacularly at that. I chuckled at how random the clips that were selected and the editing were there. Like, the Eddie - Venom banter worked because there was "banter". Cut the audio out and show just clips of Tom Hardy and the CGI creature moving their mouths? It's just stupid.

The end takeaway of the Venom Trilogy (?) is that Tom Hardy is so good that he can carry a comically inaccurate, badly written adaptation of a popular character for three whole movies and still make me wish to see more of him. Well, maybe not as THIS Venom, and not with this (lack of) creative direction, but better. 

Two stars for Tom Hardy and his back that needs immediate medical attention from carrying the entire Sony Marvel Spin-off franchise.

Name: Terrifier
Review:
I was super grossed out on my first watch of Terrifier, but now, not so much. Damien Leone's special effects and makeup are still impressive though, with the kind of budget they had, and also, old school practical effects that seem so obviously fake are kinda the appeal here too; they didn't have the budget to do CGI gore even if they wanted to, and they're better off because of it. There's barely any plot here or actual characters, as the movie just creates a scenario for the killer clown to murder people in. Showcasing creepy imagery and the gory special effects and makeup is a big priority here, and not "storytelling". David Howard Thornton is great as Art The Clown, and it's this unique portrayal of a pretty unique villain that's the USP of this movie, other than the impressive low-budget makeup and special effects. Art The Clown as a character too has elements that make him so much creepier, starting from his look. Also, he doesn't make any sound. He doesn't talk, there's that, but also we don't hear him breathe, groan, shout, grunt, scream, or make any such sounds that even other iconic silent movie slashers like Jason and Michael Myers make. Plus, so much of his movements and gestures are cartoonish and like actual clowns and mimes, so that also makes it more interesting. Plus, he's also unhinged and unpredictable and doesn't really always follow the standard slasher movie conventions. 

Anyway, other than Art, apart from the actresses that played Tara and Victoria, the acting is very amateur. But in a movie like this, bad acting and low production values are, yk, it happens. The music was great and gave the movie the atmosphere of those old timey slasher movies. It tries to do that aesthetically too. Sometimes it works, sometimes it looks like an Instagram filter. But there are many effective shots of Art The Clown just staying completely still that are way scarier than all the gratuitous violence on display here.

Also, though it's trying to emulate old slashers, it doesn't really have the judgmental eyes on teens who have sex or the Virgin final girl cliché. Well, we don't even know much about the characters other than them becoming mutilated flesh and blood afterwards; there's that. The characters had so many opportunities to escape out of this situation though. 😭

Name: Meiyazhagan
Review:
Yes, it's cheesy and melodramatic and follows the tried and true formula of the grumpy introvert person learning love and empathy through the initially annoying but well-meaning extrovert. In Tamil movies, usually the manic pixie dream girl/loosu ponnu has the duties to fix the grumpy men, but this time, Karthi has the loosu ponnu duty, hehe.

Aravind Swami plays Arul, who left his village during his youth though he loved the place and the people there, and then completely disconnects from there as he starts a new life in the city. Arul has to reluctantly attend a wedding back at his village, and there he meets the Karthi character with "protect this man at all costs" energy. As wholesome as the Karthi character is, the whole bit involving his name was kind of dumb, but the way the movie plays with it is pretty cute though. Also, I didn't care that much about the Jallikkattu episode or Arul's savarna tharavaad nostu. 

The film is cheesy; it gets too melodramatic at times, but yk, it's got its heart in the right place when it focuses on just human relationships and how even one small act of kindness or love can make a big impact in someone's life. It's also refreshing to see a calm and peaceful Tamil movie with the men being emotional and sensitive individuals rather than screaming, shouting psychopaths. The chemistry between Arvind Swami and Karthi was great, and there were so many cute and emotional moments.

(Then there’s me, who’d check a number on Truecaller even if I already know who it belongs to.)

Name: Terrifier 2
Review:
Many of the Art The Clown mutilation scenes from the first movie that disturbed me on my first watch didn't really make me flinch the second time. But the bedroom murder scene in Terrifier 2 is still nasty and so sadistic. The effects look so obviously fake, but it's so well done to create the intended effect, which is to look fake enough to disconnect from reality and yet seem brutal and disgusting. Leone has a lot of fun executing these old-fashioned gore effects, the sound effects help a lot to sell the violence too. And this is a more proper film than the first one. Because it's not just setting up a scenario for gratuitously violent kill scenes; this time we have an actual protagonist, some backstory, lore, and mystery here. I hope the supernatural elements and the lore do add something in the future, rather than being a goofy excuse for kill scenes yet again. 

Lauren Lavera as Sienna is a great protagonist, and this movie does actually revolve around her rather than letting David Howard Thornton as Art carry it like the first film. Also, seeing her beat the shit out of Art at the end was very satisfying. Sienna doesn't really entirely fit into the traditional final girl stereotype either. The music is also effective in maintaining the throwback vibe, and the visuals too this time look more similar to an old timey slasher than the first film. There are so many throwbacks to classic slashers here, gratuitous violence included, but it also seems kind of modern at the same time, fitting into the "good for her" group of movies. 

The budget constraints and amateur acting are occasionally apparent here too, but on the whole, it's a better-made film with more effective scares, thrills, and an actual plot. Well, maybe it was a tad bit too long.

I've seen criticisms about the terrifier movies being incel porn. But I for one have no idea what incel would get turned on by a dude getting stabbed in the penis repeatedly after which it gets ripped out of his body.

Name: Amaran
Review:
I can watch Sai Pallavi being in love forever. Even when it's a badly written arc that's just screaming cringe like in Maari 2, she's the kind of performer who can turn it around with her own energy and light up the screen. Amaran too felt like such a film. Yeah, Sivakarthikeyan is out of his zone; he put up muscle and does physical army person stuff, but it still felt like Sai Pallavi carried the film whenever she came on screen. Their love story and family life wholesomeness were the best parts of this movie. Sai Pallavi is so good here that I don't even care that her Malayalam accent was rough and didn't really make her sound like a native Malayali.

Whenever Sai Pallavi is not on screen though, we get an underwhelming military-action movie with an overload of jingoism, balancing gimmicks, stereotypical template Muslim terrorist villains, and a portrayal of the conflict in Kashmir that glorifies and pookiefies the Indian Army. Like, yeah, that's basically almost every Indian military movie. I don't think I've ever seen an Indian film other than Vishal Bhardwaj's Haider that looked at Kashmir through the lens of the civilians who are affected, rather than the Indians good- Pakistanis/Muslims bad binary. The film even has the Indian soldiers use "Bajrang Bali Ki Jai" as their warcry and every terrorist using "Azaadi (freedom) for Kashmir" as their warcry. Even if it's factual, in India's current climate, is this doing any good? I don't know how much of this film is based on actual facts for these Kashmir portions, but is the Indian Army always the perfectly honorable warriors of justice as shown here, though? Do we really need more films that glorify war?

Compared to the army parts that looked like every other jingoistic Army propaganda movie, the parts that showed Mukund's personal life seemed more honest and real, and you can tell the real family was involved in creating these tiny personal moments. Like, these parts are so good, and Sai Pallavi is so great that I wish this was entirely centered on just her life as an army officer's wife. Even towards the end, the emotional core of this film lies in the personal relationship portrayed rather than any patriotism.

Anyway, Amaran could've been more personal, less devotional.

Shyam Mohan as Sai Pallavi's angry brother says the P word here as much as he says JK in Premalu, and it was funny how he then instantly transformed into a nice dude from a slur throwing asshole during one scene.

Name: Lucky Baskhar
Review:
This was fun. DQ plays a very rootable protagonist here, and it's very easy to cheer for this middle-class dude scheming his way to the top. It's formulaic and cheesy, but it's the good kind of formulaic and cheesy. There's a particular bit involving how one doesn't just have to be rich but also has to "look" rich to earn respect, which was very romaanch inducing.

Dulquer is in almost every scene in the movie, and him as the title character Baskar is also the narrator of the movie; he even occasionally breaks the fourth wall, and on the whole, this was a charming and effective lead performance that carried the movie pretty well, hitting the emotional notes and the parts where he has to look cool and clever just right. Also, I don't know how accurately the film shows the financial scams, but what's shown here is presented in a way that even a person with no idea about this stuff, such as myself, can easily understand. Even The Big Short needed Margot Robbie in a bathtub, giving us a tutorial in between. There are many clever sequences where Baskar almost gets caught that are very fun. It's basically the same pattern and beats, but it's still fun.

Baskar's character arc and beats are familiar, but even while sticking to formula, the movie can get pretty thrilling. There are moments of cheesy melodrama, but not as much as something like Sita Ramam. The family dynamics and Meenakshi Choudhary as Baskar's wife Sumathi were also nice, though the redemption arc later in the film felt rushed and "easy" with an overdose of nanma.

There's always an imminent threat looming when Baskar does his first scam at the beginning, which is kind of lost when he goes bigger in the second half and towards the end. But despite that, the film still remained pretty satisfying, and there were lots of moments that made me giggle, especially when it involved your average middle-class anti-hero giving the elite pandering part of society the finger. The movie doesn't really try to portray Baskar as a bad guy though he's committing crime, but it's okay, at least he's not a real life murderer like DQ's own Kurup. 

GVP's music was cool too. 

Good stuff.

Name: Churuli
Review:
നീ തങ്കനെ അറിയുവോ? തങ്കന്റെ പറമ്പിലെ പണി അറിയുവോ? തങ്കന്റെ പറമ്പിലെ പണിയേപ്പറ്റി റിവ്യൂ പറയുവോ?
I did actually rewatch Churuli just to log this; I have integrity, okay? A lot of the discussions on this movie have been reduced to the profanity in the dialogue, and even I didn't like it that much on my first watch, but somehow on the revisit, I could appreciate it, and it's one of LJP's unique movies where the filmmaking choices actually compliment the narrative. Churuli is so much more than the therivili. The way it sets the atmosphere and eeriness is perfect. The place, the people, the greenery, all look appropriately weird, though there's no grandiose "otherworldly" production here like Malaikottai Vaaliban or something. It's just people and places that look so normal otherwise, which has been made to feel just off. The fact that the place just looks like your average Kerala village makes it creepier. It invites us into this inescapable, fucked-up space. I do wish the movie maintained the ambiguity of the place, whether it's just the mind playing tricks on two policemen stuck in a lawless place filled with criminals that doesn't adhere to the normal rules of society, or if it's some supernaturally fucked up piece of land. But towards the end, the movie goes full on surreal. The thing that still bugs me is the way this movie used CSA; what did they actually mean?

Name: Lubber Pandhu
Review:
At one point in the movie, Harish Kalyan's character questions his friend for understanding caste discrimination but failing to understand misogyny. Thing is, this movie too has an imbalance regarding how it addresses caste—acknowledging its role in local cricket tournaments—but when the two protagonists initiate their rivalry and the women in their lives get caught in the middle, as always, they're expected to be unconditionally loving and forgiving.

Now this is a way better film than Parking though, so it's not fair to pair this with that movie just because Harish Kalyan is in it and it's again based on petty male ego. Here the rivalry makes sense, the drama is better, and even the resolution is pretty wholesome, though it does have the abovementioned expectations on the women. It was a satisfying watch, and there were plenty of cool moments. 

Attakathi Dinesh singam maathiri walking in slow-motion with Vijayakanth music in the background is the definition of Geththu.

Also, yet another movie set in the present digital age where people don't see the photo of the groom during a wedding alliance. How da?

Name: Terrifier 3
Review:
This felt like the best movie in this franchise.... till the ending happened. Still, Leone's growth as a filmmaker is pretty evident here, as this film almost looks like a mainstream indie horror movie, yk, like the ones A24 and NEON make. The visuals and production values get a major upgrade, and it's not just the new aspect ratio making Terrifier 3 look better. There is the occasional instance of amateur acting, but the funny part is, the worst acting in the movie came from Chris Jericho, a wrestling veteran (I guess Jericho was going for "I'm a famous wrestler, look at me hamming it up" vibes).

David Howard Thornton as Art too, has perfected the character at this point. I guess having friendly interactions in character with actual people in conventions after the success of Terrifier 2 has helped him in developing the more "fun" side of Art The Clown. There's more of Art being silly and being an actual clown while also being deranged. The clown is even genuinely funny at times, before things get extremely deranged, sadistic, and fucked up. The kills have gotten more violent and cruel, with Damien Leone's special effects and prosthetics game also being impressive (which is something that's stayed consistently impressive since the first movie). I guess Leone also took the accusations of the Terrifier movies being misogynystic incel porn seriously, because there's more brutality on men this time around, and we also see male genetilia getting chainsawed in half. Yeah, I'm not kidding. It's not just the dudes though; there are kids being killed too (it doesn't directly show it though, which was a good decision), which is a line that slasher movies rarely cross, except for exceptions like the other more famous creepy clown that eats kids and Freddy Kruger's flashback. Bonus mention to the sound effects that make every act of brutality sound so gruesome. 

Art shares a lot of characteristics with Freddy Kruger, where he's a psychopath with a sense of humor. But Art also has his own individual characteristics, both on the fun side and the sadistic side. It's more like if one of the cute and fun silent characters like Charlie Chaplin's Tramp or Mr. Bean suddenly became a supernatural serial killer. The actual clown-like body language and facial expressions add so much to the character, and it's not just the gratuitous violence at work making him memorable. He slayed in that Santa look, literally. 

Lauren Lavera's Sienna is our protagonist this time around too, but she has way less to do here than being in PTSD about the last movie, which is fair. We also get further development on the bigger lore and demonic connections, but not enough to make everything seem properly fleshed out (pun intended) yet. But still, it at least seems like Leone is going with an actual plan in mind for the future. We've seen way too many slasher franchises that start out strong and then go off-rails with no cohesion. The music too tries new things, like a Christmas jingle during a particularly violent scene, with Art himself being so giddy and fun mutilating someone. The end credit song was a surprise, and that also made me chuckle. 

Still though, as the movie builds up to the eventual confrontation between the Art-Demon Possessed Victoria duo and Sienna, it just felt so dumb. Victoria was a great addition though, and gets a lot of effective creepy moments in, and was a great counterpart to the entirely silent Art (who still doesn't make any kind of human noises). But compared to the previous film's ending, which had a badass fight scene, here the initial part of the confrontation was just, yk, meh. The bit involving the Christmas present too had me laughing at the movie because it was so bad. There is a great fight scene between Art and Sienna afterwards, though. It's always satisfying to see Lauren Lavera kick the clown's ass. And then the movie ends on a cliffhanger, of course. 

Anyway, I'd still watch Terrifier 4!

Name: I Am Kathalan
Review:
Firstly, I appreciate the accurate portrayal of hacking so much in I am Kaathalan, and I'd even rate this movie high just for that sole reason, just because most movies don't even bother to make the effort on show here. Also, it stays away from the stereotypical depictions of what a hacker or a tech-savvy person is and even makes a joke out of that. 

The film itself has a fairly simple and straightforward storyline where a personal vendetta develops into a motive for cybercrime. Vishnu, played by Naslen, is our protagonist here, and at first glance, he's a lot similar to Sachin from Premalu; he's also an underachiever; he's also clueless about life; and the way Naslen plays the two characters is also pretty similar. But the thing is, Vishnu is not a relatable innocent dude who's pookiefied by the movie like Sachin. Sachin had micro-red flags, but the movie still treated him kindly. But Vishnu is pretty close to being an anti-hero. The way he deals with his insecurities and pettiness isn't exactly earning him any sympathy points, and the movie too doesn't try to justify or balance his wrong choices. Vishnu's character arc is pretty interesting; like, the movie doesn't actually show him as an absolute villain or anything, but still, among the "relatable loser" Girish AD protagonists, Vishnu, written by Sajin Cherukayil, is the more gray person.

There were many fun sequences, like the one involving a wifi modem and a network switch. Even with the hacking being shown as close to reality as possible, the movie still presents the technical stuff in a way anyone can understand, and the way the hacking is shot and conveyed is pretty cool. Like, when it's just command prompt windows instead of a colorful animation video showing "Hacking 100%" you'd have to get creative with how the action on screen is shown to seem cool and clever, and that's exactly what Girish does here whenever the hacking is shown. The background score was cool too. 

The supporting cast was good, and there too, the characters stay away from being stereotypes, even when they come close enough. Anishma Anilkumar's Shilpa was a character that I really liked, as she subverts the expectations on how such characters usually react to the protagonist being a dick. 

The movie was consistently fun, and yeah, and it was cool to see a cyber crime movie that's so rooted in Naadan aesthetics than borrowing from the west. That girl with the dragon tattoo reference was perfect.

Name: A Different Man
Review:
This movie and The Substance can be a great double feature. Both involve the main characters undergoing a big transformation to become a version that they thought they wanted to be, but with consequences. Both movies deal with it very differently, of course, and the philosophical areas they cover are also quite different.

A Different Man's main character, Edward, played by Sebastian Stan, does undergo the procedure to cure his disfigured face with no added complications and gets the conventionally attractive face that he had always wanted. People no longer looked at him with disgust or sympathy; he gets to experience pretty privilege, and yet he still doesn't become the person he wished to be. As he tries to become that person, Oswald enters his life, someone with the same condition that he had, which then further fuels Edward's identity crisis.

The movie is very well made. I loved the cinematography, the editing, and the score, especially the main theme music. The narrative flow is great, as the abrupt jumps never felt jarring. Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, and Adam Pearson were great, and I liked the way the movie handled Reinsve's character's relationship with both the men and then how the relationship with Edward gets echoed later. Oswald was also an intriguing character, and the way he pushed all the right buttons to trigger Edward. Edward himself too was an intriguing protagonist to follow around, as he's in the entire movie, in every scene. The way the identity crisis and its unraveling were portrayed by Stan was great.

Still though, one big decision that Edward takes after getting his new face still bugs me. Like, it kinda makes sense that he wants to live as a brand new person with the new face rather than as the old Edward, but still he tries to return back to his old life afterwards, so why'd he make that decision anyway? He could've just been Edward. It just didn't make sense. Or was that the point?

Name: Black
Review:
Well, I appreciate the effort to do a paradoxical sci-fi movie like this in Tamil. The movie does underestimate the audience a bit, but yk, even Christopher Nolan movies have done the kind of exposition dumping that's present here, so that's okay. I don't want to think too hard about the concept here to find loopholes because that'd make my head hurt. Anyway, very interesting padam, and it maintains the mystery and intrigue pretty well. Still, enthokkeyokkeyo missing and could've done more with it.

The empty villa property was a great creepy setting, though the movie then shortens itself to the single house. It initially reminded me of Vivarium, but that movie made its setting a lot more creepy and off-putting than this. 


Anyway, happy that Tamil cinema is taking swings like this.

Name: Gladiator II
Review:
The initial setup of Gladiator 2 was great. I mean, when we see Paul Mescal's character and what he goes through, it instantly mirrors Maximus' tragedy from the original. But the thing is, the Maximus parallel isn't just for him; Marcus Acacius, played by Pedro Pascal, also has an arc that mirrors Maximus. But both these men are put on opposite sides of vengeance, and this is eventually leading up to their big fight inside the colloseum that was featured heavily in this film's marketing. Now that setup was very meaty, and I was genuinely intrigued to see how it develops. Paul Mescal's character's true identity is kept as a secret initially in the movie, but the promotions of this thing have been pretty open about who he is, so I'm not sure I should talk about who he is here.

Anyway, though the leadup to the Mescal-Pascal colloseum confrontation (yeah, it rhymes) is excellent, everything afterwards felt generic and comparatively dull. But still, the film consistently looks gorgeous, the action looks badass, and it shot very well; the visual effects that show the epic scale of Rome and the production design are great; Harry Gregson-Williams' score recaptures the essence of Hans Zimmer's score from the original; and then there's of course Denzel slithering his way through the movie as an evil snake of a person. The legend he is.

The CGI animals look like CGI animals, and this one scales up the ridiculousness of the action to video game proportions with monkeys, sharks, a rhinoceros, and did I mention the sharks? All within the arena. The ending didn't give me the emotional gut punch that the original's ending did. But my man Denzel almost singlehandedly saves the third act. Still though, Paul Mescal does deliver; he looks and feels like a badass gladiator. But still, the writing doesn't give him the depth that Russell Crowe's Maximus had, so he has to work with what he has. Pedro Pascal's character too is interesting, but idk, his Ancient Rome (British? Britamerican?) accent just seemed off. Compare that to Denzel, who's just being the Ancient Rome version of Alonzo from Training Day, and it's awesome. Joseph Quinn as the emperor too seemed pale compared to Joaquin in the original (no pun intended). Connie Nielsen, the returning cast member from the original, got some emotionally powerful moments, but it felt like her arc could've had more going for it. Maybe this one too will get an extended version like Napoleon?

Anyway, Ridley Scott can still deliver on the epic scale, action, and cinematic drama, which is seen here too. Like, with better writing, he could still direct the hell out of it and deliver something as good as the original Gladiator even in his 80s.

(Denzel walking upto Paul Mescal while saying My.......... Champion! Was everything)

Name: Gladiator
Review:
Gladiator's ending still makes me cry every single time, which is an emotional response that the sequel never got out of me. Russell Crowe is magnificent in this movie, and so is Hans Zimmer's score, Scott's direction and Joaquin Phoenix as Commodus. Iconic.

This movie has one of the best on-screen death scenes ever filmed.

Name: Saturday Night
Review:
This is the kind of biopic that I enjoy more, because it's not about how Lorne Michaels grew up or how he got the idea to do SNL or how the show succeeded afterwards. This just puts us in the middle of the chaotic 90 minutes before the first episode went live. It isn't even waiting around to do so; without much context or setting up, we're right there. There is conventional storytelling happening here, of course, and various kinds of fan service and references for people who have followed the show, but still, when it's told through this real-time event, with Lorne Michaels and co. barely having a coherent show to go live, it just makes things more interesting and unpredictable.
