I loved the style of the camerawork and editing here; it follows the characters as they walk around 30 Rock a lot, and it feels like taking a walk through the chaos as they're happening. We do visually experience Lorne's anxiety and panic at times, but the movie is not a full-on Safdie Bros. style panic attack experience. It does take breathers. I don't know how many people who are not interested in SNL or sketch comedy will be into something like this, though. Because, as much as the movie occasionally tries to fill in context, a lot of times it does expect us to already be aware of the people we're seeing on screen.

The entire cast was great; I loved the music and the production design. The film captures the 70s vibes really well, and even though it has a few clichés of the genre, the whole chaotic setup and the real-time narrative make up for it. It also doesn't shy away from showing the workplace sexual harassment, misogyny and racism during that period either, though SNL itself gets off kinda clean without any harsh criticism towards itself.

Anyway, the movie also ends without having any epilogue or post-credit context about how it eventually went down for the show. It's just 90 minutes of chaotically setting up a big live show, a slightly polished inside look into the panicky side of showbiz as people run around to set up a live show. Well, Tina Fey's 30 Rock also did that for multiple seasons, and they even did a live broadcast episode about setting up a live show. But this one was also cool.

Name: After Hours
Review:
How bad can one night get? A lot worse, where a meet-cute flirty encounter and the expectation of a date turn into a nightmare. A very funny, trippy and hilarious nightmare though, as the situation gets progressively worse for our protagonist Paul, when all he wants is to get home, but he keeps encountering weird people and weirder circumstances. The film is so brilliantly made, as Scorsese is making us follow Paul and his misfortunes on this single night, so there's no Montage Scorsese here. Thelma Schoonmaker's editing is brilliant too, and the movie is filled with so much memorable imagery, and the atmosphere of the city at night looks so great. After Hours is laser focused on putting Paul through hilarious misery, though. As he runs for his life to the sound of an ice cream truck and sees someone get murdered, and then says, "This'll probably get pinned on me too", was the cinemaest moment in After Hours. I lovedddd the music too, and how it eventually ends made me laugh like crazy.

The movie is meet-cutophobic anyway. It's a romantic comedy fan's nightmare.

Name: Smile 2
Review:
Smile 2 felt like an improvement over the original. Parker Finn's original take on this concept did have some very effective scares and atmosphere, but it still felt like a thin, short film premise being stretched too much to be a feature-length film. The premise of the smile parasite curse and the creepy smiling people stays the same in Smile 2, but Finn makes many smart choices here to not only make it different from the first film but to also seem like a much more solid narrative. 

So this time we follow popstar Skye Riley in a great lead performance from Naomi Scott, and it's a setting that's pretty new to this kind of film. The way the entity starts tormenting Skye is similar to Rose from the first movie; it starts with seeing random people with creepy smiles, and it eventually turns into aggressive hallucinations. But Skye felt like a much more interesting character, plus the celebrity angle gives a lot of flavor here, both to the scares and to the way Skye's life is fed on by the creature. 

The scares are also consistently effective here, and unlike the first film that felt like a barely connected collection of cool scare sequences, here I was actually invested in Skye, so the unexpected jumpscare and the occasional creepy smile hit a lot more. There's a lot of memorable creepy imagery too, from the little girl with the braces to the creepy backup dancers to the ending that fires on all cylinders to be dark af. There are multiple instances of gnarly-looking gore and violence here too. This is also yet another movie that uses exaggerated sound effects effectively to sell violence. The mix of CGI and practical effects for the gore was great.

The music was great, both the horror soundtrack and the original songs done for Skye Riley. Naomi Scott is convincing as the popstar and as a horror lead. Since the movie follows Skye almost entirely after the title is shown, and she's the character slowly losing her mind, the lead actor matters a lot here. Scott's performance helps Finn in conveying the terror a lot. As Skye loses her grip on what is real and what's not, that doubt clouds the audience too, and I realized that though the first movie had the same premise, I was not into it like this at all. It's also interesting to look back and see the various clues peppered throughout. 

Despite having the same basic premise, the new setting and creative use of new characters and scare situations made this feel like an improvement over the first movie. But still, I'm not sure if a third movie with the same structure will work once more. But yk, Finn surprised me here, so I hope he surprises me there too. The setting up for the third movie towards the end is definitely more interesting and not your average horror movie sequel bait.

Name: Sookshmadarshini
Review:
We have always seen the snoopy stereotypical neighbor lady character in films as an inconvenience or an annoyance, the one who pries into someone else's private business. MC's Sookshmadarshini actually breaks this trope by presenting the protagonist, Priyadarshini, as someone with a sharp attention to detail and detective skills. So when she finds her new neighbor a bit suspicious and starts prying, is it her just being nosy or her having great deduction skills? 
 
Sookshmadarshini is a very effective Nattinpuram thriller set in a small neighborhood. The film quickly establishes the neighborhood, the characters, and Priyadarshini herself. Basil Joseph plays the sus next door instead of the boy next door here, and both Basil Joseph's performance and the way Manuel is presented by MC and his co-writers are interesting. Because Sookshmadarshini is very precise and smart about the way it provides information to the audience. Though Priyadarshini is the protagonist and the audience's window (quite literally) into the mystery, the audience gets to know more than Priyadarshini does, and then MC skillfully plays with this to maintain suspense and build scenes that get progressively more thrilling. Sookshmadarshini is the kind of movie that plays with audience expectations and interpretations while not insulting the audience's intelligence at the same time. It's even rewarding to notice small details here. So it's the kind of movie where a rewatch will feel like an entirely different experience. 
 
Nazriya as Priyadarshini is a great protagonist and a great lead performance. According to the director, she's inspired by his own mother, and we get to see her being clever and resourceful in daily life scenarios even before the main mystery begins. It's so easy to root for her. Priyadarshini and the lady gang are the chill, nosy group of the neighborhood. Their whole dynamic and interactions were very fun to watch. I loved both Akhila Bhargavan and Pooja Mohanraj's performance as the co-snoops. Also, Siddharth Bharathan was so hilarious. The rest of the cast is also pretty great. The movie is almost very tight and precise, with almost every scene and character being important one way or another. The only part that felt out of place was a subplot involving Priyadarshini's husband Anthony's workplace. It didn't feel like it belonged to the rest of the movie. The vibe was completely off. But that's quickly brushed aside (phew), and the rest of Sookshmadarshini is laser focused just like the titular microscope. Christo Xavier's playfully mysterious and sneaky-vibe score doesn't let the tone get too dark and yet provides the intended uplift as things get more tense, Chaman Chacko's editing that's as precise as the narrative, and Sharan Velayudhan's cinematography—everything complements each other. I also loved the sound here; movies not being too loud is not supposed to be a compliment, but as ear assault is a trend in Indian cinema these days, I might complement every movie with audio that doesn't cause a migraine. 
 
Anyway, Sookshmadarshini will be one of the examples that I'll use in the future whenever I have to talk about great suspense thrillers. The way this film is clever about the way it communicates with the audience to maintain suspense is so impressive. Moments of humor are incorporated into the mystery in a very fun way, with an adequate amount of laughs and thrills. It's a "good for her" movie that also gives us a great female protagonist in Priyadarshini in 2024 Malayalam cinema, just as the year is about to end. Almost perfecto movie, except for that one subplot and some kunj flaws that I didn't really mind.

Name: Rear Window
Review:
The way the suspense is built in this movie is the stuff of legends. We're confined to the pov of the titular window; the set itself is brilliant, and the entire space is used so beautifully. The way the protagonist's passing time habit of peeping into other people's lives eventually builds up to a mystery is amazing. Hitchcock plays with information and exposition brilliantly, like literal textbook stuff, as so many filmmakers have been inspired by this.



In this era of social media stalking and voyeurism, a person confined to a single room like Jeff would mostly be on their phone and laptop, no? Instead of directly peeping out through a window? There have been multiple films inspired by Rear Window, but I'm kind of wondering how the same thing would work adapted to the digital age.

Name: All We Imagine as Light
Review:
This gem from Payal Kapadia was a beautiful and meditative experience. The pacing is in no hurry; as the film moves through these characters, we see the daily lives of these working-class women. The way this film deals with intimacy is what hit me the most. Intimacy and the yearning for intimacy are portrayed, both physically and emotionally. The film looks so beautiful, with gorgeous visuals of Mumbai intercut between scenes with the characters and certain voiceovers. But it's not like portrayed as a magical "movie" place. There's a cute cat, a couple in love, and moments of warmth, but the film is still very much grounded too. It feels real and kinda "filmy" at the same time. I loveddd the use of colors and the nighttime cinematography. It looked gorgeous when the setting shifted from Mumbai towards the halfway point too.

There's a balance between wholesomeness and melancholy here that's so well done; there's no clear line that separates the sad parts from the happy parts, which is kinda the way life is. The music felt so beautiful too, and all of the cast were great. Also, pretty great Malayalam dialogue and character interactions for a non-Malayali production.



(I couldn't understand a lot of the non-Malayalam dialogue because the screen I watched in didn't have subs 😑)

Name: Bagheera
Review:
This could've been a great subversion of South Indian Supercop movies by making the honest and perfect Supercop turn into a murderous vigilante anti-hero, blurring the lines between justice and murder, sorta like a hybrid between Batman and The Punisher. But this is not it at all. Our murderous vigilante doesn't have any shades of gray here. So when he decides to brutally murder criminals the first time, the movie uses rape as an excuse to justify the brutality towards the criminals. Like, how long would Indian movies keep doing the sexual assault as a lazy plot device thing over and over again? Then I thought, at least they didn't show an insensitively shot rape scene, and then, just as Vedanth/Bhagheera starts murdering the goons, we get flashbacks of the insensitively shot rape scene. Because the movie wants us to remind us that the criminals deserve to get sliced and smashed. It's bad. It's insensitive.

Then the movie turns into a full-on vigilante film. There's a lot of cringe to unpack, but the truth is, I don't even remember most of it; I lost track. It tries to replicate Prashant Neel's style but falls so flat. And it's also unsure if it should be grounded and dark or if it should be cheesy and masala. KGF didn't hesitate to go full masala, but this movie does. Then there's also hilarious stuff like how this dude recruits random strangers to his Batman team, including a child. Well, yk, Batman himself has recruited kids to his team, but even that had a more natural development unlike how it's shown here.

Rukmini Vasanth is the most important reason why I decided to watch this movie (crush crusheyyy), but she's barely in this movie, and the whole romance arc is so bad that even she couldn't save it. Also, the movie does her dirty at the end, ending up being yet another lazy cliché. Srimurali fits the character with his physicality, but after initially showing some promise, the character just becomes one-dimensional and hollow. He's just heroic. There's no questioning of the morality of murder or of the mass murdering affecting his psyche.

Bad attempts like this make me appreciate amazing Indian vigilante films like Bhavesh Joshi more. Even that one had a not that great lead performance, and yet that movie is so awesome.

Name: Here
Review:
The idea behind this movie is something that I really love, and it's something that I've thought about too. Like, what kind of things happened on the land my house is on before me, or even before the house existed? What kind of stuff will happen once I'm gone? Like, a piece of space on this earth will have so many memories and people associated with it, and I've always had a fascination for it, before knowing that an artist named Richard McGuire created a graphic novel out of the same thing.

I've not read Richard McGuire's Here, the source material for this movie. But I did see photos of a few panels of it. It's fixed at a single angle, at the same geographical place, and then it nonlinearly depicts multiple events happening at that space, sometimes at the same time, sometimes one event at a time. Now, since I've not read the whole novel, I can't compare the entirety of the novel with the film. But the film does try to emulate the graphic novel's panels visually, as small rectangular frames within the main frame of the single location depict multiple events happening in parallel across decades and centuries, and these overlay frames often lead to scene transitions too. There are so many creative scene transitions and instances of events from multiple points in time happening here. But this occasionally felt like it would have looked cooler as a montage sequence or some short-form narrative situation than a full-on feature film (though it's only under 100 minutes). But sometimes it does work beautifully. 

I really wanted to love this movie a LOT, but yeah, I kinda understand where the negative reviews are coming from. But at the same time I can't completely hate it either. Forrest Gump itself was like an episodic mishmash of American history and pop culture, but what held it together was Tom Hanks' Forrest, his innocence and likability. This one, on the other hand, doesn't really let us know its characters any better other than the few interactions they have in the space we're seeing, which is their living room. Well, it's also kinda realistic that these characters are not having every single interaction in their living room. The unique fixed perspective and narrative of the film become a double-edged sword here, as parts of the film just feel like a clip show of random moments in time where we don't feel anything for the people on screen, though they're having very human moments. But still, some parts of the film do work really well. Because it taps into basic human emotions, resonating over the span of centuries, where us knowing these people doesn't really matter. So for those sweet moments that did genuinely move me, and that Alan Silvestri score that filled up my heart, I can't hate this movie.

Deepfake technology still hasn't evolved to make people look like actual people. It works as a short video or as a small cameo character, but when it's a full-length character and the film itself is about the human experience, the deepfakes occasionally produce the opposite effect of the film's intentions. Tom Hanks looked okay; I could buy him as a person, but Robin Wright looked weird and unnatural throughout this movie, even in the scenes where she was playing close to her actual age. In both their cases, the deepfakes show their limitations whenever the characters move closer to the camera. Hanks is at least a bit better from a distance. But still, yeah, deepfakes need work. Something like the deaging technique from The Irishman would've worked better because even if it didn't make them convincingly look like young people, they'd have at least looked like people. This is still one of the best uses of deaging technology though. 

The film has a great idea, and I do think the same source material and idea could've been adapted into a superior film that did address mortality, love, loss, and life happening at the same place over centuries and millennia beautifully. Maybe as an animated film, or perhaps at a time when technology did evolve enough to make actors look exactly like their younger selves. Still, though, there are places where this movie is soo sweet and wholesome, and towards the end, when they show a montage of the house throughout various points in time, without the people, it tugged my heartstrings a bit. Also, yeah, the way it's been edited and the way it's been conceived around the same space evolving over time on a production perspective is brilliant. The production design was also great. The narrative is where this film needed to do more with this idea. That's where things got a bit messy and incoherent. 

I don't know. I have nothing but respect to Zemeckis for taking a wild swing like this, no matter how the result ended up being.

Name: Bloody Beggar
Review:
This was a surprisingly fun and cool movie. It was very engaging and consistently funny. I even felt like it had better-executed dark humor than the producer Nelson's films. Because unlike Nelson's films, this film maintains a darkly humorous tone throughout its runtime. Yes, there's a traumatic flashback and some really dark and violent stuff happening in between, but the film still bounces back to being a dark comedy, while the dramatic beats do hit at the right places.

After a brief intro for the film's villains, a group of very despicable and easily hatable rich folk, we get introduced to the protagonist, the titular Beggar. He pretends to be handicapped and begs for a living. So he's basically more of a con artist. We see his daily routine, which is still pretty modest, and he's still underprivileged, but he has a smartphone, he does Instagram reels, orders pizza from Swiggy, and watches movies in the theater in his spare time. Yk, he's just living life on his own terms. He's also got this confidence and arrogance about him. Still though, his entire portrayal had me confused if this was like disrespectful towards the actually disadvantaged and underprivileged section of the society. He does have a tragic backstory, though it doesn't really explain why he is the way he is. But still, everything becomes better once the elite villains enter into the picture and our protagonist unwittingly becomes a part of their sinister plans. Then the whole movie is about these greedy, rich people and this poor, underprivileged man trapped in a big mansion with them.

The movie has all kinds of twists and turns; some are funny, some are dark, and some are both. It just goes from one twisted scenario to the next, and overall it felt very consistent in what it wants to be. Kavin was a great lead; all the rich villains were easily hateable and had a variety of personalities (some of the performances are a mixed bag, but we're supposed to hate them anyway). The entire ensemble of characters was interesting, and even Redin Kingsley was tolerable and funny here. I liked the music, the direction, the cinematography, the production design (which was going for a very specific look) and of course the darkly humorous tone. Kavin did look like a lighter person who's been brownfaced, though. But he did do his part well, performance wise. The main character's arc was a bit confusing on the whole, but still, in a film where the protagonist is stuck in a scenario where everyone except him are rich evil fucks, it's easy to root for him. 

The way the rich people have been portrayed here is really great, like they're greedy, they lack empathy, they're psychopaths, and then they have the audacity to look down upon people like our underprivileged protagonist. So the way the class difference becomes a part of the narrative here, without really being a "serious" film, makes me kinda give a pass to the way the initial depiction of the beggar's daily routine wasn't that serious either.

It's an eat the rich movie, of course I'll rate it high!

Name: Valliettan
Review:
As cool as the visuals look on the new remastered version, I just hate it when they alter the music and add new opening titles to these old movies. A remaster should always preserve as much of the original movie as possible. So when Valyettan had new opening titles and a re-recorded theme music, it already lost some of its appeal. 

I have watched Valyettan on Kairali as a kid; we had a Doordarshan dish antenna, and Kairali was one of the few Malayalam channels we had. Anyway, now I don't remember much from the movie, so it was like watching something completely new to an extent. Ranjith's writing is so bad here, except in parts. And I'm not just talking about the ways in which it's regressive and problematic; that's been covered ever since Orkut was relevant. Even the drama is bad; like, there are other movies from the same era with much better writing and drama, and even older movies written by Ranjith himself, so it's not just an age thing.

What made the remastered version a fun watch, though, is seeing peak Shaji Kailas doing peak Shaji Kailas things, along with Ravi Varman's amazing cinematography that the new version lets me appreciate even more. This was Shaji Kailas before he went all Kalam Kalam effect and poo viriyunna effect. This movie is stylish and chaotic in the best of ways. During one fight scene in a market, Kalabhavan Mani even falls onto some background actress who was running away; we don't see stuff like that anymore.

Then, of course, it's the joy of seeing Ikka as a hypermasculine feudal beast of a man. The way he delivers the dialogue, especially when it's just pure rage, and the way he carries himself, is the real deal. He basically carries the whole movie. Every awful scene is followed by Ikka saying or doing something cool. Even his intro scene has this pistol with exploding bullets being shot at him, and he even sells that with so much conviction. Then he drives to the villain's house and delivers this long af monologue in a single shot, with flashback exposition, punchlines, threats, and self-promotion all at the same time. Yk, it's one of those moments where this movie peaks. "Mulavecha kozheede ara kinnam paal tharum Njan". I mean...

Anyway, I won't call Valyettan a great movie; there is great Ikka fan service here and a throwback to the time when Shaji Kailas was the real deal. I did have fun watching this; it alternated between laughing at the bad parts and romancham at the badass parts. It's more of a nostalgia thing, yeah. 

I was waiting to hear the Valyettan theme music in the new version and got so disappointed when they played an alternate "updated" version. Niranaazhi Ponnil song sounds pretty much like how I remember it, though.

Name: North by Northwest
Review:
Visually this film still holds up, it might even be timeless. All the visual effects here are either hand painted, projected or pure cinema trickery using miniatures And It's so brilliantly done. That crop duster chase scene is legendary stuff. The film feels so big in scale, and Cary Grant is great as the protagonist, with his sense of humor and charm, the music is cool and the way the thrill builds up is also great. If there's one thing that hasn't aged well here it's the romance. I didn't really feel like Roger and Eve had a genuine chemistry between them. Though both were great as individual characters. Though some of it's dated, this movie was ahead of its time in a lot of ways too. 

I also loved how the movie was funny while being thrilling. That final transition was so abrupt and jarring that it's kinda hilarious and brilliant, don't ask me why. I'm ending this opinion abruptly too.

Name: Pushpa 2 - The Rule
Review:
I remember reading that Pushpa was supposed to be a single film but was split in two because of there being too much plot for a single movie. So after a first movie that made it seem like it was like playing a video game on Easy mode for Pushpa to become a sandalwood smuggling kingpin, we get this collection of random scenes as the sequel. I mean, this movie is so scattered, random, and incoherent that I can't even remember a lot of it. Sometimes it felt like scrolling through a collection of very expensively made TikTok videos. I think parts of the actual sequel that Sukumar had conceived are still in here, but it's been filled with so much unnecessary stuffing that the end product in no way looks like it had "too much plot" to be split into yet another sequel.

So where do I even begin? Well, let me start by saying that I was not bored for much of the 3.5 hours of Pushpa 2. Now that's a lot of movie, but this thing is so disjointed and almost episodic that it doesn't feel like watching a single film in the first place. It comfortly falls into the "so bad it's good" category as I was laughing at it too. I have no issue with splitting this into a trilogy (or however many movies this is going to be stretched into), but a movie needs to justify its existence as a movie, right? 

Allu Arjun as Pushpa is the person barely holding the movie together. His performance is great; he brings in the kind of power and aura that a larger-than-life character like Pushpa needs, and he's effective in showing Pushpa's vulnerable side, even when the writing is weak in terms of humanizing him yet again. Pushpa on his own is an interesting character with a unique arc, even while his larger-than-life antics and self-praising punchlines are pretty generic. Because Pushpa's over-inflated sense of pride and self stems from a lifetime of being seen as inferior. It's easy to understand his over-the-top stubbornness because of that backstory. Still, though, his whole backstory, where his half-brother doesn't let him use his caste surname instead of it being, yk, actual casteism, felt confusing in the first movie itself, and it does here too. Pushpa still faces classist remarks due to his origins as a blue-collar laborer, despite being rich enough to own an island. And yet, they still had to maintain his upper caste origins with the "He's from Tharavaad, but he can't use the Tharavaad name" thing. Rich Pushpa still maintains his roots in his style, though. His catchphrases, gestures, and body language are maintained too. He even owns his own branded merchandise. He rubs his beard with his hand, he rubs his beard with his two hands, he rubs his beard with horny Srivalli's foot, he rubs his beard with a dismembered hand, and so on. Even Fahadh Faasil as the villain does almost all of Pushpa's gestures and mannerisms here. Pushpa is a brand indeed.

Srivalli's arc was bad in the first movie, and it's bad here too; I can't even tell which one is worse. Srivalli, the sigma's babysitter in Animal, how does Rashmika Mandanna specifically do these awful characters in big movies? Srivalli's entire arc in Pushpa 2 is that she's horny about the mere fact that Pushpa (her Saamy) exists. She gets the peelings (horny) just from a mere touch from him, and the entire first half is her being just that. When she walked into a pretty dramatic scene towards the interval, I thought that she was going to catch the peelings there too. She gets horny for Pushpa even when Pushpa is getting all sexy with the young dancer played by Sreeleela during the Kissik song. Threesome perhaps? No judgment or kink-shaming here. Just that at the end of 3.5 hours, the horniness is the only takeaway from the character, despite Pushpa saying stuff like how he listens to his wife and respects her, the movie doesn't. She does get a big emotional monologue at one point regarding caste, family name and identity, and then that monologue is made pointless at the end. 

Fahadh as Bhanwar Singh Shekhawat was built up to be the big bad guy at the end of the first movie. Just as Pushpa defeats the existing big bads easily and becomes powerful, this new threat enters, and the sequel tease there was that of a big showdown between these two dudes. And, Shekhawat is just a sore loser in this movie, where the "showdown" is pretty one-sided, and it's also the same scene being repeated over and over again. Again, this movie is almost 3.5 hours long, and the scenario where Shekhawat has a plan, thinks he's won, but Pushpa easily gets the upper hand is repeated over and over again, after seeing the scene first play out right before the film's titles even appear. Fafaa played Shekhawat in the first movie when Shammi was the Fafaa character that was trending. So Shekhawat in Pushpa 1 was very Shammi and an over-the-top psycho. But the Shekhawat in Pushpa 2 is a mix of Rangannan, Shammi, Indian Pranayakadha, Njan Prakashan, etc. Well, there's not much of a character written there, and the scenes here seem to have Fahadh reenacting scenes from his existing movies that Sukumar probably liked. We even get a scene that looks like the dumb charades scene in Aavesham, just that it's shitty. It's not that I mind Fahadh doing a role that's "beneath him". I don't have an issue with Shekhawat embarrassing himself or doing Pushpa Charades or swimming in Pushpa piss; it's just that after the end of the first film being pure setup for him, he's just a clown who's nothing to Pushpa.

It also felt like the film lacked confidence in letting Pushpa himself carry it. Because it's packed to the brim with making Pushpa do stuff that was a hit in other movies. We have Pushpa getting a montage of how powerful he is, like Rocky Bhai in KGF did; we have Pushpa dressing up as a deity and doing an intense religious dance with Hindu aesthetics and music, like Kaanthara did; he has an action scene with the same aesthetics, like Kaanthara did, but Pushpa 2 also has a romantic duet song in between the religious dance and the fight scene, which Kaanthara didn't have. Take that for originality! Pushpa does slow-motion posing that emulates Hindu deity imagery, like in RRR. And yeah, there's a bit involving the Indian flag and Desi pride too, because why not? Pushpa, being the stubborn and proud narcissist "brand" he is, made to replicate stuff that other dudes did, is funny.

The way this movie transitions into the songs is funny. Someone says "Pushpa Pushpa Pushpa" and then we transition to the song with the same name; Srivalli talks about her "peelings" and we get a song with the same name. When they say "Kissik Kissik" we get the song with the same name. And of course Srivalli breaking into song just when Pushpa has an emotional breakdown that makes him do a duet dance just as he got finished with an intense solo dance. The music was okay.

The first film had a scene where Srivalli is about to be sexually assaulted and Pushpa saves her. Pushpa 2 also uses sexual assault as a plot device to have Pushpa punish the criminals, twice. Even delivering a line like "I'd kill you if you do this to girls". Pushpa should say the same to the writers and filmmakers over here in India who are constantly using insensitive portrayals of sexual assault for shock value and just for giving motivation for the male protagonists to brutalize some other men. 

The incoherence hits this movie very badly. And it's there from the very beginning, even the "Icon Star Allu Arjun" title, meant to make the audience erupt into cheers, is put in the front of the movie like it's a production company logo, and it gets followed by the production company logos. Like, they can't maintain the high even in the title graphics, and this sentiment carries throughout. As awesome as Allu Arjun is in embodying Pushpa, the film is a letdown, dramatically and as mass masala, and it yet again ends on sequel bait without having moved much plotwise from the first movie. The action and slow-motion shots looked cool, but again, I didn't feel anything. The violence and action lacked the impact that I felt in Sukumar's own Rangasthalam (I have the same opinion on the action in Pushpa 1 too, though). 

Also, Pushpa 1 had this framing device where it was a story being narrated to us by Pushpa's right hand Kesava. But in Part 2, Sukumar just, forgot about it? 

Despite all that, would I still watch Pushpa 3? Of course I will! Thaggedalleee.

Name: Pushpa: The Rise
Review:
This is more coherent as a film than the sequel. I'll give it that.

But the funny thing is, the final 30 minutes or so are pure setup for Fahadh's Shekhawat in Pushpa 1, where he's introduced as an unhinged psychopath; he wounds Pushpa's inflated pride like no one else has, and then Pushpa easily humiliates him. He was the right kind of villain for a character like Pushpa, whose whole deal is that he bows down to none. But on rewatching this, I just realized that the sequel just replays this whole Shekhawat scenario from the first movie over and over again for most of its runtime without the existence of a proper face-off that's teased at the end of this movie, and then it just switches to the random kidnapping plot.

I know I ranted too much about Pushpa 2, though I'm supposed to talk about Pushpa 1 here. Apologies. Thaggedhelee.

Name: The Outrun
Review:
The non-linear narrative is a bit messy, and the movie feels a bit aimless at times, but everything is tied up beautifully, and it does have a reason to be scattered like it is, because the protagonist herself is mentally scattered, and as she heals more, the movie too becomes more stable, linearity-wise, with fewer jumps. It's a story about a woman's recovery from alcoholism, and it alternates between different points in that recovery journey. Saoirse Ronan plays the protagonist, Rona, with all her heart. Her performance holds the whole thing together as it jumps between timelines. This movie has one of the most deeply moving portrayals of alcoholism and recovery that I've ever seen. 

I loved the music and cinematography so much too!

Name: Kanguva
Review:
Kanguva is like a failure on multiple levels, so I'm not elaborating much about what's bad here.

The version available for streaming has cut out a major chunk of the opening present-day portions of the movie, so I never knew why that viral chettan wanted to sjsjdhdudhdjddj Redin Kingsley's head. Redin Kingsley is reduced to a background actor in the new cut, and the trimming is so jarring and obvious too. I'd rather have feasted on the bad scenes for ironic enjoyment. Like, what's left intact is also so bad, so why'd they even bother? 

Anyway, during the initial present-day portion, Suriya, as Francis, matched Siva's freak, because just like the movie, its leading man was also being horrible. But I'd blame only Siva for that; even Daniel Day Lewis will be shitty as Francis. Then the movie goes into the flashback, which is where the major chunk of the movie unfolds. Here, Suriya is better as the title character, Kanguva. He has genuinely put in some effort, but the character and the scenes are so badly written, and it's so badly made that I just felt sorry seeing Suriya on screen high on energy, being so physical (a lot of rope pulling) and screaming most of his lines. Bobby Deol's bad guy is also shitty; he basically does the same scene of being established as a terrifying dude who wants to kill Kanguva until he gets killed by Kanguva at the end. Oops, spoilers.

Now, the whole formula of a grumpy warrior being paired with a child and a paternal bond forming between them is a tried and true one; so many successful movies and even video games have executed it brilliantly. Siva rips off Stranger Things with the AI-generated photo gallery lab and the kid escaping out of it and then running into Francis, but he couldn't replicate the Eleven-Hopper arc. Appa paasam is what saved a dumpster fire Siva Movie like Viswaasam too. But here, I just didn't feel anything. Suriya shouts, "Poruvaa! Poruvaa!" over And over again, it reminded me of Ranbir from Animal doing the same thing with "Papa! Papa!". Well, I'll give credit to Poruvaa and Kanguva for having a better Father - Son relationship than "Papa meri jaan, I'll peek at your penis while you pee". 

The action was underwhelming; the production values were tacky. There's a motel at the beginning that looks so fake, there's not even any staff working there; the place looks deserted, and of course it gets destroyed by a bazooka later. Apparently a lot of money has been poured into this thing, but it just looks so... cheap. Even a "smaller" movie like Thangalaan, with its more grounded tribal setting, looked way better even with its CGI limitations.

Anyways, the movie ends with a tease for a sequel that'd probably never get made. As it shouldn't.

Siva underestimates his audience too much if he thought showing AI-generated images would pass for actual humans. Like, wtf?

One star just because Suriya Anna really did put effort into this, though it went fruitless. I think he genuinely did feel that this is a "neruppu maathiri padam." Paavam, I feel sorry for him.

Name: Pretty Woman
Review: The movie is all kinds of dated and problematic, but I won't deny that I smiled and giggled almost every time Julia Roberts was on screen. What a queen.

Name: Heretic
Review: Well, this was very thrilling and engaging. It was also very fun to see Hugh Grant play the exact opposite of the green flag men he built up his career over. He's the exact opposite of charming and cute here, but he is smart; I'll give him that. I also liked the way his character, Mr. Reed, is introduced, like he's just a normal middle-aged man, very non-threatening. He doesn't get a horror villain intro. But a person who's seen the promos for this thing or even a poster knows that's not the case here. As the two Mormon missionaries, Sister Paxton and Sister Barnes, played by Chloe East and Sophie Thatcher, interact more with him, he tries to initiate a debate, and his vibe's a little off from your average potential convert. As they talk about religion and as Reed gets more and more skeptical and philosophical, tiny red flags arise, and the situation soon develops into something beyond your average casual religious debate. The thing is, as an atheist myself, I was able to buy into a lot of the things Hugh Grant's character was saying, but without spoiling anything, his methods to prove what religion is all about are not so ideal, to say the least. But still, I was curious about how the film would deal with the subject of faith, despite being a horror movie, and it's done surprisingly well, tbh; it lays out some solid philosophical debate, makes the titular "Heretic" the villain, and yet wraps up without being religious propaganda. Bit of a tightrope walk, but it did alright. I can't expect radical atheism in every movie I watch, and I'm the kind of atheist who loves Scorsese's Silence, lol. Anyway, coming back to the horror thriller part of the movie. It maintains the suspense pretty well; I was always curious about what Mr. Reed's next move was going to be or what was going to happen to the girls next. There were some genuine shocks in this movie, and it kept me gripped till the very end. The film was more fun in the initial half when it was uncomfortable conversations with a dash of philosophy and religious debate, which was a new kind of angle to a horror movie. There's an Indian film, PK, that did something similar, but that was a comedy, and there the protagonist was an innocent alien who questioned religions. During the latter half, Heretic becomes more similar to familiar horror movies, but it's still a lot of fun. The production design was amazing, and the house did seem like a labyrinth. The cinematography was great too, and I also liked the way Hugh Grant's character was shot in a different way once he starts to make the girls feel scared. Anyway, I liked that as a religion-themed horror movie, it's still kind of solid philosophically; it ended up being more about "faith" than religion. Atheist me gives a pass. Also, Evil Hugh Grant is a LOT of fun. Let me go and watch Notting Hill. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Kneecap
Review:
It's like that high on energy, aggressive, political, unapologetic, IRISH in all capitals Irish movie. Also, I didn't even know this was a biopic starring its real-life subjects. Film festival picks work in mysterious ways.

LOVED the style and those doodle animations, plus the music of course.

Name: Vermiglio
Review:
Too uneventful and slow for my taste. Proud of myself for maintaining my attention span though.

There are some great scenes in between, and the performances, cinematography and locations were great. But I felt that it was too long.

Name: Watusi Zombie!
Review:
The movie looks really cool despite the limited budget and the fresh crew. It has a very specific look and style to it that I really dug. The editing, the scene transitions, and the way the music was used were nice. Really cool soundtrack too, BTW.

Dry and deadpan humor is something that I really enjoy, and Cyril does show some promise in that area. There's stuff involving awkward silences and weird exchanges between characters that was fun to watch. The editing was really nice during these bits too. 

As far as the writing goes, it felt more sitcom-y. There's even a reference to Friends that's played out like a "hotel aanennu karuthi barber shopil kayariya vridhan" kind of thing, and I appreciate any kind of Friends slander. But that's not the sitcomminess I was talking about; it's more along the lines of something like Curb Your Enthusiasm, where the inciting incident is very petty, in this case, just a casual comment on someone's performance on stage, and then it just gets passed on from person to person in a way the protagonist never expected. It's non-linearly structured by presenting the story as a flashback in between a podcast interview, and the way the time jumps were shown was cool. But as it ends, the structure doesn't quite hold as a coherent narrative; the podcast bit doesn't have a payoff or something. Like, when it ended, it did hit me with a "That's it?". 

So anyways, it felt more structurally like a sitcom episode than as a film on the whole. But I don't mean that too critically. Cyril definitely has some skill in doing deadpan humor, wacky character interactions, and a unique style about him. The performance by the cast was pretty good too. I had some fun.

Name: Queer
Review: The cinematography, performances, music and the cool looking visual stuff and dream sequences don't make me completely hate this. And Luca can still make physical intimacy look really cool. It's just that I was so out of this movie, like, when I watched Challengers I was completely IN it, but here, nope.

Name: The Room Next Door
Review: Performances and colors were nice.

Name: Me, Maryam, the Children and 26 Others
Review:
Surprisingly wholesome.

Also, person with a lonely existence, put in a situation where they're among a group of people, initially being frustrated by the situation, but then appreciating the hustle, bustle and company around them, and yet also wanting to get back to the peace and quiet of being alone. Is this a biopic or what?

Name: Anora
Review:
I didn't expect it to be as funny as it was. The comedy is so well done. So was the drama and the main character herself. 

Mikey Madison is a star! And we finally have a version of Pretty Woman with accurate rich people representation.

Prettay Mothafukin Womahnnnnn!

Name: Seven Samurai
Review:
Might be my biggest flex ever that when I watched Seven Samurai, it was on a cinema screen with a full house.

Wammaaalaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!!!

Name: Conclave
Review: As a person who doesn't care about who becomes Pope, by the end of this movie I was HEAVILY invested in who becomes the Pope, that's great cinema. The way the narrative builds is awesome, the staging of scenes and the performances are great, the cinematography is beautiful, and the music is also amazing. It's also political, and does stretch the politics quite a bit while being set in the catholic church. But still, yeah, it does stay a bit limited in how much it criticises the church itself.

Name: Misericordia
Review: Big Priest Energy.

Name: Caught by the Tides
Review:
This just seemed like a random collection of footage with barely any narrative holding it together. Then after watching the movie when I searched about it, it was indeed repurposed footage over the span of 22 years and even footage from the director's previous movies. Well, I got a sense that I'm not watching any sets and extras when China from the early 2000s was shown, and the two leads were visibly aging on screen. But without much context about what this movie is, and the director himself, I was lost and confused about what really was going on. A lot of people were even leaving the screening. But I stayed back because I just had to know if it all meant something, and got the gist that it's about time passing and the evolution of China over the last two decades. Yeah, that was basically it. Great success.

Isn't this what Mr. Bean does to the Willem Dafoe movie in Mr. Bean's holiday though? Don't kill me arthouse bros. 😭

Name: Sangarsha Ghadana - The Art of Warfare
Review:
I liked Krishand's style choices in his last two movies, and even this one had moments that made me laugh. But as much as I had fun watching this, I had fun watching it as just a gangster revenge movie. Whenever it started reciting lines of Art of War with the Pramod Pappanic approach narrator voice, or showed slides about actual wars and conflicts, as if they're parallel to the main narrative involving the small gunda sangham (it really isn't), I was instantly out of it. Like, bro, you already have a pretty solid and funny gunda comedy padam, and the police officer characters were a riot, and scenes like the villain gunda team discussing lime sodas were hilarious, but the moment it tries to be allegorical and serious in a way it really shouldn't be, I was conflicted about what this is. The only part where the whole Chinese gimmick worked is for the aesthetics and music (when I say aesthetics, I don't mean the AI art). The Palestine reference was also totally unnecessary. Like, bruh, don't.

In short, Art of War was Fart of War whenever it pretended to be an adaptation of Art of War and did stuff like comparing the petty conflict in it with something like the genocide in Gaza, that too using AI images. I mean, I'm not saying it's wrong to make an allegory where a small petty gunda issue has parallels to wars and conflicts across history and the Art of War. It's just that this isn't it. This is not serious enough for it, even as a dark comedy. Not rating it too low because of the few parts I did enjoy. (I have no clue about giving numbered ratings to subjective opinions anyway.)

Name: Chicken for Linda!
Review: So cute and beautiful.

Name: Victoria
Review:
This was a gem. The film covers a single day in the title character's life as she works in a women-only beauty salon. She's dealing with relationship issues, family issues, work, and a rooster. The film is filled with these great long shots, and the performances and dialogue felt so natural. Nothing in the movie felt forced or artificial, especially the way patriarchy is addressed and how the salon itself is a place just for women. Everything from the art direction to the writing to the performances was great, and the film made such great use of the space it's set in. The main character's stress and anxiety are portrayed effectively.

With so many long shots in a space with multiple mirrors, multiple characters, with all kinds of banter and activity between these women going on, the cinematography has all my love. 

The director certainly has her own unique voice, and this has so much love put into it. Loved it.

Name: Emilia Pérez
Review: Except for Zoe Zaldana's performance throughout the movie and the music numbers with her, and the performances of Karla Sofía Gascón as the title character and the rest of the main cast except Selena Gomez, this was pretty meh. I cannot emphasise more on how bad Selena Gomez was.

Name: Animal | Human
Review: The whole time I was wondering how they made the bulls do all that stuff. Also, the parallels between the animal and the humans work well, and more points for how it doesn't glorify bullfighting and addresses the animal abuse unlike something like Meiyazhakan over here in India.

Name: The Girl with the Needle
Review: Someone told me that this was going to get dark, and I DID NOT expect the actual dark twist here. The black and white cinematography was so great and the performances and the music too. Very effective stuff.

Name: Memories of a Burning Body
Review: This was such a beautiful film from the perspective of older women, their sexuality and their lives. So I felt so bad that I dozed off for parts of it though I was so into the movie. Have to watch it again after the streaming release to catch up with the parts I missed. Apologies.

Name: Linda
Review: When you do a movie about rich people being horny for their maid, not addressing class at all is a bad decision. The movie just lingers over the same point over and over again till it just ends. There are some laughs here and there, and the way she's absolutely repulsed by the men while she flirts back with the women was cool. But yeah, even Saltburn did this better.

Name: Holy Cow
Review: Very very wholesome movie. Loved the cast, the cinematography, the music and the overall vibe. The little kid was the MVP.

Name: Black Dog
Review: Best doggo actors of 2024.

Name: Kill the Jockey
Review: Dozed off a bit at the beginning. The rest of it was fun though.

Name: Rifle Club
Review:
I fucking loved this movie. Rifle Club's pace is super fast, and as a result, yeah, the drama doesn't really land, and the characters lack depth and are just all about their quirky characteristics. But I think that's the vibe the film was going for here. It's fast-paced, hyper-stylized fun, with jokes, one-liners, and bullets flying all over. Even when the film fails to maintain momentum, it doesn't linger around too much, and something cool will quickly happen, or Lord Rex Vijayan will bless us with sangeetham from the heavens. Loved the cast, the banter, the ookkals, the one-liners, and how every single person gets to be a badass. Also, though he's playing a generic bad guy here, this is the only South Indian movie so far where Anurag Kashyap has put in an effort with the dialogue by doing it himself.

Just fun big-gun energy, double meaningey.

Name: Barroz: Guardian of Treasures
Review:
This is not that well-made a movie with bad dialogue and writing that drags on and on aimlessly, and scenes that drag on for no reason, and I'm sure the 2D version would be ripped apart even more. The gimmicky 3D effects and stuff popping out from the screen (including A10's head breaking the 4th wall) were fun. But the thing is, in this age of weak attention spans, where I've seen kids skip through even Spider-Man: No Way Home, I don't know if Barroz would get love from even its core audience. Because instead of doing a cute, simple plot with jokes and fun sequences like My Dear Kuttichathan, this movie is unnecessarily verbose and plotty, and at the same time, there isn't much plot here, and we don't feel much for the characters and their relationships either. The girl and the ghost are supposed to bond over the runtime, but we never feel it happening. The girl is Gen Alpha because she takes selfies with everyone; that's the level of character work at play here. Not elaborating further on that. 

Anyway, there was a good plot buried beneath all this involving a colonizer forcing a slave to guard his plundered treasure, a present-day plot involving clearing a slum (occupation parallel again) to build a casino, and yet, this movie still makes the Black voodoo witch the villain and the white colonizers seem better? Like, I know this is not the kind of movie that's meant for political readings, but why bring in colonization and slavery to half-ass it like this?

The movie looks and feels like those Indian TV serials made for kids from the early 2000s. Couldn't compare it with my dear Kuttichathan because I'd watched the re-release as a kid, and that movie still took me in. It just drags on aimlessly with occasional colorful 3D stuff happening. The CGI work was pretty solid in some scenes in the movie, and horrible in some others. The sets looked fake, but that could be an artistic choice. A10's performance ranged from looking unnecessarily spaced out and drunk to giving monologues that don't really mean anything. How does a ghost even get drunk? Idk. He delivers the same monologue about his undying loyalty over and over again, like, get a hint: you were a slave; you were murdered to guard plundered wealth. 😭. I did feel bad for poor Barroz the ghost. The CGI doll ends up being the most normal and reasonable character in the movie (pretty good animation on him too; he might be the best fully CGI character in Malayalam cinema, all things considered). 

The dialogues were unintentionally hilarious, and some of the scenes are so absurd. The attempts at building up drama do tend to go towards "thenga udaykk swamiii" territory.

Bad as it is, I did feel that A10 cared about this movie. But I don't know how I'm supposed to feel about that.

Name: Marco
Review:
Haneef Adeni was smart in realizing the potential of the incel-core audience, because just like Animal, adding in a few gimmicks that cater to a particular male audience, they'd forgive that the rest of the movie is fucking horrible. There's the gratuitous violence, the love interest who randomly appears to call the protagonist a toxic red flag, for him to respond that his toxicity is his love, and then she appears again to be subjected to gratuitous violence, and for the homophobes, a character's arm is mutilated as soon as he says that he's bisexual (a dude in my theater was taking a video of this scene on his phone, wtf for?). So yeah, enough deliberate and obvious incel baiting is present here for this movie to be praised as testosterone max, masculinity max, "real man" cinema.

So it's funny that the protagonist in Marco is a fucking moron here and pretty useless for the entirety of the movie. Is that peak male performance? Well, okay then. Unni Mukundan stars as Marco, a dude who cares the most about his drip in this world, though he says he cares about his family the most in this world. This is the only man who'd first think about styling himself to look like John Wick after witnessing the worst tragedy in his life. He looks stylish, has the physicality of an action hero, can't pull off smoking cigars in style, and acts terribly. He pukes during his intro scene, and that's about the most honest that performance is. Puke. And no, ripping off action set pieces and aesthetics from superior films just doesn't matter when you utter lines like "Yudhathil kollaanolla sothanthryam und" like you're reciting the Malayalam textbook at school. He even asks a friend, "Vedhanikkunninda?" after that dude has his fucking arm chainsawed off, like wtf? The drama is so weak, the dialogue is horrible in a very funny way, the acting across the cast is bad, and there's even a senti song that's edited with fast cuts like a KGF montage for some reason. Nothing really happens for most of the movie either, till there's enough excuse to throw violence at our faces.

There are violent, lackluster action set pieces with Marco bashing, slashing, and shooting through waves of goons—mostly inferior rip-offs of action sequences from better films—that didn't really make me feel anything. Plus, the way the final action set piece is set up makes Marco look more like a sore loser than a badass, and not in a tragic hero kind of way, but in a "You could've made more of an effort to prevent the tragedy from happening in the first place instead of waiting it out to get a shower and get dressed for the big fight, you fucking idiot!" kind of way. Like, dude does a dress-up montage right after going through something so traumatic; how tf is this film supposed to be taken seriously? But the thing is, towards the end, it felt like Marco mutilating thugs was not the kind of violence that Haneef Adeni was interested in anyway. Haneef Adeni's films have always had a fixation on violence towards children, and it's at its most deranged and insensitive form here. It's supposed to provide a tragic motivation to the protagonist, but the insensitive violence towards the women and children showcased here is so gratuitous and so extended in a way that the violence towards the villains just wasn't. Now, as someone who enjoys gory action movies and slasher movies, I might sound like a hypocrite for criticizing graphic violence in one movie while enjoying others, but the way Haneef Adeni fetishizes the violence towards women and children made me uncomfortable in a way that I don't want films to make me feel, even with the scene being as badly made and badly acted as it is, like the rest of the movie. And even after the scene is finished, it's replayed over and over again through flashbacks, as if it wasn't already burned into our heads. Even something like Terrifier 3, which was gratuitous violence galore, had children being killed off-screen. That, plus the fact that Sreejith Ravi is in the cast of Marco (just Google why he was arrested), makes me question a lot of things. And fuck any parent who brings kids to watch this shit. Usually I appreciate gore effects and makeup in movies; here too, apart from some bad CGI blood (which looks worse than video games), the gore is effective at times, but what it actually accomplishes doesn't really make me appreciate the work that much.

And the way this is then getting celebrated is so fucked up. This is badly made, insensitive, violence porn just for the sake of it, where it's overloaded with excessive gore just to hide how bad the movie is. It feels like the creator just has some deranged fetish or something, and it's not even fun. What the fuck are we celebrating here? If the biggest MERIT of a film is that it shows kids being murdered in a gory fashion, I don't know what brand of "real masculinity" that is. Yeah, they fulfilled the "promise" of being the "most violent." For that, my only response is a big, fat, "Ayinu"?

This movie also has the laziest obligatory sequel-bait post-credits scene that I've seen this year.

Half a star because Letterboxd doesn't allow a proper 0 rating or minus ratings. 😭

Name: Carry-On
Review: After a wobbly exposition-heavy initial setup, this movie just takes off once it gets to the main incident. It's all familiar old-school single-location thriller stuff, but done very well, and it's very gripping. Taron Egerton's very rootable protagonist is put in a situation where he's almost entirely helpless, and it obviously kept me on my toes. Jason Bateman was very effective as the bad guy as well. Moving forward, there are plot holes and logical issues, and a weird highway action scene where the movie momentarily becomes Fast and Furious, but I didn't really mind the flaws because this movie was just so fun and thrilling.

Name: Mufasa: The Lion King
Review:
Looks lifelike, felt lifeless. 

Mufasa has solid narrative beats for a great Lion King follow-up, but the writing just doesn't flesh them out properly at all. Scar and Mufasa being a cute found family of brothers, eventually leading up to one murdering the other, was ripe for all kinds of powerful storytelling, but here, everything is so undercooked narratively.

Then there's the photorealistic animation, which looks gorgeous and is a sight to behold, and this time they do ditch absolute photorealism to make the animals emote a bit more, but it's still not enough. While watching the first photorealistic Lion King, for someone like me who had seen the original, the gaps made by the emotionless animals were filled in by my memories of the original 2D version (which is still the definitive Lion King), but here, that doesn't exist, which further causes a disconnect. It looks very pretty, but it doesn't work towards conveying a powerful emotional narrative, and the underdeveloped writing doesn't help either.

The music and the songs were pretty forgettable, and the only bits that struck were the reused themes from Zimmer's score from the original, plus the bad guy singing the "bye-bye" song was so goofy and felt like a misfire at pulling off something cheekily evil like "be prepared." Timon and Pumbaa are there to do some meta-commentary on the prequel story, a version of which was great in the 2D animated Lion King 1 1/2 movie, but here most of the jokes fall flat, and they just end up being annoying.

Anyway, the animation work is truly amazing, and the film is gorgeous to look at. Seemed like a Disney movie more than a Barry Jenkins movie, though.

Name: Singham Again
Review:
So this is a case of a movie assuming that its audience is a way lot dumber than the movie itself. This clusterfuck was written by eight people, apparently, and it does seem like random ideas and rip-offs being thrown at a wall rather than anything that resembles an actual screenplay.

It's also hilarious to see how this movie underestimates the audience so much. Let's take the Cop Universe's big female empowerment "girls get it done" woke moment, for instance. Deepika Padukone gets an intro scene beating up some goons, and she's doing the exact same thing Singham does where she steps out of a drifting car, and if an audience member doesn't remember that this is a callback to Singham, as she walks we see clips of Ajay Devgn as Singham walking in the same pose intercut with her. Now it's pretty obvious to the audience that she's the female version of Singham, and we can stop the spoonfeeding, right? Wrong. Then in the background, the chorus sings, "Lady Singham! Lady Singham!". So yeah, it's been established she's Lady Singham; now we can move on, right? Wrong! A dude then tells her she's not Singham, and she replies that she's "Lady Singham." And... It's not over. A few scenes later, Singham himself meets her and reminds her (and the audience) that she's Lady Singham. Like, can't she just be her own person? Wrong movie for that.

The rest of the movie is jingoistic right-wing propaganda and copaganda mixed with manipulative efforts to tap into Hindutva emotions with the unnecessary Ramayan parallels angle, of course. In that case too, it's so obvious that the Ramayan cutaways, "Jai Shri Ram" background score, and references were a lazy effort to invoke some emotions from the Hindu majority audience rather than putting in any kind of effort to create a solid action movie. There's a lot of PR to the BJP's "new India" and their brand of nationalism; Modiji is not referenced directly, but he's more of an omnipresent entity here than Ram ji. And of course the villain is Muslim and gets murdered by a pole with a saffron flag while "Jai Shri Ram!" is heard in the background.

This also might be the laziest Rohit Shetty production. As shitty as Sooryavanshi was, I do remember that movie having some solid action, but here even the action is shitty, and the final "Avengers" moment, with even ripped-off musical cues from Avengers, was pathetic. Even the jokes are bad, whether it's the Gen-Zingham jokes at the beginning or Simmba's efforts to become this universe's Deadpool that made me want to fire a bazooka at him. A big A-list Bollywood cast and a team of eight writers assembled together to deliver the cinematic equivalent of a cow fart.

Name: Bhairathi Ranagal
Review:
Shiva Rajkumar's performance was the only part of Mufti that I liked, but even in that movie, his character being set up as a ruthless gangster only to be revealed that he's a pookie at heart was weird. They couldn't just commit to making him a proper anti-hero.

But the prequel here begins like it'd be an interesting take on such a character. Because Ranagal's rise to power doesn't really involve a quest for power and money. After a childhood episode that establishes that Ranagal can go to extreme and violent lengths for justice, he's seen as a lawyer, fighting for the justice of working-class people. So this well-meaning lawyer is made to face a powerful corporation, and when he realizes that he can't fight them with the law, he becomes a powerful gangster. But that's the biggest problem in this movie. He just becomes a powerful gangster. We don't get to see any buildup regarding how he accumulated the power, wealth, men, and resources to be such a big deal. One day he decides to switch his lawyer costume for the Bhairathi Ranagal costume, and voila, he's just Bhairathi Ranagal from Mufti; men, money, helicopter, and all, and the corporate villain is reduced to nothing in front of him instantly. 

A rise to power story should show an actual rise to power instead of the character just instantly becoming powerful without any proper setup. So after an interesting setup where a proper buildup is given to the conflict involving Ranagal facing the corporate mine company, him just instantly becoming a larger-than-life gangster makes the movie fall flat hard. This could've been about someone with noble intentions being forced to be morally corrupt, and how he gains power through violent means and gets trapped in a cycle of violence. But no. 

Shiva Rajkumar's performance is great here too, though. They don't even make an effort to make him look like he's in his mid-30s, but that's okay; better than misfire deaging, I guess. Rukmini Vasanth is cast as an inconsequential love interest, but at least she's not a plot device to inflict violence on like in Bhagheera. She's such a great talent; yo, give her more Sapta Sagara-ish characters! The background score was cool, and that one Asuran-ish action scene towards the middle was great with Shivanna being an absolute badass. 

But yeah, promising initial buildup, and then it falls flat spectacularly.

Name: Girls Will Be Girls
Review: I love films that are melancholic in a very peaceful way. While I lack the perspective to talk about the themes of this movie, there's a lot to appreciate here. The film is very gorgeously shot, well written and acted. Also, gave me a lot to think about as it ended.

Name: Identity
Review:
Just when I believed that Henry Cavill in Justice League was going to be the only creepy-looking CGI mustache shave I'll ever see in my life, Aju Varghese in Identity happened. It was fun to spot the actual clean shave and the CGI shave; sometimes it's within the same scene.

Anyway, enough Aju Cavill lore; onto Identity, which lacks any identity. They had this really interesting angle here involving Trisha's character and the peculiar way in which she's a witness to a crime, but it's pretty much used up after the initial reveal, even though Shammi Thilakan gives us an extended lecture about the situation, with examples. The movie does this a lot, btw, just useless extended scenes of exposition, which don't mean anything. There's the initial Shammi Thilakan monologue about the main character Haran (Tovino Thomas), his unique family situation, and how he developed OCD. Does this matter much to the rest of the movie? Nope. The movie even forgets about his OCD after the initial hour or so. Tovino is playing this hyper-intelligent, socially awkward person with OCD, except that the movie isn't that consistent about him as a character, and hence he just becomes nothing more than a blank protagonist after a while. I even questioned his heightened intelligence when an extended scene during the third act in a commercial airline flight had him struggling to figure out a piece of info he could've figured out easily before he even got on the plane.

Like, I enjoy dumb movies when they embrace the dumbness or at least are fun enough to forget about the dumbness and plot holes, but this thing is dumb in a frustrating kind of way, and worse, it pretends to be smart, complex, and sophisticated when it actually isn't. The Tovino character is smart because he recites Wikipedia pages about various topics whenever an opportunity presents itself. Bro Wikipedias his way through both conversations involving crime solving and when he has to talk to a family member who just went through trauma. Trisha's character was the most unique part of this movie, but she's reduced to the background after a while. Vinay Rai was okay. There's also a lot of talented actors being wasted in trivial or underwritten roles. Aju Varghese had a mustache that the film crew definitely didn't plan for.

There's so much redundant exposition and unnecessary filler in this movie, and by the end it's trying to do too many things at the same time, a lot of which could've been cut down. Some sequences are set up just for pulling off some weak twists, and boy, are those twists stupid. But credit where it's due, there are two great action sequences in Identity. A car chase and a fight scene inside an airplane. The car chase was a surprise; there were other vehicles on the road (Malayalam movie car chases happen on empty roads most of the time). It's very eventful, the visual effects are solid, and, yk, pretty impressive. The plane fight scene too was well choreographed and well shot. And I just wished these scenes were part of a better movie. Jakes Bejoy's background score was loud and overused. There is pretty solid CGI work throughout the movie too, except when it involved Aju Varghese, his face, and his mustache. 

The production company Confident Group's chairman's confidence has to be mentioned, which is evident in their logo itself. When the movie shows the flat all the main characters are staying in, there's a text graphic that says it's "Confident Blossom Heights," though it doesn't matter if it's Asset Homes Blossom Heights either. Then the filmmakers betray his confidence by including a scene that shows that Confident Blossom Heights doesn't have proper power backup during a power outage. Greatest anime betrayals.

At one point, a character remarks how disgusting it is to use sexual assault as a part of their plan. That's a question that can also be asked of the writers of identity: Why do you need to have that here at all when this movie could've worked without that, and when are we going to stop seeing this overused trope of sexual violence towards women being used to give the men motive to play hero?

Name: Bhool Bhulaiyaa
Review:
It's a pretty respectable remake, which stays a respectable remake mainly because of the atrocities P. Vasu did towards Manichithrathazhu with his multiple remakes. But yeah, the original is still superior. And I'll be a completely annoying Malayali about it. 

While this one stays faithful to the original, it lacks the charm. It looks pretty, and perhaps too pretty. The old tharavaad and the thekkini that hasn't been opened for decades in the original actually did look abandoned and old. Here, the mansion looks too pretty, and the abandoned area looks like a well-put-together set rather than a real place. Akshay Kumar doesn't have half the rizz A10 had, and hence him recreating the same scenes but without that natural A10 cuteness makes him seem more weird and annoying. The way some scenes are altered is also weird; when KPAC Lalitha narrated Nagavalli's story at night, both the narration and the mood of the scene create this eeriness, but here the same story is recited during some public temple ritual. 

Also, instead of Johnson's iconic score from the original, we have loud, generic horror movie music; the background score for the climax exorcism sounded so funny. Ami Je Tomar is a great song, though, and the Hare Ram song and its music video don't belong anywhere in this movie here.

Name: Sonic the Hedgehog 3
Review:
They understood what worked the most in the last two movies and gave us just that. The cute CGI animals are front and center; there's more Jim Carrey, in a double act, essentially making him the human lead, while James Marsden and Tika Sumpter take a backseat in this movie.

Jeff Fowler brings in animation film sensibilities to these live-action CGI hybrid Sonic films, and it's fun. And whenever Jim Carrey is let loose to do his thing, there's all kinds of gags, meta jokes, his signature slapstick, and general Jim Carreyness for the grownups to enjoy, while the rest of the movie is generic, lighthearted kid movie stuff. Well, kid movie stuff that involves grief, vengeance, and blowing up the earth. But still with kid movie sensibilities, which grown-ups with their inner child being still alive can enjoy, hehe.

Idris Elba was my favorite voice cast member. He's appropriately silly and deadpan and adds so much personality to Knuckles. Ben Schwartz as Sonic still sounds like he's somewhere stuck between being a video game character and a movie character, but that's the goal, I guess; these movies care a lot about keeping the video game fanbase happy. Shadow just sounds like Keanu Reeves. And Tails sounds like Tails because Colleen Ann O'Shaughnessey has always voiced him. In the case of the live-action cast, it's a Jim Carrey show all the way. It's fun when the movie transitions from a kids movie to a crazy Jim Carrey comedy whenever he steps in.

The animation and visual effects look pretty, the characters are cute, the action serves its purpose, the movie is genuinely funny, and there's a good amount of formulaic fun here.

Name: Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2
Review:
The initial setup was interesting, and there was some fun, though I found Karthik Aryan to be annoying af and it didn't really feel like there was a proper romantic chemistry between Ruhaan and Reet (Kiara Advani). Then it enters generic horror comedy territory, with a constant supply of unfunny scenes. Tabu stood out though, it takes a legend to give a performance like that in a movie that doesn't really deserve it. There's a good Tabu movie buried deep inside this unfunny Karthik Aaryan horror comedy sequel with some aesthetics and music borrowed from the Manichithrathazhu remake. I did feel that the movie overused musical cues from the Hare Ram song too much, especially in that final atrocious alternate version of Ami Je Tomar. 

But still, the initial setup had me thinking that a better spiritual sequel to a Manichitrathazhu remake would've been something like a remake to Chathikkatha Chanthu (2004), where there's no actual ghost, but a ghost is still a part of the movie, and it's just about conning someone about the existence of a ghost. 

 Well, A10 and Priyan did do Geetanjali, so namukku voice illa. 😭

Name: Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3
Review:
As a stand-alone movie, this is just as bad as Bhool Bhulaiya 2, but the thing is, a lot of this movie is just recycled bits from Bhool Bhulaiya 2, so that makes it a bit worse. Karthik Aaryan is playing the same dude from the last movie. Well, kind of; he has the same name and wears the same costume and acts the same way, but it's an alternate universe where none of the stuff from the previous movie happened, and he's a con artist instead of a rich entitled brat. Which is just how Bollywood sequels work, and we just have to deal with it. Not being a rich, entitled brat did make me hate Karthik Aaryan less in this movie.

So basically we have an overlong horror comedy that is neither funny nor scary, well, except for that Jawan bit, which did make me chuckle a bit. The Pandit gang was insufferable apart from that. Tripti Dimri had nothing to do besides looking pretty; at least the Kiara Advani character had more relevance in the last one.

How much can Ami Je Tomar and Hare Ram be milked over the course of two whole movies? Not enough, says Anees Bazmee. The two songs have been overused to the extent that they'd appear in my nightmares soon. The same goes for the name Manjulika. I wish instead of Jawan, Joju George from Churuli appeared during the climax to say, Manjulikede.....Allel venda.

Bhool Bhulaiya 2 itself was an unfunny movie riding on top of references to Bhool Bhulaiya. And this is an unfunny movie riding on top of Bhool Bhulaiya 2. Not even Madhuri Dixit and Vidya Balan could save it, though I did unironically like their Ami Je Tomar duet.

This one too had some good ideas, especially towards the end, that could've been part of a better movie, but too much fluff, too much recycling, too much brainrot, too much bad CGI, and not enough fun.

Name: Kathodu Kathoram
Review:
It's an 80s Malayalam senti padam and pretty much a product of its time. So idk how to give it a "rating". Such beautiful locations though, and I love the way they do close-ups in older Malayalam movies. I don't know how to quite explain it, the closeups in almost all old malayalam movies have this distinct quality to how the actors emote. They seem very natural in closeups despite the material being so melodramatic like this movie here. 

The soundtrack is iconic though, I've been listening to these songs for years, and I'll keep listening to them. Plus, the Ikka and kid scenes were very cute. But Ikka willing to let the kid's mom get raped to get him back from the dad, wasn't 💀.

Also, the tragic ending didn't really hit me emotionally. It's too quick, and the scene also looks kinda goofy.

Name: Rekhachithram
Review:
It's a procedural crime drama that's not really focused on being a mystery movie. It's more about the police officer played by Asif Ali finding more information about a single person, literally starting from scratch and slowly forming a complete portrait of the title character Rekha, played by Anaswara Rajan.

Rekha's story is connected to the production of the real-life 1985 Malayalam film Kaathodu Kaathoram, and there's quite a bit of film history and film trivia involved here. While the movie references, connections, and trivia were my favorite parts of Rekhachitram, it's also weird when people would drop random movie trivia to the officer investigating a murder, like they're doing a mini episode of Charithram Enniloode or something. Or that's just how movie people talk, I guess. How would I know?
