The movie does feel like it could've been shorter and tighter; also, I thought the movie had ended some 20-30 minutes before the actual ending, when there was an entire flashback and a song still left. Idk if that's just me or if the film does have a third act problem. Because the movie really is about finding out about this person so that she could be connected to the crime. But it's also about connecting the crime to the individuals responsible for it. I was confused about which of these the movie prioritized. 

Asif Ali in police roles is a different beast. Whether it's his body language or the way he speaks, or even his angry outbursts, he's amazing. There's a particular scene in a washroom that's all kinds of badass. He's so good at the emotional bits, and when we have to see him being helpless and frustrated. He's the kind of actor who can give depth to a character even if the writing doesn't. Anaswara Rajan was also great, as she's the emotional core of the movie, and even with limited screen time and not a lot of depth writing-wise, she makes an impact. Zarin Shihab was another great performer in this movie. She's the next big thing in Malayalam cinema if she gets the opportunities. 

Also, yet another movie with a Sreejith Ravi casting jumpscare. Idk how the film industry gave a pass for his crimes, but dude's an uncomfortable presence on screen for me, ever since I knew about what he did. ☠️

Name: Nunakkuzhi
Review:
It's one of those light uchayoonu watches with enough laughs and fun that I didn't feel like I wasted my time watching it. Still, though, the bits with the drunk dudes played by Siddhique, Binu Pappu, and Manoj K. Jayan were the most unfunny parts of the movie (except for a surprisingly good Althaf Salim). Jeethu Joseph is not the kind of director who could extract great performances from an ensemble cast; even his thriller movies have horrendous performances from the supporting cast, even when the lead performances will be pretty good. Here too, Basil, Grace Antony, Baiju, Nikhila, and a few others were fun, but yeah, Jeethu Joseph movies with bad supporting actor performances curse still continues.

The narrative involving the multiple intersecting storylines and multiple lies leading to multiple fuck-ups had more potential. Like this could've been the 2020s equivalent of Vettam, which was what it was because of Priyadarsan more than Udayakrishna—Siby K. Thomas. The movie is still fun on the whole, though it doesn't reach its full potential.

Name: It
Review:
So recently I saw this Malayalam movie that used a graphic scene where a child's head is getting smashed with a gas canister to produce shock. IT is the first movie involving child murder that I'm watching after that. And the difference in sensibilities is so apparent.

IT is an R-rated horror movie about a monster that eats children that disguises itself as a clown mostly. While being pretty gory and graphic, IT never really directly shows the monster murdering the kids. Even the initial kill scene involving Georgie, we see the monster bite Georgie's hand. There's no gore. We don't actually see the hand being dismembered. Then we see Georgie desperately trying to crawl away; this time we do see that his hand has been bitten off. It's scary imagery, and then we see the clown pull Georgie into the drain. We don't see the aftermath, but it's not hard to guess what's going to happen to Georgie. That's minimum violence on screen with maximum impact... Well, it's still a child getting eaten by a clown.

So yeah, I remember this movie coming on the back of Stranger Things' success, so a lot of the vibes are shared, but, yk, both are inspired by 80s teen movies as well. The Losers Club was an easily rootable group of protagonists. We don't see them bonding much, especially with Mike and Ben, but still, they were cool. The initial parts of IT can seem like just a random collection of scare sequences, but I remember the TV movie being like that too (I haven't read the book). But then the story does get interesting. And Bill Skarsgård's so damn effective and creepy as the clown. So were the visual effects that showed him being all kinds of distorted, weird, and terrifying. Pennywise the clown gets more violence inflicted on him, on screen, than the violence he inflicts on the kids. When the kids do fight back, it's so satisfying.


Anyway, now onto the second one: I remember dozing off a bit the time that I saw it in the cinemas. Now for a proper watch. 

(All this because I didn't get to watch Nosferatu).

Name: Pani
Review:
Long story short, Giriyettan is an entitled, privileged asshole, and his friends are pretty much the same. There's no reason for us to like or root for this dude, even when considering him as an anti-hero. He isn't even doing much in the film except driving expensive cars around Thrissur. But sadly, he's not Ryan Gosling from Drive either. So of course Joju George doesn't put much effort into fleshing out the lead character that he himself is playing. So, this being a revenge plot, the next step is to make the villains be as despicable as possible. But the villains here are two underprivileged, small-time criminals. The protagonist and his friends are a group of privileged criminals. So how to make us hate the villains instantly and root for the privileged assholes? Cue the insensitive portrayal of sexual assault.

So yeah, Pani is yet another movie where sexual violence towards women is used merely as a plot device and an excuse for manipulating the audience into feeling that the villains deserve all the extreme forms of violence that could be inflicted on them. Which is really cheap and lazy, tbh. Because apart from giving the protagonist this "motivation," the survivor doesn't even matter to the movie. She fades into the background after this assault scene. The movie is just about the men afterwards, with a few tokenism moments thrown in for claps. Like, even during the aftermath of the assault, the theme music kicks in to our protagonist's angry face to convey that he's in beast mode; it's about him, not her.

The opening of this movie showed some promise, though. The whole Thrissur round opening sequence had some great cinematography; a lot of it had been shot at the actual place as far as I could see, and it was a great way to introduce us to the setting and the characters. As bad as the movie is, it captured Thrissur really well in this opening. But the movie just derails afterwards. It's just one lazy decision after another. Like, if both the villains and Giri had been written better, this could've been a great gangster revenge drama that didn't even need the unnecessary and insensitive sexual assault angle. There was a class and privilege angle that could've been explored here, but it's all gone to waste.

There are a handful of moments where this film actually showed promise, but, yk, clusterfuck on the whole. When someone very close to Giriyettan is attacked and he gets in his car and drives for the nth time in a row, I actually laughed. Yes, Joju George is a big man, and the puny villains are nothing to him physically, but the ending just felt very meh, like some violent fantasy was being portrayed on screen or something. Maybe this ending was written first, and then showing an insensitively shot scene where the villains rape a woman was the way to justify the violence towards them and make the audience cheer to it. Fuck this movie.

Name: It Chapter Two
Review:
While there are some creative scares, some great use of visual effects, and a great cast, it lacks the charm of the first one. Not just because of the main characters growing up. This could've been more fun even without the 80s teen movie vibe the first one had. Because there were moments of fun banter and chemistry between the adult losers club. Plus, the casting was perfect. The second act was just tiny jumpscare episodes as the losers club splits up to look for their totems. I didn't even properly understand how the totem thing worked. Then there's the ending stretch, which was pretty great, tbh, except for the part where they bully the monster to defeat. It just seemed dumb, pun intended. The ending, the totems, everything could've worked if the movie maybe focused more on the lore and worldbuilding instead of scares.

The first act of It: Chapter 2 is indeed pretty plotty compared to the first one. But afterwards the movie becomes all about the scares. Chapter 1 was simple enough, and the ending was simple enough to not seem confusing like this one. This opinion is from someone who has not read the book, btw.

Bill Skarsgård was great as always. Especially that scene without his makeup. Chilling.

Name: Rifle Club
Review:
Sexy padam on the rewatch as well. 

The characters, the quirky dialogue and the banter are sooo 😙🤌

Rex Vijayan's score is soooo 😙🤌

Badass Padam. Badass club. Several satisfying high moments. And they actually got the job done in protecting their family and loved ones from the villains. 

Fuck Marco. This should've been the bigger hit.

Name: Pravinkoodu Shappu
Review:
Pravinkood Shaap was a delicious murder mystery to experience. Firstly, the way it's structured is so unique, and the way it's been edited is magnificent. We have the crime, the night of the crime, the events that led to the crime, and the investigation and witness statements related to the crime. The initial half of Pravinkoodu Shaap has a crazy non-linear structure that shows all of these together in parallel. But whether it's the filmmaking, the writing, or the editing, it's very precise with the way the narrative unfolds and the way information is revealed to the audience. There's no confusion in the structure; it felt like the writer-director, Sreeraj Sreenivasan, had a proper unique vision in mind.

Basil Joseph plays Santhosh, a wannabe Sherlock Holmes cop, who thinks he's better than other police officers and tries to flaunt that he's better than the others. The character is a subversion of the lead investigating officers in police procedural movies on so many levels, and I just loved how the movie even kinda switches to being a parody of police procedural dramas in scenes involving him. Then there's Chemban Vinod Jose as Suni, Soubin Shahir as Kannan and Chandini Sreedharan as Merinda in the main cast. But I'm unable to talk about all the characters and performances without spoiling the plot. But everyone gets their moments, even the supporting cast, and there's a lot of fun, memorable moments in this movie. The film also has a darkly humorous tone throughout. There's constant banter, one-liners, and jokes, and I liked this tone they were going for here. It's not about all the jokes being laugh-out-loud funny; it's more about the vibes. Hehe. Vishnu Vijay's score was also fun, especially the very sarcastic theme song given to the police. 

Also, there's some brilliantly staged sequences here, and I cannot emphasise more on how gorgeously shot this movie is, Shyju Khalid's cinematography shines along with Shafique Mohamed Ali's editing. There's a great oner fight scene, two great scenes involving two-wheelers, and the entire section involving the fire at the end. The stunt work and visual effects were pretty impressive. The production design was also great, and I loved the way the film set up the space and atmosphere that the story takes place in. The titular Shaap, the surrounding area, and the houses nearby, the space is well established, and even with the non-linear structure, it never felt jarring or confusing. The mystery unfolded with a purpose. Yes, it does get a bit exposition-heavy at a point, but I didn't really mind.

Anyway, this was a very satisfying murder mystery. Very unique, very cool. I'd recommend.

(I don't know why they darken a light skinned person instead of just casting a dark skinned actor in these movies though).

Name: Notting Hill
Review: I wished to grow up to be Hugh Grant from Notting Hill (1999). But I grew up to be Hugh Grant from Heretic (2024). There's a sweet spot in between the late 80s and early 2000s where so many great cheesy romcoms exist in almost all languages around the world. The cheesy era of cinema keeps me sane. Bring cheesy back. This movie is so funny and charming, and the romance just works. Both Julia Roberts and Grant are so cute. Sure, the movie is cheesy and unrealistic. But it's totally realistic that a rich movie star will fall in love with a broke bookstore owner if the broke dude is Hugh Grant. William Thacker being the supreme pookie he is, is the unrealistic bit. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Thazhvaram
Review:
I'm letting this movie sink in. This is such a great portrayal of revenge, where it's not just about violence and vengeance. The protagonist, Balan, is also grieving; he feels betrayed by the person who was once his friend, and he's always in conflict with the murderous rage within him and the fact that, in reality, he doesn't have the capacity for taking someone's life. The tension between Balan and the antagonist Raju is so well developed. The cinematography and the landscape are amazing, and the way the movie uses close-ups and wide shots is indeed so Sergio Leone coded. Johnson's background score too mixes the western sensibilities with the naadan sensibilities. Giving us sequences with Mexican standoff-like framing, even when there are no guns involved. Balan goes to the valley purely for vengeance, but within the valley he again finds humanity. It's such a great way to treat a revenge saga. 

You can't find your average action movie heroism or badassery here; when Balan slowly walks towards Raju as Raju throws bombs at him, he doesn't flinch, because Balan has got nothing to lose at this point. That end shot with the beedi and the walk is objectively badass, but then as Balan walks away, Balan is still shattered; his grief is still within him. Would he find happiness beyond the valley? I don't know.

MT and Bharathan were two legends being legendary here. Plus A10, as Balan was so brilliant. He added so many layers and so much emotional depth to the character.

Name: Nosferatu
Review:
It's so refreshing when an artist makes an adaptation their own while also paying homage to it. This film is a modern remake of the original silent film of the same name, and at the same time, it adapts extra elements from Bram Stoker's Dracula that were not in the original, and Robert Eggers makes some changes and additions of his own to the vampire lore as a whole. The thing is, this didn't feel like a rehash or a tired retread of a very familiar story that has been adapted on screen for decades. Nosferatu by Robert Eggers has all his signature flair in doing horror and his mastery at maintaining a dark and dreadful atmosphere.

The performance that impressed me the most here is from Nicholas Hoult. This movie takes its time till we see the titular monster, AKA Count Orlok, on screen. And even when he does appear, we don't get a good look at him for a significant amount of time. The film follows a less-is-more approach for Orlok. He's not shot like the other characters in the movie; just like in the original film, the goal here is to make him seem like this inhumane thing, rather than a person. The way he moves, the way he takes those heavy breaths, the way he speaks, nothing about him remotely even seems human. Bill Skarsgård's performance here is more about being this embodiment of evil, this presence that's feeding off of misery. It's more about how Orlok affects the other human characters than Orlok himself. So Skarsgård really only gets a handful of moments to give a full performance on screen; otherwise, he's more of an evil presence in the shadows. Especially in those earlier scenes with him and Hoult's Thomas Hutter, where more than Skarsgård's very effectively scary Count (I didn't feel that the mustache was goofy, btw), Hoult's reactions of sheer terror made the scenes more effective. Hoult is incredibly talented in portraying pure fear, like his soul just left his body, and this film doesn't wait around for Thomas to realize how terrifying Orlok is; he pretty much realizes it in minutes. I also loved the way Orlok is treated almost like a disease in the film. 

So many iconic moments from the silent film are recreated, but everything's been given the Robert Eggers treatment. Also, the scene where Orlok walks around town by carrying his coffin was so goofy in the original, so I'm glad this darker take had that omitted. That doesn't mean this movie doesn't have some comedic flair. It surprisingly does. The intentional comedy comes from Willem Dafoe as Professor Von Franz, while the unintentional comedy comes from Aaron Taylor-Johnson as Mr. Harding. Dafoe was a delight to watch on screen, as he hammed it up just the way the movie wanted him to. While Aaron Taylor-Johnson just seemed goofy and over-the-top in scenes where I don't think he should've been. Because I don't think his monologue after suffering from a horrible tragedy should've made me chuckle a bit.

Then there's Lily-Rose Depp's Ellen Hutter as the true protagonist of the film. There's a scene where Ellen gets possessed, where her performance is so brilliant, I don't even think there was much VFX or film trickery involved there; it was just mostly her. Eggers' Nosferatu has Orlok being a presence that had been abusing Ellen for years. There's a sexual abuse analogy here that wasn't really explored in the original film or in the other Dracula adaptations I've seen, especially Francis Ford Coppola's one, which had an entirely different take where Mina is the reincarnation of Dracula's lover, and Dracula is truly in love with her, and Mina is kinda into him and goes on dates with him. That's not the case here at all; whatever Ellen and Orlok had was messed up, and he definitely became a malign presence to her. Though this film has the exact same ending as the original, this extra layer makes it even more tragic.

Anyway, Nosferatu is a brilliant work of art from a director with great command over horror. The cinematography, production design, makeup, music, and visual effects are all top tier. Most of the frames in this movie are ART, including that closing shot with Willem Dafoe. The film is also very creative about the way violence is portrayed. 

Aaron Taylor-Johnson kinda making me chuckle after a very dark and tragic scene is the only reason I'm not rating this a 5.

Name: Dominic and the Ladies' Purse
Review:
I'm so disappointed in Dominic and the Ladies Purse because there was potential here for this to be a great detective comedy, because Ikka as CI. Dominic is a fun enough character who's not just another Sethuramaiyer. There's a lot of interesting quirks to Dominic, like how he's semi-incompetent at what he does, how he's almost lazy, though he's played by a big star, he doesn't really win every fight he's in, he isn't exactly completely heroic, and the various quirky one-liners and silly character beats. But the thing is, Dominic as a character isn't that consistent either, and as for the "and the ladies purse" part of the movie, the case and the investigation just end up falling flat, with a lot of flat and unnecessary scenes and an end reveal and climax that's laughably bad. 

I won't get into much detail here; this did have a vibe that could've worked for a better movie; Ikka being cute and quirky was the only saving grace, but he just looked so slow and stiff in the action scenes (Turbo and Kannur Squad at least covered up his physical limitations in some ways). Sushmitha Bhat was great too; the rest of the cast? Meh. The film would've been a lot better if it leaned more into being a comedy and took itself less seriously (parts of it do, parts of it don't). 

By the end, I was disappointed enough to say, "Fuck this movie". 

One star for Dominic and the wasted potential, one star for Ikka.

Name: The Apartment
Review:
It's so wholesome and brilliant, movie-wise.

The themes and the nuances of relationships and being stuck under the control of a manipulator are still golden decades later, relevancy-wise.

The portrayal of corporate culture and manipulative, gaslighting corporate men was also pretty surprising in a movie from that era, with the protagonist, C. C. Baxter, being the only pookie among the men over there, who just reluctantly becomes a pawn for these powerful men.

So it's so easy to root for both Baxter and Miss Kubelik, with both Jack Lemmon and Shirley MacLaine being so great, cuteness-wise.

Billy Wilder is amazing, legend-wise.

Name: Paprika
Review:
It's such a brilliant, gorgeous, and innovative movie. Also, some of the innovations here are stuff I thought were innovative in Inception, so Satoshi Kon was the original dream master after all. The music, the art, the crazy imagery, and the dream sequences were all so trippy and amazing. There's crazy stuff here that could never be translated to live action.

Just that, every time the film impressed me and pulled me in, the unnecessary fat-shaming pulled me out. Though there's a wholesome twist at the end and all, the fat-shaming was not worth that twist. Which is why this is not a 5/5 for me. Because this is such a great work of art in my eyes otherwise.

Is this why almost every anime character is skinny or jacked? Chubby people or people with an eating disorder won't probably survive most animes.

The greatest trick Christopher Nolan ever pulled was convincing the world that Inception was original. 😭

Name: Love Actually
Review: Love Actually is not charmingly cheesy like a Notting Hill. There's a considerable amount of bad cringe here, and some of the plotlines are just plain stupid. But still, it had enough wholesome cheesiness and smiles to distract me. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Ponman
Review:
It's unfair to put Ponman in the "male ego clash" category of films, because yeah, some of those elements are there, and the film does mostly revolve around the men, but there's so much more here. Ponman is centered around the institution of patriarchal arranged marriages and the very transactional nature of them, specifically involving dowry in the form of gold jewelry that the bride has to wear for the wedding. Ponman is set around one such wedding, or a "transaction" tbh, but instead of putting the focus on just the families involved, our title character, the titular Pon (Gold) Man, is an employee for a jewelry store who arranges gold for weddings. This character, Ajesh, played to perfection by Basil Joseph, is the heart and soul of this film.

Ajesh is a "protect this man at all costs!" kind of protagonist. He's just a working class man doing his job, and he's not driven by any ego or masculine rage, just by his helplessness and desperation. What Ajesh has is unlimited confidence, but it's not coming from an arrogant or cocky place. He's not even a physically intimidating person, compared to Mariano, the character played by Sajin Gopu. And yet, Ajesh is on a mission, and it's so easy to root for him, and he's also very empathetic. He has all these interesting personality quirks, including the line "Ajesh aada Ajesh!" that add so much flavor to him. Basil plays the part with so much earnestness, both in the parts where we're laughing at Ajesh and where we're so in sync with what he's going through. Then there's Sajin Gopu's Mariano, who's so much more than just a one-dimensional villainous brute. Mariano too is a victim of patriarchy and the whole system involving transactional marriages. But not more than Steffy, played by Lijomol, who gets married to someone she doesn't know, and then everyone cares more about the ceremony and the gold than her life anyway.

Usually similar stories sideline the women, but even though Ponman mostly follows the men, Steffy's POV is well established in the scenes that she has. She's not merely a plot device to set up the men's conflict, and Lijomol plays the character really well. Steffy's marriage is supposed to be about her own life, but the institution she's stuck in is all about the transactional aspects of it and about the whole face value of "marrying her off" before she's too old. She doesn't even know Mariano; she doesn't know if he's a compatible partner; she's agreed to the wedding just because it's what her mother wants, and all everyone else cares about is the gold she'd be wearing.

The film doesn't wait around to set up its conflicts; the inciting incident is right at the beginning, where Bruno (Anand Manmadhan), Steffy's brother, sets up the conflict that eventually leads to Ajesh being stuck in turmoil. The few interactions that Steffy and Ajesh had and the soft chemistry in them were wholesome. Yes, there are a handful of moments of cringe, but a lot of this movie has some great drama that develops and builds up really well, with just the right amount of comedy and quirk in between. Even "Ajesh aada Ajesh!" has a payoff. The way the conflict is set up is fun, and with the way Ajesh is played by Basil and the way he's established, we know this is not going to end with Ajesh heroically beating up everyone and walking in slow-mo, so that makes it more interesting too.

The film is so rooted in the region that it's set in and within working-class people, and the production design, by the director Jotish Shankar himself, was great. Though the transactional arranged marriages and dowry situation have been covered in a lot of movies, Ponman does offer enough of a fresh perspective that moves away from the clichés just enough and highlights an issue and a "culture" that pretty much still exist in one form or another, across families in all parts of the society.

Basil Joseph is a star who doesn't have to call himself a superstar. 🌟

Name: About a Boy
Review: Hugh Grant in the cheesy era could play the biggest asshole in England, and he'd still seem like such a gentleman. In this movie, he starts off as an asshole and then evolves into the kind of Hugh Grant that we expect from Hugh Grant anyway. The movie was a warm, wholesome, and funny little thing where a rich, shallow dude who doesn't even have to work for a living pretends to be a single dad to hook up with women, and that leads to him actually being a reluctant father figure for a kid. Well, the kid ends up helping the dude grow up too. There's some cool music. Grant and little Nicholas Hoult were delightful, Toni Collette was cool, and Rachel Weisz was a goddess in human form, and this was a nice little found family movie. An adult Nicholas Hoult tried the same thing with Count Orlok, and it didn't go the way he planned. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: The Wizard of Oz
Review:
It's so wonderful and delightful, full of childlike innocence. It's the kind of film that requires an adult to switch off the adult brain to enjoy. And I did. The musical numbers were so wholesome. The sets, costumes, makeup, everything aged so well. 

That monochrome to color transition was the greatest thing ever.

Name: Wicked
Review:
One thing that really bothered me in Wicked is the colors and the lighting. Because I watched this right after watching the technicolor magic in the 1939 Wizard of Oz, and Wicked just looks less magical in comparison and more like generic post-Marvel Hollywood. This needed to look like how La La Land looked. Despite that, the musical sequences were very well made and choreographed, and the costumes and production design looked great. The movie was appropriate amounts of goofy and silly, with enough character work and drama being set up.

Cynthia Ervio was a great lead, and I was rooting for her from the very beginning, so I so wish this doesn't actually end the way the Wicked Witch's arc ends in Wizard of Oz (I'm not going to read the plot of the source material). Ariana Grande as G(a)linda was annoying af, but that's just the way the character has been written; her performance was pretty good otherwise. She's just made to play her as the annoying rich mean girl character. The few moments of warmth between Elpheba and Galinda were wholesome, but overall, Galinda just doesn't come off as a genuine friend. Jonathan Bailey was great as the love interest too, in a very predictable love triangle situation. The initial parts of this movie are very generic high school movie coded, though the musical numbers were fun. It really picked up towards the end, as they go to the Emerald City. Then the way it eventually leads to Elpheba becoming the wicked witch was really well done. With some great performances from Ervio, Grande, and Jeff Goldblum as Oz.

Now I'm thinking I should've watched this right before the second part's release.

Name: Vidaamuyarchi
Review:
I don't have the opinion that big movie stars should only play larger-than-life characters. There's a really bad trend of Instagram reel movies right now, where basically most "mass" movies are starting to look like the same collection of fan edit reels on Instagram. So big actors at least attempting to do genre films is a step forward rather than backward. The problem with Vidaamuyarchi then is not the fact that Ajith Kumar sheds the star persona and doesn't have many over-the-top moments in the film or even slow-motion poses that's meant to make the crowd go crazy; the problem with Vidaamuyarchi is just that it's not a very effective genre film. I think adding in more fan service would've made this movie worse, so that's one of the few good things about Vidaamuyarchi.

I haven't seen the original Breakdown (1997), but the plot itself does have the potential for a good thriller (which I'm assuming the original was, for it to get remade). The movie does require Ajith to shed the star persona and seem human. Because him being beaten down and helpless is very important to the eventual payoff. But the thing is, when it reaches the point where this person is pushed to a corner and has no choice but to fight back, though the buildup was great, he just starts fighting like a trained badass rather than an ordinary person who was pushed to fight back. Like, as much as this movie grounds the character, he does get Thalafied towards the end, not to the extent of a Siva film, but yeah. Basically makes the movie neither fully a genre film nor a fan service film. It lies somewhere in the middle.

Then there's all these weird decisions in the film. Firstly, Anirudh scores the whole thing like a star film rather than a genre film. Then, there's the setting of the movie. When Lokesh did Kaithi, he adapted 80s and 90s Hollywood action movie elements and rooted them in a very Tamil aesthetic. Here the movie has been set outside India so that they can adapt a Hollywood movie without making any effort to adapt it to Tamil sensibilities, ig? Idk, I think setting it in India itself would've been more interesting, Vidaamuyarchi does look cool visually though. I did appreciate that there's no rich protagonist vs. poor villain thing in here, though. The villains are rich too, but we definitely didn't need to see their unnecessary backstory.

On the other hand, showing the lead couple, Arjun and Kayal's romance and eventual separation, was important to the movie. The whole nonlinear flashback structure to show their relationship was nice. Afterwards, when the wife goes missing, it's not just a race to find her; it's also their relationship being put to the test. That whole angle of a relationship drama being integrated into a thriller was nice, like, "Perseverance" is not just about Arjun as a person, but also about their relationship. But the thing is, instead of keeping us guessing about what's true and what's a lie, the film itself chooses to lie to us at times, presenting lies that characters say as big reveals. So instead of maintaining some kind of ambiguity, this only pulled down the movie and weakened the drama. The relationship drama part was pretty well done though, and in a way that doesn't enforce misogynystic stereotypes. Which is good in an era where incel movies are becoming more popular. 

Once the movie switches to action towards the third act, Anirudh gets to spam us with the theme music. That whole fight scene inside the moving car, when Arjun finally decides to fight back, was great. The rest of the movie too has some great action, though yeah, at this point, Arjun is not just a normal person stuck in an awful situation anymore, he's a full on action hero, but there are tiny tidbits in between to still ground the thing, like, despite fighting for his life, seeing someone get murdered does horrify him. He's still in real danger at times, and he does show visible fear at life-threatening situations. He's not really making anyone fly, but he does fight like he's trained for this his whole life and goes around kneecapping thugs with precision like he's the dude from Person of Interest.

Anyway, I wouldn't call Vidaamuyarchi a bad movie. I appreciate the decision for Ajith to be presented as a somewhat grounded character a lot. I liked his performance; I liked Trisha too. Arjun and Regina Cassandra as the villains, not so much. The cinematography was amazing. The action bits were great and fun, and as much as I think Anirudh's score was misplaced in a genre film, it was cool to listen to 😭. But yeah, this could've been A LOT better.

Name: Wolf Man
Review:
Sure, it's not as good as Upgrade or The Invisible Man, but this is still a pretty solid monster movie with well-executed body horror elements. The practical effects and prosthetics were really well done, and the way the werewolf transformation progresses, both internally and externally for the protagonist, was really well done. Christopher Abbot was really great. He doesn't even have dialogue for almost half of the movie, but still the pain, agony, and the inner humanity of the man slowly transforming into a monster were well portrayed. The action and cinematography were cool too. There was an especially tense sequence where they try and start up a car. I also liked the way the movie showed the werewolf transformation as a disease and an infection rather than as something supernatural. I just wished it explored the body horror side of it more, instead of being this hyper-fast survival movie set in one night. Julia Garner was also great, and there's a perspective shift that happens in the movie where the movie is locked on to Abbot's character till he starts transforming, and then Garner's character becomes our POV character, and the way that shift was visually conveyed was great. So was the way the protagonist Blake slowly started perceiving things differently.

There was some family drama being set up at the beginning, which doesn't get any payoff afterwards, unlike The Invisible Man. 

Overall, this was a pretty okay body horror monster movie.

Name: Game Changer
Review:
I have revisited some Shankar movies over the last few years. So when I see a dated, unfunny, problematic comedy scene in one of those movies, like when a character is introduced who can only walk sideways, and the joke in the introduction is that a woman mistakes him for staring at her breasts, honking sound effect included, in a Shankar movie from the 90s or even the early 2000s, I'd have maybe given that a pass that it's a product of its time, even the original Indian has those awful body-shaming jokes. But this fucking scene is a part of Game Changer, a 2025 release, which just shows that Shankar is still stuck in the past. Shankar is so out of touch that the lyrics in one of this movie's songs praise our honest, perfect protagonist who wants to help every ordinary citizen to live a great life by comparing him (positively) with Elon Musk.

Shankar's understanding of politics and India is the same as a school student writing a political essay on a class test, then and now. He has picked off random headlines and factual information and then filled it to the brim with bullshit. Movies like Indian, Sivaji, and Muthalvan at least had some pulpy fun, but here, the same thing is recycled with the same sensibilities, and it's just sad. Ram Charan's protagonist was soulless and lacked any personality, and the quirks given to him, like the anger management thing, were just goofy. He was better as the father with the speech disability in the flashback, though. But Ram Charan giving a good performance as a person with a communication disability in a political drama set in a period rural setting? Bro, that's just Rangasthalam, and it came out like 7 years ago and is the superior movie. Shankar's "politics is bad" philosophy bleeds into this flashback as well, but yeah, this was the place where there were some flashes of good filmmaking.

Kiara Advani is there in this movie only to get objectified and to be at the receiving end of jokes about ogling her body; they even integrate that shit into the song. Shankar has all these unrealistic advices to make India a better place, but he still can't write female characters well, or even consider them as human. I also think a major chunk of this movie was edited out, because when Ram gets to know about his birth parents and his biological mother, that information is not even acknowledged properly; the movie just goes into a flashback. And then the tragic ending given to his mother is also so goofy that I laughed.

Shankar has spent a lot of the budget on the songs, but just to show that he has spent a lot of the budget on the songs. It's mostly just rip-offs of other Shankar songs, with technology, big sets, and big crowds of background dancers being thrown in, because why not? They even put CGI abs on Ram Charan because the song lyrics have "six pack" on them. The action sequences are bad; the robotic camera is overused to the point that I thought it might've hit Ram Charan's face. There are occasional flashes of Shankar's grandiosity here, like that bit involving the JCBs. SJ Suriyah is made to do the screaming psychopath preset, without any interesting quirks or scenes like Saripodhaa Sanivaaram had, and Jayaram continues the trend of Malayalam actors being cast in Shankar films just to make a fool out of them.

Ram says to the villains that he's unpredictable, but Shankar's very predictable at this point. Predictable to the point of his former assistant Atlee seeming better at doing the whole grandiose masala movie thing. Thaman was also predictable. Even the ironic fun I had from watching Indian 2 was missing here.

Name: Mickey Blue Eyes
Review: Were critics too harsh on this movie? This was very fun; it was like Hugh Grant accidentally walked into a Sopranos episode. The two worlds don't fit together at all, and that was the best part. Hugh Grant even tries to do the New York mobster accent here, and it's so hilarious. This movie made me laugh at several points; James Caan was also very funny, delightfully hamming it up. It's so silly, cheesy and weird, I had a good time. Dumb, but the good kind of dumb. Perfect weekend light-watch. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Better Man
Review:
I'm giving this movie 5 stars without any hesitation, because apart from being such a towering achievement on a technical and visual effects level, it's also a pretty solid musician biopic film that didn't deserve to bomb at the box office at all. Way worse generic musician biopics with way less creativity, stylistic flair, and love poured into them have made a lot more money. I mean, wtf? And this is also coming from someone who also doesn't know much about Take That or Robbie Williams, apart from watching the Rock DJ music video's skin-peeling bit on the TV, giving me nightmares as a kid. So if my insignificant validation on Letterboxd means something, here it is. 

So Better Man is Robbie Williams as seen by Robbie Williams. Which also means he's a chimp. And that also means everything we're seeing is Robbie's side of things, story-wise. Whether everything is factual or not can be set aside because the whole framing device is him telling us his story himself, so it's natural that it'd have his biases. At times, I even felt like Robbie Williams' therapy journals were the source material for the screenwriters. The movie doesn't shy away from showing Robbie as a narcissistic person, or his insecurities, and his self-deprecating tendencies, which can be both destructive and cheeky (like the fact that he's a monkey in this movie). The film is more focused on Robbie's psychology than his career and covers his struggle with depression, addiction, and suicidal tendencies with a surprising amount of emotional depth. It does get dark, and the CGI monkey isn't making it any less dark.

Towards the end, there's a cheesy redemption arc, but everything before that felt like it came from his own real inner demons. So even the redemption felt like it's just how he made peace with himself. In a movie dealing with such heavy emotional themes and mental health issues, the protagonist is a CGI monkey, and they do make it work. The monkey didn't feel like a running joke or a one-note gimmick. Recently, in the Kneecap biopic, Kneecap played themselves. Here, something similar is achieved by showing us a chimp modeled after Robbie himself. It feels like we're seeing Robbie's version of himself, not the actor Jonno Davies playing Robbie. Plus, Jonno's dialogue and Robbie's narration and singing voiceover blend together so well that it never feels like two different people are doing the same character with superlatively brilliant visual effects work from Weta. This whole movie would fall apart if CGI Robbie doesn't seem like a person, but he does! And Jonno Davies is so good in those moments where we see the chimp Robbie being vulnerable. Like, even if the chimp is a gimmick, it's a brilliantly executed gimmick with some of the best visual effects artistry ever. 

This is not a straightforward biopic either; Michael Gracey has poured in a lot of style over here, there are many amazing song sequences and scene transitions (the Rock DJ oner and the Knebworth concert scene were the stuff of legends), and moments that are pretty unique to this particular movie. Plus, the movie has that distinct British sense of crass and crude humor. The cinematography and editing were very cool too. For a film with a CGI protagonist who's in every scene, a lot of it has been shot on real locations. There are also fantastical sequences that'd only work for a CGI protagonist, especially one where a big concert turns into a nightmarish dream sequence. Apart from a handful of moments where he does chimp noises and movements, chimp Robbie is a human character otherwise. But the thing is, even while covering familiar beats from a musician biopic, the movie is focused on Robbie's psychological trauma. When there's a montage about Robbie's solo career taking off, it's more about him being overwhelmed by all of it, and the whole thing is edited like an anxiety-inducing horror montage. The abovementioned concert nightmare also appears during a moment that concert biopics usually depict as triumphant.

A lot of the depictions of Robbie and his life come off as an internal and personal perspective rather than an external one, even the redemption and closure he gives himself at the end. That's actually kinda cool, and I don't care about the factual accuracy when they're completely honest about the fact that this is all coming from Robbie himself; dude is taking full accountability, and it's also easier to separate chimp Robbie from the real Robbie. Like, he's still a self-deprecating, self-aware narcissist at the end, when the camera zooms in on his monkey face and he says, "I'm the best, fuck you."

Name: Bridget Jones's Diary
Review: The good kind of cheesy with enough fun, jokes that land, a very lovable and cuteee lead played by a great Renée Zellweger, plus Hugh Grant delightfully playing an irredeemable asshole, and Colin Firth as the green flag, and both of them have the greatest fight scene in the history of cinema in this movie too. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason
Review: I don't know why this movie has atrociously bad reviews. Sure, it's not as good as the first one by a long shot, and there isn't much happening in terms of plot, and Bridget as a character does come off as a bit annoying here at times, while she was super wholesome and relatable in the first movie. And yet, Zellweger is cute, charming and funny as ever, Firth is dependable again as the nicest guy in Britain, and Grant is also great as the charming dickhead. There's yet another epic fight scene between Firth and Grant that was so much fun, and the entire movie had enough wholesome cheesiness and fun that made me smile and laugh. Can't hate it. The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon

Name: Painkili
Review:
Showing the movie's title during the third act is a unique creative decision and all, and it is a great way to confuse people who sit around waiting to take pics of movie titles, but when you show the title that later into the movie, it also kinda creates the assumption that the movie has ended, when that's not the case, right? Idk. Enough about the title sequence of Painkili; now about Painkili.

Painkili, as the title and promo materials suggest, is not a romantic comedy. It's a very silly comedy, and as a person who's into silly chaliyadi and movies being funny just for the sake of being funny, I had fun. Sajin Gopu was great as an FB cringe bro, and I hope to see more of him as a lead actor. There were many one-liners, visual gags, slapstick bits, and even song lyrics that made me laugh. I even liked Anaswara, Jisma, Abu Salim, Roshan, and the rest of the cast. The over-the-top performances and the silliness of the whole thing worked for me. Just like Aavesham, there's a moment where the silliness warps into a more uncomfortable situation too. But yeah, there are loose threads and underdeveloped character arcs writing-wise. The movie is a bit aimless, better writing could've helped a lot especially in the third act, but on the whole, it was okay. It's not like we were seeing true love on screen, the protagonist is always shown as a shallow loser, than some charming lover boy. He doesn't grow and isn't really getting some kind of redemption either. Dude is a major red flag by the third act and the lack of a full-on redemption arc was a good choice. 

Kuzhappilla.

Name: Bridget Jones's Baby
Review:
It's a slight improvement over the second one; again, it has enough cheesy wholesomeness and humor that made me smile and giggle.

To be Bridget Jones, single throughout most of her life, but whenever she's romantically involved, there are multiple handsome men fighting over her.

I'd have hated this movie for unceremoniously writing Daniel Cleaver off if I didn't already know that Hugh Grant is back as Cleaver in the fourth one.

Name: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy
Review: It's got the elements of a Bridget Jones story, the two love interests, the humor, the cheesiness, the wholesomeness, and Renée Zellweger stepping into Bridget and her British accent as if she's been living as her for all these years. But this one adds something a little extra. It begins with a literal stab to the heart; instead of a lonely Bridget hilariously crying while lip-syncing to "All By Myself", we see an older Bridget struggling with grief and struggling to be a mother. It's a pretty heavy introduction compared to the other movies, but it's still done in a Bridget Jones-ish way. What follows is not just a romantic comedy where Bridget once again has a meet-cute and two good-looking potential romantic partners; this movie is also about dealing with grief and dealing with growing older. It's such heavy themes for a cheesy Bridget Jones movie, but there's a surprising amount of emotional depth here, and a heartfelt exploration of middle age. And it's not just for Bridget herself either. Daniel Cleaver is back, and Hugh Grant finally gets to play Cleaver as a green flag. Well, kinda; he's still the flirty Daniel Cleaver, but in a cuter way. Daniel Cleaver only gets a few scenes here, but even his own lack of any meaningful connections in his middle age is explored really well, and Grant is a joy to watch too. It's got the cheesy wholesomeness expected from a Bridget Jones movie for sure, but it also unexpectedly hit me with the emotional weight of the whole thing; Bridget Jones feels much more like a real person by the end. Very touching. Watching all four Bridget Jones movies together over one weekend felt like watching something like Boyhood. It's the same person over 20 something years, growing and evolving, getting her happy ending at the end of each movie, and then life having other plans for her. I'm so glad my The Great Hugh Grant Cheesathon coincided with this movie's release.

Name: Captain America: Brave New World
Review:
It's got all the makings of a corporate product that was put together with multiple rewrites, studio notes, reshoots and all. Unlike a Captain America: The Winter Soldier, it never felt like a coherent or thrilling movie. There are attempts made to not look like generic superhero slop, but by the third act, that's exactly what this is.

Anthony Mackie and Harrison Ford were still great though, all things considered. And Mackie's Captain deserved a way better movie with way better action.

As an Indian, the scariest villain in this movie—and possibly the entire MCU—was the Narendra Modi lookalike Indian Prime Minister. Do not let him exist in the MCU too Kevin!! 😭

Name: Companion
Review: There's a 30-minute buildup until the big reveal about the protagonist Iris (with some very obvious foreshadowing). Now the promo material and even the poster for this movie make it pretty obvious who she is. But still, if there's anyone who doesn't know and wants to see the movie completely fresh, stop reading right here, the movie is awesome, go and watch it... . . . . . . Because yeah, she's a robot. There's this bollywood movie called Teri Baaton Mein Aisa Uljha Jiya which made me feel very icky in the way it portrayed a human - robot relationship. The robot woman had zero autonomy in the movie; she was completely in control of the man who had admin access. She doesn't even understand the concept of consent, and he's basically in "love" with her because she's hot and obeys anything he says with no hesitation. Now this was supposed to be a colorful Bollywood movie with dance numbers and stuff where we're supposed to sympathize with the male protagonist, though to me, the entire scenario seemed fucked up, and I thought about how that movie would've been if it actually acknowledged the red flags in that whole dynamic, and Companion is that movie. Sophie Thatcher is amazing as Iris; her character is pretty similar to Dolores (and in some parts Maeve) from HBO's Westworld, and she performs really well as a robot protagonist who's so easy to root for because the human cast is almost uniformly awful people, led by a dependable Jack Quaid. Quaid can play both the green flag and the red flag disguised as a green flag with ease, and here he's the latter. Companion is surprisingly very funny too. The dark humor pops up at unexpected places and was well executed. Lukas Gage was great in this movie too, but I won't give too much away about his character. The music was nice, and I liked the cinematography and the overall visual choices; even the futuristic stuff is done minimally, and it works. There are many memorable scenes, like the one where Iris speaks German. The movie is also very dependent on Sophie Thatcher to carry it with her performance, and she does it so well, true star. Companion isn't entirely original; everything from Westworld to Ex Machina was reminded to me, but yet, it is a great take on a robot-human dynamic and the whole philosophy of "Do we get to decide what's a thing and what's a person?". Now it might hit different in the present era where AI is no longer a sci-fi concept, but that's the point, isn't it? If we develop these things to the point where they're not that indistinguishable from a human and can think and feel, can they be considered a person? Then do we have the right to enslave them? Even Blade Runner and Spielberg's Artificial Intelligence put up the same question, even before ChatGPT or Siri existed. But yeah, Companion asks the same philosophical questions, and then combines them with a toxic and manipulative romantic relationship dynamic, which is exactly what I wanted the above mentioned Hindi movie to be. Also, this movie was very tightly paced, thrilling, and entertaining. Very fun.

Name: Officer on Duty
Review:
Well, firstly, fuck this movie. Not only does it have insensitive portrayals of sexual assault that make it all about the men, with no empathy for the victims, it also goes out of its way to say "police ammaavanmar paavaaa" despite the police dudes in the movie, including the protagonist, being absolute vile pieces of shit. This is the kind of movie where the majority of the female characters are sexually assaulted to be plot devices. 

Even the introduction scene of the protagonist has him being abusive beyond redemption. But the thing about this movie is, there's not even an attempt being made to give him a proper redemption arc. We're just supposed to feel sorry for him and root for him because the villains are worse. The movie conveniently forgets about how cold, abusive, and psychotic the protagonist is once the villains are introduced. The villains themselves are an unintentionally funny bunch. Like, they're written in a way that I don't think the actors could've saved those characters. Because this is a pure boomer police-ammavan POV of young people, and the actors who play the villains are stuck doing the randomest shit. All these characters do is take drugs in shady places and then commit murder. They have no other life in between. All of their scenes are written and performed so badly. But I wouldn't blame the actors too much because at the end of the day, they have to follow the boomer writing and direction. 

I wouldn't call this an entirely Pazhanjan padam technically, though it is Pazhanjan af writing-wise; it's like Chinthamani Kolacase sensibilities or worse. The lighting and cinematography are so good at times, except when the villain gang is involved, and they're lit in shades of red to seem sinister; it's hilarious. There are two scenes that I really liked, one where the protagonist has a mental breakdown, and the other was a pretty well-done fight scene inside a mortuary. 

But I'm putting the lowest possible rating here because the writing of this movie is colossally bad. You don't introduce a protagonist like THAT to make it a "paavam naayakan, paavam police" movie. And just like in Joju George's Pani, it felt like the insensitive sexual assault (that too of minors in this movie's case) was a lazy writing choice for enough shock value to make the villains worse than the psychotic protagonist. And the balancing with the villains' motives just makes it worse and even more insensitive. The protagonist in this movie doesn't deserve any forgiveness, and yet, he's the one receiving an apology by the end. The movie is also filled with so much unintentional comedy. I've never laughed like this at someone doing pushups or someone being poisoned to death. There's dumb and lazy writing all over this movie. 

Stop writing movies like this. 

Kunchacko Boban seemed like the better actor because most of the supporting cast was so bad, especially the villains. 

And lastly, fuck this movie.

Name: Daaku Maharaaj
Review:
Urvashi Rautela's inclusion in this movie is so random. She's playing a sub-inspector guarding this family who's under attack from criminals. When our protagonist, played by Balayya, enters the family property to work as their driver, she's doing yoga inside; the camera pervs over her body, and then she starts crushing on Balayya. Then the bad guys attack, Balayya murders them with precision, and this sub-inspector accompanying him, instead of feeling sus, fantasizes about dancing with him while getting spanked by him. And then, there's a home invasion scene where she's hit in the head but survives. And then, she has disappeared from the movie and is not even mentioned. As bad as Urvashi Rautela's acting is, not even good acting could save this terribly written character who's just there to get objectified. The one song was very infectious, though. It's still not leaving my head.

Now about the rest of Daakku Maharaj, which, except for the parts involving Urvashi Rautela, is a completely different movie. And I won't lie, it was pretty fun. The action moments looked cool; the epic, over-the-top buildups and slow-mo stuff were badass, and Balayya was a true singam through it all. I'm not a fan of Boyapati Srinu's brand of mass masala (fuck Akhanda, I hate that shit), but the stuff Bobby Kolli has done here worked for me for the most part, like even the funny one-liners seemed intentional, as in a bit more self-aware than a Boyapatti movie. It's supposed to be watched with a particular mind space because that's how Balayya movies roll. You really can't expect a normal movie, even though this is supposed to be one of the tamer ones. The plot beats are all generic and familiar, with a Daakku skin put over it. Thaman was firing on all cylinders in this movie. 

Balayya movies seem to be getting progressively woke, this one too has him be a savior of the underprivileged, against rich villains. He teaches women to be badasses and all. But still, unlike Bhagavanth Kesari, this movie does have an unnecessary dance number and the Urvashi Rautela character, who's just there to get objectified. So no woke card this time.

This movie did make me unironically go Jai Balayya at times.

It was hilarious to see Balayya randomly walking in with an instant noodles packet and cooking noodles in the middle of a home invasion scene. A clear rip-off of the baby formula scene from Vikram, but it was so random.

Name: The Gorge
Review: Anya Taylor Joy is brilliant as the title character, though they misspelled the word GORGEOUS. Jokes and celebrity crushes aside, this was fun but could've been a lot better. The initial bonding between the leads was very cute; Miles Teller and Anya Taylor-Joy were very dependable leads. But once we get into the actual gorge, the film becomes a generic sci-fi mishmash, with the novelty so far wearing off. But things pick up towards the end, though. The scenes set within the gorge were ironically the weakest parts of the movie, while everything else and the central romance were pretty cool. The score was amazing, and then I checked who did the music, and I was like, "Yeah, makes sense." The CGI at times made it look more like a low-budget TV show than a movie with Oscar-caliber A-list leads. There was one moment where they'd used prosthetics, which looked pretty nice.

Name: Shōgun
Review:
This is a textbook on how historical fiction should be written and filmed. It's so rooted in the culture of the era, and the world-building is so dense and deep. The moments of violence carry such weight and meaning, and it's not hacking and slashing just for the sake of hacking and slashing. The characters are so well defined, the psychological exploration of power dynamics is so well done, and the acting is brilliant.

I wish the complexities of Indian history were also explored along similar lines, instead of most historical movies and shows being political propaganda that glorifies certain rulers or communities.

Name: The Brutalist
Review:
There's some supreme filmmaking, cinematography, music, and acting being showcased here. I was glued to the screen for the entirety of the film's pretty long runtime. Lots of brilliant use of long shots, and the entire thing looked gorgeous. The colors, the costumes, the production design—I can go on and on about how every filmmaking tool at my disposal was used brilliantly. It's worth appreciating every film that has a unique and cinematic look and feel to it nowadays. This is also so clearly a product of a unique artistic vision. 

It's about a conflict between the artist and a capitalist; it's the story of America from an era when WWII survivors were seeking refuge there. The drama is pretty intense and gripping, and the actors are amazing. As impressive as the filmmaking is, the film didn't sweep me off my feet either; I did have some issues with the writing and themes at times and that ending. But yeah, engaging stuff.

Name: A Real Pain
Review: Firstly, hats off to the title of this movie, because there's no other title that'd give justice to the themes of this warm little movie. It's all about living with pain; both Benji and David live while carrying their pain, and it's such an emotionally rewarding experience to see them bonding over their Poland trip where they discover their Jewish ancestry. It's more of a personal piece, and Jesse Eisenberg is great as a director and writer behind the scenes. Kieran Culkin is playing one of those reach-into-the-screen-and-hug kind of characters. It's hard to not like Benji even at times when he's annoying, and I feel David so much when he says that he's envious of Benji's charm and ability to just light up a room and connect with people instantly. The Chopin piano pieces were well integrated into the movie, Poland looked gorgeous, both the leads were fantastic, and the movie touched me.

Name: Heart Eyes
Review:
This is a mashup of two of my favorite genres that I never thought would be in the same movie: slasher and romantic comedy, and by integrating clichés from both slashers and romcoms, it then also works like a parody of both too. This is the kind of movie with many intentionally dumb scenes, like, a romance motivation monologue by the main character's friend towards the end is just titles of popular romantic comedies strung together ( the phrase "Crazy, Stupid, Love, Actually" is actually spoken). The slasher kills are gory and over-the-top, with well-executed special effects that are meant to seem campy rather than genuinely disturbing. Also, it's so absurd to see the two main characters bond and have their meet-cute moments while there's a killer out there brutalizing people, like, in the middle of a killing spree, there's a bonding moment where they say to each other that they're having a great day, after seeing multiple people getting murdered and mutilated in front of them.

The Heart Eyes Killer as a villain doesn't really have any unique touches; the killer just seems like an amalgamation of Jason, Michael Myers, and other silent slashers, wearing a 😍 emoji on the face. But this movie is more about the cursed marriage of a slasher with a cheesy romcom, and when it works, it works great! I can't really criticize the dumb parts of it because most of them are clearly intentional for laughs, and this movie does get very funny at times, with a lot of memorable jokes ("These muscles are not meant for violence; they're for cuddling!!").

I had fun.

Name: Mickey 17
Review:
You know, when I started my working professional era, one of the things that I found absurd was how these companies refer to a person as a "resource". Like, that was my first thought, "Why am I being called a resource? I'm me! I'm a person!". But that's it, right? Only your position matters, and in most of these jobs, who you are as a person and your individual expression are really secondary or even unnecessary. And it's really set up so that you're easily expendable, like, you're made to believe during certain situations that it's life or death if you don't get something done, but it's not really, if you die, you get replaced, if you get fired, you get replaced, that's all you are, an expendable.

So enough employee whining, and now onto Mickey 17, where our main character Mickey is a literal expendable, where his bosses don't even consider him as a person. Mickey is there to die, as in, be the test monkey and easily replaceable person for tasks and tests they won't send out another employee with basic rights to do. Because Mickey can get reprinted through a human printer that uses waste as its "ink" with his memories and personality uploaded into it every time he dies. And then, the next Mickey will be put through death once again, being less valuable as a life than anyone else, because he's an expendable.

This theme of the dehumanization and exploitation of the worker in a sci-fi capitalist setting really hit home for me. It's looking at corporate exploitation the same way something like Severance looks at the same through the way it presents a fucked-up version of work-life balance. But Mickey 17, rather than sticking to Mickey and his darkly humorous existential dread, branches out into various other political themes during its two-hour runtime too. There's the Trump-coded Kenneth Marshall played by Mark Ruffalo and his partner Ylfa played by Toni Collette. They're very caricaturish fascist villains, and there's a lot of satirical scenes that poke at real-world imperialism, capitalism, classism, racism, how religion and popular media come into play to manipulate, how such leaders are willing to commit genocide without having the tiniest bit of empathy, and even the use of cute CGI creatures like in Okja is present. 

Like yeah, after the initial half, it does get a bit messy on how it tries to convey a lot of ideas at the same time, whereas other Bong Joon Ho films were laser-focused on just the one thing, like how Parasite or Snowpiercer dealt with the class system in their own unique ways. But still, I had fun watching this movie. Robert Pattinson was great as the various Mickeys; there was an innocence in him that felt like the heart of the movie, and his comedic timing was on point. I also loved Naomi Ackie as Nasha, and all the Nasha-Mickey interactions were cool. Ruffalo jumps in at the opportunity to mock Trump and appropriately hams it up; so does Toni Colette. Steven Yeun was also good. The movie is solid, acting-wise.

Mickey 17 looked solid technically. The cinematography, the editing, the visual effects, the production design, and Bong's filmmaking: it's got a unique look and feel to it, despite being so CGI-heavy, and that's so rare for a big-budget Hollywood movie these days, and I can't help but appreciate that. This is Bong Joon-Ho's own movie, and not a studio movie. There are so many well-crafted moments in this movie, but yeah, writing-wise, it does try to do too many things at the same time, and I wish it stuck to just the Mickeys.

Name: Nadaaniyan
Review:
Aww, how can I hate on this movie when it ends by showing all the principal cast and crew's photos with cute music in the background? (I still will) 

Now I enjoyed it as a cringe watch as much as I enjoy cringey Malayalam Vineeth Sreenivasan movies, but this movie does make Vineeth Sreenivasan look like Richard Linklater. 

There are three people being credited for writing this thing, and by the photos, it's a younger writer and two older writers. But this thing felt like it was written by either AI or aliens or rich people who have no idea how normal humans behave, or all of the above. There's a literal scene in the movie where the lead couple gets romance advice from an AI. So yeah. I won't go in deep about how bad this movie is because that rant is enough to fill a book. 

It's not that I couldn't relate to the rich kids being shown on screen; they just didn't feel like real people, that school didn't feel like a real school, every time the lead characters do something, everyone in school gathers around them to watch, whether it's their romance or their drama, "Go to your classes!" yo. The young cast in this movie is more convincing as fake 3D-printed humans than Robert Pattinson ever was in Mickey 17. Netflix has even put subtitles for facial expressions in this movie. The writing and filmmaking are so bad, the acting is so bad, the drama and conflicts are so dated, petty, and stupid, and the whole thing seems like pretend Gen Z rather than any representation of actual Gen Z. Like, this one has an actual young writer involved according to the credits; it didn't feel like she contributed much insight about how young people behave to this script. 

Everyone is rich in this movie, but Ibrahim Ali Khan's Arjun is not rich enough that his family owns a business empire; his parents are "just a doctor and a teacher". And yet, the other rich kids and even his romantic subscriber's mom look down upon him because he's only normal rich and not "owns a personal zoo" rich (I refuse to write a plot summary, fuck you). Anyway, when an elitist bully confronts Arjun that he's not rich enough to be the debate team captain, he then flashes his abs to convince everyone that he deserves to be the captain because money doesn't matter; abs do.

You know what, no. They show cute photos of everyone at the end; I shouldn't be so rude. So instead of saying "fuck this movie", like I always do, I'm giving this movie a six-pack out of five, which is something that both Letterboxd and I don't have.

Name: Nickel Boys
Review: It took me a while to get into this movie, not because of the first-person camera; watching multiple seasons of Peep Show had made me pretty comfortable with that, but it was about the way it was paced and structured. It takes a certain amount of time till I got to know Elwood as a person rather than just as the eyes through which I'm seeing this story unfold. Then when Turner comes, the film switches back and forth between them; their friendship also evolves, and this whole POV does have a big payoff at the end, and it was a fresh way to look at a drama like this. Also, the horrible mistreatment of Black and Hispanic students in the Nickel Academy was conveyed with zero violence portrayed on screen. It was either through sounds or by verbal descriptions, and it worked. The film was more about the way these characters found friendship and humanity even while being mistreated and dehumanized. Also loved how reflections were used to sell the POV thing, but yeah, the POV thing is clearly not accurate during a cafeteria scene when we see the same scene play out through both the protagonists (in Elwood's POV he'd be looking at Turner, while in Turner's POV of the same interaction, Elwood is clearly looking down at the food when he's talking). But on the whole, it's pretty well executed, and by the end, it serves its purpose. Great acting and filmmaking too!

Name: Narayaneente Moonnaanmakkal
Review:
This movie had its moments; there's some solid filmmaking and performances at times, and also, I love calm dramas that deal with family dynamics and drama. But by the end it felt like wasted potential, like it had its moments, but it could've been a lot more. Themes like caste, family pride, intercaste marriage, grief, and the tension between estranged siblings are all still there, but so much is left unexplored.

Then there's the matter of the cousins. The progression of that whole arc is pretty good, actually. They're both in a vulnerable state, and they're both basically strangers to each other because of how their parents were estranged, and they're bonding with each other because they have no one else there. But then the way it proceeds to a romance is what gave so many people the ick.

Still, among South Indian Hindu families, cousin marriages are common and even encouraged—specifically when the cousins are the children of a brother and a sister. In such cases, the relationship isn’t seen as problematic and is widely accepted. However, when the cousins are the children of two brothers (or sisters), the relationship is considered incestuous and taboo, which is what's shown in this movie. The whole system is weird though; even movies as recent as Saripodhaa Sanivaaram have cousins being romantically involved, but it's okay when their parents are brother and sister? Idk.

Anyway, the problem with this movie is not the fact that it depicted a situation where cousins get romantically involved; it's just that it's not really saying anything or giving it any proper payoff. It isn't even talking about the "mura" system I mentioned above.

And that's the case with everything depicted; there are flashes of good filmmaking and heart in this movie at times. And that calm atmosphere was great, the music was great, and it was great to see Joju George play a chill and sensitive man instead of a raging lunatic after a long time, but still, yeah, I didn't understand where the movie was going with everything.

Name: The Apprentice
Review:
This was like watching a supervillain origin story like The Penguin or something, just that the villain is pretty real. I also liked how everything is played so straight in this movie. There are moments of dark comedy for sure, but the movie takes itself seriously for the most part, and Donald Trump is a layered character other than a satirical clown. Another movie I could think of was the Dick Cheney biopic Vice, but even that one was more comedic in its tone, and while it too showcased Cheney as a villain, The Apprentice just seemed more evil and tragic.

Now, it's not like the lawyer Roy Cohn takes a poor, innocent boy named Donald and transforms him into a monster. Donald at the start of the movie is ambitious, racist, and pretty much a dickhead too, but he's also pretty soft and insecure, but Cohn just gives him the means and the advice and the guidance for him to be a ruthless, narcissistic monster who'd do anything to win no matter who he hurts in the way. In that process, Cohn becomes a bit too successful in his project of mentoring Donald, and by the time Cohn realizes that, it's too late.

Like I said, I liked how the movie didn't treat Donald Trump like a cartoonish caricature. As much as I love satires too, this hit differently. Sebastian Stan's performance captures his mannerisms and vibe in a way that doesn't play like a comedic impression. This is not a good person turning bad kind of character arc; it's a bad person becoming worse and more powerful, and Stan's performance captures each stage of that so well. We can even see his body language and mannerisms slowly evolving into something that resembles the present-day Donald Trump as Cohn molds him. Jeremy Strong as Roy Cohn was also a brilliant performance, and he gets to do the flawless Kendall Roy sad face towards the final act of the movie, while at the beginning he's the most confident person in every room.

The movie doesn't hold back any punches, even while depicting Trump's abusive first marriage (and even an instance of sexual assault). I also liked the recreation of 80s documentary footage aesthetics and the way it's been edited. Ali Abbasi's filmmaking is solid. The music choices were great too.

And in the end, the whole thing is pretty tragic, even when both Trump and Cohn weren't good people to begin with. It's also tragic that this man is the most powerful person in the US at the time I'm writing this opinion too, of course. Like I said, pretty evil movie, in a good way.

Name: Flow
Review:
I have only praise for Flow. The art looks gorgeous, the animation is so good, the music is beautiful, and without any dialogue, the entire movie is just visual storytelling at its finest. The virtual cinematography and the editing are also so great, and the whole thing is paced perfectly. The animal behavior is so on point, striking that balance between being realistic and cartoonish, and they're so expressive! Especially the cat, with the tiny pupil variations and the cat body language quirks, you know, it's even like how Disney animated movies with animals used to be, before they shifted to lifeless photorealism (minus the talking, of course). It's so easy to root for these animals, and especially our protagonist, the cat, and their moments of bonding and their moments of crisis are very effective. I couldn't take my eyes off the screen. The narrative and emotional beats are simple enough, and the movie is so well crafted and pulled me right into it. By the end I was all, "PROTECT THIS CAT AT ALL COSTS!". There are so many cute, wholesome, and memorable moments, and even some that are very thrilling and harrowing.

Like, this is pure artistry and cinematic vision on screen. This movie can be used as the equivalent of "TONY STARK WAS ABLE TO BUILD THIS IN A CAVE!" whenever people try to justify bad animation with a lack of budget and resources.

The emotions I felt while watching Flow were so similar to how it felt to watch WALL-E. And the fact that this is a way smaller production than WALL-E makes it even more impressive.

Name: Borderline
Review:
Hit or miss movie. Parts of it were funny and appropriately weird; parts of it were very dull. Lots of instances of the direction and staging of scenes really pulling the movie down.

Ray Nicholson was great at doing the kind of insane character that Nicholson Sr. used to love doing, though. The scenes between Samara Weaving and the French psychopath were fun; the movie needed more of that energy. The bodyguard was the most boring character, and somehow he's the protagonist of this thing, not the more interesting characters.

The movie has a really great soundtrack though. I was searching for the songs throughout.

Name: Inside Out 2
Review: I was going to write a long-ass opinion about how this movie is not as good as the first one in expanding the already slim mythos, but how all the puns and therapy speak references were fun and all. But then, it made me cry at the end, so

Name: Adolescence
Review:
Adolescence is a very important and relevant show, especially when violent tendencies and violent influences in children are a topic being discussed everywhere right now. 

Very sad, but very real. The acting is phenomenal and the show is so brilliantly made as long single shots. Must watchhh!

So many brilliant and memorable moments and nuances that I don't want to spoil here tbh, just watch and experience!

Name: Lucifer
Review:
Lucifer is an onion movie. It has a huge supporting cast of characters, lots of events happening, and lots of references to international crime syndicates and Kerala politics, and yet, it's just layers and layers of nothing while on the inside it's just a hollow masala movie that gets fun only when it doesn't take itself seriously and gives in to being a masala movie. And it's so boring whenever A10 is not on screen doing something cool, which is not much, screentime wise. 

There's like 10-15 minutes of Lucifer where A10 looks very badass, and his star aura is on full display, so I'd still appreciate Prithviraj for those handful of moments, like the Pillere Thodunnoda and the two fight scenes ("Aara Stephente Thantha?" ; "Po" still makes me laugh hard, though).

The rest of the movie is somehow worse on my rewatch. A lot of it is unnecessarily bloated, the drama is flat and boring, the filmmaking is rough, and sometimes even so badly written that it seems like a soap opera (Bobby wants to find out why Priyadarshini hates Stephen so much, so he randomly walks into her room and just happens to stumble on her diary where she has explained in detail why she hates Stephen, like, how can you write scenes like this and then give interviews about how brilliant your own writing is? 😭).
