I understand if the audience interprets Murali Gopi's shallow writing here as complex and layered, because, you know, we choose how we interpret a film, but Murali Gopi and Prithviraj pretending that their masala movie with a bad dance number (which just goes on forever till it tested my patience) at the end is some complex and layered work of art is just hilarious, I'm sorry. 

Like, I understand the appeal of Lucifer; there are parts of it that are pretty effective at cashing in on Mohanlal's star aura, even when Stephen/Ab'raam as a character is pretty shallow and uninteresting. Like, the good parts of the movie are when Prithviraj gives into commercial cinema sensibilities to present his star, and the bad part of Lucifer is almost everything else. Especially Murali Gopi's bad writing, which of course includes his shitty political takes. Like, dude, stop. Well, he didn't; we are getting two more movies, and as I'm walking into L2, I just hope his tendencies to balance or pookiefy the right wing aren't present in that movie (first partil just miss, he just gets off by saying both Congress and Communist parties are bad). Just let me enjoy A10 badassery in peace without any triggers will you?

Name: L2: Empuraan
Review:
My opinion of Lucifer was that it's an onion movie that pretends to have Layers with a capitaL L (we have an L fetish now) while it's actuaLLy shaLLow. The same goes for the sequeL Empuraan too, but with an even Lesser amount of A10 doing cooL A10 things. I'm gonna stop putting emphasis on the L's now as it's very annoying, just Like how it was in the fucking movie. 😩

Like, I get the desire to build a huge world within the film involving international crime syndicates, international espionage agencies, and then Kerala/Indian politics going on along with it. But man, the whole thing is a mess; the writing is bad, half-assed, and the film is just dragged on aimlessly for no reason. Like many scenes are stretched out just for the sake of it, and a lot of it involves unnecessary slow-mo walks, I am not kidding when I say Mohanlal's screentime would be reduced by more than half if we remove the slow-motion walks. When there's an action setpiece involving gunships, we see the gunships shooting for way too long, just because they paid a lot of money for setting the whole thing up, I guess. An explosion is shown in multiple angles, with slow motion and without slow motion, and then we see the same explosion play out with the same footage again. When Govardhan sees an old photograph of Stephen, we get a long-ass unnecessary flashback of A10 getting out of a car in slow-mo and walking to a stage in slow-mo. The editing was basically, you know, L, pun intended. So many scenes exist solely to showcase that they were filmed in specific foreign locations, even when the interactions could have easily happened through a phone call, text, or email. Why did they go through all that effort to shoot in the London Tube when it could've easily been a set—and we wouldn’t even know the difference? I get the ambition to make most of the film feel 'real' (is Nolan to blame for this?), but sometimes that effort feels unnecessary. Aren’t illusions enough? After all, some parts of this movie do use sets and CGI, so… why?

Then there's Murali Gopi's L writing. Bro brings the Sangh to the picture in this L world at last. But the thing is, just like his own Tiyaan, it felt like he tried to play it safe. He still shits on Congress and Communist parties as a whole, but when it comes to the Sangh, is he criticizing the Sangh and their communal ideology that wants to divide the nation and destroy it from within, or is he just talking about the villainous Balram? Then there's the balancing by showing Muslim terrorists who want to destroy Hindustan, but Hindutva terrorism is explained by a character as a problem with "politics" as a whole? Idk. The movie seemed anti-Sangh only on a surface level (But even that's a big deal under India's current circumstances), while it reduces the left and Congress to insignificant clowns who are terrified of the Sangh. Also, the "Indian Muslim" kind of Vinayan dialogue And the "Jai Shri Ram - Allahu Akbar" secularism from Sita Ramam aren't something that I expected to see in the complex layered L world (I totally did, and I laughed, hehe). So the politics of the movie left me confused; Murali Gopi's understanding of national and local politics is still L. I mean, it's apolitical shit that's even anti-democracy. But even this attempt at a safe and balanced take, which addresses hinduthva terrorism by referencing a real life incident like the 2002 Gujarat massacre by hinduthva terrorists, is triggering and exposing the Sanghis, so that's good, I guess. It's satisfying to see them cry tbh, a W from this movie in between the Ls.

But even if we disregard the lackluster political POV of the movie, it's so lacking as a commercial entertainer too. The main character of the movie has very less screentime and he is just walking in slow motion for most of that screen time. The only time I felt some A10 romanchams was during that fight scene at night in the forest, which was pretty cool, and what this movie needed more of. The climax fight duet felt like editing L, choreography L, and filmmaking L. Did the fight choreographer think he's doing choreography for a dance scene or what? A10 is smiling at times as he's killing goons, and for some reason he just looked cuter than sinister. Also, the costumes for A10 when he's being Khureshi-Ab'raam were so bad, with him even looking kinda uncomfortable in them. Give the man his mundu and shirt back! Manju Warrier got some cool moments in this movie, though, and she slayed. The film is filled with a big cast of shallow supporting characters just like the first one, and there's a lot of unnecessary scenes like the first one, and the movie feels even more bloated too. And emotionally it was all a big nothing. The film does the insensitively shot gruesome violence towards women plot device for shock value and "emotional impact" at the beginning (fuck this movie for being that exploitative about the portrayal of sexual violence even when it's based on a real incident), and then, the revenge payoff for that afterwards just seemed weak and meh anyway (Was the revenge supposed to be personal or political? Or both? Idk). Also, how's this a U/A certified movie with the kind of violence that's shown on screen?

Like, I admire the ambition behind the thing, but it felt like the writing and filmmaking didn't quite match that ambition. Plus, Murali Gopi should really stop acting. I mean, he's not in this movie's cast as an actor, but he should stop acting like he's written a brilliant, complex political drama and international crime drama crossover that captures Indian politics, international conspiracies like The Illuminati (ndi) and power dynamics brilliantly. It's dumb; the political takes in it are shit; it's supposed to be a hero worship movie, and if this sequel leaned into being a hero worship movie as much as its prequel or even a bit more, then it would've been at least a bit more fun. And Rajuvettan, you don't need to show the gunships shooting for all of eternity to emphasize your big setpiece.

The tail end is where Khureshi Ab'raam felt more human, but then there's a tail tail-end with a flashback glimpse that made someone audibly sigh in the theater I watched in (I felt bad for you know who, paavam).

The Malayalam subtitles for English dialogue just being Manglish were also funny (the translation for "Snipers are in position" was "സ്നൈപ്പറുകൾ പൊസിഷനിലുണ്ട്").

There's so much hilariously bad dialogue too. Could and should? Ninte thantha?

The Khureshi-Ab'raam mercenaries had way more time to chill and relax in this movie since they just had to make their dramatic entrance and stand there while their two bosses did most of the work.

Oru load L. The movie was so committed to L that it ended up being L. 

Link of the Link. La La Land. Laila O Laila.

 (Update: The fact that Sangh outrage is leading to this movie getting trimmed sucks, fuck political Censorship, freedom of expression matters, even for a movie that I loathe. It’s so disappointing that this film’s team caved to the Sangh outrage like that, and that apology from Mohanlal was so embarrassing. What an L).

Name: Veera Dheera Sooran: Part 2
Review:
It was very thrilling and engaging. The movie unfolds over a single night with a flashback that unfolds over a single day. It's very tightly packed with little to no filler stuff. It does structurally falter at times (maybe it's the editing?), and occasionally Arun Kumar is confused whether to make this a grounded thriller or a star vehicle for Vikram, the balancing of the two isn't that seamless. Vikram, Suraj, SJ Suriyah, and Dushara were great, and the acting is pretty solid on the whole. The cinematography was cool as well, and that oner towards the end with all the action and drama going on was soo impressive. Like, even though it has some elements that are supposed to massify Vikram's protagonist, he's pulled down to the ground at times too, like very rarely do we see the protagonist lose a fight in Tamil action movies. The action was gritty and cool, especially in the oner and the action scene that followed; it was only weird on a few instances, like that quick gun assembly that doesn't quite properly pull off the feel of the protagonist quickly assembling a gun and shooting it.

Anyway, fresh aanu, fun aanu, kinda like a crossover between The Departed and A History of Violence that happens over a single night. GVP's score was nice too.

Name: Dragon
Review:
Of all the recent backbencher-core movies that I've hated, like Don and Vaazha (not to be confused with Maari Selvaraj's Vaazhai), Dragon is the one that I hate the least. It's also the one that hits home the most for me, because the asshole protagonist is the same age as me and even studied the same course in college and was academically terrible. But is it a "literally me" movie for me? Fuck no. I took the traditional route of clearing all my back papers by myself and then getting an IT job that lets me write Letterboxd movie opinions for fun. But this dude doesn't even clear his papers and cons everyone into being insta-rich. More on that later.

So basically, the way the movie treats his protagonist is confusing. At times he's really shown as the pathetic dickhead that he is, but at other times the movie expects us to sympathize with him, find him likable, see him as a badass, and even cheer for him. The whole thing is leading up to a redemption arc too, and while the redemption is not terrible like in Don, it still doesn't feel like the character has earned it. But I'd be lying if I said I didn't have fun while watching this movie and that it didn't emotionally engage me. It did both in parts, but at times it just instantly made me disconnect as well. Basically any time the movie expected me to see this dude as anything other than a piece of shit, I sighed, but parts like the initial section of the second half where he's facing ridicule for his past mistakes and cringe, it was fun. Plus there's a touching monologue at the end from George Maryan that made me tear up.

Anyway, this movie's basic plot beats are pretty good, actually. But the screenplay doesn't do a good job at fleshing it out. At times it's clear what it wants to be. It's an asshole's road to redemption; it's a subversion of the trope where the irresponsible bad boy is always shown as being cool and heroic. But the character work for the protagonist doesn't know whether to show him as an anti-hero or a hero, so even before the whole redemption thing, parts of the movie were frustrating to watch and gave me major second-hand embarrassment at times. Also, bro, I think I've had enough work experience to know that that's not how IT companies operate, and that's not how life would turn out for IT employees within 4 years. I hope teens watching this movie don't get the same idea about working in IT, though it presents the college part of the situation better by putting an emphasis on how important studies are. Bro bought an Audi car and a huge house after 4 years of working in IT, and there's me paying EMI for my earbuds. He's a singam; I'm asingam. A character even jokes earlier that the protagonist should get rich over the length of a song—and then that’s exactly what happens, through IT job grinding of all things. 

I remember a friend saying that this film treats its female love interests like they're trophies, and I felt that's a pretty much accurate description after watching the movie. It even shows one of them apologizing to him and feeling guilty for doing something that she was totally justified to do. I cannot emphasize more how an absolutely unlikable protagonist Mr. Draghavan is. And then the female love interests are there to fix him or service him. Plus, with a protagonist this unlikable, I didn't really care about his love life anyway. And scenes like the one with the checklist seemed like cringey care ettaayi reels. 

Pradeep Ranganathan's performance ranges from kind of good to kind of trying too hard. Like, even when Don was a worse movie than this, Sivakarthikeyan played that character with a certain ease and charm, and that doesn't quite come to Pradeep. But he is occasionally good, like at times the film did fool me into caring about its shitty protagonist, with his performance and some clever filmmaking choices (it would then instantly pull me back to reality, though). The movie does have a great supporting cast, especially Mysskin and George Maryan. Mysskin's principal was a good subversion of how such characters are usually presented in similar movies. The two female leads are reduced to just looking pretty mostly.

Anyway, the same plotline involving an asshole having to revisit his past to correct his mistakes could've made a way better movie, even with the redemption and messaging at the end. But this movie has too many bad creative decisions and expects us to like an unlikable protagonist even before he gets his redemption. And at times, especially at the beginning stretch, there was so much cringe and scenes that caused secondhand embarrassment; you can say that the movie DRAGged ON. Hehe.

Name: My Neighbor Totoro
Review: From the onset, this film captures the innocence and the wonder of the two sisters beautifully. The art and character designs are gorgeous, of course, but so is the overall filmmaking style that designs the movie more like how live-action dramas are made than cartoons of the era. Also, all the artistic touches given to the animation and the movements, even the more subtler ones, are so brilliant. There are exaggerated character movements and poses that only work in an animated format, and with it, the entire narrative is so touching and wholesome. It's the kind of movie that makes me cry in the best possible way. We instantly bond with the girls, their love for their parents, how they find comfort and peace in the village, the forest and the creatures, and all the absurd and wacky ways the creatures operate (the fluffing catbus!!!), and how the thought of a parent not being well shakes the very core of these kids. Like it's a simple narrative, but it's an extremely well-crafted simple narrative with beautiful imagery, amazing animation, and some great music and filmmaking. It's also a very peaceful watch, there's a calmness and heart to the whole thing that I loved. I have only praise. Discovering Ghibli

Name: Howl's Moving Castle
Review: I might change my definition of what an anti-war movie is after having watched this. Because yk, the entire plot happens while a huge war is going on, but we rarely see any violence. The movie doesn't care about who wins or loses the war, and the movie couldn't be any clearer about the fact that it's against the mindless violence, it's against people being forced into committing acts of violence, it's against people in power profiting off the violence, and the best part is that it does all this while being a gorgeous children's movie with cute characters, beautiful music, and plenty of humor. The movie is about humanity, love, friendships, found family, empathy, and yk, the real important stuff in life. Of course, it also has that calmness and warmth about it that I've seen in the last two Ghibli movies that I've watched too, even when it's dealing with heavy political themes. The protagonist, Sophie, is cursed into being an old lady, but she's just doing her best to live with it. The wizard Howl just wants peace, and every time he has to use violence, he literally turns into a monster and finds it hard to be human again; the psychological metaphor is right there in our faces. There are so many beautiful and memorable moments in this movie, in terms of the art, the animation, and the narrative itself. Also, it packages the political themes into a sweet and emotional narrative perfectly so that even children could relate to the larger themes at play here to an extent. Discovering Ghibli

Name: The Monkey
Review:
Even though Longlegs was stuck somewhere between being dark and being camp, I did feel that Osgood Perkins had it in him to direct horror really well, and The Monkey also solidifies that opinion. This time there's no tonal or thematic confusion, though; the movie is pretty sure about what it wants to be. It's a campy horror comedy with pitch-black humor centered around death, and there's a lot of death.

But still, it's also pretty obvious that the source material is a short story because the movie doesn't really have enough material for a 90-minute feature. That's not to say that it's boring. The movie is consistent in delivering hilariously over-the-top and cartoonish death scenes and other forms of dark humor. Just that I felt that it had stretched out a tiny premise regardless of the whole thing being pretty fun. It also has the expected Stephen Kingness, like the characters being indifferent in their reactions to extremely gruesome deaths and how some of them even cheer it on. The deaths and gore are pretty tastefully done, striking that balance between being cartoonish while being bloody and gory, sort of like a Looney Tunes cartoon with gore. The violence and gore here is not meant to disturb but in service of the dark humor. 

There are touches of horror, though, especially in the way Perkins chooses to show the titular monkey toy (great creepy design there, BTW) and some creepy dream sequences. But yeah, it leans more heavily into the comedy than the horror. The kills, though they're freak accidents like the Final Destination movies, are sudden gags instead of having tense buildups to them. There are several deaths here that made me laugh, but yk, the movie is designed that way, so don't judge me. During one scene, they cut to the funeral photo before showing the actual death, and it was hilarious.

Theo James was great as the twins, and I thought this movie would have way more Tatiana Maslany than we got. Which was disappointing.

Anyway, this was a fun watch. I'm a sucker for dark humor, though I agree that the plotline here was more like a 40-50 minute anthology short material than feature film material.

5 stars if it had a Robbie Williams song or reference.

Name: The Naked Gun 2½: The Smell of Fear
Review:
This one too just throws in joke after joke like the first one, just that unlike the first movie, it's more misses than hits. Also, at times Leslie Nielsen plays it like he's doing a comedy, whereas in the first one, the thing that made it more hilarious was the fact that he was being dead serious with the material, if that makes any sense. There's a sense of repeating the same jokes over and over again too. 

 That's not to say it didn't make me laugh at all. It did. Nielsen is still a legend at this.

Name: Novocaine
Review:
There's an Indian action comedy movie named Mard Ko Dard Nahi Hota (which was unofficially called the "Indian Deadpool" at the time by Indian internet), which was a quirkier and more unique take on a protagonist who can't feel pain. The trailer for Novocaine immediately reminded me of that movie, but the similarities stop at the genetic disorder shared by the protagonists and being action comedy movies.

The protagonist Nathan Caine is not a trained badass or someone equipped to fight or kill people. He lives a pretty isolated life, always being scared and careful about unknowingly causing serious injury to himself or even dying without even realizing it. His only friend is the guy with whom he plays an online video game. So when this 30-year-old loner has a meet-cute situation, and then that girl gets kidnapped by bank robbers, of course he'd throw away all caution and try to save her, even if it kills him. It's not that hard to believe that someone that lonely would fall in love like this with the first real person to show him some sense of empathy.

Nate is no John McClane; he's not a badass fighting through pain. He's a non-badass who doesn't feel pain. The lack of pain is the only thing going for him in a fight, while he's outmatched in terms of skill and strength by every single opponent. So that added a fresh layer to the fight scenes. Though Nate doesn't feel pain, the hits and injuries he has to endure are pretty nasty here, and the movie does a great job of setting up how not feeling pain could be fatal to Nate, the dude's even afraid to chew food. Though the movie addresses the extent of his injuries several times, he still stays alive and functions with those more than a normal human being would, pain or no pain. Anyways, almost all fight scenes have Nate doing something nasty that harms his own body as well as the person he's fighting. All the injuries are pretty gory too; it's stylized and over-the-top gore, but still gore. So for someone like me who enjoys tastefully done gore and dark comedy, it's fun. But for someone who's not into a protagonist getting pummeled, burned, stabbed, and mutilated constantly, the movie might be a painful watch, pun intended.

Jack Quaid was the perfect leading man here. He brings in a certain innocence and vulnerability here, and it's easy to buy him as Nate. Because this is the kind of action movie where the protagonist not seeming like an action hero adds to the appeal. Amber Midthunder was also great. I was disappointed to see her as just a love interest and a damsel in distress after seeing her as a badass in Prey, but the movie makes up for that towards the end. But yeah, the romance arc was a bit rough. Ray Nicholson was a great villain as well, though his character is not that well written. He has fun playing a sadistic psychopath. Him being the villain makes this a Nepo Baby vs Nepo Baby movie was well, something that happens in Indian cinema a lot, but not that much in Hollywood. xD

There are instances of dumb writing here, but the movie worked for me on the whole. Even though it operates on an unrealistic terrain, it's fun that the movie still addresses Nate's serious injuries—the thought put into showing his medical condition during action scenes, and how that's reflected in Quaid's performance. At one point, Nate even gives someone bank robbery money for helping him, and then, he advises them to launder it, lol. Despite all the gore and violence, the movie has a very unserious tone, even having Marvel movie-ish quips during action scenes, but I enjoy that sort of thing, so issokay.

If this was a Malayalam movie, it could've been called Pain-Kili.

Name: Good Bad Ugly
Review:
Amarkalam, Dheena, Vaali, Attagasam, Billa, Varalaru, Villain, Red, Vedalam, Mankatha... Ahem… I forgot that I'm supposed to talk about Good Bad Ugly for a moment and started writing its screenplay instead.

There are different ways to do a "fan tribute" movie for a star. There's the way Karthik Subbaraj did it in Petta, which is by far my favorite, where the Rajini references and Easter eggs are there for the fans to notice and enjoy, but the movie and the character Petta/Kaali stand on their own, with or without nods to Rajinikanth's filmography attached. But Adhik Ravichandran's brainrot-coded (or Thala-rot Hehe) fan tribute does not walk that line. Here, Ajith Kumar plays AK. We do not know what AK stands for, but it probably stands for Ajith Kumar, because he's just being the star persona on screen here. We're reminded that he's Dheena and Billa right at the beginning, and then it's repeated over and over again. Dheena, Billa, Vaali, Varalaru, Attagasam… this movie cares about most movies in Ajith Kumar's filmography more than itself. Like, if you weren't familiar with Ajith's entire library of films, this movie will burn a lot of those movie titles into your brain.

Anyway, this is a surprisingly self-aware movie, or it just doesn't give a shit that it's badly made, and it does seem like whatever Adhik Ravichandran wanted was what we got. We get the full force of the reel creators'—ahem, director's—vision. Parts of it look like a parody movie too, so I did audibly laugh in at least three places, but I don't know if I was laughing with the movie or at the movie. One involved a hilarious bit involving an underworld WhatsApp group, then there was the moment which was building up to seem like it's going to reference another Tamil superstar towards the interval, and that's exactly what happens, then there's that flashback. Like, we see multiple references to AK's past and how he's the biggest and scariest badass and the literal dragon of the underworld, but when we finally get the full flashback of his rise, it's a silly parody sequence straight out of the Thamizh Padam series with some absurd cameos and references, like it's the sort of sequence that we'd expect for Agila Ulaga Super Star Siva than Thala Ajith (Again, the joke where he doesn't want to be referred to as Thala also made me chuckle). Did I mention that the actor Ajith Kumar had acted in films like Amarkalam, Dheena, Vaali, Attagasam, Billa, Varalaru, Villain, Red, Vedalam, Mankatha?

We shouldn't look for logic in a movie like this, I know, and the movie knows; that's why it's so blatant about how dumb it is. When we see photos from AK's past, they're literally screenshots from Ajith's old movies. When we see video evidence of events from this movie, it's just scenes from this movie. The core plot of this movie is Viswaasam without the paasam, involving AK and his love for his son. But the movie doesn't care about its own characters or itself. I wouldn't even say it cares about Ajith, because as fun as he is to watch here doing comedy, action, and slaying in all kinds of drip and hairstyles, the movie isn't giving him much room to perform like how something like Mankatha did; now that was an effective "fanboy sambhavam". Ajith actually looked better while behaving naturally in the BTS footage shown at the end of the movie, than in the movie itself. Adhik cares more about making references to his older films. The movie does have better fight scenes than Siva's Viswasam, Vedhalam, and all; I'll give it that. The cinematography and choreography for one of the fights even reminded me of the theater fight from Thallumaala; the way the hit sounds were synched to Ilamai Idho Idho playing in the background was also cool. Also, it was pretty fun to see Arjun Das doing this kind of silly material with that voice and he's a good dancer.

This is a very unserious movie. It doesn't want to pull us into its world and characters; it just wants to movie. At one point, Adhik himself even breaks the 5th wall (we're way beyond the 4th one) and talks to Thala himself; lines of dialogue string together Ajith movie titles like they don't even give a shit if the dialogue makes any sense in the context of the scene. Parts of the movie look worse than amateur short films where it's tough to believe this is a big-budget production with a huge star attached. There's a scene where the foreign actors playing henchmen give over-the-top reactions of frustration at something that made me laugh at how bad the acting was. They don't even make an effort to make the sets seem convincing. Like, when people say this is an Insta Reels movie, don't think that they're being sarcastic or insulting; that's just what this is. I don't know if this is a tribute or parody of Ajith Kumar's star persona and filmography, seriously. No other fan tribute movie might've repeatedly shoehorned in the movie titles from the star's filmography like this movie has. A filmography that includes Amarkalam, Dheena, Vaali, Attagasam, Billa, Varalaru, Villain, Red, Vedalam, Mankatha, and so on.

GVP's score ranged from being pretty cool to giving me Thala vedhana. The editing was constantly underestimating the audience's attention spans, making the whole movie look reel-ish. Like, even Ajith's intro sequence looks more like a mashup video or a trailer for a movie than something from an actual movie (it's so fucking awesome though 😭). KGF did irreparable damage by popularizing the trailer/mashup editing style within movies. I don't know, maybe the reason why the movie titles were constantly repeated too was because Adhik didn't trust the audience's attention spans enough to remember all those Ajith movies being referenced. Yk, Amarkalam, Dheena, Vaali, Attagasam, Billa, Varalaru, Villain, Red, Vedalam, Mankatha, and so on. Characters even say that AK is back multiple times, as if we didn't hear it the first ten times. We get reminded of AK's past constantly too. The movie also conveys a lot of the plot by just directly narrating it rather than, you know, showing it. Because the plot is secondary or even just an excuse to make this seem like a feature film, at least on a surface level.

There might be fans who find joy in seeing Ajith being presented like this with constant nods to his filmography, but I'd personally prefer something like Mankatha over this. This felt like brainrot/Thala-rot slop through and through. It's like we're being tricked into thinking it's a celebration of Ajith Kumar, when it's really just a bunch of gimmicks slapped together. At times, it even felt like the director was looking down on Ajith's fans rather than actually paying tribute. There's lots of bad dialogue, bad filmmaking, a Redin Kingsley dance that I want erased from my memory, and female characters who solely exist to confirm that Adhik bro hates women.

I had the best crowd to watch Good Bad Ugly, though; they were screaming "Kadavuley Ajithey" even through the anti-smoking ads. The crowd was so ON, so that helped to hate the whole experience a bit less. In addition to this being a reels movie, the dude sitting behind me had filmed Ajith's intro scene and was rewatching the clip on his phone in full volume over and over again while the rest of the movie was going on. He didn't care about the plot stuff; even if there was very little of it, he's just there for the vibes and the reels. Was he the target audience? So, you know, to each person their own Thala, I guess. 

I won’t lie and say I didn’t have any fun watching this movie—I did. But afterwards, it left me feeling the same way I usually do after spending time doomscrolling, if that makes any sense.

The movie does have some cool 3D animation and 2D artwork, though. But very lackluster VFX and production design otherwise.

So, in the end, what I want to say is Amarkalam, Dheena, Vaali, Attagasam, Billa, Varalaru, Villain, Red, Vedalam, Mankatha.

Name: Alappuzha Gymkhana
Review:
Khalid Rahman's Thallumala was the kind of movie you could watch for the vibes; it was not really plot-driven, and the characters kinda stayed the same people without going through a traditional character arc. Just being about the vibes was one of the reasons why I enjoyed that movie so much and have even revisited it. Alappuzha Gymkhana is also a movie I had fun watching. But unlike Thallumala, it does try to execute some drama and character development at times, and the weak writing makes such attempts fall flat, and what's left intact is, of course, the vibes. There are some great, well-directed sequences in this movie, especially the action, so Khalid Rahman as a director is still a champ who can deliver a knockout, but some of the writing choices here are so confusing. 

Contrary to what the marketing had me believe, this is more of an ensemble movie, though Jojo, played by Naslen, is our POV character, and he's in every scene in the movie if my memory is correct. Jojo as a character is... confusing. He's stuck somewhere in between being a Manavalan Wazim-like protagonist who doesn't grow much over the movie or someone who does grow and evolve. Because the movie wants to give us a sense of Jojo growing into someone better, but he doesn't at the same time. When the movie begins, he's a good-for-nothing loser who just failed his 12th exams. But when the movie ends, he's an amateur boxer with his own boxing gang, but that evolution could've been written better. We get hints of Jojo's family and some apparent financial issues there, but that doesn't get any payoff. There's Jojo's romantic kozhi escapades, where he flirts with every girl he has a crush on while he does have a girlfriend. This doesn't get any payoff either. Like, it's fine if the intention was to show that he's an immature kid who simply doesn't grow; my issue is with the fact that this movie, by the end, shows Jojo having gone through a journey that makes him a better person, but I don't think the writing made the character completely earn it. Naslen is dependable with his charm and wit, though, and there are lots of opportunities in the movie for him to flex his comedic skills, in addition to the new boxing and fitness flexes. He still has a Kodungallur slang despite his character being from Alappuzha, but maybe Jojo migrated to Alappuzha from Kodungallur or something; idk. 

The movie does have a great ensemble cast. Actors like Ganapathy, Anagha Maya Ravi, and Franco Francis are absolute badasses in their respective boxing sequences, I wish they had more to do in the movie. The boxing scenes are very well made; we feel each punch when a character is getting pummeled on the ring. The slow-mo shots are so effective in conveying the impact. The cast is pretty effective in pulling off the comedy; they have great chemistry with each other, and it's easy to like the gang. There are some kattachalis in between, but it's forgivable cringe. The cast, the quirkiness, and the direction do more towards rooting for these characters during the movie than the writing does. 

This is not your typical sports comedy either. Winning doesn't really matter here, and the movie deliberately sidelines Jojo than giving him the hero treatment, it's more about the team. Well, it was fresh to see a sports movie where the ultimate buildup was not towards some victorious triumph, because at the beginning itself, the very unserious stakes of Jojo and his friends deciding to learn boxing just to get enough grace marks for their studies and to beat up other dudes were set up. They don't all need to be underdog stories, yk, and it doesn't always have to be about winning, sometimes we just lose and we move, so I liked how sports movie tropes were subverted here, even in the way Jojo himself is presented. Despite the low stakes, some of the boxing matches are set up for us to root for the Alappuzha gang to win, and those emotional beats are well executed filmmaking-wise, because during those moments the film did emotionally engage me. All the action, including the brawl at the end, looked very cool and was well choreographed and performed. 

But again, the writing had me confused about whether the movie was going towards a character journey route or a "just for the vibes" route. At times, the entire vibe of the thing reminded me of Cobra Kai, how it makes amateur martial arts the backdrop for teen drama and silliness, and how it’s not always just about winning. But that show does give its characters a whole journey and eventually becomes about the winning rather than staying fully unserious, though. 

Vishnu Vijay's score fit the movie; the soundtrack might not be in my on-repeat playlist like the Thallumala album is, but it was okay. It fit the vibe. The movie has some really cool editing, especially during the action scenes. Very cool cinematography too. 

Anyway, this was a fun watch despite the flaws.

Name: Maranamass
Review:
This movie made me laugh a lot. Like, in the entire hall, I must've been the person who laughed the loudest, like, not just chuckles, big loud laughs. So as a dark comedy movie, I was part of the target audience for Maranamass, and I had lots of fun. The writing could've been a bit better and tighter, and it felt like the movie was a bit too long than it had to be, and that's my only complaint. 

For me, the comedy was more hits than misses; I didn't mind the jokes that didn't land when the fun was consistent. The cast performances and the visual style were apt for the movie, the cinematography and lighting were cool, and there are so many hilarious sequences involving visual gags, slapstick, and verbal humor. It's not just verbal jokes and punchlines; the director has a great eye for pulling off visual humor too, even during the one fight scene. The darkly humorous tone was also mostly very well done, with only a few instances of tonal imbalance.

There are attempts at executing some drama, which doesn't really land, but the movie quickly switches to unserious mode after being serious for a few moments. The character arcs weren't properly developed, but it didn't bother me because the movie was just tonally silly. The background score and songs fit the movie, and it was cool to find jokes in all the production design details, text, and even T-shirt designs. We were pointing at funny stuff on the screen and laughing. The pop culture and meme references felt tastefully done. I even enjoyed the Basil Joseph title card gags; I wish they hadn't put them in the trailer. Yes, the characters randomly saying words like sigma and pookie are cringe; they know, the movie knows, that's what's supposed to be funny about it! Even the one big cameo was well placed.

Anyway, it has its flaws, but how can I even pretend that I didn't like this when I laughed my ass off! 😭

"Comedy is subjective, Murray."

- Joaquin Phoenix as Tony Montana, Taxi Driver (1976)

Name: Malcolm X
Review:
The movie begins as it shows the American flag burning over the credits as a fiery Malcolm X speech is going on in the background. The flag burns up to form the letter X. It's a pretty powerful opening, and then the opening stretch of the movie with a young Malcolm Little was surprisingly unserious, with the most unserious character in the movie being played by the director Spike Lee himself. The moments involving Denzel and Spike Lee playing around and dancing are such a different thing from the rest of the movie. Malcolm's own very serious backstory involving how his family and he were victims of racial discrimination does come interspliced with this sillier section of the movie, though. 

Anyway, we get into serious territory and get locked in there only after Malcolm gets put in jail. The change this man goes through is huge as he converts to Islam, becomes a Black Nationalist and becomes an entirely different person, and it's also something internal. It might be impossible to put in film how exactly Malcolm Little becomes Malcolm X, but the movie and Denzel's amazing performance do a pretty good job at that. The movie goes through key moments in his life afterwards; we see Malcolm, his ideologies and sense of identity evolving. We see him become a voice for oppressed Black Americans and then reevaluate how he should work toward securing rights, equality, and the eradication of racism for Black people. There's a stretch of the movie that's just Malcolm giving various speeches, but yk, you can't make a Malcolm X movie without the politics and the man's ideology in it; the politics being loud and direct is a requirement here. Even the portrayal of religion here felt like it was more about faith and community. 

I did feel that the initial unserious Malcolm Little portions could've been shorter so that we could've seen more of Malcolm X, though the movie already clocks in at around 3.5 hours. But it's a great character portrait anyway. The ending stretch involving Malcolm's assassination was brilliantly done, with the sense of dread and the eventual acceptance of death being conveyed really well. Denzel was firing on all cylinders in this movie, the legend that man is. The epilogue was also very moving.

Name: Bazooka
Review:
There's so much I want to rant about this movie that I'm not even remembering every single thing properly. Anyways, by the end, as a fan of Mammootty, Bazooka left me sad, disappointed, angry, and even traumatized.

Now, recently, Good Bad Ugly was a dumb movie that embraced its dumbness and didn't even bother to seem smart even on the surface level. Bazooka, on the other hand, is an even dumber film that pretends to be smart with dumb gimmicks, making it even dumber. Deeno Dennis' version of having done "research" is showing the Google search definitions and Wikipedia intro sections of stuff. Like why the fuck would an IPS officer get a sketch of Super Mario because the criminal he's chasing uses the codename Mr. Mario? What the fuck? Game thrillerinte Andi. The stupid game references sound like they were written by someone who hasn't even played Candy Fucking Crush. Fuck you. Then there's the effort to shoehorn in social media references to seem "new gen." But said social media references include a Santhosh Varkey cameo and making Mammootty say a casteist FFC originated slur word like "kannaappi." It's bad enough to see slurs like colony and kannaappi being normalized with a lot of people being oblivious about their casteism; it's another thing to make a star like Mammootty say it while delivering a "mass" dialogue. Even the shittiest Midhun Manuel Thomas screenplay is an upgrade over this clusterfuck. This is an Ammavan screenplay masquerading as a new Gen techno-thriller. References like Peter Griffin and "shoopperaada" were relevant on mallu social media like two years ago, but the movie is even more outdated. Apparently when Ikka read this script, he's the one who suggested that Deeno Dennis himself should direct this movie instead of pitching it to another director. Ideally, Ikka should've told him to shove this script up... Ahem… Moving on.

Mammootty seemed like he was sleepwalking through the movie. Then the ending happened. And it was heartbreaking. This man has been praised by countless critics and audiences for the nuances of his voice modulation and his expertise in dealing with different dialects and how he can transform into an entirely different person using just his voice. And for the first time ever, like not even Pattanathil Bhootham has done this, for the first time ever, Mammootty's voice and mannerisms made me physically cringe. Like, wtf was that? Ikkolas Cage? Whatever it is, please never do this again. Like, till then, this was just a bad movie, but that ending stretch broke the heart of the Mammootty fan in me.

The attempts to be stylish like an Amal Neerad movie were pathetic. Like, this is the closest thing to a Pramod Pappan movie that Ikka has had to act in since Thaskaraveeran. Every time a car is shown, we get shots like it's an ad for that car. The background score is like all current mass movie BGM clichés combined. The acting is bad across the whole cast, but yk, with material like this, where even Mammootty is turning in a bad performance, only the director can be blamed for that. The things GVM has to do to clear his debt. Naming Shine Tom Chacko's character "Stonerman", though? Genius. 

There's nothing here, nothing. Letterboxd doesn't allow a 0 or negative rating, so I'm putting half. And that half is for the work that the people who did the animation and VFX for the movie have done. 

The movie made me feel the opposite of what a fan mashup movie like Good Bad Ugly would make an Ajith fan feel, like I'd prefer a reel mashup like that over whatever the fuck this is, tbh. During Mammootty's intro, there's a cool animation sequence where his face morphs into a few of his characters. Fuck this movie for doing that; you have no right to touch the man's legacy. Well, maybe just the shitty characters like the one in Shylock, because that's good company. The interval scene of Bazooka has Mammootty standing next to a burning middle finger, as one of the I's in the text "Intermission" is this middle finger. It was the movie telling me, "Fuck you." And it's totally right; fuck me for watching this.

I'll probably need a triple shot of Big B, Bheeshma Parvam, and Rajamanikyam scenes to recover from this. YOU WERE GOING THROUGH A RENAISSANCE, IKKA, WHYYY??????

This movie uses a casteist FFC reference to seem cool, while the asshole who created FFC makes money off making fun of this same movie on YouTube. Circle of myr.

Name: Kadaisi Dhum
Review:
It's a very simple idea: smoking kills pretty instantly. The execution was thrilling, the atmosphere was set really well, the tension building was on point, and I was glued to the screen. The use of lights was really cool, and the background score was great as well. They did have some limitations on how the violence is conveyed; it's a low-budget student film, but yet, it was done pretty well; that one fall was pretty effective.

Name: G20
Review:
This is the kind of movie that doesn't actually require an Oscar-winning acting powerhouse like Viola Davis in it, but she's still so committed to the character, and her performance is really great. It's one of those low-effort streamer action movies otherwise; usually it'd have people like The Rock or Chris Evans in it, but here we have an acting legend like Davis. Davis' physique here also makes her look like an action hero, and the movie still wants to do exposition at the beginning about her military background and show us her practicing martial arts. But it's very believable that she can kick ass in a Die Hard-kind of hostage situation. But the thing is, the movie is so dumb.

Firstly, it's hilarious to see a badass American president trying to bring the world together and then save it when I'm writing this on 17th April, 2025, and with whatever the fuck Trump has been doing. Antony Starr has fun playing an over-the-top villain, and he's given lines and motives that justify his actions too, like when he calls out the unnecessary war America created in the Middle East for oil and all, but it's all surface level. The villains are white mercenaries for a change, not the usual brand of Muslims or communists, and there are attempts to balance out stuff, but in the end, this is still an American president saving the world kind of movie. I can't buy them trying to save anything, lol. And I don't know if this movie was made with the utmost confidence that Kamala Harris would be the president when it releases.

Anyway, it could've at least delivered on the action, but the fights are quick cuts galore, and the action is lackluster. Anyway, I'm not rating it too low since Viola Davis's and Antony Starr's performances were pretty good here.

Name: Sinners
Review:
Sinners is a sexy movie. Thematically there are elements that it shares with what Ryan Coogler did with the Black Panther movies, a celebration of Black art and Black culture that also has political themes attached to it. But this time it's a monster movie with vampires.

Unlike Black Panther, Coogler isn't constrained with making this a full-on Marvel superhero action movie. He takes his sweet time to establish the film's world, the characters, and their relationships, there are some moments of humor and it's sooo good. Michael B. Jordan plays the Smokestack twins, and Coogler does a pretty smart thing the very first time we see them on screen. We see them sharing a cigarette. What this did for me is this kinda turned off that subconscious part of my brain that keeps on telling me that it's the same actor playing both parts. The double act is well executed here by Jordan, with Smoke and Stack having just enough differences with each other to tell them apart, and with the visual effects and filmmaking choices being effective enough to just see the characters instead of seeing two Michael B. Jordans.

Smoke and Stack are former criminals who return to their hometown to start a juke joint just for Black people that celebrates Black music. The film begins by establishing that things didn't go well at the juke joint on its opening night, as we see an injured and traumatized blues musician Sammy, the twins' cousin. Then we see that single day unfold, from the moment Smoke and Stack buy the building to the opening night. The characters and the world are so interesting, the relationships and drama are so well done, the performances are great, the music is amazing, and the movie is so well shot and edited that I was totally into the world and even forgot that it's supposed to be a vampire film. The buildup to the club's opening is so well done. And when we finally get to see the club, we get an amazing sequence where a blues performance from Miles Caton as Sammy quite literally transcends space and time (that moment was unreal in IMAX), and then the vampires turn up. The tension building is spot-on, and the tonal shift, the horror elements, and the change in atmosphere are executed really well.

The vampires are a pretty obvious colonialism and cultural exploitation metaphor; the lead vampire (a white man) initially even appears while being chased by Native Americans. Then the vampires try to infect and hijack a safe space for Black people that they're celebrating their culture and art in. The metaphor is pretty direct, plus it also plays with the fact of the oppressed having to deal with different forms of oppression, where one poses to be better than or a solution to the other form of oppression, and it also addresses the kind of oppression where the oppressors try to take their art away from the oppressed. Even for the vampire Remmick, his own experience of losing his land and community as an Irish person is mentioned. The violence and gore are well executed, and the final action setpiece was very thrilling and chaotic. I watched the IMAX version, so the way the aspect ratio expands just as the fighting begins was very cool. The whole movie was amazing in IMAX, and it's one of the best IMAX experiences I've had.

The movie looks soo gorgeous, the cinematography by Autumn Durald Arkapaw is soo good, the drama, the romance, the comedy, the action and the political themes and Black history are so well integrated, and as a vampire movie too, it just works. It does have some monster movie tropes, but unlike Black Panther, Coogler gets much more flexibility to not lean into formula here, and the cast was soo good. It was also very cool to see Hailee Steinfeld as a character like this. Ludwig Göransson has yet another banger of a soundtrack that integrates various styles of music. Also, Ryan Coogler's growth as a filmmaker is also very evident in this movie; there are lots of brilliantly staged sequences here. This might be my favorite movie of his.

Also, the mid-credits scene of Sinners is not just some throwaway scene; it's a proper epilogue and pretty much a part of the main film. So don't walk out when the credits roll!

Name: The Pink Panther
Review:
It's easy to see how Sellers and Inspector Clouseau hijacked the entire franchise. He's the only likable character in the movie, tbh, and the movie becomes genuinely fun only when he's on screen, except for the scene with the two gorillas and the way the final chase scene was staged, maybe. The main theme music and the opening credits are iconic too of course. 

I've only watched the Steve Martin Pink Panther movies, which were louder and more cartoonish. The originals didn't have any appeal for me then. But now I could appreciate how smooth Peter Sellers' slapstick is. The best part about Clouseau here is how all the gags seem like genuine mistakes and how he's trying to be a serious person all the time. Sellers is so smooth and straightfaced through the slapstick, it looks effortless and that makes it even funnier.

I didn't really care for the rest of the plot, though, but since the rest of the franchise chose to stick to Clouseau (for the most part), I'm watching the rest of those movies. 

Also, brownfaced white people playing South Asians. Eww.

Name: Daveed
Review:
It wasn't that bad, actually. The narrative beats were actually solid; the way the conflict was set up between a world champion boxer who'd literally murder his opponents and a lazy former underground fighter was all going well. But then, a large stretch of the movie is kind of flat; it's obviously building up to the big fight, but the buildup was missing, for lack of a better word, a punch. That flashback section didn't help either.

And when the big match finally happens, the editing choices are baffling, as the beginning of the match is intercut with the protagonist's training montage scene. I was confused if this was the actual match or the protagonist's imagination or dream or something. The ending did properly hit some emotional notes and drama and was pretty well done. The action and buildups worked there. But still, after building up the villain to be a literal killer, he was so out of character at the end xD. Like, yeah, there too the narrative beat makes sense; it's him going through a transformation through this journey too, but man, the writing doesn't properly convey it.

But on the whole, this movie takes a Rocky-ish underdog sports drama plot, and it misses the one ingredient that makes the drama in such formulaic boxing movies work.

Name: Whisper of the Heart
Review: One of the best parts of this movie is how the cat behaves. Instead of giving him neutral animal expressions, he's highly expressive. We see that he's bored, uninterested, playfully smirking, and going about his business; that's the kind of attention to detail that I love so much in these movies. The movie itself is the first Ghibli movie that I've watched that's entirely rooted in reality without any fantasy elements. The only time we get fantasy imagery is when we see the characters' imaginations unfold. This is Shizuku's love story and coming-of-age story. As an animated teen movie, this has a lot of detail and love put into it. Shizuku's emotions are very well understood: the wonder and happiness of seeing a great view, the warmth of meeting new people, even a new cat, the joy in music, the joy in imagination, the joy in creating art, and of course, falling in love with someone who is into the same weird shit that you're into. It's all there, and it's all so beautifully portrayed. The family scenes, the scenes with her friends, the scenes with Seiji, the wise grandpa, the various wholesome iterations of Country Roads, the overall sense of warmth and calmness... My heart wasn't whispering; it was full watching this movie. I'd like to believe that they did get married and create violins and stories together. Discovering Ghibli

Name: Thudarum
Review: Thudarum had a great plotline, and Mohanal embodied a character in ways I've not seen him do for years, and yet, it doesn't become the great film it could've been either. The screenplay fails in fleshing out the very promising plotline and the potential for drama in there. The dialogues are so bad at times, and some of the lines sound like they were written by ChatGPT while some A10 references were given as input to it. It's cute to have references to Mohanlal's career, but the ones in here belong in a movie like Good Bad Ugly or Aaraattu, and this is not supposed to be a Good Bad Ugly or Aaraattu. Even some of the serious dialogues sound so bad and dated, but thankfully Mohanlal's character Shanmugham/Benz is a man of few words in the second half after the movie becomes serious, and that lets the legend do his thing without his lines pulling him down. I like the way certain dots are connected in the narrative, but it feels so badly fleshed out. Things could've been a lot better. It even shows a social message text towards the end, while the narrative doesn't even address that social issue properly. But hey, points for having evil cops as villains; I always appreciate reverse copaganda. Operation Java is the only Tharun Moorthy film that I've seen, and yeah, I'm not a fan of his work. The things I hated about that movie are present here too, whether it's the bad dialogue, the cringe… Sorry… The crunch (hehe), one-dimensional characters, the kind of bad melodrama that frustrates me, and a Binu Pappu performance that I didn't like. But where I appreciate Tharun Moorthy here is in the way he has presented Mohanlal. We have A10 being a working-class everyman. He gets to be a cutie, he gets to be emotional, he gets to be helpless, he gets to be wounded, he breaks down, and then he gets to be a menacing and intimidating beast. When we're fresh off a Mohanlal film where he played a powerful international criminal, this movie makes even that powerful "overlord" seem less intimidating than taxi driver Shanmughan. So yk, it's just not about having Mohanlal; it's also about how he's presented. Both Empuraan and Thudarum have similar setups where Mohanlal stands in the darkness and he's revealed by lightning flashes; he's just a much more terrifying presence when the same thing happens in Thudarum. There are so many great close-up shots that just let Mohanlal emote and do his thing, and so many scenes where he could shine and flex his acting muscles. Tharun Moorthy understands what the people want from Mohanlal and gives us just that, instead of making Mohanlal reenact Telugu masala movies. So those moments are what made me forget about everything that I hated about the movie. While A10 is in beast mode, the action was so badly made and the editing during the action scenes was atrocious. Both A10's character after a point and the cool background score by Jakes Bejoy gave me Mundoor Maadan vibes, yk, the untamable beast kind of man. But the thing is, either Tharun Moorthy and co. could've taken what Sachi did in Ayyappanum Koshiyum as a reference or even what Priyadarsan did with A10 himself in Oppam as a reference, because the fight scenes here are just so bad. I can't comment about the choreography because the editing was so bad and fast-cut diarrhea that I couldn't even see wtf was going on. The only thing that made the crowd cheer and me feel anything was the occasional moment where A10 was doing something cool in slowmo, or striking a pose. In his whole presentation of Mohanlal, the action sequences are where Tharun Moorthy fell so flat; just imagine A10 getting the Mundoor Maadan treatment instead. Even the fights have small moments and touches where Mohanlal grounds Shanmukhan as a real person pushed to his limits rather than as a superhuman, at the same time, he's so agile and intimidating, but all that's lost when the fucking action editing is too fast and jarring. Another thing I appreciate is the fact that evil cops are the bad guys here, instead of glorifying systemic violence. And when the movie shifts genres, though it does have some hero worship moments, the violence is not treated lightly or casually. It's pretty brutal and it has consequences. That consistency in tone was nice and the movie is not treating the way the main character's life unravels lightly. But it could've made more of an effort to flesh out his family and show how everything that happens affects them as a whole (Ahem, Drishyam). I really expected more out of the Mohanlal and Shobhana combination, but after the initial section of the movie, they don't really get many scenes together, and Shobhana herself is criminally sidelined. The way the women are written in this movie is sus in general. I have mixed feelings about the supporting cast, and the main bad guy's performance and dialogues made me crunch at times. I don't want to rate this movie too low only because of one person, and that's MALAYALATHINTE MOHANLALLL. A celebration of Mohanlal involves actually giving material to Mohanlal that he can work his vismayam with and not throwing L's at the screen. He was soooo good in this movie. The entire film stands on those strong, slanted shoulders. Without him, the bad writing, the bad filmmaking choices and the crunch would make the movie crumble worse than that awful-looking CGI landslide in this movie. But yeah, this had so much more potential. I wish someone else got to flesh out the same plotline. Also, Sreejith Ravi casting jumpscare. Why though? (The rating is more about A10 than about the movie if it wasn't obvious)

Name: Until Dawn
Review:
I don't have the opinion that this movie is an unfaithful adaptation of the video game. I thought it was pretty smart to adapt how it feels like to play Until Dawn instead of just directly adapting its plot. The game was basically an interactive horror movie where the players could make several narrative decisions that'd decide whether all, some, or none of the characters die as the night ends. The best possible ending is obviously the one where all the characters survive, so players would have to keep replaying the game and changing up their decisions and gameplay choices with the hopes of getting that ending. In my case, I played the game exactly once, got a mixed ending where some of the characters didn't survive, and that was it for me; that was the ending of Until Dawn. This movie makes it a time loop scenario, and it's about the same night playing out with different kinds of threats each time and the characters trying to get this "best ending" where none of them die.

So yeah, the time loop thing in the case of adapting a game like Until Dawn is something that I liked here, because Until Dawn as a straightforward single playthrough story is just an interactive generic horror movie; adapting it straightforward would just make it look like a generic horror movie. But this movie actually makes the interactivity and different player choices a part of its narrative. The acting was okay throughout the cast, the gore was really well done, and I could tell that a lot of it was practical old-school film trickery. The monsters, too, relied more on prosthetics than CGI, and they looked positively creepy. David F. Sandberg does get some effective scares in, and he's pretty skilled in executing horror and practical gore on the whole.

The writing does have issues, and it's cheesy and generic. The movie is pretty short, but it does lose steam once the loop starts and feels stretched out, like it maybe feels too much like replaying the same video game over and over again? After a point we just get horror setpieces on a loop and not much happening narrative-wise. The filmmaking is pretty competent, and the scares make up for it, though. I think clever editing and dummies were used even for the exploding bodies, and if it was CGI, that's some amazing CGI.

Peter Stormare is the only returning actor from the game, but they do show a picture of Ramy Malek's character from the game, but it's funny that it's just a screenshot from the game of Ramy Malek's CGI model rather than a photo of the actual Ramy Malek.

In the end, their ultimate superpower was vlogging.

Name: Retro
Review: Enter The Suriyan! I've always loved Karthik Subbaraj's sensibilities and conviction in doing action because he cares about actually pulling off great action rather than just giving moments for his lead actor to look cool. The martial arts choreography and presenting Suriya as this Bruce Lee kind of agile martial artist badass was something I really dug in this movie, so I'd love this movie just for that, even when it has its flaws. So I'd rate this movie high just for that reason. The plot itself is a lot similar to what Karthik did in Jagame Thanthiram and Jigarthanda 2 with some tweaks; we have a reformed gangster helping an oppressed community here too, the three movies are a trilogy at this point. Even a moment during the ending seemed like it was mirroring Jigarthanda 2 in some way (not that well executed though). The writing has issues and is incoherent, but man, Suriya was so great, and the action was so badass, so for me, the flaws are manageable. Santhosh Narayanan's score and songs were cool and fit the mood. Pooja Hegde got an actual character to play instead of being eye candy, but her character still is pretty monotonous and ends up being just a person who motivates the protagonist to move the plot forward; the brown makeup was a bit distracting too (maybe just cast a brown actress?). Though the love story is an important part of the film, her character and the romance arc felt underwritten. The protagonist's arc and moral dilemmas were portrayed well, though. There's a big supporting cast, but a lot of them are just, yk, there, without having much to do. I liked the political angle but there's also a divine angle in the movie that I didn't really like, it felt like this movie didn't actually need that to pull off its chosen one plot point. The smile and laughter plot element was fun though, the buildup to the protagonist finding his smile was nice. There's a pretty impressive oner sequence at the beginning during the wedding, and there are several moments where Karthik Subbaraj unleashes himself. He's got his own style and identity, and I dig that. I had fun, and it's always great to see well-shot, well-edited, well-choreographed badass fight scenes. Suriya also was very convincing in seeming like a trained martial artist, with the choreography being done in a way that suits his physicality. The various homages and references to the retro era and several films were cool too. Anyway, Retro has its flaws, but i enjoyed it a lot. And also it's an anti-oppression movie. The way Karthik has approached the action here is something I hope more movies would do! I don't know if other people will dig this movie like I have, but I really do hope this is the Suriya redemption, I really loved seeing him as a character like this. 😭❤️❤️😭❤️😭❤️😭❤️😭❤️❤️

Name: Death of a Unicorn
Review:
This felt like an interesting one line that could be a very good trailer, but with not enough stuff for a feature film. The characters are all one-note and unlikable, even Jenna Ortega's character, who's supposed to be the only sane one (at one point she gives the worst possible presentation to the others to convey the fact that they're all about to be kebabbed by unicorns).

I don't mind the plot beats being predictable and similar to other monster movies when the concept and characters are interesting enough. But here, apart from the killer unicorn angle, it just becomes this eat-the-rich slasher with unicorns that's just flat through most of its runtime, even with the kind of acting talent in the cast. The unicorn CGI and animation being rough also doesn't help. The movie does have some cool nasty and gory kill scenes, though, but the movie also lingers around the same point of the rich people being greedy to exploit nature thing and doesn't really blend the comedy, horror, social commentary, and fantasy elements together well. 

The movie also suffers from the "character saying obscure bullshit instead of directly getting to the fucking point" syndrome for Jenna Ortega's protagonist. And this might be the most annoying Paul Rudd character that I've seen (not in a good way).

Name: Bromance
Review:
When I was a kid, my parents bought me a DVD for the Transformers movie when we visited the town, but it's only when I reached home that I realized that the DVD was of some movie called TRANSMORPHERS. Both the title and the poster looked deceptively like it's a Transformers movie, though, and I'm pretty sure the intent here is to trick people into watching the movie thinking it's Transformers. An Arun D Jose movie in that sense feels like the Transmorphers of a Girish AD movie. It'd have actors from the Girish AD films and would seem like that universe on the surface level, but it lacks the charm, humor, and relatability. 

I won't lie, this movie was fun in parts (teeny tiny parts), especially Sangeeth as the hacker, and also the translator jokes made me chuckle, but the rest of it is just misfire after misfire, whether it's the writing, the Gen Z references, the whole anger thing with Mathew's character, or everyone trying to ham it up and scream their lines in a way that's not really fun. I did laugh at times, but I was laughing at the movie with cringe rather than laughing with it during all the anger outbursts and weed brownie stuff. Shajon with his deadpan delivery also seemed better, just because the others were worse. The Gen Z references, social media references and the " Gen Z anthem" at the beginning made me physically cringe. There's a whole buildup given to honeybees, but that payoff falls flat. The final action scene is an attempt at doing chaotic slapstick humor and all, but that's also meh. We've seen better comedy road movies with similar plot setups. This was just an Elixir Kundi movie.

Name: Thunderbolts*
Review:
There are very few Marvel movies that seem like there are artists putting their soul into it, as lots of them get dumbed down to look like the same kind of corporate-manufactured products that lack an identity of their own, possibly because studio notes and involvement form those movies more than any independent artistic vision. The last one I remember that seemed like the creator's film was Guardians of the Galaxy 3, and now comes Thunderbolts.

The director, Jake Schreier, has a background in indie movies and directing episodes for comedy-drama shows like Kidding and Beef, and those sensibilities are surprisingly present throughout Thunderbolts. The screenplay itself is pretty formulaic and goes in the ways we expect it to go; it's a group of former villains and supporting characters from the MCU reluctantly teaming up together. But there are these small touches and creative choices that make these characters seem so much alive and flesh them out a lot, even when we've seen all of them in other Marvel films, and it doesn't seem like another Guardians of the Galaxy or Suicide Squad as a result either. 

This is a Marvel movie with way less green screen and lots of nicely done practical stunts and action, and along with that, there are several other choices that set Thunderbolts apart. Take the opening scene, for instance; it has this big stunt where Florence Pugh as Yelena actually jumped off a building that they heavily featured in the marketing campaign. But the thing is, Thunderbolts' narrative is very much focused on one thing more than anything else, and that's mental health. All of these characters are fighting their inner demons and trauma, though it's Yelena and Bob (Lewis Pullman) that we have the most focus on. So during the initial action set piece, instead of focusing on showcasing the action, it's more about Yelena's feeling of loneliness and emptiness. Spectacle takes a backseat here, and that's like one of the last things we'd expect a Marvel movie to do.

Signing on Florence Pugh is one of the smartest decisions Marvel took post-Endgame. She's the kind of performer who can add so much to a character way beyond what's written, and she gets to play a very flawed, human, and real-seeming Black Widow that, honestly, Scarlett Johansson never got the opportunity to play. Scarlett's Black Widow was reduced to eye candy and stereotype for a long time before she got to actually do something with the character, but Pugh is getting those chances pretty early on. Another one of Jake Schreier going indie in this Marvel movie comes in a moment when Bucky (Sebastian Stan) reveals something about John Walker's (Wyatt Russell) family. When this happens, John and Yelena look at each other, and there is so much emotion being conveyed just by these looks—there's shock, empathy, sadness, and shame—and yet, it lasts just a few seconds. Like it's the kind of moment where a theme park becomes an "absolute cinema."

Lewis Pullman as Bob/Sentry is also a standout from the cast, as by the end the movie becomes about his mental health (male loneliness epidemic fr). There's this oner action scene that showcases his powers that indeed make him seem like one of the most powerful Marvel characters. But the thing is, this movie still focuses more on its emotional narrative beats than on delivering spectacle, even during the third act, which is the place where these movies usually try to unleash spectacle. The Void's design was also very creative and effective. Yes, it's way smaller than any other Marvel movie as a result, but that becomes a strength rather than a weakness.

The cast itself was great and had great chemistry and banter with each other. Whether it's the deadpan humor from Hannah John-Kamen, Wyatt Russell, and Sebastian Stan, the silliness from David Harbour or then Florence Pugh who stays somewhere in between silly and deadpan, the cast was great here, and they do make us care about this team and these characters, so that (it's already been spoiled by Marvel) when they become New Avengers at the end, that payoff is also well executed (it also works that the credit sequence consist of all possible social media comments for these characters becoming the Avengers). The humor and fun do land here, and it's done in a way that doesn't weaken the drama either. And Valentina is just Veep's Selina Meyer without the profanity here. 

At the end it's a movie about saving ourselves more than saving the world; even with superhero movie elements present, Thunderbolts never loses its focus on being about companionship, confronting trauma, and finding your weirdo group of friends. I respect that. Yes there are dumb parts in the movie too, but there's enough good stuff to forgive that. I also have to mention Son Lux's score, which was really cool and memorable, it sounded like a superhero movie score and at the same time it didn't. This is the smallest Marvel movie with the biggest heart. A warm hug from trauma bonding buddies is the most powerful thing in any universe, cheesy, but effective. 

This movie made me care about Marvel movies all over again. Start making creators do their thing themselves, Kevin!

Name: Grave of the Fireflies
Review: The most important but often overlooked perspectives and stories during any war are those of the civilians. The people who were never a part of any fight, who stand to lose everyone and everything just because they were living in the wrong place at the wrong time. Even in the case of films, we see more stories about the soldiers, the leaders, and even the guy who made the bomb than of the people on whom the bomb fell. As I'm writing this in May 2025 as an Indian, the last few days were also a testament to the lack of mainstream Indian media that represents how war affects ordinary lives. Most of our war films involve action heroes defeating the enemy and claiming victory. Clips from those movies were being shared on the Internet, and songs and background scores from those films were used as people were craving revenge, destruction, and death. The "glory" of war is what those films sold, and not the tragedy, and people's reaction to the possibility of an actual war, expecting this glory and victory, seemed scary. Safer Indians were celebrating war while other Indians were losing their lives at the border. Those lives are merely numbers and collateral damage to those who celebrate and glorify, they're just a "part of" war. Well, they shouldn't be, and this is exactly the kind of film that shows why they shouldn't be just numbers, that the people matter the most, not your pride, not your revenge, not your political aspirations. I know I took the worst time to cover the darkest Ghibli movie that's basically about how two kids tragically suffer during a war, right as a threat of war was looming over me as an Indian citizen. But by watching something like this now and then feeling everything I felt as this movie broke my heart into a million pieces and made me break down crying, I realized that I should indeed never be the kind of person who'd think anything good would come out of war. Grave of the Fireflies also has moments of warmth and innocence that I've seen in other Ghibli movies, just that this time, it's also about the loss of that innocence, about war taking that warmth away from these children. The film doesn't even wait around to deliver its tragedy; it begins outright with the death of its protagonist, and then we're just seeing their eventual journey into starvation and death, which makes all the happy and warm moments they share seem more bittersweet and painful. The filmmaking is very precise, with beautiful art, music, and animation that really invites us into the lives of these kids, their bond, and their love, as they're also trying to survive while facing fear and helplessness with death and destruction all around them, and as the audience we're aware how this is going to conclude, making everything sadder. Through beautiful animation, we see fantasy and reality blending in the most heartbreaking and poetic ways. This film should be re-released frequently; this film should be shown as educational material, like, it portrays who loses the most during any war perfectly. How can someone still celebrate war or wish for war and then call themselves a patriot? I'm not merely recommending this movie; everyone SHOULD watch this. Even when the experience is very heavy on the heart, it was a hard watch for me (just because of how affecting it is), and it did destroy me. But it's a very very very important work of art. Discovering Ghibli

Name: Havoc
Review:
The Raid movies are one of the first ones that pop up in my head whenever there's a discussion about the best action movies, so obviously I'm a fan. But unlike the Raid films, Havoc does try to be more than just the action; it tries to set up a world, an ensemble cast of characters, and some amount of drama, but the problem is that all of these attempts fall flat. The movie spends a considerable amount of time setting up its key players and conflicts until the big action scene at the club. Even something like the first John Wick took a considerable amount of time till it switched gears into the action, but there, the lead character was interesting, the world was interesting, and the buildup was interesting. But here, not so much. There's a CGI-heavy car chase at the beginning that felt pretty underwhelming too.

Now, about the action and violence, I felt that the exaggerated CGI blood and practical gore combo was a stylistic choice, and when it worked, it worked well. I have no idea why the characters in this movie would keep shooting someone over and over again even when they've shot them enough to kill them, or I've just been spoiled by the precise kill shots in John Wick and its clones. The club sequences started up pretty cool, the hand-to-hand combat did have the Raid flavor, and it looked pretty visceral. It looked like they were also using VFX to make it seem like the hits were actually connecting to the bodies, similar to what the Roadhouse remake did, and it looked pretty cool.
