Once it then became a shootout, though, it just seemed confusing and chaotic. Don't get me wrong, Gareth Evans is better than most directors at using shaky cam and frantic camera movements, whether it's in the Raid films or here, but the club scene just lost me once the bullets started flying. The next big action setpiece was the climatic showdown in the cabin. Now, that was some badass and visceral gunplay. The instances of slow motion were on point, reminding me of how it used to feel to play Max Payne. The bullets ripping through wood, the furniture, the things in the cabin, and the henchmen were all effectively executed. The violence is gory and visceral, and the whole scene was thrilling. That was the kind of energy the rest of the movie needed, and that's why I'm not rating it too low.

The characters were all one-dimensional, but Tom Hardy is the kind of actor who could look good even as a one-dimensional stock character. He did perform well during the action scenes, though. The movie also maintains a pretty good sense of internal logic, like yk, when Tom Hardy's Patrick, a police officer with basic hand-to-hand combat skills, faces off against a superiorly trained martial artist, the fight goes exactly the way we expect it to go. It brought me flashbacks of a similar fight scene from Raid. Jessie Mei Li was the only person in the movie who was not permanently brooding; she was good, but I wish the movie had more of her.

Havoc also looked really cool; the night shots had a certain noir appeal about them. But yeah, kinda disappointed that the Tom Hardy-Gareth Evans collab was just "okay" rather than making me go ‼️‼️‼️. There's still some cool action in this movie, so I'm not rating it too low.

Name: Mission: Impossible
Review: These movies have always tried to ground Ethan Hunt in some way, but this must be the most grounded Ethan Hunt. Tom Cruise in his 30s, in his prime, hangs from a CGI helicopter in front of a CGI background in this movie, while he hangs from real planes at actual high altitudes in his 60s. This is an Ethan Hunt who gets knocked down with just two hits, and everything about this movie is quite different from the MI we know today, apart from maybe all the twists, betrayals, reverse betrayals, and mask disguises stuff. The final action scene does defy physics, but it's still tame compared to what has followed. This is primarily a commercial espionage movie with 90s sensibilities; it's not the showcase of big action set pieces and daredevil antics that MI became afterwards. The biggest practical stunt Cruise does in this movie is probably the hanging from the ceiling. There is the big train set piece at the end, which is all 90s CGI and film trickery, which does hold up despite the primitive visual effects thanks to pretty solid filmmaking from De Palma. Also, it's so nice to see the retro tech in these 90s movies, your keypad phones, CRT monitors, how the internet looks, how the hacking is shown, and especially the floppy disks and then Cruise doing sleight of hand magic tricks with the floppy disk. Nostalgia raahhhhhhh!!!!!! Anyway, cool movie. Short haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible II
Review: Aah, the John Woofication and Matrixification of Mission: Impossible that sticks out from all the other movies in the franchise. And yet it did set some elements that'd become hallmarks of this series. The first movie was not heavy on big action set pieces and the showcasing of elaborate practical stunts; this is where that started. Ethan Hunt's intro sequence has him climbing a cliff in the most badass way possible. Why? Because Tom Cruise can. When Ethan and Nyah have their meet-cute, it's an elaborate high-speed car chase where their cars hit and spin together in slow motion and Nyah almost falls down a cliff. Why? Because they can. Tom Cruise nearly had his eye stabbed during the climactic fight scene. Why? Because he's Tom Cruise. Plus that amazing chase sequence at the end is one for the history books. I used to be one of the people who considered this the worst Mission: Impossible too, because there's an extra layer of campiness and unseriousness here, and Ethan Hunt himself is not as grounded as the rest of the movies, but that's exactly why I loved it on this rewatch. John Woo has a very distinctive style, and he made a full-on John Woo movie. I mentioned The Matrix at the beginning. This movie does have an overdose of slowmo and dramatic slow-mo stares like The Matrix, but the action sensibilities and the style are more John Woo than Matrix. Still, both Cruise and the villain rock black leather jackets and shades during the finale, which is clearly because The Matrix made that cool 1 year ago. The Matrix aesthetics and style choices were such a big deal then, they even made their way all the way over here to Indian cinema. This movie also has some of the best cheesy dialogues in the entire series. You have an Oscar-winning thespian like Anthony Hopkins saying, "This is not Mission: Difficult, Mr. Hunt; it's Mission: Impossible. 'Difficult' should be a walk in the park for you". I mean, ICONIC. The action, of course, is John Woo-coded. There's the slow-mo, there are the dives, the doves, the dual wielding, and everything being so hyperdramatic. That whole lab shootout has Hans Zimmer blasting that amazing score that blends operatic music with electronic guitars, and it's so awesome. The climatic showdown has an epic bike chase scene that has some of the best stunt driving work in this franchise. Also, Cruise on that bike emerging through the flames in slow-mo? ICONIC. It's also interesting that despite all the over-the-top stunts up upto that point, when Ethan and Ambrose finally fight each other, it's a pretty dirty and nasty fight choreography rather than dance-like martial arts choreography. Also, this might be the Mission: Impossible with the most interesting setup. The entire movie happens just because Ethan Hunt goes on vacation and the IMF decides to substitute him with a dude who's clearly sus. Ethan deserves to have his PTO, though. Anyway, I'm not going to rate this low. John Woo was all style and badassery here, Hans Zimmer was awesome, Cruise was Cruise, and this is the movie that made me have a crush on Thandiwe Newton. Fabulously long haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible III
Review: Gone was the Matrix-era slow-mo of MI:2, and in was the Bourne-era grittiness and shaky cam of MI:3. This was the time when every action movie tried to be Bourne, and of course both Mission: Impossible and James Bond had their Bourne-era movies. But still, this one doesn't go full Bourne like Quantum of Solace did; Tom Cruise still likes to show stunts with as few cuts as possible. This movie lies somewhere in between Brian De Palma's sensibilities from the first movie and a gritty Bourne movie. This is the first appearance of Simon Pegg as Benji. He's a pretty minor character here, but making him a franchise regular along with Luther is one of the best decisions they've made. Also, 3 has the best villain of this franchise in Philip Seymour Hoffman. Now, the character is a generic one-note villain, but Hoffman adds so much weight during the few scenes that he does get. His threats have a certain bluntness and coldness that just makes him seem so sinister. If Ethan Hunt ever had a foe who made me feel like he could completely destroy him, it's this guy, sorry Henry Cavill. This movie makes it a point to differentiate itself from the more campy and unserious MI:2. This is a pretty serious affair; there are still instances of humor and fun, but on the whole, this is more of an espionage thriller than 2 but still has more action setpieces than 1. But the finale is surprisingly a small-scale shootout inside a building rather than some huge setpiece. Might be the smallest MI ending scene. Ethan himself is more grounded than he was in the last movie. He loses his cool many times, he gets beaten up a lot, fails a lot of times, has so many near misses, and in the end his wife saves him (2020s incels might call this forced woke lol). The Vatican mission remains memorable for showing us the mask printing and voice imitation technology in action; that transition from Tom Cruise to Philip Seymour Hoffman was so smooth. It was also cool to see Hoffman actually play Ethan Hunt. The bridge explosion with Cruise flying and hitting the car is also an iconic image from this movie. Plus, the ending has us seeing the full iconic Tom Cruise run in this franchise for the first time. It's a JJ Abrams movie, so there were lots of lens flaress and close-ups of sweaty faces as well. Also, pre-Breaking Bad Aaron Paul sighting! Short haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol
Review: The three movies so far were all drastically different from each other, with different visions and different sensibilities. But Ghost Protocol is the sweet spot where Mission: Impossible started to shape up into more of a unified vision, and though Christopher McQuarrie is the person who took the franchise forward afterwards, Brad Bird's entry set up several elements and the tone that McQuarrie would build upon. Firstly, Simon Pegg's Benji is promoted to main character status here, and also, though Ethan is still front and center, from Ghost Protocol onwards, the team gets more prominence, and we get more team banter and team action. Jeremy Renner as Brandt was also such a great addition to the cast ("Next time I'm seducing the rich guy", lmao), it's kinda disappointing that we only got one more movie with him. Paula Patton as Carter was also a great addition, though the flirty energy between her and Ethan is left unexplored, and she never appears in the franchise after this. Luther is reduced to just a cameo in this movie for some reason. This was the first proper digital age Mission: Impossible with all the holograms, touchscreens and digital gadgets. The 3D fake background projection screen thingy is still so fun. Brad Bird approached this thing with sensibilities not so different from something like The Incredibles (he even snuck in the Pixar A113 in here), and it's awesome. There are more crazy gadgets in here than in any of the last movies. The finale in India is also an extended BMW ad, but even that product placement is done very smartly. The Dubai mission in this movie is Mission: Impossible at its best, it's espionage thrills and tense buildups, combined with Tom Cruise doing badass practical stunts, the near-misses, the doubt, the fails. Like every single piece is placed perfectly, the Burj climb and descent is not just an amazing feat of stuntwork; it's a feat in filmmaking as well, with proper tension buildup and payoffs. But it's a bit anticlimactic when we cut back from the practically filmed action to that not-so-great-looking CGI sandstorm. This movie also has the best opening intro sequence in the franchise; the Christopher McQuarrie movies afterwards would go for an intro that's similar to the first one, which itself was based on the intro of the original TV show. But this was a blend of that with quirkier sensibilities. The villain, Hendricks, was just a generic placeholder character, though; he doesn't really have any personality or any defining characteristics. He's just there as a threat, but he is a pretty formidable threat that keeps Ethan and the team on their toes, leading to some thrilling and edge-of-the-seat missions and moments, but yeah, he might be the weakest villain in the franchise. There's so much fun in this movie. Of course they do sitar music when they show India. Long haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation
Review: If I had a penny for every time the IMF was disbanded and Ethan and the team had to save the world from a highly intelligent terrorist while being hunted as criminals, I'd have two pennies. Which isn't a lot, but it's weird that it happened twice. We're officially into the Christopher McQuarrie era with Rogue Nation, and this for me is the definitive Mission: Impossible movie. It's the perfect blend of badass action and great stuntwork with adequate espionage thrills, moments of humor that do not cut down on the urgency of the plot, romantic tension, campiness, cheesy lines, shirtless Ethan Hunt escaping being tied down to a pole by jumping up like a gymnast, and Ethan Hunt with a beard. It's got it all. Lorne Balfe's score also brings back the classic Mission: Impossible theme in its full glory, and elements of it are reused throughout the score. Christopher McQuarrie also brings back the classic Mission: Impossible intro sequence in this movie. The cast is also great; Rebecca Ferguson was such a great addition here, and the way she played off of Ethan was great (watching this movie made me resent what happens to her in Dead Reckoning, though). It was also hilarious when Alec Baldwin's Hunley went from wanting to capture or kill Ethan Hunt to being his ultimate hype man in a second. "Hunt is the living manifestation of destiny." Not even Hunt's best buds, like Luther or Benji, will say that. Also, there are so many exhilarating moments of action and thrills here. Whether it's the opening plane stunt, the opera sequence, the underwater heist, or the chase (which is also this movie's BMW ad opportunity), everything is memorable, with the climactic run-and-gun being the only small-scale action scene here, but even there that great fight scene with Rebecca Ferguson and the eventual payoff to the Lane-Hunt face-off make up for it. This movie is just so well put together, and it's always on such high energy. And it's always satisfying to see Hunt get the upper hand after losing and almost dying throughout the movie. Solomon Lane was a pretty good villain too. Long-ish haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible – Fallout
Review: Out of the six missions I've rewatched so far, this is definitely the prettiest-looking one. Man, I cannot emphasize more how gorgeous this movie looks, so much so that I googled who did the cinematography, so shout out to Rob Hardy's amazing work here. This too is a movie I have little to no complaints about. The action and stuntwork are spectacular; it's shot so well, the filmmaking and editing are on point, and the cast is fun with enough banter and chemistry, though I did miss Jeremy Renner as Brandt. Also, not enough good Rebecca Ferguson moments like Rogue Nation did, apart from that fight scene at the end. But yeah, this movie is stacked; it might even be the Mission: Impossible movie with the most amount of action. All the previous movies had a heist and escape kind of situation, but this movie goes all in on all kinds of fights, shootouts, chases, and a HALO jump instead. Fallout also chooses to end with a big action setpiece, while the last three movies decided to go smaller with their endings. The finale helicopter stunt was glorious, and even the fight scene where Benji and Ilsa face off against Lane was great. Henry Cavill as Walker was a great addition to the cast; also, the Superman mustache meme exists because of August Walker, amen. He's also such a physically intimidating presence, and it's no surprise that when a fight happens between Hunt and Walker, it's pretty one-sided as the bigger, stronger, and younger Walker overpowers Hunt. Hunt then has to think smartly to get rid of him. If any star should take any note from Tom Cruise (other than the Scientology), it's this: he doesn't mind getting beat up, looking weaker, or even losing in a fight. It doesn't make Ethan Hunt any less of a badass because he occasionally loses or gets overpowered. It's more about delivering on the action, drama, and thrills. Ethan Hunt is always about not being in control of the situation, losing to the villains, taking big risks and gambles, and even relying on dumb luck, because yk, the stakes being impossible is pretty true. It has an appeal, and it makes these movies more thrilling, even if we know that at the end Ethan would indeed save the world. Anyway, Lorne Balfe's score was also great; Christopher McQuarrie found the best possible ways to show all these action pieces, shout-out to the cinematographer Rob Hardy again, Cruise pushed himself to the limit in this movie and even broke his foot. 5 stars, fuck yeah! Short haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning
Review: If I had a penny every time Ethan Hunt was branded a criminal by his own government for trying to save the world.... Anyway, after watching 7 MI films back to back, I can confidently say how Ethan Hunt is consistent as a character, yes, even in the second one. Like they mention in Rogue Nation, he is indeed a gambler; he relies on chance and dumb luck a lot. Most of the time he has no idea what the outcome of the mission will be or how exactly he'd even get it done. There are lots of instances of him just winging it, nearly dying, and nearly losing; the wins are mostly last minute. Anyway, with a protagonist like this, the AI entity that can predict every possible outcome with precision seems like the perfect and most dangerous antagonist, more than a human villain would. Lorne Balfe is badass for all the marching band arrangements of the original MI theme. Anyway, I don't think this movie deserves the hate it gets. So I'm bumping up the rating from my first watch a bit, though my opinion remains pretty much the same. Also, short haired Ethan movie.

Name: Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning
Review: As I sat in the theater and watched this 62-year-old man hang off a plane flying thousands of feet above the ground, it was a reminder that nobody else does something like this; nobody else would probably even try to do something like this. I cried a bit. Mr. Cruise, you are THE action star. So despite the issues that I have with this movie, it's literally impossible for me to rate this movie low after witnessing just how insane and committed both Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie are at executing breathtaking action sequences at the scale and risk that they have here. They're as much badasses IRL, or even more, than what they show Ethan Hunt to be. The movie itself does have some issues in the writing level. One of my takeaways from Dead Reckoning was that the entity seemed like a very formidable threat to put Ethan against. Ethan's mode of operation has always been about being emotionally driven, gambling under impossible stakes while dealing with lots of uncertainties. And then we have this AI that knows everything and predicts every outcome and thinks logically instead of emotionally. I was excited to see how Ethan would tackle a threat like this in this movie, but that just doesn't happen here. After a promising setup that shows a dystopian AI-infected world, the AI is reduced to just being a world-ending ticking time bomb plot device, while the actual villains are indeed humans and the circumstances that Ethan and the team are put against. Even something smaller in scale like the TV show Person of Interest explored an all-powerful AI being a villain really well, but The Final Reckoning avoids those possibilities altogether, whether it's the AI's capabilities or Ethan and the team being forced to make use of analog tech, there was so much more potential. The high-stakes, literal apocalypse prevention Mission here is still set up to be Impossible and thrilling though. There are also too many moving pieces at times when a simpler approach might've worked better. But at the same time, there are moments where the parallel events sync together beautifully, like a fight scene that alternates between Ethan and his team that's beautifully edited to flow through each person, or the final setpiece after the whole messy setup to it, which was edge-of-the-seat perfection. There are lots of callbacks and references to previous movies, and the movie does cut back to footage from those movies to remind us, which is okay; not everyone is crazy enough and has the time to binge through all seven movies before watching this movie, like I did. The connections made to the first and third movies were nice, though. I can't complain about the supporting cast not getting enough time to be fleshed out when the movie is already packed to the brim. The two big Ethan Hunt setpieces here, the one underwater and the one in the air, were breathtaking. The underwater scene is placed beautifully where, in that moment, the movie is locked to just Ethan and doesn't cut away to the other characters; there's no dialogue at all, except for a single line of pretty necessary exposition. The production design is also amazing here, and the way it's been shot and edited is also brilliant. The same goes for the climactic scene in the air, which is where I cried. It's an incredible feat of filmmaking, stunt design, and stunt performing. I can't help but feel massive respect towards everyone involved in pulling it off while being as safe as possible. It's amazing stuff, like, the commitment it takes to pull off something like this is the actual Mission: Impossible. In promoting Dead Reckoning, they made the mistake of hyping up the jump so much while it's a quick moment in the film itself (it's still an amazing stunt), but here the whole aerial fight scene is way more impressive and exhilarating than the promotional material ever had me believe. The ending itself is set up similar to how the final sequence in Fallout was, but the helicopter chase in Fallout now just seems so tiny compared to what's seen here. The score was great, and McQuarrie again cleverly uses the music, choosing not to use it at some moments to let the sound design build up the tension. His direction is so on point here, and the way he approaches action and the thrilling setups and tension builds are still great, even when his writing falters. There are plotholes that are a bit too on the nose to ignore, but even then, when this movie works, it works gloriously. The cinematography was great too, especially during the two big action setpieces. There's a big cast of supporting characters, but a lot of them are, yk, just there to move the plot, apart from Ethan, of course. Hayley Atwell's Grace very well could've been Rebecca Ferguson as Ilsa instead, and nothing would've changed. Pom Klementieff gets some cool moments, though. There was a returning cast member who was a pleasant surprise, and Mister Milchick from Severance saying the word "Mister" constantly was fun. Anyway, the insanity of Tom Cruise performing stunts like this on camera, when movie magic could easily do the job, I can't help but respect that. And it does make a difference that the stunts are real; when he's high up, and as the wind hits his face and his body reacts to gravity and the G-force, there are several factors here that visual effects just can't replicate. The Mission: Impossible movies are never completely CGI-free, of course; they don't make that Christopher Nolan claim. They do use CGI to enhance the action, but the amount of in-camera action filmed makes all the difference. There's only one Tom Cruise, and I doubt if there'll ever be another one, and this has been such a journey to watch 30 years of Ethan Hunt back-to-back, seeing this dude run (A LOT), jump, drive fast, dive deep, climb and hang from stuff, and barely save the world under impossible circumstances. Made me feel emotional. Long haired Ethan movie.

Name: Padakkalam
Review: It's great to see a fantasy comedy in Malayalam; the whole body control and body swap situation was very fun, and within the cast, Sandeep, Sharaf U Dheen, and Suraj were great. Among the boy gang, one of them was very plain and monotonous, though he does get a big laugh with a T-shirt joke. The comic book references and pop culture references were fun, and it was nice that the characters were pretty smart; even that Google Translate joke came just as I thought the same. But the rules of the central game situation weren't all that well explained, like something like Jumanji was; it could've improved upon several areas, though it's pretty engaging till the end. Sandeep has all the potential to be star material.

Name: Predator
Review:
I love the part where the movie ends like we just saw a fun sitcom or wholesome comedy movie with the cast looking at the camera and smiling, while most of them get brutally murdered in the movie by an alien for fun. Absolute cinema.

The way this movie is set up is also fun. As in there's absolutely no setup, we have no idea who Dutch is as a person; he's Arnie, he's got big muscles, he's in the military, he has a mission, and the mission just begins right from the get-go. The most muscular handshake in the history of cinema between Arnold and Carl Weathers is right at this introduction. We know exactly what kind of men these men are; they're the men men, the hypermasculine, jacked-up, alpha warrior kind of men. Even the camp ambush scene afterwards has Arnold lifting a truck with his bare hands, impaling a dude with a knife to a wall ("Stick around"), and killing enemies with ease. With all the muscles, strength, and alpha-ness on display, we'd think this movie is going to be all about Arnie and the gang being cool badasses, and we're dead wrong. All of this is misdirection, because the real alpha here is the Predator, and all the badassery and muscles these dudes just displayed is just making them fun for it to hunt and kill.

I forgot just how much of Predator is just beefy men walking through a forest. The way this movie switches from a hypermasculine action movie to a slasher horror flick is so smooth. These men are immediately emasculated by the Predator after they get a chance to show off their strength. All they did was make it more fun for it to kill them. It kills everyone with ease. The one woman escapes just because she's unarmed and it didn't see her being the kind of prey that's fun for it to hunt. Even in the climactic confrontation with Dutch, he's absolutely helpless against the predator in a direct fight. It's stronger and better trained than he ever will be, alien steroids, I guess. Dutch only gets an upper hand when he exploits its weaknesses and plays it smart; there too he barely survives out of sheer luck. I think it was a deliberate choice to have Dutch's voice sound so high-pitched in the Predator's POV as it's beating the shit out of him. He's that weak and small to it. Those Arnie muscles don't mean anything to that thing. It's just playing with him because he's the only one that gave it a proper fight.

This movie is memorable for a number of things: the predator itself (the special effects and makeup are still amazing and stands the test of time), Arnie, every single word that comes out of his mouth, da choppah, and the whole beefed-up muscular dude energy of the thing. But ever since I watched it as a kid, the one thing that I could never forget and stuck on was Alan Silvestri's iconic score. The music in this movie is the stuff of legends.

It's also political isn't it? American soldiers land in a foreign country and are exerting their power over their natives, and then the predator, a being from another planet comes and wipes all these soldiers out for fun. 

Predator, where the campiness is its muscles, and muscles. 

Shane Black acted in the original Predator only to write and direct a Predator movie with an Iron Man predator suit.

Name: Predators
Review:
I thought Shane Black's pussy jokes in the first movie were the most offensive the Predator movies could get, and then Walton Goggins says that 5:00 PM line in this movie ☠️. When I see the title "Predators", I think creepy-looking murderous aliens, not, you know, PREDATORS. 

This was the best Predator sequel (which was not a high bar) until Prey happened. Adrien Brody got jacked for this movie and channeled his inner Arnie. He talked very little, which is amazing acting, seeing how he’s yapping IRL in his award speeches. Alice Braga was also great. That samurai fight with the Predator was badass. But the Predator vs. Predator fight was underwhelming.

Also surreal to see Walton Goggins and Mahershala Ali in this right before they got their big breaks.

Anyway, pretty fun.

Name: Narivetta
Review:
The real-life issue being highlighted here is important, and the film is a good reminder of the darker sides of Kerala's history, where the system absolutely failed. But still, the film itself had issues. Though the film is about the real-life shooting and police brutality against tribals, it chooses the external POV of a police officer named Varghese, played by Tovino Thomas, rather than that of the tribal community itself. My issue is not that the film has an external POV, just that it's not done that well. Even something like Killers of the Flower Moon was pretty self-aware about it being written and made from a white perspective, but here, it's different. 

Firstly, we didn't need that much of a backstory on the protagonist; we didn't need to know about his love life, as that doesn't really matter to the main incident being portrayed here at all. Afterwards, the massacre scene itself was pretty affecting and dark, and it did trigger an emotional response in me, but at the same time, the tribal people were reduced to just being victims here. I wish the time given to show the protagonist's love story was spent on the tribals themselves. I mean, look at Kammattipadam; it had Dulquer Salman as a Savarna man at the center, but it smartly places him in a way that the movie still ends up being about Ganga and the community of underprivileged people who lost their land and homes. But here, it somehow ends up being more about Varghese and his redemption than about the community, and he ends up being their savior, in an ending that doesn't really fit in there after the movie shows us the ugly reality of the real-life situation.

The movie also relies too much on generic tropes, and I have mixed feelings regarding the acting as well. Jakes Bejoy's score was good, but parts of the movie were overscored. 

Is it an important movie that may lead to important discussions? Yes.

Do I like the fact that a movie that exposes systemic oppression exists? Yes.

But yeah, I had some issues with this one. Movies like this need to exist, though, the anti-Shahi Kabir kind, I mean, but they need to be better too (as in inverse Copaganda, I hate Copaganda, clearly).

Name: Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning
Review: I just felt like rewatching this in IMAX, and I'm so glad I did. The two big action setpieces were glorious in the large format, especially the aerial stunt. Though it was a bit hard for me to sit through all the exposition-heavy setup at the beginning for the second time, it was so fucking worth it. I also noticed how once Ethan starts chasing Gabriel at the end, from that chase in the jeep onwards, he doesn't have any lines at all. Ethan is completely silent for the rest of the movie, even in the epilogue. For a movie that was so heavy on in-your-face exposition dialogue, the finale and epilogue are so much less talky (along with the submarine sequence). The plane stunt was almost like a modern and advanced version of silent era action scenes, yk, Buster Keaton style. Even Gabriel's end is comical. I could yap about that stunt sequence for ages. It's the stuff of legends. It's so interesting that the last 30 or so minutes that we're seeing Ethan Hunt has him being a silent character. This movie deserves so much appreciation and love. I have issues with it, but to me, it's a 5. Long haired Ethan movie.

Name: Sikandar
Review:
We have a protagonist who is the king of a nation with infinite wealth and resources, who is beloved by the people in his kingdom, and they exist as a utopia separate from the inferior democratic world, but then, the king must step out of his kingdom to save the world. No, this is not Ryan Coogler's Black Panther that I'm talking about; it's A. R. Murugadoss' Bhai Panther. They even have the king's warrior bodyguards here, like Black Panther, but instead of badass women, it's buff men, of course.

I see two possibilities here: this is either a rejected script for Sarkar, where Vijay was supposed be a king with infinite wealth instead of a techbro with infinite wealth, or Murugadoss wrote this by telling ChatGPT to write him an A. R. Murugadoss movie. The movie is so random at times, and the dialogues just sound so random and robotic, and Bhai, for some reason, delivers everything like he's a robot 😭. Like, this is one of the very few movies where I've laughed at a person going through grief. Bhai goes through a huge loss here, and he's like, "I'm done, bro." Talking about his performance, he was struggling with moving his facial muscles here, like I think lifting weights might be easier for Bhai at this point than moving his face. There are moments where his entire face remains stationary while only his mouth moves, like a muscular Muppet. It's so weird. I have no idea what's happening here and why he's behaving like he's a Terminator while he's supposed to be a person. Sometimes it even feels like he doesn't even want to be on set and act. Also, the movie randomly gives him the badass theme music even when he's walking sadly after a death in the family. Rashmika Mandanna's character was the most hilarious running gag in the movie. I won't spoil why. Murugadoss movies occasionally at least have good action, but here the action is shit too. But that's the only time Bhai doesn't seem like a mannequin. 

The whole kingdom setup in the movie felt like it was the wet dream of every surviving family member belonging to the families who used to rule parts of India once upon a time. The movie ends with Bhai becoming king of the world through Instagram, and the post-credits scene has him dancing with a corpse. I'm not joking.

Name: HIT: The First Case
Review:
Vishwak Sen was Pretty good and believable as a cop, but they overplay the tortured cop bit, and it doesn't really affect the investigation that much either. The buildup of the mystery was great, and the way the clues were being gathered was interesting; the movie convincingly made me buy the protagonist's attention to detail and all. There was a certain amount of groundedness and realism here that Telugu cinema lacks even in the fight scenes. But then in the third act it kind of falls apart. Instead of using his smarts, the protagonist is suddenly torturing and beating up suspects for getting information, which is how Indian police operate, of course, but I hate it when it's shown as part of the police procedure rather than as inhuman torture. Also, then the reveals happen, and it just felt like they were trying to trick us for the sake of shocking us, rather than building up an intriguing twist that actually makes sense. Both the twist and the way the protagonist reaches the conclusion didn't feel that smart. Then the movie ends with a cliffhanger. Let me check out the second part anyway.

Why is it named the First Case when it's clearly not his or the department's first case?

Name: HIT: The 2nd Case
Review:
This one seemed comparatively better than the first one, but it's hilarious that the first one ended on this big cliffhanger and then it's reduced to an insignificant B-plot here with its protagonist on vacation. xD

This one doesn't play with the tortured cop stereotype; instead, we have a chill and overconfident cop being pushed to his limits. Also, it shows the police department actually being shitty by torturing suspects without properly investigating and even going as far as to murder a suspect just to close a case. In the first one, torturing and beating up suspects to get information was just "a part of the job", this one does show them fucking up. Yay!

The mystery also seemed better, even if the whole premise of an incel killer isn't that well written or explored. The plot beats are all familiar and generic. The twist seemed a bit better than the first one, but the way they reach the conclusion is still so dumb. I mean, why did the killer put up an ___ for his ___ the way he did in the first place? The end confrontation was also dumb, with some bad CGI.

I already hate fucking Arjun Sarkar, though. This movie takes a stand against encounter killings, only to introduce the next protagonist, who's a psychopath who doesn't hesitate to beat up and murder innocents? Anyway, my hopes aren't that high for the third one.

Name: HIT: The Third Case
Review:
I've never laughed as hard as I did watching a dark, gory action movie than the moment I heard "Abki Baar Arjun Sarkaar," LMAO.

This movie completely ditches the murder mystery procedural format of the last two movies and makes it a hero-centric action movie starring Nani as Arjun Sarkaar. The biggest mystery here is them completely forgetting about the existence of the first movie's protagonist, Vikram, and that whole murder attempt cliffhanger.

Anyway, I find anti-heroes very interesting, but the movie is pretty confused about whether it should treat Arjun Sarkaar as an anti-hero or a hero-hero, and when it's police brutality that's being glorified, with Arjun's whole deal of brutalizing every single person being shown with a cool background score, that confusion is an issue, and then towards the end he's a hero-hero anyway. Add an awful romantic subplot to it, and the movie starts to feel like a parody. Ideally Arjun should've broken up with her the moment she showed him that creepy animated video with his mother's old photo, but instead he cried. Aww, such a softie. We even get a scene where the love interest gets turned on by Arjun beating up and shouting at people, of course. Kalippante Kaanthaari thanne.

Arjun Sarkaar himself is just an angry and violent dude with not much depth. He's like a Sandeep Reddy Vanga character in a non-Sandeep Reddy Vanga movie, just without the penis fetish. The cock obsession is something that's so specific to Vanga, and I don't think a normie like Sailesh could even try to imitate his dickness, SRV. I'm at a point in my life where I hate all kinds of copaganda, but the last movie did at least make an attempt to show the police being shitty with their torture methods and encounter killings, but that's all ditched here. The funny part is that Arjun gathers zero usable information while brutally torturing his suspects and only gets something useful when he manipulates them mentally. I remember the torturing of suspects being absolutely useless in the other HIT movies as well. Is Sailesh actually mocking the police here?

NGL, there were some cool fight scenes in this movie, and Nani is dependably good even when given awful material to work with (but he's also the producer of the movie so idk), though in the attempt to be edgy and gory, the not-so-well-executed CGI blood and gore occasionally make the thing look more cartoonish than gritty and brutal. Still though, we get a cool hallway fight scene and all, only for it to get very comical afterwards. Everything except the occasional cool moments of action was colossally bad in the final act, while the rest of the movie was just bad. 

Anti-heroes can be so complex and interesting, but this is not it. Arjun Sarkaar is so unfazed by all the violence, murdering, torturing and blood and we never really know why he's like that. If he's a cold blooded psychopath inside, why doesn't the movie explore that Dexter-style, instead of just putting him on a hero pedestal? Idk. 

Also, all those ugly AI generated images and videos when the characters were giving "smart" explanations were so funny. This movie is so dumb in the most hilarious ways. Also, keep Al Pacino and Robert De Niro out of your fucking mouth. 😭

There's an Avengers-type team-up at the end, and at that moment, the team became the Super Homicide Intervention Team (SHIT).

Name: Premam
Review:
Premam released right before I was about to begin my first year of college, so I was able to experience firsthand just how big of a cultural phenomenon this movie was. I've seen no other Malayalam movie make the impact that Premam had made, and it still maintains its longevity; it's still infinitely rewatchable, and along with the cultural impact, I also have so many memories associated with this movie, its music, and its moments that rewatching Premam also felt like revisiting a version of myself, if that makes any sense.

Yes, it is an episodic collection of three short films. Alphonse Puthren hasn't followed any conventional format in writing and cutting together this movie, and sometimes it's even so random, but it works beautifully. The whole thing has so much life poured into it. Most of the cast consists of Puthren's friends, and you can just tell that a lot of the movie has their lived-in experiences put into it. The characters feel so real, and their banter and interactions feel so real despite us not knowing much about them. There's all sorts of detailing and teeny tiny touches that Puthren has added in that add so much to this world and breathe so much life into it, but at the same time it has a gleefully cheesy energy; the songs have a distinct filmy energy; there are lots of crazy framing and blocking choices that nobody else does; there's the "butterfly" cinematography by Anend C Chandran and the eternally iconic score from Rajesh Murugesan and Govind Vasantha. I can probably write a "Why Premam is a masterpiece" thesis if I go on.

The movie is lighthearted for the most part, but the little bit of drama that hits during the second chapter still makes me cry ugly. Whether it's the music piece Unfinished Hope by Govind Vasantha or the way Puthren has shot and edited together that sequence and that montage, it gets the melancholy across perfectly. We haven't even seen George and Malar being a proper couple, but the movie is so damn successful in visually conveying that feeling of budding love and then the heartbreak of losing it. The final glance that George and Malar share was also a great emotional payoff (La La Land came after Premam, and I remember the ending glance in La La Land reminding me of Premam).

Despite college-era George having this macho alpha exterior, he's still a softie inside; he's a sensitive person, he gets shy, he has this playful way of flirting with Malar, and when he's heartbroken, he cries. Portraying George as this sensitive and emotional being adds so much to him as a character, rather than being just another alpha male fantasy cutout (there is some amount of male fantasy here too of course). Though most dudes ended up channeling the kalippan part of college George in their personalities while I was in college. We even had the college chairman saying in his speech on the first day of college that Premam is the kind of film that spoils the youth and that nobody should imitate George from Premam. I took that advice seriously, BTW. I'm only two years away from being 30, and I'm nowhere close to being a successful café owner. Anyways, this was 2015; neither Sandeep Reddy Vanga nor Andrew Tate had infected Mallu youth yet, so we had a pookie romantic like George David being public enemy no. 1 because he drank and smoked in college and got into fights.

Lines or moments from this movie are still used in memes or quoted in everyday life. This movie is the reason why a black shirt and mundu became THE onam dress code for mallus for almost a decade. There are movies that might've made more money than Premam, but the cultural impact and the impact this movie made on the youth, I've not seen anything come close to that scale. Alphonse Puthren really made something special, and while popular movies are shifting more towards loud, violent action movies, I'm so glad that this wholesome Poompatta padam is among one of the biggest movies in Malayalam cinema. I don't think anyone else can make a Premam; I'm not sure if even Puthren himself can make something like this again.

Watching Premam brings back so many memories, like how the soundtrack was playing in my head as I pursued my college crush (ouch) and how the first ragging assignment that I got from seniors was to take a Java class for them like how Vimal sir would and how our actual Java professor started the subject by saying "Java athra simple alla" (I failed Java on the first attempt, btw). If I start going on about how this movie has been a part of my life, I might have to write a whole-ass autobiography.

Butterflies are mentally mental, and so was Premam.

Name: Valkyrie
Review:
On watching this after an MI marathon, what struck me here is the fact that the basic structure of this movie is so similar to the way McQ had written his Mission: Impossible movies. We have a mission with impossible stakes here too, which is to kill Hitler and take back control of Germany from the Nazis. Half of the movie is expositionary exchanges about the plan, how to get it done, and what the steps required to get it done are, and then we see that plan in motion. But unlike Mission: Impossible, where Ethan Hunt beats the odds and succeeds in getting it done, here Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg and his team fail in their mission. This isn't a spoiler, as we know Tom Cruise didn't kill Hitler; Hitler killed Hitler. Plus, the text shown at the beginning makes it clear that this isn't going to be an alternate history kind of situation either.

So the enjoyment of Valkyrie depends on how invested one is in seeing a doomed mission unfold; it's anticlimactic, just like it was IRL. Also, all the action is through analog communication and conversations; there's not much "action" action. Tom Cruise doesn't even do the run here, even when there are explosions in the beginning. I felt that Bryan Singer's direction and narrative style should've been more panicky and frantic, like this should've unfolded more like an Uncut Gems; then maybe the tension and anxiety could've been dialed up even when we know that these men are going to fail. But yeah, what they did was very brave and they deserve respect for trying to end an oppressive regime from within by putting their lives on the line. 

It was nice to see a toned-down and subtle performance from Cruise. I didn't really care about the accents and all.

Name: Karate Kid: Legends
Review:
The Cobra Kai show was already the best follow-up the Karate Kid franchise could get. It took characters and storylines from even the less loved films and used them to create something special. It subverted, parodied, and paid tribute to the underdog story formula of the Karate Kid movies with enough cheesiness, melodrama, and self-awareness that the whole thing was always fun, I cared about those characters and the drama worked. This movie comes just a few months after Cobra Kai had ended, so of course my mind would make comparisons.

This is a pretty short movie, and it moves at a super fast pace. But the thing is, there's too much plot going on here for a 90-minute movie, and the rapid pace means the drama doesn't strike hard. I don't know if a lot of scenes were just cut away to make the movie shorter and faster paced. Basically there are two movies here; one is a reverse Karate Kid, where the kid becomes the teacher for an older man, with even a version of the Karate Kid scene where the sensei saves the kid from his bullies with the roles reversed. Then there's the second movie, which sticks pretty close to the OG formula where Li, who is a Kung Fu martial artist, must fight in a karate tournament, and Mr. Han and Daniel LaRusso join together to train him. The way these two movies intersect kind of makes no sense. Han just quickly shows up to New York, recruits LaRusso, they start training, and the tournament happens—it's all in the blink of an eye.

The other Karate Kid movies (the better ones) all operated with simple plotlines, but the drama and character work always hit the right notes. Here, the initial setup was good: how Li adjusts to his new city, finds new people, and how their problems become his problems—that was all fine. But the selling point of this movie was the Jackie Chan and Ralph Macchio crossover, and the movie's crumbling point is sadly when that happens too. Everything is just moving too fast then. This should either have been done as two separate movies, or it should've been a season of television like Cobra Kai. Because, you know, the plot beats here make sense; it's just that the movie becomes too fast after a point, whether it's the rival dojo, the loan shark situation, Li's grief, Han's decision to come to America and train Li for this tournament as a solution, Li's mom's disapproval of him fighting, or the connection between Miyagi and Han. All these plot beats make sense, but in this movie, the drama just ends up being weak as they're all just glossed over.

There are moments of fun here, though; the training montage had good moments of comedy, and the banter between Han and LaRusso was also great, but again, at the pace this movie's going, there's not enough of anything, not even the good stuff. LaRusso even appears very late into the movie, though he's literally in the poster. We don't even spend enough time with him to see him managing with New York and the new people there. He's just a part of the gang and just there. This is especially a bummer when, out of all these characters, LaRusso is the one who had multiple years' worth of character development going for him. Mr. Han is featured more in this movie, but even he doesn't get to do as much as he did in the 2010 movie. Ben Wang makes a promising debut, though; he's great in the fight scenes, and his body language is perfect to portray a martial artist. He even displays some Jackie Chan energy during the alleyway fight. His acting and line delivery need work, but he'll get there. The action was pretty nice here, but then again, the tournament at the end of Cobra Kai hit its emotional highs and payoffs so perfectly that something tamer like this feels like more of a bummer.

Underwhelming, but fun. 

The cameo at the end had me giggling, though. Badass energy, fr.

Name: Mountainhead
Review:
It's not so much satirical when you know that the real-life tech billionaires are completely capable of fucking up the world like what's shown in this movie. Anyways, the movie was an interesting watch, and there's some sharp commentary on Gen AI, social media misinformation, how it can literally lead to the apocalypse, and how indifferent these billionaires are to death and destruction that won't affect them in any way. The thing is, the conversations that they have here, and even that whole plan of taking over the world? It doesn't seem so far-fetched.

All four leads were great; there were some hilarious exchanges and dialogue. Jesse Armstrong has definitely infused this with Succession energy. The movie does get a bit repetitive towards the middle, but then three of them get together to plan something, and the rest of the movie is again hilarious. Steve Carell's freak-outs were giving me flashbacks of the good old Michael Scott days at times.

Name: The Family Star
Review:
There were these Malayalam Jayaram movies in the early 2000s, where Jayaramettan would play this perfect family man person, who's everything to his family, the epitome of care and love, and would slap his romantic partner at least once. The Family Star, in that sense, felt like Sandeep Reddy Vanga's Jayaramettan, just without the penis fetish. Nobody else is obsessed with dick like Vanga in Indian cinema; sorry, Parasuram, you don't have the dick commitment to be SRV adjacent.

Don't get me wrong, this is a shitty movie, but this is the kind of shitty movie that could've been a good movie. Firstly, the music and songs by Gopi Sundar were good and reminded me of the time when this dude peaked over here in Malayalam. Then, Vijay Devarakonda is actually a good actor, but for some reason he can't help doing shitty films and characters. Mrunal Thakur tries to give a good performance too and looks gorgeous, of course, but unlike Sita Ramam, here the writing is too bad for just the romantic chemistry to save the movie. Even with a pretty good soundtrack.

Now, about the movie, somewhere buried deep within layers and layers of shit is a good plot that examines the class system and how the elite perceive the middle class. There's an anthropology element here too. While the inclusion of anthropology and a thesis is laughable in the film itself, it kills me that there was a deeper plot here that Parasuram didn't even realize. Firstly, it's supposed to be about a middle-class family man, but the portrayal of the middle class here just seems so distant from the actual middle class. Like, despite the main character's financial situation and his tight spending routine being shown, the movie itself feels like a privileged person's fantasy of the middle class rather than the actual middle class. Vijay Devarakonda's protagonist seems so far away from being middle class from the very beginning. 

The main character, Govardhan, is supposed to be a perfect, loving, emotional gem of a man whom others should see as a true representation of a common man and as a superhero and role model. Just that there's a moment in the movie where, as a response to a loan shark saying that he'd forget about a loan if Govardhan's sister-in-law slept with him, Govardhan takes his entire family to the loan shark's place on an auto (I have no idea how 3 women and 6 children fit in that single auto). Then Govardhan tells the kids to pay attention as he's going to teach them a lesson. Then this guy beats up the loan shark's goons in front of these kids, blood and broken bones all around, and then, in front of the kids and the women of the family, Govardhan threatens to sexually assault the women in the loan shark's family. This scene is so bad, and it makes Govardhan seem like such a terrible person, and yet the movie never addresses how wrong everything he did in this scene was, and it then keeps on reinforcing this idea that he's this perfect gem of a person till the very end. No amount of emotional manipulation or long monologues about how loving this person is can work when your idea of heroism was him making a rape threat, and his emotional outbursts include slapping and shouting at a woman. That's just Sandeep Reddy Vanga universe behavior that has nothing to do with the whole wholesome family man persona they're trying to show here. Later on in the movie, when Govardhan himself is being harassed by some women and he's clearly shown to be uncomfortable, that's shown as being comedic by the movie.

All the fight scenes are bad and seem like they're making this seem like a parody movie. And the way the fights are so cartoonish also distances Govardhan away from the middle-class family man persona that they're apparently showing him to be. He's a psychopath, and idk why his family doesn't ever acknowledge this. This movie's version of a middle-class person trying to be upper class is him buying an iPhone and throwing his Android phone to the ground. But this movie is so fucking stupid that it's definitely not a critique on how certain brands are also associated with how class is perceived by people.

I've seen so many types of betrayals and dramas in shitty movies, but this is the first shitty movie to bring an anthropology thesis to be the central conflict. The whole thesis situation is so hilarious. It's some of the most fun this movie was (ironically, of course). The least fun and objectively horrible parts were whenever it tried to show Govardhan being intimidating and during all the action scenes, including the rape threat out of nowhere. And while being about the class system on a surface level, it ends up being a "money will solve everything" kind of movie, in a bad way. I don't think for a second that Parasuram actually had any idea about the complex themes while writing this.

Govardhan is shown as a very intelligent person in the movie, but he's such a fucking idiot. His idea of representing Indian culture was building houses with Savarna Hindu aesthetics in the US. India is not just Savarna Hindus, moron! And yet, everyone in the movie thinks it's brilliant. He's also the kind of idiot who will join to work in a company named Indu Group without even doing a Google search on who that Indu is. 

Fuck you, Govardhan, you're not a Family Star; you're a Family Scar. No family should have a Govardhan, and no middle-class person should try to be a Govardhan; that should be the only message here.

Name: Thug Life
Review:
This movie had all the makings of something that they were just making up as they were going. I don't know if that's what happened here, of course, but this movie just seemed so lazy, dumb, and insincere. It cannot be compared on any level with Mani Rathnam and Kamal's best work; hell, even something like Chekka Chivantha Vaanam is a far superior gangster drama than whatever this is.

The plotline and the various twists and turns are all nothing new in the gangster genre, but even if that's the case, a well-written screenplay, good characters, and filmmaking choices would've saved this film. The first half felt comfortably mid, an inferior version of Chekka Chivantha Vaanam. CCV understood what it was, the dynamics of the brothers, how the outsider Rasool fit in, and the power struggle; it was all developed enough, and the movie was thrilling enough. Here, every character, including the leads Shakthivel and Amaran, was shallow. The characters repeating their own names over and over again doesn't add any depth to them; it just makes them seem like Pokémon. 

The big dramatic turn occurs when a conflict with an opposing gang and a power struggle within Shakthivel's gang lead to a betrayal. It's a familiar Julius Caesar moment in a gangster drama; the movie even leans in on the Shakespearean influence by having an "Et tu, Brute?" moment too (not quite a spoiler when the trailer and the posters have spelled it out). But the whole betrayal just comes out of nowhere, with characters willing to jump ship so quickly that we're meant to believe this gang and their relationship were so fragile. But like I said, comfortably mid till then. 

And then, the second half happens. For a few minutes we see the opening of Johnny English Reborn on screen, with Kamal Haasan even looking like Johnny English, just that we don't see him pulling a rock with his testicles. I have no idea what kind of thought went into putting together Shakthivel's look in the second half, especially when Kamal was already trolled for a similar look in Indian 2. This is pretty much the same thing, just without thicc prosthetics. This guy has the most out-of-place-looking hair and costumes for the rest of the movie. The movie is supposed to be dead serious, but I audibly laughed a few times Shakthivel appeared on screen in his monk look. Sorry, KH. 😭

There are betrayals, death, grief, and all sorts of things happening, and I felt nothing. Even the action seemed basic, apart from that one-on-one brawl between Shakthivel and Amaran at the end. But that brawl itself was unnecessary, and the buildup to it was so weak that even that fight scene is wasted. The ending too is so stupid on so many levels because there's no way those characters have lived their lives for so long in the same place without discovering each other, especially when one of them is the most notorious gangster in the area whose origins are known by everyone. And yeah, Ali Faizal plays a villain who randomly spawns out of nowhere in the movie at times that my mind went, "Nee evidunnu vannedaa malambhoothamey?" The female characters are badly written and just there as an extension of the men and to get killed. One of them even has a meta line of dialogue where she says that these women are there just in service of the men. 

A. R. Rahman has provided a good soundtrack for this movie; Anju Vanna Poove is a beautiful track, and that song is the heart of the movie. The rest of the soundtrack and the score? I don't even know if the songs and that score were meant for this movie because they seemed so out of sync with what's happening on screen a lot of the time. Even some basic conversation scenes are overscored with music that sounds so out of place. Even though Anju Vanna Poove is a beautiful track, when it appeared in a highly emotional moment at the end, it just seemed comical to me. The editing, too, was weird at times. One that I remember is during that scene on the beach with Amaran and Indrani, where there were random inserts of Silambarasan and Trisha standing on the beach together in the middle of their conversation. It felt like when people try to recreate Mani Rathnam frames on Instagram, but just that this is Mani Ratnam himself doing the same 😭. The way some of the dramatic scenes have been executed here makes no sense. They mostly border on unintentional humor. The bad CGI doesn't help either. 

Nayakan was the Tamil adaptation of The Godfather. This one, with its whole setup, reminded me of The Sopranos, the Shakthivel-Amaran relationship that had shades of Tony and Christopher. Shakthivel's marriage and mistress situation also reminded me of the Sopranos, as did the power struggle here. Just that the drama here was so badly executed that it threw all that potential that a Kamal-Mani Ratnam reunion had out of the window.

In the end, it's just a movie where nothing quite fits in, not even the title Thug Life. It's the kind of disappointment that made me feel sad.

Name: Jaat
Review: I won't say "SORRY BOL!!!" to the people involved in making this shit because I chose to watch this shit despite being aware of exactly what kind of shit it is. JAAT: 2 Idly 2 Furious is a romantic revenge saga of an angry man seeking revenge for his idlis, and on the way he realizes that he must save 40 villages and India too, but he was already beating up people in the name of idly anyway, priorities. I guess they were trying to put a quirky spin on the Yojimbo/A Fistful of Dollars formula of a badass stranger arriving in a village controlled by ruthless villains and ending up saving it. We have Sunny Deol beating up people and asking them to say sorry for knocking down his idlis for half of the movie. And no, dirty minds, idly is not code for his balls; it's literally just idlis. This is not a Vanga movie for having male genitalia erotica. Anyway, the movie begins by showing some police officers going to arrest the main antagonist, Ranatunga. We'll never forget the name Ranatunga because every character finds some excuse to say that name, and even Thaman's background score screams Ranatunga. Ranatunga is ruthless; he'd murder people without a second thought. Ranatunga is super rich but still stupid enough to have a big, framed, AI-generated image on his wall. Whoever conned the ruthless Ranatunga into paying for that AI image, thinking it's an actual painting, is the real hero, not Idly Wick. Anyway, as these police officers approach the villain's house, all the men are afraid to go anywhere near there, and they run away. Only the women remain. The women bravely march into the villain's house to arrest him. At this point I'm thinking this is going to be some Atlee-style woke situation, but I was wrong; it's a Telugu cinema-style misogyny situation. These women immediately get stripped of their clothes and sexually assaulted because "they're women." And this line is spoken by Ranatunga's wife, played by Regina Cassandra. If that's this movie's idea of female representation and empowerment, it's disgusting. So that's the kind of female representation here. Every woman is either sexually assaulted or murdered; not even minors are left alone. Telugu cinema has been stuck in this cycle of regressiveness and dated sensibilities for a long time, and instead of evolving, that formula is just spreading all over Indian cinema because of its cash-grabby possibilities. S. S. Rajamouli made a Baahubali, and now there's a Balayya movie without Balayya in Bollywood, but tbh, even recent Balakrishna movies had better sensibilities than this shit. Jaat is by no means a Bollywood movie; it's a Telugu movie through and through. Most of the supporting cast are Telugu actors, most of the principal crew are Telugu, the thing is set in Andhra Pradesh, and Sunny Deol is essentially just playing Sunny Deol as Balayya here. I'm pretty sure this thing was written for Balayya. About our protagonist, apart from being an Idli lover, he's also an India lover, and he's also a Lord Ram lover traveling in a train to Babri Masj.. Ahem, Ayodhya, though the Ram thing doesn't even matter to the rest of the movie. Basically he's a hypermasculine dude who fits a very conservative right-wing mold of what a man should be. He will protect and stand for women, but not by supporting controversial non-sanskari stuff like feminism or something. During his introduction, he's eating an idly from an old woman's shop, a goon knocks it down, he asks the goon to say sorry, and when the goon doesn't, he destroys the old lady's shop while beating up all the goons. That's the most feminist thing he does in the movie because by destroying the old lady's livelihood, he's saving her from the patriarchal constraints she was living under. Fly, Grandma, fly! The fight scenes were more Jai Sunnyayya than Dhaai Kilo Ka Haath. It's the expected kind of Telugu cinema action with a superhuman protagonist, which is fun for those who are into it. But pretty soon I got bored of these repetitive, one-sided fight scenes of goons just flying and bouncing. The villain is built up to be cruel and ruthless by showing him kill a whole lot of people, but even he's just a bug for Dhaai Kilo Ka Haath. There are literally no stakes in these movies; there's only one way to go. There's an entire fight scene in a police station with the sentence "Respect the Ladies" on its wall, and this movie's version of female empowerment is so regressive and condescending that it borders on being a satire. The movie also has the thing where supporting characters randomly hype up the protagonist. Bulldozer Saar, Patriot Saar, Tiger Saar won all wars in the world, Saar... Saar.... Thaman also blasts surplus Balayya background score here. This movie is so loud that my windows started shaking. Sunny Deol only speaks in catchphrases here, and it's so obvious that the dialogues have been translated from Telugu. Also, our protagonist is the kind of hero who'd save people only after getting them killed. He'd wait for his intro till a few more people get killed for emotional impact. He loves his idly... ahem... country (add some jingoism on steroids) and the women of the country a lot. Just don't let him eat in your restaurant. The old lady with the idly stall got the worst trade deals in the history of trade deals. Even if she gave him two more idlis for free, it'd have been less of a loss for her than when he destroys the entire store afterwards. It was satisfying to see the director and star of Swatantrya Veer Savarkar getting the shit beat out of him, of course.

Name: Chotta Mumbai
Review:
It's been ten years or more since I've watched Chotta Mumbai in its entirety. I had watched it in the theaters back then as a kid, and then I got the Moserbaer DVD for this movie that I rewatched on a regular basis. I even remember what the DVD menu music was. Now, while watching the theatrical re-release, most of the scenes, shots (no pun intended 😭), dialogues, jokes, one-liners, background score, sound effects, and even certain scene transitions are still burned into my subconsciousness like I've never stopped rewatching it.

I've always referred to Chotta Mumbai as the last great A10 movie that utilized him as a star. Thala is a standalone character who doesn't need references to Mohanlal's career. Added to that, he has character quirks, a personality, and a vulnerability of his own rather than just being a superstar avatar person. The movie itself is a perfect blend of commercial cinema sensibilities, comedy, melodrama, action, and immaculate vibes. Anwar Rasheed has such a great eye for crafting these great, fun buildups, like how the Thala intro remains iconic. It's the kind of commercial cinema sensibility that was unique to him, and it was not just about copying what Tamil cinema, Telugu cinema, or Kannada cinema were doing. Anwar Rasheed later stepped back from this zone since Ustad Hotel, though the energy from Rajamanikyam and Chotta Mumbai was present in one of his production ventures, Aavesham, of course.

Chotta Mumbai has aged better than most films from that era; only a few bits haven't aged well, like all those SA jokes. Also, we needed more of Parakkum Latha. Kalabhavan Mani as Nateshan was also a great and memorable villain; he just shifted the mood of the movie from fun and jovial whenever he came on screen. 

That soundtrack is also one that's always been in my playlist for years, from iPod to Spotify.

Cochin Carnival peeps were unhinged for carrying on with their New Year celebrations even as a man got crushed and burned to death right in front of their eyes. 

I'm big on theater etiquette and all, but re-releases like these are also meant for the vibes, so people getting out and dancing to the songs and the vibes being recorded on video get a pass from me in this particular case. 🙈

Name: Hurry Up Tomorrow
Review:
Hurry Up Tomorrow felt like it was conflicted in between being a film and a music video. The ideas here are fine for a music video, the cinematography is gorgeous, the editing is good on a technical level, and there are some well-directed scenes here like that opening Wake Me Up performance, but again, the writing and filmmaking seemed to be in conflict with whether this is a film or a music video.

Our main character is The Weeknd, played by Abel Tesfaye. He was alright. I'm unable to call Abel Tesfaye a bad actor for this performance for a number of reasons. Firstly, he's playing himself here; only Abel Tesfaye knows how Abel Tesfaye emotes; we've only seen The Weeknd. Also, on a personal level, I cringe whenever I see videos of myself because I have the weirdest, non-photogenic body language and expressions. So if either a professional actor or I am to portray me on screen, it'd have to look as awkward as I am in those videos, and in turn it'd look like bad, cringey acting. So in that sense, I'm watching this performance and thinking, what if this is just how Abel Tesfaye is irl? So how can I call this bad acting?

But the thing is, we don't know anything about this fictional version of Abel Tesfaye. He's going through a breakup, he's suffering from insomnia and depression, and he has a weird relationship with his manager. His relationship with his mother is mentioned, but we don't get enough context on that either. I don't know anything about the real Abel apart from listening to his music. Everything shown about Abel's inner turmoil, sadness, and trauma—yeah, I didn't get that; I just saw this rich and famous sad boi, and he was no Bojack Horseman. The same goes for Jenna Ortega as Anima too, though her performance is great and adds so much to an otherwise hollow character. We get to know little to nothing about these characters. Even the whole modern retelling of Stephen King's Misery with the meta twist of the celebrity being played by himself is nice, but this movie just doesn't treat even that nicely. Barry Keoghan is wasted as well.

All that said, these ideas would've worked better as a music video, but as a film, when the film is trying to build an emotional narrative, there must be an effort to flesh out the characters more. I'm sure it was traumatic and humiliating when The Weeknd lost his voice mid-concert IRL, but even that moment looked sadder in audience videos of the real-life incident than in its recreation here. When it happens in the movie, he just leaves and randomly hangs out with a fan from the crowd. Idk. 

The music was great, though, whether it's the score or The Weeknd's songs being used on the soundtrack.

I'd like to know what kind of creative thought went into the scene where Jenna Ortega dances to The Weeknd's songs when The Weeknd is tied to a bed. Hmm…

Name: Big B
Review:
Malayalam cinema wasn't ready for a stoic badass and the deadpan one-liners in 2007. Even I wasn't then, I liked Ikka as a Rajamanikyam or Gulan kind of character at the time, and Bilal, to me as a kid, just seemed boring. But kids are wrong about so much stuff.

On revisiting Big B, Bilal is the best thing about this movie. Firstly, the look and style of this movie is something Malayalam cinema wasn't familiar with, and though Amal Neerad's filmmaking in his debut is a bit rough, when it works, it's massss. The plot of Four Brothers isn't all that special; what made this movie cool is the stuff Unni R., Amal Neerad, and Ikka added onto it rather than whatever Marky Mark and his brothers did in the original. Bilal is both a grieving son and a vengeful badass, and the kind of energy Mammootty brings into the role with the deadpan delivery and body language is pretty amazing. He emotes so much with his eyes, and also he rarely even smiles in the movie. The smiles I noted were during the flashbacks with Mary Teacher and towards the end as he imagines Mary Teacher looking at him from the house. 

A character like Bilal works on a thin line and can easily be perceived as being monotonous and uninteresting, like what I initially thought as a child. But almost every single line he speaks is either darkly humorous or plain badass, and then the "Yo Big B" music kicks in—absolute cinema.

More than wanting to see him be Bilal again, watching Big B made me feel how I'd love to see Mammootty do deadpan humor, because I never realized how funny Bilal actually was. Ikka could pull off something like De Niro's character from Meet the Parents to perfection (we can forget De Niro from Analyze This becoming Current Bhargavan for now), or even a dark crime comedy or something.

Name: The Surfer
Review:
Nic Cage is the Surfer, but he doesn't get to surf, and he goes insane over not getting to surf. The initial buildup felt like it'd eventually lead to Nic Cage beating up or even killing the dudes who are ganging up on him and bullying him. But he just takes all the bullying, embarrassment, and multiple levels of fuck-ups, pain, and suffering to transform into a psychotic person, even questioning his own reality. Yeah, shit gets real fast. He gets plenty of opportunities to leave the place, but he just doesn't. And by the end, this is more of a psychological piece than a revenge movie, with Nic Cage doing unspeakable things to a rat. Though the villains here are a bunch of rich alpha dude bro surfers, this is more eat the rat than eat the rich, literally.

The setting does offer Nic Cage plenty of opportunities to unleash the Cage Rage. The way the protagonist unravels and loses his sanity is the kind of Cageness he excels in, and the movie pulls it off really well. Also, I get the larger themes at play here too, how joining the oppressors seems like the easier choice than actually fighting against oppression. But the ending could've packed more of a punch.

EEEEEAAAAATTTT THE RATTTTTTT!!!!!!

Name: Viduthalai: Part I
Review: Director's Cuts of Part 1 and Part 2 It takes a Vetri Maaran to do an ACAB commie movie with a cop as the protagonist. (compliment) Kumaresan becomes a cop with very idealistic ambitions of helping people and being a hero. But pretty soon he realizes that the system that he's a part of won't let him or any cop be a hero no matter how well-intentioned they are. They're made to commit crimes and be complicit in horrible crimes and atrocities, and they're no better than the criminals they're trying to capture. Kumaresan finds humanity only with the woman he falls in love with, and even that eventually leads to tragic consequences. Though this movie and the subject matter is dead serious, I found some fun in the way Kumaresan escapes from getting killed without even realising it during multiple instances, like he's a Looney Tunes character or something xD. In Part 1, just like my first watch, the only thing that seemed out of place was Raja's music at times. But the music situation was better in Part 2. There are some beautiful songs and background score pieces here, I'm not invalidating the entire score BTW. Viduthalai braves to show the ugly reality. It blurs the lines between who's the real terrorist. Is it the ones fighting for freedom against oppression and exploitation, or is it the oppressors who murder and torture the people while wearing uniforms? This is why showing the militant leader Perumaal's story and perspective seemed important in Part 2. Perumaal's story involves a big transformation: he goes from being betrayed by the system to trying to fight the system and its oppressors from within as a communist leader, and then getting radicalized, and then finally realizing that the ideology that speaks for the oppressed and the working class is bigger than any one individual or group. Perumaal's politics and his whole journey are very integral to the narrative, and they connect to everything. The irony is very clear when the system doesn't care about people and casualties, but the "terrorists" do. A good amount of philosophical debate and political theory is there in the movie, and so it becomes the closest thing I've seen recently in Indian cinema to something like Spike Lee's Malcolm X. There are a few technical issues here and there, and Tamizharasi's fate is left hanging. Some of the dialogue is a bit on the nose; I'm not talking about the political themes—those being direct is almost a necessity—but there were some other instances of clunky exposition as well. But this is important cinema. The politics and the reality shown here are important; the way it questions and exposes the system is important. Perumaal's journey starts and ends the same way when we think about it, and that whole ending stretch was very hard-hitting. "Ideas are bulletproof"

Name: Ronth
Review:
For almost a third of this movie, I felt like it was going to be a Shahi Kabir movie that I'd actually like, but no, then the end stretch happens with exactly the kind of elements that made me hate Shahi Kabir's previous work.

I liked the whole idea of following two cops during their night patrol on a single day, the combination of the veteran with the idealistic rookie, and how what they encounter is a mix of the mundane, often funny, and often dark and depressing. It's this grounded portrayal of police work that we rarely see being portrayed on screen.

There is even an instance where the veteran tells the rookie to keep his communism and social justice away from his uniform when he gets angry with a privileged brat, as the police have no choice but to be in service of the privileged. He also says stuff like how people fear the police not because of cases or courts but because of the fear of getting beaten up. It's a justification of police violence, of course, but we get where he's coming from, yk, that's just how the system conditions cops over here (That line's intentions are still sus though, especially when considering how the sensibilities in Shahi Kabir's previous body of work were). Dileesh Pothan embodies the character perfectly, whether it's the body language or the dialogue delivery.
