As a trope of the genre, he has a tragic backstory, but the performance is so good that even though one starts to hate the way he behaves to his rookie colleague, there's depth to him, and he does understand being a cop more than the rookie, as a scene involving Dileesh Pothan's character and his performance was the only saving grace in a finale that I otherwise hated. Pothan's Yohannan felt more like a proper working-class police officer than the abusive psychopath from Officer on Duty, a big upgrade. Roshan Mathew was also good as the rookie police officer who's yet to experience the harder parts of the job. Some of the situations they have to encounter are interesting, and the fear in Roshan's character felt real. There are some very well-directed scenes here and some that are very depressing. There's also a scene in a dark house that was very atmospheric and horror-core. 

So the movie progresses while we see these two officers on their night patrol, with some interesting cases, some tension and banter, and some moments of bonding. There's one big case going on in the background since the very beginning, and that's where the movie then falls apart towards the end. At the end, the movie becomes a repeat of what Nayattu was; it makes systemic oppression towards dalits just a plot device to show cops as victims, other than properly addressing the system and holding it accountable. The whole ending stretch is so lackluster and has all the issues of Shahi Kabir writing this from the perspective of a police officer, while his lived-in experience as a cop is what made everything before that good. I watched this movie right after finishing Viduthalai, so it's easy for me to see how Viduthalai directly addresses and questions the system and addresses the dalit community, while this movie, "cinematic universe" or no, just inherits everything wrong with Nayattu with that end stretch. Plus, the random forced tragedy angle just for shock value at the end doesn't help.

This would've been a 3.5 to 4 movie if that ending stretch didn't exist. The night cinematography looked cool, the performances were great, and Shahi Kabir is a good director, but I just wish he'd have some co-writer who'd help to filter out the koppness from his copness.

Name: Ace
Review:
This felt like a failed attempt at executing something like Soodhu Kaavvum with nothing that made Soodhu Kaavvum special. Vijay Sethupathi is given a bland character, Yogi Babu is given an annoying character, and neither of them could save the badly written characters just with their performances, though Vijay Sethupathi tries his best to do his cute wholesome softboi mannerisms during the romance portions. We should've just gotten a straightforward romantic comedy with him and Rukmini ideally. Even the mystique behind VJS' protagonist falls flat. The attempt to make him seem like a super smart man with a plan doesn't work. The movie started off with a potential for fun, the romantic subplot was cute, but then it just became so absurd, in a bad way. There's a poker game, a heist, and a lottery win back-to-back. I did like the idea of the graphics shown during the poker game with the winning chances, though. It was way more effective to make a civilian like me who doesn't understand poker understand the game on screen than how it was to see the poker game in Casino Royale. The movie also suffers from the Money Heist professor syndrome of dumb luck masquerading as a brilliant plan. The dumb writing in this movie is off the charts. Some of the comedy stuff felt more frustrating than funny. 

Anyway, as much as I'm a fan of Vijay Sethupathi, the main reason I watched this was because of Rukmini Vasanth (🥰🥰🥰). I think this is one of the better roles she got after Sapta Sagaradaache Ello, but just like with VJS and Yogi Babu, she too doesn't get more to do as a capable performer, but she was soo 🎀🎀🎀🎀🎀🧡.

[Spoiler] 
The best part of this movie is when everyone completely understands why VJS would rob a bank for Rukmini Vasanth, including Rukmini Vasanth.

Name: How to Train Your Dragon
Review:
I have mixed feelings about remaking animated films into live action. Disney has been doing it for more than a decade, and it's the first time DreamWorks is stepping into it, and it manages to be better than most of Disney's efforts. TBH, How to Train Your Dragon is indeed something that translates well into live action compared to other DreamWorks films. I see no chance that a live-action Shrek or a live-action Madagascar would ever happen, and if it does, it'd be a disaster. This movie manages to recapture everything that was good about the original; it captures the heart, wholesomeness and fun of it, which is the most important thing. The creator of the original animated trilogy being the writer-director here helps, of course. Dean DeBlois gets it. 

One of the best decisions here is making the dragon design and animations exactly the same as the original. They are given a photorealistic CGI upgrade, of course, and they blend together so well with the real sets, real locations, and actors. Removing the expressiveness from the animals to make them seem "real" was the worst part of Disney's Jungle Book and Lion King remakes, where the animals were CGI anyway. The visual effects work is so good, and they pull off making an otherwise cartoonish-looking Toothless seem like an actual living creature. The behavior and movements of the dragons are an exact copy of the original, of course. Toothless, in specific, seems more like a cat than a reptile compared to the other dragons. Towards the end, Toothless even becomes a doggy.

This is like too faithful a remake, as some scenes are even shot-by-shot recreations of the original; even the dialogues are the same. There are a few additions, and that climatic scene with the Kaiju dragon felt bigger in scale here than in the original. The live-action cast is also good, and it's very easy to see them as the new versions of their animated counterparts, with the exception of Gerald Butler, who just gets to play the character that he originally voiced in the flesh. The movie also looks very beautiful, and the visual effects, animation, and production design look great. John Powell returns with an updated version of the original score too; that flight test scene is still a delight, both as 3D animation and as... well, 3D animation with a live-action actor composited on it.

Anyway, even if it's cash grabby to have a remake of a 15-year-old movie, Dean DeBlois and the team didn't half-ass this effort. It recaptures what made the original special pretty well, the visual effects are great, Toothless with the photorealistic detail is still cute af, it was a fun, wholesome watch and I had a great time.

Best of all, I can con my friend, who avoids animated movies, to watch How to Train Your Dragon now, though this movie is still mostly animated xD.

Name: Final Destination Bloodlines
Review:
I just loved how unserious, goofy, and self-aware this movie is. It's been some time since I've watched a Final Destination movie, but I don't remember them being this hilarious. The plotline itself is grim and dark and involves an entire family being targeted by death, but it's just so funny. There's funny banter between the actors, the gory deaths have some kind of goofy spin on them to make them seem like gory Looney Tunes, and the whole movie is just such fun. The gore effects and CGI are pretty solid, the performances and the characters are quirky and interesting, and all the deaths and death buildups were awesome. There were multiple deaths that made me laugh out loud. I don't know if that makes me a psychopath (especially the one early on that involves a piano). There are dark and shocking deaths too, of course. This is the perfect movie to watch with a crowd, so I'm so angry that the cinema near my home didn't have it. 

Also, the Tony Todd farewell was very wholesome and heartfelt. RIP, legend.

Name: Friendship
Review:
I've been a fan of Tim Robinson and his specific brand of cringe comedy ever since I randomly discovered his sketch show I Think You Should Leave on Netflix. Friendship, written and directed by Andrew DeYoung, shares a lot of its energy with I Think You Should Leave. Well, firstly, the main character, Craig Waterman, played by Tim Robinson, is in every scene of the movie, and he's our POV character. We're following this socially awkward and misguided man from one uncomfortable situation to another as he struggles for approval, acceptance, love, and just some good company.

I started watching this movie expecting a comedy-drama, but sometimes it cut too deep on how it portrayed male loneliness and the protagonist's inability to form social connections. So at times Friendship was a horror movie where the situations Craig had to go through seemed too real. Whether it's his wife and son seeming like they're in their own world that he's not a part of, the joy of finding a new friend who takes him on exciting adventures that are new to him, the awkwardness in feeling like the odd man out with his new friend's existing friend circle and that feeling of not having any friends at work while his colleagues seem like they're all friends with each other, and then, how Craig's constant attempts for approval and to fit in just fall into self-sabotage, to the point of him engaging in self-destructive behavior. After a point I just wanted him to stop taking the worst possible decision during every single scenario. 

Like, these scenarios didn't just feel like setups for cringe humor. The emotions and Craig's insecurities seemed so real. Tim Robinson can be called a master of cringe humor; whether it's the awkward pauses, his reactions, or his body language, he can brilliantly make any scene look sad and uncomfortable while being funny. This is a funny movie, but the fun here depends on one's tolerance for secondhand embarrassment and uncomfortable social scenarios too. There's a deep sadness and loneliness in Craig; he's not just a funny character. The rest of the cast, including Kate Mara and Paul Rudd, were great too, though Paul Rudd's character felt so random in his behavior at times, while Craig's erratic behavior after a point at least made sense because of his desperation for validation and company. 

This is the anti-buddy movie in that sense. I felt that the movie succeeded in what it set out to do: show the uncomfortable, cringey, and sadder part of friendship, or the yearning for friendship, and also be funny. A good companion piece to The Banshees of Inisherin in the Male Loneliness Universe (MLU).

Name: The Phoenician Scheme
Review:
Michael Cera has fulfilled the reason for his existence. He truly is the chosen one. That whole scene with him in the forest was hilarious.

This is like corporate espionage, assassination attempts, death, slavery, communism, succession, and daddy issues, all wrapped into a silly and whimsical package because it's Wes Anderson. I had no idea that the next guy to do a plane crash scene after Tom Cruise will be Benicio Del Toro in a Wes Anderson movie. Also, great to hear an Alexandre Desplat score in a Wes movie again. It was very weird to see serious and heavy themes being treated so unseriously. But it was just so fun, and it just works. 😭

The acting was great across the whole cast.

Mia Threapleton is also a star in the making.

This is a 5-hand-grenades movie.

Name: Vyasanasametham Bandhumithradhikal
Review:
Despite being a comedy, this movie shows an extremely accurate Thekkan middle-class Savarna Hindu Maranaveedu. The depiction of a rural Hindu funeral in South Kerala is pretty accurate here; the village itself, the characters, the conflicts, the funny quirks—yes, there is a layer of comedic flair, but everything is so real at the same time. Written and directed by Vipin S, Vyasanasametham Bandhumithrathikal seemed more like a genuine movie and didn't seem like shallow and plastic reel compilations like a Vaazha or Guruvayoor Ambalanadayil.

The characters and the world were set up well; there's a band practice going on next door as the funeral is happening, and that music sometimes becomes the background score to the events happening at the funeral, and it's so well done. There's a lot of stuff happening at the same time with lots of characters, but it's still coherent and well structured; there's lots of cool detailing in the writing, the characters are memorable, and the performances are good (with a few exceptions), especially Anaswara, Azees, Noby, and a few other supporting actors. It manages to address grief despite being unserious, because the whole scenario is that the family is not even able to grieve properly because of all the dysfunction and chaos around them. The digs at NSS Karayogam and casteism were very accurate, and the movie also addresses sexism. Even the few pop culture references were nicely done. The movie is mostly silly, but when it gets a bit serious, that shift too is done nicely. 

There were plenty of laughs and fun. A lot of the situations were very relatable. The whole thing of the mom not getting names right reminded me of my own mother 😭❤️. The movie gets the specific Thekkan Kerala rural vibes very well, and the Trivandrum dialect everyone used sounded natural too. The movie sets up multiple subplots, but not all of them are resolved properly by the end. But as much as I thought the ending should've been better, it does shift back to being about the grieving, which was good. The movie has its heart in the right place for the most part; the rural character quirks seemed authentic, especially the women, as we don't see movies represent rural Malayali women like this, with their various quirks, often. 

It was fun and seemed more like an honest film than other Vipin Das Universe projects.

Name: Prince and Family
Review:
Sharis Mohammed is not that old, but he still manages to out-ammaavan actual ammaavans. This movie is all over the place before settling on something that resembles a narrative. The first half has an unmarried middle-aged man with the burden of providing for his whole family, including his brothers. He tries to get married, and he's struggling financially, has an inconsequential romantic subplot that wastes so much time on a joke that doesn't even land and just makes Prince seem more shallow, and then he finally gets married to a 24 year old. At this point this becomes an entirely different movie that's supposed to be a commentary on social media influencers that's not even really about the middle-aged protagonist at this point.

Some of the things in this movie are thoughts that have come to my mind as well, but Sharis' uncle gaze is so shitty that any potential that the movie had is in the trash. Like, I've thought about how influencers would draw a line between their life and their content when their life itself becomes their content. Another aspect here is that Prince's wife is half his age, and though the movie addresses Prince being an older man repeatedly, the generation gap that exists between them is also just unexplored (I shouldn't be this kind to a movie this shitty).

Anyway, Sharis treats a female influencer like she's a psychopath or an alien or something. It's not about whether she as a person is struggling with balancing her life with her public persona; she's reduced to just being that public persona. The movie never judges Prince, the way he rejects an older woman's proposal (who's still younger than him) and then emphasises how his young wife is just 24 repeatedly (to the degree of sounding creepy). Prince is just an innocent and sensitive gentleman full of love and kindness as far as the movie is concerned. But his influencer wife, Chinju, is not even treated as a person with feelings and emotions by the movie. She's heartless, soulless and only cares about followers, views, being viral and sponsorship collabs. There were these Jayaram movies like Njangal Santhushtaraanu, which were all about "fixing" the evil modern wife who doesn't "respect traditional family values", this comes from the same patriarchal ammavan sensibilities, just that it's an influencer in 2025 and not a woman who wears jeans and t-shirts. Towards the end there are just lines after lines of preaching about influencers, the media, truth and half-truth, and this is where the movie tries to sneak in some Dileep PR as well. Lines like "you'd treat someone like a criminal just because they were called in for questioning" sound too specific to think they're not related to the actual crime accusation towards Dileep. Tbh, using even his movies to paint himself as a "victim" like this only makes him seem more sus. Even hyper-intellectual Murali Gopi's Kammaara Sambhavam had a line like this. Absurd. 

The jokes don't really land; Dileep is really struggling to pull off humor here, but by the second half, the movie becomes more about Chinju anyway. Raniya Ranaa got horrible material to work with, and the direction given to her was to enact an ammavan's version of what an influencer is, but despite everything, it's really hard to pull off a character who's always so dialed up like this; maybe she'll get well-written characters in better movies in the future. The evil background score that's constantly given to Chinju towards the end reminded me of Malayalam mega serials—hilarious. It was also funny how Dhyan Sreenivasan occasionally appears out of thin air and then completely disappears at the end and leaves for Canada.

You know that dated, misogynistic sensibility of "putting the wife in her place" kind of thing? That's what this movie is, but it's the Instagram/YouTube version of that. Belongs in the "fuck this movie" category, of course.

Name: F1
Review: Formula Won I consider the best kind of filmmaking to be the kind that just pulls me into what's happening on screen and shuts off the part of my brain that looks for how it's done. The race sequences in F1 did that for me. I did not care where CGI was used, I didn't care how the stunt driving was done, and I did not care how they cleverly integrated the fictional APXGP race team into real races and footage from real races while being seamless. In fact, I only read about the crazy ways this movie was shot right after I watched it. It's formulaic writing and filmmaking, but it's Formula (d)One well (see what I did there? Because Formula One, hehe). I was completely pulled into the drama and conflicts here, formula or not. The racing scenes are masterfully shot, the cinematography and editing are on point, the sound design is amazing, the stunt work is great, the visual effects are seamless and Hans Zimmer's score is goosebumps-inducing. We can feel the wind, the kinetic energy, the tension of each turn, and the close calls—just amazing filmmaking on full display—and the choreographed scenes blend so well with the footage of actual races that I didn't even realize actual race footage was used till I read about it. I don't follow the actual F1; I only realized actual F1 drivers and teams had cameos in this movie when the rest of the theater erupted into applause whenever some of them appeared on screen. The movie still does a pretty good job at explaining the stakes and the rules of each race and how certain strategies and technical details work, without it feeling overwhelming to the casual moviegoer. They do this both using the F1 commentators and the dialogue between the team. The way the drivers' perspectives were captured while conveying that they're actually doing the driving on the track was also well-executed. We have a by-the-numbers underdog story here, with an old-school has-been racer and a hotshot rookie racer trying to score a win to save a horribly performing team. Brad Pitt's Sonny Hayes did remind me a bit of Tom Cruise's Maverick from Top Gun: Maverick, while Damson Idris as JP reminded me of Tom Cruise's Maverick from Top Gun. Then there's Javier Bardem as Ruben and Kerry Condon as Kate, rounding off a cast of likeable characters. Yes, the narrative beats and conflicts are familiar, but the execution here is immaculate. Kosinski knows his stuff; he knows how to land those emotional beats, he knows how to set up tension and conflicts, and he knows how to deliver the euphoria of a win or the disappointment of a loss or the shock and tension of something worse happening. It takes skill to build up a "he's flying" moment and make the audience feel exactly like how the dialogue described it. Kosinski makes it look so effortless and seamless that maybe this'd just be seen as a formulaic sports movie; making people forget about the technicalities of it all itself is a skill, especially when you read up about the crazy ways this has been shot. But this is so much more than just a formulaic sports movie; this is a Formula One sports movie. High-speed cinema.

Name: Viduthalai: Part II
Review: Director's Cuts of Part 1 and Part 2 It takes a Vetri Maaran to do an ACAB commie movie with a cop as the protagonist. (compliment) Kumaresan becomes a cop with very idealistic ambitions of helping people and being a hero. But pretty soon he realizes that the system that he's a part of won't let him or any cop be a hero no matter how well-intentioned they are. They're made to commit crimes and be complicit in horrible crimes and atrocities, and they're no better than the criminals they're trying to capture. Kumaresan finds humanity only with the woman he falls in love with, and even that eventually leads to tragic consequences. Though this movie and the subject matter is dead serious, I found some fun in the way Kumaresan escapes from getting killed without even realising it during multiple instances, like he's a Looney Tunes character or something xD. In Part 1, just like my first watch, the only thing that seemed out of place was Raja's music at times. But the music situation was better in Part 2. There are some beautiful songs and background score pieces here, I'm not invalidating the entire score BTW. Viduthalai braves to show the ugly reality. It blurs the lines between who's the real terrorist. Is it the ones fighting for freedom against oppression and exploitation, or is it the oppressors who murder and torture the people while wearing uniforms? This is why showing the militant leader Perumaal's story and perspective seemed important in Part 2. Perumaal's story involves a big transformation: he goes from being betrayed by the system to trying to fight the system and its oppressors from within as a communist leader, and then getting radicalized, and then finally realizing that the ideology that speaks for the oppressed and the working class is bigger than any one individual or group. Perumaal's politics and his whole journey are very integral to the narrative, and they connect to everything. The irony is very clear when the system doesn't care about people and casualties, but the "terrorists" do. A good amount of philosophical debate and political theory is there in the movie, and so it becomes the closest thing I've seen recently in Indian cinema to something like Spike Lee's Malcolm X. There are a few technical issues here and there, and Tamizharasi's fate is left hanging. Some of the dialogue is a bit on the nose; I'm not talking about the political themes—those being direct is almost a necessity—but there were some other instances of clunky exposition as well. But this is important cinema. The politics and the reality shown here are important; the way it questions and exposes the system is important. Perumaal's journey starts and ends the same way when we think about it, and that whole ending stretch was very hard-hitting. "Ideas are bulletproof"

Name: Jurassic World Rebirth
Review:
A corporation hires a group of hot mercenaries and a hot scientist to go to a secluded island filled with dangerous CGI creatures on a super secret mission, and they have no idea what's waiting for them on the island. This is Kong: Skull Isla... Ahem... Jurassic World: Rebirth.

Though the promos for this movie looked generic, it was written by the writer of the original Jurassic Park movie, and it had Gareth Edwards as the director, so I was interested despite the lukewarm reviews. Firstly, I had fun watching this. Not having Chris Pratt taming dinosaurs and riding a motorcycle with them itself makes this the better one among the Jurassic "World" movies. It puts the focus back on survival and introduces horror elements seen in the first movie, which was great. The storyline and the characters are indeed generic, and there are plot holes and conveniences and all, but also, a few moments stood out where Gareth Edwards did execute effective monster movie thrills and scares.

Something that I always admired Gareth Edwards for is his sense of scale. Whether it's Godzilla, the Imperial Walkers in Rogue One, or the various structures in The Creator, he has this skill to convey scale that's truly unique. Here the dinosaurs are not as big as Godzilla, but still, the sense of scale is still conveyed. There's a scene involving a T-Rex, which might be the most memorable and thrilling T-Rex scene in this franchise since the iconic one from the original. The invinsible inflatable raft is the only thing that kind of made the scene a bit silly. Whether it's the CGI on the T-Rex as it's chasing the characters through a river or the way the scene has been shot, it was thrilling and pretty scary. The same goes for the opening scene, which looks more like something out of the Alien movies than Jurassic Park; well, the D-Rex looks like a giant Xenomorph anyway. Towards the end too there's a moment involving a helicopter that was pretty scary.

The music sounded pretty distinct and like a horror movie score, apart from the occasional throwback John Williams theme from the original. The movie also doesn't rely too much on nostalgia and references and tries to be its own thing, which ends up being Kong: Skull Island. The cast is packed with great actors, but they're stuck doing generic roles, though all of them looked fabulous, Scarlett Johansson looked more badass here than she did in Marvel. Jonathan Bailey's character's glasses stay on his face for the longest time through all the action, though. As a person who wears glasses, I consider this a superpower.

Anyway, 

Kong: Rebirth

Jurassic World: Skull Island

It was pretty fun.

Name: Dheeran
Review:
Devadath Shaji's Dheeran has the characteristics of those older Malayalam comedy padams set in villages, but it's also pretty modern in its sensibilities, whether in its non-linear structure or the way a couple trying to have a casual relationship in a conservative village is portrayed and so much more. The movie is smart in its narrative structure and pov as well. It has an almost episodic format where the title character, played by Rajesh Madhavan, doesn't even become the main character of the story until way later. There's a big ensemble cast of characters with their own character arcs and quirky personality traits, and the title character is absent for a large portion of the initial half as they set up the village, the people there, the existing conflicts, and how these characters must now travel together because of the main character. The structuring is almost like a comedic version of what Lokesh Kanagaraj did in Vikram.

Then all these characters and plotlines collide with each other in the second half. There's moments of comedy and fun, plus the drama is well integrated too. It does feel a bit janky and abrupt at times, and the confusion comedy aspect of it could've been explored more, but it's still comes together pretty well and there was fun there. Another thing about this movie that reminded me of those classic village comedies is something I realised only when a friend wrote about it. All of the comedy here is situational and the movie doesn't really rely on social media references and meme references for its humor. The way the movie pokes fun at conservative and misogynystic men in a way that blends in with the plot was also nice.

The cast was great, with good performances from both the older and newer batch of actors. It was great to see actors like Sudheesh, Ashokan and Vineeth as characters like this. Rajesh Madhavan was great as the titular Dheeran too, and its such a disappointment that one of his best lines in the film was censored by the CBFC. The music was nice too. Anyway, it's a good watch.

Name: Sthanarthi Sreekuttan
Review:
I've never seen such a high-stakes class leader election. This movie succeeded in drawing me into its world, which we see primarily through the eyes of the kids, and the main plot concerns a single classroom and the choosing of its class leader. It sounds silly, but the movie takes it very seriously, just as the kids do. Each tiny scenario is treated as a big dramatic event, and it comes off more like a genuine expression of seeing the world through kids than being gimmicky. The cast full of talented newcomer kids also helps towards that; they just disappear into their characters and that world, their Trivandrum slang is natural, and all of them seem like stars. Among the adult actors, Aju Varghese had the most memorable performance as a cruel, unprofessional, and abusive teacher, who's the kind of person I've seen in the school I've studied in but was questioned by no one. The way he is built up as this uncomfortable presence was very effective here.

The movie has lots more adult characters and plenty of subplots. While the acting was nice, I felt maybe there could've been fewer characters and subplots going on, there was also a bit of a lack of clarity here and there, but still though, the movie is a pretty fun and wholesome watch. I couldn't help but love these kids and root for them. Even the studious first bencher breaks the usual stereotypes, and the kids feel like individuals with personalities rather than an adult's stereotypical version of children. There are also lots of meta jokes and pop culture references, though the kids themselves reminded me more of kids of my own generation than Gen Alpha kids. There are some attempts to make parallels to real-world politics here and there too; revolution begins in the classroom, hehe. The editing and some of the montages vere very cool. Even with a modest budget they've pulled off some cool stuff here, like that title sequence. The music and the songs were really good as well. 

Anyway, it was a nice watch. The movie felt fun and genuine enough to forget about the flaws. It had its heart in the right place.

Name: Superman
Review:
James Gunn's DC Universe's big cinematic debut is everything I hoped it would be and then some more. I did expect something that'd embrace its goofiness and mix high-stakes drama with comedy, because that's what Gunn has been doing with every single comic book adaptation so far. I expected a portrayal of Superman that'd fly closer to the do-gooder symbol of hope, but even then, this movie's Superman surpassed those expectations with how much of a literal ray of sunshine he is. But what surprised me is how political this movie got. Despite the constant supply of silly humor and superhero madness, the film deals with serious and heavy themes here, and it's also very successful in setting up the DC Universe for the future too, which doesn't seem like a clone of the MCU at all.

David Corenswet's Superman is defined more by who he is than what he can do. He's not Superman because of his superpowers; he's Superman because of his ability to be a selfless, empathetic embodiment of goodness, which comes from within him and not because he's an alien who gets superpowers from the yellow sun. An international conflict is also a part of the narrative, and I can't help but make parallels to Israel and Palestine there. Superman chooses to protect a country without a powerful military from an invasion by a heavily armed nation that’s also a U.S. ally. Like, think about it even from a fictional narrative standpoint, rather than as a political stance. If Superman decided to join the US in aiding their ally to commit genocide, that'd make him Homelander and not Superman.

And the movie never makes us forget how good of a person this Superman is. He's the kind of hero who'd give the same priority to saving the world and saving a cat. During every fight scene, he'd prioritize saving people, and even animals, over the fighting. He'd ask people if they're alright; he'd desperately try to convince every foe who tries to kill him to change for the better. Like, at the end of the movie, you'd feel the biggest superpower he has is this unlimited capacity to do good and be a literal symbol of hope. Corenswet portrays that innocence so well, we can even say this Superman is a bit too naive in the amount of hope he sees in people. Superman is a true pookie here. 

Then there's Nicholas Hoult's Lex Luthor being the perfect kind of evil antagonist to this version of Superman. He's envious of Superman and the love and adoration that he gets from the public, and also doesn't want a presence in the world who's more powerful than him, and he also refuses to believe in Superman's capacity to do good and wants everyone to hate Superman the way he does. Lex is also the film's main outlet for satire, with parallels made to Elon Musk and tech billionaires in general, with one of the most hilarious depictions of social media hate PR that I've ever seen. Lex Luthor does do some goofy stuff here, as an over-the-top comic book villain, but we also really feel the hate, indifference, ego, and self-centeredness of this person. It's the kind of villain that we'd love to hate, and Hoult finds that perfect balance of villainy and goofiness. Luthor is such a pure hater here. 

The biggest contrast between Superman and Lex is that Lex would consider a human life or any other living being as just collateral damage and a number, as long as he gets what he wants. He's like the embodiment of corporate imperialism here. The kind who'd start a war and only care about the land, money, and wealth they could get or how it'd help them defeat their enemy, rather than about the lives being lost. Superman, however, cares so deeply about saving every living thing he possibly can and doesn't want people getting killed by anyone, anywhere, and he'd jump in to protect and serve those at the receiving end with no hesitation and with no thought. Is Superman saving a country full of brown people kind of white-savior-y? Well, yeah, but also no. He's not even human, and though he looks like a Caucasian man, we don't know how the racial situation in Krypton worked. He's treated more like an outsider and an immigrant than as one of the white people by the US government itself too (he'd still enjoy white privilege while he's being Clark Kent though, it's complicated). The plotline involving his origins and its connection to who he is as a person was also very interesting. It's something we've seen before, but the way it's handled here is very good, especially that heart-to-heart that he has with Pa Kent towards the end. The way Corenswet changed his voice and posture in between Clarke and Superman was also great. Just like how we saw more of Batman in full costume than Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' film, we're getting more Superman than Clark Kent here too.

The movie has a huge supporting cast, but it doesn't seem too crowded either. Rachel Brosnahan is such a great Lois Lane and gets a lot more to do in the movie than just being the love interest. The chemistry between Lois and Clark was great, and so were Lois' scenes with the rest of the Daily Planet gang and then Mr. Terrific. The rest of the Daily Planet staff also has talented people like Beck Bennet and Wendell Pierce playing the characters, but they don't get much screen time. Still though, the Daily Planet journalists are cool enough to have their own spin-off TV show here. The Justice Gang was cool too, with the standout being Edi Gathegi as Mr. Terrific, who was equal parts funny, badass and cool. Nathan Fillion and Isabela Merced were also great additions to the cast who also get their own cool moments. 

Again, even with so many characters, the film always seemed super focused and coherent. All the subplots mattered, every cast member had something to contribute, and the cameos and references hit the right notes. The iconic John Williams Superman theme comes up at just the right moments, where Superman is at his Supermanest. Plus, the movie never loses track of what it's about, it gives us one of the purest depictions of Superman as a person, and it lets us forget all the darker depictions of the character. The sun literally shines from his back during a scene where he's making one of his pure-hearted speeches. This is also a Superman who can get defeated, who can get beat up, who barely holds it together during a fight, so it's not like we're seeing this invincible god either. There are several moments where he's literally almost dying, and I always appreciate a hero who's grounded and can lose over someone who's overpowered and undefeatable. It makes the action more thrilling and adds in more stakes.

The action in the movie does not deviate from the familiar James Gunn style; there's even a oner with a retro song moment here like his previous movies. There are familiar superhero movie action tropes like the city destruction setting towards the end, but there are all these cool touches added in here that make the drama and the fun seem unique, with some truly great Superman moments. The flying looked cool and kinetic, and the CGI on Krypto the dog was also great, with him joining the likes of Groot, King Shark, and Eagly in the James Gunn universe of cute, chaotic, and deadly CGI animals. John Murphy and David Fleming's score was good enough, but the most memorable moments in the music were always when John Williams' theme kicked in.

I remember watching an interview where James Gunn talks about making the decision to have Superman wear the red trunks outside his suit. He was afraid of the trunks looking silly, but David Corenswet then apparently told him that maybe the trunks are supposed to be silly. When children see this flying man with superhuman strength who can shoot lasers from his eyes, when he's wearing a bright costume with his trunks outside, it makes him look silly and disarming. This is the kind of philosophy that Gunn has applied to the movie as well. It just felt very genuine and from a place of love, rather than like churning out some "content" for cinematic universe purposes. The movie has a big S-shaped heart. 

Anyway, it's not a flawless movie; I'm sure there's plenty to be nitpicked here, but the thing is, I got exactly what I hoped from this movie, with the political and philosophical themes being the icing on top. So I can't give anything less than a perfect score over here. This is such a great start to James Gunn's DC Universe while being a great standalone film on its own. There's HOPE in DC now. Being kind is the real punk rock, yes it is. 

Also a side note as an Indian audience member:

FUCK THE INDIAN CENSOR BOARD, AKA THE CBFC, FOR CUTTING MOST OF THE KISSING BETWEEN LOIS AND CLARK. THEY RUINED TWO REALLY GREAT ROMANTIC MOMENTS IN THE FILM, AND THEIR CRIMES TOWARDS CINEMA WILL NOT BE FORGIVEN. YOU'RE OKAY WITH SHOWING SEXUAL ASSAULT, BUT CONSENSUAL KISSING IS WHERE YOU DRAW THE LINE? WHAT KIND OF "SANSKAAR" ARE YOU PROMOTING HERE, DICKHEADS?

Name: Superman
Review: I just knew I needed to rewatch this on IMAX 3D, and it was so worth it. The entire movie has the expanded aspect ratio, so it's more fit for the taller screen. Plus, whether it's the Guardians movies or this, when a James Gunn movie is released in 3D, the 3D is worth the extra price; the depth is used very well to convey scale, and things keep popping out of the frame in cool and non-gimmicky ways too. The movie begins with a beaten-up and bruised Superman and ends with a smiling Superman while the sun shines on his face. It felt symbolic of where this movie is taking Superman, from where he was in general. I'm not just talking about Zack Snyder's Superman here, but apart from Adventures of Superman and Superman & Lois on TV, there's been an overabundance of dark Superman adaptations, which were frankly more popular. There was the Snyderverse Superman, the Injustice Superman, Homelander, Omni-Man, and James Gunn's own Brightburn (which now feels like him getting any trace of dark Superman out of his system before writing his pookie Superman, though he was officially only a producer there). A dark Superman got popular to the point where there are people who believe that's the accurate depiction of the character rather than an alternate take. But what James Gunn does here is start the movie off by showing a hurt and bloodied Superman, in line with a dark iteration, and then immediately turn it over on its head to give us an innocent and softboi version. The contrast is even more apparent during that reveal from the third act, where we feel that Corenswet's Superman is so different from the previous darker iterations, when the other character reminds us so much of that darker and more aggressive iteration. Lex's arc involving validation and adoration is also something that has the potential to span over multiple films. My thoughts on the movie remain pretty much the same from my previous longer yapping. Just that on the IMAX rewatch I could appreciate its scale a lot more. Gunn has deliberately chosen a style that makes this seem a bit cartoonish at times, because the visual effects work is consistent here, so it's not a botch; this is really just them going for a very specific look. But at times it's also close to reality, whether it's the politics or that back and forth between Lois and Clark that feels like a conversation that would happen if Superman existed for real, and I'm pretty sure that the social media accounts that cultivate outrage for bigots are a bunch of monkeys. Even if the Boravia and Jarhanpur conflict wasn't written with any parallels to Israel and Palestine in mind, a mainstream superhero movie having such a great anti-imperialist take that just outright opposes war, murder, capitalism, and colonialism and that holds a mirror to real life in a way that triggers actual bigots, that's punk rock, man. This is the kind of movie that we can confidently show kids and actually expect them to learn some values from, whether it's political or even on a personal level, like an anti-incel antidote that says being kind, being soft, being sensitive, and being empathetic are the coolest things ever.

Name: M3GAN 2.0
Review:
Actual AI had developed exponentially in between the three years in between the original M3GAN and its sequel M3GAN 2.0. The original movie was like a "What if your Amazon Alexa murdered people?" kind of thing, which was like a sci-fi Child's Play kind of thing, which is what the reboot to Child's Play was too, well, Chucky was on camera saying that M3GAN is a rip-off of him, so... Anyways, the sequel tried to do something new instead of rehashing the same formula as the first one, but in that process it's borrowing the formula from Terminator 2 and even Leigh Whannel's Upgrade.

Anyway, the reason I talked about the growth of actual AI in real life is that we're living at an age where AI is no longer science fiction; there are actual AI tools available right now that can do stuff that fiction has said AI would do, and we're not far away from person-like AI existing. A movie like Companion found ways to address this in interesting ways, but M3GAN 2.0 just dumps exposition on us and lines after lines of AI this and AI that, which just seem very shallow and uninteresting.

The basic setup of the film is just a Terminator 2-ish thing where M3GAN is now the protagonist instead of the killer robot. But there too it's an interesting turn because unlike the T-1000 from T2, who was reprogrammed to be a protector to John Connor and wouldn’t possibly turn against him, here M3GAN kinda learns and chooses to be a good person, while Gemma doesn't trust the AI that murdered four people and a dog, and there's some ambiguity to whether M3GAN actually wants to help or does she want to kill everyone. The new villain in the far more advanced Amelia too is yet another T2 situation. But every show of promise this movie has is shot down by something dull and generic. It's like they deliberately tried to make each creative decision go a generic route than an interesting route.

M3GAN was an interesting character, taking the creepiness out of her also just made her less interesting.

Name: Heads of State
Review:
To quote the famous Idris Elba and John Cena meme from The Suicide Squad, this movie does exactly what those Dwayne The Rock Johnson action comedy buddy movies do, but better, like way better. And the main reason for that is the movie not taking itself seriously. Like, apart from one final speech about America helping other nations (man, STFU), the movie doesn't even have any jingoistic energy despite the main characters being the heads of two powerful western nations. This is not a "president kills terrorists and saves the world" affair like in Air Force One; it's more of a "two dudes survive an inside job" situation. It was also nice that the villains were white people, and the brown woman was actually more in charge of saving the big muscular lead dudes' asses than being a terrorist or love interest. This is one of the better roles I've seen Priyanka Chopra Jonas in, and she gets her moments.

The best part of the movie is, of course, the chemistry between Idris Elba and John Cena and all their banter and the way they play off each other. It's a bit similar to how their chemistry was in The Suicide Squad, but in a more buddy kind of way, with Cena playing a nicer hero person than a lovable asshole anti-hero like Peacemaker. The way they eventually bond and become buddies is, of course, following the conventional playbook of Buddy comedy action movies. Also, these streamer action comedies usually are lazy about their action, but not this one. There is some great action here, some fight scenes with slapstick comedy energy, and some great chase sequences with pretty great visual effects and production values. It was consistently funny too, and I loved those "how did you get here?" montages, very Edgar Wright coded.

Anyway, I'd have liked it more if it just stuck to being a buddy movie in some parallel universe where the American government doesn't commit war crimes, instead of going on a speech about how America "helps" foreign countries.

Name: Queen of the Ring
Review:
There was a great show on Netflix called GLOW (Gorgeous Ladies Of Wrestling), which was about these characters running a female wrestling promotion. That show hit the drama, the comedy, and the heart of it just right, and I was so disappointed when it got canceled right before its final season (fuck you, Netflix). Anyways, Mildred Burke's real-life story of how she pioneered women's professional wrestling is very powerful and inspiring, but even at almost 140 minutes, Queen of the Ring still seemed like it only scratched the surface.

It's appreciable that they tried to do a period drama of this scope under a limited budget, but at times the budget limitations were pretty apparent as well. This is a story that takes place over multiple years, but the only true difference I ever felt was Millie's son being played by different actors as he grows up. Otherwise everyone just looks the same, and we never feel that sense of time passing or their lives evolving that much. A lot of big events just aren't portrayed like they're big enough. Like, this is big-budget studio movie material in an indie movie package. But even with those limitations, I think the drama could've hit a bit harder, and the events could've had more of an impact than just passing by like they don't have much significance. 

 The performances are great, though, with Emily Bett Rickards being perfect as the lead, both performance-wise and in her physicality. Whether it's all the flexing and posing muscles-wise or the moves, body language, and agility, wrestling-wise, you can tell a lot of hard work went into this performance. That sort of earnestness deserves all the praise, and she carries the movie so well. Josh Lucas as Billy Wolfe is yet another standout performance as a guy you can't help but hate. The female wrestlers consist of both actors and actual professional wrestlers like Kamille and Toni Storm. 

I don't know the technicalities of professional wrestling, but I liked how they approached those scenes, especially the climatic shoot match, which has some stakes attached to it since they're wrestling for real instead of it being scripted (within the movie, of course). This felt more like an honest depiction of female professional wrestling, the risks involved, the athleticism required, and the business side of things than something like WWE's promotional propaganda biopic Fighting With My Family did (great Florence Pugh performance in that movie, though). And of course, in an era where women's wrestling was outright illegal, it addresses the sexism of the period too. The real Mildred Burke was an absolute badass to become who she did by overcoming everything that she had to overcome. This movie does pay respect to that, but the thing is, I think the real Mildred was far more amazing than what's shown here, and her story deserved to be portrayed bigger, despite Emily Bett Rickards' great performance. Maybe it should've been a series like GLOW. 

Even with the writing being as weak as it is, I can't rate it any lower because it's got some great acting and it's got heart.

Name: The Fantastic 4: First Steps
Review:
Even when the writing is familiar, the way this movie looks, feels, and sounds is so unique that it does manage to stand out and differentiate itself from any Marvel movie that came before or even any other superhero movie that came before. It felt more like a sci-fi movie than a superhero movie; after that initial montage, the four sparingly use their powers and engage in superhero action till the finale. What we get instead is a sci-fi family dramedy with world-ending stakes.

The four main characters are instantly likable, and had great banter and chemistry with each other. All the little touches given to Reed and Sue's chemistry as a couple were nice too. I knew Matt Shakman as a director on It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia before he did Game of Thrones or WandaVision. Just like how Sunny took place mostly inside the gang's bar, a lot of this movie takes place inside the F4's headquarters, and the four of them are together in most of the scenes as well. I can't really explain why the whole thing reminded me of Sunny, though The Fantastic Four are selfless heroes with heart, not selfish assholes with spite like the gang. 

Matt Shakman already played with recreating retro television aesthetics in WandaVision. Here he's recreating both retro television and retro film vibes together. The color scheme is very unique and consistent; the visual sensibilities and production design are great too. None of the movie is set in a "normal" environment; it's either retro, retro-futuristic, or sci-fi all the way, and I won't be surprised if the production design gets attention awards-wise.

Michael Giacchino's score is yet another standout in the movie. The Fantastic Four theme music is simple and instantly recognizable; like in the next Avengers movie, when the music hits, we'd know it's Fantasticin time. Nailing the theme music and making it memorable is a major win for any superhero movie, and Giacchino succeeded here (the "FANTASTIC FOOUUUURRRRR" vocals also help). The score is a mix of 60s music sensibilities and epic themes with all those cool vocalizations, and the music has so much more personality here than seeming like your average generic superhero movie score. 

Pedro Pascal was a great Reed Richards, someone who's conflicted between being a scientist, a superhero, and a father. The newer Johnny and Ben dynamic was also nice, I liked Joseph Quinn's more softboi version of Johnny Storm. Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm was my favorite from the cast, she's just pure aura. Mother energy indeed. The movie being set in the 60s also changes up the way they are, of course. 

Ebon Moss-Bachrach is a great actor, and he did do all of the performance capture for The Thing in person, but unlike CGI characters like The Hulk or Thanos, who have human faces and skin, The Thing with rocks for a face would be harder to animate because the skin is supposed to be rigid there and not elastic. It's an understandable trade-off for a character like this. So that does mean the subtleties of the performance can't quite be recreated by the animators like they did for a Hulk or Thanos. But despite that, Ebon Moss-Bachrach does emote a lot with his eyes, and the animators do try their best to capture his performance in the CGI character. The Thing does feel like a person and blends in (except when he's holding the baby; I'll get to that); the CGI work on him is amazing. 

In contrast, Julia Garner as Silver Surfer and Ralph Ineson as Galactus do get to put more of a performance there, mainly because the characters are modeled after their own faces and it's just them in CGI essentially. The Silver Surfer in particular looked amazing, and all the reflection detail was unreal. The character felt underwritten, though. We have someone who has been aiding a giant dude in committing genocide, who suddenly has an internal conflict because of a pretty boy on fire? Idk. 

Galactus was an interesting character, though. He's portrayed more as someone suffering from a disease than as someone who commits mass murder out of hate. What he really wants is to stop eating planets, intergalactic dieting, folks. He was scary as a villain as well in that final stretch where he comes to New York. There was a moment with Reed that was making this seem like a horror movie for a while. The scale and power of this thing were conveyed really well, making our heroes seem really tiny in comparison and making him seem like a very dangerous threat. 

But ironically, the one person who doesn't blend in and sticks out through most of the movie is the often CGI and often composited baby. CGI babies can always get creepy, and I imagine composting a baby that's being held by The Thing might've been hell for the VFX team. But the baby just sticks out a lot of the time. It's not as bad as Twilight or Squid Game, but it's still a bit uncanny valley. James Gunn's Superman also had a CGI baby, but that baby not exactly being human helped.

Anyway, this was a good time. It was a great way to introduce this version of the Fantastic Four; they're given a great theme music by Michael Giacchino that Marvel can use forever, the cast was great, the aesthetics and production design were on point, the action and the way they showcased the powers looked good, the drama worked, the characters were likable, it had enough heart and the visual effects were great too, apart from instances of uncanny valley baby. Anyways… FAAANTAAASTIC!

Name: A Shot in the Dark
Review: This one is a big improvement over The Pink Panther because there's more Jacques Clouseau and more Peter Sellers. Clouseau being the protagonist means more Peter Sellers slapstick gags, and I couldn't get enough of them. Sellers is effortlessly hilarious with the physical comedy and deadpan delivery. The movie is a so-and-so murder mystery, but the thing that keeps it afloat is the constant supply of gags; they manage to squeeze jokes in for every single scene, and there were several moments that made me laugh out loud. There are some brilliant comedy set pieces here, and the score is iconic as well. It succeeded in making me laugh, so..

Name: Happy Gilmore
Review:
I remember loving this movie from watching this on TV as a kid. But on the new rewatch, at the start I was confused if it was the same movie that I loved, with Sandler being too cartoony and the jokes not really landing. Then the golf stuff started, and I remembered why I loved this movie. Happy Gilmore gets so much fun and hilarious once it gets into the golf. A working-class guy (with a subway sponsorship) and his fans invading a rich people-only game? Gold. Sandler does the same thing in almost every comedy movie of his, and this is one of the few where it works the most. Chris McDonald as the shooter was also so hilarious. Plus, it manages to be a pretty good sports movie with a protagonist to root for despite being so goofy and unserious.

Also, Julie Bowen looked so pretty in this movie, instant childhood crush, before I knew Modern Family even existed.

Name: Happy Gilmore 2
Review:
The first few minutes of this movie were horrendous, with some ugly deepfakes, and it had me thinking that it's another one of those low-effort shitty comedies Adam Sandler's been doing for Netflix. The big shocking twist at the beginning especially triggered me, and I hated it. But afterwards, the twist does make sense plot-wise to do a comeback story for Happy, and something similar to this twist happened in the first movie itself, so I was trying to set it aside and enjoy the rest of the movie.

Happy Gilmore 2 alternates between being a tribute and follow-up to the original, with heart and humor, and being absolute brainrot. It's filled with callbacks to the original from start to finish, and it even mocks the original at some places; the "happy place" sequences were especially hilarious. But it also does too many cutaways to footage from the original, and it's unnecessary a lot of the time. Most people who have seen Happy Gilmore will remember Ben Stiller saying, "You're in my world now!" so there was no need to cut back to the original footage when he says the same thing here, and this is a recurring thing; some callbacks are clean and normal, and the others have a "remember that this happened in the first movie too?" attached to them. Shooter is still a great character, and the interactions between Shooter and Happy were all hilarious, especially that graveyard scene. And Sandler does slip back into Happy with ease (not that he was that drastically different from Sandler's usual comedic persona).

Plus this movie has LOTS of cameos, like LOTS. A lot more than the first movie. They're either Adam Sandler's friends or celebrity fans of the original movie. It's also funny that Benny Safdie, one of the directors of the best Adam Sandler performance of the last two decades, plays the villain here and has fart breath. There are even wrestler cameos, where AEW wrestler MJF plays one of Happy's sons and WWE wrestler Becky Lynch plays one of the villains. Then there's Travis Kelce, lots of real-life golf personalities, lots of musicians (I especially didn't expect that one cameo of the Jackass dude's son), and Adam Sandler's family. Adam Sandler has one of the most family-looking families. As in, both his daughters resemble him and his wife and each other, so when one of his daughters plays his daughter in the movie, and then his wife and the other daughter play characters who are not related to him, it's so obvious that these four people belong to the same family.

Regardless of everything, the movie did make me laugh, and there was fun here. It was fun to spot the cameos and the callbacks, though I wish the movie actually didn't underestimate my ability to understand the callbacks by using clips from the first movie. The plotline involving traditional golf vs. brainrot golf was great for a sequel like this. There were plenty of moments of cartoonish fun and running gags here. Just like the first movie, the golf scenes are still fun, and it still manages to be a pretty serviceable underdog sports movie, and though the grief situation is set up to be unserious, it ends up having some amount of heart.

Can't rate Happy Gilmore: The Clip Show too low because I did laugh and have fun.

Name: The Fantastic 4: First Steps
Review:
I saw people hyping up the IMAX version so much that I had to check it out. This is more about the IMAX experience than the movie; my feelings about the movie remain the same from the first watch. Just that I noticed some of the plot holes more, but I'll give it a pass. It's still fun. 

And yeah, the scale of the movie rises exponentially in IMAX, especially in any scenes that involve Galactus. There's a big wide shot where the four and the surfer are facing Galactus, which I don't even remember seeing in my first watch. There are only like two big action setpieces here and most of the movie takes place indoors. Unlike a Dune 2 or a Superman, the taller screen doesn't add much otherwise, but when the spectacle is on, it's ON. Also loved the 3D in IMAX better than my first watch; I could really feel the depth during almost all the scenes, even simple dialogue scenes. 

The creepy CGI baby looked way creepier in IMAX, though.

Name: 28 Weeks Later
Review:
It's not as good as the first one by a long shot. But not that bad either. The most frustrating part was the way the infection starts spreading. Fuck you, Don. I mean, a normal patient at a normal hospital would have more people to look after them and monitor them than how these people kept a patient infected by the rage virus in quarantine. And Don doesn't make sense as a character other than being there for the plot whenever something shitty has to happen.

There are some effective scares; there was an instance of an eye injury, which looked very scary. Also that scene with the helicopter blades and the infected was very cool, though it made zero sense that the kindhearted helicopter pilot would do what he did to a civilian. The movie has sharp political commentary, and the way the US military was used to show that they'd murder civilians with no hesitation, instead of as some kind of saviors, was cool. The entire rage virus disaster getting out of control is because of the US military's incompetence when you think about it. This is not even like a Walking Dead situation where the bites would take a long time to infect someone; the rage virus turns someone instantly, so it makes no sense when the military does shoot civilians that are definitely not infected, but civilians being murdered by the military in the name of "safety" is a real thing across the world. So, that's totally something the armed forces can do.

The makeup and the infected effects were really nice, and though the movie looks more "movie-ish" than the first one, it does do the shaky cam and rapid cuts during scenes involving the infected, and it does make those scenes seem scarier, visceral, and like someone's shooting documentary footage of the attacks. Just that it was overwhelming in some scenes, and I couldn't really register what was going on; could be a me thing too.

Anyway, it's not a bad movie, but I didn't really bond with the characters the way I did in the first one, and again, the way the infection begins is really, really dumb. Fuck you, Don.

Name: Sorry, Baby
Review:
This is one of those movies that seems simple at first, but the more I think about it, the more complex it feels, and I appreciate the sheer brilliance of Eva Victor. Sorry, Baby is about the main character Agnes dealing with trauma. But it's not entirely somber and depressing either. There's humor, heartfelt moments, and warmth, all without undercutting the seriousness of what the main character goes through. The movie never gets monotonous; every experience Agnes goes through adds meaning and depth, and Eva Victor is great both as the creator and as the actor playing Agnes, with the movie having lots of memorable moments that carry so much emotional weight and insight. The portrayal of trauma too seemed sensitive and empathetic to the survivor, and the moments of humor that come it between never makes it seem light. 

There are so many quotable lines too; especially the lines regarding how Agnes sees adulthood sounded so real. She looks at a baby and says something like "You don't even know that you're alive yet" I mean... 😭

Anyway, brilliant stuff.

Name: Coolie
Review:
Coolie has "first draft" written all over it. Like, there were so many ideas, so many plot points, so many characters, and twists and turns that just refuse to stick together as a coherent narrative. I won't say that it's because Lokesh is incapable of doing a complex narrative with multiple subplots, because that's exactly what his debut feature, Maanagaram, was. Forget Vikram, Kaithi, Leo, Master, and all; the person who wrote Maanagaram writing something like this all these years later is both disappointing and sad.

We have a basic revenge plot here, just like Vikram did, but Vikram was better at filling that up with lots of supporting characters, subplots, and a fun kind of narrative structure, while Coolie just throws in ideas and references to other films that just seem lazily put together. I expected throwbacks to older Rajini films here, but what I got was somehow scenes that parallel movies like Petta and Jailer, which themselves were movies that were referencing other Rajini movies, so what's this, a copy of a copy? Like, I'd expect Lokesh to get inspired by Karthik Subbaraj, since Petta to me is the "fanboy sambhavam" at its finest, but what I didn't expect was so many scenes and elements that were cut and pasted from Jailer (I don't like Jailer, btw). I mean, ripping off Petta more would've made me like this movie. Lokesh ripping off a Nelson movie and failing is a sentence I never thought I'd say. 😭

(Some mild spoilers below) 

Rajinikanth plays Deva, who alternates between looking confused and being intimidating. Some of the plot points and twists here seem too comical for a movie that takes itself seriously and is trying to be "more DC than Marvel." There's a Manmadhan body disposal device that has no business being THAT important to the plot, a zombie situation, twists that seem straight out of the Tamizh Padam franchise, a villain waiting around for a character to finish doing a phone call before trying to kill them, people reveling important information randomly, people being unnecessarily cryptic, and characters randomly acting stupid and nonsensically. There are lots of layers of shit to unpack here. At least something like Good Bad Ugly has some level of self-awareness in being brainrot, but this is brainrot that takes itself way too seriously than it has any right to be.

But at least Lokesh movies had great action before, but this one's meh in that regard too. Rajinikanth is obviously restricted physically (and yet, look at what Karthik did in Petta), so the fight scenes go how we'd expect a Rajinikanth fight scene to go, and when the character does get agile at times, the head replacement looks so obvious. At least Leo had some great fight scenes except for that scene in the forest. Here, the action just falls flat without any stakes or thrills. There's a siege situation in a closed building at one point, and when I thought maybe Lokesh would do another Kaithi here, that too became just about the slo-mo posing and the badass Kannada superstar cameo. I also got annoyed by that thaam thakida track for some reason. Also, even though Deva gets injured and tired during the action, the movie just refuses to acknowledge him being physically worn out in any way. I mean, the protagonists get injured more than any normal human being could survive in Lokesh's previous movies too, but at least he managed to write that into the plot in some way. Here Deva gets a major injury to his back that the movie just forgets about. This movie has an A certificate, but the violence doesn't pack the impact that the action in Lokesh's previous movies had at all. It just seems too choreographed and superficial. 

Speaking about forgetting, the movie also keeps forgetting who the villain is. We think it's this one person, but then apparently there's another person, and then there's another person. And when the movie is focused on one villain, the other villain appears, reminding us of their existence, and then disappears, and then reappears, but there's a new villain, but that's a cameo, but is it a friend? No, he's a villain, but is he chill? My brain fried trying to decode the villain situation here, basically, and exactly what the fuck happens during the big cameo at the end. 

Credit where it's due, the deepfakes in the flashback looked pretty nice most of the time, except when the faces were out of focus. The old movie filter and audio were also a nice choice. But does the flashback produce the intended buildup apart from making the audience cheer for seeing a young Rajini on screen? Idk. Tiger Muthuvel Pandiyan had a more intimidating buildup to him, as much as I hate that fucking movie. Rajini does deliver the monologue about the flashback in a single shot, so, well done, Thalaivar ey. (Also, that baasha tribute was badass, all things considered). 

There's a big supporting cast and a few cameos, but with the movie seeming so incoherent, Rajini doing Rajini stuff was the only thing going for it. While I was glad to see Soubin Shahir getting such a substantial part in the movie, a lot of the unintentional humor in the movie comes through him, but it's not his fault but the movie's fault, so yeah. Nagarjuna gets an opportunity to ham it up and be a psychotic villain and just ends up being a forgettable villain. Upendra plays Shiva Rajkumar from Jailer (such swag tho), and Aamir Khan plays pookiefied Rolex from Vikram, in a part that's written like it's revenge for him remaking Ghajini with a bigger budget. (Lokesh is Suriya's friend and Kamal's fan, just saying) 

Anyway, I'm not rating it too low because at least Ani-nna gave some cool tracks that I could add to my playlist. Monica song's random placement also turned out to be worse than how Kavalayya was placed in Jailer BTW, and I don't even want to elaborate on the male savior trope situation in this movie. Also, when the death of a female villain makes the men in the theater cheer just because she’s a woman, you need to realise there’s a problem with the way you write women, Loki bro.

Also, I can't believe Lokesh made Shruti Haasan say that "I'm 29 years old, girls my age are in love or getting married" line. Bruh.

Also, the movie introduces its protagonist with the messaging that drinking booze is bad, and then the movie wraps up by saying how cool it is to smoke beedi. 🥹

Name: Eddington
Review:
Ari Aster found a scary group of villains yet again, and it's... white people in America. Initially Eddington seemed like the most "normal" Ari Aster movie. It's a satire set during the pandemic; all the scenarios are things that have actually happened during the pandemic. Even the George Floyd murder and the BLM protests are a part of the plot. Tbh, I struggled a bit to get into this movie during the first two acts, but then, things get a lot crazier during the third act, and the ending just goes all guns blazing. 

Joaquin Phoenix plays the worst kind of straight white guy here as the protagonist, and it's this despicable human being that we're following the most in this movie. There is a big cast of supporting characters, but after a while the movie becomes just about Phoenix's sheriff. I was especially disappointed about how underutilized Emma Stone was in this movie. Pedro Pascal too doesn't get much apart from that one confrontation scene.

By the end the movie seemed very anti-American (complimentary) and anti-white people, whether it's the free access to guns, virtue signaling, making even a justified outrage an excuse to murder people, subtle and obvious ways in which racism still exists, women and their trauma being used as political tools, misinformation and conspiracies online, Facebook bashing, police violence, corporate exploitation, or the fact that the protagonist has covid throughout the movie, after having a first scene where he's so adamant about not wearing a mask. There's a lot here in terms of satire; I might not have gotten all of it, and the ones that I did get didn't entirely land for me, but still, it was interesting. America did elect Trump for a second time, and they're fucked up in more ways than one, so a movie that shows how fucked up America is makes sense.

Name: 28 Years Later
Review:
Everyone born in 1997 is wondering why their age is associated with a zombie movie in 2025.

The original 28 Days Later largely inspired stuff like The Last of Us, whether it's running zombies or the humans being worse than the monsters angle or the way the characters, their dynamic, and the drama are explored. So it's interesting that 28 Years Later seems so Last of Us adjacent when it's just a natural expansion of the first movie.

Now, there was a 28 Weeks Later in between, but this movie is not so keen on acknowledging its existence. That movie was more like an imitation of the first movie, but this one is more like an expansion; it's way bigger in scale, and no, that's not a reference to the Alpha's penis.

This one's a perfect follow-up; they try new things with the frantic style they use to show the infected, and it works so well. Whether it's the bullet time effect, the editing, or the cinematography, it's very effective. It's not just for the infected, though; sometimes I noticed that the movie even uses that style to convey non-infected characters expressing rage, which was interesting, and it feels like something they'd explore further in the future. The naked infected and the head-pulling alpha were pretty scary, and the helplessness of the characters was conveyed well, the violence and gore too was meant to disturb. The characters themselves had layers to them, and it was easy to root for them too. The ending was very emotional, and we don't see big movies choosing drama over spectacle like this that often.

Anyways, I'm excited to see where this story moves forward.

Name: I Know What You Did Last Summer
Review:
This movie used to play all the time on the TV during my teens, and I had no idea that it was a slasher. The title and the scenes that I did see made me think this was some high school drama. But then I watched Scary Movie and then got to know that it's spoofing Scream and this movie together. So I actually watched I Know What You Did Last Summer after watching its spoof.

This is one of those very 90s-coded 90s movies; whether it's the acting, the style, or the dialogues, everything just screams 90s. And though Kevin Williamson wrote both this movie and Scream, this one doesn't have the self-aware edge that Scream had. Plus the characters really aren't that interesting, and it takes quite a bit of time to get into slasher territory and get interesting. And even then, I have no idea why most of the characters in this movie make the random choices that they do, including the killer. The killer is not just a bloodthirsty psychopath here and acts on a defined motive, but he conveniently also switches to being someone who'd just kill at random because the movie needs more gore and kills, he's just a mix of the two I guess. The fisherman's outfit and hook are a nice look and memorable, though not really practical for hiding the killer's identity (like I have no idea how he could tell that the one guy he initially threatens couldn't see his face, or maybe he wasn't even trying to hide the face), but yeah, it's good enough for a slasher villain.

This was the peak Jennifer Love Hewitt era, though. I had the biggest crush on her.

Name: I Still Know What You Did Last Summer
Review:
The biggest surprise in this movie was when the guy I thought to be a Jack Black impersonator playing one of the minor characters turned out to be the real Jack Black.

The first movie tried to be a thriller/mystery along with being a slasher, but this is more of a conventional slasher. The fisherman says, "I still know what you did last summer," but they did that two summers ago at the time this movie is set in so how is it "last summer" now? And the twist at the end of the first movie reveals that the fisherman himself did more than what Julie and the gang did, and he kept on murdering people who had nothing to do with his murderous revenge quest too, so the "I know" thing is more of a calling card for a killer than a threat about something Julie did at this point, if that makes any sense.

Anyway, this one was just generic slasher content. Jennifer Love Hewitt looks gorgeous throughout the movie, and they choose to sexualize her more in this movie than the first one. It's pretty much a product of the 90s, just like its predecessor, except that the first one had something a bit unique going for it with the premise, and this is just a normal slasher. 

 I won't trust the cliffhanger ending again after the first one's cliffhanger fooled us once.

Name: I Know What You Did Last Summer
Review:
I thought that this was an improvement over the first movie, despite this one getting worse reviews. Because this one had the thing I thought the first one didn't: a sense of humor and self-awareness. It is a cash-grabby legacy sequel, and it doesn't hide that one bit. "Nostalgia is overrated," lmao. The self-awareness doesn't reach the levels of the Scream revival, but it still made the movie more fun. There were plenty of jokes that made me chuckle too, like the "hot widow" exchange right after the first murder. Critics would maybe say that's dumb and out of character; I'd call that fun.

It also addresses the practicality of the Fisherman costume in hiding the killer's identity; the mystery is more intriguing, and as stupid as the final twist is, it's still a fun and campy reveal where the movie still maintains a sense of humor, and I couldn't complain. The cast of characters was interesting; Chase Sui Wonders was great, and of course Jennifer Love Hewitt's return was an appropriate amount of legacy aura farming. Even the Fisherman's victims seemed more in line with the motive than seeming like the killer is randomly picking off people in between the revenge spree.

As a campy whodunit slasher movie, it's fun enough and funny enough, and so I can't rate it too low.

Reduced half a star from my initial rating when I remembered how pro rich people this movie is. Eww.

Name: Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra
Review:
You know all that noise that said a female-led action movie will never work in Malayalam cinema, or even in Indian cinema, because people won't care about watching them and only male-led action films can draw in crowds and find financial success? The noise that says leading big action movies are just not "meant for girls", this movie and the success it found with the audience is firstly one big step in proving how stupid that noise was, and hopefully this'll lead to more such films being made. Also, the team chose to begin their cinematic universe with a film led by Kalyani Priyadarsan as Chandra, when they could've easily gone the other way with a male-led film when the producer Dulquer Salman himself is a leading man, despite the above-mentioned noise possibly being presented as "market analysis" to them too, but they took a swing and it worked.
