The Brahmin dude's "instincts" didn't really matter much in the movie, and the movie does emphasize his Brahmin roots to explain his abilities to sense the supernatural (the scene where he sweeps his house shirtless and adjusts his poonool wasn't forced exposition of his Savarna caste at all, hehe). He could've very well been a normal person. The Brahmin exorcist is one "traditional" trope that I wish modern movies would retire. Even if him being a Potty is a connection to the Potty lineage in Bramayugam, it made me feel a bit sus about Rahul Sadasivan. Bramayugam itself had a criticism that it's addressing oppression while also glorifying the "ideal Brahmin" in parallel. I didn't fully agree with it then, but this movie is making me a bit sus in that regard. 

Also, the malevolent spirit here is of a working-class church-going Christian, while the protagonists here are a rich Savarna Hindu and a middle-class Hindu Brahmin who is supernaturally gifted. I thought this would involve some kind of Satan worship or occult situation, but no, the bad people are just Christians, and then Christian symbols are shown with scary music. Meanwhile, a Pooja room with vilakku and pictures of Hindu gods is shown as a safe haven for the Brahmin dude where the evil Christian spirit won't enter. I'm still not sure if these are intentional; like I said, it just makes me feel a bit Sus. Or yk, the writing just needed more clarity about everything.

Name: The Writer's Room
Review: The framing device of this documentary is quite fun, and that's what makes it unique. Because this is not a "day with G R Indugopan" or a formal interview with G R Indugopan. Murali calls himself "The Interruptor" in the credits, and that's what it feels like; it's this annoying dude interrupting G. R. Indugopan on a normal day and making him speak a bit reluctantly. It's a blend of actual interactions and some scripted elements, and it's just a very fun way to look at an artist. Along the way Indugopan talks about how he sees art, how he writes, and how he develops a story or rather lets his characters develop the story for him; sometimes they just feel like random unfiltered thoughts, and sometimes they're very insightful. There are also lots of clever and cheeky references and instances of humor; Murali, as the interviewer/interrupter, has some pucham in his tone, and Indugopan has pucham in return, and the whole back-and-forth banter is fun to watch. The whole first-person camera technique was also nicely done. I'd have loved this one a lot more if not for the music. The music is very bad at a few instances; the music really took me out of the documentary whenever it became more prominent. In the beginning, the most irritating bit of music in this documentary is playing while [irritating rap] is shown as its subtitle; at least we're self-aware. Once the interactions with Indugopan begin, the music is pretty minimal, and that helps. Then the music becomes prominent towards the end too, and it's bad. Anyway, Murali's little slice of Indugopan does indeed feel like him barging into Indugopan's room on a random day, and it's so fun and unique. Streaming on YouTube

Name: Predator: Badlands
Review:
Cute and lovable are the last adjectives I thought I'd use to describe a Predator, but that's exactly what this movie pulls off, and it does so while also being very faithful to the Yautja/Predator lore and mythos set by the previous movies, way more than Shane Black's Predator movie was. We got a likable, pookiefied, empathetic, badass protagonist Predator in Dek; it should've never worked, but it does.

Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi plays Dek. I couldn't even tell if he was fully replaced by CGI or only parts of him were, because there are pictures of him in full costume on the sets. Maybe those were for lighting references, or maybe only parts of him were replaced, but the fact is, the CGI here is so good and seamless that Dek feels more like a person that exists than as a costume or a CGI render. Dek's face, of course, is fully CGI, and it's the Predator face we're familiar with, but the thing is, even with a face like that, the animators are able to translate Dimitrius' performance onto Dek; we see his eyes and his face convey all kinds of emotions with that face, and it's pretty impressive that Dan Trachtenberg and team pulled this off. Dek also speaks in this movie; I don't remember the Yautja speaking in any of the other Predator movies I've watched (Edit: I watched Killer of Killers and they do speak in that). His dialogue is entirely in the fictional Yautja language, which is also fun to listen to, btw, as all the creature sounds that I do remember that a predator makes are a part of the Yautja language and how they communicate. The film's score also integrates Yautja vocals similar to how Avatar's score had Na'vi vocals, and that was also very cool. Dek only speaks a single English word throughout the entire movie, and the decision to have all his dialogue be in Yautja was also a great one. Like, just think about it: he has a CGI alien face of a monster who was originally meant to be scary rather than likable, he speaks an alien language, this is the first time that this franchise is making one of them a protagonist instead of a villain, and yet, Dek feels like a fleshed-out, easily rootable protagonist.

Elle Fanning is the principle live-action cast member of this movie; there's also Cameron Brown as the drone synthetics, but those are like the enemy NPCs in a video game rather than actual characters. Fanning is basically the main human face that we see throughout the movie, though she's not playing a human, and she's the one with all the English dialogue too. The universal translator thing was a nice in-universe excuse to have her interact with Dek in English while Dek responds in Yautja. There are these little touches given to Fanning's Android character Thia too, like the way she glitches when she talks, and also, half of her body is missing for most of the movie; the effect is so seamless, and that's an impressive technical feat that they've achieved too.

Both Thia and Dek are driven by directives set by external forces; for Thia it's a mission she's programmed to do by a corporation, and for Dek it's the way the Yautja tribe has operated for centuries, where they're predators seeking dangerous game to kill to prove their worth as warriors, and the movie essentially makes Thia the yappy one and Dek the grumpy one in a buddy movie combination, and it's very fun to watch. Elle Fanning is so charming and likable, and it's a delightful tone shift when these two finally meet and decide to travel together, with cute moments of humor peppered in between. We also have the cutest little CGI animal in Bud. 

The visual grandeur and scale of this movie is a sight to behold; it looks gorgeous, the CGI work is amazing, and it blends so well with the real sets and locations. The action scenes are all thrilling, there are some cool slo-mo moments and plenty of badassery, and it felt cool to actually root for a Predator instead of seeing it as a threat. Towards the end there's even a fun reference to Arnie's battle prep scene from the original. I watched this on a 3D screen, and the 3D too is well integrated, with plenty of spears and sharp stuff poking at us and the depth being used to convey scale. I thought the movie would be tame in its violence since it's not rated R, but it actually isn't. This one goes all in on the violence and dismemberment as much as the R-rated Predator movies have; it's just that there are no human characters here. Every character is an alien or a synthetic, and I guess alien and robot blood and gore don't qualify as hardcore violence xD.

Are there familiar sci-fi tropes and genre tropes here? Sure there are, but it's done so well, and so many aspects of this movie are huge unique challenges from a filmmaking perspective. But I didn't think of those challenges or how they achieved what I was seeing on screen while I was watching the movie; I was fully immersed in the characters, the action, and the world that Dan Trachtenberg had set up here. The fact that Dek as a character was portrayed so believably is a feat in itself, never sticking out from the narrative. So much of this movie is so visual and cinematic, and it's the kind of cinema that makes me glued to the screen. The music and sound design were also very cool, I missed hearing the Alan Silvestri Predator themes though. 

What the people who say that this movie “ruins” The Predator should understand is that it clearly places Dek as an outcast: he’s smaller than the other Yautja, he’s not the big ruthless hunting machine the rest of them are, and that’s precisely why they consider him a weakling. The fact that he’s so different from the other Yautja, both physically and mentally, is part of the story itself, it’s literally about an outcast Predator who discovers empathy and heart and realises that there’s more to life than the hunt, and your complaint is that he’s not like the others you’ve seen in the franchise, when Dek being different is the whole point of the movie 😭. I found it very cool that Dan Trachtenberg decided to shake up the existing formula of a Predator movie here. And he already made Killer of Killers with all the ruthless Predators, it's not like the other kind of Yautja ceased to exist and we'd never see them again in future movies. This movie doesn't alter or rewrite the Predators, Dek is just an exception from the rest. 

The original Predator movie was all muscle; this one's all heart.

Name: Predator: Killer of Killers
Review: The art and animation are gorgeous, the action is amazing, the music is cool with plenty of usages of the classic Predator themes, and just so much fun on the whole.

Name: Frankenstein
Review:
I haven't read Mary Shelley's original novel or watched the other adaptations of the actual storyline. I've only been aware of the character named "Frankenstein's Monster" or "Frankenstein," you know, the square-headed guy with the bolts, and a basic idea of how the story goes because of pop culture, and I've seen other interpretations and depictions of it, from Hotel Transylvania to DC's Creature Commandos, but never the real deal.

Firstly, this movie is absolutely gorgeous; it has some of the most beautiful shots with the sky in the background that I've seen recently. I have no idea if digital trickery is involved, but the production design, costumes, colors, and the cinematography; everything follows a very specific look, and it's beautiful to look at. Fuck Netflix for not giving this movie a proper wide theatrical release, because the way this movie looks and sounds is so meant for the theatrical experience, Del Toro didn't make a "streamer" even when he would've been aware that this won't get a wide theatrical release window. The music too captures the tone and the tragedy of the storyline perfectly.

There are plenty of instances of pretty effectively done gore in this movie; it's a mix of CGI and practical effects and looks pretty horrific at times. The creature's brute strength is conveyed really well, right in the beginning, as we see him throw people like they're nothing and punch off half of a person's face; we'd believe he can crush a person to mush with his bare hands. But the thing is, this isn't a horror movie, and he isn't a monster, but at the same time, this is a monster movie.

The film is divided into three chapters: a prologue, Victor's Tale, and The Creature's Tale. The character development is so clear and well done; we're following Victor from his childhood till he brings life to the creature. The movie switches gears once the Creature is introduced; Victor changes, and he becomes an oppressor, even though he himself has lived his life under an oppressor. He presumes the creature to be a savage brute when he actually isn't. And then we switch to the creature's perspective, who is childlike and innocent and doesn't really want to hurt anyone. We see how with enough love and care, he could've lived like a person, but Victor created him in a way that makes the world see him as grotesque, and that forces him to be violent. But still, this version of the monster only attacks those who wish to harm him or in self-defense (though he's unkillable).

Del Toro loves his beautiful monsters, and the creature here might be his most human-looking one yet. All of Jacob Elordi's facial features are kept intact by the makeup; there's no attempt to make him look grotesque. It's more like Victor stitched together corpses to give birth to something beautiful, except that the world around him doesn't see him as the beautiful and innocent person he is. The makeup on the creature conveys that idea beautifully. I initially thought Jacob Elordi was cast for his tall frame and facial features alone, to make the creature be physically towering and yet handsome at the same time, but he's great performance-wise too. The creature is basically "growing up" throughout the movie, from a baby to an adult, and each step of that transformation is portrayed really well by Elordi, in his body language and even how his speech eventually evolves. By the end, he can speak sophisticated English, but yet, there's something that still makes him just a little bit unnatural compared to a human who was born and not made. The creature just wants companionship and a normal life, basically. It's such a great character and performance that perfectly captures innocence, loneliness, and longing, along with the reluctant rage.

Oscar Isaac also plays the titular Frankenstein really well; he's this vile person who thinks he's a better man than he actually is, and both the film and his performance capture Victor Frankenstein's constantly shifting morality, his inflated ego when he's playing god, his insecurities, his selfishness, and the way he eventually makes peace with his creation really well. Victor and the creature are opposites to each other; Victor is trying to hide who he really is, while the creature is not allowed to be the person that he actually is. 

Casting a person named Mia Goth in a Gothic film is in itself a casting W. But I wished the movie had more Mia Goth, though, but yeah, none of the characters except Victor and the creature get the multi-layered and complex treatment.

I really liked the way violence was treated in this movie; it has a sort of tragedy attached to it. The violence is not just for show or for the scares; it carries some weight, and the shocks are pretty well delivered. The practical and CG special effects are done really well, and so are the makeup and costumes. There's a moment where the creature is walking down some stairs while holding a corpse; it looks so beautiful and almost fantasy-like, but the moment is supposed to be tragic, and that tragedy is not lost on us. Moments like this made this movie more beautiful.

Anyway, I'm sure there are flaws to be nitpicked here, but just like The Creature, I guess the flaws add to the beauty here, or yk, I'm just giving five stars to any and all movies that I love now. xD

I watched this movie late at night and was glued to the screen till around 1:30 AM. My attention being locked in like this during a home watch is extremely rare, okay?

Name: The Running Man
Review:
I've not read the source material, but this is a very 80s and very Arnie movie. But at the same time, the dystopian post-2017 society shown here isn't too far removed from the actual reality of this era, and I was surprised by the amount of stuff this movie gets right. Like if we were to take a list from the most basic stuff, like voice-activated smart homes, to the more serious stuff, like the manipulation by state-controlled media, popular media being used to push fascism, and deepfakes and fake news being a means of controlling the narrative, it's all real, and all of it exists right now. All the villains are missing is the slogan "Make America Great Again" or a lotus flower to make them resemble the real deal. The dystopia even ends up being less futuristic and fucked up than the real present. Even entertainment TV shows that sell negativity and have their viewers behave like they lack basic empathy also exist right now. The Running Man doesn't push for a Hunger Games-level extreme dystopia but for something that closely resembles reality. 

Arnie himself is everything we expect from Arnie from the 80s. We get introduced to him from the first scene, and he's just Arnie. We don't judge Arnie's performances like this based on his actual performance; it's purely based on fun and the vibes. Because he's not so good at the drama stuff here, but he's awesome at being Arnie. We see his flexed biceps some 10 minutes into the movie. He asks a guy "need a lift?" to pick him up and throw him like a rag doll. So that's a recurring theme here; we're reminded of Arnold's muscles and how ridonculously strong he is frequently, plus most of the lines that come out of his mouth are quippy one-liners. Even "I'll be back" is in this movie, and Arnie smoking a cigar is in there; you get the idea.

So this is a pretty political sci-fi dystopia most of the time. Richard Dawson as the villain was also a great performance, with a perfect blend of evil showman and cowardice. The social commentary is sharp and still relevant. Like I said, I'd even mistake this for a contemporary satire rather than dystopian sci-fi, but Stephen King wrote the original decades ago, before the world progressively developed to resemble the version in The Running Man. But the thing is, this is like two separate movies. Whenever Arnold is on screen, this is an Arnold movie: muscles, muscles, one-liner, one-liner, which feels separate from all the serious social commentary and satire shown in the rest of the movie. But it's still fun to watch Arnie being Arnie.

Now to see what my goat Edgar Wright has done with this source material and a leading man with fewer muscles.

Name: The Running Man
Review:
While Edgar Wright's adaptation of The Running Man does make some references to the 1987 film adaptation, like whose face is there on the "new" dollar bills and a sneakily integrated "I'll be back", this is a far more direct adaptation of Stephen King's original novel than the 1987 film, which was an Arnie movie with only some elements from the novel in it. I'm glad I checked the plot of the novel only after watching both movies, so the new movie surprised me throughout.

Ben Richards is a much more rounded and vulnerable protagonist here; he's not the invincible jacked-up hunk like the Arnold version. He's desperate, he's angry, and he's empathetic; it's established very quickly. This film leans more on the sociopolitical side of the story, presenting an exaggerated dystopian version of corporate media manipulation, how hate sells as entertainment, and how people are manipulated into cheering for and encouraging murder and violence. Glen Powell is an effective leading man; Ben Richards is shown as capable of handling himself, but he's still grounded and human, so each near escape feels like a near escape; we feel that he's running for his life and barely surviving. Powell also mastered the Tom Cruise run here and gets several opportunities to show it off in long shots. Uncle Tom would've been proud. Ben losing his shit and expressing his anger was also very fun to watch. 

Edgar Wright is so good at pacing. This movie moves at exactly the pace it needs to, as once the show begins and Ben is running for his life from being murdered, it's a non-stop thrill ride till the very end. Even in the more quiet scenes we feel the threat looming in the background. Ben is so easily rootable, and each of his near misses and his desperation are easy to connect to. And also, it does feel like he's genuinely overpowered by the hunters and the militarized force that wants to kill him. Unlike the Arnold movie, Ben Richards is not using his muscles to defeat the enemy; he's using his brain muscles and being smart.

This movie leans heavily into anti-capitalist messaging, and so it was so funny when a character who is supposed to be this anti-capitalist revolutionary pulls up a Monster energy drink; that's like product placement and a meta joke combined. The satire and political commentary is pretty direct: "They make us hate each other and then steal money from us," oof. The Running Man as a fictional TV show itself has only the murder separating it from existing reality shows that do feed off hate and encourage its audience to be hateful. These people don't truly understand that they're rooting for and supporting murder. The worst part is that the audience is made to be a part of the murdering too, by having them report the runners to the authorities (a fucked up version of how some actual reality shows have audience voting to eliminate contestants). But these people don't see the runners as real people who get murdered, to them it's just a TV show and entertainment, that's how deep the manipulation is. The movie even had its own version of the Kardashians, which is Ben's favorite show. I also liked how much of the world building is done along with the storytelling instead of relying on a text crawl like the Arnold version. 

The class politics side of it is explored here, and the movie pretty much says "viva la revolución" without actually saying it, with a Monster Energy ad attached xD. I'm assuming the Monster Energy drink popping up was a meta joke poking at anti-capitalist messaging in corporate-funded movies like this one, but that might just be me.

Also, just like all Edgar Wright movies, it's edited together so well; the signature Edgar Wright scene transitions are there, and so is that dark sense of humor. In this era where actual deepfakes exist, the thing from The Running Man where the network creates fake footage of characters to manipulate people isn't so science fiction. But still this movie finds fun ways to use that whole thing of how the footage the network broadcasts is unreliable. I wish the movie had more of that, but the stuff that it has is cool too. I'm aware that people would have mixed feelings about the ending after how everything builds up till that point, but it was satisfying for me, and I felt like cheering at the end.

Just like all Edgar Wright movies, the music was also cool here. The production design, visual effects, and depiction of a not-too-distant future were also done pretty well. The action was really great too, with lots of cool practical stunts and explosions, and it does sneak in some one-liners and humor in between like the Arnold version, but the action sensibilities are different here; this is more about Ben surviving than showcasing machismo.

Anyway, my goat Edgar Wright delivered, and it was a joy to watch on the big screen. So I'm putting five in spite of the flaws it has.

Name: Kaantha
Review:
I could just tell that Dulquer Salmaan was putting everything into his performance. It's quite a challenge to play a character who is supposed to be a "great actor". Because then when there are scenes that are supposed to show the said "great" acting, the pressure is on the actor to perform in a way that justifies the validation from the characters in the story. Dulquer does that really well in multiple instances here, because this is a pretty tricky character to pull off. He has to both perform as this particular person with modern drama sensibilities, and then when he's performing, he has to bring in that exaggerated dramatic flair from back in the days of Indian cinema. Bhagyashri Borse pretty much had the same challenge to pull off, and she surprised me with just how expressive and lively she is. Bhagyashri even steals the spotlight from Dulquer during some of their combinations. So I'm glad she got that space to perform and show off her dramatic flair in this movie. This is a very talented actress, and I hope her career path has more roles like this and less of being objectified eye candy. Samuthirakani was also great and gets some good moments towards the end. 

Anyway, the movie itself had lots of good ideas going for it, but somehow not everything is held together as a coherent package. I always love movies about movies, and this one does set up the drama and conflicts pretty well. Some of the scenes where they're making the movie were really fun to watch. The way the movie transitions between color and black and white was also very smooth, and we quickly get pulled into that visual style. But then towards the middle, it becomes a different kind of movie, and Rana Daggubati enters as a cop. Rana's cop character felt like he belonged in a different movie, and this does become a different movie for a while, only shifting back to the drama that it had going for it in the first half towards the end.

This one does have some good drama, interesting character dynamics, a budding romance that's portrayed really well, great performances, great production design, and cool music, and it did make me feel emotionally invested. But also, it should've either been a full-on character-driven drama or a full-on Agatha Christie-ish murder mystery; trying to be both seemed a bit incoherent. Like, during the investigation parts, I was waiting for the rest of the ongoing drama to play out rather than being in suspense. Rana's character not being as likable as the main characters we were following so far doesn't help either.

Again, this is a film with some really great ideas. I don't think it's a misfire, just that the ideas could've been tighter; maybe the movie could've been a bit shorter, because this had even more potential. Dulquer and Bhagyashri were delightful on screen.

Name: Dude
Review:
Out of the three movies Pradeep Ranganathan has played the lead in so far, only one of them was written by himself. And yet, all three movies have him playing basically the same guy, an unlikable asshole who thinks he's way cooler than he actually is but who the movie would have us believe is this charming, lovable, sympathetic person worthy of redemption and admiration. He'd be placed as the absolute catch and the coolest and most desirable man in the city; he's not judged harshly for his actions, no matter how bad they are, and by the end he's a well-meaning baby. There was an era of Tamil cinema in the early 2000s where Dhanush and Simbu were competing with each other in doing incel movies; it's a phase that they eventually moved on from, but it seems like that's the sort of energy Pradeep Ranganathan movies have, just with some incel meme culture and social media references in them. But what makes Dude worse is that instead of committing to being a full-on incel movie, it actually tries and pretends to be progressive and makes the protagonist say social justice speeches. 

So Pradeep is playing this unlikable dude named Agan, whom the movie wants us to see as this cool dude, complete with his own special mannerisms and stylish actions, which end up looking more cringe than stylish, the Dairy Milk product placement is hilarious in a bad way. Constantly throwing and spinning phones, Dairy Milks and sunglasses with a sound effect doesn't make every hero character a Rajinikanth, especially a character this pathetic. Some fifteen minutes into the movie, Agan's cousin Kural, played by Mamitha, proposes to him, and he rejects her (cousin romances and marriages being normalised among certain communities in India is another weird topic altogether and I'm not touching on it further), and we see it leading to extreme heartbreak that even makes her put her hand in a toilet bowl (don't ask). But the thing is, up to this point, we haven't seen anything that makes Agan a charming and lovable catch whose rejection should shatter someone. He's just been annoying, he ruins his ex's wedding, his first reaction to seeing her propose was to ask her why she's on her knees like in a porno movie(?). We haven't seen any sort of genuine chemistry between Agan and Kural that makes us feel bad that these two didn't end up together; we feel nothing for these people, and when the movie starts blasting sad music and shows them crying, I just felt a huge load of meh.

This is a recurring theme in this movie. Agan will behave like an incel dickhead most of the time, being annoying, inappropriate, crude, and just borderline repulsive, and then he'd drop some pearls of progressive wisdom or empathy, and by the end we're supposed to see him as this selfless hero who'd sacrifice anything to protect those he loves. The entire conflict in the film is a result of Agan's fuck-up, but the movie never acknowledges this and then finds ways to blame Kural for everything that's happened and make Agan seem like a gem of a person in comparison. There's even an emotional manipulation attempt with Agan wearing a clown nose and juggling CGI balls. Kural makes fun of him, which is firstly so out of character for Kural, and then his friend goes on this emotional monologue about how a pure soul like Agan is being hurt by her. So basically every character in this movie serves one purpose, which is to make Agan seem like a gem of a person with a heart of gold, while he's not that great a person, and he's not even that charming. It's like a grand illusion that's supposed to make us think that he's so great while he behaves like an incel. That he's owed a hot woman and him being rejected then is the woman's fault, and yet, he's an amazing person who'd go to great lengths to help that woman.

This movie has all these moments of conflict and melodrama that made me feel nothing. How can I feel for any of these characters when they lack chemistry, I don't feel anything for their romance or emotions, and I either hate or feel indifferent to everyone? Then there's the way caste violence and honor killing are introduced in the movie. Ngl, that reveal was the one moment in this movie where I felt something. Sarath Kumar's performance was great at that moment too. But the way that angle is then handled is also very shitty. The character from the oppressed caste community is like an empty shell without any personality and an immature loser who needs Agan's help to get everything done and needs Agan to save him from everything, and the movie clearly wants us to see that Agan is way cooler than him. Like, when you're speaking up against casteism, the upper-caste dude being shown as the cooler savior is just weird, bro. And then in the end, as if redeeming someone as shitty as Agan wasn't enough; it's a redemption arc situation for the murderous casteist as well, which is like the worst way to write an honor killer's character arc. When Agan's brilliant plan and intervention cure him of his casteism, he embraces his oppressed caste son-in-law, as if he didn't hate his community enough to murder his own blood. And then a smiling Agan walks away from this honor killer's happy family in slow motion, looking proud because he solved casteism, eating a dairy milk, which reminded me of how AJ Bhairav videos end with that guy walking in slow motion looking all proud. This is pretty much the same sensibility and the same (low) quality of writing, just that it casts actual actors instead of AJ Bhairav in filters and wigs. 

Tbh, Oorum Blood is a song that I really liked when it got released as a single. But this movie overuses that track so much, and it pops up in the cringiest of scenes and when Agan is supposedly farming aura while he's actually farming shit. Sai Abhyankkar is low-key multipurposing this song by having it pop up in happy, sad, and mass scenes. We've heard of masala movies, but Oorum Blood is a masala song. Oorum Blood and all its versions and the rest of the songs in the soundtrack are still peak though. I love this damn soundtrack no matter how much I loathe this movie, so no disrespect to the isai arakkan 🙏🏽. You go kid!

I don't think Pradeep is a bad actor. But after each release, the assumption that his priorities lie with catering to the incel crowd just grows stronger. Like, why can't he just play characters who are actually charming? Then I'd believe that he's charming and likable. Mamitha Baiju is wasted in a badly written character who is just there to make the hero seem cool and sympathetic, even though we can see him for the asshole he is. 

I'm putting the lowest possible rating because this incel-core movie decided to pretend to be progressive in the worst ways possible. Just make incel movies about human penises like Sandeep Reddy Vanga, bro. 

Agan ends casteism by being an insufferable asshole. Being an asshole is the answer to defeating the caste system, guys.

Name: Eko
Review:
There's lots to admire in Ekō: the way it's been shot, the gorgeous landscape the story's been set in, the beautiful yet eerie atmosphere, and the way the narrative unfolds layer by layer, taking us deeper and deeper into its world, or should I say, into Kuriachan.

There's a certain kind of narrative that I really admire, and it's the kind where we see a person depicted through other people's eyes rather than directly seeing them. Bram Stoker's Dracula, the novel, never gives a sense of Dracula to the reader directly; we're only reading up about what the other characters wrote when they encountered Dracula. It's the same monster, but each of them has their own version of him. Even in KG George's Yavanika, which is structured as a murder mystery, basically each of the characters paints a portrait of a vile human being named Ayyappan, and they each have their own reasons to loathe him, before showing us Ayyappan directly. In Ekō that character is Kuriachan, as we hear characters talk about Kuriachan and his many chronicles and his very absurd and eventful life.

Kuriachan is this invisible presence the entire film revolves around, as basically every character is talking about him or wants to find him. There's this mystique around this person, and every piece of information that's revealed about him makes him more interesting. For the same reason, when Kuriachan does stop being someone we just hear about and we do finally get to see him in the flesh through flashbacks in the movie, Saurabh Sachdeva as Kuriachan didn't quite make me feel like it's the same person that everyone was talking about so far. Him not being a Malayali also restricts the performance here, as he's not matching his lips with the Malayalam lines either. Biana Momin as Mlaathi Chettathi is another non-Malayali presence as a major character in the film, but in her case, her presence does match the character she's meant to portray even if she's having a dubbed voice too. Anyway, showing Kuriachan in the flesh kind of lessens the mystique given to the character up to that point, and I wish he just remained as a person that we only heard about but never saw through flashbacks. Or he needed to be the kind of presence in the flashbacks in a way that justifies the image the other characters' versions of him portray.

Another important presence in the movie is the dogs. This is the second Bahul Ramesh screenplay involving dogs, and this is superior to Kerala Crime Files in the way the dogs are used. The analogies given to "protection vs imprisonment" and "pet vs prisoner" were all great, the way the dogs have been integrated into the film and become an integral part of the narrative was nice, and the movie succeeds in making the dogs seem scary in very smart ways. It's all cinema magic, clever editing, filmmaking, and sound design most of the time, but they succeed in making these dogs seem scary and intimidating; the way the tension builds up during such moments is pretty brilliant.

I also liked the fight choreography in the movie, which didn't seem choreographed. It really looked like people were really going for it, trying to hurt or kill the other person, just violently hitting and hurting each other. It's very chaotic, very messy, and pretty realistic. Sandeep Pradeep was good as Pious (Peeyoos ig); he can be called the lead of the movie screentime-wise, but this is more of an ensemble piece that revolves around Kuriachan. Vineeth was also great, and I lowkey wished he was Kuriachan instead (I think he dubbed for Sourabh as Kuriachan too; I'm not sure). The supporting cast was solid on the whole.

I won't be talking about the plot that much because, just like Kishkintha Kaandam, this movie is best experienced fresh, and it does get progressively more thrilling and intriguing as it moves forward. But just like Kishkintha Kaandam, it can get a bit exposition-heavy, but it doesn't make it any less engaging. The music was very atmospheric and cool too; especially towards the end, I got chills listening to the score during the ending. Also, the atmosphere set by all the greenery and the mountain landscape was also very beautiful and moody. The hill, the dogs, and the house at the top, it's effective imagery.

Anyway, I'm glad that people like Bahul Ramesh and Dinjith Ayyathan pursue unique stories and storytelling opportunities like this one. Cinema needs to be vibrant; cinema needs to be unique.

Personal Note: I almost got hit by a car while I was on the way to watch the movie, and I was pretty distressed when the movie began, and yet, it pulled me in, and on the way back, I was more afraid of getting attacked by dogs than I was of getting hit by another car. xD

Name: Zootopia
Review:
They used cute animals, animal metaphors, and animal puns to make a movie about how wrong it is to hate somebody on the basis of an identity that they were simply born with. Like this can be translated to racial hatred or religion-based hatred or any kind of such prejudice. Beyond just how fun and hilarious this movie is, Zootopia is also one of, if not the, most political Disney Animation movies.

The DMV scene still makes me laugh out loud; there are so many great jokes here, so many pop culture references, cheeky puns, fun action, and very beautiful design and animation, and each and every frame of this movie is oozing with so much creativity and innovation. This reminds me of a time when Disney wasn't just a factory churning out sequels and live-action remakes of existing properties. Judy and Nick are such lovable leads and have great chemistry with each other, and that chemistry feels earned. The music and the one Shakira song were also so cool.

Watching this was like getting transported to a different time in my life. I'm excited to see the sequel. (I'm aware that I just took a dig at Disney for producing sequels in the previous paragraph, but yk 🫣.)

Name: Zootopia 2
Review:
There were two big Hollywood movies this year that dealt with Americans being hostile towards immigrants. One starred Leonardo DiCaprio, Chase Infiniti, and Sean Penn; the other stars a fox, a bunny, and a snake. 

This time, Zootopia is using animal species metaphors to talk about immigrants and land occupation with some anti-capitalist themes thrown in (Disney movie, I know; it's called a hustle, sweetheart). It's an extension of the themes present in the first movie, where it was about seeing a person beyond our preconceived prejudices related to their identity. Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde single-handedly putting an end to animal racism is a bit of a stretch, so I'm glad this movie is a little bit realistic about the first film's ending. It's not that Judy and Nick were able to rid everyone of their prejudices; it's just that they solved a conspiracy that would've dehumanized (should I say deanimalized) a certain community and painted them as potential killers. And similarly this time it's about the reptiles and aquatic animals.

Make no mistake, this is still a pretty fun comedy adventure movie. Just like the first one, the political themes are integrated in a way that maintains a light tone just enough. In terms of the humor and animal puns and references, there are lots, though there wasn't a scene that made me laugh out loud like a crazy person like the DMV scene from the first one here. There are lots of pop culture references too, and though this is a kids' movie, I'm pretty sure references to movies like The Godfather and The Shining were meant for the adults. No child watching this would be like, "OOH, IT'S THE THEME MUSIC FROM THE SHINING AND THE MAZE FROM THE SHINING!" There was a Ratatouille reference that had me laughing too. 

Judy and Nick are still loveable leads; their chemistry and the conflict between them were all well developed, and all the therapy speak was accurate, insightful, and hilarious at the same time. Gary the snake was also a great addition, and all the snake puns were fun too. I had a lot of fun watching this movie; it was great to see Flash again too. The sloth always eats up the scene in the Zootopia movies. The music was nice, and the Shakira song was cool too. The art and animation looks gorgeous and I was glued to the screen. Every character and every environment is beautiful. The movements of each animal has so much thought put into them, especially the snake. 

It's an overall faithful sequel to the original that's fun and political in an entertaining package. It does lack the novelty the original had of course, I don't know how to quite explain it, but it does lack a teeny bit of something special that the original had. Or maybe it's just that one hilarious DMV scene. 

At the same time, it's funny to see Hollywood release the nth mainstream movie about how occupying and colonizing a community's land is wrong while a lot of them still defend Isra... Ahem, it's called a hustle, sweetheart.

Name: Bugonia
Review:
BUGONIA reminded me so much of Yorgos' earlier movies, and this might be the most satisfied I've been watching one of his movies after the favourite. It manages to strike that perfect dark comedy tone of being disturbing, scary, and yet funny at the same time. I'm conflicted whether to laugh at this or be disturbed by it, and that's because the movie works. The filmmaking is so precise, the production design is amazing, and the performances are brilliant.

People complain that Emma Stone is in every Yorgos movie now, but also, she doesn't get other opportunities to deliver such performances in her other movies; like, she was barely in Eddington. Her performance is amazing here, and so were Jesse Plemons's and Aidan Delbis's.

The movie constantly kept me on the edge about where it's all heading to and found new ways to be absurd and funny. I won't talk about the plot because this is the kind of movie that's better experienced when it surprises us. But yk, it was so brilliant. Credit goes to the original Korean version too, of course.

Name: Kalamkaval
Review:
Ikka Renaissance is back on track, babyyy!

Honestly, it was great to see Mammootty as a proper antagonist here, this truly malicious psychopath who seeks out his prey just for the kicks. He doesn't have a tragic flashback, he doesn't have a sympathetic side, he's just venomous. Mammootty is clearly choosing characters that are fun for him to dive into as an actor rather than sticking to a certain brand value as a star, or right now, being unpredictable about his choices might precisely be his brand. He does this thing with the cigarette in his mouth in this movie, and just his face and what he's doing with the cigarette convey the terror and the violence of the situation more than showing any actual gore. A truly great supporting performance from the cigarettes in this movie. The prologue of this movie has this great buildup that's less on the background score and more about the dialogues. The way the tension builds in the scene and how a casual conversation slowly turns sinister is a legend at work. He adds so many layers to the character, way beyond what's written. Whether it's the menace or the moments where he does show weakness beneath. He elevates this movie so much with his performance and presence. 

Vinayakan plays the police officer protagonist Jayakrishnan/Naththu. Initially the performance felt a bit jarring, and I wasn't sure if it was a misfire or if this is just how Naththu is supposed to be. But then the performance slowly grew on me later on too. There were many moments where I did like the performance; one is a scene where he's with his daughter, and the other is towards the end, where the fact that most of the people in my screening cheered was the biggest W from this movie.

I really liked the non-linear structure too; at times you don't know whether what you're seeing is happening in the past or present as the movie alternates between the two. It adds a certain uncertainty to the proceedings as Naththu and team are trying to find this criminal, and he keeps slipping away. Now, this is the kind of police procedural that begins by showing us who the killer is. It's more of a howcatchem than a whodunit. The thrill is in whether the protagonist would get to the killer or not, and here lies one of the issues I had with Kalamkaaval. As much as it was a joy to see a villainous Mammootty performance, some of the scenes where the villain is stalking his prey and seducing the women ended up being a bit repetitive, and they were just making the same point over and over again. This is a predator who preys on these women's loneliness and manipulates them, but the writing doesn't convey how exactly he succeeds in trapping them. Fleshing out a few of the victims or conveying how exactly they were manipulated would've improved the movie. 

The music was pretty great, though occasionally the movie felt a bit overscored. That prologue scene played around with silence and awkward pauses and a subtle background score, and it added to the terror there. The main theme music given to the villain and that retro song were cool, though. 

There were several cool memorable moments in the movie, like that pre-interval scene. This movie strikes a balance between presenting a star as a villain while not glorifying the villainy like how Kurup did. The narrative itself so clearly wants us to root for Naththu to catch this guy; it's a pretty straightforward police procedural that way. The plot conveniences and all didn't bother me that much. 

Spoilers

People cheered in my screening when Naththu finally catches up to Stanley and pins him down, which is such a win because people are only caring about the characters and not about who's playing who. I was glad that Vinayakan's character got his hero moment towards the end. I also liked the duality of the two characters. It's not a vigilante justice situation here; Naththu is shown to enjoy murder just like how Stanley does. That's what's making these men be parallels to each other. Stanley preys on lonely women, while Naththu satisfies his urge by murdering criminals. Naththu is pretty much a murderous psychopath too. It reminded me of Dexter, yk, the serial killer who only kills criminals, not the kid with a secret laboratory. Treating Naththu as another killer who enjoys murder, rather than as a vigilante hero cop executing "true justice", was an interesting angle, which connects him with the villain Stanley on a deeper level, and I wish the movie explored it a bit more.

PS: I was just thinking about how I wouldn't be able to describe even someone I see on a daily basis to a sketch artist to accurately draw them when that sketching scene happened. That conductor had supreme photographic memory ig.

Name: A Nightmare on Elm Street
Review:
This is a very corny movie, but it's corny in a fun way. All those practical special effects are so fun to watch, even the goofier ones like that doll through the door at the end. Some of the deaths are still scary, and sometimes that sense of horror and dread is conveyed well, and some other times the movie is straight up hilarious. Freddy Krueger is not full-on goofy in this movie, and yet it's so funny when he turns into one of the Home Alone bandits at the end and screams in agony while setting off booby traps. The blood geyser is still a very chilling death scene. Also, such an iconic background score. 

Also, I forgot how much of a mindfuck this movie is; after a point, we never know if we're watching a dream or the reality, and I had no idea about that when the ending happened either.

"THIS IS GOD"

Name: Jay Kelly
Review:
"Can I go again? I'd like another one."
Noah Baumbach has this skill to invite us into the vulnerable emotions of his characters in the most beautiful ways while also being funny on a very human level. It doesn't matter if it's someone deeply relatable like Frances Ha or someone who is so far removed from who I am like Jay Kelly. Jay Kelly immediately reminded me of Bojack Horseman, though they're very different from each other. Jay Kelly is not as dark and depressing, but this one is also about a rich actor confronting his past while also having an interesting relationship with his agent, it makes fun of show business, except that Jay Kelly is still a pretty relevant movie star, and he doesn't have an addiction problem, and George Clooney is not a cartoon horse. It's just that he's really lonely and disconnected. Jay spends three decades of his life pretending. When he's doing his job, he's pretending to be other people, and when in the public eye, which he is most of the time, he's putting on the persona of a movie star named Jay Kelly. In between this, he forgets to live as himself. Which makes him neglect the people around him who did care about him. He could play a loving man on screen, but he could never be one, and then over a couple of days he's forced to confront his past and his many mistakes, which ironically is leading up to him getting a tribute for his career. What we get is something funny, charming, heartwarming, and often melancholic. I use the word "melancholy" because this is not an inherently sad movie or a heavy drama of Marriage Story proportions. Jay is held accountable for his mistakes; this is not a "the world did this poor baby wrong" kind of situation. Jay was an absent father and a bad husband, and even when his manager Ron treats him like family and gives him as much attention as he gives his actual family, Jay has a way of treating his employees as, yk, his employees. So this is not just the "pains of being a rich star"; it's just showing how the choices Jay Kelly took towards favoring his star persona just made him lonely at the end. Just like that Bojack Horseman quote, everybody loves him, but nobody really likes him. Noah Baumbach's way of writing and directing conversation scenes always has me in awe. After White Noise and Barbie, which were operating in a different terrain, with this movie, Baumbach, along with co-writer Emily Mortimer, is back in familiar Noah Baumbach movie territory. Every conversation has so much texture and personality; they're funny and insightful, we get to know so much about these characters, and each interaction feels so real. Towards the end, there's a very important phone conversation, and Baumbach makes the choice to represent that conversation as if the two characters are actually walking and talking, instead of using split screen or cutting back and forth between them on their phones. I loved that choice because this is exactly the kind of scene that he's so great at. There are also some beautiful moments where just the music and the visuals carry the emotions, like when Jay has to travel in a train, in economy class, and he just takes a pause, seeing ordinary lives play out in front of him, and he looks at the other passengers like a curious child, and we can just tell that he hasn't seen people like this for a long time. There are a few flashbacks in the movie, but they're also treated like Jay walking into a set where slices from his life are playing out. And then there's the tribute that the entire movie is building towards, which also felt like the perfect way to close his film as both Jay's career and personal life cross over. George Clooney was delightful as the title character; he conveyed the perfect amount of humor and vulnerability. Jay Kelly is the kind of character that we do feel sorry for, but at the same time, we do understand why he's lonely. We'd feel like giving him a hug, but at the same time, we don't know if he'd actually consider that a warm gesture. Clooney makes the title character likable and relatable, but in a way that the character's flaws are also visible. The movie is aware that life is not a movie where retakes are possible, and that's the kind of character arc that Jay gets. It felt so real when he cried in this movie. Also, George Clooney is one of the few Hollywood faces who still has lines and wrinkles on his face, and that definitely adds to the character, if that makes sense. Adam Sandler as Ron gets more prominence here after Clooney; Ron's point of view is important because it eliminates the misinterpretation of Jay being a victim of circumstance. It's through Ron that we see Jay as a privileged man-baby who doesn't consider others' lives as much as he does his. There's this moment where Ron and Jay are talking to each other, and Jay only wants to talk about himself and doesn't even want to listen to Ron. It says so much by saying so little. There are other talented actors in the cast, such as Laura Dern, Greta Gerwig, Riley Keough, and the co-writer Emily Mortimer, and then Billy Crudup and Patrick Wilson. Most of the cast get their fair share of good moments, while some are just "there", though Clooney and Sandler get the most. Sandler's daughter plays his daughter, because I guess that's to be expected in every Adam Sandler movie these days? Anyway, Jay Kelly has all the elements of the Noah Baumbach kind of movies that I've known and loved. It might have its flaws, but I'm judging it solely by feels here, and the feels were definitely there, and my heart was full. Also, beautiful music from Nicholas Britell.

Name: Wake Up Dead Man
Review:
Three movies in, it's so cute that Daniel Craig is visibly having so much fun playing Benoit Blanc, perhaps more fun than he ever had playing James Bond. All three movies of this series so far have a similar structure where all three movies have their own protagonists: it was Ana De Armas' character in Knives Out, Janelle Monáe's character in Glass Onion, and Josh O'Connor's character in this one. But this one in particular felt more protagonist-driven than like an ensemble. O'Connor's Reverend Jud is our point of view character for most of this movie; we rarely switch away from him. We get to know the others mostly through what he experiences, and that includes Benoit Blanc. Out of all three, this might be the one where Blanc felt the most like a supporting character, though he still gets to do his "checkmate moment" at the end and deliver some Big Blanc Energy.

The movie was funny, entertaining, and thrilling enough; the mystery was engrossing, and the reveals were done in a very fun way. Rian Johnson can still write a good detective story. Also, the idea of faith and religion is explored in a really fun way in this movie, and unlike Hugh Grant from Heretic making atheist arguments, Benoit Blanc roasting religion is far more satisfying. The fact that Hugh Grant played Benoit Blanc's husband too is a fun trivia here. The cast has a lot of talented actors, but not all of them get their moments. I also liked the look and atmosphere of this movie, which set it apart from the other two movies and yet had some visual elements from them at the same time (especially those camera moves).

Anyway, I hope Daniel Craig and Rian Johnson keep on making these.

Name: The Mastermind
Review:
Taking everything you know about doing a heist film and doing the exact opposite of that seemed to be the assignment here, and I'm saying this as a compliment. Like, where else would you see the thiefs picking up and arranging the all of the loot in all it's mundane glory? We never saw the dudes in Ocean's Eleven put all that money in all those bags, but this is not that kind of heist. This is like a heist and chase presented like your average mundane day, with occasional laughs in between, including that ending.

Also, Josh O'connor was great as the anti-Danny Ocean.

Name: The Chronology of Water

The movie was very trippy, disturbing, and insightful, even with that chaotic structure where memories are presented like messy mashups. 

Kristen Stewart knows ball. Also, Imogen Poots WAS brilliant.

Review:
It was very funny, with an ensemble of a lot of talented newcomers. The rural culture, constant dose of humor, all those big visual comedic moments like that big fight were very well done. So was the way animals were integrated into the movie. 

 It's a bit unfocused at times, but still, the fun makes up for it. The music was very cool as well.

Name: Broken Voices
Review: Expected something like Whiplash but this one's taking another route. I was very disturbed by the end. Such great acting from the whole cast.

Name: It Was Just an Accident
Review:
Jafar Panahi is a filmmaking badass in the way he just refuses to be silenced. This one is not that politically charged, the narrative is operating on a thriller/dark comedy terrain, but still, Panahi is able to integrate his political voice into this, and as a result, even when the moments where the political perspective is addressed is lesser compared to something like No Bears, it was just an accident still feels like it has a powerful political voice against an oppressive regime, the same regime that has been trying to silence Panahi for years. But like a true badass, he'd make cinema, however he could, with whatever he has. I would give this the full rating because Panahi is the kind of rare artistic voice that deserves all the love in the world.

Also, the movie was very engaging, with great characters, great acting, great use of long takes, great dialogue and it's also surprisingly funny and heartwarming even when the subject matter is heavy.

Name: No Other Choice
Review:
Can capitalism and unemployment be terrifying, depressing, dreadful and then funny at the same time? Park Chan-wook says hell yeah. 

This movie was thrilling, funny, sad, tragic, all the actors were amazing, the music was cool and it's up there with Parasite in how it deals with the theme of capitalism making desperate people do terrible things. This movie manages to be consistently funny while having such a tragic and dark storyline otherwise. That's just mastery at work there.

Name: Resurrection
Review:
I had no clue about what was going on most of the time. But then again, the movie is showing us dreams and actual dreams do tend to have that quality, I didn't fully grasp all of the themes and emotions being conveyed regardless, but still, I'm planning on reading up about it.

Anyway, as an audio-visual experience this movie was on another level. Each of its chapters are like their own self contained movies, with lots of gorgeous and unique visuals and crazy sequences. So many people were leaving the screening early on and they missed out on this crazy long unbroken shot towards the end which is a brilliant technical achievement, with the amount of locations, characters and events happening on screen. 

This is one of those movies where, I was too dumb to fully understand it, but I sure as hell appreciated the craft in it.

Name: Sentimental Value
Review:
This movie reminded me of that Laura Dern monologue from Marriage Story where she says how people would always accept an imperfect dad but the women will be held to a different, higher standard. Here, I couldn't help but feel that the movie sides with the absent father, make him sympathetic and expects the daughter to be the bigger person and forgive him. Now, I can't say for sure that this is the same kind of bias that Laura Dern was talking about, but yk.

Anyway, the acting was great, I really adored a lot of the character interactions, but I just wish the movie was more about the daughter played by Renate Reinsve than the dad, as good as Stellan Skarsgård's performance is. Nora was the far more interesting character and the movie needed more of her. My favorite scene from the movie was also the conversation between the two sisters towards the end. This had an interesting enough family dynamic and meta-narrative possibilities to be even better, though.

Name: Franz

It's a pretty looking movie, and there are lots of penises. I don't know if that falls under being kafkaesque.

Name: Amrum
Review: At one point, this movie asks a question, whether the children of hate filled bigots have accountability for the violence and hate even if these children themselves don't carry the same hate with them. Sometimes such parents fail at filling up their children with the poison of hate, and that itself is a miracle, but still, it puts the kids in a spot where they still have to consider these people family even if their hate and prejudices are unacceptable. This film is showing this in a WWII Nazi Germany context, but I know friends whose parents are sanghis who have questioned themselves the same way this movie's protagonist had.

Name: The Secret Agent
Review: I lacked context about the political scenario in Brazil at the time to fully understand this movie. But still, being hunted in the name of opposing an oppressive regime, having to live expecting death from every corner, an oppressive regime that'd resort to anything to silence voices against them, the storytelling here is pretty universal. It's very well made with some cool music too and Wagner Moura was really great.

Name: Once Upon A Love Story
Review: Whoa I didn't expect the other reviews about this movie to be hating it to this extent. I found it kinda charming, the landscapes and architecture in Vietnam reminded me so much of rural Kerala, the film looked visually beautiful, the music was cool, yeah, the drama was a bit dumb at times, but I didn't hate this movie. All the three lead actors were great too.

Name: Miroirs No. 3

Name: Avatar: Fire and Ash
Review:
The Avatar movies were formulaic and 90s coded from the very beginning; the unobtainable mineral in the first movie was called unobtanium, ffs, so it's pointless to judge the movies for sticking to the formula or being predictable in their dramatic beats. This is pure big commercial cinema from one of the absolute pros of doing such spectacle movies. It's not without its flaws, but when it works, it's glorious.

The film is almost three hours and fifteen minutes long, but as dazzling and magnificent as it is to look at this world and the top-of-the-line visual effects artistry, there's too much movie going on here too. The first Avatar dealt with the colonizers trying to take away land and minerals from the natives. The second movie brought in the whale hunting angle, and now this movie is a combination of the two: the humans find a way in which they can finally occupy and colonize Pandora, while there's a whale hunting plot happening in between. While the first Avatar was simple and basic in its narrative, the second one brought in more characters and subplots, and this one also has multiple characters having their own thing going on. It's packed to the brim with stuff, and I wish it had less stuff and kept things tighter.

Jake and Neytiri are pretty monotonous during the beginning stretch of the movie, and while I still don't care enough about the kids to even remember their names, man, the villains get so much cooler in this movie. I'm not talking about the corporate creeps, of course; I'm talking about the Colonel and the fire lady. Stephen Lang and Oona Chaplin are so much fun to watch as Quaritch and Varang; they get some of the best lines and most memorable moments in the movie. Quaritch even has the most interesting character arc here; his moral dilemma is pretty much the same as the last movie, but it does seem to be something that Cameron seems to be interested in further developing. The funniest parts of the movie involve Quaritch, and he has come a long way from the stereotypical beefy military villain from the first movie.

The stakes and the drama do get more interesting after the halfway point; Jake and Neytiri's arc involving the human vs. Na'vi conflict being a part of their mixed family, and them having to choose between the battle for Pandora and their own family also becomes interesting. Human civilians are shown for the first time in the franchise, and of course they're mindless colonizer idiots who want to shoot everything with their mobile phones. Pretty soon they'll say that Pandora was promised to them, maybe? Anyway, there were several moments where Zoe Saldana and Sam Worthington showed Neytiri and Jake's vulnerability and moral turmoil that worked really well. But the thing is, I really didn't care about the kids this time as well, when three of them are front and center here. The most I remember is teenage Sigourney Weaver having a cool Aliens callback moment.

As an audiovisual experience, this movie is extraordinary. They push the technology and visual fidelity further forward in this film too, whether it's the characters or the environments, and it's a sight to behold. So is Cameron's skill at executing huge action sequences and old-fashioned drama. All the action sequences have his signature all over them, and even when the writing falters, the drama, the thrills, and the storytelling during the action scenes still drew me in. It's nothing Cameron hasn't shown us before, but damn, he's so good at it.

Anyway, I'd still revisit Pandora, as, even with its issues, Cameron's world is still so dense and filled with wonder and beauty, and the anti-occupation narrative is more relevant now than ever.

This is the second Disney movie over the span of a month to have a narrative that's against colonizing, btw; one had a bunny and a fox, and this one had blue people. Funny.

Name: Now You See Me: Now You Don't
Review:
Ah, the fast and the furious with magic is back.

I've forever been fascinated with the art of magic, both as a kid when I thought it was real and as an adult when I realized they were just tricks. That feeling of getting fooled right under our noses is always very fun. Which is why I loved the original Now You See Me when it came out. Sure, I'd wish for a magic-themed heist movie to be more grounded, with tricks that are possible to be done irl, but these movies mix real tricks with impossible movie magic and CGI trickery, but it's still fun. It's dumb, but in a very fun way. This one also follows the same principle. It's not the most intelligent thriller movie, but it's still fun; the twists are fun, and the action looks unserious but again, so much fun. Like, this is the only franchise where the good guys would perform free magic tricks for the bad guys who are trying to kill them, so...

Rosamund Pike was a joy to watch as a goofy and over the top German villain. She even does the Absolute Cinema pose in this movie 😭

And God bless Brian Tyler for the coolest theme music ever.

The movie didn't have enough Ruffalo in it.

Name: The Terminator
Review:
It's hard to believe that James Cameron was just starting out here given the amount of control he has over his craft in this movie. There are so many cool decisions that just work beautifully. Firstly, Arnie is given that forever memorable "duh duh duh duh" background score since his very first appearance. It's instantly memorable, and then it just becomes an indicator of his presence, even in moments where he isn't even on screen.

Then there's Arnie himself; he was built for this role, not just born for it. Legend has it that he was actually approached to play Kyle Reese, but then he had all these notes on how the Terminator should be played, and then Cameron eventually got him to play the Terminator. And boy is he perfect. Whether it's his imposing physique that a normal person just doesn't have, or his movements and the way he carries himself, the way he speaks, or the way he showcases his power. Even Arnold's limited acting range adds character to the robotic nature of the Terminator. It's that perfect of a character for him.

This movie is just full-on old-school fun. Linda Hamilton is great as Sarah Connor, and so is Michael Biehn as Kyle Reese. The way the tension builds up as both these men look for Sarah is great, and once the chase begins, it's even more thrilling. Even while being a smaller film compared to the other Cameron action spectacles, this movie still delivers on visceral, high-octane action. The animatronics and the prosthetic makeup on the Terminator also look so great; sure, the stop-motion endoskeleton at the end looks rough, but this movie still mostly holds up due to just how great Cameron's vision and filmmaking are. It's also interesting to see his tendency to show badass women here too. Sarah is not the trained badass that we see in T2 yet, but still, she's not a damsel in distress either; in every escape, she and Kyle have to work together against the terminator rather than him always having to save her. Even in the end, Kyle is out of commission, and she has to fight on her own.

This was also basically the first time loop movie I'd ever seen, and I didn't even realize that it was a time loop as a kid. That whole idea of both Skynet and John Connor existing in a closed loop where both of them only exist because of the other is so trippy and genius.

Name: Sarvam Maya
Review:
This movie does one single thing really well, and that's presenting Nivin as the charming, funny, and cute pookie person that he's meant to be. Nivin is in his comfort zone here, playing the goofy softboi, and he's a joy to watch throughout the movie. The movie itself felt like a mixed bag, I didn't like the whole brahmin glazing angle, the way it expects an atheist to think faith is the right path, and the movie didn't really give me a proper closure towards the end.

When I watched Diés Iraé, I didn't really buy into the Brahmin exorcist angle in that movie, and here's this movie, again involving Brahmin exorcisms and ghosts. But somehow this is a better depiction, but yeah, brahmin glazing is present here too and it's not exactly opposing the caste system or addressing savarna privilege or Brahmin purity or something, the gaze is pretty much from a privileged POV. We have an atheist Brahmin protagonist, who's still a vegetarian though he doesn't actually need to be (dietary choice, I guess?). At least he's not intolerant towards a Muslim eating meat near him hehe (Why should the Muslim guy even ask him if he's okay with it, actually?), he starts doing poojas to make some money on the side while he lands a musician gig while still being a non-believer, and then he encounters a real ghost. This film was kinda casual about religion and faith, showing it as someone's personal thing rather than being too serious about it despite operating in a fantasy area, which is what Diés Iraé did, but it still pushes faith to the atheist protagonist instead of yk, letting him stay an atheist. I was afraid that this would be about the protagonist embracing his Hindutva Brahmin purity, faith, and identity, but I was a bit glad that the movie isn't really about all that but I hated the fact that there was some balancing here to satisfy that side too. The movie also borderline shows all the poojas and exorcisms as a hustle and is generally casual and unserious about those rituals, pretty clearly showing the Namboothiris caring only about the money, doing rituals that don't actually mean anything. 

Anyway, this is a light and breezy little ghost movie with the protagonist encountering a manic pixie dream ghost girl who fixes him (of course). Reminded me of a similar Malayalam movie from a couple of years ago (which itself was a remake). Though this was marketed as a Nivin-Aju movie, it's more of a Nivin-Riya Shibu movie. There were fun moments, and the leads did have some chemistry together, but it was mostly Nivin carrying the movie with his charm. Like, he's adding so much to the movie here, and I doubt someone else could make the same impact. And then towards the second half, the movie just wanders around a lot; a new love interest and a romance subplot are introduced out of nowhere, and every plot thread is rushed to an ending. I didn't like certain elements in the movie that clearly come from a privileged gaze like everything involving the main character's privileged savarna identity or like the joke involving homeless people ordering KFC from Zomato. Like, even if we leave elitism out of it, the whole "look at poor people doing rich people things lol" is just a dated and unfunny trope. 

This movie has a major third act problem, which is a recurring thing in newer Sathyan Anthikad films and his sons' films, as they set up all these character relationships and plot threads only to just tie everything up in the most underwhelming way possible, giving a sense of "Ithreyullo?" But still, it's still a light and easy watch, with no unnecessary noise. It did have some heart and feels, but yeah, it felt somewhat incomplete also. Grief as an emotion has been a main part in all of Akhil Sathyan's works so far and that always carries some emotional weight in his movies, that's true for Sarvam Maaya too. I liked the way the main character's grief was portrayed and how it tied to his atheism, even when the eventual closure in how his atheism is handled is underwhelming, and I loathed all the Brahmin glazing and balancing stuff too.

Also, Arjun Ajikumar/Aesthetic Kunjamma got attacked by both a terror ghost and a pookie ghost in 2025, such a unique achievement.

(The rating is more about seeing a charming Nivin on screen than the movie itself btw)

Name: Terminator 2: Judgment Day
Review:
T2 is an upgrade over T1 in every single way, and it's no wonder that this movie is one of the first ones that pops up in anyone's mind when talking about sequels that overshadow their originals. Cameron makes sure that we know that right from the beginning. The visual effect from the first movie that looked the most rough was the Terminator endoskeleton from the ending, so this one outright begins by showing gorgeous-looking Terminator endoskeletons that look and move realistically; that's a major flex right there. We also see a major upgrade in the future war sequence, bigger in every way compared to the first movie, and then the titles roll with the dun dun dun dun dun... Myru Absolute cinemaaa 😭

Arnie had become a way bigger star in between T1 and T2, and that stardom is clearly visible in the way that he's presented. In T1 he's a threat, with Kyle and Sarah being people trying to survive and escape this threat. In T2 Arnie is a full-on action hero badass; he looks cool, does cool shit, and says cool catchphrases and he has big muscles. I know everyone walked into this movie while already knowing that Arnie plays the protector this time and not the villain, but I wish I got to watch this without having that knowledge. Because though the film's marketing back then and pop culture have spoiled it for everyone, the film itself starts in a way that's very similar to T1. We see both Arnie and Robert Patrick looking for John Connor; the film doesn't specify which one the killer is, and it's only revealed in the mall hallway that Arnie is the good guy. It's a pretty awesome buildup.

The film is filled with such epic action scenes; Cameron's vision and execution here are unparalleled. Also, though the primitive shape-shifting CGI on the T-1000 and certain effects at times show their age, the vision and the filmmaking involved are so competent and amazing that they still blend in with the narrative, never taking me out of it. That's the power of cinema, baby. Also, in T1, when the terminator's face is damaged and we see Arnie in his half-man, half-machine look, it's not actually Arnie, but a puppet. But here, they were able to achieve the same look with prosthetics, and it's very impressive; there are several close-ups of the damaged terminator's face, and it looks perfect. The visual effects work in this movie is legendary, man.

Also, though T2 is Arnie in star mode, he's still the kind of action hero who gets beat up by the villain. The fight at the end is pretty one-sided, as the far more advanced T-1000 dismantles our hero with ease. Robert Patrick was very effectively scary and intimidating throughout this movie, despite not being as imposing as Arnie physically. It creates so much drama and tension and then gives that much satisfaction to the final payoff. It's that kind of balance between the action star sensibilities and character building that makes movies like this work. The relationship between John and the terminator feels real and earned. I'd still say the scarier T1 was the best Arnie performance, but this one is a more human terminator, so to speak. He was a pookienator, basically. Arnold was spiritually a cat in T2; don't ask me to elaborate.

The only part in this movie where I always feel a bit off is when the constant chase from the T-1000 takes a pause and the Miles Dyson Skynet plot happens. Sure, it ends in an epic action scene, and that's integral to the judgement day in the movie's title and the end farewell, but still, it pulls the movie a bit back from being a full-on chase situation like the first movie. But T2 still holds it tight, and it's still iconic af. Arnie saying "I'll be back," slowly walking towards cops through smoke while being shot and damaged, and then kneecapping them? Myru, absolute cinema 😭

Also, Linda Hamilton in this movie was like the first jacked woman that I ever saw as a kid. She was also all kinds of cool here as a trained and more battle-ready Sarah Connor. The thing with James Cameron is that he never made a boys' movie. All of his movies have female leads who are equally or more capable than the male leads of being badasses. Just like in the first movie, even though a protector from the future is present, Sarah can still take care of herself, and they take down their threat by working together and not by the terminator doing everything on his own.

Hasta la vista, baby.

Name: Terminator: Dark Fate
Review:
This movie is like good ideas mixed with absolute misfires. It has multiple writers attached, including Jim Cameron himself, so that tracks. This is the third attempt to relaunch the Terminator franchise, and I'm going to talk about it like it's a sequel to T2, also because I watched this right after rewatching T2 and I don't remember much from the other movies in between.

It's understandable how the killing off of John Conner pissed off people; at the time I didn't mind, because there were multiple timelines in this franchise already and this is just one of those alternatives. But now after watching T2, this is like making everything set up by T1 and T2 seem useless. But we move. Because it's from this change that the best part of this movie comes from too. Both Linda Hamilton as Sarah Connor having to live without John and Arnie as Carl.

Carl is a novel and philosophical way to look at a Terminator. Every Terminator that we had seen so far had a mission they were programmed to do. But Carl is different; he already completed his mission. Frankly, he doesn't have a reason to exist, and yet, he built a life around him, found love, and did something other than being an infiltrating killing machine.
