He didn't quite become human, but he came close. It's a great parallel to the arc the Terminator from T2 had. But it's also one the film doesn't spend that much time on. Carl only appears halfway into the movie, and just as we get scenes of him introspecting his very existence and him even feeling something resembling guilt, we switch back to action.

Tim Miller is a great action and VFX guy for sure, and the initial portions of the movie do have some cool action, but it fails to sustain it, and as a result, even with more advanced CGI, the action set pieces in something like T2 feel bigger and more thrilling. That whole CGI fest at the end on the plane and near the reservoir wasn't it at all. The more intimate standoff inside the power plant was way better though. I didn't care for the new characters the way I did for Sarah and Carl; the new protagonists were basically Kyle Reese and Sarah/John in a new skin too. Also, the whole "not a man thing"? Terminator never made it be about John being a man; he was a man raised by his badass mom, who prepared him to be the leader of the apocalypse. It's supposed to be progressive that a girl leads the resistance and all, but the thing is, weren't the Terminator movies always woke?

Anyway, apart from Arnie and the action, the most interesting part about Terminator was the closed time loop it created. John Connor wouldn't exist without Kyle Reese being sent back to the past. Kyle Reese was sent back by John because Skynet sent a Terminator to the past. Skynet wouldn't exist if not for the remains of that same Terminator being found by Cyberdyne Systems. This was at the core of the first Terminator, a very self-contained movie. T2 then added to that pretty well and concluded by closing off that loop. This one just throws all of that out, and despite that, we won't get to even see where it was building up to because it flopped anyway. 😭

Very cool music from Tom Holkenberg, though.

Name: Nobody 2
Review:
Well, it did what's expected from it, nothing more and nothing less. The Night Comes for Us was one of my favorite action movies in the way it's just excessive in the most fun way possible. With the same director attached to this, I thought Timo Tjahjanto would bring some of that energy here, but what I saw was just things from the first Nobody in a different package. But yeah, it's a fun package; the action is still great. Nobody chooses to cast white American dads in action movie roles, whether it's Bob Odenkirk as the protagonist or Colin Hanks as one of the antagonists, and it works. Sharon Stone's main villain is hyped up as this very scary threat that's deadlier than anything Hutch has faced before, but by the end, she's just a villain; there's nothing extra scary about her when the confrontation does happen.

This movie was funny and thrilling enough for a smooth weekend watch. I liked the hand-to-hand fights more than the shootouts. Plus, Hutch not being invincible and being pretty much vulnerable to getting shot or beaten up and improvising on ways to survive and hit back works here, and it's where Odenkirk brings his everyman appeal and dad energy too. That's what makes these movies different: in the beefed-up action heroes of the past, this is the last guy we'd expect to kick ass, but he does.

Name: The Smashing Machine
Review:
I haven't watched the HBO series Ballers, but most of The Rock's film career has been him playing the same dude over and over again. He'd be this big, strong alpha macho dude; the movie would always emphasize how big and strong he is, and he'd never lose fights (which is apparently a part of his contract). There's a certain formula to a movie starring The Rock, even in something where he does shake things up like the Jumanji movies, and that's part of the reason why he's so perfectly cast in this movie too. He’s so good in this movie, and it genuinely feels like he’s playing a character instead of just being The Rock, so I’m going to call him Dwayne Johnson for the rest of this.

Dwayne Johnson plays MMA fighter Mark Kerr. The way Kerr has been presented in this movie is like everything I said about how a Dwayne Johnson character is expected to be, but they're the things that make him more vulnerable and flawed than a perfect hero. Kerr has never lost a fight when we meet him in the movie; he doesn't even expect to ever lose a fight, so when a loss does happen, instead of moving on, it's devastating for him and internally breaks him. That's how fragile this man is. Also, Mark Kerr IS a big strong man by all accounts, but the thing is, that also feeds his insecurity; he becomes agitated when he's not treated like one. He literally cries and says, "I'm not a boy; I'm a man." He uses his strength and aggression to show power when he feels weak about his masculinity. Like, all those hypermasculine traits are used in a way to show how pathetic this person is, basically. Though the movie gives mixed signals on how the audience is supposed to perceive its protagonist. The movie eventually becomes about him being more at peace with accepting defeat. 

The Safdie brothers, as a director duo, were always doing these super fast-paced, anxiety-mode movies that were relentless and often showed a continuous chain of events. But this is a biopic; this is a story happening over multiple years instead of something that takes place over the course of a few hours or days. Benny Safdie opts for fast-paced storytelling here too, but the story itself doesn't have any kind of panicky energy to it, and it just made me feel distant from this particular narrative when events were just whooshing past. There have been biopics that have opted for fast-paced storytelling, of course, but this just felt messy. It's like a collection of random events from someone's life and then the movie just ends. The drama and the character journey doesn't quite stick. 

Raging Bull seemed like an inspiration here, but unlike Raging Bull, where Jake LaMotta was an absolutely irredeemable terrible person whom the audience is never meant to like, this movie is confusing in the way it expects the audience to perceive Mark Kerr. On one hand we see his career side of things, his struggle with addiction, and his recovery from said addiction; it's in the conventional sports biopic side of things where we're meant to sympathize with the protagonist and root for him. But then, there's the personal side of things, where we see the relationship between Mark Kerr and his girlfriend Dawn, where Mark is just a terrible partner to her; he's selfish, cold, rude, and emotionally abusive and just basically makes her life miserable. She does everything for him like a mom/maid stand-in, and yet we don't see him show much respect towards her. We don't see any acts of physical abuse from Mark, but he constantly hits and breaks things around the house, including a whole fucking door during their arguments, which makes Dawn horrified, and yeah, it's not shown to be a healthy relationship at all. Dawn has her own issues too, but we don't see enough of her perspective either. 

The real Mark Kerr was a part of the development of this film, as we see him during the final scene and also in photos during the end credits where he's on set and training with Dwayne Johnson. While it's appreciative that he allowed himself to be portrayed as a horrible partner to his ex in this movie, it's the fact that the movie also expects us to feel sympathy towards him that's confusing. I could only feel concerned for Dawn during these arguments, as it's very valid for her to feel sad, angry, and terrified during these. The movie also chooses a weird way to conclude the Mark and Dawn arc before abruptly transitioning to the final sports tournament. We see the real conclusion of where Mark and Dawn end up only as a text graphic towards the end, but I think something as significant as that needed to be a part of the movie rather than just being post-movie text. Dawn's character's handling in the movie is very confusing in that sense. Like, this would be a very different movie if it followed her perspective more. While the movie itself sides with Dawn mostly, at least I thought it does, it still wants us to consider Mark as just flawed and sympathetic and even find him likeable. I don't know about that.

The fight scenes were like watching a broadcast fight basically; there's not much dramatic flair in them, and most of them just looked pretty similar. Johnson and Blunt were brilliant performance-wise. With Johnson really bringing in the vulnerability, insecurity, and fragility of Mark Kerr really well. Emily Blunt was also great; honestly, this movie has better verbal fights in their argument scenes than all the physical MMA fights. This movie was more interesting when it focused on the relationship than the sports stuff, and in the relationship, Mark was clearly the bad guy, though the movie kinda expected us to feel for him and see him as a flawed good guy? 

The movie's got a great soundtrack and an interesting visual style, though.

Name: Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines
Review:
This was my introduction to Terminator, okay? Not the Cameron films, this. So imagine my surprise when I watched the original afterwards, where Arnie is the villain, after the way he sacrificed himself to save the humans here.

Anyway, on revisiting after watching the James Cameron originals, I can see how this is inferior even while having Arnie and more advanced visual effects at their disposal. Everything about this movie is just trying to replicate what made T2 so iconic, rather than doing something original with the Terminator mythos. The only few instances of not being an exact copy might be the connection they make between this particular terminator and John and that dark twist at the end. Other than that, if T2 was about being bigger and more epic than T1, this one was just about being another T2.

There were many ways they could've taken this other than a T2 replica too, but I guess this was a safe bet commercially (this is the last Terminator movie that did well in the box office to my knowledge), and being a heroic Terminator like this might've been better for Arnie's political campaign at the time too. But that's the thing too, in T2 the Terminator is a blank slate at the beginning, a machine with a mission. He develops a personality and starts cracking one-liners only after he starts interacting with John and adapts something that resembles a human personality from John. Here, he's just Arnie as the Terminator, as pop culture remembers him from the very beginning. There's no gradual development to his character in a way that leads to his eventual sacrifice; he's just this cool hero guy. The Terminator does get damaged in his very first action scene, though, and all the damage makeup looked amazing; even that CGI face towards the end with half the skin and flesh torn off holds up really well. That one cameo from T2 was also hilarious.

The TX was just the T-1000 from the last movie in a new skin (or endoskeleton). Her ability to control technology was something they could've played with more. She was an intimidating threat, though the CGI during some of her scenes does show its age. This movie does have some pretty cool action at times, but of course it lacks the thrills and chills of T2.

Also, that Sergeant Candy scene is hilarious, and given how messy and convoluted the Terminator timeline became anyway, that needed to stay in this movie. Imagining a Terminator that sounds like Benoit Blanc makes me laugh out loud. "I'll be back, y'all."

Name: The Roses
Review: The casting decisions did more for this movie than everything else. Even Allison Janney who pops up for just one scene was so cool. Both Benedict Cumberbatch and Olivia Coleman had great chemistry with each other and the movie does strike a balance in dealing with the two protagonists. I honestly can't choose a favorite, and the movie itself gives both the main characters their own flaws and their own fuck ups that it's tough to root for or even hate just one of them. The movie also stays away from reinforcing gender stereotypes despite centering around a hetero married couple. The conflict just keeps on escalating to crazier and crazier levels till THAT ending. I've not read the novel or seen the previous Danny DeVito adaptation, so this was new to me. The movie made me laugh at multiple instances, it was very entertaining, the ensemble cast was hilarious, and the way it ends was very memorable.

Name: Akhanda 2: Thaandavam
Review:
Where do I even start? Firstly, fuck this movie, and I'm so glad that it flopped at the box office, rare Indian audience W. The first Akhanda itself was Hindutva propaganda in a Balayya masala movie skin, and it was so fucking shitty, but somehow that became a hit. In this one's case, Boyapati Sreenu dials up the Hindutva propaganda. I don't know if it was overconfidence or the desire to go "bigger", but this one's far more on the nose about the Sangh propaganda than the first movie, like, to the extent where it seems like it's a parody of Sangh propaganda movies. There were people who justified the first film by saying that it's just showing mythology and not all mythology is propaganda, but this one throws the opportunity for any such arguments right out the window.

So this movie is set in a fictional country called Bharat. It's not the country called India that I live in, because India is a secular country where people who practice all kinds of religions live, along with people who do not believe in any religions, but in this movie's Bharat, everything is Sanathana Haindava Dharmam; only Hinduism matters, and Hinduism is the only reason why the country exists. Such propaganda movies usually choose Muslims and Pakistan as their villains, but this one stays away from Muslims thankfully but instead has Chinese villains. The Chinese are played by Indian actors; they speak Telugu and Indian-accented English, and the depictions of China boil down to rooms that are decorated with dragons. It's pretty clear that the level of research into the Chinese that went into this movie was limited to having food from a Chinese restaurant. Plus, this movie is so racist towards the Chinese; it outright says Bharat people are a superior race to the Chinese, that our religion and god are way better than theirs ever would be, and even mocks Chinese cuisine, so Boyapati probably got diarrhea from said Chinese restaurant to be so frustrated towards the Chinese food too?

The evil plot of the Chinese villains, and I'm not kidding here, involves making Bharat people lose their belief in Hindu gods, as the reason why Bharat is so awesome, unstoppable, and prosperous is because of their belief in Hindu gods. So they poison the water in a religious festival and then make a dude tell the people that God doesn't exist because lots of people died from this poisoning, and then people just believe this and stop worshipping God. I mean, is this movie showing that Hindu faith is that weak? One dude could just tell them to drop God, and people just will? That's why I said earlier, this is a parody of Hindutva propaganda movies, if anything.

Balayya plays, well, Balayya, the Hindutva propaganda version. He's either defying physics, biology, or chemistry or reading off WhatsApp forward bullshit in long speeches in this movie. The entire movie is written like it's a compilation of Sangh WhatsApp forwards, and Balayya reminded me of even Facebook posts that I've seen as a child. His Hindi speech reminded me of a Hindi elocution competition I participated in as a kid. Everything is crammed in here: scientists and technology using Hindu mythology and Vedas, Chathrapathi Sivaji references, Balayya's house being filled with calves, surgical strike references, and multiple references about Hindus being the most superior race in the world (the movie assumes Bharat is a Hindu rashtra, like I said). This guy even tortures the Chinese villains with these long racist rants about the superiority of Hinduism before killing them; death might've felt like a relief for them.

I really hate Boyapati Sreenu's brand of masala films, even when it's not Hindutva propaganda. Everything about it is so cartoonish and soap-opera core. People talk so weirdly; they are behaving weirdly. Wind machines are so overused that at times it seems like Balayya is just aggressively farting. At one point, literal fire is blasting out of his ass; even his face looks like he's holding in a fart most of the time. Balayya is warding off the evil eye by doing Pooja with a goon's head; he's massacring the Chinese army in his "Surgical Strike", plus the expected science-defying Balayya shenanigans in a Boyapati Sreenu movie. There are two Balayyas here; one has divine superpowers, and one's a normal human, but both of them can make a crowd of dudes fly with a single punch the same way, so do the superpowers even matter? Balayya made me laugh a lot in this movie. The movie is so dull when he's not on screen, actually. When he's not on screen, it's shit, but when he's on screen, it's fun shit.

Samyuktha is in this movie to do the mandatory dance song with Balayya and then die. At least the female lead from the first movie got to survive that movie and die off-screen before being replaced by a new woman who also dies. Harshaali Malhotra plays the damsel in distress, the 17-year-old scientist who found a miracle vaccine by reading the Ramayana, daughter of human Balayya, and nephew of the hairier Balayya. It's so weird to see her in a Hindutva propaganda movie, after her most popular role before this was a movie set in a secular nation called India, where a Hindu dude helped a Pakistani Muslim girl, and she played that girl. Thaman blasts his background score to try and save this dumpster fire, but it felt like it's just the same few tracks on repeat. One good thing about watching this on Netflix was that I got to lower the volume, as I'm sure this would've been an attack on the ears in the theater.

This was written with the assumption that it'd be a right-wing Hindu nationalist's wet dream, but instead, the extreme honesty in the propaganda backfired, and the Hindu right-wing cheered for softer, disguised propaganda like Dhurandhar instead. Or maybe BJP HQ saw this movie and thought, "We can't fuck with the Chinese like this" and that's why this movie didn't get the aggressive BJP IT Cell PR that Dhurandhar got. Akhanda 2 is so desperate for validation from that side too, from chest-thumping nationalism like an Indian soldier killing a Chinese soldier with a single punch, references to the Indian army being the best in the world (due to Hinduthva), to showing Lord Shiva himself and having him do a duet thandavam with Balayya, and having Balayya do speeches on the superiority of Sanatana Dharmam. But right-wing Hindu nationalists preferred Akshaye Khanna dancing to Arabic hip hop instead in December.

Akhanda 2 was clearly designed to be a blast but ended up being a fart even for its target audience. It's a perfect parody of Sangh propaganda movies actually, it even fooled the CBFC into releasing it uncensored while it's actually insulting the Hindutva more than any left or liberal movie that I've seen. 

I really wish Letterboxd would register proper zero ratings, even the 1/2 is too much for this movie.

Name: Parasakthi
Review:
It's hard to judge a movie like Parasakthi, actually. The movie felt so disjointed and incoherent, but I can't tell if it's disjointed because of the writing or Sudha Kongara's filmmaking, because the movie itself was heavily censored by the CBFC before release. If I've said this once, I've said it a million times: the CBFC is scum that's been ruining cinema in this country for years, and not just Indian cinema; not even foreign films can release over here the way the creators intended in this country. But in the case of foreign films, we can at least catch the actual version of those after the online release, but in the case of Indian films, we're stuck with the versions that the CBFC had butchered. It's so obvious that they'd let any kind of right-wing Hindu nationalist propaganda release without any issues but try to silence any other voice that doesn't validate the Sangh agenda. The fact that they're able to keep on doing this in a country that's supposed to be a democracy is very sad and scary. The kind of censorship and silencing they're carrying out is meant to silence any and all artists who won't cater to the Sangh agenda, and yeah, we're so fucked.

Onto Parasakthi, I'm not that aware of the actual protests and events that this film is representing; the film itself is a social drama that's pretty much by the book and reminiscent of many films in the past, both in terms of writing and imagery. The cast was pretty good, especially Sivakarthikeyan and Sreeleela, Ravi Mohan's villain was generic, and GVP's music was adequate, though it did feel a bit overscored at times or like the music was a bit out of place. It felt like the system should've been more of the villain than just the one dude? Since the protests were against the system after all, and police violence is systemic, not just about this one guy. The half Tamil background given to the villain is also not explored that deeply. The bad CGI took me out of the fight scene at the end, though (there was a shot involving a character on fire at the end that just looked funny). Some of the dramatic highs land, and some don't. We do feel the fire of the protests, though. The songs seemed out of place. Great production design and costumes through, the sense of scale was also conveyed really well. It did feel like a big movie. 

During the initial stretch there was some tonal imbalance too, but like I said, I can't say if the incoherence in the film is a flaw from the writing or filmmaking side after watching a version that's been butchered by the CBFC so heavily. The film is set around the anti-Hindi imposition protests in Tamil Nadu in the 60s. I wish Hindi imposition remained as a thing in the past, but it didn't. The Sangh are trying to impose not just Hindi but also Hindutva onto the whole country, and institutions like the CBFC are aiding them in that. They even muted the villain saying "anti-national scum" because it's a term that they still use against opposing voices. This film is not even a radical portrayal of a political movement, there are even several attempts at balancing and playing it safe, but even then, the censoring happened.

Given what the movie is about, the amount of censorship that it had to go through is very ironic. The film talks about India's unity in diversity and letting each Indian speak their own language and have their own culture, and how it's important to fight for our identity and rights as citizens, but given where the country is right now, I wish people would continue to do so now too, instead of staying silent while they infect everything. The director of this movie herself ironically called the CBFC a "democratic" entity in a pre-release interview (which was shot before this movie received its censor certificate, afaik), but nothing about the CBFC is democratic. Like, even if someone makes a better, deeper, more political film about such issues, wouldn't the CBFC just butcher that too? 

I'm sorry that this is more of a rant about the CBFC than about Parasakthi.

Name: Ithiri Neram
Review:
I love conversational movies and movies that deal with themes like former lovers reuniting after never getting to be together. This one, on the surface, should exactly be the kind of movie that I should love, but I ended up hating it.

It kept disappointing me in everything it set out to do. When the whole movie hinges on the relationship between these two former lovers, the first thing it should do is for the leads to have some great chemistry and for me to care enough about these people so that their emotions and yearning make sense to me. Here, the chemistry between the leads is so awkward and inconsistent, and the dialogues sound awkward and like they're just actors doing scenes rather than, you know, two people with a history conversing, which only felt more fake once they start drinking and act drunk. Also, there's too much background score in this movie, and the background score just tries too hard to convey emotions that just don't exist on screen or in the lines of dialogue otherwise. Like, is the scene supposed to be sad? Blast sad music. Is the scene supposed to be funny? Blast goofy music. No offense to the music director, but the background score was like very stock music core. Like it's the stereotypical sad music, stereotypical funny music. The attempts at comedy involving the two work colleagues also felt so flat. 

Plus, the movie expects us to care for these people and feel sad for their lost love when they're, like, being terrible people too. I mean, I understand depicting flawed people on screen, but I don't think the movie actually treats them as being as flawed as they actually are. The dude has a very loving wife who's nothing but supportive and caring of him, and yet, he talks about her like she doesn't mean anything to him and that he's just bearing with her because he needed a partner, and I just felt that this guy is being such a prick, but no, the movie still wants us to shed a tear for him not being able to marry his ex. The fact that he doesn't even tell his wife that he's going to meet his ex is also sus, but like I said, I gave this movie the benefit of the doubt until it proved without doubt that it thinks its protagonist is more sympathetic than he actually is.

But then, halfway through the movie, the conversational ex-lovers reuniting thing is dropped, and this becomes about dragging around a passed-out person. Like what? That entire stretch just made my head scratch tbh. One of the work colleague guys is even a major pervert, and he says all kinds of offensive and disrespectful things about the woman, but by the end, a sorry is enough, and everyone's smiling and jolly. Even Jis Joy hasn't attempted the levels of nanma at display here.

Even at the end, the guy doesn't show any signs of consideration for his wife, and the ex-girlfriend is treated like a burden for half of this movie, and we're supposed to have feelings for these people?

There were like tiny moments in between where I felt something, mostly because of the actors involved, though the performances were all over the place, but on the whole, I was so disappointed.

I want a good conversational romance in Malayalam so bad. 😭

Name: Thalaivar Thambi Thalaimaiyil
Review:
Contrary to what the marketing and posters for this movie look like, this is not a typical hero-centric movie. I don't think Jiiva's lead character, Jivarathnam, in TTT can even be called a "hero"; he's basically this local politician trying his best to support and help people, resolve conflicts, and be a public servant, and the film puts him in the middle of a conflict between two neighboring homes where a marriage and funeral happen in parallel. The movie doesn't actually revolve around Jiva, and he's not a larger-than-life figure with solutions to every problem. He's trying his best, and the situation keeps getting out of hand and heading to more chaos.

Like I said, the movie is more of an ensemble piece that's very situational and dependent on a large cast of characters than revolving around a sole lead. Jiva is basically helpless through most of the movie while the others are just fixated on their ego and grudges. I don’t have a complaint that Jiva should've been more like a hero who has intelligent solutions and does cool things, but at times the movie does make it seem like Jiva is about to do something, or that he must do something, but instead he continues to be helpless while everything goes wrong around him. Even the way he's introduced is a kind of foreshadowing to his entire character arc throughout the movie. 

The setting was definitely interesting, but I thought this movie had more potential to be more chaotic, funnier, and even more emotional. The backstory given to the conflict between the two houses and the impact of that past tragedy didn't really hit me like it should have. The humor works most of the time, and the movie does keep the energy up, but the focus is lost occasionally. The ending was the best way to wrap up this conflict, though, and I really felt for Jiva when he finally delivers some brutal honesty to these people. The bride and groom's arc also felt sweet. The movie judges most of the people in the village pretty harshly, and with good reason.

Anyway, it's a refreshing watch in Tamil for sure, because so much of it is Malayalam cinema coded. Vishnu Vijay's music is dependably awesome, the songs were all cool, especially the title track, the performances from most of the cast were great, and yeah, seeing an evil village movie instead of a goody-goody village movie was also nice, like there's no expectation for people to resolve everything through a pep talk or a lecture on empathy here; sometimes people are just awful to each other, and we move on.

Name: Bha. Bha. Ba.
Review:
I'd call this movie Pa Pa Pa, Pathetic Panna Padam. So firstly, fuck this movie. People rated this movie half stars over here at the time of the release as a way of showing solidarity with the survivor, but imagine the actual movie turning out to be so pathetic and awful that they actually did the movie a favor by giving it even those half stars. I'm also putting half stars here, just because Letterboxd doesn't consider empty ratings as a zero rating. There's absolutely nothing good about this movie; there's nothing original about it, and it's a chore to sit through and a pathetic failure in almost every regard. 

Like, every "entertaining" aspect of this movie is ripped off. And it's not even ripping off other films; it's ripping off social media. Like, feed some memes and social media references to AI, and even something that lifeless and derivative can shit out a screenplay that's better than this. Anything "fun" is a reference to social media. Anything "mass" is a reference to social media. When the Mohanlal cameo happens, he's presented like it's meant for someone who only knows Mohanlal through Instagram. I won't even say this movie is made like a compilation of Instagram reels because I've seen Instagram reels and memes that are way better made, funnier, and more original. 

I'm not against meta jokes and 4th wall breaking; in fact, I love them, but this is like a desperate attempt, an easy out to make people laugh in movies like these. These are jokes written by people who lack any sense of humor. The references are also done in such a lazy way. That fight scene with all the hit adichupoli Malayalam songs playing in the background was also such a desperate attempt at getting a reaction from people. The way the entire movie's been shot and edited is bad, and the action scenes are among the worst. Cigarettes in mouth, loud music and slo-mo, mass aayi, eduthondu podey. The movie is even insecure about its references; we hear about Vineeth Sreenivasan coming from Chennai thrice before we see him, as if we didn't hear the same lame joke the first two times. We hear that Dhyan Sreenivasan is an "interview star" twice. Sense the pattern? Devan plays Dev G and says the "ippo parayaan pattilla" line, hehehehe. Thuuuu. 

Then there's the Mohanlal cameo, the only reason why this movie at least made some money before getting washed out and flopping. I misunderstood initially by thinking that this is Mohanlal helping Dileep to have the comeback he's desperate for, but no, this is Gokulam Gopalan and Dileep fucking A10 over. The A10 cameo is so pathetic, and it actually seems so disrespectful and like they're insulting what he is to Malayalam cinema rather than giving any sort of a fan tribute to him. What they have is, of course, references. But these are social media references that don't seem like they come from a place where they love Mohanlal because of his films or his characters. Like, they literally treat him like a circus monkey in this movie, with a character played by the film's producer Gokulam Gopalan of all people giving him commands for mundu madakkal and meesha pirikkal in a scene, which he does for them, and a crowd of people cheers him on. I felt secondhand embarrassment when this happened. Even the way he's framed and the way he looks in the movie is so bad. Like, while they're recreating iconic moments from his past films, we can just tell how bad this version looks compared to the iconic original, whether it's Ravanaprabhu or Spadikam. Maybe their reference was vertical videos of those shots? Every single scene with Mohanlal is making him seem like a clown; even hosting Bigg Boss was less embarrassing for him. Ithinte valla karyam undayirunno etta? ( You deserve this for supporting this desperate comeback attempt hehehehe.) 

As for Dileep, comeback ennu 50 vattam BGM and dialogue vechal comeback aavilla. Like, even while setting aside the case and all the controversy surrounding him, he's just an outdated actor now. No amount of PR and desperate attempts at brainrot fan service can fix that. He lacks any charm; he sticks out like a sore thumb most of the time. Even when the movie makes several excuses about "madness" and "no logic", the performance is just very bad, even for an over-the-top character. Illatha aura undennu thettidharikkal at its peak. Don't get me started about all the indirect references about his own case and arrest to try and paint himself as a victim. This person is still trying to manipulate the audience and repair his public image using his movies and you still want to have a "separate art from the artist" conversation? 

Like, it's pretty obvious that everyone who made this clusterfuck was so confident about this being a hit. Talk about underestimating the audience, because people already love these references in social media, right? What could go wrong? They thought this would be such a huge comeback for Dileep that the word is spoken through music or dialogue repeatedly. It's like they're forcing us to believe that this is a comeback. Another proof of their comeback overconfidence backfiring is the fact that the OTT version cuts out references to the actress assault case that became controversial, and it also cuts out the scene where Dhyan Sreenivasan has dialogues that mirror Prithviraj's response to the media during the case. Which makes it so obvious what the exact intention of those scenes was. They didn't expect it to backfire so spectacularly (rare Mallu audience W), and when it did, they cut those scenes out.  I hope the word "comeback" haunts them now. 

The music was also generally bad; there were some cool-sounding themes in between, and of course, use of existing songs and background score because reference, hehe. The lyrics were so bad, whether it's the rap or the lyrics to Azhinjattam. Vineeth Sreenivasan's villain's theme music was "No More Painkili", maangatholi. Everything about this movie is so laughably bad, yo. 😭

ANYONE who said this movie is any good either has shit taste in cinema, or they only cared about desperately pushing for a Pettan comeback even for something this awful. This is not spoof; this is poop. Fuck this movie.

PHA PHA PHA!!!

Name: Rental Family
Review:
I love movies that feel like a warm hug, and I generally just go with the flow with such movies instead of nitpicking for flaws. This was one such easy watch with enough warmth and emotions.

Firstly, Brendan Fraser is so great in this movie. He's like the perfect guy to be cast as a wholesome, sensitive, huggable and emotional man, and that's what he does here. He's playing a lonely actor who starts working for a rental family service where he pretends to be a part of the lives of total strangers. The plot moves in exactly the way we expect; he forms emotional bonds with these people, treats them as the family that he doesn't have, and eventually things get complicated.

The movie flows at a steady pace, the cinematography and music are beautiful, the performances are wonderful, I really felt all the emotions. Also, the movie is set in Japan, and the dialogue is a mix of both Japanese and English. The switching is done pretty seamlessly, and the flow of the dialogue never breaks. There's no fish-out-of-water situation here; the American protagonist, Philip, can understand Japanese and even speak a bit of it. He's been living in Japan for 7 years, but still without much interaction with Japanese people in life, the Japanese culture is still distant to him. The way this movie navigates through Philip's loneliness, his yearning for human connection, cultural differences, and how he's distant from the rest of the Japanese characters was nice.

This premise had a lot more potential, though, maybe even to be turned into a series rather than a single feature-length film, but still, what I got still felt emotional and heartfelt, and I had a smile on my face as it ended.

Name: Chatha Pacha: The Ring of Rowdies
Review:
I've been fascinated with pro wrestling ever since I was a kid. And actually the fascination only increased once I knew that it's scripted entertainment rather than a sport. I've not constantly followed the pro-wrestling scene, but I've always been in and out of it. But still I had enough pro wrestling nostalgia and knowledge to understand all the references made in Chatha Pacha, so it can be said that I'm a part of the target audience of the movie. And as a member of the target audience, all I can say is that this movie is wasted potential.

There was this Netflix show called GLOW, which was about a few women setting up an independent pro wrestling show. That show found a great way to invite the audience into this world of pro-wrestling, the showmanship of it, the athleticism and skill required, and all the other related drama. Netflix canceled the show right before its final season, though, fuck them. Anyways, Chatha Pacha is also an underdog story about a group of working-class wrestling enthusiasts trying to do their own pro-wrestling show in Fort Kochi. 

But the movie also kinda assumes that the audience watching the movie are all wrestling enthusiasts too, which is not the case. Like, I know that exposition, or "spoon feeding," is frowned upon by many, but in this case, a bit of exposition on pro wrestling might've added to this movie's experience. But this is a general issue I felt in this movie, not just with how the movie rushes through how pro wrestling works, but also how it treats its drama. Idk if it's because the movie doesn't trust its audience's attention span, but it just whooshes past setting up its drama, characters, and character conflicts, and most of it doesn't quite stick the landing.

Like, when you set up your core conflicts, maybe let us understand these characters and their relationships before all these big changes happen in their dynamic? A lot of the detailing is left vague, and stuff just happens randomly and quickly. The writing was either lazy, or they were writing for an audience who'd be on their phone with the movie playing in the background, like how Netflix does.

Even when we get into pro wrestling, of course, I don't want the movie to spell out every single reference to WWE, like, the moves, how Savio does Shawn Michaels' Wrestlemania zipline entrance, the taunts; things like that can be left for the WWE nostalgia gang to appreciate. But what I would've liked was at least a refresher for the general audience to tell them how pro wrestling is more of a performance art than a sport event, how there's a face (hero) and a heel (villain), the storytelling involved, how there's athleticism and a physical toll involved despite being a scripted performance, and how there's a risk of real danger even when both the performers try to do the moves while being as safe as possible. To me these are the things that make pro wrestling itself interesting, and that first Friday fight night scene, as great as it is, could've benefited from giving the audience some more context before rushing into it. But after this, the movie drops the scripted pro wrestling aspect anyway and becomes more about actual fights happening in the pro wrestling stage, so yk, if there was more context provided about what pro wrestling actually is, then that shift where the fights turn real could've landed better, but instead, after the first fight event, the movie goes into montage mode for the rest of the wrestling action till the ending happens. There's even a buildup given to the choke slam: initially Little says that we can do a choke slam only if the other person jumps up to support the move, and then at the end of the movie an actual choke slam happens without the opponent's support. Even that payoff could've landed better. Other things being set up, like Little's asthma, are also forgotten in the second half. 

Again, the drama between the foster brothers and the core conflict being set up is very weak because they're rushed, and the way it resolves is even weaker, though it comes after this amazing fight scene. The action in the movie is very well done on the whole. The wrestling moves are very accurately recreated, with only a few exaggerated things, but even that's done well. The wrestling sequences and fights are the only parts where the movie truly gains some life, as everything else falls so flat. The scripted fights in the first fight night were super fun, and it does show that pro wrestling is more about giving entertainment than who wins or loses. And when it then transitions to actual fights, the fight between the two brothers was one of the best one-on-one fight scenes that I've seen in Malayalam cinema, actually. The camerawork and editing were so on point, and the choreography was also great, and both Arjun Ashokan and Roshan performed really well, but then the way the fight ends is a bummer. Then the cameo happens. And even the way the movie ends makes no sense. It ends while properly addressing none of the drama that's been set so far, actually, but talking about that further would be spoilers. 

Amal Neerad has been able to do so much aura farming with Ikka in a Fort Kochi setting twice. But here, the problem was that Walter is built up to be this larger-than-life person; they got Mammootty, who can just exist to seem like a larger-than-life person, but several of the choices here to portray Walter, from the accent to the look and the overall presentation, just felt off. Everyone except Roshan is pretty goofy in the movie, so it's okay if Walter is goofy, but Walter comes off like Michael Appanum aayilla pakshe Gulaanum aayilla. The way my theater erupted when ikka appeared on screen and immediately went silent when he delivered his first line of dialogue. 😭😭 

As for the rest of the cast, everyone's put their all into the action scenes and the wrestling, and the whole cast and stunt team is great in that regard. But in terms of the performances, Vishak Nair tries to be a Meesho joker yet again. He's very irritating to watch and got on my nerves, but his character is supposed to be irritating too, so yk, great job? Every character is poorly written, and the performances are pretty basic, Roshan Mathew was great even with the monotonous way the character has been written though, I also loved the little girl that played Rosamma, she understood the assignment. The songs were cool, and so was the background score.

Like I said, I can see a way better movie about pro-wrestling here, but this movie, with its very rushed writing that just randomly moves from one event to another, has weak drama, forgettable characters, and a cameo that felt like a misfire, but it has got some great action, and it's got its heart in the right place when it does work. I'd be lying if I said I didn't have some fun watching this movie when it stuck to straightforward, formulaic storytelling and action. All the WWE references and callbacks were cool to spot too. It's also obvious that they planned way more direct references to WWE in the movie but didn't get the rights to use them; that self-censoring is so evident throughout the movie. Why so cruel, Paul Levesque?

Name: Marty Supreme
Review:
Now this felt more like a Safdie movie than Benny Safdie's Smashing Machine did. Once more, we have a narcissistic, overambitious, morally all-over-the-place, and yet somehow rootable protagonist desperately trying to hustle in some money, with a ticking clock in the background. It's clear that he's not a good person, when this asshole even jokes about "dropping the atomic bomb" when he's about to go up against a Japanese opponent, but that's part of the fun here. Though the sport of table tennis is involved and there are several intense table tennis matches in the movie, this is more about the character of Marty Mauser and the desperate lengths he'd go to for achieving success and greatness than being a straightforward underdog sports movie. It's him constantly and desperately spiraling for greatness. 

Being just loosely based on a real person and not really being a straightforward biopic also lets the movie go crazy. Something randomly crazy or crazy hilarious happens in this movie at regular intervals, just when things seem to go normally. That frantic Safdie pacing and panic energy is present in several scenes too. Many of the intense conversations and set pieces are so brilliantly directed and written, and the filmmaking and editing are so precise here. The comedy also works really well. I won't spoil any of the surprises and absurdities here since they're best seen on screen. And the performances are amazing too, headlined by the best Timothée Chalamet performance that I've seen yet. He just truly gets into the skin of a desperate narcissist and gives so much life and innocence to the anti-hero that is Marty Mauser. The villain of this movie is a capitalist pig playing a character named Milton (hehehehe). Gwyneth Paltrow and Odessa A'zion were also great, playing women that Marty clearly didn't deserve. 

Then there's the music in this movie; whether it's the songs used or the original score, the music was always so perfect. The music and sound design were insane, and the way the music synced in with the songs was absolute cinema. The original score was very unique and might be my favorite movie score from 2025. I can't find words to express how impressive and unique this film sounds. And as many people have already said, that opening credits sequence was also one of the best I've ever seen.

The movie is all about how capitalism pushes desperate people to do crazy things to achieve their dreams, how even sports and skills are controlled by corporations and sponsorships, and that makes the choice of who was cast as the villain funnier. 

Anyways, great stuff.

Name: The Rip
Review:
The beginning few scenes of this movie seemed pretty bad, with clunky exposition and a very rushed setup, which, if I'm to believe Matt Damon, is more about the scenes being written according to Netflix content policies than the writers themselves. But ngl, once the core event of the movie, the titular Rip, happens, this becomes more fun. All the seeds of doubts about each character's intentions and the twists were also so 90s and early 2000s thriller-movie coded and fun. Also a pretty cool cast of zaddies and baddies. The action scenes were pretty basic, though. Nothing memorable there. 

Anyway, it was fun, had a GREAT cast, and of course Damon-Affleck collabs always tend to be entertaining just for their bromistry. But seriously though, NETFLIX NEEDS TO STOP TELLING WRITERS AND FILMMAKERS TO MAKE MOVIES AND SHOWS FOR PEOPLE WHO PLAY MOVIES AND SHOWS IN THE BACKGROUND.

Name: Feminist Fathima
Review:
I liked how the movie kept things light and natural, rooted in the setting, doesn't steer towards being melodramatic and Fathima feels like a real person. There's nothing big happening in the movie; the entire conflict is set around the need for a new mattress, and one of the important parts of the plot involves turning on the ceiling fan. It's all small daily life stuff, but it's all part of the religious conservative patriarchal household that's holding Fathima down. There's all kinds of detailing all throughout the movie that adds so much to the characters and the story. Though occasionally it's pretty direct about the satire and what it's trying to do too.

I liked how when eventually Fathima decides to do things for herself and be financially independent, it's not treated as some big progressive transformation or enlightenment; it's a very natural decision from her, and when she gets asked if she's a feminist for that, she's like, "Yeah, okay." The movie does get a bit direct about its messaging at times, but I liked scenes like the "Inj Feminichi aano?" better. Amazing performances from the whole cast, especially the lead couple; we really feel for Fathima, and the husband really gets on our nerves, and the ending was very satisfying. The dialogues were really great and the movie was funnier than I thought it would be.

Name: Anaconda
Review:
There are two things I remember from watching this movie as a kid. One is that the snake gave me nightmares; the other is that I found the lead actress to be very pretty. Revising it all these years later, JLo is still gorgeous and slaying, and the snake is not so scary now. The filmmaking in Anaconda doesn't have the timeless quality that something like Jaws or Jurassic Park does. The scenes that rely on CGI show their age, so those scares don't really land. But ngl, the animatronic snake still looks pretty scary, and there are still moments where the movie delivers on some solid monster thrills.

In a 90-minute movie, it takes almost 45 minutes till the characters even encounter the snake. The kills happen pretty much the same way, with the snake jumping and wrapping around people. It's not so effective at building up the tension initially. Jon Voight as the villain was the most fun to watch. He has, like, a different accent in every scene; the dude is so obviously evil from the very first moment we lay eyes on him, and yet it takes the leads a long time to figure out that he's manipulating them. He's also a snake here, in the other sense of the word, but in case we didn't understand that, JLo practically spells it out too. It's also fun to watch this after being more familiar with the celebrity cast. Especially Owen Wilson. He's just playing disposable snake food here, but it's still fun to see him. The dialogues are so bad though, but bad in a funny way.

The text crawl at the end talks about how anacondas regurgitate eaten prey and all, but we only see that in action at the very end, that wink was hilarious though. It was also hilarious to hear old-timey punch sound effects during the fight scenes. Also, when they finally kill the snake, of course Ice Cube yells "BITCH!" at it.

Name: Anaconda
Review:
This is a dumb and unserious movie, but this was a very fun and unserious movie to watch, so I can't really hate it. This is a parody of 90s monster movies disguised as a reboot of a 90s monster movie while the vibe is pretty much like the kind of silly comedy movies that Jack Black, Paul Rudd and Steve Zahn used to do in the early 2000s. I do wish that this was R rated and more unhinged though.

This is the kind of movie where there's a whole long scene dedicated to making a character pee while a huge deadly snake is chasing the main characters. The CGI snake is very CGI snake, the original too had a bad CGI snake, but it also had a very scary animatronic snake, and this movie only properly focuses on the snake till it's like the third act. But yeah, i already knew to not expect a monster movie here. Plus the movie maintains that unserious tone throughout, even with a deadly snake in it, that whole chase with the pig on Jack Black's back made me laugh out loud. I wish they didn't spoil that through the trailers though. 

It was funny, entertaining and it made me laugh. So yk, can't hate it.

Name: Vaa Vaathiyaar
Review:
After a pretty interesting opening stretch set in the past, this movie just immediately went downhill once Karthi appeared as the unlikable grown-up protagonist, Ramu. Like, I couldn't even believe Nalan Kumarasami directed something this bad. We had an unlikable protagonist, a bad romance arc, a female lead who's just there to be eye candy, songs popping up in quick succession, and just really messy. Santhosh Narayanan's songs and score were cool to listen to as standalone tracks; even the music videos are shot well, but they just felt like they didn't belong in this particular movie.

Things got interesting once the alter ego in the form of Vaathiyaar appeared on screen. I haven't seen any MGR movies to understand the references or judge the accuracy of the portrayal here, but then again, it's not the real Vaathiyar we're seeing on screen; it's an embodiment of how a fan chose to see Vaathiyaar. But the whole alter-ego vigilante situation was portrayed in a pretty fun and quirky way in this movie, not taking it too seriously like an Anniyan. Some of the Vaathiyar portions were the ones where this movie did feel like a Nalan Kumarasamy movie, and there were some really great fight scenes in there too. But yeah, it had more potential, and Nalan Kumarasami is supposed to be better than this. Didn't expect to be jumpscared by an AI-generated video in this Nalan movie too.

Name: Send Help
Review:
The writing or concept isn't novel here. The trailer itself reminded me of Triangle of Sadness from 2022, which had the exact same scenario where rich people and the help get stranded on an island and the power hierarchy inverts because the underprivileged person had survival skills. This movie also reminded me of the recent Korean dark comedies with capitalism and class hierarchy as their themes, like Parasite and No Other Choice, where capitalism makes desperate people take very dark paths, but in a comedic yet tragic way.

Even when the writing has shades of other films on it, this movie makes up for it through how Sam Raimi approaches the material and how Rachel McAdams carries the whole thing with such a powerhouse performance. The main character, Linda, just straight up fails to function properly in the real world. She works hard, but she's treated like crap at work and not given the appreciation she deserves. Every attempt at making social connections is shot down. In that whole corporate circle, she's the person who doesn't quite fit in and is looked down upon and mocked. And of course she faces workplace misogyny too from these men. But then, getting stranded on the island changes everything, and she finally gets to be the one in charge, and she wants to keep it that way. Linda's whole transformation is portrayed really well by McAdams; even when the things she does become progressively darker, it's conveyed where she's coming from and how she's processing the whole thing. It's a performance that's a mix of comedy, drama, and the crazies, mixed in the perfect amounts. 

Dylan O'Brien as the privileged white-collar asshole boss turned dependent/prisoner/bff/whatever was also great, and the best writing in the movie involves the ever-evolving dynamic between these characters, their unique chemistry, their constantly shifting relationship, and how it turns into these psychological games that get physical by the end. McAdams and O'Brien play off of each other really well, and these two are the only actors present for most of the runtime, so the movie depended on it, and they deliver big time.

Then there's Sam Raimi finding every opportunity to go crazy with his filmmaking. Even before the island there are scenes where he does extreme close-ups and his signature stylistic touches. Even in scenes involving CGI animals, he'd find some way to make it seem gnarly and ultra gory so that the scene still does what it's supposed to do, which is the same thing this guy pulled off in the Evil Dead movies back in the day with the very obvious-looking dummies and makeup effects. There's violence, lots of blood, over-the-top gore, and even some jumpscares peppered into the movie, which are so Sam Raimi. 

The dark comedy is also very nicely executed; the whole thing is very fun to watch despite very nasty stuff happening. I was curious as to why this movie has a 3D release, but man, the 3D is so worth it, whether it's the depth or the kind of stuff that pops out of the screen. Watch this movie in 3D if you want to know what Rachel McAdams puking on your face would look like.

Anyway, despite the premise being not so original, the execution here is very original and very Sam Raimi; both the leads are great together, and their constantly shifting dynamics are fun to watch, with Rachel McAdams giving such an amazing horror lead performance that already puts her on top of my list of favorites from this year. It's very easy to understand why Linda does everything that she does, which is a message that the movie is very direct about: Linda knows that life outside the island would just immediately put her at the bottom, to be mocked and exploited by the people on top, which makes her tragic and evil at the same time. I don't want to spoil the ending here, but let's just say that I LOVED it.

Name: Dhurandhar
Review: It feels like an insult that Thuurandhar was among one of the few Indian movies that popped up in the highest-rated action-adventure movies list in the Letterboxd year in review when the action was mostly shit and there was nothing adventurous about sitting through 3.5 hours of dragging propaganda slop, and "Thuurandhar" is not a typo. So let me start by saying FUCK THIS MOVIE. Obviously, fuck the propaganda in this movie too, but even without the propaganda, this didn't feel like it had the "craft" that several people were raving about. The success this movie had feels more like a very successful PR campaign than anything, while the movie itself is an elaborate PR campaign for the Modi-led BJP government. There are several true events being referenced in this movie, with real archival footage and audio recordings being played for those too. Out of those, the 26/11 scene seemed the most manipulative and disrespectful, where the screen turns red and a real recording from the terrorist attack is played. It's there to invoke an emotional response, but you have to decide if that response is a generalized hate towards a community or empathy towards the victims and martyrs of the terrorist attack. It doesn't serve any purpose in the plot; the purpose of the use of factual information and archival videos and recordings in the movie is only to validate the fictional propaganda that they're sandwiched in between, like, this makes it possible to use "Well, this did happen for real though" as a counterargument when the propaganda in this movie is called out. To me, that felt like an exploitation of tragedy and was disrespectful toward the victims. Would the CBFC ever allow Hindutva violence to be shown the same way? Would Aditya Dhar ever show Hindutva violence or the ways in which the current BJP government fucked up the nation? If not, he's a coward. The Hindus in this movie are either victims or heroes, while Muslims are mostly vile or violent. Let's talk about Ajay Sanyal, the most obvious BJP propaganda surrogate in this movie, who feels like he's the BJP IT Cell as a person. The two attacks shown in the prologue of the movie happened when BJP was in power in India under Vajpayee, but of course Ajay Sanyaal or the movie doesn't acknowledge that, the corrupt and cowardly government is mentioned only in scenes set during the Manmohan Singh-led Congress government's rule in India. The movie begins by quoting the Gita, and then when Ajay tries to make the hostages of the Kandahar hijack say "Bharath Mata Ki Jai," he's intimidated by a terrorist, and the terrorist says something like, "You Hindus are a bunch of cowards, eh?", see, you can say this movie is only showing evil terrorists and not feeding hate towards the Muslim community or trying to show India as a Hindu rashtra and showing Hindus as a morally superior community. You can say that; it's a choice. Later on, when Ajay Sanyaal talks about UP, he talks about a certain "them" in UP who enable terrorists, about how Indians are the biggest enemies to Indians, and about how Pakistan only comes second. You can say that's not a generalizing reference to the Muslims in India, putting them under suspicion for aiding terrorists; you can say that. It's a choice. Ajay even finds an excuse to hype up a future UP leader who would "care about the nation and help solve this problem" in this scene (Yogi, lol). After a point, while the rest of the movie is set in the Pakistan underworld, Ajay Sanyal would pop up at regular intervals in repeated scenes that basically convey the same thing: "The current [Congress] government and ministers are bad; we have to wait for the leader and government who care about the country to save us; the chosen one will stop the flow of fake currencies forever with demonetization." At the time of writing this, new Epstein files were released, and it's confusing if it's the nation or Donald Trump your chosen one cared about, Ajay/Aditya. Apart from the Ajay Sanyal scenes, Durandhar is a so-and-so overlong gangster movie that's a very bad spy movie. I say bad because it fails in the most fundamental aspect of a spy movie, or even something a gangster movie like The Departed nailed, which is building tension around the protagonist who is stuck in a foreign land with dangerous criminals gathering intel while pretending to be someone else. A great spy story would lean into this double life, how he manages to fit into this world, and how he manages to be a spy in between while not being caught. Ranveer Singh's protagonist just seems like he's playing the spy game in easy mode. He keeps staring, asking too many questions, reacting to events in a way he shouldn't react if he didn't want to get caught (reacting to 26/11 the way he reacted, by being visibly shocked and disturbed by it, while in a room full of men celebrating the terrorist attack, could've blown his cover instantly), and barging into conversations. Like, he's so visibly sus and stands out; realistically, this is the first guy who'd get killed when they start hunting for a mole. Durandhar takes itself too seriously and makes the choice of blending in real events to give it the "it's just a dumb movie" pass. We don't even see how the protagonist's morality is tested when he has to pretend to be one of these very terrible people committing crime and violence. The only time an emotional response comes out of him is when Indians are killed. Violence and murder towards Pakistanis is treated very casually by the movie, like they're NPCs in a video game. It's obviously not just other criminals and terrorists that Rehman's gang or the protagonist is being violent towards, and yet the protagonist is chill about that, and so is the movie. The action scenes mostly have cool iconic retro songs playing in the background, but man, most of the action and visual effects work is so tacky and bad (which is another reason why this movie ranking above the film with the most groundbreaking visual effects work of the year in the letterboxd year in review ranking pisses me off). Overuse of gore is basically how the movie tries to mask the very basic action, which is mostly unnecessary shaky cam, janky editing, beauty shots like it's a shampoo commercial or an Instagram reel, and often looking like it's a GTA game (when that autorickshaw spins around and the cartoonish CGI person flies from inside it like a ragdoll and all). The only action block where I did feel something is the one in the climax, that fight inside the car, where the movie's very cool title track plays, it was cool as a standalone thing even with the cartoonish CGI and all, but even that scene is stupid because they had guns and could've easily shot the protagonist dead. But man, I was exhausted by the time the movie got there. This thing did not need to be 3.5 hours long at all. Some scenes are too long for no reason; there's so much unnecessary filler here. The Ajay Sanyaal scenes themselves can just be cut out to be used as ads for the Modi government to run. At other times the movie is so Instagram Reel coded in the way it's edited and how certain lines pop up as text captions on screen. There's also a very bad romantic track, where the protagonist has zero chemistry with the poorly written teenage love interest, with the usual alpha male tropes, including a very bad romantic chase sequence that looks straight out of the YRF spy universe and a scene involving physical intimidation, and I guess we'll have to wait till the sequel to see whether him being in a relationship with a teenager serves more meaning to the story. The most impressive thing about this movie was Akshaye Khanna's hairpiece. The hair and makeup department deserves praise there. Instead of giving him a thick full head of hair, the hairpiece here looks more natural, like, I'd believe it's his real hair if I didn't already know he's fully bald. His whole look was very well put together. His performance was also the better one among the cast, though that's not a high bar. I didn't feel the immense aura that was being praised. Most of the time he just had the same smoldering expression. It was hard for me to take Ranveer Singh's undercover protagonist seriously when his character was being visibly bad at the undercover thing. He looks the way he looks in the movie for pan-Indian hypermasculine blockbuster purposes, I'm assuming. But I just found his look, the tight costumes and the way he walks and stands around to be funny at times. Anyway, this was overlong propaganda slop that was hard to sit through. Cool music and a magnificent hairpiece don't make me love this when everything else was mostly shit. It's mid as a gangster movie, shit as a spy movie, and successful as a propaganda movie. All those bullshit takes that "set aside the propaganda" and praise "the craft" are proof that it's successful as a propaganda movie, and so is this movie ranking above films like Avatar: Fire and Ash in Letterboxd's top-rated action-adventure movies from 2025. I won't judge the Sanghis who would celebrate and praise a movie like this; it was made for them, and it's supposed to be celebrated by them. But the rest of y'all who'd call out the propaganda in films like The Kerala Story, but will choose to "set aside" the propaganda and rate this movie high for its "craft"? Idk. 0.5 seems appropriate for this movie, which I won't be separating from its propaganda. Even if I was hypothetically "setting aside" the propaganda, it felt like a 2 or a 2.5. There are multiple references in this movie about India being cowards at the time who won't strike Pakistan back, subtly hyping up the Modi govt's several strikes, with the "Naya Hindustan" line from URI (which the BJP has used as a campaign slogan) literally popping up at the end. If Aditya Dhar finds India before Modi to be such pathetic cowards and the India after Modi to be so perfect and brave, it's not the country, its soldiers, or its people that he's showing respect and love towards. And of course, fuck this movie. Dhurandam. Update: The sequel was exactly what I expected it to be. Aditya Dhar finally gets to goon to his real hero, and it becomes a full on advertisement video for the BJP.

Name: Roofman
Review:
Jeff Manchester might be the pookiest armed robber ever. He only hit corporate franchises, was always nice to the employees, made them wear their coats before locking them in the fridge, and would even give his own coat if they didn't have their own. Like, this is the kind of guy who'd get a 5-star rating on Thiefboxd from the people he robbed if Thiefboxd existed. Even the reason for him committing the crime is to be a better provider for his family, because capitalism and patriarchy, and also because he was pretty greedy about that. But somewhere along the way, he enjoys the crimes too; it makes him feel smart and adventurous, but then he eventually gets caught. The movie begins here and is about how he later escapes prison and goes into hiding by living inside a toy store, eventually being in a relationship with one of the employees there.

Derek Cianfrance has made some of the most depressing movies that I've ever seen, so Roofman was kind of a surprise from him, since this is a pretty calm and chill movie. Like, it could've been a thriller; it could've also been a somber and sad movie, but Cianfrance decides to tackle this true story in a light, funny, and kind of wholesome vibe. Even the prison escape in this movie might be the most chill prison escape I've ever seen. It does get sad, but it's a different kind of sadness, because once Jeff starts getting closer to Leigh and her daughters, we're aware that this relationship is built on a big lie and can fall apart so quickly, and so that adds a layer of sadness over all the happy and wholesome moments and the bonding between them. The movie maintains this calmness even through the end, where it could've easily switched over to a more dramatic thriller mood.

The actual story itself is pretty amazing here, of how this guy managed to survive living in a toy store for so long without getting caught; the ways in which he makes the store his home were very funny and interesting to watch. Also, living in a big toy store like that was the ultimate dream for me when I was a kid. And you can't help but feel for the guy a bit in spite of him being a criminal and a liar. He genuinely feels bad for being a criminal, and even then, can't help it. We feel like he could've had a nice life if he didn't make these terrible choices and became a criminal. I had such conflicting feelings about him, and that made it more interesting. Him being the narrator and POV character also adds a layer of bias towards him, of course. Because from the point of view of Leigh and her daughters, they were lied to and manipulated, but then again he seemed to genuinely care about them and like he genuinely wanted to make them happy. Channing Tatum is so good here and is exactly the guy to cast as a big beefy guy who also looks as innocent and caring as a puppy. Kirsten Dunst was also great as Leigh. Cianfrance is so great at doing romantic scenes and scenes where the characters are flirting or being intimate with each other; that's here too. I really liked the closure towards the end too. 

This might be the funniest and least depressing Derek Cianfrance movie that I've ever watched, and even that has some form of the sad in it. The music was also very chill, just like the movie. Also, do not miss the real clips that they show during the end credits; it made me smile and laugh, especially hearing the real Leigh talk about Jeff.

Name: The Housemaid
Review: This was pretty fun to watch, and this might be the movie where I liked Sydney Sweeney's performance the most so far. Amanda Seyfried was great too. I enjoy these kinds of pulpy thrillers even then they're not blowing my mind and are pretty dumb, the ending was very satisfying to watch. I saw that big reveal coming from miles away of course.

Name: Twinless
Review:
I've asked a friend who has an identical twin sister how it feels to share a face with another person, and she told me that her sister has always felt like a separate person from her; like, to her, it doesn't feel like it's the same face. So imagine my surprise when the same question pops up in this movie too. Twinless is about twin brothers who did grow up like they're the same person but then get estranged when one of them indeed becomes different than the other, and then what happens after one of them dies. Specifically when a new third person becomes a part of the grieving brother's life. 

It's a hard movie to talk about since there are some surprises in there that I shouldn't spoil. It begins on a sad note, showing a main character grieving, but then, the way the drama builds up is pretty brilliant, and after a point, it's funny, emotional, and heartfelt, and it keeps building tension up to the point where it keeps us wondering whether everything will fall apart or not. There are two scenes I really loved in particular. One is this long closeup shot on Dylan O'Brien that really tells us everything we have to know about his relationship with his brother without the need for any flashback sequences. The other is a party sequence that makes very brilliant use of split screen and sound. There's even a pretty impressive fight scene in here. James Sweeney knows his stuff. Amazing performances from the whole cast. 

It starts off as a sad movie, but it doesn't stay that way and becomes something much more. There are happy and wholesome moments, with drama and tension building up in the background, and it's about how different people deal with grief, just that sometimes it can be a bit fucked up. But I liked how the movie doesn't judge the characters too harshly for their mistakes. It's just people dealing with loneliness and the need for human connection in absurd, yet understandable ways. James Sweeney's portrayal of homosexuality also felt personal.

Name: Tere Ishk Mein
Review:
This movie fucking sucks, but I won't put it in the "fuck this movie" category because it's bad in a very fun way, there were lots of laughs to be had. Bollywood has been going through something that can only be called incelification or the Sandeep Reddy Vanga effect. It's this urge to be edgy and violent and show fucked-up romantic dynamics. Even BJP propaganda videos like Dhurandhar wear this incel skin for popular appeal. Tere Ishk Mein, in comparison, doesn't entirely commit to the incel thing; it's trying to replicate being a Raanjhanaa, which had its own issues on how it showed stalking and a one-sided crush, but still, I can't help but think that there was this pressure to seem like a Kabir Singh-adjacent fucked-up toxic dynamic here too. But this is no alpha male showcase movie; Shankar, played by Dhanush, is indeed an angry, violent, psychotic dude, but Anand L. Rai, unlike Vanga, is not so devoted to the penis, so the woman gets to be a shitty person who fucks over the alpha guy too. It's impossible to talk about this movie without talking about its absurd plot.

The protagonist of this movie is a 2200-page psychology PhD thesis. Mukthi, played by Kriti Sanon, needs to have a real-world example in her psychology thesis about how a violent person can be turned into a pookie in order to get the thesis signed and get her PhD. Fortunately, the most violent and psychotic dude in the college, Shankar, thinks Mukthi is hot. So basically she pretends, but not really, but pretends to be in love with him to turn him into a non-violent pookie and gets her PhD signed. Since this is a spiritual successor to Raanjhanaa, it's pretty obvious where it's heading towards: Dhanush is doomed to be rejected by the tall North Indian girl. But this is worse than Raanjhanaa because at least there, she never shows any feelings for him. I have no idea what kind of thesis or theory she had on those 2200 pages, turn violent men peaceful by being hot and manipulating them? Bruh, who'd want this person to be their therapist? After Vijay Devarakonda's The Family Star, this is the second film that I've watched with a plot point where a woman pretends to be in love for a PhD thesis. Men in Indian cinema seem to really hate PhD scholar women for some reason.

It's not like she doesn't get opportunities to reject him either. When she goes out on a date with her fancy guy friend, Shankar goes and makes a scene in the club, douses himself and the rich guy with petrol, and tells her to set the man she's rejecting on fire. She could reject him then for his psychotic behavior, but she doesn't. She goes to his house, has rice and sambar, and then tells him to meet her dad. Her dad, a rich privileged asshole, berates Shankar's working-class financial status in a full-on classist and casteist rant (though I checked and Shankar is supposed to be a Tamil Brahmin, but it's just that Mukthi's dad only cares about North Indian Savarnas?). But even then, there's no rejection; Mukthi makes her dad tell Shankar to clear the UPSC prelims to agree to the wedding. At this point, Shankar vows to clear the exam and cuts all contact with her for plot purposes, and then he grinds for 3 years and clears it. And when he finally goes to her house to tell her about it, of course she's getting engaged to another dude. This makes Shankar set the engagement venue on fire with molotov cocktails while reciting what he studied for the UPSC exam, in behavior that once again proves how effective Mukthi's PhD study and her job as a psychologist were in taking the violence out of him. So finally, after Shankar commits arson, Mukthi delivers the rejection to him, and it's like the worst and funniest friendzoning scene in the history of cinema.

Like, he asks her why she didn't just reject him in between all the opportunities he got, and she was like, she knew he couldn't handle rejection and was afraid of what he'd do if rejected. The funny thing here is, firstly, she's the one who supposedly cured his violence and wrote a thesis about it and got a PhD for it. Secondly, if Shankar is supposed to be a volatile psychopath who'd put this woman at harm, and that's why she never rejected him, the movie also tries to make us feel sorry for Shankar, and that's confusing in a "both sides are grey" kind of narrative, and finally, HE JUST SET FIRE TO YOUR ENGAGEMENT PARTY. TF ARE YOU TALKING ABOUT THIS BEING THE BETTER STRATEGY? By this point Mukthi's PhD should already be revoked, and she should not be allowed to be a shrink to anyone ever. The guy here is a psychopath who'd commit arson out of rejection, and scenes like these want us to feel sorry for him, and when classism is thrown into it too, it's a weird mix. And when Mukthi finally calls Shankar "mere dost", I audibly laughed. Later on, Shankar ominously walks up towards Mukthi during her wedding celebrations, looking all beaten up, pulls out a bottle, making the people around assume that it's acid, and he pours Ganga jal on her to bless her. We're supposed to pat him on the back for not pouring acid on her there. 🫩 

As a "flawed people entangled in a fucked-up love story" movie, the movie didn't feel self-aware at all. Creating one edgy scenario after another and building up to a tragic ending seemed to be the writing blueprint here. Just that the scenarios and the way these characters behave don't make sense at all. They're like different people in different scenes; tragic stuff or sad stuff happens at random because the movie wants them to happen. Anand L. Rai does succeed in making the violent psychopathic man seem like the poor victim here, better than Vanga ever did. The positioning of Shankar as underprivileged had something to do with that too; Vanga's protagonists have always been privileged. 

A. R. Rahman delivered a great soundtrack here, though. Plus Dhanush and Kriti delivered great performances, though Dhanush was Pradeep Ranganathan from Dragon for a bit during the college scenes.
