This movie takes itself way too seriously, so the goofy CGI during the army bits was also unintentionally funny. The film itself falls in the "why don't I deserve the hot girl?" category of incel cinema, while simultaneously making the girl be a terrible, self-destructive person. Like, when both of these characters die at the end, I felt nothing except "good riddance", and that says something, either about the movie or about myself.

Name: Call Me by Your Name
Review:
I don't know if the age difference not really being addressed or not even considered to be that much of an issue within the film is because of the period or the place the movie is set in. It is the most controversial and most debated aspect of this movie, and yeah, that's confusing…

It's a beautiful film, though. The visuals, the Italian landscape, the atmosphere, the music, and the acting: the vibes are just immaculate. Luca Guadagnino is one of the best in the business at showing physical intimacy and the kind of romance that really emphasizes touch, and that's explored here as well. There's both heterosexual and homosexual intimacy being shown here, but the homosexual touch and intimacy are clearly made to look more romantic, and that's necessary and deliberate from a character point of view as well, as the entire film is in Elio's point of view and about Elio discovering his sexuality. The film doesn't portray the relationship like Elio was manipulated or exploited by the older Oliver; it's portrayed as a mutual connection. They're both distant at first; they form a closer bond, and then the bond starts to get romantic, one that Oliver is even hesitant to make since he's also aware that it's more than just physical and that it can't turn into something long-term. For Elio, it's his first time experiencing a bond like this with another person, his first time experiencing true yearning. That whole emotional narrative builds up quietly while we see these characters spending summer and going about their days at a breezy pace.

The pace of this movie is important because it has the same pacing till the end, which also makes the heartbreak at the end feel so real. Nothing over-the-top, dramatic, or tragic happens; it's just life in its motions, and Elio's dad's monologue articulates it perfectly. This is Chalamet's breakout performance, and I can see how this launched him into having the leading man status that he currently has. Elio is the most precious thing about this movie; the way he navigates life, love, and heartbreak, there are all these touches to the way he shows his emotions. Even towards the end, on the phone call, little details like how the way he breathes changes when Oliver says something that breaks his heart but then chooses to hide it were all done really well. Also, the film chooses to end on this close-up shot of Elio looking at the fireplace, crying and smiling as if all the time he had with Oliver is playing back in his head, which is what Sufjan Stevens' Visions of Gideon playing in the background is implying too, while the end credits roll beside Elio. It's a very emotionally powerful ending, and even after the screen blacks out, Elio and his yearning linger around.

Name: Masthishka Maranam
Review:
Right as the movie begins, we get a narration about the future city of Neo-Kochi, the dystopian version of Kochi that the movie is set in. The narration talks about the class divide, capitalism controlling everything, AI-generated propaganda, and then… Most of that doesn't really matter to the rest of the movie. The main plot device in the movie involves this tech that allows memories of a person to be extracted and experienced like a virtual reality video game. The movie really wants us to understand that concept because the same thing is explained by the characters over and over again at least three times. This tendency to repeat points that the movie already made is present throughout.

There are things to appreciate here, like the main satirical plotline of how an actress is treated like an object and a commodity by those around her and how that connects with the memory experience tech and a murder case. There are really funny jokes in between, but lots of unfunny and confusing moments of attempted humor too. There are jokes that rely on stereotypes, like when a short person appears, there are jokes about his height; then there are jokes about sexual orientations, and also the mannerisms of one of Frida's assistants are being used for laughs too. There's lots of reference humor here; some of them went past the screen before I could read them, and some others were straight out of social media memes. Sometimes the movie even reminds us that a particular line is a reference to something else, like when one of the main characters says, "Enthina chetta chumma vaayil thonniyath vilich parayunnath?" to the media, which is something Dileep said at the time of his arrest, and another character stops and says, "Ith avante allaa." Usually only Pettan movies make reference to Pettan's case, but here's a non-Pettan movie doing that. The moments of humor that really worked for me were the ones where local flavor was mixed in with the dystopian setting, or the actors' performances and slang were doing the work. For a movie set in "Neo-Kochi" a lot of the characters have thekkan or Trivandrum slang. But that thekkan flavor made it more fun actually.

We follow Niranj's character for most of the initial half; he was just… Okay… I really liked Divya Prabha and Vishnu Agastya; as they became more prominent towards the second half, they got some fun lines to perform. Santhy Balachandran's character and the whole TV executives satire fell so flat, both performance-wise and writing-wise, like they're the most generic evil corporate media people you could find. The veterans Jagadish and Suresh Krishna were dependably good. Most of the cast consists of people who were already in Krishand's other films and web series, with the new addition being Rajisha Vijayan as Frida Soman. I liked her performance; her costumes and makeup and whole demeanor were also great, and the moments where she stops pretending to be the perceived image of herself and brings out the real person underneath. Her character is used to critique how the media, the industry, and even the audience members dehumanize an actress and treat her like an object; how she herself is forced to navigate an environment of perverts, being pressured to look a certain way and do procedures on herself, always being treated more as a commodity than as a person, and by the end, she just snaps.

While the movie's whole messaging is about the sexualization and objectification of an actress, the movie does sexualize and objectify Frida throughout its runtime. That one dance number is spliced up and replayed throughout the movie, as is the "memory experience" scene with her where perverts are getting intimate with her in the virtual reality simulation and those are used for laughs by the movie too, which felt weird. It can be argued that sexualizing her in this way is a way of exposing the icky gaze by the others within the movie, but also, the movie itself was marketed using that same dance number and her sexualized image. Is that irony or meta-commentary? I'm not so sure.

The movie uses plenty of AI in it too. Krishand's last movie, Sangharsha Ghadana, had used AI-generated images in a way that I didn't really like, but in this one, Gen AI is really a part of this dystopian reality where ads and even film stars are AI-generated. Plus, in 2026, films and ads do use AI, as at least two real AI-generated ads played in the theater just before this movie started. So filling a movie with AI slop when a part of the dystopian world-building also involves AI slop makes it different from the last movie's context.

I didn't really mind the low-budget production values, but the world being shown did seem inconsistent; sometimes it's super dystopian, and other times it's just "the not-too-distant future." Plus, all the information about the society given in the opening narration doesn't really matter that much; most of the time, this is just an exaggerated 2020s Kerala with a dystopian filter on it. The VFX work also looked pretty basic, but at least they're trying out these ideas even with the limited resources. They even show BTS sketches and VFX breakdowns at the end, probably to let us know that not everything was AI. The visual style was pretty unique, the editing was cool at times and weird at some other times, with some jarring choices. This movie is like very fast and yet very dragging at the same time pacing-wise. The music was really cool though. 

Anyway, the movie did have some solid ideas, and I did have genuine laughs and fun in between. But it also has lots of repetition, whether it's repeating information, repeating something the film had already established, or even repeating the same scenes or footage. Sometimes it can be tedious; even with the rapid pace, stylistic choices, and constant supply of jokes, the jokes falling flat at times also doesn't help. The efforts at anti-capitalist satire also have mixed results, some of the choices the movie made confused me, and then the movie ends without a proper closure with a sequel-bait cliffhanger.

Name: Hamnet
Review:
I'm not familiar with Maggie O'Farrell's book of the same name, so I can only talk about this film that she co-wrote with the director, Chloé Zhao. This film can be split into two equal halves; the first half consists of love, and the second half consists of grief, with an ending where love and grief blend together into beautiful everlasting art.

I don't know how much of this is fact or fiction, but in a film where William Shakespeare is a main character and his emergence as a writer and how he creates Hamlet is a part of the story, the film chooses to not really be about Shakespeare himself or his body of work; we don't even hear the name "William Shakespeare" until right before the ending, if I'm remembering correctly; he remains unnamed till then. Because the film chooses to focus on an emotional narrative and not a biographical one. It's a story of love and grief, and it chooses to begin and end with Agnes, Hamnet's mother and William's wife.

Chloé Zhao is a true empath because the way this movie visually conveys emotions is just amazing. Restricting a filmmaker like this with studio notes and cinematic universe guidelines might be the evilest thing Kevin Feige has done. Jessie Buckley is so brilliant here throughout the movie, especially in the ending, where she barely has any lines and yet says so much with just the way she reacts. If I'm being a bit silly, the ending of this movie might be the most cinematic and emotionally powerful audience reaction video ever shot. 

Paul Mescal is also great as Will, who does play the character as this vulnerable and grieving father instead of bringing any kind of literary genius energy, though it's conveyed that Will is very good at what he does too, but this portrayal is more concerned about what he's going through emotionally than who he's about to become. Will uses his art as a way of processing his grief and to share the love he had for his son with the world with the play Hamlet. But even then, the film makes Agnes the emotional center; at the end, it's both her and Will being connected by the love they had for their son and so many strangers who never even knew their son sharing that love and grief through the art Will created, and I won't lie, I was weeping towards the end. On the Nature of Daylight by Max Richter has successfully managed to make me cry every time it has popped up in a movie or TV show episode that I've seen. The movie also looks so gorgeous and is edited beautifully. Even with all the time skips, the emotional narrative never skips a beat. It's beautiful cinema.

Name: Train Dreams
Review:
It's tough to explain what this movie is about; even the official synopsis by Netflix sounds bland and doesn't really sell you on what Train Dreams is. Because it's not about the story or the period American setting, what's special about this film is the feeling it creates while it drops you into this person's life, and that person is Robert Grainier, who's just a working-class [white] man navigating through life, working as a logger and trying to find other ways to find work in a post-World War America. Robert is no historic figure, nor does he have an extraordinary life; he's just human. He's just living his life as time passes by and the world changes around him, and we're essentially just seeing Robert's life play out as he navigates through the happy, mundane, and tragic parts of his life, and it is so beautiful and emotional. Again, a film like this is more about the feels, and this movie delivers on the feels beautifully, and I was in tears by the end.

Firstly, this is one of the best-looking movies of the year. This movie is gorgeous from beginning to end; like, as a Netflix movie, it really made me think about how most of Netflix's original content is so generic and flat compared to this. Most of the film is set in the backdrop of nature, and natural lighting is used throughout; cinematography by Adolpho Veloso deserves a big shoutout. The editing and filmmaking are also very precise; all those dream sequences and the montages, especially the one towards the end, were so beautifully edited. The score was also very beautiful and really drew me into the many emotions the film navigated through, be it love, loss, or just pausing and reflecting on life.

Also, the movie uses a third-person narrator really well, in a way films rarely pull off.

Overall a very beautiful film that hits right in the feels.

Name: The Bride!
Review:
I can't believe they turned Frankenstein's monster into a literally me character (complimentary).

This might be the most overused analogy about this movie, but I can't think about anything else that's more accurate. Just like Victor Frankenstein's creature, Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride also feels like it's stitched together from parts of completely different films. I did have fun watching this movie, with both Jessie Buckley and Christian Bale being absolute hyperanimated beasts on screen, but also the movie is just trying to be too many things at the same time instead of being one coherent and focused thing.

On one hand it's surreal and meta, with direct references to Mary Shelley, a possession angle, and Frankenstein existing both as a real person and a fictional character in this world; it was all very David Lynch. But then, it's also a crime thriller but also a fucked-up love story; it's about loneliness, it's about fitting into the world, it's about female autonomy, it's about consent, and then after a point there's a revolution? There's a cop who has a history with the bride? It's like throwing all the ideas from the idea board at us instead of focusing on one solid thing from start to end.

As much as the writing is very messy and random, this was still entertaining. The amazing performances from the two leads, the visuals, the music, the dance numbers, the overall politics, and the comedy—there was always something that kept drawing me into the film's world and the characters despite its flaws.

The most important aspect of the movie was Frank's loneliness and isolation leading him to create a bride for himself, without her consent. Her sole existence is on the basis of being this one person's companion, but she herself doesn't have a say on whether she should even exist or whether she should even choose to be this person's partner. And then there's the fact that even in her past before her death, she didn't have any autonomy as a person. Frank, the sad and lonely monster, ends up seeming better than the men that the Bride was surrounded by before her death. The film should've focused more on this fucked-up dynamic of theirs, the Bride's autonomy, and the contrast between the Bride and Frank, which were my favorite parts of this film, instead of doing every subplot idea that ever existed for a movie like this.

Name: The Lost Bus
Review:
I was aware of this movie's existence, but I didn't get around to watching it until it got nominated for an Oscar in the Visual Effects category and the dudes at Corridor Crew were reacting to its very impressive VFX work. The Lost Bus is a disaster survival thriller based around the real-life 2018 California Camp Fire. Though the film also touches on the fire & rescue efforts from the fire department and the authorities, the main focus is on a school bus carrying children from their school that gets caught in the fire. Matthew McConaughey plays the bus driver Kevin, and America Ferrera plays the kids' teacher Mary.

The film has a pretty short initial setup that's set in the day before the fire, showing Kevin's daily routine and a bit of his personal life and struggles. We do hear warnings about a possible fire in the background, but mostly it's just about Kevin and his family. Then the next day begins, and the film becomes a full-on thriller. Paul Greengrass is the shaky cam guy who makes movies documentary style, and that's pretty much the predominant style here too, apart from some aerial shots and these really scary and effective POV shots where the fire and wind are shown to be this destructive entity spreading all over, like the evil entity from the Evil Dead movies. The documentary style really adds to the film feeling more real, and there is real footage from the real fire spliced up and inserted in between too. But the thing is, the visual effects work is so damn good and seamless that after a while I forgot to look for what's real and what's not. This is a very VFX-heavy movie, and that makes it even more impressive that it doesn't feel like a VFX-heavy movie for the most part. It just pulls us into this catastrophic event, and there's some great thriller filmmaking on display.

While this movie is a 10/10 as a disaster thriller, with characters we really root for and scenes that are edge-of-the-seat thrilling, the character-focused drama elements, like the ones that are about Kevin's life and his family situation, and the dialogue in these scenes, seemed kind of detached from the rest of the movie that was this laser-focused thriller. Like, maybe it's just me, but I wish I cared more about Kevin's personal life than just about him and the kids getting out of the fire alive, which is just basic empathy that would've worked even without me knowing about his personal life. McConaughey was so great in these emotional scenes, though; that did add some weight to them.

But even with that tiny lack of connection I felt, this is a very impressive thriller and some of the best visual effects work from this year, very worthy of the nomination.

Name: Blue Moon
Review:
This is yet again a film based on real people where I have no clue about the people and events being portrayed. But on the other hand, the kind of loneliness being portrayed here felt so real; many of the conversations and emotional beats felt so real, so by the end, my heart was fully into the movie despite being clueless about Hart and Rodgers or even the musical "Oklahoma!". And of course I have no idea how much of what's portrayed is real.

Lorenz "Larry" Hart is the protagonist; the film is set in a single night after the premiere of his frequent creative partner Richard Rodgers' hit musical that he did with another creative partner. But the film chooses to start with Hart's death and then shows this night, not that long away from his death, as a flashback. Doing so adds a layer of tragedy to everything that follows, even when those scenes never imply that he doesn't have that long to live.

As we see the night unfold in the bar, Larry is constantly yapping to the bartender, the pianist, and even to a fellow writer he manages to spot in there (which is part of a really cool Easter egg). Basically, Larry is just yapping on; it doesn't matter if the other person even asked him something or is interested in listening to him. The film doesn't use any flashbacks to show what Larry was before this night; it's all purely dialogue from this point onwards. But we get to know a lot about him; we get to know how insecure he is, how lonely he is, and how sad and miserable he is, and how his alcohol addiction affected his life, all while he's just yapping on while maintaining a very thin mask of confidence, pettiness, narcissism, and intelligence. As the night unfolds, Larry's mask does slip away at times; his vulnerability is exposed, and we get to know a lot about this person just from these various interactions. We also get to know about his ambiguous sexuality, his voyeurism kink, and his attraction and fascination towards a 20-year-old girl half his age. He's a weirdo. And even with a character who should give the audience the ick and be unlikable, Linklater manages to open up some room for empathy. Which makes Larry more complex than black or white.

Ethan Hawke was very brilliant as Larry. To make Hawke appear as the 5 ft Larry, the movie resorts to old-school movie magic for the most part, like clever set design, props, and using clever cinematography and forced perspective shots, rather than going the CGI head replacement or compositing route. But it's not just the filmmaking techniques doing the work here; the way Hawke carries himself and even talks and emotes is all very different from any Ethan Hawke performance I've ever seen. Though there are great supporting performances from Margaret Qualley and Andrew Scott, Hawke really carries the whole movie, providing so much emotional complexity to someone who's lonely pretty much because of himself.

Like I said, Larry and most of the things Larry felt seemed so real, even with Larry not being so likable as a person. Richard Linklater flexes his skills in doing amazing conversation scenes that feel so alive, and there were some real emotions here. Larry is surrounded by so many people but is so alone and left out basically; even with the 20-year-old Elizabeth, it's more like a yearning for intimacy, emotional included, than just something purely sexual. It's amazing the amount of emotional complexity this film has while being mostly set in the same location, in real time, and driven entirely by the dialogue and the performances.

Name: Aadu 3 Part 1
Review:
Only the first movie was actually about the Aadu, and the next two movies have nothing to do with Aadu, so that lack of Aaadccuracy while having Aadu in the title infuriates me. Anyways, I watched the first Aadu in an almost empty theater with my Amma, and it was one of the films that I loved as a kid. I'm pretty sure I had the Dude theme as my ringtone on my first phone. I didn't want to rewatch the previous two movies before watching the new one because I don't think they have aged well, especially the jokes that make fun of Vinayakan's skin color, which was like a recurring element of almost every Vinayakan movie pre-Kammattipaadam (I noticed one such joke in this one as well). Well, on the first watches anyway, I liked the first movie and found the second movie so-so, with only the Dude scenes staying on my mind all these years later. It's pretty obvious at this point who my favorite character is.

The first one had a pretty simple setup: there was this thing that everyone's after, Shaaji Paappan and gang get a goat, the goat eats the thing everyone wants, and everyone now wants the goat. Makes sense why the movie is named "Aadu" too, ahem. All of the characters are idiots; everyone gets their own intro scenes and individual theme songs. Basically this is the same formula in the third movie too, minus the actual goat. I mean, they literally do an Aadujeevitham joke in the movie and then call it Kazhutha jeevitham, when Aadu is literally in the title of this movie 😭 (I don't think anyone else is more frustrated about the lack of Aadu than I am).

Anyway, though it's the same setup, this one tries to be a bigger movie and blend in some sci-fi elements that were absent in the previous movies, and the results are messy. There's too much filler in the first half. Character intros with individual intro songs are a staple of the Aadu movies, but the movie spends too much time on these intros, some end up being basic, and there are scenes where basically nothing is happening. There were laughs in between, but when the comedy is more misses than hits, then watching the movie gets tiring. Then the second past timeline is introduced; the main guys get their own alternate theme songs and intros in that timeline too, and then those scenes too feel like filler, were tiring to watch, and it's in the past timeline that most of the jokes miss too.

The only intro that did make me feel something is again, Dude. But Dude has so much less screentime in this movie. Vinayakan appears in the past timeline in the first half, but Dude only appears in the second half, and again, it's his scenes that I enjoyed the most, though there was very little of him. New additions include Fukru's Gen-Z Instagram addict, who's this unfunny millennial representation of Gen-Z, leaving no impact. Canadian actress and stuntwoman Alleya Bourne plays the main antagonist, who's again just a basic villain with no real personality, but she does get to show off some cool action moves. The rest of the cast tries to still be their earlier selves, but it's not the same. Again, I'm talking from childhood memories and not a recent rewatch. But still, it's more about the writing and the fact that most of the movie feels like filler material, with a past timeline section that frankly I didn't really care about. Things like that 6 7 joke came out of nowhere and I laughed, ngl. 

It's the second half where the plot actually gets moving, where the characters actually start doing something, and the familiar setup from the Aadu movies plays out. And then just as it's starting to get interesting, the movie just abruptly ends with a "to be continued…" text. To have nothing happening for most of your movie and then slap in a cliffhanger ending when something just starts to happen is just diabolic, bro 😭.

I liked how the visual style changed in between the past and the present, and it's not just the aspect ratio; they actually seemed like two different films visually and yet seamlessly transitioned between each other. The music was also very cool, and I can never get tired of hearing Shaan Rahman's original themes and their variations. 

Also, seeing the criminals in Aadu 3 who stole the demonetized currency plates suffering from that failure is funny when Aditya Dhar's demonetization erotica is also playing in the cinemas right now. 😭

But still, on the whole, Biriyani tharaamenn paranjitt ulliyum achaarum maathram thannitt, Biriyani naale tharaam enn parayunna pole aayi.

Name: Is This Thing On?
Review:
I end up loving every movie that I've watched that has Under Pressure in its soundtrack, and this is another addition to that list. This movie uses Under Pressure twice; at first, when the main characters' kids are practicing it in the background as they're having a conversation, it sounds all messy at first, but gradually it starts to sound like the song. The second time is at the very end; I won't say the context because that'd be a spoiler.

Bradley Cooper's "Is this thing on?" is about this newly separated couple; the husband, a finance guy, then finds an interest in doing stand-up comedy, but this is no gender-reversed Mrs. Maisel. The film is very much about the relationship between Alex and Tess, why they decided to separate, and how both of them deal with the separation. The first time Alex does stand-up, he just wanted to get into a bar for free, since non-performers have to pay $15. He just talks about his marriage and the separation, and since he's a naturally funny guy, he gets laughs, and then he finds love in performing comedy, which is always about his own life and relationship. Tess is also dealing with the separation in her own way and trying to reignite her past passion. The film's leaning more towards Alex's POV, but Tess is just as important.

Will Arnett and Laura Dern are amazing in this movie, and they have such great chemistry together, which is hard to pull off while playing a separated couple. Because here we're seeing two people who are currently distant from each other but who used to really love each other; that history and love are really felt in their interactions even without any flashbacks about their past relationship. The writing is so good in several of the Tess and Alex scenes, especially towards the end when the movie starts directly addressing the reasons why they separated. The supporting cast is also very cool; Bradley Cooper himself plays Alex's weird friend. Maybe he always wanted to know what performing as Alan from The Hangover would feel like, though his character is not nearly as weird as Alan. It was also cool to see Will Arnett and Amy Sedaris sharing a scene in person, where she once again is playing a talent manager of sorts, after listening to their voices as Bojack Horseman and Princess Carolyn for so many years. 

The way Bradley Cooper chose to film the stand-up scenes was also very unique. The camera is always very near Alex's face; it doesn't cut back to audience reactions, and the background laughter also sounds genuine. It's not like Alex is this hilarious comedian making everyone burst out laughing; the stand-up sets performed by Will Arnett as Alex were funny enough to justify those laughs. This film isn't really about his stand-up career or him becoming famous. There's only a single instance where the film chooses to cut back to the audience during Alex's comedy set, and you bet it's the only time that matters. I liked how the movie never lost its real focus.

The film closes by playing Under Pressure, and it is a very valid Under Pressure moment.

Name: Point Nemo
Review: Surreal and weird in a really fun way. It plays around with the form and format of what a film is supposed to be throughout. The DVD logo screensaver opening titles were cool. Some of it didn't make sense, some of it made sense, something weird is going on almost all the time, there was fun stuff and really creative imagery and choices throughout, and it is a pretty unique watch.

Name: Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man
Review:
Tommy Shelby has been faced with death throughout the original show, and in all those times he chose to accept it. So as a lonely man who is haunted by the ghosts of his lost family and with nothing much to live for, it's a pretty justified conclusion for the Shelby family and Tommy himself. Just that this conclusion probably needed a full season of television, and the movie just didn't give these big losses room to breathe.

Firstly, there's the offscreen death of Arthur. Paul Anderson was written off the movie because of his real-life drug charges, and that's pretty much the way Arthur's death has been written too; his drug addiction makes him a burden on Tommy, and one day Tommy loses it and kills him. We've spent multiple seasons seeing these characters having each other's backs, but this just comes suddenly. Not having Paul Anderson reprise Arthur when it's a major dark twist like this doesn't help at all. Tommy killing Arthur works in theory; we've seen something similar in The Sopranos, but that death had a proper buildup to it; this doesn't. The same film has Ada dying too, which had more impact because it has a proper buildup and Sophie Rundle is on screen playing her.

I don't hate this movie, though. There are things I appreciated here. The WWII setting was the perfect way to conclude Peaky Blinders; beginning from the aftermath of WWI and ending in the middle of WWII makes it seem full circle. That parallel to the very first episode of the show, when Tommy is riding his horse through a war-torn Birmingham with a somber version of Red Right Hand playing in the background, was powerful. Cillian Murphy is also absolutely brilliant as Tommy, adding depth to the character that the writing didn't have the space to, and of course, plenty of aura farming. Barry Keoghan was great as well, but Rebecca Ferguson and Tim Roth didn't really get much to do. The music and the aesthetics were pretty on brand for Peaky Blinders, though the scale is way bigger this time, and the war is shown in its full scale.

I think more than the various twists and the conclusion itself, what I felt was that there wasn't enough time to flesh out everything. Which is similar to what I felt about the Sopranos movie, The Many Saints of Newark. There was simply too much story for a two-hour movie. This is something Vince Gilligan dealt with smartly in El Camino. El Camino was not a proper follow-up to Breaking Bad the way Better Call Saul was. It was not trying to be a bite-sized version of Breaking Bad. Instead, it was like this self-centered epilogue just for Jesse to give him some closure, which never felt like it was a season's worth of story getting condensed.

Anyway, despite some disappointments, the ending still made me emotional, and I'll always remember Peaky Blinders fondly.

Name: Mazhameenukal
Review: This sweet and small movie is only 10 minutes long, and it manages to be beautiful and emotional in that short amount of time. I could resonate with it in a different context because I've had a lonely childhood myself, and I've thought about how my childhood would've been if the lovely people I got to meet later in life were also a part of it where we got to share innocent memories before whatever adulthood is took over. Mazhameenukal is this sweet portrayal of love and companionship established with very few dialogues and some beautiful visuals. The very beautiful song Aaro Nee was then like a warm hug holding it all together. A good melody in Sooraj Santhosh's voice is always healing. Sending love to Sreehari and everyone involved. 💖

Name: Project Hail Mary
Review: Peak literally me cinema. I have not read the novel, so I'm just going to be talking about the film adaptation here. Project Hail Mary has shades of sci-fi films I've seen in the past; there's Interstellar, Arrival, E.T., and even the other Andy Weir adaptation, The Martian, being reminded to me. But the thing is, this film still manages to be original, funny, thrilling, and so wholesome on its own, and it's so well made with so much heart and care poured into it that I don't even have any complaints. Watching this film in IMAX was a core memory for me. Project Hail Mary has a perfect blend of science, sci-fi, and heart. It takes the science so seriously that the sci-fi just feels like a natural extension of that; showing analog equipment and physical machinery instead of modern screens also felt like a cool production design choice. At the same time, all the expositionary dialogue and science stuff is accessible enough, and it never takes focus away from the central emotional narrative. It's a story about saving worlds, but portrayed with a very personal point of view, and it just works beautifully. The film begins with the protagonist Ryland Grace waking up in space with no memory of who he is. How exactly Grace got there is then slowly revealed to us as he himself is slowly remembering those events. The transition to these flashbacks is very cool, using these match cuts to transition back and forth from the present-day space scenes. The aspect ratio also changes to wide-screen for the flashbacks, while the space scenes are taller. The transitions are so seamless, not just visually or in terms of the editing, but also in how the flashbacks are introduced narratively. The payoff to why we're seeing past Grace and present Grace in parallel while we already know where Grace ended up is worth it. Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace and is in pretty much every scene in the movie. I only counted a single scene towards the end where he was not in there. Gosling dependably carries the film with so much grace (pun intended) and earnestness; his signature sense of humor and charisma are all a part of the character, and he gets to wear some really cool and hilarious t-shirts. Grace is this lonely loser-core character (OMG, he's literally me!) who is suddenly responsible for saving the world. He's flawed and vulnerable, and his whole character journey is defined by hope and love, and that's where Rocky comes in. Rocky the Eridian is the second star of Project Hail Mary, the cutest rock alien person in the entire universe. They made the choice of portraying Rocky through puppetry instead of going the CGI route, which is also funny when Rocky also performs his own puppet shows. Puppeteer James Ortiz also voices Rocky, and Rocky always felt like a very real creature full of life and a personality. Even though Gosling is the star of the movie, Rocky gets some of the best lines here; the way the whole communication aspect was treated by the movie was really fun. We really do get to see these two characters bond over time, and the relationship is so well formed. Gosling's face is the only one we're seeing, as Rocky is faceless, and it's all the movements and the voice giving life to him, so mostly it's the way Gosling interacts with Rocky and reacts to Rocky that adds life to their friendship. Sandra Hüller also gets some really memorable moments in the film, especially the karaoke scene and the scene towards the end. It was also cool to see Marcus from The Bear (Lionel Boyce) as Carl, and he also gets some really cool deadpan comedy moments. The film builds up the emotional narrative beats really well and makes us care about these characters on a personal level that whenever things switch gear to scarier thriller/action territory with the challenges they face in the mission, it's very edge-of-your-seat stuff. Action with a purpose and a heart always lands better than action that's purely spectacle. It puts us over the edge, as both these characters are in grave danger, and either of them could die, as they're not set up as invincible action heroes at all. And the amazing part is that this movie delivers on the spectacle as well. The space scenes are always gorgeous to look at, even when things get scary. Cinematography by Greig Fraser really gives the film its own unique look and personality. There were multiple scenes that made my jaw drop and my eyes sparkle, like, of course, the moment where Grace is outside collecting samples. The visual effects, the set design, the practical effects—everything here is impressive, but they're always there to uplift the narrative and pull the audience further into the characters and the emotional stakes. The music by Daniel Pemberton and the songs used in the soundtrack were also very cool and, likewise, uplift the film. The film gives new meaning to "Sign of the Times" by Harry Styles and "Two of Us" by The Beatles, a sentence I never expected to say. This film made me tear up, laugh, have the widest smile on my face, and touched my heart in more ways than one. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller had a canceled TV show named The Last Man on Earth that I really loved, which also had this lonely loser in a post-apocalyptic scenario suddenly having to deal with situations he never had to. I can't quite explain how, but I could see a bit of The Last Man on Earth here too. This is the kind of experience that cinema is all about, the kind you need to watch on the biggest screen accessible to you. This is the kind of film that those big premium screens are built for. It's technical finesse with a purpose; it's peak Ryan Gosling (but you'll still remain in my top 4, La La Land), and everyone deserves a Rocky in their lives. AMAZE! AMAZE! AMAZE! 👎🏽 👎🏽 👎🏽 👎🏽 👎🏽 🧡

Name: Dust Bunny
Review:
This has the whimsy and colors of a children's fantasy movie but is then filled with assassins and death. The colors and the set design were amazing; the movie's got a very distinct atmosphere and feel to it and looks beautiful most of the time. It's nice to see unique visual sensibilities in a time when movies, especially kids' movies, are starting to look the same. The humor and the chemistry between Mads Mikkelsen and Sophie Rundle were also on point. It's also always cool to see Mads flex his gymnastic skills. The way the movie kept teasing whether a monster actually exists or if it's just a little girl's coping mechanism was also cool. Just that, the CGI didn't look so great most of the time, as beautiful as the production design and cinematography were otherwise.

It was a fun and nice watch, but the CGI occasionally took me out.

Name: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die
Review:
This is like all of the anxiety and worries an artist might have about the present AI-brainrot era all packaged into a weird dark comedy. A generation gap is also a factor here, because you know when older people say Gen-Z are just screen-obsessed zombies? This film even manages to make that a part of the plot, but in such a smart, twisted, and funny way that I can't dismiss it as someone from the older generation not getting the vibe of the younger generation.

Sam Rockwell stars as a man who looks like the last person whom we'd expect to be the time-traveling savior of the world. How he wants to save the world is also interesting, because he doesn't want to destroy AI. He knows AI is inevitable and some form of it will emerge from one place or another. He wants to regulate AI, which is darkly funny in its own way. There's a lot of crazy stuff happening in this movie, and it's best experienced completely fresh without much context; a big nightmarish AI slop monster even appears at one point.

Some of the ideas here felt borrowed from Black Mirror, while some of the others felt very real and like they were coming from a place of genuine concern over where the world is currently heading with the advancements in AI and the popularity of brainrot. The ending was a bit disappointing, lots of instances of characters delaying to do stuff they should do as quickly as possible for dramatic effect and a final confrontation that felt like the characters were just mouthing the writer's talking points on AI. I have no issue with direct messaging as long as it somehow fits into the context and characters of the movie, but the confrontation at the end just felt... Off. I really liked the epilogue that came afterwards. 

Anyway, this one has some great performances, it's funny and entertaining enough, and it does some delightfully weird dark comedy with the topic of AI and brainrot. Though it loses steam towards the end and leaves so much stuff unexplained. If you've ever sought validation from AI chatbots, this one's for you.

Name: The Drama
Review:
I think this movie is best experienced without being aware of what exactly all the "drama" in it is all about, so I'll keep silent about that. We're essentially following this couple, Charlie and Emma, on the days leading up to their wedding; it's all fun and cute until something is revealed about one of them that changes their whole dynamic. What follows are several uncomfortable and darkly humorous scenarios.

Both Zendaya and Robert Pattinson are great in this film and have great chemistry together, both in the rom-com awkward-in-a-cute-way mode in the beginning and the dark-comedy awkward-in-an-absurd-way mode later. Zendaya's especially amazing in the way she really sells the absurdity of it all and brings so much vulnerability and empathy to her character. I loved the non-linear storytelling and the way this film has been edited. The editing really gives a unique energy to this movie, both in terms of comedy and drama. Even when this is like a really small plotline, the precise and unique editing style really gives it life and makes it more engaging. The music is also cool, and the movie also looks very beautiful. I also liked how the movie balances its empathy between the two characters, instead of making it all about the guy, which is how such stories usually play out.

True dark comedy is achieved when you laugh but you're unsure whether you should even laugh at that, which is what The Drama pulls off; that scene with the photographer towards the middle was especially funny in a delightfully fucked-up way.

Name: Scream 7
Review:
Firstly, Free Palestine. Secondly, fuck spyglass for firing Melissa Barrera for speaking against a genocide. But no, I didn't hate this film on account of the firing or because of the producers being Zionists. I'd have hated this film even if those circumstances were not present. Because this is simply the worst Scream movie I've watched.

Firstly and most importantly, it takes itself way too seriously; the self-aware, semi-parody vibes are gone, and what we get is exactly the kind of legacy sequel that Scream 5 was making fun of. Even the kills are not that good, and there's too much goofy CGI gore involved. The last two Scream films directed by Radio Silence did manage to recapture the style, humor, and campiness of Wes Craven's four Scream movies to an extent, but this one, even with original Scream writer Kevin Williamson directing, seems miles apart from those sensibilities, despite having the same writers attached. The writing seems so lazy; it's not thrilling, it's not funny, the characters are just cardboard cutouts, and there's too much dumb shit happening. Bringing back Neve Campbell also seems so unearned on her legacy when we know this is damage control casting when the same series lead was absent from the last film because the same people didn't pay her enough.

The killer reveal is also very dumb and has to be the most pathetic killer reveal in the series. Bringing back previous killers to do cameos made me appreciate how the whole Billy Loomis gimmick in the last two was so much better. Anyways, it takes a different level of suck to bring back the original series lead in a sequel and make it feel so lazy and tacky.

Name: Vaazha II
Review:
I'm someone who hated the first Vaazha, but I decided to watch the second one only because Hashir and gang are the leads, and unsurprisingly, one of the main reasons why this one is a huge improvement over the first one is because of them. The writing improvements are way fewer; there are a few changes from the first movie's sensibilities that I appreciated, while the Instagram reelness and corny melodramatic stretches that felt tiring at times and unnecessary preaching carry over from the first one. But still, I did tear up a bit towards the end; the performances and the music do wonders here to uplift the not-so-great writing.

I'll start with what has improved from the first Vaazha, and it's the fact that the leads are more likable and easy to root for. Hashir, Alan, Vinayak, and Ajin are pretty much playing the versions of themselves we've seen on their reels, but there are extra sides of them that we've not seen on those reels also present here. The movie obviously wants to cater to the fans of their Instagram content too, since there are multiple references to their own content, whether it's Ada Gommaale being turned into a love song of all things or enthaada kochu keralathil nadakkunnath, and I noticed that during some scenes, even the shots were set up like how Hashir and gang shoot their short comedy videos on their phones rather than a conventional cinematic blocking of actors. 

The leads are very fun to watch, and they carry the film really well. Hashir, especially, was so charming during the few moments we saw him in loverboy mode. This movie doesn't have a good love track for him, but still he's so great with whatever he got to do that I wish I could see him in a well-written full-on romcom very soon. But whether it's the funny scenes, the action scenes, or the emotional ones, they were pretty dependable leads performance-wise. And unlike the first film, these guys were more convincing as school students too. There were several moments that made me laugh out loud, and their delivery and performances were a large part of that.

Also, the key difference in writing this time around is that the guys in Vaazha 2 actually try to do something with their lives. Vaazha 1 had the guys do absolutely nothing towards making their lives better or even get jobs, and then the movie expected us to feel sorry for them and blame their parents and the society for not being kind towards them. Vaazha 2 actually shows the guys trying to study, work, and survive at adulting. It even shows how migrating to the UK is not so much the dream life that's usually advertised on social media for someone not from a privileged background. That feeling of being left alone while your friends migrate away also felt real.

The preaching scene with Alphonse Puthren was all sorts of stupid. He's a cop taking a class about what parents and teachers should do to make sure kids don't become drug addicts, and it's like so absurd. Yes, physical activity should be encouraged among school students, but no, bro, kids not getting to play football is not the reason why they become drug addicts (? 😭). Also, when a teacher then slut-shames female students, our upadesham cop's response towards it is to slut-shame the teacher (😭?). I mean, upadeshikkan ulla wisdom onnum illel mindaathirunnoode hei? I did like that, unlike the first film, which didn't give any accountability towards its leads, this one does show the boys being equally responsible for their mistakes and facing the consequences. But still, Vipin Das ini upadeshikkaan varallu, pls.

Along with the leads, the other big pillar of Vaazha 2 that's saving a lot of scenes is the music. The songs were all a delight, even for the most corny scenes in the movie. The ending of this movie is exactly like the first one, which is 4 senti scenes running in parallel, but just as it was starting to feel too long, the Koodepirannor track hits, and yeah, it did make me tear up. But the thing is, the movie ends with that song on an emotional high, though it leaves so many important threads hanging, but then when we're just settling down on that emotional ending, the dudes from the first movie randomly pop up, and there's a fight scene with Hey Bananey playing in the background. This is the exact sort of Instagram reel sensibility that pulls the movie down. 

The film has a theme of sibling bonding running through it, but still, the way Alan's sister is absolutely sidelined by the movie after something traumatic happens to her felt weird. Yes, the movie is supposed to be about the "bros", but the female characters are reduced to just being plot devices, which also dampens that ending. Alan's and Vinayak's arcs in particular have many weird choices in their writing towards the end (Vinayak is still waiting for his paracetamol). There's even a dumb Johnny Sins joke, which has nothing to do with that paavam character otherwise.

Vaazha 2 has its flaws, mainly in the writing; several scenes go on for too long despite it being an Instagram reel-core movie, but still, there is some very cool music in this movie, the emotions and themes work well when the performances and the music carry their weight, it's a well-directed film too and I did like this a lot better than the first movie. The four leads were really good, and I wish to see them in more films, hopefully ones with better writing. I hope Hashir has already been cast in a great romcom (If Girish AD is reading this, get cracking).

Can't rate this movie too low because of the fact that i absolutely adored leads and the music. 🫶🏻

Name: Bharathanatyam 2 Mohiniyattam
Review:
Bharathanatyam was like a family dramedy that also acted like a Balettan spoof. The only complaint I had back then was how it became melodramatic towards the end by having the same tropes it had been subverting so far. So it's interesting that this is the biggest change in the sequel. Mohiniyaattam is this full-on irreverent dark comedy that maintains a comedic tone throughout its runtime, carrying on the plotline and characters from the first movie but by being an entirely different kind of movie.

Where the first movie was a Balettan spoof, this one is like a crazier Drishyam, where the family is dealing with a crime cover-up instead of just the patriarch's infidelity creating clone sons. The jokes are constant, and there are a lot more hits than misses. Even the most ethical use of an AI-generated image in movies I've seen must be in this one because that particular image looking as ugly as it does because it's AI kinda makes it funnier. There are also lots more meta jokes and parody situations this time; it's more self-aware, and it takes itself way less seriously than the first film. Some of the meme references and meta humor didn’t work for me, like that Vasu Annan joke and the chapri joke (I don't like movies casually using such casteist - classist internet slurs in general), but on the whole I was laughing constantly throughout the movie.

Sai Kumar is missed from the first part in this movie, though Bharathan Nair pretty much drives the plot this time too and gets the best "mass" scene in the movie; mixture and sambhaaram will never be the same. The rest of the cast is also great, with Saiju Kurup as Sasi being more like a part of the bigger ensemble than being front and center. Kalaranjini gets some of the movie's best moments like she did in the first movie, several of her reactions made me laugh. New additions like Baby Jean, Suraj, Jagadeesh, and Vinay Forrt were also great.

Music by Electronic Kili was also cool; Baby Jean gets this song where he's always staring at the family being all sus, which is like this movie's own version of the Dexter sus meme. I also loved the way the movie has been edited; there's a lot of visual humor conveyed through the editing and scene transitions. 

Anyway, Mohiniyaattam made me laugh a lot; it plays up the strengths of the first movie and even brings a new twist to the formula with the crime angle. There are more hits than misses in the comedy, and I hope Malayalam cinema plays around with dark comedies a lot more.

Name: The Super Mario Galaxy Movie
Review:
I'm not really against movies that are meant to sell stuff as long as it's a good enough time. The LEGO Movie is one of my favorite movies, and it even redefined American 3D animation as a whole from every animated movie looking like Pixar. Illumination itself started from a Pixar-adjacent path and now is more about growing the minions' corporate empire. The Super Mario Galaxy movie also feels more like a commercial than a movie.

What we get is gorgeous-looking animation, beautiful art, very cool music, a lot of famous celebrities doing pitch-corrected voice-overs, and heaps upon heaps of video game references. As someone whose only connection with Super Mario is playing the original Super Mario Bros. back in the day, all the references to the later games flew right over the head. It's still fun, with lots of cartoon action and a regular supply of jokes, but still, at the end, it's really a nothingburger. The artists and animators have clearly put in a lot of effort, as this movie is visually stunning, but the writing is just the bare minimum fan service and nostalgia baiting and whatever excuse they need to throw colorful visuals and references at us.

The Bowser and Bowser Jr. plot reminded me of the one from Sonic 3, yet another video game adaptation, but Sonic 3 had a way better version of the same plot; Sonic 3 actually gave more of a shit. I did like the throwbacks to the classic Mario game towards the end and some of the action scenes, but on the whole, this movie is like a shameless cash grab commercial, and it was successful, so we can see more of this happening. But at least the art, animation, and music are great, and I loved Yoshi.

Name: Sambhavam Adhyayam Onnu
Review:
This movie is very rough around the edges. The acting, the dialogues, and the filmmaking have a lot of room for improvement, but still, as a debut work, it does show promise, and I can't be too harsh on its flaws. Once the movie gets into the central mystery and we get a sense of what exactly is going on, this movie did pull me into the mindfuck of it all even with its several limitations, which is something timeloop movies are supposed to do.

Malayalam cinema has lots of unnecessary sequel baiting these days, but here the cliffhanger felt earned, and if the team does make another one, I'd definitely watch.

Name: Lee Cronin's The Mummy
Review:
I like how flexible the Mummy movies are. The 90s Mummy movies were Indiana Jones coded as an action adventure with just some horror elements; the Tom Cruise Mummy movie was, well, Tom Cruise coded, and this one is an Evil Dead coded body horror movie. Bugs entering human mouths is just about the only thing this one has in common with any previous Mummy movie. It's pretty much a demonic possession body horror movie set mostly in an American household, there's not much of Egyptian lore being explored than what's necessary for this setup, and there's definitely no instance of the cast being all hot and farming aura like in the 90s Brendan Fraser - Rachel Weisz movies. 

The narrative is pretty fast-paced and straightforward. We have a scary cold open that sets up the mood of the movie; we're introduced to the family, the child goes missing, she gets found years later as a mummy, and creepy shit starts to happen. The movie doesn't really wait around and gets straight to business. Now it's in the creepy shit that Lee Cronin starts to do his own thing. The movie finds so many ways to be disturbing, gory, and disgusting, and while this is not as relentlessly and continuously gory as Evil Dead Rise, when it does get nasty, it gets REALLY nasty. There's lots of skin peeling, nails doing stuff nails aren't supposed to do, and teeth doing stuff teeth aren't supposed to do, and just like in the Evil Dead movies, even when things are deranged and traumatic for the characters, the movie can occasionally have this twisted sense of humor, though I'm the only person who laughed during certain scenes, and maybe the rest of the people in the audience judged me.

The performances are good too, but the kids impressed me more than the adults; all three of the young actors got some really twisted material to work with, and they pull it off really well. I understand why May Calamawy had those stitches on her throat in this movie's premiere, eesh. The visual effects and practical gore are very effective, and almost every gory scene managed to make me squirm. The ending felt a bit easy; all things considered, it's the conclusion I wanted, but I just wish the way there was a bit more fleshed out. In the very fast pace and the priority given to scares and gore, the narrative beats can feel a bit rushed, and that's felt the most in the third act, where everything is supposed to build up to a conclusion. Sometimes the characters' actions don't make sense, but I didn't mind.

But anyway, this movie successfully managed to creep me out in multiple instances, so it's a pretty effective horror movie.

Name: Michael
Review:
There is a CGI monkey in this movie, but he's not the protagonist. 

I like biopics that feel a bit personal, even if they're not a hundred percent historically accurate. Michael never felt like it wanted to look at the king of pop as a person. The film always feels like it's only pushing this curated surface-level public persona of Michael Jackson, one that is only meant to sell more music and merchandise. So Michael is this supremely talented, pure, and innocent soul who has no flaws and no vices. Michael himself says in the film at one point that he'd like to stay mysterious and let the music and dance speak. This film too falls flat whenever there's something resembling a narrative going on and only gains life when there's music and dance on screen. It depends solely on Michael Jackson's star power and influence (which is like as big as it gets) and Jaafar Jackson's ability to channel that showmanship for the most part, and not so much on writing or actual filmmaking. 

Jaafar Jackson stars as Michael, along with Juliano Krue Valdi as young Michael. There's been a lot of care given to make both of them look and move like the real Michael. Jaafar in particular has his genetics doing the work for him, but the makeup and hairstyling were so on point too. He looks almost exactly like Michael Jackson in some of his profiles, and the film keeps choosing these particular angles to always show him, and it felt like the blocking in those shots was more about him looking like his uncle as much as possible than a narrative choice. Well, most of them are low-angle shots, so it does help him look big and like a star too, a win-win. Jaafar looks the least like Michael in moments like the Thriller recreation, where they have to use the same angles as the original video. But still, it's a great, stardom-worthy lead performance, as he's amazing in every recreated Michael Jackson performance. The writing itself doesn't give Michael any depth as a character otherwise, and his voice, too, comes off more like an impression. But any time he's singing or dancing, he's Michael, he's able to channel Michael Jackson's physical presence really well. But still, it's the kind of portrayal where we keep subconsciously comparing how accurate the recreations are, and even the praise the movie gets is just about how close Jaafar seems to the real Michael, instead of the film drawing us into its narrative (which it barely even has anyway), this is the sort of flaw that you solve by making your protagonist a monkey, guys. You were too unfair on Better Man. 

Colman Domingo stars as Michael's father Joseph Jackson, who's pretty much the villain here. He's also not given much of a personality to him other than being abusive, manipulative, and exploitative. And unlike Jaafar as Michael, the prosthetics given to Domingo look like he's perpetually stuck doing the same facial expression, and it's easy to tell that it's restricting his performance by a lot. I even wondered if the prosthetics were meant to make Domingo look more evil than to resemble the real Joseph. 

None of the Jackson family members except Michael himself and Joseph (the villain of the story) get much prominence in the film. All of Michael's siblings and his mom are glorified extras. But the movie does give one person a lot of importance in this film, and that's Michael's lawyer, John Branca. Branca is played by Miles Teller, the most famous (and probably most expensive) established actor of this cast. Branca in the film is this [white] savior who swoops down from heaven to help save Michael from his exploitative father. There's even a good amount of buildup given to Branca when he appears on screen for the first time. He's there every time Michael needs support, legal or emotional. One quick glance at this film's credits will tell you that John Branca (the real one) is the co-producer of this film and is also the co-chair of the Michael Jackson Estate. Frankly, Branca's self-glazing and the way this movie chooses to portray Michael make it seem like Branca's seeing Michael pretty much like a product that he gets to sell, like the way Joseph is shown to see Michael in the film.

It's well recorded that this film was supposed to have the child sexual abuse allegations against Michael as a part of its storyline but then had the entire third act reshot because they couldn't legally portray that on screen. But it felt like some part of that storyline still remains in this film. Yes, Michael is shown to be different than other adults; he has a fascination with Peter Pan, his home is basically a zoo, and then he's a kid at heart and likes to be around kids. At one point in the movie, they show Michael Jackson buying lots of toys and kid games from a toy store and asking his brothers to play with him. But his brothers would rather play basketball and go on dates with girls. Poor innocent adult Michael, who is a kid at heart, is shown to not have any other kids to play with... This particular plot thread doesn't really progress any further in this movie. But it just felt weird when watching it with added real-life context. Maybe this was supposed to lead on to how Michael hanging out with those kids in Neverland was completely innocent and pure. In that sense maybe it was good that the child abuse storyline was edited out, and maybe they shouldn't do the sequel about what happened after 1988 that would have this plotline in it. There's a high probability of the ick there.

The new third act instead has multiple recreations of MJ performances, which include Billie Jean, Thriller, Beat It, Human Nature, Bad, you get it. The quick rewrite basically included nostalgia overloads, with a quick wrapping up of the storyline around Michael getting out of Joseph's control and manipulation. The Pepsi commercial accident is also covered. Michael's various physical conditions are covered well by the film, including his vitiligo, the nose job, and the nerve damage and issues from the fire accident, even when his personality and creative process only get surface-level treatment. The closure with Joseph also doesn't feel that earned, but it's followed so quickly by a closing performance of Bad. As basic as Bohemian Rhapsody was, the closing Live Aid show was still shot really well, even Baz Luhrmann's Elvis was loaded with a unique style and personality of its own even with its basic writing, here the recreations really depend more on Jaafar's performance than any stylistic filmmaking flair. 

On the whole, other than the amusement of seeing Jaafar Jackson recreate some iconic MJ performances and moves, there's nothing much happening narratively in this by-the-numbers rise to fame biopic that just becomes less of a film as it progresses further. The unnecessary white savior halo given to the lawyer doesn't help either. Only I was happy in my screening to see yet another Mike Myers as a record executive cameo in a musician biopic.

It's really, really bad, Shamone. But the two stars are for the two amazing performers who tried to embody the unique showmanship of Michael Jackson the best they can and those recreated performances.

Name: Apex
Review:
This is one of those streaming movies that pretty much looks and feels like a streaming movie; it even has those "considerations" to make it appropriate for background watching. Also, you can tell when there are real stunts going on, and both the actors and the stunt artists are doing some impressive stuff on screen for real, but whenever it goes full CGI, it looks so obviously fake. It doesn't quite blend the practical stunts and CGI the way the best in the business, like Mission Impossible, do.

It's a very basic premise and setup; you can see all the twists and reveals coming from a mile away if you're not background watching the movie. Taron Egerton was delightfully weird and creepy, though, and gives this movie his all. Charlize Theron gets a monotonous character to work with, but for her too, lots of physicality is involved, and she pulls that off very convincingly, whether it's the water stunts or the climbing. If there's a reason I'm not rating this movie too low despite not really finding it that good, it's the actors.

I wish they played around with the chase element more, because the movie just goes a different route towards the end, and I expected more. The two leads were really great, and this had more potential.

Name: Patriot
Review:
Flaws aside, I can't help but appreciate the ambition here. Patriot is this large-scale genre film that's pretty much plot-driven rather than moment-driven. Given the star power on screen, there is a little amount of fan service peppered throughout, which even I expected out of this when Mammootty and Mohanlal are in a movie together. But this is pretty much a film driven by the narrative and the characters more than the stars.

The biggest star in this particular film for me is Sushin Shyam; the background score was so cool, and the score itself gives a sort of Bourne trilogy-ish energy to several scenes. The editing and the non-linearity were also good at times, but still, I think this could've been a shorter movie. The movie is too dragging at some parts and too rushing at others (look at me sounding like Fletcher from Whiplash). There's a lot of exposition and information being dumped on us; some of it is repeated and reemphasised, some of it is unnecessary, and I think maybe a better way at exposition might've benefited the movie. The fight scenes also had too many fast cuts and uneven choreography for my taste. Only the slow-mo aura farming in between made me feel something.

Also, the writing in Patriot seems somewhat stuck in between being plot driven and character driven. Like, there are so many great plot-driven thrillers where we don't know anything about the characters other than what we see them do in the particular situation that we're seeing them in. Patriot is like that at times, but then it also needs us to know about these characters' backgrounds. Daniel and Rahim's friendship is a central pillar of the film, but we don't even see enough of that, and every emotion we feel for that bond is mostly because they're Mammootty and Mohanlal. A central relationship in the movie is later revealed to be an extra marital affair, but idek what was even the point of that. The movie does suffer from characters who are just "there". The flashback given to Fahadh's villain also seemed pointless apart from having to see Fahadh with a Henry Cavill CGI shave.

The thing with super fast-paced thrillers where the protagonists are constantly on the run from enemies far more powerful than them, like the second and third Bourne movies, is how laser-focused and relentless they are. Patriot does lock in like that at times, and when that happens, it's great, but the lock ins are just not consistent. The whole techno conspiracy and privacy invasion angle was pretty interesting and relevant, remember the real Indian government trying to make it mandatory for every phone to have the Sanchaar Saathi app installed? The dissident vs the system chase was an interesting angle too, but there was some amount of filler and unnecessary detours that could've been avoided to make this lean and mean and more thrilling. The awkward dialogue at times don't help either. The social evaluation angle is just mentioned in a few lines of dialogue and then immediately dropped. If I felt any emotions watching this, it was mostly because of seeing Mohanlal and Mammootty on screen and not because of the writing, so I guess star power did overpower the plot in that context. Fahadh crashing out on a regular basis was also fun to watch. 

Anyway, I can't rate this too low because there were parts of it that I really enjoyed, even the little amount of fan service, and I appreciate what Mahesh Narayanan was trying to pull off here, despite the flaws. It's a movie named Patriot about people trying to save the country without any jingoism or Sangh propaganda included, which is not what's celebrated in Indian cinema right now. Plus the music was VERY cool.

Name: Eternity
Review:
It's great to see original concepts like this. The last time I saw a unique and original take on the afterlife was in The Good Place. But here there's no good or bad place; there's just "place," and every person gets one, even the terrible ones. The setup itself is worth exploring for so many types of stories and characters, but the afterlife itself is only the background here, with some jokes like the various worlds like the man-free world, capitalist world, and Marxist world appearing in the background; eternity, otherwise, remains focused on the central relationship between Joan and her two husbands, Luke and Larry.

Luke and Larry represent two different parts of Joan's life. Luke was the first love who died before she got to live her life with him properly, whereas Larry is the one with whom she did end up spending most of her life. And then in the afterlife, she's having to choose between the two of them. The movie is charming and funny; the love triangle situation is truly unique here, and the whole cast is delightful. I really loved the design and look of the afterlife, Elizabeth Olsen's costumes, and the background score too.

Name: Mortal Kombat
Review:
There was some cool action and fatalities, but this was your most generic-ass chosen one plotline thrown in with some Mortal Kombat references. Like the way the characters drop lines from the game don't even make sense here, but it's so fun.

Great cast though and Lewis Tan is a really cool martial artist, just that he got a bland character like Cole Young. I really love the Scorpion vs Sub Zero fight at the end. Perfect casting in terms of all the characters from the games, especially Sonya, Kano, Sub Zero, Scorpion (fucking Sanada, man), Kung Lao, Liu Kang, Raiden.. Everyone's memorable in some way and that says something.

Name: Mortal Kombat II
Review:
This one has the exact same director as the first movie but it feels like and entirely different movie. Because this time Jeremy Slater's script is treating it as a legit Mortal Kombat movie than as a generic action movie with some Mortal Kombat references in it. This thing fully embraces its video game origins in more ways than one, including recreating entire game mechanics and scene by scene recreations of the game's 2.5D camera angle. Mortal Kombat 2 is way more comfortable in being unserious, camp and just let the action, gore, jokes and references carry the movie.

Lewis Tan returns as Cole Young, but is barely in the movie. I get that they're addressing the audience complaints of Cole being a bland and uninteresting protagonist, and I get it, but him being so irrelevant despite the entire first movie revolving around him and his prophecy is still weird. Instead we get Kitana and Johnny Cage and they're both welcome additions. Karl Urban being called a cunt instead of calling someone a cunt was funny. So was his constant pop culture references and the way he was so unserious. Speaking of unserious, Kano is also back, and is a highlight of the movie. Death isn't permanent in the Mortal Kombat games and it's not permanent in this movie either. Kano and Johnny together was so fun to watch and I wish the movie had more of that.

Joe Taslim is back as sub-zero but he's just a glorified thug in this one after being the main villain in the last one. Also unlike the last one Joe Taslim doesn't really get action where he gets to be, yk, Joe Taslim, the badass martial artist. Instead in general most of the action in this film is very CGI heavy and over the top. It's more video game accurate of course, but I missed the more martial arts focused action from the first movie. It's not entirely devoid of it though, the Liu Kang vs Kung Lao fight was great in that regard, and the Johnny Cage vs Baraka fight was just so fun and hilarious to watch.

Anyway, I love it when campy movies embrace their campiness.

Name: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
Review:
I don't remember enough of the first movie, but it was the beginning of the "eat the rich - good for her" series of movies. This one picks up immediately after the first one ends, there's even a superhero movie suit up like buildup given to Samara Weaving's grace wearing that same bloody wedding dress once again. Just that this time we get two protagonists to root for, with Grace's sister Faith played by Kathryn Newton.

The setup is pretty much the same, we get a new reason for a group of new rich people to try to hunt and kill the two sisters. I don't mind formula as long as it's fun, and this movie is fun.. For the most part. It also tries to have this bonding arc between the sisters, they're estranged and don't really hate each other and throughout this traumatic experience of rich people trying to murder them, they try to work out their problems. But the thing is, they're having a lot of this pep talk and sibling arguments while they're actively being hunted, and it just doesn't make any sense and my mind kept saying "go somewhere private and safe to argue yo!". It felt like the sibling drama was pulling the movie down than making it an upgrade compared to the first film. Lots of plot conveniences happening towards the end too. But the ending was still fun though. Samara Weaving is still dependably great as Grace, it was also weird to see a doctor from the Pitt as a murderous psychopath. Kathryn Newton as Faith seemed a bit inconsistent performance wise or that could've been just the fact that her character itself was inconsistent in the writing.

Name: Primate
Review:
This is basically Cujo with a chimp, but it also feels like they were going for the movie seeming like an extended version of the Gordy's Home scene from Jordan Peele's Nope. But the thing is, that one scene from Nope is still far more effective in what it's trying to do than Primate is.

I do appreciate the practical effects in this movie, whether it's the very impressive practical gore effects or the chimp itself. But still, as impressive as the chimp suit and animatronics are, it still looks more like a person in a suit than like an ape. After seeing all these photorealistic CGI monkeys in films, going back to an actor in a suit does make him look like an actor in a suit. Gordy from Nope had this innocence to him, and we really do feel that sense of the animal abuse triggering him to go savage when he feels unsafe. Here, Ben the chimp is designed to look scary, even in the prior scenes where he's being friendly, and the rabies turns him into a slasher movie villain rather than an innocent animal having uncontrollable violence. It's not Cujo when the animal is like, so intelligent and calculated, like Robbie Williams as Michael Myers. 

There were some effectively thrilling sequences, though, and Ben is shown as a very dangerous threat. The kills are nasty too. But there were also multiple instances of the characters being too stupid under the circumstances. Multiple instances of accidentally turning loud shit on or making the absolute worst survival decisions (why do they stop and stare at the monkey after closing the glass door instead of running as soon as possible?!). I was holding my breath through the scenes where Troy Kotsur returns to the house, not because of the movie or its writing, but simply because it's Troy Kotsur playing the character. There could've been more of him in the movie, though. That one scene where his deafness makes him unaware of what's going on was thrilling. A deaf protagonist facing a killer is something Mike Flanagan's Hush had already covered, but it'd have been interesting to watch more of when the threat here is a murder monkey.

Anyway, as much fun as I had watching this, the Gordy's Home scene from Nope still mogs this, and Robbie Williams killed way more in Better Man than this monkey did.

Name: Athiradi
Review:
Athiradi is a basic ego-clash template movie that had enough fun, payoffs and competent cinematic moments that kept me entertained. The humour is pretty reference-heavy for the most part; whether it's movie references or social media references, some of the jokes fell flat while some did make me laugh. For every miss, something did come up that kept me from being pulled down completely.
