As likeable as Basil Joseph is, and he does have this natural innocence about him that makes us root and sympathise for him, I couldn't help but feel that he was miscast as the college student Samkutty in this movie. Basil clearly took an effort to lose weight to seem younger here, but he still seems like a man in his 30s or at least late 20s. But the funny thing is, most of the college kids, except Samkutty and his friend Parasu, played by Shelvin, do seem like Gen Z kids, and these two grown-ass men stand out among them like Ikka from Johnny Walker. Samkutty's love interest is played by Riya Shibu, another actual Gen Z actor who seems clearly Gen Z, and I couldn't buy for one second that these two belong to the same generation. The whole romance arc falls apart because of this; the writing doesn't help either, but also, maybe a Naslen or Sandeep type as Samkutty might've been better. Because even when I start forgetting about Samkutty seeming older than everyone, another Samkutty and Swathy scene will popup as a reminder.

Tovino Thomas as Kuttan was really great, though; he was the right mix of funny and intimidating, and the buildup given to him was also great, though I expected more from the David and Goliath setup of the conflict between these two than what eventually goes down in the second half. Vineeth Sreenivasan and Shaan Rahman were also surprisingly fun. The performances from the cast were a mixed bag on the whole. There were multiple cameos too, among which a particular one made the theatre go crazy and was worth the hype, while another cameo was there for an unfunny joke that already played out in a far worse movie before.

The emotional stakes given to the whole college fest didn't make sense to me, while Kuttan's arc involving a failed attempt at being a better person kinda did. But despite all the flaws in writing, this movie did keep me entertained. It was funny enough; I'm perpetually online enough to get the social media humour, though, like I said above, when more movies start to rely on references for their humour, they end up recycling the same source material and seem the same. How many interview star jokes, Azhukka Chekkan jokes, Chennai jokes and Devji jokes are too many? The conflict is simple, but the buildup was good; the movie is pretty competently made, and the large scale is definitely felt. Though it could've been a shorter film, parts of it felt stretched out. Towards the end, Vishnu Vijay's music does the heavy lifting. The music on the whole was great and really complements the movie. That theme music given to Kuttan was badass. 

Anyways, I had a pretty good time, maybe the audience being so active helped, and as someone nearing 30, seeing dudes older than me as college students makes me feel younger. 🥰 

That Alpenliebe line made me laugh way more than it should've.

Name: Karuppu
Review:
I'm the kind of atheist who enjoys a good divine movie as long as it's not glorifying the wrong idea of divinity. I've loved OMG back when I saw it, and it was a simpler time when Akshay Kumar wasn't a bigot bootlicker and Paresh Rawal wasn't a visible bigot too. OMG had this unique idea where instead of God doing divine stuff to magically solve everything, he just assists the protagonist in getting justice through the legal system. Karuppu is also set around a particular court and legal system. Karuppu Saamy is not a deity who belongs to the Brahmin concept of what god is supposed to be; he smokes cigars and enjoys eating mutton legs, which sets Karuppu apart from Hindutva divine movies (looking at you, Akhanda). But Karuppu alternates between being a serious Saamy padam and an unserious Saamy padam, and sometimes it wants to give Hari movie fight scenes to Suriya. There are several good ideas scattered throughout, but they're not really fully realised.

The film focuses more on the villain, Baby Kannan, played by RJ Balaji, and how he tries to scheme his way out of being in conflict with a literal god. So the initial setup, though a bit dumb, is interesting, where God must actually fight from within the system to defeat this sleazebag instead of relying on his supernatural, divine powers. But it's dumb because in this stretch of the movie we feel like God is listening to the wishes of the villain more than the devotee who actually summoned him. This was a setup that was adjacent to OMG, but it doesn't stay there for too long. Then it becomes a more traditional Saamy Padam, with RJ Balaji writing himself a scene that's a remake of a very popular Jim Carrey scene, but it was kinda fun to watch. The back and forth between the god and the villain becomes pretty one-sided after a point, and even when the bad guy eventually finds a loophole to strike back at the god with, the conflicts and challenges are simply resolved with "God does God things". That kind of makes it narratively boring, apart from seeing divine aura farming from Suriya and hearing some amazing tracks from Sai.

Sai Abhyankkar is the MVP of this movie, and he consistently uplifts this movie, even when the sound mix is a bit awkward at times. He gives both an unserious song like "god mode" for the god, a mass hero song like Verappa and a legit folk Tamil-style song like Karuppa Koode Vaa. So this is not an Oorum Blood situation where alternate versions of the same theme music are used; here all three Karuppu themes are alternatively used based on which one we want to see on screen. Do we want fun aura farming? Do we want the mass hero? Or do we want the god? Even as the movie ended, the thing that stuck with me the most was the soundtrack, especially Karuppa Koode Vaa, that was out of syllabus isai from Sai. Went so hard. 

Suriya is the kind of actor who'd give his all to a role no matter how mid or awful it is. Like, he cared more about Kanguva than Siva himself did; that's Suriya. Here too he does his best with the material given, seeming all kinds of divine, charming and badass. Even that trance scene towards the end was really well done by him; it's just that RJ Balaji throws all kinds of VFX and stuff instead of letting us see more of the performance, which is a problem Rishabh Shetty didn't have when he himself did the similar performance in Kantara, but at least RJ Balaji lets the camera capture everything when he himself is doing the performing as Baby Kannan xD.

Credit where it's due, Balaji does show some competent commercial filmmaking flair at times. Suriya is presented really well and looks amazing throughout the movie, which is not that hard to do, but Siva fucked even that up, so... The film follows the Shankar film pattern of a large stretch of social injustice being shown to us for the hero (in this case, god) to then swoop down and fix everything. The song 'God Mode' was shot really well; it looked appropriately grand. Some of the fight scenes were also cool at times, except for when they involved that bright red CGI stuff. And of course, like most star movies these days, there are a lot of references to the other movies the star has done. And I'm not just talking about Suriya here; all of RJ Balaji's directorial movies are referenced here. A lot of the references were fun ngl, including the chocolate coffee, but everyone who watched that particular movie knows that the character did something terrible even before he entered that cafe, so is making him a peaceful person just in the cafe really forgiving him of his past sins? The whole mind-control-to-reduce-crime logic is very flawed if we choose to think about it. 

Sometimes, watching Karuppu does feel like Balaji wrote it initially with Baby Kannan, the bad guy that he plays as the main character. During the initial stretches especially, we're just waiting for Karuppu to pop up, with these long stretches of Baby Kannan conning innocent people being shown. Like even in that case, a bad human outsmarting a god and the god trying to fix the system instead of just killing or beating up this one bad guy is good as an idea; it could've been done as an OMG-adjacent kind of story, but sadly Balaji doesn't commit to it. So the movie just feels like ideas and disconnected scenes barely being held together with Suriya and Sai Abhyankkar in God Mode.

The heart is for iSai arakkan. You go kid!

Name: Oru Durooha Saahacharyathil
Review:
Can this even be judged as a single movie when the production issues and the fact that the director didn't have full creative control are so well known?

So it's basically one movie till the third act and becomes something entirely different towards the end. Sajin Gopu has the widest and sweetest smile when he dances and it's so wholesome to watch.

Name: Drishyam 3
Review:
Arranged marriages are scary... What if...

The first Drishyam hasn't aged that well in big 2026 in terms of the acting and the melodrama during its initial hour, but the whole murder cover-up angle and the way someone with just cinema knowledge cooks up a fake alibi and confuses the hell out of the police are still great. There's also the big reveal at the end, but the first Drishyam held on its own and was thrilling while building up to that point too; it's still a great crime drama plot. Then Drishyam 2 happened, which did have interesting ideas for a follow-up, but it felt like such a downgrade, and for many people, including me, it was a nothingburger except for the twist, which didn't make much sense, but at least the movie acknowledged that it's mostly luck. Georgekutty having to carry this burden and live his life in fear as a kind of penance was also a nice ending. So when Drishyam 3 was announced, I wasn't really excited to see what would happen if Varun Prabhakar's spiritual corpse was dug up again, but yeah, it was.

I can't talk about this movie without talking spoilers. Firstly, was the two years' worth of scheming by Prabhakar really to bribe four marriage brokers to get Georgekutty's daughter arranged married to that one specific dude? In big 2026? It's one of the stupidest evil plans ever, bro. 😭 It depends on too many variables, including the fact that Ancy won't find a partner for herself, would like this guy enough to get married to him and that Georgekutty and family won't rely on online matrimony for marriage proposals. Like, everything else in the movie felt silly just by the fact that this evil plan is so silly. This is the big weapon in the Prabhakar-Sahadevan gang's hand, while most of the movie is spent on them investigating Georgekutty's cover-up just as a distraction. I mean… The previous two Drishyams at least didn't feel THIS silly.

Sahadevan's back as an antagonist this time, with the most red I've seen a Malayalam actor's eyes being since Saniya Iyyappan's stoner face in Lucifer. This works as an idea, like at first they couldn't incriminate Georgekutty because they had no real evidence against him, and the second time, Georgekutty used legal loopholes to escape conviction, so the next time they're really being flexible with their own morality to trap Georgekutty and family. But the way that's been executed was just too silly and unserious here. Sahadevan's daughter and Sahadevan work their asses off to incriminate Georgekutty, but none of that even matters because the real plan is the matrimonial frame-up.

The interactions between Georgekutty and family were always the parts of the Drishyam movies that I enjoyed the least. In this one too, the family scenes seem so artificial, writing-wise and performance-wise. That whole pattern of "Georgekutty or Rani would say something boomer; younger daughter materialises from thin air to say something progressive or new-gen" was so rinse and repeat. I'm not going to be too woke police on Georgekutty and family seeming like an average rural conservative family, but it's tough to buy them as a real family when everything about them seems so artificial; every interaction feels so staged. They even use one of the family scenes as a full-on ad for Kalyan Jewellers; it reminded me of that scene from The Truman Show. The family have clearly designated jobs; Rani is there to be nagging and then get shouted at by Georgekutty, Anu is there to be the "modern kutty" stereotype, and Anju is there to be a trauma placeholder. Three movies in and this is still all we know about these women in Georgekutty's life, apart from them being someone Georgekutty needs to protect. They don't have much active involvement in the narrative, and Jeethu Joseph still refuses to acknowledge the whole "women's honour/purity" morality aspect from the first part.

As to be expected in Jeethu Joseph movies, the filmmaking and dialogues are so megaserial core, and most of the supporting performances are too. There were multiple instances of Veena Nandakumar carrying a bucket while looking evil, and it made me laugh every time. Which rural Mallu family says "saadhikkukayilla" and all to each other? I have no idea. Murali Gopi was surprisingly good in this movie, and he was pretty much always saying exactly what an audience member might be thinking, always having the right and practical take. He was the most logical and level-headed character here, and the performance too made sense, except for that speech on politics influencing the police, which again, has nothing to do with the movie. Joke's on Akshaye Khanna for ditching the best character in Drishyam 3 to ride the Dhurandhar wave, though.

The last two movies had these scenes that looked like throwaway scenes that ended up being important to Georgekutty's plan. Here, a lot of those scenes are just indeed unnecessary scenes that make us think they might somehow add to the story, but no, they're just there. The writing is all over the place in this movie and so random. I don't think this'd survive a rewatch after knowing all the twists and reveals the way the first Drishyam had. What was even the point of Georgekutty producing a 100Cr club blockbuster movie, then that movie getting leaked online, and then the director coming to talk about his next movie with FaFaa and all? Maybe it was just Jeethu Joseph flexing to the audience that he made a movie named Drishyam once that was the highest-grossing movie in Malayalam at the time? What else was the point, bro?

Georgekutty's arc involving him having to live with this crime and his instinct to protect his family at all costs – that's been the running theme of these movies, and that's carried over here too. His whole character arc culminating in him surrendering while also acknowledging that he did hurt people while trying to protect his own was the only good thing I felt here. Of course Mohanlal does a great job; he's pretty much the only actor in the lead cast who fits naturally into his character even when he too gets to deliver bad lines. But even then, I felt like towards the end, when Jeethu Joseph had that pressure to deliver the twist moment, Georgekutty stopped being Georgekutty and became Shanmughan from Thudarum, beating Sahadevan up, screaming threats. Like, yeah, I get it; he's been pushed to his limits, and everyone wanted to see Sahadevan getting beaten up by Georgekutty when they saw the first one, but still, Georgekutty was always about his brains, so this just seemed off to me. Sahadevan is reduced to a goofy thug squirming at Georgekutty's violence, which was a goofy scene that made the entire theatre laugh as well; the crowd chasing him away in the first movie was a way better ending for him, and it also didn't goof up his character like this. Also, Georgekutty tragically beating up his own daughter to frame evidence? Why didn't he just explain the situation to her and then work together to do the framing? That was such an avoidable trauma for both him and the daughter. 😭 Ansiba's performance during this scene wasn't helping either. That plus the way it was shot and the absolute overkill on the violence Georgekutty is inflicting on her made that moment look unintentionally funny.

Like, even when reevaluating everything about this movie, that stupid plan from Prabhakar still sticks out like it belongs in a comedy movie. Also, Siddique's performance when Prabhakar reveals himself to be malicious was also comically goofy. Whatever kind of detailing and practical writing this film had, like addressing the logical loopholes and issues within the last two movies and this one itself when characters talk, is lost because of the stupid evil matrimonial arranged marriage plan. Anju should've tried dating instead.

AND OF COURSE THIS ENDS WITH A SEQUEL BAIT CLIFFHANGER BECAUSE THIS IS JEETHU JOSEPH'S CASH COW.

Also did you know that there's a Kalyan Jewellers in Thodupuzha?

Name: They Will Kill You
Review:
As a burnt-out person looking for something to just distract my mind with, this was the perfect watch. The premise involving a woman being trapped with a satanic cult of rich people who are trying to kill her is very similar to Ready or Not, but this is not following the same horror comedy formula. This is instead more of a full-on, over-the-top action comedy with very tastefully done retro B-movie elements. The gore, the visual effects, the cinematography, the editing, and the music all have this very cool B movie energy; they even make the CGI elements seem like the stop motion visual effects from the analog days. The action is over-the-top gory, but it's gore that's meant to be silly rather than disturbing; Zazie Beetz looks like a total badass during them, and it's very well choreographed and shot.

This is the kind of movie that cares more about its setpieces and gags than the narrative or characters. So the writing is pretty loose and just quickly sets up the stage for the mayhem. So it's not the most original movie writing-wise, but it's a whole lot of fun. I could just sit back and have fun watching those cool fight scenes. The director Kirill Sokolov definitely knows how to do gory, over-the-top B movie action really well.

Name: Faces of Death
Review:
I was watching the 2026 Faces of Death, an okayish modern slasher, and then this movie was directly referenced in it. Then I had this urge to watch this one for context, which is a chore I shouldn't have committed to. It took me a week to sit through this. This thing is framed like a documentary about different kinds of death, but it has scripted death scenes that they filmed for this movie too. But the thing is the scripted violence is spliced up in between footage of actual death and gore, so it's hard to pick out which is a real corpse and which is just latex and jelly at times. Some of the scenes, like the monkey brain and the paranormal investigation, were easier to recognise as staged scenes, while the existence of real deaths and corpses disturbed me whenever that popped up on screen (if they even were real, of course). I can do fake movie violence, but watching real death, real gore and real blood on screen is something I'd never do for entertainment.

I guess in that way this movie did succeed in confusing people and blurring that line between reality and fiction. But what was even the point? It's just using the deaths and misery for shock value, and also this movie is evidently racist at times too.

Name: Faces of Death
Review:
I regret watching the 1978 movie first to get more context on this conventional slasher movie because I hated it, and it was completely unnecessary. Well, kind of. The original Faces of Death was controversial in its confusing mix of real and fake footage of death scenes. Which is kind of the core theme of this film too. A real serial killer films his real death scenes as if they're stylised horror scenes that are low-budget remakes of the scenes from the original Faces of Death and posts them on social media. The protagonist Margot feels like the deaths in the videos are real but has a hard time making anyone believe her.

The film alternates between being a generic slasher movie and being this satire about how in the age of social media, even murder will be memed, and the tech corporations who thrive on engagement would have no issue as long as the content passes certain criteria. The killer, in his own words, exploits the "attention economy" and gets off on the validation that he gets, and people would post joke comments no matter how serious the content is. While the protagonist is almost comically incompetent in getting him exposed. The movie does suffer from "people making the stupidest possible choices in tense situations to build more tension" syndrome, but some of it's to be expected and realistic. The killer here is a white man, and in America's history there are multiple psychotic white male serial killers who operated for years without getting caught whom the cops didn't take seriously.

It's a pretty okay slasher movie. With its whole satirical vibe and the obvious movie connection, it did remind me of the Scream movies a bit, and this movie felt like more of a Scream movie than the newest Scream movie. Dacre Montgomery was great as the bad guy as well. 

Charli XCX randomly appears as Margot's co-worker in a role that definitely didn't need Charli XCX.

Name: Over Your Dead Body
Review:
I haven't seen the original, so I'm going to judge just the remake here. This was a fun watch for the most part, with some great performances from the whole cast and some great instances of dark humor and gory action. I didn't expect this movie to go this all out on the gore and violence, but it does and it's pretty fun and tasteful about it. Samara Weaving being stuck in fucked up violent scenarios is one of my favorite genres at this point. Despite being a comedy, the action is pretty brutal and relentless. The movie's just a continuous action sequence after a point anyway. I also liked the whole flashback plot device whenever there's a new reveal. Lots of Chekhov's guns in this movie too. The initial fucked up relationship dynamic murder plan plotline was more interesting than the home invasion thriller this later becomes though, but it still remained fun, except for one moment. 

But while talking about being tasteful with the dark humor, there is a confusing instance in the movie where there’s an attempted sexual assault against a male character. I'm not sure if the way that sequence plays out was sensitive. It felt similar to instances in Pulp Fiction and even recently in The Boys where men being sexually assaulted is played for laughs. I'm conflicted about the dark humor in that particular scene.

Name: Hokum
Review:
Ngl, Adam Scott's character Ohm is such a dickhead in the opening section of this movie that I was rooting for something terrible to happen to him. But yeah, the film is atmospheric horror done right for the most part with some solid jump scares and build-ups. There's also the added psychological element which keeps the extent of the supernatural that we see on screen ambiguous. The whole setup did remind me of Twin Peaks at times, but without the sense of humour and goofiness, of course. The pacing felt off at times, though, like there were some jarring transitions, and sometimes favouring shocks over story can feel a bit confusing.

But yeah, this is a pretty effective horror movie with its own unique sense of identity. I need to check out Damien McCarthy's Oddity too, which has been sitting on my watchlist for a long time.

Name: undertone
Review:
This movie has some of the best sound design that I've heard in a horror movie, so I urge anyone who'd want to watch Undertone to use headphones or a surround sound speaker setup. I was curious how a film like this where the protagonist is sitting in a room and doing a podcast for a lot of the runtime would be visually interesting as a film, but both visually and in terms of sound, Undertone finds so many ways to be scary and creepy. I was watching the movie alone at night, and I was positively creeped out by the end.

There are only two visible characters in this film: the protagonist Evy and her bedridden mother, who we never see in a conscious state. Evy does a podcast where they discuss supernatural phenomena, where she's the sceptic and her friend Justin is the believer. When they start to play some audio files they received as an anonymous email during the podcast, things start to get weird for Evy. It's here that the film gets creative with the way it uses sound and the space that the film is set in. The camera never leaves Evy's house and lingers and pans through it constantly. The house is really well established to the viewer, and this is important when things start to go wrong. Sound-wise too, the ambient sound in the house is muffled when Evy puts on her noise-cancelling headphones, and once the audios start playing, both Evy and we as the viewers are unsure where the noises are coming from. The soundscape of this movie is pretty incredible.

Evy's struggles as the sole carer for a dying parent and the weird supernatural events are happening in parallel and affecting her psychologically; that's visually conveyed by the film too. With a setting and narrative that's so confined, this film still manages to be visually so rich. It ends with this long single shot that has some of the most memorable horror filmmaking I've seen lately. Ian Tuason really impressed me and I didn't even care about the logical issues and plotholes. Definitely creeped me out.

Name: Mother Mary
Review:
I didn't understand some of the very complicated dialogue, mostly spoken by Michaela Coel's character in this movie, and I'm glad I parallel-watched this movie with my much cooler friend because that's how I got some sense of the overall metaphor here too. Towards the middle point, after spending a significant amount of time showing two people talking in a single location, the movie just unleashes its surreal energy. It's amazing to look at too, with great cinematography and editing, and some of the sexiest scene transitions I've seen. Anne Hathaway and Michaela Coel were amazing, with Hathaway really doing justice to the goddess energy pop star she's playing. The surrealism had this David Lynch energy to it, and my cooler friend again pointed out how David Lowery and David Lynch even have the same initials. Close enough. Welcome back, David Lynch.

At its core, this is a breakup movie and how the pain of a separation affects the two people involved in different ways and how they process it. Just that the processing involves a blood cloth ghost, which I won't elaborate on. David Lowery said that Mother Mary was inspired by Taylor Swift, but most of her songs are about men and she's engaged to Travis Kelce, while there isn't a single male character in Mother Mary and not even the existence of a single man is mentioned. I'd argue that Mother Mary is cooler.

With no male characters and no mentions of men, this might be one of the movies with the highest Bechdel test scores.

Name: Kara
Review:
Kara has got the familiar Tamil commercial movie formula of a corporate bank being the villains who prey upon innocent farmers and trap them in debt. The protagonist Karasaamy, played by Dhanush, is a former thief who turns into a robber who targets just this specific bank for his personal reasons. Kara was a bit different from the usual formula of such films because Karasaamy faces so many failures and setbacks. He's not like the cool hero who'd always have an upper hand on the bad guys. He's shown as an ordinary person facing a system way bigger than him under unpredictable circumstances. 

So the middle portion of the movie, once the heist is set into motion, was interesting because the movie wasn't playing by star movie logic, and the stakes being built up really makes us root for Kara to get a win. But then the ending is just all kinds of messy. Clearly they set up impossible odds against Karasaamy and then set up a new, bigger motive for him just 20 minutes before the movie ends. It's at this point that Kara stops being grounded and thrilling, and it transitions into a star movie, with slow-motion walks, cool-sounding theme music, instant payoffs that don't feel earned, the whole deal. I'd have loved this movie if the final payoff didn't feel this easy after the whole buildup.

Also, the movie is tonally all over the place; idk why some parts of it were silly in a way that undercuts the seriousness of everything else. Dhanush has long been praised as having the kind of face that'd let him play any age, but no, bro, he and Mamitha weren't believable as a couple who don't have two decades in between them at all. Mamitha is made to play a token wife character who just stays in the background; sadly, she got more to do in Meesho Dhanush's movie than Original Dhanush's movie. Suraj Venjarmmoodu as the cop, Jayaram as the evil bank manager and Abu Salim as a goon round out the very Mallu cast of this Tamil movie. The performances, characters and the tone of the movie felt very inconsistent, including Dhanush himself.

Anyway, there is a middle part of the movie where it did draw me in and kept me invested, but the ending was too nonsensical and silly for my taste.

Name: Mollywood Times
Review:
I have to talk about my biggest issue with this movie first, which is that it's pretty casteist.

So to make the point of "mediocrity is always celebrated over greatness" in Mollywood Times, the mediocrity comes from a filmmaker belonging to a marginalized caste who writes a script that has his underprivileged perspective in it, and Mollywood is this fictional place where an underprivileged filmmaker's mediocre film will be celebrated and given awards just because of his caste background. "The privilege of being underprivileged" is an actual line of dialogue that this character in the film says to refer to the fact that reservation gives him opportunities. This is the kind of perspective that'd rather blame reservation for giving "unfair advantages" to the underprivileged than address why reservation exists in the first place. It doesn't talk about how unfair the caste system itself or savarna privilege is; it would rather show the underprivileged character be ashamed of his identity than hold a mirror to the society that shames him.

Which Mollywood is this film actually talking about? Can the director himself name any mainstream filmmakers from marginalized communities in Malayalam who make superhit acclaimed films from an underprivileged perspective, mediocre or not? Indian cinema doesn't even have the kind of token representation and diversity that liberal Hollywood does and is predominantly savarna male-dominated, avide aanu underprivileged aaya privileginte kindi.. The said mediocrity had to specifically come from the character belonging to the marginalized caste and not from someone privileged or from a nepo background, which was pretty sus. This comes off like the Savarna casteist who says, "Reservation is bad and unfair bro" being fused with the cinebro who says, "Cinema is too woke, bro". The film directly refers to this character's marginalized identity only once; at other times it's referred to as his "background" that gives him special treatment and unfair advantages even in cinema.

Casteism aside too, this film falls into the mediocre category rather than the greatness category. With Mukundan Unni Associates (a movie that I loved), a main part of following a narcissistic asshole anti-hero through it was that the film didn't expect us to like this person. There weren't any attempts to justify his actions, and he was just being unapologetically evil and selfish for his own success. That movie being generally unserious in its tone also helped, but this one expects us to take it seriously at times too. Here, the protagonist Vineeth Madhavan is designed to be likeable and sympathetic, and there are attempts to justify his actions and to explain his side of things, but the thing is, he's also an unlikeable narcissistic asshole like Mukundan Unni, and just by the fact that he's being played by Naslen, who has an innate innocence to him, is not enough. 

Even the worst thing the protagonist does in the film is justified using a sentimental speech about the writer/director having sole ownership over a film and that they can do whatever they want with it. I hope the director doesn't actually feel this way about his films, because it's very disrespectful towards everyone else that works in that film, big time. It's pretty much self-sabotage instead of any "struggle" there, and the "villain" he fucks over has every right to be bitter about it. How can we root for an unprofessional filmmaker who only cares about himself, makes wrong decisions, then justifies it as artistic integrity and then blames everyone but himself for his fuck-ups? Athinte koode reservation konayadi vere. I just felt like saying the same "Oombu Myre" to him that Arjun Hariharan did.

The oombithettal dialogue from Mukundan Unni was a big hit, so the humor in this film, which got the most laughs from the theater, mostly consisted of reactions to hearing Malayalam swear words like oomb, myru which we don't usually hear in our movies. The censor board muted all English swear words but kept all the Malayalam ones, which was weird. Maybe this was censored by non-Malayalis? I'm not against films having swear words in the dialogue at all; in fact, I actually encourage more of such films. Aavesham would've benefited from Bibi saying 'myru' instead of 'malaru'. Just that, were the laughs because those scenes were funny or because we rarely hear these words being used like this in a comedy? I laughed too, so I really can't judge.

The world and the characters also seemed pretty fake and distant. We're seeing a struggling filmmaker who doesn't have to care about any money or financial struggles at any point, which is okay; his parents might have enough money to fund his cinema pursuits, Aavo. He doesn't even have to convince producers or pitch his projects, producers just seek him out and every script he writes is a potential brilliant sureshot blockbuster to everyone. And then the portrayal of Mollywood seems very Smalliwood, with very few people involved and everything seeming small. The snippets and names of Vineeth Madhavan's films don't scream the "greatness" that the film constantly hypes up. But suspension of disbelief, I guess. That first low-budget short he does as a teenager was cute though, but the rest that are hailed as masterpieces? Idk. The more I think about this movie, the more obvious the several plotholes and inconsistencies are. 

The film is set from the late 2000s to the early 2010s, and yet there are lots of AI images. The attention to detail in the retro era to show the old film posters, handycam footage, DTS logo, and all didn't extend to showing film posters and photos that fit the era, and the movie just got lazy with it by using AI slop. Some AI-generated clips are shown during the flashback at the beginning too. The AI poster for "Manushyan" looked like the kind of thing no mainstream movie would ever use. A movie that preaches about the purity of art, originality of art, the pain of an artist's creativity being stolen and the greatness of true artistic expression using AI slop is so ironic, bro.

Most of the time the characters just spoke like one-dimensional mouthpieces for the creator to make his points and disses towards people in the industry, with dialogue that just sounds weird and overdramatic at times. Among which the lines given to the underprivileged character were the worst; maybe the creator shouldn't have been THAT honest about how he feels about reservation and filmmakers from an underprivileged background. The second half was a tiring watch that felt repetitive.

Naslen was great and does carry the film well, but not enough to actually redeem the bad characterization; I liked Roshan as well. There are parts of this movie that I did enjoy; the music by Jakes Bejoy was nice, and I liked the aesthetics and style at times whenever AI slop wasn't involved, but yeah, on the whole it's still MEDIOCRE, even if I set aside the casteism. Still not giving it the lowest rating because of the parts I did enjoy. 'Please don't be this honest with your thoughts' is what I want to convey to the creator of this thing. 🙏🏽

Name: Normal
Review:
The long buildup in the beginning is very fun; it's not the kind of thing where we impatiently wait for it to finally be an action movie. The characters, the town and the weirdness the protagonist notices in the town are all interesting on their own. Bob Odenkirk is dependably likeable as the lead, and once the bullets do start flying and the bodies start to drop, there is some great dark humour and action, with some hilarious accidental deaths too. Some are very Looney Tunes coded, but with blood and gore, of course, it's some great dark slapstick humour. And this movie might quantitatively have the most amount of literal Chekhov's Guns.

The finale felt like the movie was already over and they just needed something to go wrong for a big action scene at the end, but nevertheless, it was also very chaotic, brutal and funny. The action-comedy mix was really great throughout the movie, with the right amount of balance between being grounded and being silly. It never gets too dark despite having so much death, blood and gore.

Name: Blast
Review:
Blast is like a mashup of the Shankar vigilante format with the Lokesh Kanagaraj Kaithi format, but instead of being a male savior movie, here the women kick ass too and are placed as equals with the men. Arjun is the male lead and does get the bigger intro than the two leading ladies, but when it comes to the action sequences and the way the movie plays out, unlike what we usually see in Indian movies where women do get to do action, this movie clearly places both Preity Mukundan and Abhirami as equals to Arjun's character. Preity's character in particular gets more badass moments than all three leads. Some of Arjun's preachy woke dad dialogues and the way the scenes were staged reminded me of other movies where men do such preaching, like Atlee's Bigil a bit, though xD (Abhirami says something a conservative mom would say, and Arjun would say something woke; repeat). 

This could've been a leaner movie, though. So much time is spent setting up the pieces, establishing several characters, elements, and the villains. Heaps and heaps of exposition are thrown at us, and then the same information is repeated again and again. When the village is mentioned again towards the end and then an emotional song comes out of nowhere, I almost laughed because it was so unnecessary and out of place. Which is why I mentioned Kaithi at the start. Most of the main events of this movie do take place over the course of a single night like Kaithi, but Kaithi established everything very fast right at the beginning, and by the time Dilli pops up, the plot is already in motion and the chase begins. Blast would've benefitted so much from the pacing being similar to that.

I did have a lot of fun watching this, though. I watched this while I was going through a bit of a hard time personally (TMI alert), so this was the perfect distraction to take my mind off. There were lots of well-choreographed, well-shot, and well-performed action scenes; the leads seemed every bit like the badasses they were supposed to be. Preity Mukundan surprised me the most out of all of them. How many such potential badass characters are we missing out on seeing just because women are accessories to the men in Indian action movies most of the time? There are some genuinely cheerworthy moments in this movie, where the cheers are purely out of the cinematic buildup and payoff instead of a star or stardom. Other than having Arjun's iconic "therikke," there aren't even any references to past roles here; everything is purely character-focused.

But still, after spending so much time building up the villains to be so ruthless, cruel, and powerful, and just making us anticipate the hell out of them eventually getting beaten up, the payoff felt a bit easy. It was satisfying, of course, but still felt like everything got over so fast. Setting up the protagonists to be a normal family and then making them seem pretty chill about committing murder was also like video game logic at play. But at least one of the characters is shown to be hesitant towards murder, so at least it's somewhat addressed.

Ravi Barsur's music was too loud and over the top at times; the heavy metal screaming noises' theme music given to the main villain became comical after a point. But on the whole this was a fun time where the kind of "man saves women and the society" formula familiar to Tamil cinema is turned into "man and women save themselves and the society."

Name: Obsession
Review: They who have mastered silence have mastered cinema. I was putting off watching this one in the cinemas despite the hype and peer pressure, since I was aware that the version running in Indian theaters has been censored by the fuckass Indian censor board whose only job is ruining good cinema and supporting Sangh propaganda slop. Obsession has some of the best uses of silence I've seen recently in cinema. Curry Barker doesn't use silence just for creating tension and eeriness; it starts from the very beginning. Every conversational scene is so well written and well made; the pauses and the awkward silences carry a lot of meaning. When we finally get to see the main characters Nicky and Bear together on their own in the car, we can get a feel of their dynamic even without seeing their whole life played out. The way one person talks over another, the awkward silences, the chemistry, or the lack of any chemistry; it's all laid out to us even without directly saying it to us. It's the choices like these that elevate this from just being a horror movie. Then the wish happens, and things start to get weird. During the darker and creepier moments too, Barker uses the silences and pauses really well to elevate the horror and discomfort of the situation. That there, takes skill. Almost the entire film is told through Bear's perspective; he's there in every scene, and we're experiencing everything through Bear's eyes, and yet he's the villain here. This could've easily been a guy movie where it's just about a wish gone wrong that torments the poor guy who just wanted love. But no, in several points in the film, Curry Barker clearly lays out that Nikki is the real victim here and that Bear is essentially holding her hostage inside her own body and just using her body without her consent. The wish itself can be given the pass that he thought the willow was just a stupid toy and just said something he wished for. But everything after that is what makes him the bad guy. If he really wanted the real Nikki to love him, he'd not have gone with it when she was clearly not being herself. He gets enough signs of that fact, and his friends even spell it out to him, and he still stays in this "relationship" with her and essentially sexually assaults her. This is further reinforced when the real Nikki occasionally peeps through the body and is horrified every single time. Even when she does get the chance to communicate with Bear, and this is at a point where it's obvious to Bear that his wish is the only reason for Nikki acting this way and that the real Nikki had friendzoned him, she begs him to kill her to free herself from this torment, and his response still reeks with entitlement; he asks, "What's so bad about being with me?" to which she replies, "I was never with you." It's this exploration of interpersonal dynamics and the male entitlement of a "nice guy" that elevates Obsession from just being a supernatural horror movie. The horror feels real and human here; the supernatural twist, the one wish willow, is only a conduit that unlocks the darkness within Bear. The way Nikki's manufactured obsession with Bear escalates to bloody and gory proportions is also done so well. Nikki is shown as being in the darkness or with her face cut off in multiple shots right from the start, post-wish. Even when the time we spend with the real Nikki is brief, the transformation is very obvious, also thanks to Inde Naverette's star-making, show-stealing performance, of course. There are multiple layers to the character than just being weird, creepy, and terrifying after the transformation happens. Of course that's there, and she does that brilliantly, whether it's the smaller off-putting behavior or the way weirder ones and the whole absurd body language; that feeling of a person not really acting like a person is being conveyed really well. And whenever the real Nikki does take control or we see her struggling from inside this body at one point, it's both sad and disturbing at the same time. Michael Johnston as Bear, too, plays the character as the shy rom-com nice guy at the start, and even after the wish, he's not very evidently acting like a villain but more like a victim. But despite being the POV character, this is the kind of movie that makes us follow around the bad guy and see him just be passively evil and abusive. Like, rarely do I watch a film where I want the protagonist to kill himself so bad when they finally reveal how the wish can be canceled. Bear was essentially lying to himself too that this is a real relationship, so locking us into his POV really sells that. The horror setpieces are brilliantly done here, even the jumpscares are. There aren't many jumpscares in this movie, but the ones that are in the movie are brilliant. There's one where Bear and Sarah are talking inside a car; the whole scene is blocked in a way that every shot shows a car window behind Bear and Sarah, with enough space behind each of them for Nikki to pop in anytime. So we're anticipating a Nikki jumpscare from the very beginning, and at the same time the conversation itself is interesting, and it's not just filler till the jumpscare happens, and even when I expected the jump from the very beginning, I jumped when it happened. But fuck the Indian censor board for trimming what happens afterwards, of course. The way the atmosphere is built up is masterful as Bear's grandma's house becomes progressively darker as an environment. The movie still finds some dark humour in between too in moments that are fucked up and funny at the same time. The pacing of this movie was just perfect. The weirdness just creeps up, and every weird encounter between Obsessed Nikki and Bear is written, filmed, and performed brilliantly. Like I said, what makes it scarier is that there are no ghosts or monsters; there's just a person acting not quite like a person. It's just the supernatural being a conduit for even the nice guy having sinister intentions masked as love. This movie even has the most uncomfortable romance montage I've ever seen, though it plays it completely straight like it's a real romantic montage; Curry Barker even uses an AI couple photo during this montage to further show us that the "romance" we're seeing is artificial. Obsession did remind me of last year's Companion a bit, but there the main character, Iris, was a robot manufactured to be used as a romantic companion who lacked autonomy from the very beginning, by a similar "nice guy," and when she finally gained autonomy, she got to fight for it, and the oppressive nice guy villain was very obviously acting like a bad guy. Here, Nikki is a normal person who loses her autonomy and doesn't even get to fight for herself, and the oppressive nice guy villain acts like a victim and is the POV character too, which makes it more tragic. But Companion would be a great, ahem, companion piece to Obsession.

Name: Hoppers
Review:
Beaver, Beaver, Chopped Wood, Chopped Wood, Heart, Heart.

Hoppers is the Avatar sequel that James Cameron never thought of. It has all the elements of the Pixar movies I hold close to my heart. It's centered around a very personal relationship a girl has with her late grandmother, which is connected to a glade and her love for animals and nature, and it's also about her transferring her consciousness to a robotic beaver.

The characters were all lovable and easy to root for. King George might be the best and cutest king in the entire world, just empathy personified in a cute beaver body with a cute beaver mustache. George sees too much good in the world, and he's easily the most huggable character in the world. Mabel is the protagonist; her character arc also involves heartfelt emotions and adventure, and then she commits murder. Not even kidding. There's a considerable amount of death in this movie that I never expected.

The whole visual device of using black eyes and cartoon eyes to distinguish between an animal acting like an animal and the animal acting like a person was so smart. The movie was cute enough, funny enough, heartfelt enough, looked amazing, and was Pixar enough.

The voice cast was great too; I was checking the credits to see who voiced whom, and suddenly I went, THE INSECT QUEEN WAS VOICED BY WHO NOW?!!!

Name: Disclosure Day
Review:
It doesn't reach the levels of past iconic Spielberg sci-fi films, but it was still a solid watch. Spielberg's filmmaking techniques and John Williams' score still maintain their timelessness, and despite being so serious in tone, the film does find moments where there's a childlike wonder and whimsy to the proceedings, especially towards the end in a scene involving invincibility. This is basically one feature-length chase that drops us right into the middle of the conflict and then just explains everything along the way piece by piece. But towards the end there was some repeated exposition, though, showing us things we already knew as flashbacks, but I felt like those flashbacks were more about the feel of it than the information. The action setpieces and chases were very thrilling. 

Also, I can understand why that ending would leave people wanting more or make them feel, "That's it?" but I get what they were going for here, and this is not a movie about aliens; it's about the disclosure of the existence of aliens.

If I had a nickel every time there was a big sci-fi movie in 2026 where aliens are more empathetic than humans, I'd have two. Thematically this felt like a spiritual successor to both ET and Close Encounters. But that end message doesn't apply to all human conflicts, does it? Seemed pretty simplistic, seeing how the real world is affected by the actions of narcissistic genocidal psychopaths in power. I don't think kind aliens can fix us. Which is probably why the ending kept it open too.

Name: Backrooms
Review:
By the time Kane Parsons reached the age where he could've even comprehended the existence of different video formats, digital HD and SD cards already existed. So, both in his YouTube series and in this movie, Kane's level of understanding of the 90s media and aesthetics as a person who has never actually lived in that era amazes me. I've watched 17 out of the 22 videos in Kane's Backrooms series, so I can say that this film feels more like an extension of the found footage episodes that center on ordinary people who encounter the Backrooms (like the very first Backrooms short he did when he was 16) than the others that are more about the Async Research Institute doing their various experiments and research on the Backrooms.

Kane's audiovisual sensibilities are so on point in this movie. The opening scene is very similar to Kane's first found footage Backrooms short and presented like it's video camera footage on VHS. Then it becomes a traditional film, and we get introduced to the characters. Here too Kane makes some interesting choices. Clark and Mary are the main characters here, and the film only ever switches character perspectives while we're seeing the outside world. When any of the characters are inside the backrooms, the film chooses to trap us inside the backrooms with the characters without ever intercutting to the outside world in between.

The film is called Backrooms, and of course most of it is set inside the creepy and weird liminal spaces that seem like they go on forever. The backrooms in Kane's YouTube videos were a digital render, while this one combines outstanding production design with some seamless visual effects to get the effect. The atmosphere buildup is immaculate, and the sound design is a big part of that. The constant hum of fluorescent lights, the unnatural silence, that sense of another presence being there with the characters, and the sound design and sound mixing really place us in the middle of this eerie and mysterious infinite space where every part is weirder than the last one. Backrooms plays with being both a traditional film and a found footage film, with an extended found footage section towards the middle, which makes such great use of locking in the audience to the POV of a single character holding a camera. I'm not exaggerating when I say that I see a bit of David Lynch in 20-year-old Kane Parsons. Lynch has also played with such spaces like the Red Room in the past. Backrooms did give me Twin Peaks flashbacks. 

Where Backrooms lost me is in its writing; Mary and Clark both have their individual character arcs and issues they're dealing with. But still they seemed underdeveloped, and when a certain character switch happens at a point in the movie, it just felt very abrupt and confusing. I know abrupt character switches and leaving things unexplained are also something from the David Lynch school of things, but still, this just seemed a bit incomplete rather than intentional. Idk. The writing is pretty loose here, and it's mostly just for Kane to play with the horror setpieces and all the weird ways he can take the backrooms concept and imagery with a way bigger budget. There's even a part where the several "levels" of the backrooms are shown, which looked as beautiful as they were weird. It's more about the vibes and the atmosphere here, and I dig it. 

This is also one of the most brightly lit and colorful horror movies I've seen. The outside scenes look so vibrant and beautiful, probably to contrast with the yellow fluorescent lighting in the backrooms. The cast is amazing; I loved Renate Reinsve in a scene towards the end, where she even brings some unexpected comical energy to the situation. The music was also great, mixing both original material and themes from the YouTube episodes.

The film doesn't expect the audience to have watched Kane's YouTube episodes, but watching them does fill in several gaps on who Async is and why the backrooms exist that the film doesn't quite explain. It's also very obviously setting up things for the future, whether it's more movies, TV shows, or YouTube stuff. The original Backrooms creepypasta originated from the photo of a furniture store, so setting this movie in a furniture store was also like a full circle moment.

Name: Double Indemnity
Review: It would've been so cool to watch this in the cinemas, every line that Keyes delivered would've gotten applause.

Name: Dridam
Review:
We talk about movies where we can see the twist coming from miles way, but this is the kind of movie where we can see the twist coming from lightyears away. The foreshadowing attempts and some of the dialogues and performances make the entire thing obvious even before the conflict even begins, which is not so great when the entire movie is building up towards this big reveal. How much foreshadowing is too much foreshadowing is the question I had after finishing the movie.

Shane was good as the protagonist and I really felt bad for the guy. It's so hard to fit into a new workplace friend group as a fresher when they're all already a gang, and a big criminal conspiracy happening in the town in between doesn't help. The supporting cast's soap opera coded performances and dialogues really justified the "Jeethu Joseph Presents" title. There was a really great fight scene towards the end though, which hit solid narrative beats in between the action, with the protagonist essentially transforming into a cornered feral animal.

But this movie was not without potential. The protagonist's whole turmoil was interesting. Maybe instead of Agatha Christie, Alfred Hitchcock should've been the inspiration here; by not hiding the full mystery from the audience, this would've been a different kind of movie, maybe even making it feel more cat-and-mouse coded than having to wait so long for such an obvious reveal that we might've already guessed.

Also, the movie's title doesn't have much to do with the plot.

Name: Balan - The Boy
Review:
The central mother-and-son relationship being explored in Balan was VERY interesting, and my one complaint is the fact that the film chooses to not focus on that relationship after a while. Both halves of the film felt like they were telling entirely different stories.

The first half was about this unnamed mother who is very clearly escaping her past, not trying to get attached to anything or anyone but her son, who also remains unnamed. They assume random identities, which are the only names we know them by; she cooks up elaborate backstories for them and teaches her boy those backstories. Her first priority is the safety and survival of her and her son, and she'd do anything and hurt anyone for that. But this also means that the boy has a very unstable childhood, no identity for himself except the backstories his mom imagined, no friends of his age, and basically none of the experiences most of the boys his age get to have. This whole relationship and how the boy essentially doesn't get to be a boy was very interesting; there's even a scene where he enters a classroom for the first time and seeing so many other kids his age is very disorienting for him. He struggles to fit in with other children.

But the thing is, the film doesn't stay to explore their relationship or how he doesn't get to have a boyhood, but instead becomes about something entirely different in the second half, which I won't spoil. It felt like the second half condensed this to the kind of Amma paasam storyline that we're more familiar with, when the relationship this mother and son had was anything but familiar or ordinary. It just becomes something entirely different and then bounces back only at the end. This is a well made and well shot film (Shyju Khalid my goat) and the music is so beautiful throughout (Sushin Shyam my goat), so it felt like that end moment being so beautiful is also thanks to the music and the way it was shot. Because the film lost me for a big portion of the second half and then pulled me back in right at the end. There are several logical issues and plotholes too, but I'm not nitpicking on those for now. 

Both the boys (Sinan and Adisheshan) who played the title character were great performers; Farzana as the mother was also good, though the performance did feel a bit too dramatic during a few scenes (might be an intentional choice though), but her presence conveyed the kind of passively unhinged person the mother was really well. Also, as much as I loved Ammamma and felt that she was a true baddie and enjoyed all her scenes, again, exploring the very unorthodox lifestyle and dynamics this mother and son had was more interesting to me, and this was like a feel-good comedy movie in between that.

As for the production design, things did look a bit too aesthetic, curated and put together at times when the characters and settings were supposed to be working class, or that could be just me. But it was still nice to see a cinematic-looking "film-film" in an era where Malayalam cinemas are more inclined towards being Instagram reels coded. The film also had such beautiful use of colors. Anyway, like I repeated several times, I wish Balan explored the two main characters and their relationship more than what we actually got. 

And Sushin Shyam should release the full OST ASAP. 🛐

Name: Dr. No
Review: Watching this film is like visiting a historic landmark. There are several elements in their infancy here that defined not just the biggest film franchise in the world but also cinema and pop culture in general. This was a cultural milestone whose impact echoes even today; even people who've never seen the movies or know about the books know who James Bond is and what 007 means. So the rating I've put here is completely an honorary rating for the cultural phenomenon that this film is. And for context, I've only watched the Daniel Craig era of Bond films. This is a pretty small-scale film, and the big action set pieces and scale that have defined the Bond franchise are not really present. But of course it begins with the iconic gun barrel sequence and the Bond theme music, but this one puts the title sequence right at the beginning, while big action sequences in the cold opens would become a staple of the series moving forward. The way we're introduced to Sean Connery as James Bond is so smooth and classy with the "Bond, James Bond" to this day. Connery's performance as Bond and the way he looks and carries himself is the one timeless aspect of this movie. The man is just oozing charm. The one-liners were delivered so smooth and sound so cool with that accent. Of course, before the more balanced, multilayered, and vulnerable Daniel Craig version, first there was the hypermasculine, perpetually flirty, chauvinistic womanizer that was Sean Connery's Bond. Does he have morals, try to save people, and kill bad guys? Yes. Would he seduce most of the women he encounters, even one whom he's certain wants to kill him and then hook up? Absolutely. Most of the women who we see on screen either sleep/have slept with Bond or want to sleep with Bond. "Honey Ryder" is the main bond girl in this movie, and I'm pretty sure her inclusion in this film was just about eye candy, as she doesn't have anything to do in this movie other than look hot and tag along with Bond. And I'm aware that Honey Ryder is only the start of the not-so-subtle Bond girl names. I'm aware that this was a low-budget production even for 1962. Bond didn't have the Aston Martin, Omega watches, or other brand deals attached to him either. Gadgets are also completely absent here, Bond uses only his body, guns and his unlimited rizz. Despite being smaller in scale, the production design and overall look and feel do feel like a condensed version of what the franchise would eventually become. The evil lair and the costumes and all, especially as someone who watched only Daniel Craig Bond films and Austin Powers, the older Bond films reminding me more of Austin Powers are also going to be a recurring theme. The action seemed pretty endearing; lots of throws were involved, and the spider scene made me laugh for some reason. It's not high octane action, it's more simple and cute. There's even a car chase and several explosions. Pretty impressive for the era tbh. The plotline itself is a very simple and straightforward one, or maybe this feels simple and formulaic because it was one of the first of its kind on top of which so many films built. Everything just seemed too east for Bond, there wasn't really any mystery or suspense to it, the title character Dr. No is introduced and dispatched within 15 minutes or so. So Dr. No doesn't really leave much of a mark as a memorable villain despite being in the title, the only memorable thing about him is his mechanical arms, which is also a Bond movie staple where a villain would have some kind of a handicap or scarring. There are also several long scenes that amused me. A long decontamination scene where it's Sean Connery and Ursula Andress being stripped and passing through a conveyor belt shower thingy; the way Bond prepares his room before leaving to see if anyone has broken in (it has no payoff, we're just seeing routine); the iconic James Bond theme playing even during scenes where Bond's not even doing something impressive or badass. There was a silly energy to this, and I enjoyed that. Of course this is a movie from the 60s, and parts of it haven't aged well. Much has been said about the misogyny and objectification of women in the pre-Daniel Craig era Bond movies, so I don't want to elaborate on that. The title character of Dr. No is a half-Chinese man, played by a white man in makeup, which is also something that wouldn't happen in a modern Bond movie. But yeah, this was a historical milestone, shaken, not stirred. Bondathon, James Bondathon.

Name: From Russia with Love
Review: From Russia With Love was a big improvement over Dr No and felt more like a proper spy thriller. It has a cold open before the opening titles, and though it's not a big action scene here, it does act as the start of a long-standing Bond tradition. Then there's the credit sequence itself, which has text being physically projected onto a woman's body. It's indeed treating the woman as an object but is also very cool and very imaginative. The villains and their threat seemed like a proper threat to Bond; after Dr No's tease of SPECTRE as the big evil organisation, we see Blofeld for the first time – well, we see Blofeld's cat for the first time. It was funny that even though his name is not even mentioned, Blofeld is listed as a character during the closing credits, but the actor playing him is listed as "?". This is the longest time a Bond movie made me wait till James Bond (the real one; the fake one in the opening credits doesn't count) actually popped up. I was also surprised to see that James Bond did the rubber mask disguise thing way before Mission: Impossible did; I thought it was a Mission: Impossible thing all these years. Bond himself is pretty much the same he was in Dr No, but the threat is more interesting this time, and the Bond girl Tatiana Romanova is very much an important part of the story rather than just being eye candy like Honey Ryder from Dr No, and even gets involved in the action towards the end than just tagging along with Bond, but yeah the women in the Bond series are still treated like accessories. Bond is still a chauvinistic womanizer and would sleep with any attractive woman whom he comes across, sees them as objects of desire, and would make objectifying comments. Except for the evil Russian lady (who reminded me so much of her Austin Powers counterpart), the women are there for eye-candy purposes, and Bond's presentation is still very hetero male fantasy core. The flirty banter with Moneypenny is always fun to watch though. The part where British intelligence listens to Bond and Romanova's recording which was partially Intel and partially pillow talk was also hilarious. Sean Connery's charm and screen presence are so magnetic, and you'd believe this man is seducing and charming his way through his mission. Even in later scenes like the whole train sequence, Connery plays it in a way that makes us doubt whether Bond is being oblivious to the double crossing or just playing around with his suspicions. Connery just embodies everything that's cool about Bond perfectly, and the action sequences have improved here from Dr. No and actually seem thrilling instead of seeming cute and goofy. We also get the first intimidating Bond Thug in Grant, the deadly person sent by the villains to kill Bond in these movies, that is. The fight scene with Grant looked raw and gritty, the punches and throws carried weight, the multiple chases afterwards looked big and explosive. The helicopter set piece also holds up even to this day and was very impressive. This one doesn't quite shift gears into action mode till the end, but when it does, the action is several steps ahead of Dr No in every way. This one also introduces gadgets into the Bond series; there's nothing over the top here, just a suitcase and a compact sniper rifle, but the payoffs with the gadgets are always fun in these movies. The Bond and Romanova romance arc is the most dated part here; their dynamic doesn't have the kind of depth and emotional weight the Vesper and Bond romance from the Craig era did. Connery's Bond is very cool; he looks like a sharp and handsome badass and is very charming, fun and magnetic to watch, but he still feels pretty much like a hypermasculine fantasy rather than a real person. But yeah, this was way more solid as a spy movie than Dr No, and I was able to take this one more seriously, though it's still silly in a few places.. In a fun way. Also, I realised that a James Bond movie having multiple endings was also not a new thing, because this thing ends like 3 times, there's so much stuff happening in the last 10 minutes alone, including a boat chase, a scene in the SPECTRE lair and a fight inside a hotel room. Talk about rapid pacing. Also, both these movies end with Bond being with that movie's Bond girl romantically, who's absent in the next one and is never mentioned, which is funny. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: Goldfinger
Review: Goldfinger introduces more recurring Bond elements into the series. This one's bigger and more action-packed than its predecessors; we have an action scene in the cold open, and the Aston Martin with all its cool gadgets is introduced, and it gets crashed. Dr. No was the last Bond movie named after the villain, where No doesn't even properly appear until there's only like 30 minutes of movie left, but here, Goldfinger, the titular bad guy, pops up pretty much right at the beginning and is far more of a persistent villainous presence. Goldfinger as a Bond villain carries more weight; he's a few steps ahead of Bond for most of the movie and gets some very memorable lines. "I expect you to die, Mr. Bond" was iconic both as a line and in its delivery, and I wasn't even aware that it's one of the most popular Bond villain one-liners from this franchise. I expected him to be connected to SPECTRE since that was a running theme in the last two movies, but no, he just wants to fuck over America for the love of the game. This was a more intentionally funny Bond movie; it's not funny because of its age, it's funny because it wants to be. Bond would crack a funny one-liner at any given opportunity; Goldfinger also hits back with funny evil one-liners. Sean Connery also plays Bond with more of a cheesy energy. The Bond girl's name is "Pussy Galore," and Bond says, "You're a woman of many parts, Pussy," with a straight face. The opening scene has Bond using a girl as a human shield, which is something that apparently would return again in the series. And then we have the always smiling and hat-throwing Oddjob as a Pookie Bond heavy. The fight scene between Bond and Oddjob was equal parts action and equal parts comedy, and this time this movie wants it to be a bit silly. Also, this movie has a single karate chop from Oddjob knocking Bond out, which I thought was an Austin Powers thing, but it's an OG Bond thing. The opening song again has images projected on a woman, but this time it's a gold-covered woman, and scenes from this movie are projected on her while the credits run beside her; it's pretty cool and my favourite opening song so far (well the opening theme of Dr. No was basically just the James Bond theme music though). Bond being a cocky womanizer and underestimating Goldfinger also leads to the other iconic imagery from this movie, which is a woman lying dead while being covered in gold. Bond's meddling ending up in women getting killed is also a recurring theme that carried over even to the newer Craig-era films. I'm aware that Pussy Galore was a character in the original novel too (I had to double-check if Ian Fleming himself actually cooked up this name), but bro, how can we even take that name and that character seriously? Of course the Pussy and Bond scenes (yes, I'm aware how this sounds) again showcase some good old Bond misogyny; that scene in the barn was pretty weird, putting Bond in the predator category rather than the womanizer category for a moment, but of course Bond's mojo appears to her "maternal instincts," so Bond gets a pass, I guess? Now I know why Austin Powers valued his mojo so much because Bond saves the day purely by seducing Pussy in this movie (yes, I know how this sounds 😭). Tatiana Romanova from the last movie is by far the only woman who's been written to be a bit more than an object so far, which is not such a high bar either. Pussy's character basically remains Goldfinger's thug, then Bond forces himself onto her, she resists and throws him, they have a judo throw session, Bond throws her over, gets on top of her, and kisses her (forcefully), then she kisses back, and now she's working with Bond and is in love with him. The hypermasculine fantasy in the 60s, ladies and gents... This is by far the most fun I've had watching these movies. The franchise is getting closer and closer to the template that comes to our minds when we think "Bond movie"; there was some cool and fun action, the Aston Martin scenes were dope, and the ending was pretty thrilling. But yeah, if there's a part that hasn't aged well in this movie, that's the barn scene between Pussy and Bond and how and why she switches alliances. It left such a bad taste, I don't like the idea of James Bond seeming like a predator. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: Valathu Vashathe Kallan
Review:
This is the Korean revenge thriller format mixed with elements similar to Netflix's Adolescence, which Adolescence did way better.

As in all Jeethu Joseph movies, the performances by the supporting cast are bad. There are scenes that end up goofy just because of the performances and the way they've been directed, and sometimes it's because of the writing too, like a scene where a character is watching a pre-recorded video and a lady is shouting "Onnum cheyyallenn para saaree," and I couldn't resist laughing. There's even a tragic suicide scene at the beginning where the dialogues, the performances, and the way it's been shot just make it seem so silly.

The writing screams first-draft energy, because towards the end, when the reveals start happening, the movie does gain some life, but it's too late at that point, and the whole decoding thing was also silly. Like, it seems so much like 2 hours of oppikkal just to reach that particular reveal and conclusion. There could've been a good movie with the same storyline, but I don't think this is it. 

It's not a Jeethu Joseph movie without a woman getting beaten up on screen or worse.

Credit where it's due, there's some solid de-aging work to show young Biju Menon in the flashback scenes. It looked like frame-by-frame de-aging visual effects similar to what they did in Thug Life, not an AI deepfake; the scenes being black and white also helped, but still, it looked very natural and blended in. So most of my rating goes to the VFX team.

Name: Supergirl
Review:
Every DCU canon movie or series released so far has had direct involvement from James Gunn either in the writing or both the writing and directing. So they all carried James Gunn DNA through and through. James Gunn is not officially credited as a writer for Supergirl, but the James Gunn elements are still present here; we have the retro soundtrack, a lead character who carries around a music player that plays the said soundtrack as diegetic music, we have weird aliens doing weird alien stuff like in Guardians of the Galaxy, and we have a found family storyline where one of the main characters is looking for revenge. Even the sense of humor seems pretty much like James Gunn's work. But still, this one doesn't have the James Gunn sauce the previous DCU stuff has, so it's pretty obvious that it's someone else trying to replicate a James Gunn-style movie. 

When Gunn said DCU will always focus on giving filmmakers and writers their individual voices and styles, I didn't expect this movie to try to be so Gunn coded. The only parts where it did recapture Gunn's style were during that first meeting between Clark and Kara, with David Corenswet's Superman being the adorable goofball that he was in his own movie. This was the best scene in the movie and it needed more of that energy. This is a pretty formulaic affair, but it's not strictly the superhero formula. There are no world-saving stakes here; there's Kara's search for the bad guy to get the antidote for the poison he shot Krypto with, and there's Ruthye's search for the bad guy to get revenge for killing her family. It's more like the Mad Max formula being combined with westerns like True Grit, where a girl seeks the help of an older drunk badass to get revenge.

Milly Alcock plays Supergirl, who's in her early 20s, and Eve Ridley plays Ruthye, a 13-year-old teenager. Even though there's like a 10-year age difference between the two (both the characters and in real life), this didn't feel like an adult and child duo but like they're two teenagers, due to Milly seeming younger than she actually is. Maybe a smaller child should've played Ruthye? On the villain side, there's Krem and the Brigands, ugly dudes belonging to an all-male race who'd kidnap girls to breed. I think this was a missed opportunity for some satire, which is something James Gunn has done in all the previous DCU stuff; the Brigands could've easily been a parallel to Andrew Tate podcast incel bros; their leader is even bald and ugly. But yeah, this one does have this whole gender angle going for it, with an all-male race of villains and two girls (and a Lobo) being the good guys, but it's pretty underdeveloped. Jason Momoa returning to DC as Lobo was fun to watch, but it's like they're just teasing him a bit here, and we're going to see a much more explicit, cursing, violent version of him later on.

Everything about the movie was just adequate, like there wasn't much that I REALLY loved or like swept me away. Kara's powers are limited for most of the movie, so it was very satisfying to see the action during the moments where she does get to let loose; there was a slo-mo moment towards the end that was pretty James Gunn coded. I couldn't really feel any stylistic flair from Craig Gillespie himself, which I saw in I, Tonya or Cruella, and like I said above, this just felt like a movie that was trying to be a follow-up of James Gunn's style. This was a coming-of-age movie about Kara finding herself by getting to help someone else. Trying that kindness stuff that her cousin's all about. It does have some heart, but it doesn't reach the levels of hope core that her cousin's movie did. 

But yeah, I did have fun; it's not as bad as some reviews are making it seem to be; it's just adequate. Millie Alcock was great and is a true star and I do hope to see more of her as Supergirl, in better movies. I've had the Woman of Tomorrow book with me for quite some while now, but I couldn't get around to reading it. But I should get to it.

Name: Thunderball
Review: This was the Bond movie that bored me the most so far. I understand that the underwater sequences were a huge technical achievement at the time, and even watching them in 2026, I can appreciate the efforts, especially during all the underwater action scenes. There's some really great underwater action in this movie that has aged really well and remains impressive. But there's also too much underwater stuff here. Too much footage of people swimming underwater. Like, did we really need to see how the SPECTRE employees load and unload the bombs underwater in such great detail?
