SPECTRE itself was way closer to Dr. Evil and gang from Austin Powers than ever before, including Blofeld killing a minion by electrocuting their conference room chair, the whole evil plan involving holding the UK and the US for ransom by stealing nuclear weapons, and a dude with an eyepatch being Number 2. There was also the pool with the man-eating sharks too. Apart from the opening fight scene and the jetpack, most of the action in this movie happens underwater. The climatic boat sequence with all the speed ramping hasn't aged well. But yeah, there's still some explosions and large-scale action happening, but I found Goldfinger to be more fun than this. The title sequence and song weren't that memorable either; there was more underwater stuff there too. The movie lacks Bond stuff when Bond is underwater and unable to speak for a chunk of the movie. But when he does, he's, of course, the same kind of charming, with the funny one-liners and smoothness. This movie has another instance of Bond using a woman as a human shield. Misogyny returns, of course; there's another instance of Bond being kinda creepy towards a nurse, but it's not as bad as the barnyard scene from Goldfinger, and she does seem to be reciprocating later. And after they've been together, she seems to love him and can't get enough of him, which is typical of the male fantasy that Bond represents. Afterwards, there's like one good Bond girl and one evil Bond girl; they're both accessories without much of a personality beyond being seduced by Bond and hooking up with him, except that one of them wants to kill him too, but this is not the first time Bond has slept with a woman who he knows wants to kill him. But yeah, the girl does get multiple opportunities to save Bond's life in this movie, which is as close to using the women as more than just accessories that the Bond movies get at this point. What the hell was that jumpscare transition from the sex scene to the guy blowing a horn at the parade though? Made me physically jump. Absurd editing choice, bro. Also, the ending with the airlifting looked cool af with the Bond theme playing over it. The behind the scenes drama regarding the rights to both the novel and SPECTRE is more interesting than the film itself. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: You Only Live Twice
Review: SCREENPLAY BY ROALD DAHL?! Right off the bat I knew this was going to be an upgrade over Thunderball because this has the best opening credits sequence and song in the Sean Connery era so far. It kind of reminded me of Skyfall, how the credits begin from a seemingly fallen Bond. More Austin Powers core elements are present too, like the evil lair in the volcano and, of course, Dr. Evi... Ahem... Ernst Stavro Blofeld, played by the legendary Donald Pleasence, had such a fun, campy energy and goofiness that my only complaint was that he had way less screentime. You could just see how comfortable the kitty was while getting cuddled by him. We also have the deadly piranha pond and the big and tall Bond heavy. I can't believe I'm saying this sentence, but this movie does misogyny better than the last two Bond movies. And by that I mean the misogyny here is like goofy, dated sensibilities that make me laugh, rather than being truly uncomfortable to watch and process scenes like the Goldfinger barn scene. Of course there's a gang of Japanese servant women dressed in their underwear there to bathe and soothe the men, with Mr. Tanaka saying, "In Japan, the men always come before the women." We have 3 Bond women, two good ones and an evil one. This time all of them just instantly fall for Bond, which is understandable when Bond looks and sounds like Sean Connery, way better than Bond forcing them into submission. This is the first appearance of Asian Bond girls too, and they both actively save Bond's life and help him in his mission, but of course, during the final stretch, the Bond girl has to be in a bikini with no apparent practical reasoning to be in a bikini. Of course Bond is still a chauvinist and treats women like objects. But at least he's not a predator in this one. Another funny part was the part of the movie where Bond is made to be "Japanese." I assumed it was about him learning about Japanese culture, but no, he's given fake eyelids and a wig to "make him Japanese." But most of the cast here are actual Japanese people, and it's shown to be the Japanese people themselves doing this. There's even time taken to show a Japanese wedding for Bond. Connery NEVER looked like a Japanese man for a second in that makeup. It's the kind of dated racism that made me laugh, but also, I remember Bond fanboys crying over Lashana Lynch playing Agent 007 and saying it "ruins the franchise," when the franchise literally has Bond dressing up to be Japanese. The Cold War references were more direct here, and obviously the film inclines towards the US, though the evil plot here is SPECTRE trying to make the US and Russia destroy each other during the Cold War so that they can control the world. There are very few gadgets in this movie; there's the mini helicopter with all the weapons, and then there's the cigarette missile. The action is pretty great too, and a lot of the practical stunt work and miniature special effects have aged well; only the rear projection stuff hasn't. It was also fun to see Sean Connery's Bond immediately run when being surrounded by multiple thugs who aren't even armed. That's when I remembered that Bond might be an action hero, but he's not an invincible action hero; he can't take on an army on his own. He gets knocked out, beaten up, and intimidated and must rely on his instincts, intelligence, and sometimes pure luck to overcome these situations. Sean Connery's charm and his one-liners remained consistently iconic so far. I know this isn't his final Bond movie, but I'll miss him while I watch Lazenby in the next one for sure. I had fun, even the things that were bad about this one were somehow fun. Most of the stars are for Blofeld's kitty btw. The real star of this movie. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: The Sheep Detectives
Review:
This had the vibes of the 90s and early 2000s talking animal movies that I used to love as a kid, combined with a very unique idea for a murder mystery. The murder mystery vibes themselves felt Knives Out adjacent, but there's no Benoit Blanc here. Instead, the film stars talking sheep who investigate the murder of their shepherd. Though we can hear the sheep speak, the humans in the film can only hear their "baaa"s. So this is a detective movie where the main detectives can neither question nor even directly accuse the suspects and witnesses. For this they need to basically use the simple-minded yet good-hearted town policeman (Nicholas Braun as a cuter, British and kid-friendly version of Cousin Greg) as their surrogate to find the killer. 

Hugh Jackman is the biggest and top-billed star in the cast, but of course he's playing the murder victim. Though he has only a limited amount of screentime, George is set up as such a kind and wholesome father figure, with Jackman being all sorts of lovable. I couldn't help but feel sad when the death happened, rather than it just being about the mystery. That's another part of this movie too; there's an overall emotional plotline going on here about George and his sheep. The sheep flock has unique traits given to them, like their beliefs about sheep turning into clouds and their ability to erase memories, and then each individual sheep is given their own unique quirks too. 

The CGI character designs strike this balance in between seeming like real sheep and being more expressive and animated than real sheep. And the integration is seamless. They do feel like actual creatures that exist within that world, but they also seem like these intelligent, human-adjacent characters speaking in English. The lighting and character detail are just amazing; the sheep never feel out of place with their surroundings or the real human characters at any point. The film uses real locations and sets, and the CGI sheep blend perfectly in them. This film definitely does photorealistic animals better than Disney's Lion King remake did, because these sheep actually emote and convey so much through their faces. 

The main mystery is solved pretty quickly, but it's understandable since the detectives being sheep is a pretty big limitation to drive the story of a human being murdered. This was marketed as a Hugh Jackman movie, but then it slowly becomes a Nicholas Braun movie instead. Like, him as Inspector Derry could pretty well have his own franchise where he goes around solving crimes with the help of cute animals. The best part of the Knives Out movies is the gotcha scene where Blanc lays out the entire mystery, and here the gotcha scene is all carried by Braun. 

The film itself is very well made; the emotional beats are done really well; the sheep feel like people; the main sheep characters have well-defined character arcs, though some of the supporting human characters are intentionally underwritten (the movie's told through the sheep's perspective mostly); the cast, both human and sheep, is good; the cinematography is beautiful, and it's very well edited too. Just the kind of movie that used to fill my heart up as a kid, but it's also a pretty solid enough murder mystery with just enough feels.

Name: Alpha
Review:
YES, I'VE RATED THIS HIGHER THAN DHURANDHAR BECAUSE THIS WAS ACTUALLY ENTERTAINING ON SOME LEVEL.

You can tell there's a better director behind this movie than the last few YRF spy universe movies because the action scenes get a major upgrade. But the writing and dialogues are still bad; the plot is so dated that not even modern aesthetics and pop music can hide it, and then there's the YRF spy universe and general Bollywood insistence that the leads must look like they're ready for their modeling photoshoot all the time. Like, when the characters roll around in dirt and on the floor and try to kill each other, maybe make them also look like they've just been through all that physical stuff instead of cutting to them looking fresh and fabulous with no hair being out of place. And no, it's not because the leads are women; Pathaan had SRK's hair being shampoo ad levels of fabulous even when he was getting the shit beaten out of him.

This movie has one of the most dated Indian melodrama plots of all time, yk: siblings being separated at birth, one being raised by the bad guy and the other being raised by the real father, and them eventually meeting as adults. No matter how much modern action movie aesthetics and pop music you throw at it, ancient writing is still ancient writing. Even the dialogue writing is so odd. A random cringey line would pop up at times, either making me cringe or laugh. That whole lioness line before the interval might be a cool girl power line in isolation, but the way it's placed makes no sense contextually when the bad guy isn't shown to be a misogynist (who literally says weakness doesn't have any gender at one point) and Anil Kapoor's very serious and straightforward character, who sets the line up, isn't shown to be the kind of character who speaks that way up until that point or even after that either. 

The randomness in writing is evident throughout. The way the two characters are shown to be raised does open the doors for an interesting kind of dynamic, but mostly they're just the emo one (Alia Bhatt) and the cheerful one (Sharvari); the writing is that thin. When they meet for the first time, the emo one literally tries to kill the cheerful one through shooting, stabbing, and strangulation, and then they talk, and a flashback later, the emo one says, "I just wanted to talk to you and not kill you," when being a trained badass and having her dad as backup is the only reason why the cheerful one is still alive.

The fight scenes were really great, though, even when some of them were clearly derivative. First and foremost, this is not as CGI and bad greenscreen-heavy as the previous YRF outings; most of the fight scenes happen inside physical sets. That itself makes it look way better. The fights are well choreographed, well performed, well shot, and well edited. They also acknowledge the size and strength differences of the characters in the choreography and mix gun combat and hand-to-hand martial arts together really well. I did really get into the action, with only the occasional case of obvious CGI head replacements and the characters doing their model poses in between taking me away. The goofy explosion at the beginning, which Alia Bhatt so unconvincingly seems like she's running away from, is the only CGI moment that felt War 2 levels of goofy. Even Hritik as Kabir got a better action scene here than what he got in his own movies. 

These are beautiful women being badasses; I just wish they'd look like they've actually been in an intense fight or through an intense forest trekking situation rather than always looking so perfectly well put together. Like you can just tell these are actors that are onscreen wearing well-curated and aesthetic costumes and perfectly placed scars and makeup instead of feeling like we're seeing those characters. The characters doing model poses and getting time to show off how sexy they are is a general YRF spy universe thing and not something specific to Alpha. Tbh, this one is light on the posing and sexy energy when compared to Pathaan, where even John Abraham as the bad guy got his beauty shots.

This one does make so many references to Hindu mythology when compared to previous YRF spy movies, which were more balanced. Pakistani Muslim bad guys are present too, but this one's still in the pre-sanghification of Bollywood era of patriotism and nationalism, rather than having Aditya Dhar's absolute conviction of sucking sanghi cock. Even with all the Dhurandharcels continuously attacking this franchise ever since that shit released, they're not pandering to sanghi gooning here like Dhurandhar yet, which reduced the ick considerably. But was that one flashback supposed to be a Dhurandhar parallel though?

Anyway, there were moments I found cool, including the one cameo and over-the-top, stylized fight scenes that I really enjoyed. Alia and Sharvari do get their moments to be badasses, though Alia's character bounces back and forth in between being stoic and expressive, but the writing isn't giving them much to work with either. The writing still feels very dated, and the dialogues don't help. It's the first female-led YRF spy universe movie, but it still feels like it could've been way better at being that, the sensibilities are pretty much like a dude coded movie. Competent filmmaking and action saved the bad writing at many places.

I still want this movie to do well though, just to see Dhurandharcels lose their shit.

Name: War 2
Review: They couldn't fully commit to make this a gay romance.

Name: Locked
Review:
If there's any subgenre of thriller movie I have a bias towards, it's the one where the protagonist gets trapped inside a closed space on their own and should survive and escape. So when I saw that this is exactly that kind of movie in a VFX breakdown video, I had to check it out.

This is a survival thriller where the main character gets trapped in a remotely controlled car. But this movie expects a huge suspension of disbelief from our side. We need to accept how the car has enough battery throughout the movie's runtime (it's not clear whether it's being charged in between, or if this custom built torture car has sci-fi battery capacity); we need to accept that the police don't care about and pursue a car that drives erratically in the city, plus several other logical inconsistencies that pop up throughout the runtime if we really think about it. But the thing is, all of this stuff really didn't bother me much, because the movie was fun enough, and it's really well made on a technical level, plus Bill Skarsgard and Antony Hopkins (mostly through voice) were clearly having fun in their roles.

The Corridor Crew video where they react to the very first oner where Eddie, played by Bill Skarsgård, breaks into the car is what made me watch the movie. The filmmaking choices and the technical finesse are impressive; I just forgot that an actual camera can never move around a real closed car like it does in this movie and just immersed myself in Eddie's turmoil. For a film mostly set in the interiors of a car, they find ways to make it visually interesting, and the back-and-forths between Eddie and the car's owner and his tormentor William (Hopkins) were great. With William acting like a vigilante executing justice, but really he's just more like a privileged classist psychopath. The sequence that happens when the car finally gets out of the parking lot was also thrilling, as was the ending where we finally see William in the flesh. There was also a legit scary moment involving Eddie's daughter. 

But yeah, if you're the kind of person for whom logical holes would ruin the enjoyment of a movie, then this may disappoint. I can forgive logical issues as long as a movie pulls me into its action, and this movie did. 

Also there's a moment towards the end where Eddie lets out a smile while his face is covered in blood, and that's the most Pennywise that Bill has looked in a non It project that I've seen. 

It's also funny that there's a movie named Locke, which is entirely set in a car that Tom Hardy is driving, and this is Locked, which is mostly set in a car that Bill Skarsgård is locked in.

Name: I, Nobody
Review:
Raju Pilgrim vs. The World

Mass hysteria is a pretty real thing; people can judge way too quickly, apply a label on a person, see them only based on that label, and pretty much ruin their life. So I loved seeing this multi-layered portrayal of how an ordinary man unintentionally gets judged as a criminal by everyone around him, how that pretty much ruins his normal life and the relationship with his family, and how he's forced to be a violent version of himself that he never wanted to be. And I'm talking about Sethumadhavan from Kireedam, btw, which is re-releasing right alongside I, Nobody. It was funny to me how Malayalam cinema's best portrayal of mass hysteria would be playing right alongside a movie that makes mass hysteria seem so goofy.

The opening stretches show a bit of promise; we have Rajeevan, a normal guy with a normal office job, accidentally getting important in a bank heist. This opening stretch where we see what actually went down during the heist, piece by piece, was very engaging, as were the little touches, like how the plastic bag put over Rajeevan has a print that looks like he's doing a winking face. There's an air of mystery surrounding Rajeevan and his intentions. But as the movie goes forward, we just understand that there's not much to Rajeevan, and he fights like a trained badass just because he's a commercial movie protagonist.

Some degree of silliness is fine when a movie doesn't take itself so seriously as well, but this one does, and it pretends to be smart as well. When it eventually becomes the mass hysteria situation where people start to judge Rajeevan as this bank heist mastermind who got away with it, the encounters range from a (unintentionally) hilarious scene with bullying kids, the entire city being in chaos to find the loot while the police do fuck all, and random goons and service staff (who are also surprisingly good at martial arts) trying to beat up Rajeevan. 

Now I'm a fan of action movies and well-made fight scenes. And this movie does have some well-choreographed and well-shot fight scenes, which are pretty grounded. We feel every hit, and Rajeevan is not that invincible and gets hit a lot in between too. But the question is, when the whole deal of the movie is that he's a "nobody," at least give some reasoning for how he's able to fight like a trained soldier, yk? Like how Thudarum clearly establishes Benz as a stuntman in his youth. Maybe there was a boxing or martial arts trophy in Rajeevan's home that I missed? Plus, the fight scenes start to feel repetitive, like they're stretching out the story other than adding to the story. Rajeevan is in no way an office employee "nobody" after a point; he's Puthiya Mukham. Some of the goons even try to straight up kill Rajeevan when the whole point is to get him to tell them where the money is? Rajeevan himself stabs and slashes these people with the knives with no hesitation. Like, these work as individual fight scenes, and Rajuvettan feels like an absolute beast through them, bringing enough vulnerability and physical exhaustion to the character as well, but do they fit into this particular film narratively? I didn't feel so. 

There are several moments where the filmmaking style looks really cool, but in terms of writing and storytelling, it feels like a letdown. Like when Rajeevan remembers about the relationship that he has with his wife, we get this stylish sequence that pans over the whole apartment while we see those memories across various points in time play out. Is it cool to look at? Yes. But does it provide much depth to their relationship? No. The family relationship remains very surface level, so when it becomes important towards the end, it feels so silly, because we don't know these people enough for such emotional payoffs.

There was so much potential that was built up in the initial half that dies down so quickly. The movie kept repeating itself; the same stuff kept happening, or the same thing that was already established was given flashbacks to re-establish it. Which really adds towards making it a tiring watch. There's a lot of supporting characters, and since this is a movie that focuses on how the public and the mob behave towards the protagonist, lots of background artists are involved too, and the performances are pretty over the top. 

The second half involves an elaborate plan and an extortion plot and makes the Kerala police look like incompetent losers who just sit around and have chaaya and snacks. Like, they won't even bother to do a basic investigation and just do anything but their jobs. Meanwhile Rajeevan has fight scenes with random goons to deal with, and then towards the end this thing brings in politicians, the media, and social media and acts like a goofy satire. Rajeevan is far from being a nobody at this point; he's the most important person in India. The movie overestimates the power of social media and the media and komalifies politics to the point where I had to check whether this is not a Sharis Muhammed and Dijo Jose Antony joint. Hashmi from 24 News' monologue with mass bgm playing over it in a movie? Really? Also, was Anoop Thottathil a reference to Rahul Mankoottathil? If it was, the way it was placed was pathetic.

Rajuvettan was really great as Rajeevan, and he gets several opportunities to shine, whether it's in the action or the more dramatic moments. It was good to see him as a character for the most part, though sometimes, like that scene with the politicians at the end, he's Rajuvettan. Rajeevan is a very one-dimensional character, and any dimension that he does have is given through the performance. The scenes that didn't have Rajeevan were the boring parts; he tries his best to carry the movie. Rajeevan's morality is tested at a point, but in no place is it properly addressed. He just remains a closed shell, but not in an interesting way. Parvathy's character was also monotonous, and it didn't look like she had much to do there. Here's a mom in a loveless marriage suddenly being a center of attention in a crime plot, but she's just... there. Both the kids were delightful performers, though, especially the younger child.

Jakes Bejoy has overscored this thing with a soundtrack that sounds like most of it belongs in a different movie. Things get louder than they have to be at times. Why does every movie have to sound like a mass movie?

Anyway, the initial portions really did show some promise, then it just kept on getting stretched out and kept on getting sillier until somehow reaching one of the worst Kalamudaykkal third acts I've seen this year.

Name: On Her Majesty's Secret Service
Review: We have the first Bond recasting, and it's George Lazenby. The way Lazenby is introduced as Bond is also fun, since this was the first time the world was about to see another person being Bond. We see a scene with Q, Moneypenny, and M, all being played by returning cast members, as they wonder where Bond is. Then we cut to Bond, face obscured, and after a small buildup, he saves a woman from drowning and then looks at the camera while he introduces himself to the woman with "My name's Bond, James Bond." And then in true Bond cold open fashion, there's a fight scene, and then the woman, Tracy, just leaves, which makes Bond address the camera again; this time it's meant for the audience themselves, as he says, "This never happened to the other fellow," and we get to the opening titles. This is one of THE best ways I've seen a character recast being introduced. It also sets up George Lazenby as a different kind of Bond than what Connery was, too. The opening titles have these animated silhouettes, lots of blue and clips from all five previous Bond movies (without showing Bond/Connery). Which also establishes that this is set in the same continuity, though it's a different actor. The theme music was also amazing and very James Bond. But Lazenby's Bond is very different from the Connery version, not just in the performance but in the writing as well. Connery's Bond had a rough edge to him; he was charming, but it was a different kind of bad-boy charm. Lazenby comes off with a softer gentlemanly energy, which is also charming in it's own way. Connery's Bond came off like a womanizing flirt, while for the first time, Bond is a romantic in this movie. He actually falls in love with a woman, emotionally bonds with her, and even spends time with her doing more things than just sex. This is the first time that the '60s Bond is showing any sort of affection towards a woman that's more than a casual fling. Bond himself says how, as a spy, he must have a lonely existence and that he's willing to let that life go for her. Even the other instances of seducing women he does in this movie are solely for the mission. This is the most human and emotional version of Bond so far, rather than just being a hypermasculine fantasy. He seems more like a person for once. So does the female lead, Tracy, who is not an eye candy character like past Bond girls and has some agency and identity for herself. The starting beats of the whole romance,, where Bond follows her, she commits suicide, Bond saves her, she flees, and then he follows her again, and then they hook up, were a bit weird, but afterwards, Tracy is the kind of woman who sees through the fact that Bond has agreed to marry her just out of an arrangement with her father, who wants Bond to "tame" her. And then these two actually hit it off, and we see a romantic montage for the first time ever in a Bond movie. This is one of the endings that everyone knows, but I'll still not spoil it, but even at the end, the way Bond reacts to what happens seems so genuine; the movie doesn't treat it lightly like how previous Bond films treated such moments. I really felt bad for the guy. This one also doesn't have many gadgets and stuff, other than things like the safe-cracking machine, and is more of a serious spy thriller like From Russia With Love for at least half of it; things get into cheesy Bond territory when we reach Blofeld's facility and meet the brainwashed assassin women and all. Lots of Dr. Evil coded moments in these scenes. It's also funny how even though Bond and Blofeld have met each other, Blofeld doesn't recognize Bond, but it's okay for us because it's literally a different actor. But I preferred Donald Pleasence's sillier Blofeld than this far more British one. The action only kicks in towards the end; the speed-ramped action scenes and the close-ups with rear projection have not aged well, but there are still some impressive miniature works and practical stunts being showcased during the snow portions and a pretty great car chase. The snow plow chase at the end reminded me of the Grand Budapest Hotel. It was also awesome when the James Bond theme kicked in at the end when Bond and Tracy's dad's gang storm Blofeld's facility. The music in the movie is amazing on the whole. Anyway, I think people were too hard on Lazenby; he was a good Bond, and the best thing is that he never tried to imitate Connery in any way. Also, why was that moment in the dining room scene where the women eat their food edited frantically like it's some panicky thriller scene? Foreshadowing about them being brainwashed? Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: Evil Dead Burn
Review:
There are enough moments of very nasty gore and over the top violence which are executed really well, including a makeout scene from hell. While I can appreciate the technical finesse like the practical blood and gore, the seamless CGI integration (except for the very obviously CGI burnt dude) and stylistic touches, including a very impressive single shot action scene, this one doesn't quite add anything to the Evil Dead Formula the way the last two Ash-less Evil Deads did. This is pretty much a basic movie with basic and pretty unlikable characters, from whom it never seems like an Ash equivalent survivor badass rises. There are teases with garden tools and even the chainsaw, but they just end up being teases. It's not just the likability, it's also the fact that both the characters and the deadites are constantly stupid in this movie.

Like, the deadites want to get a dagger from the family, everyone knows where the dagger is, the people that the deadites have possessed know where the dagger is. And yet, they're interrogating and tormenting the family instead of just getting the dagger? And it's not even hidden or something it's just laying around in some cardboard box, like why? Like this movie would be over so fast if either of the normal people or the possessed people just didn't take the stupidest possible decisions.

Name: The Furious
Review:
The dialogues sounded a bit off in this movie, and I was confused if I even had the right audio track. But then again, the characters were mouthing their lines in English too, just that the American accent voiceovers felt detached from their acting, which is common in Indian movies where ADR is more common than sync sound; here, it made it seem like an American dub of a movie that's actually mostly in English. But apparently the Chinese version of the movie does have the characters speaking in Chinese-accented English rather than the American accents?

Anyway, this film is not about the dialogues, anyway, and the protagonist is mute. This is all about the action, and this movie delivers on that in spades. The fight scenes not only look cool but also have actual stakes attached to them and actual threats that the protagonists should deal with. The pain and violence seem brutal, but the choreography and stunt work are the stuff of legends. The action scenes are not just about looking cool; they actually move the story forward, and each of them presents a new challenge, and they keep doing new and unexpected things with the action and violence. There were only a handful of moments where a set piece felt a bit too long or repetitive; otherwise, I was on the edge of my seat. The movie even acknowledges the size and strength differences of the characters and balances being stylized and grounded. 

It's a so-and-so common man vs. criminal empire movie with just enough of a narrative for the fight scenes to exist, and the fight scenes are amazing, so no complaints, really.

Name: Minions & Monsters
Review:
I was one of the people who started to find the minions very annoying after a point, and I've even referred to them as an evil corporate empire. But this movie surprisingly has heart; there's genuine love for cinema as a medium at times and a celebration of the rich history of cinema. James the minion is such a lovable protagonist, with his love for telling stories and creating art. This is still a Minions movie with plenty of slapstick humor and Minion stuff, but yeah, it had surprisingly more heart than the past ones, it got some genuine laughs out of me, and the movie is filled with so many old Hollywood references and historical references that were clearly not meant for its target audience of Gen Alpha kids. But if the Minions out of all things make little kids check out film noir, silent films and Citizen Kane then why not. 

The animation also looked beautiful, and there were all these throwbacks to classic cinema, including one chase scene that's straight out of silent cartoons and direct cameos from both Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. John Powell's score was also great. One plot point literally involves the minions being huge movie stars in the silent era, being unable to adapt to the talkie era of movies. That plot point was literally also there in Damien Chazelle's Babylon. 

If there's any complaint that I do have, it's that this could've been all about cinema, like the minion version of The Fabelmans or the Minion Cinema Paradiso. It didn't even need the monsters and the big final battle and all, but that's the thing kids would watch this movie for anyway. I just mean both the storylines and characters like Dort could've been integrated better into a single thing than seeming like fragmented pieces. The whole cinema storyline was the most interesting piece of it, for me as a Letterboxd snob, at least.

This is the first movie in this franchise after the very first Despicable Me that didn't feel like it was just cute slop to sell toys and merchandise. It does have a storyline and Minion leads with some personality. But still, Illumination could learn a thing or two from Pixar and DreamWorks on how they told mature storylines while still having enough kid movie content in them.

Name: Diamonds Are Forever
Review: This was Sean Connery's [official] final James Bond movie. On Her Majesty's Secret Service ends with a very dark character moment for Bond, where his wife is killed by Blofeld right in front of him. This one also starts with Bond relentlessly pursuing Blofeld and then murdering him. But Bond's dead wife or his grief is never mentioned, so it's unclear if everything George Lazenby's Bond went through is even relevant to Connery's Bond here or if he's just continuing his own storyline from where You Only Live Twice ended. Nine years had passed since Dr No, and Bond himself felt different as a character, like it wasn't Sean Connery playing the same guy. Bond has changed with age, but he still has the charm, the wit and the tendency to drop the occasional one-liner. Diamonds Are Forever did feel a lot more intentionally comedic, though; even the opening credits sequence is like kitty-themed and focused on Blofeld's kitty. There's a pair of assassins who feel like a comedy duo, who are the only bad guys we see for a while in the movie till the person behind it all is revealed, which is obviously Blofeld. The end set piece does have many SPECTRE goons, though, but this time SPECTRE is not called SPECTRE, and Blofeld is only ever referred to by his last name, and he has hair as well. I'm assuming this is when EON stopped using SPECTRE because of the rights issues? Both Blofeld and Felix Leiter are played by a different actor in each movie, and it's so funny. There are two Bond girls, Tiffany and Plenty (Plenty O'Toole, these names, bro 😭), and yeah, after Tracy from the last movie being so much more than just eye candy and a woman just being there for Bond to seduce, we're back to the Bond girl situation where they're just there as accessories and don't really contribute much. Though during the end set piece, Tiffany randomly being in a bikini and the whole cassette tape switching stuff were straight out of Austin Powers. The relationship between Bond and Blofeld was also funny here; Blofeld gets plenty of opportunities to kill Bond, but he never does. After revealing his evil plan, and after Bond tries to kill him, he just politely asks Bond to leave in an elevator and then knocks Bond out in the elevator and tries to kill him in a way that makes it possible for Bond to escape. Even at the end Blofeld would rather give Bond a tour of his facility than kill him. The whole crane and submarine thing was also very funny. There are so many parts of the movie that are just intentionally silly, like a chase in a moon rover from a set that looks like a fake moon landing, the car chase that ends with Bond tilting the car, and how most of Bond's lines are a quip ("But the wrong pushyy"). But even when Q is present in this movie, there aren't any gadgets being used. With the movie being as silly as it is, I did expect more gadgets than just the grapple gun. Anyway, Sean Connery's run as Bond did have great moments even while there were problematic parts as well, and he made Bond the icon that he is today, as it's obvious how so many stylistic touches of the character were his contributions that even carried over to the Daniel Craig version that I'm familiar with. He perfectly fits the charming yet lethal description, has this edgy sense of humour, and that accent is truly inimitable. But yeah, Diamonds Are Forever just sits in the middle among his Bond run for me; it didn't bore me like Thunderball did, but I didn't have as much fun as with Goldfinger and You Only Live Twice, and it's not in the serious thriller category like From Russia With Love at all. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: Live and Let Die
Review: The Connery era is [officially] over, and this is the start of Roger Moore's pretty long run as Bond. Moore also plays Bond as an English gentleman like Lazenby; Connery's unique Scottish accent brought an edge to the character that would forever belong to him. But still, Connery's Bond did possess a sort of lethal energy to him, like we can feel this guy has a license to kill and is dangerous. Daniel Craig's Bond also possessed that same edge to him, but Moore seems more like a lighter action hero, though his Bond also doesn't hesitate to go violent or kill. I've been familiar with Paul McCartney's Live and Let Die even before I watched this film, and it is one of the best opening theme songs of the franchise and goes to weird and whimsical places that only a Paul McCartney song would. The title sequence with the African tribal women and flaming skulls was cool and appropriately weird too. This film ditches the save the world plot, cold war tensions and international terror organisations for a plotline involving drug trafficking. This also might be the Bond movie with the most amount of black cast members. I searched up a bit and saw that it's borrowing blaxploitation elements. But aren't blaxploitation movies also supposed to star black actors instead of starring a white Englishman? Idk the black representation seemed more like stereotypes, but Yaphet Kotto was a great Bond villain though. He was clearly having fun with the material he got. There are two bond girls here, including the first black bond girl. Moore's Bond does come off as less of a chauvinist than Connery's, at least in this movie, there's no instance of him forcing himself on women, but he does do tarot card manipulation tactics for seduction at one point. He's still pretty much a raging flirt and a womaniser. And the movie clearly favors the white bond girl over the black bond girl. As for gadgets, there's the magnet watch, a very obvious Rolex product placement, and the shark gun at the end. All the cars being the same model also seems like another instance of product placement. There is an amazing boat chase sequence in this movie, though, which is where this movie peaked, the stuntwork and visual effects there still hold up, with a goofy redneck sheriff who's like the kind of stereotype that I'd give a pass for. The fight scenes seemed silly though. There were also far more obviously silly and campy moments here, like the one involving crocodiles and the ending. The boat chase and the delightfully cheesy finale are the reasons why this movie left me pretty happy. Bondathon, James Bondathon

Name: The Odyssey
Review:
Matt Damon desperately needs to get back home... Wait a minute...

Matt Damon doesn't remember who he is, but his instincts are still intact... Wait a minute...

I've never read the Iliad or The Odyssey or even watched any of the movie adaptations like Troy. My relationship with Greek mythology is mostly the God of War video games, Disney's Hercules, and one Percy Jackson movie. This film does provide plenty of exposition and context that's enough to follow along and understand this particular story set around Odysseus' journey back to his home, but still, a Greek mythology crash course would be good for the uninitiated to fill in the missing gaps and the details surrounding the Trojan War and the involvement of the Greek gods that the film doesn't really cover. Folks in the West learn most of this stuff in school, but Indians don't really dabble in Greek literature in school; at least I didn't. 

Anyway, onto the movie, this is brand new territory for Christopher Nolan, whether it's the fantasy element or the setting itself. Several elements in this film, including choosing to have contemporary English dialogue, Agamemnon looking like the Greek Batman, the music, the filmmaking choices, and even the font used for onscreen text, make this a very obvious modern adaptation. Hearing ancient characters say words like "wanna," "gonna," "dad," "mom," and "stuff" instead of the very formal English that such adaptations usually have was interesting. And lemme tell you somethin, Jon Bernthal playing a Greek king sounds exactly like Jon Bernthal as every other character, and I'm glad it does.

Like most of Nolan's filmography, The Odyssey also follows a non-linear structure, and I just loved the way Nolan played around with time and character perspectives. The narrative of this film is this interconnected web of events (definitely not a Tom Holland pun) that reveals itself non-linearly not just for suspense but also for several emotional reveals and payoffs, the editing by Jennifer Lame was amazing. We see different accounts about what went down at Troy when Odysseus and his men got inside the city walls using the Trojan horse. Both play out very differently; one is an action scene and one is a horror scene.

Speaking of horror, throughout Odysseus' journey, he faces several terrifying circumstances, and here's where Nolan creates these amazing horror set pieces, with each one seeming different from the rest. The Odyssey does this thing where throughout all these moments the perspectives are locked on Odysseus and his men experiencing the terror. When the Cyclops or the big sea monster appears, we only ever get glimpses from their perspective. This is clever in terms of the same kind of "less is more" tactics that classic monster movies like Jaws used to employ, and it also helps to ground the movie and make it more real. 

This is a BIG movie and marketed as a big IMAX movie, but unlike a Dune movie, the taller frame is not just used for showing scale or vastness here. It's mostly used for locking us in with the characters; whether they're inside the Trojan horse, or the ship, or the cave, it's trapping us in with the characters. There's also the brilliant use of lighting. This is the first Nolan movie where the night scenes have to depend entirely on fire for the lighting (I'm not saying they actually used fire to light the scenes; I have no idea about that). The night scenes were amazing, whether it was the ones at sea, the dark cave with just one fire as the light source, or grander places like Odysseus' palace or the one that I loved the most that did show scale, Menelaus and Helen's palace. The dark places look actually dark, and these rooms do look like they have only those fire lanterns lighting them up. I mean, yeah, duh, it's just rarer than you think in such movies. 

Lots of fantastical things are happening on screen, but it's always seen through the perspective of humans; there are no sparks flying or lighting emerging from human hands. The gods exist as real entities, but their intervention is almost always through nature itself. When there's a sequence involving witchcraft, it's done with body horror finesse, with clever special effects and cinema trickery. Portraying the supernatural as if they're something that can possibly exist in the real world like this makes it scarier. Also, the direct supernatural elements are present only in scenes that are presented as Odysseus recollecting his lost memories. He could just be an unreliable narrator as well. There's that possible interpretation that mythology could just be human stories that had fantasy elements added to them as they were passed on from person to person, the opening text "A time of apparent magic" also implies something like that. The combination of practical effects and visual effects is pretty seamless and grounding; everything really made me forget about what's real and what's not. 

There's also the brilliant use of sound and the way the score builds up several moments. Ludwig Göransson's score is absolutely amazing; it's the perfect merge of modern music with elements from the setting and even from the story itself. In moments like the first Troy flashback, the way the music helps in building up the tension was brilliant. The siren scene was another great example of sound being used really well. And then in the third act, the horror portion of the story is over, and it's Odysseus' eventual return, and then the themes get more epic and action movie coded, and Nolan actually treats Odysseus' return to Ithaca like how he treated Batman's return in The Dark Knight Rises with Matt Damon seeming like an absolute badass. During a key moment where Odysseus is leaving Eumaeus' house, the way it's been shot and the music seemed soo Batman to me. 

The film makes a very compelling argument that men are pigs (wink, wink). Samantha Morton was an unexpected standout in this cast who was not really present in the promotional campaigns; her whole sequence and her monologue on how men who participate in war enjoy the violence and murder they commit regardless of whatever duty, righteousness or discipline they're acting on behalf of hit the right places. I even liked her definition of what a disguise is. This connects to the bigger theme of the film too, which keeps haunting Odysseus throughout his journey. Odysseus being traumatized by his own actions during the war and the violence that he himself was the reason for ties this movie directly to what Oppenheimer was trying to say too, but I felt that The Odyssey does those anti-war themes better and actually holds Odysseus more accountable for his war crimes than how Oppenheimer handled it. Odysseus loses years of his life that he could've lived with his loved ones instead because of this war, and he just wants to return to them. This character motivation of being stranded away from loved ones and desperately wanting to return also connects The Odyssey to Nolan's own Interstellar and Inception. 

Matt Damon was amazing as the lead, and it's pretty obvious on screen how physically demanding it was, but Odysseus' mental turmoil, including his guilt, trauma and the toll the whole journey took on him, is portrayed really well by Damon. Odysseus' long and painful journey does seem like a long an painful journey and that's this movie's biggest achievement. There's plenty of visual spectacle here, but on the whole I felt Nolan's action when it involved cars, planes, guns, and explosions in his other films was better than the ones involving swords, bows, and spears in this one. But yeah, Odysseus stringing that bow and being lethal with it was still all kinds of badass. The rest of the cast has lots of big names, but the smaller names on the supporting cast who didn't really feature that heavily on the promotional campaigns left a lot of impact, like Himesh Patel and Samantha Morton, as I mentioned above. Anne Hathaway as Penelope felt sidelined at the beginning but then gets some really great moments moving forward, especially the scene with Robert Pattinson and the ones with Tom Holland and then Matt Damon afterwards. Along with Samantha Morton's character, Penelope also makes a very compelling argument in the movie that men suck, but she's forced to be a part of a very patriarchal arrangement where men see her as an object. Robert Pattinson as an evil snake of a villain was also very fun to watch, he was also kind of hilarious, especially at the end when he's like screaming weapon names. Tom Holland gets some great moments too, but at times I wasn't able to separate Peter Parker out from him, especially towards the end when the way he's in the action scene is so Peter helps Mr. Stark core. Could just be a me thing. 

The rest of the cast has lots of big names as well, but it's already too much material for one movie, and not all characters get to be so well defined. Elliot Page gets a very memorable character to play whose presence is echoed throughout the movie, but when we think about it, he's only really in like three scenes, but of course, he's amazing in every scene he got and leaves a big impact. Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Sparta doesn't get much to do though Helen's involvement in the war is also clearly marked as men merely using her as an excuse for their own violent ambitions; Zendaya as Athena is also a minor presence. And lemme tell you somethin, Jon Bernthal also only gets to be there to say things about Odysseus to his son, though Menelaus is a very central character in the Trojan War itself. Benny Safdie as Agamemnon, whose face remains hidden, probably because the film wants him to represent this large ambitious authority figure rather than ground him as human, mostly just gets to stand around in his ancient Batman armor, look cool, and get what's coming to him. But yeah, for someone who's not familiar with the Iliad, the way Agamemnon's story wrapped up is so quick, without even knowing much about who he is. But the thing is, this film is not about the Trojan War; it's about Odysseus' journey, so I understand why the rest of the characters are just there while the film is more about Odysseus' internal and external turmoil. It's not really a complaint when it's not really something the movie intends to do. 

Also, I'm aware that the film was trimmed a lot to fit into the IMAX 70mm format, so maybe some of the missing pieces and jumps are because of that. Like, as much as I want to understand (I really don't) Nolan's insistence on giving priority to a format that the majority of his audience don't even have access to, maybe sticking to a format that restricts his storytelling and forces him to cut out chunks of his film is not a good thing. As an audience member living in a country that doesn't even have a 70mm IMAX, I'd rather get the full version of the movie without the compromises made to fit it into 70mm IMAX, obviously.

It's not a flawless film by any stretch; the opening stretch has a lot of exposition. It took me some time to really get locked into the narrative, but once I did, I was really locked in, and the non-linear structure just flowed really well. There were a few instances of awkward editing choices, but I've always felt that it's a very specific Nolan thing, and not really about the editor that he works with, what's a Nolan movie without the kind of editing choices that you only see in a Nolan movie? While most of the ensemble cast fit their roles (I'm not commenting on the whole "woke casting" thing), and I didn't really mind the contemporary dialogue, Charlize Theron did look a bit out of place, she just had a specific 2020s Instagrammable face in ancient Greece. The third act had a lot of great narrative payoffs, and people were rightfully cheering at the show that I watched, but yeah, the action was missing something.

Despite the flaws, I'm giving this movie 5 stars because it's the kind of cinema that really honors the medium; there's a lot of love, care, and artistry behind each and every element. The music, the art, the special effects, the cinematography, the writing, and even the included flaws bear some soul. I support Nolan's intentions to keep cinema grounded and practical, his conviction in filming most of his visuals on camera no matter how fantastical or out of this world they are, but I love you more than the people who can afford and access 70mm IMAX, bro. Please don't stay married to a format that only a few people can see your movie in; stay married to cinema itself. 😔

The song at the end was the coolest thing ever. Bless you Travis.

I'm also happy that this film managed to piss off the same anti-woke cinebros for whom Nolan was a god only three years ago.

Name: The Man with the Golden Gun
Review: Bond is far from being a "secret" agent at this point when everyone knows who he is, what he does, and even what he looks like. This movie has the smallest threat Bond faced so far because there's no big criminal organization with lots of henchmen here. It's just an assassin and his minion Nick Nack (actual character name) and an insignificant and creepy third minion. Scaramanga was an interesting villain, though; he's like the evil counterpart of Bond, and Christopher Lee was very fun to watch. And Nick Nack was a very fun Bond heavy, and I'm pretty sure he inspired Mini-Me from Austin Powers. But yeah, Nick Nack is a little person, and the derogatory M word is used constantly to refer to him, even by Bond himself. A different time, ig. I felt that Live and Let Die was less misogynistic than the Connery era films, but this one brings back the misogyny big time. Bond is horrible and disrespectful towards his co-worker Goodnight, who's one of the two Bond girls in this movie. He very obviously sees her as someone lesser than him and as someone incapable. Goodnight, herself, is shown as a stupid woman who doesn't have much dimension to her. At one point she does reject Bond's advances towards her, saying that she's not one of the objects that he can just use and discard, and I felt maybe Bond movies did start to treat their women better, but no, that was just her trying to play hard to get, which Bond doesn't even take seriously, and she had already fallen for him. And even after this point, Bond constantly insults her, and any doubt that this is just about Goodnight being a stupid agent and not about her being a woman is cleared when Bond scoffs, "Women," when she gets kidnapped by the bad guy. And in true Bond movie fashion, Goodnight is randomly in a bikini during the ending, but this time the movie tries to give it a justification: it's because it'd be hard for her to conceal a weapon in a bikini, which is hilarious. The same logic never applied to Bond when he was captured (until woke Le Chiffre strips Bond naked in Casino Royale). So Goodnight serves as both eye candy and comic relief here. The other Bond girl, Andrea, is also your basic Bond girl who works for the bad guy that Bond must seduce for the mission's sake template. Explains why Austin Powers' Mojo was so important to him. This is a very silly movie with so many elements thrown in. Like borrowing blaxploitation elements in the last one, this one borrows Asian martial arts movie elements, just for a while. Bond is captured and trapped in a karate school and must then fight the school kids with two other karate girls. This one does have a bit better fight scenes than the last one. The goofy Sheriff J. W. Pepper also returns from the last movie very randomly. There is a very cool car chase in this movie, though, with one of the best car jumps I've ever seen at the end, which is a huge achievement in stunt work even to this day; it's just that they randomly put a very goofy sound effect when that jump happens. Though Scaramanga as a villain gets enough of a good buildup and seems like a legitimate threat, Bond defeats him too easily through the superpower of being able to get into a full two-piece suit as fast as possible. Joke's on Scaramanga for making his Bond doll too lifelike. This movie was just too goofy. Like, yeah, I don't mind a goofy Bond movie; I'm not a purist, but still... There's also the instances of goofy racism, porny names for women return, like Cheww Mee, then there's the wine called Phu Yuck. Different times omg. Another favorite hobby of mine is noticing the brand integrations in these things, like how here, every screen is a Sony screen. HOW MANY ICONIC FRANCHISES HAVE CHRISTOPHER LEE BEEN IN THOUGH?! Bondathon, James Bondathon.

Name: Scary Movie
Review:
Ts was peak brainrot to me even before the word brainrot even existed. They showed a censored version on TV, but I used to watch it every time it popped up. Of course some of the jokes haven't aged well; there are some really problematic ones, but also, there's a new joke like every 10 seconds, and a lot of them still make me laugh, especially Brenda's death scene where she's killed by the entire cinema audience instead of the killer himself. Marlon Wayans as Shorty also has so many iconic moments, like him getting shot in the lung while being so stoned that smoke comes out of it and he becomes a human bong. Anna Faris as Cindy Campbell also made me laugh so many times. She finds the exact range of goofiness for a movie like this. The 4th wall breaks and meta humor are still cool to this day though. Some of the jokes like contacting the cops and saying "white woman in trouble!" are timeless. 

And this one weirdly ended up having a far more shocking twist than the original Scream.

Name: Jana Nayagan
Review:
Bagavanth Kesari is one of the only two Balayya movies that I've watched that I kinda sorta liked. It had this whole woke girl power thing going for it; it didn't take itself too seriously, and the fight scene at the end was very fun. Jana Nayagan, on the other hand, tries to be so many things all at once. It is a Bagavanth Kesari remake on the surface, but it also has H. Vinoth's very absurd modifications to that simple masala movie plot, mostly regarding the villain played by Bobby Deol, and it also wants to be political propaganda for TVK. At times the film also pretends to be a kind of 4th wall-breaking GBU fan brainrot type for Vijay. I say "pretends" because I don't think H. Vinoth is a true fan like Adhik or even Atlee and Lokesh. Neither does he have the unseriousness to go full brainrot. What we get is brainrot that takes itself too seriously at times to be considered fun.

And on the propaganda front, this is a pre-election campaign movie that released after the election, after the guy had won. I think if the censor board did let the movie release in January, it'd have actually hurt Vijay's chances of winning the elections more than anything. I do understand why the Sangh-controlled CBFC showed resistance to a movie like this, though. The core evil plot by the savarna Hindu and North Indian villain, played by Bobby Deol, involves manufacturing communal tensions and supplying weapons to citizens so that Indians would kill each other and he could assume control as a dictator. But the movie doesn't name the Sangh or directly reflect the real world at all and is playing it pretty safe. All communal tension is a result of this one guy entering the political field with a new party; the ruling party of the nation is not addressed at all, like, why would the censor board think every bad fictional Hindu communal bigot is dangerous to them? Hmm. And Vinoth seems to really hate Africans for some reason. A fictional country in Africa is shown as the villain's successful project; this very big-budget movie shows that mostly using AI slop, and then there are repeated dialogues like "India will become Africa," "Indians are not stupid like Africans," and "Africa alla, Tamil Nadu da." What's with the racism, bro? I don't know how much of the original evil plan was altered for this newly censored version, other than the evil plan's name changing from OM to MM.

Then there's the obvious TVKfication, with Vijay's character himself being named TVK. It's funny how they kind of foresaw that the censor board might mute the name, because they did mute whenever TVK was being said, but "Thalapathy Vetri Kondan" is shown on screen as text in ways we'd never miss. Like, when someone asks Vijay his name, he literally looks at the camera, points to the corner of the screen, and "Thalapathy Vetri Kondan" appears. It's repeated every 10 seconds how Thalapathy is going to save democracy, or someone telling Thalapathy that he can't save democracy, only for him to reiterate how he will. There are multiple lectures about how Thalapathy would unite everyone and how he's a man of the people and indirect digs at how TN has been robbed by the two parties who have ruled it so far, how generational politics is bad, and how, unlike all other politicians, Thalapathy and his followers TRULY care about the people. Like, it may be indirect, as Vijay doesn't actually play a politician here but a murderous former cop, but it's no way subtle. Some TVK leaders even get cameo appearances; the TVK flag is recreated during a fight scene. Atlee has the TVK flag on his arm as threads during his cameo, like the propaganda dissection would require its own essay. But unlike BJP propaganda like Dhurandhar, Jana Nayagan doesn't have the vile intention to actually spread communal hatred; here it's more like showing India unrealistically being united by Thalapathy, and then at the end he breaks the 4th wall and asks us to "vote right." Wink, wink. The movie also very unsubtly implies that Vijay is the next MGR at least three times, with an AI MGR handing him out the whip at one point. Big movie couldn't afford to just animate MGR? 

Vijay was one of the best in Tamil cinema to perform action on screen when he got the right choreography, which only Lokesh Kanagaraj has been able to pull off for him recently. The action in Jana Nayagan is generally bad, with lots of bad CGI as well, and it makes the Balayya fight scenes in Kesari seem way much more fun to watch. Which is a sentence I have never expected to say. There are also these over-the-top elaborate scenes that are meant to build up the villain as terrifying, including his intro and several other instances, which are too long, too boring, and have too much bad CGI and even AI slop. They were just never-ending, and all of them were empty buildups anyway because after showing multiple instances of the villain easily murdering entire armies, he's always a loser in front of the god-like Thalapathy and never rises above as a dangerous threat. It proves that it's not about how much murder a villain commits on screen; Vijay Sethupathi from Master just had an arm and a punch as his weapons, and he seemed like far more of a dangerous threat to a Vijay protagonist. The villain's whole origin story and the Green Goblin-ish transformation scene were also so stupid. I remember the villain from Kesari being just some evil corporate guy. 

And this movie is a very rare instance of an Anirudh score sounding like it's piercing my ears. I did like some of the themes, but most of the score was either forgettable or plain annoying. Especially all the loud electronic music towards the end. The final act has all this sci-fi bullshit that's like so much bad CGI, AI slop, and obnoxiously loud music. I have no clue why a production this big is technically looking worse than fan films. They even had 7 extra months to fix any issues, but no, the bad CGI, bad production design, bad makeup and hair, AI slop, everything's still there. Even for something as simple as Vijay doing a Muppet voice, they're using the AI voice filter from Instagram reels, as if this big-ass production couldn't afford to just manually alter his voice. 

Vijay's performance is more like doing a checklist of things for people to cheer. So every expected mannerism is present here, and it just feels so mechanical at times. I did like Mamitha Baiju in this movie, though, and all the Singappennu stuff with her character are the scenes that are directly lifted from Kesari, and she was good during the final fight scene as well. But still, the final fight scene where dad and daughter fight together was way better in Kesari, as Jana Nayagan still has its priority to make it about Vijay's political campaign, with a TVK cameo-filled final payoff that's just so stupid. A movie starring raging misogynist Balayya gave more prominence to the female lead in the final fight scene than the one starring female-empowering VJna. 

For a send-off movie for Vijay the star, there's very little in this movie that does provide such fan service. But there were feeble little moments where the subconscious Anil in me woke up. Thalapathy Kacheri was one of them, and the mashup dance at the end of the song brought back memories. Then there was obviously the JD theme from Master popping up as the intro, though I didn't like that the new intro was for the Chief Minister instead of the actor. Then there's lots of slop and TVK propaganda instead of good fan service, and we get an emotional tribute video at the end, which did give me the feels. See, I don't like TVK Vijay at all, but actor Vijay meant a lot to me growing up, and some part of my brain can't help feeling stuff when specific things happened in the movie. But the thing is, there's very little of that sort of fan service happening in this movie, which is a vehicle for TVK Vijay rather than a send-off or celebration of Actor Vijay. H. Vinoth absolutely fails in the fan service element because again, he never feels like a true fan, or his obligation to make this TVK election campaign material clouded everything else. 

The whole scenario of goons being terrified of Thalapathy and who he is happens during multiple points in the movie. When the same thing happened in GBU, Adhik makes it so unserious and funny; Vinoth lacks that sense of humor to be truly brainrot.

There were several scenes that tested my patience, starting from that sleeping grandpa; listing every one of them would require yet another essay. And there's so much shit that I even forgot about about most of them. The writing and the dialogues were very bad in general. 

I'd have put one star if this were an Actor Vijay movie, but the title card clearly states this is starring the honorable chief minister of Tamil Nadu, and the honorable chief minister of Tamil Nadu hasn't really been acting like the savior that he played on screen. So it's a half.

Name: Scary Movie 2
Review:
This one had more jokes that made me cringe and squirm than ones that I found funny. They go overboard with sexual harassment and rape jokes here; there is a reason why such humor has died down. 

There were only a few moments that were genuinely fun, like the cat fight scene, Shorty being rolled into a joint and then smoked by a possessed weed plant, the Shorty Hannibal scene, that foul-mouthed parrot, and white people grouping together to leave the Black people to die, yk, such moments of genuine parody and not just adding poop, vomit, or pervy energy.

Then there are the not-so-great jokes that made me laugh simply because of the actors. This one adds more talented performers like David Cross, Chris Elliott, and Tim Curry. David Cross' character's entire thing is disability jokes because the character can't walk and uses a wheelchair, but he plays it so straight and is so good. And similarly, Chris Elliott's character's whole deal is his deformed small hand, and all of his character's jokes are just about how gross that disability is. And then the two of these characters have disability joke-offs with each other. But again, both of these actors are so good, though the material is so bad. Anna Faris also does over-the-top goofy stuff whenever she gets the opportunity to, and it's always hilarious. And I can never get enough of Shorty saying, "Shiiiiit, son!"

But yeah, the good joke-bad joke ratio is pretty low on this one.

Name: Scary Movie
Review:
This was actually way better than the last official Scream movie, because at least this movie was actually fun at times and has a far better twist and motive for Ghostface and even looks better.

I'm putting the same rating I put for the first movie because this felt like an extension of that movie, with a lesser amount of problematic jokes. There are definitely dated sensibilities, but it's more like older dudes whining that everything's too woke now. The trans jokes especially show that this was written by middle-aged dudes, who aren't exactly queerphobic in a very hateful sense, but they still want to make fun of it. The subway scene where old conservative folk stab a non-binary woke character to death instead of the killer having to do it (like the cinema scene from the first one) did make me chuckle just because of how absurd it was, and it was making fun of conservatives at the same time ("I like women and I like sports, just not together!!").

This is the basic plot outline of Scream 5 (or Scream) being parodied with some random comedy sketches in between. It flows more like a compilation of sketches than a movie movie. Jokes do fall flat, but still I wasn't bored. Gay Ray jokes were still the same as in the first movie, and that scene of Ray and Brenda doing prison roleplay in the shed was pretty flat. Shorty's Get Out + K-pop demon hunters parody was also just meh, but Marlon Wayans saying "Ahh, shiiit, son" still makes me laugh. 

I liked how the Ghostface mask from the first Scary Movie looked like a cheaper version of the original, but here it just looks like the original mask. But all the various alternative masks, whenever the killer changed his facial expressions, were fun designs. The Scary Movie Ghostface ends up having more of a personality than the original Scream Ghostface in Scream 7.

I did like all the meta jokes, though. It's just my kind of humor. It pokes fun at how the killer in Scream 5 was obvious from the start and how an inhaler is a lazy plot device, and then, from start to finish, the Wayans can't help referencing that this is their movie and that they didn't like how the franchise was taken away by them, so much so that it becomes the main plot point at the end. Also, how the entire thing ends up being a fake legacy sequel dressed up and released as a real legacy sequel is pretty smart. 

For an unapologetically brainrot movie, there is smart stuff here. When Cindy fights the killer(s) in this one, it's a John Wick parody, while it was a Matrix parody in the original. Also, the Wayans lean more into making this one a black-black movie. I had fun, though it had its flat and dated jokes.

Name: Spider-Man
Review:
I've watched this movie a gazillion times as a kid, but I've never watched the whole thing as an adult. So it was new in that way. This Peter Parker was the absolute worst at keeping his secret identity a secret. The very first time he discovers his powers, he drags a tray with his web while the whole school sees, and he, the bullied nerd, suddenly shows agility and superhuman strength that the other 30-year-old kids have never seen. And then when suddenly a dude who has superhuman agility and strength starts doing vigilante stuff, none of them connect the dots that it's this dude.

This is such a quintessential early 2000s movie, whether it's the dialogues or the acting. Also, Sam Raimi is essentially more of a horror filmmaker, so someone like that putting his spin (pun intended) on comic book material is fun. He can't resist putting jumpscares on screaming people even then. The whole visual style is still very cool, like at times it's like watching panels from a comic book, the way certain transitions and visual cues are handled.

So much of this movie is still goated, though. Willem Dafoe is so deliciously evil as Norman Osborn, there's no one like him. More than the goblin stuff, I loved that Thanksgiving dinner scene the most. JK Simmons as Jameson is only in like two scenes in this movie, and boy does he steal both of them. After that there are the visual effects and the action. This is like 24-year-old visual effects, and they still hold up. It's not about the level of detail; the technology has obviously become more advanced, but there is such great vision and creativity here that I still buy these scenes, and the action is still so well crafted. The blend of practical effects with the CGI is very impressive. And lastly, there's the iconic Danny Elfman score with themes that still echo in my mind.

Of course Tobey's Spidey never felt like a high school kid, and all the young characters talk like adults. But yeah, there's an everlasting quality to this movie.

Name: Spider-Man 2
Review:
I never understood as a kid why Peter lost his powers, but that whole part was the genius of this movie when I watch it now. Peter Parker is a 20-year-old with no generational wealth, trying to do college and juggle multiple unstable jobs while also being a superhero. Of course he lacks a social life, and he's unable to be in a relationship with Mary Jane despite being in love with her forever. Peter losing his powers was a result of burnout and an identity crisis. While the movie doesn't actually show how Peter then deals with all this stuff in his life moving forward, this was a very cool way to look at a superhero story.

This is an upgrade over the first movie in so many ways. More hilarious Jameson scenes, bigger and better action, so many wild stylistic swings (Spidey swinging through the newspaper will always be iconic), and the score from Danny Elfman might be his finest work. Sam Raimi's horror tendencies return too, especially in that scene in the hospital where Doc Ock massacres some other docs. All of Ock's appearances having hysterically screaming women in addition to his theme music were low-key funny, and Alfred Molina was amazing. Oh, and those swing sequences were so cool and even more dynamic than the first one. 

Two movies in MJ's whole arc is just: have a will they won't they with Peter, get kidnapped at the end, and confess she loves Peter. She deserved more. 😔

I've owned a VCD of this movie and have watched it countless times so.

Name: Spider-Man 3
Review:
Emo Peter is both the worst and best thing about this movie. Is it a very ineffective version of the whole symbiote storyline? Yes. But is it still hilarious and fun? Hell yes.

This is my least favorite Tobey era movie for the obvious reasons. That third act was all sorts of meh. But this movie did have good things going for it. The music was amazing; the bully Macguire theme music might be the most iconic piece from this movie, but I love all the emotional themes given to Sandman a lot more. The VFX for Sandman was also cutting-edge stuff that still holds up.

The writing in this movie was straight up bad. The MJ and Peter arc was a bad rehash of stuff that was already there in the last two movies: them being unsure about what they are and then MJ getting kidnapped and then them getting together. But here, there are so many other badly written dramas. Why is Peter pretending to be the mature one and MJ shown as the insecure crazy girlfriend when Peter as Spidey literally makes out with Gwen in front of MJ? Like that seemed like a pretty valid callout from MJ. Also, Gwen Stacy is just there in this movie to make MJ feel jealous, and her writing is so stereotypical; when I watched it as a kid, I didn't even realize that Gwen is such an important character otherwise.

Also, in the final fight in the last two movies, there was like blood and sweat during the fight scenes, and it grounded everything despite the cheesy early 2000s flavor of it all. Here everyone has a fresh face despite all the action going on and Peter literally getting crushed by Sandman. The Venom in this movie does make the Tom Hardy version look better; Eddie Brock is also wasted here.

Again, so much hilarious early 20s coded stuff here, but Emo Peter takes the cake. The movie does a terrible job at even showing how exactly the black suit made Peter more powerful, but every time emo Peter was on screen was delightfully cringe and made me laugh the entire time. Even at the bar scene where he's supposed to be evil. It's funny that Peter just becomes annoying instead of evil because of the symbiote.

Also this is the last time a Spider-Man movie would have an elaborate opening titles sequence for now, I loved these in all three movies.

Name: The Amazing Spider-Man
Review:
I'm among the Amazing Spider-Man devotee gang. Yes, this movie did come out at a time when every superhero IP was trying to be dark and edgy, but this one did have its own identity and several creative choices that I loved. Andrew Garfield's Peter is not as nerdy as the other two, and at the time it looked like a choice made to distinguish him from the Tobey version. The dialogue is less dramatic and more natural here; Peter always mumbles and mumbles when he speaks. And then there's Spider-Man himself; this version is more loose with his body, and at times he does move like an actual insect, like when he's covering the lizard in web at the school. He's also way more quippy and also more loose about his secret identity. Even the suit looks like something a teenager could create on his own compared to the Tobey version; the eyes being dark sunglass lenses was a nice touch. The swinging scenes and the POV shots were the cherry on top. 

The action is pretty one-sided as the lizard has the upper hand every single time, but that's pretty realistic. It's still very fun to watch; there are new dynamic things done with the webs, which weren't present in the Tobey movies. I find the mechanical shooters lighting up whenever Peter fires the webs very cool. This one also has a better romance arc. Gwen Stacy finally frees the Spider-Man love interest from the "will they, won't they, and then get kidnapped" jail. She's also more than just being a love interest here, and they have such great chemistry together, for obvious reasons. It was also cute that Peter gets the name "Spider-Man" from Gwen. 

Also, James Horner's score was so good, and I loved the main theme given to Spider-Man. Though I like Hans Zimmer's theme from the sequel, I always preferred this one, so I was glad when this was the one that played in No Way Home.

Also, this one has the best Stan Lee cameo.

Name: The Amazing Spider-Man 2
Review:
This is objectively the best-looking live-action Spider-Man movie; like, even if Brand New Day manages to top this, this is clearly an inspiration for the swinging scenes in that movie as well because this is the best Spider-Man has ever looked in motion. The suit looks so good; the fact that it's a bit loose-fitting and it makes ripples and wrinkles while he moves adds so much character. And within the movie, the top and the bottom of the Spider-Man suit being two separate pieces is way more practical than it being a single piece. The whole idea that Peter gets his powers from the Spider bite only because he shares DNA with Richard Parker was cool.
