And of course, the action, all the slow-motion stuff, and the music are all epic in this movie.

Then there's the Peter and Gwen scene; the more I see Emma Stone and Andrew Garfield in this movie, the more I realize how Tobey Maguire and Kirsten Dunst didn't have much chemistry. The whole Peter and Gwen arc involving the promise he made to her dad and them being unable to stay apart from each other regardless was so good in this movie, and when the loss hits at the end, it's devastating. If there's any place the writing on this movie shines, it's the Peter and Gwen arc; the romance arc is usually secondary in superhero movies, but here it takes center stage. Extra points to Emma Stone for that final look towards Peter that was everything.

Yeah, but other than that this movie is ass writing-wise; the writing on the villains is awful. Jamie Foxx's Max is a caricaturish nerd at first and becomes Jamie Foxx after the transformation. They managed to botch the Goblin as well. Then there are all the Sony-mandated breadcrumbs for their planned cinematic universe that never materialized. They cram too much stuff in here, and none of it sticks except the central romance arc. So this movie always gave me the impression of something that could've been great that got ruined by studio notes.

This is not a great movie, but everything good about it is so AMAZING that I can't rate it too low.

Name: Spider-Man: Homecoming
Review:
Peter starts off as a teenager in both the previous live-action iterations, but he always seemed like a mature man rather than a kid. The MCU Spidey is truly the one where Peter felt like a kid through and through; it also helped that Tom Holland can convincingly pull off a screen age of 15 in his early 20s. Pete is so lovable in this movie and has so much personality to him; we can see both the hero that he is and wants to be and how he's just a kid as well. Everyone treats him like a kid too; when the vulture ends up finding out his identity, his threat sounds more like an adult scaring a kid than a supervillain addressing a superhero. I just love how this film is structured like a proper coming-of-age movie. Though when they reference John Hughes and do a Ferris Bueller tribute, they didn't need to actually show the original scene too for us to make the connection, but I'll let it pass. 

I'm aware RDJ's presence was more of a contractual thing, but the Tony and Peter relationship was one of the most beautiful multi-film arcs in the MCU, and this movie is a big part of that. Peter learns that he is more than just his costume, plus the setting not being in the city with all the tall buildings for Spidey to swing from also made things different. There are a few scenes that stand out to me in this movie. Like the scene where Toomes realizes that Peter is Spider-Man as the traffic light is shining on his face; the scene where Peter uses all his strength to escape the rubble; that montage where Peter gets ready for the dance; and the whole Washington bit. 

Vulture was a great villain and Michael Keaton was great. Pretty solid and justified villain origin story of a corporation taking away his job as well. 

Jon Watts gets a lot of unwanted hate. So I'm giving this a 5 because this was actually a solid and well-made movie with a lot of fun and heart.

Name: Spider-Man: Far From Home
Review:
They took the Iron Boy criticisms seriously because suit lady/Karen is completely absent here (I didn't mind her or that this version of Spidey relied on more tech and gadgets), but still, Tony Stark's presence still looms largely over this movie too, but with good reason. He was the most important mentor and father figure for Peter, so obviously that loss carries weight. But this one's also kind of similar to Tobey's Spider-Man 2, in that Peter just wants to be a kid and enjoy his trip without doing any superheroing. Going to space, disappearing for 5 years, and fighting in a war to save the universe did take a toll on the kid. But this is also another hero growth arc for Peter when he's finally out of Tony Stark's shadow and being his own hero.

If the villain in the first movie was angry about Tony Stark taking away his business, the villain in this movie is angry about Tony Stark being a bad boss. Jake Gyllenhaal's Beck was okay, like, not great, but not bad either. The action during the first half of the movie was underwhelming, with all the CGI overloaded elemental stuff. But at the same time, all the crazy illusion sequences were really great; that's where the CGI and Jon Watts' experience with horror shined. The final London set piece was also cool, especially that moment where Peter breaks the illusion by depending on his Spidey senses.

This one also gives more to Zendaya's MJ, and though the romance isn't as prominent as the Amazing Spider-Man movies, it was still cute, they have great chemistry together, and the high school gang was fun too. That final callback to Peter being at his Toniest with Back in Black playing in the background always makes me smile. These movies get some hate for not letting Peter become a "man" yet, but I always liked that they took the time. It felt organic.

Also, MJ here is goated for figuring out that Peter is Spider-Man all on her own. 7 movies in, she's the only person to do that (Toomes in Homecoming doesn't count), when it's always been obvious.

Name: Spider-Man: No Way Home
Review:
I have lots of issues with this movie. Firstly, there's the way the whole spell situation's been written, like it's so obvious that they just wanted to do this crossover of different versions of live-action Spider-Men and just worked backwards from that idea. And then, May is more central to this story, and we can even say she's the emotional center of it, but the way her death has been handled is very confusing. When it comes, it's a tragic and hard-hitting moment, but then the rest of the movie takes place in pretty much the same night, and then when the movie switches to quips and banter, it feels like Peter, Ned, and MJ weren't all that affected by that loss. Like, the tone shifting to fun fan service right after such a dark scene always bugged me, pun intended.

But of course, that doesn't matter when the movie does absolutely deliver on the fan service. There are meme recreations, interactions between the Spideys that fans have always dreamed of, and Andrew's Spidey finally gets to process the grief of losing Gwen. The returning villains were also fun, but of course Willem Dafoe is the best among them, as he manages to be way more unhinged as the Goblin than he was in his original portrayal. It also helped that he didn't have the mask on him after his first appearance. It was a great creative decision there, as Willem Dafoe's face can be way crazier than anything that mask can offer. That Spidey sense scene in the apartment was also cool. 

Idk why Jon Watts gets so much hate. Any problem I have with this movie is writing-related and not about the direction. Yes, the swinging scenes aren't as impressive as the past iterations, but that's about it. Most of this movie was shot on sets, and there's a lot of CGI also because of it being shot during COVID. Brand New Day has the exact same writers, but Destin Daniel Cretton did do martial arts action really well in Shang-Chi, and that's the kind of flair I'm looking for. 

Michael Giacchino's score has been consistently great in all 3 movies, but here, with the added element of themes from the previous Spider-Man movies, it's his best work so far for Spider-Man. While the finale has all the Spidey crossover fan service stuff, the Doctor Strange mirror dimension stuff was the best-looking sequence for me. This movie also had Tom Holland getting way heavier material to work with even though the character consistency is all over the place writing-wise. He did make the movie his own despite being a crossover situation and pulled off all the emotional beats really well.

With everything that happened in this movie, Mysterio ends up being the villain that took the most from Spider-Man.

Name: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
Review:
The MCU Spider-Man gets a total shake-up here, not just character-wise, but stylistically too, from Jon Watts to Destin Daniel Cretton. It felt like Cretton was drawing from The Amazing Spider-Man 2 stylistically a lot of the time, which was the best Spider-Man movie style-wise, though it was the worst writing-wise. Along with that, there were also moments that felt like they were lifted straight out of the Insomniac Spider-Man video game, especially a fight scene towards the end with some prison guards. Cretton seems to love replicating iconic Spider-Man comic book covers and poses too in slow-mo, which looked really cool. 

The coming-of-age thread from the three "home" movies is over, and Peter is a big-city superhero fighting big-city crime when we meet him in this movie. After everyone forgets who he is, Peter starts living on his own, doesn't even attempt to make human connections, and becomes a full-time vigilante. The only person he talks to is a police detective, though even she doesn't know who he is, and they only ever talk about crime. This is meant to be taking Peter back to the basics, living on his own and with no Stark backup. But still, it doesn't quite explain how Peter is able to afford the big apartment, all his tech and make a living when he's just Spider-Maning throughout his whole day. This was such a big deal in the Sam Raimi movies, and even in the video games, it adds to the whole angle of him being a normal guy. Or he might be providing Spider-Man material to Jameson on the side to fund himself, which we don't see (or was it in the background?); Jameson is also absent in this movie. Or Peter still has access to Stark inheritance, which could fund him for a lifetime actually. All the anti-vigilante task force stuff from Daredevil is also not really mentioned, which seemed odd, maybe to avoid people having to deal with watching multiple seasons of television as homework. (Or maybe there's background stuff that I missed.)

Peter remains as Spider-Man for most of the runtime of this movie. This might be the one where we see Peter Parker's face the least. He remains masked up, and he's very guarded about his identity more than ever before. Though it's not a total Robert Pattinson from The Batman situation, there are enough scenes with an unmasked Peter. Tom Holland portrays the more adult version of Peter really well, and it does seem like a natural progression of the same character; he does still retain his kindness, sense of humor, and innocence. The transformation is not mental; it's physical as well, but that whole metamorphosis plotline had more potential. I also liked how Peter's theme music has evolved from Homecoming to Brand New Day, how the music itself shows how he has matured over the years. 

Destin Daniel Cretton is pretty great at delivering big action and hero moments. It also helps that instead of Spider-Man fighting CGI things, most of the action involves him fighting humans, except for the big green guy. The previous MCU Spider-Man movies didn't really have proper fight scenes where Spidey takes on groups of human enemies like this; there was the fight scene with Goblin in No Way Home, which was actually really great, though the mood there was completely different. Here it's more stylized; it's meant to look cool, and the fight choreography reminded me of both The Amazing Spider-Man and the video games, like I said above (complimentary). The swinging also takes inspiration from The Amazing Spider-Man 2 by giving Peter a suit that's more loose-fitting and forms ripples and wrinkles. It's pretty cool, but still not TASM 2 opening swing-scene cool. There's no self-fitting nano-suit or even the self-tightening tech suit this time. Though Peter still relies on tech and has an AI assistant, the AI assistant is more like a Siri and less like a Karen from Homecoming. The distinction given to organic web vs. web shooters in their look and even the thwip sounds was cool. In comparison to the Raimi version, this does look more like stuff that came out of a body, no double innuendo intended. 

This was a true-blue-red Spider-Man story as it started, with Peter giving his all to fighting crime and still dealing with his loved ones not remembering him. The emotional beats do hit in that regard. What I had mixed feelings about was the bigger plotline, which I won't spoil, but it was obvious to anyone who follows enough of these things and has seen the trailers. The third act had lots of cool action, but I didn't really connect to that whole plotline, and the ending also seemed just okay. It just seemed more interested in setting up future MCU stuff than adding to a self-contained Spider-Man story. 

But lemme tell you somethin, the kid-friendly Jon Bernthal Punisher was very fun to watch; they even reference the Punisher memes for comedic purposes. They somehow find the middle ground of placing him in a PG-13 comedy situation while he'd also work in the R-rated world. But it was hilarious how the Indian censor board out-censored Spider-Man, because the part where Punisher says "Motherfu..." and gets his mouth web-censored by Spidey is altered in the Indian version to mute the "Motherfu..." part too. The Indian censor board also cut a kiss from the movie during a very emotional moment for Lord knows what reason and ruins the scene. Zendaya and Jacob Batalon were great, though they get less screentime and involvement in the plot than in the last two movies. I want to make a Stranger Things reference in regard to Sadie Sink's character, but I guess we're not supposed to say anything about her. It was also fun to see Hulk being all Hulk after so long.

Anyway, this movie had exactly what I had expected from it; it had cool action, plenty of fun, good humor and some great Spidey moments and a relatable character arc for Peter, though Peter's income remains a mystery. Just that the whole bigger plotline that they kept away from the promotions didn't really feel like much. But yeah, it was fun enough and delivered on most of its promises.

Also, the end credits just being real footage of New York City being normal and peaceful was different from every other Marvel movie so far. Looked pretty beautiful and hopeful.

Name: Unmadham
Review:
I think this is the Shahi Kabir movie that triggered me the least. Which isn't to say it lacks the copaganda elements present in his movies or even the dated sensibilities, but I could let it pass rather than let it bother me too much. It's still pretty much coming from a "police will only beat up those who deserve it; people are unfair to police when they claim police are violent" kind of gaze, but this time it's a more character-focused and psychological storyline. I was confused about the jokes that were made at the expense of a husband who did household chores, and I was confused why it was emphasized that a particular police officer was a Brahmin astrologer. 

Unmadham is about a police constable who's an aspiring screenwriter. He's writing a screenplay about him writing a screenplay about a particular case, which is very Adaptation (2002) coded, and then he's also dealing with some mental health issues, and then the case at the center of it all might have a ghost involved with it. This is the most interesting and most risky part of this movie. There are, like, three layers of ambiguous storytelling possible here. What's real and what's the screenplay? What's real and what's a hallucination? What's superstition and what's supernatural?

For Malayalam cinema, Manichithrathazh is obviously the most iconic example of blending psychological drama with the supernatural while leaving room for audience interpretation of whether the supernatural exists. This film even makes a direct reference to Manichithrathazh by literally using an interview clip about it, but still, I didn't feel like I felt the ambiguity about the film's reality that much by the way it's been written. I felt that the whole setup had way more potential than this. The initial buildup was promising, but by the end it's a generic affair involving a generic reason for the crime. Things like the way a police station was very guarded and serious about their one big superstition was intriguing.

Kunchacko Boban was pretty good as a character who's either losing his sanity or seeing more of the reality. But I felt that, for this movie to actually be ambiguous about the reality it presents, it should've stayed locked to his perspective, but that's not the case here. Lijomol gets a character who lacks depth in the writing but does justice to what she got to work with. Like, the character feels less like a person and more like a wife who's just there to add pressure to the already pressured protagonist. Then there's the mystery part. Raina Radhakrishnan plays the character central to the mystery, who leaves an impact even with limited screentime, as her character's presence is felt throughout the movie, even as jumpscares.

The initial buildup made the mystery seem very interesting, but then the way it unfolded and concluded felt very easy. Towards the middle the protagonist gets stuck during the investigation, but it's not even an actual blocker; we spend some time watching his mental turmoil, and then it's back to him chasing the most obvious lead. Like I said, if this was about emphasizing the ambiguity of the film's reality, this is the place where the movie lost me in that regard. The same goes for the way everything concludes; there's even a fight scene that looks very out of place with the kind of movie that this was up to that point. Here too, the ambiguous reality justification can be made, but really? 

Something that deserves all the praise in the world from this movie is the gorgeous hand-animated and hand-drawn opening title sequence. In an era of soulless AI slop, a movie having even its title reveal being hand-animated deserves to be appreciated. There's some solid visual effects work in the movie too, with some CGI lizards and a part involving smoke, a ghost, and a LOT of lizards.

Anyway, I disagree with the opinion that this is Shahi Kabir's worst. That distinction still belongs to the dumpster fire that is Officer On Duty. This belongs in the unexplored potential category. My rating is a bit extra because of that AMAZING handmade title sequence.

Name: Ela Veezha Poonchira
Review:
Definitely the best movie involving Shahi Kabir that I've watched (Minus his assisting role in Thondimuthalum Driksakshiyum). But he's not the writer here, though, and it shows. That whole police ammavan gaze of his is absent here. This is not really a police story, but a story set around people who work for the police department. So there's not really much room here for copaganda.

It's a pretty hard movie to talk about without spoiling anything. There was a Brahmin angle that felt odd. Maybe the caste emphasis was unnecessary? This only rings bells for me because of how Shahi Kabir's other work has depicted Dalits.

The atmosphere and the buildup were great. The choice of location, the cinematography, and the filmmaking convey the isolation and eeriness really well. This is a pretty short movie, and the pacing was perfect for what it was building up towards. Shahi Kabir is a pretty good director. He just needs good writers. But yeah, definitely a very dude-dude movie where the woman is just a plot device.

Name: The Devil Wears Prada
Review:
Meryl Streep is the best part of this movie, but watching this movie as a working professional, I hated Miranda so much more for being a toxic and entitled boss tormenting both her assistants. But movie makes a good point that she must be the devil that she is if she needs to stay in the position that she worked so hard for as a woman, when the men around her do everything to have power over her.

Meryl Streep's performance is just masterclass stuff in this movie.

I miss 90s and early 2000s NYC so much though I've never even been to the place and have only seen it through movies.

Name: Thudakkam
Review:
The biggest problem with Vismaya Mohanlal's Thudakkam (its official government title) is that it's not letting Vismaya Mohanlal make it her own Thudakkam. Like, my shortest thought about this movie is "Onnu thudangaan sammathikkedey."

Vismaya Mohanlal barely stars as Meenu in this movie because the movie is actively trying to show less of her on screen and have "just enough" to justify her being the lead. It's like the people who made the film were not confident enough to just let her carry it. It's like a debut with training wheels attached. Her character is mostly absent from the first half of the movie, and even when she's shown, the editing and the scene blocking are in a way that we really don't see her performing much. And then, even when her character gets more prominent in the second half, the movie still just doesn't let it be her movie; the A10 cameo happens, and even in the climactic fight sequence, there's a visual cue that she's channelling Mohanlal through her even before she kicks ass.

But the thing is, the acting is universally bad in this movie, even from veteran actors, so in comparison, Vismaya's performance, when we do get to see it, just made me think, Maybe she'd be better when it's a better director? Like, the writing and acting is so bad across the board. There were some instances of bad acting that literally made me laugh out loud, like the guy who played the pervy jeep driver who instantly makes Vismaya seem like the better actor. The dialogues are so bad, and the writing and the way scenes play out rival Jeethu Joseph's TV serial sensibilities. The whole thing of how the public turns on Meenu and shames her, and then the whole girl power resolution of it where everyone magically ends up becoming her fans from a single speech, reminded me that Jude Antany Joseph has also made the cringefest called 2018.

Thudakkam is trying to be a girl power movie with the "if girls hit back, then men won't prey on them" messaging. Yk, the most dude-coded way to address the issue without really acknowledging rape culture, misogyny, or patriarchal society. When there's an SA attempt on the lead character, everyone just jumps in to judge her, and we're always seeing her from a distance. The dialogues by even characters who appreciate her seem like they're taking the whole thing lightly, like, she's interviewed on TV because she became viral because of her being so inspirational (there needs to be a new term called "viral ex machina" where becoming viral solves everything magically; it's been happening so regularly), and then the news anchor is like, asking her about her performance and if she'd improve if she got another chance WHEN SHE LITERALLY JUST FOUGHT OFF A RAPIST WHO ATTACKED HER. How do they write stuff like this bro? 

Vismaya is a trained Muay Thai martial artist, and it shows in her posture and movements during the action scenes, about the only time the movie itself confidently shows her on screen as well, but still, it was lacking in the kind of action design and commercial cinema payoffs that pull me in. It just felt so convenient and plastic, with a cringey dialogue with the bad guy at the end that again reminded me that Jude Anthany Joseph made 2018.

Ashish Joe Antony plays the bad guy, and both his performance and the writing of his character are just defined by one word: PERV. Like, the only thing the character does is something pervy during every scene; if there's no woman to perv over, he'd randomly perv over adult magazines. I'm assuming Sandy's character from Leo was the reference here because this is essentially that without the creepy smiling. He's just doing the same creepy facial expression from beginning to end, occasionally switching to creepy-angry from creepy-creepy.

The writing here just doesn't feel genuine. The goal seemed to be just about launching this star kid, with constant reminders about who her dad is, hitting certain checklist points of female empowerment, and family values and aesthetics that are meant to appeal to the conventional family crowd, showcasing her martial arts training, while not really letting her be a real character or giving her a chance to properly perform on screen. Telling a story never felt like the intention here, so this feels more like a product than a movie. 

Vismaya Mohanlal as a person seems cool so far; she has stood for the right causes, and I do hope she gets to do real movies and play real characters, because Jude Anthany's training wheels movie isn't it. With every new awfully directed Jude Anthany movie, my suspicions that Om Shanthi Oshaana is actually a Midhun Manuel Thomas movie grow stronger. 

Also, it's hard to do an action movie with a female lead in Indian cinema when the censor board slaps "violence against women is punishable under law" every time the badass woman is getting hit during a fight scene.

Name: DC
Review:
ACAB: The Musical

We have yet another ACAB gangster action movie from Tamil cinema. Even when there's a good-hearted cop with a sentimental family angle attached, he's also shown to be a reluctant part of a group of killers, so the system is never given a pass. So bonus points for being unapologetically ACAB, Arun Matheswaran.

Anirudh's soundtrack is as much of a star of this movie as the actors are, as this movie is rarely quiet and the music is a constant presence throughout. Songs would pop up in regular intervals to the extent that this would actually qualify as a musical, just that people are shooting, stabbing, and murdering instead of singing and dancing. Lokesh was surprisingly solid as the lead anti-hero Devadas, who's pretty much a ruthless killer, but he channels his violent tendencies towards those who deserve it or something. I liked how the character himself is pretty soft-spoken, empathetic, and very respectful towards the women he encounters, when lead characters that are styled like him in violent action movies tend to usually be incel-coded. The interactions between Devadas and the two female characters, Parvathy and Chandra, felt nice, and it was those moments where the movie breathed a bit in between all the chaos. Wamiqa and Sanjana were good, with Wamiqa as the female lead being the one getting the opportunities to be a badass in the action sequences.

The movie is operating on a hyper-stylized plane, with constant intercuts, a loud score, and stylized non-linearity. I'm not complaining much; it's style over substance done well, with just enough substance given to the characters and the conflict to root for them. The priority here is clearly about the action, all the stylish imagery, and aura farming from the leads and Anirudh with the music. 

The action was pretty solid for the most part. Somehow the movie kept me engaged throughout, with all the constant shooting and stabbing. There's even a single-shot fight sequence where blood falls on the camera lens at one point, and the fight still continues while the blood is dripping down. Now, I'm not sure if that was CGI blood intentionally added for the effect or not, but it does add to the movie instead of being a distraction. The film has these payoffs and musical cues at the right intervals to make the audience cheer, and it also helps that the villainous cops are easily hateable and our gray anti-heroes are very rootable.

Pretty much commercial action movie stuff done right, with a very cool soundtrack; I just wish that the raga of revenge track that appears twice in the movie wasn't cursed by Instagram with the image of VD Satheeshan biting his lip.

AI slop during the opening credits was disappointing though.

Name: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
Review:
This time I could forget about the plot stuff and just enjoy Destin's stylistic flair and action design, which were really unique for an MCU film, though he does take some notes from The Amazing Spider-Man 2 and the Insomniac Spider-Man video games. This is definitely one of my top Spider-Man movies and a clear case of the director elevating basic MCU writing. The end credits sequence is definitely the coolest in an MCU movie and it's just real footage of a peaceful New York.

Maybe I'd have 5 starred it if the needle drops included some Oorum Blood.

Name: The Devil Wears Prada 2
Review:
The first movie was almost completely told through Andy's perspective. I can only remember two moments that we were not experiencing through Andy: one was a meeting where Miranda learns that Emily is sick, and the other was the smile from Miranda at the end after acting all indifferent to Andy. But the sequel switches this up, and there are scenes told through the perspective of all 4 of the main cast. Though Andy still remains the primary POV character.

But the thing is, 20 years have passed in between the two movies, and there's lots of stuff that has changed in terms of media and the fashion industry, and this movie does address that evolution, but not to its full potential. Miranda has evolved a lot over the 20 years, both in Meryl Streep's performance and the character herself; we can see a Miranda who is trying to hold onto what she has worked so hard for. And we can also see a Miranda who reflects on herself and the "devil" that she was. And also a Miranda who struggles to fit into the woke internet era. Miranda was the best part of this movie, and she's more humanized than being the devil here, but it works, and Streep can never miss a beat.

But Andy Sachs, however, is not written as if she had 20 years of life experiences in between the two movies. It seems like she just walked in from the first one to this one. Same goes for Emily as well. Nigel gets his moment towards the end, so he was kind of done right.

I was confused about the priorities of the movie, like sometimes the need for product placements and promotional collabs overshadowed the narrative. Do we really need to see Andy drinking Diet Coke that much? This did have the juice to be a good follow-up, and Meryl Streep is amazing, but Miranda deserved better.

Name: The Invite
Review:
It's the kind of movie that's hard to talk about without spoiling anything, because every joke, every reveal, and every hilarious twist and turn is better seen and experienced, and I can never do justice to them by talking about it. The dialogues are so good, the acting is amazing, Seth Rogen's comedic timing is just chef's kiss, and the editing, the blocking, the use of awkward pauses, and the vibe shifts in between the interactions, I can go on and on. With four characters and a single house, Olivia Wilde found the most interesting ways to film them and let them play off of each other. It's the kind of movie that I'd keep rewatching forever.

Also a perfect example of doing sexual humour without being vulgar or deragatory.

Name: Masters of the Universe
Review:
It seemed to be aimed more towards the people who grew up with the original cartoon (i.e., millennials and early Gen Z) than audiences who are completely blank about He-Man or Masters of the Universe. This movie does find the perfect balance between recapturing and embracing the campy nature of its source material while being self-aware enough to laugh at it too. I expected it to be more of a kid friendly movie but the sexual innuendo was off the charts.

There were many fun little twists here, like Adam getting sent to earth as a child, and then how all the silly names that the characters have are just from his 10-year-old imagination, well, except for Skeletor and Evil-Lynn. Adam being a lovable general goofball instead of a hypermasculine fantasy dude and an HR employee on top of that was a fun twist. Nicholas Galitzine was great in the role; he could switch between being goofy and heroic seamlessly, like, he sells that he has the power and looks the part as He-Man while maintaining that he's more than just muscles, though Skeletor is obsessed with his muscles and his glorious sword hanging between his thighs (?), when He-Man always hangs his sword on his back. Again, the sexual innuendo is crazy in this movie. 

But it was funny to me that, unlike a Captain America situation where the muscular lead actor's head was composited onto a smaller body double, here they decided to just put Galitzine in loose-fitting clothes and expect us to believe that this dude isn't already jacked. They even show him struggling to lift light dumbbells at the beginning, but with those shoulders, that posture, and that frame, it's so obvious that he's not a weak dude, though they do give him a CGI body that turns muscular at the time he finally turns into He-Man. Jared Leto plays Skeletor, and that's also funny to me because they replaced his head with a CGI skull and altered his voice digitally to make him sound more demonic, so it's like why, bro? But yeah, it turns out to be the best character with Jared Leto's name attached to it in years and is consistently funny, mostly thanks to the chaotic and irreverent way he's been written. I wish Alison Brie as Evil-Lynn got more to do in the movie, though. Camila Mendes as Teela was great, both in looking the part and in being funny. Idris Elba was also dependable; well, he's Idris Elba.

There were some solid action sequences, and the visual effects also looked great for the most part and only took me out in a very few instances. The synth music score was so awesome, and there were some cool needle drops in the movie as well. This one deserved more love on the big screens.

Name: The End of Oak Street
Review:
When a movie gets a physical reaction out of me, it's a definite tell that it completely pulled me in, and this one did do that. The end of Oak Street is a dino movie that manages to recapture what was great about the first Jurassic Park while trying to be different from Jurassic Park in every way possible. 

Firstly, the film is set in the 80s, which avoids the characters having to refer to Jurassic Park, but also, the entire vibe of the movie, whether it's the music or the visual style, feels like an 80s tribute. The dinosaurs are fluffier here and have more feathers, and there's also more visible blood and gore; the dino attacks are far more visceral, they visibly bite and tear shit off. The 80s energy, humor, and cheesiness are a bit disarming at times right before something horrific might happen on screen. David Robert Mitchell plays with the tonality of it really well, sprinkling in moments of terror in between moments of dark humor and 80s charm. The score by Michael Giacchino was amazing work; it sounded exactly like an 80s monster movie soundtrack, also switching between charming and terrifying seamlessly.

The movie doesn't wait around much; it sets up the neighborhood and the main characters really fast and sets up their interpersonal drama right before they're being transported to prehistoric times. The kids are pretty underdeveloped, but the relationship between the parents and the financial issues they're going through does connect into the ending. The ending is a traditional 80s movie ending on the surface, but if we think about it, it's pretty grim and fucked up. Like, I think a person's perception of this movie would depend on how they walk off that ending, if they see it as a happy one or a dark one.

The CGI looked great; there's a great mix of CGI and practical sets and visual effects here. The prehistoric animals seemed like actual threats, and the sense of danger felt very real, especially during THAT scene. I'd give a pass for the characters acting impulsively and not like survival experts because they're all just normal people who get transported to a dangerous place with no clue about what to do, unlike the Jurassic Park franchise, where there are always experts involved. 

Plus Anne Hathaway was all kinds of unhinged and badass towards the end.

Name: The Last House
Review: The whole "castaway but inside a home" angle was nice, seeing how the family turns their home into a sustainable shelter when they're locked in with no way of getting food, supplies, or resources from the outside world. But whenever this movie turned into a hybrid of M. Night Shyamalan's The Happening along with A Quiet Place, it lost me. The ending made no sense.

Name: Bethlehem Kudumba Unit
Review:
There's this amazing match cut at the start of the movie that goes from a guitar strum to a striking match while introducing the main characters, Ashley and Justin, and this movie pulled me IN right at that moment. 

Girish A.D.'s movies don't really operate on a realistic plane; there are over-the-top cartoonish moments, parodies, and references to pop culture and situational humor peppered throughout, and yet, the people we see in his films always feel alive, like they have a life outside of the story that we're watching and that the settings are living and breathing places. There are always these small details and quirks given to the characters and the setting that add so much texture to everything that the films always hold up on their own, and the humor also holds up on its own. Despite having multiple instances of social media and pop culture references, this movie is not actually entirely dependent on those references to be funny. Just like Premalu, it's able to be funny just with its characters and situations, so that pure skill to write and direct comedy like this is why Girish is one of the best in the game right now.

Though every Girish A.D. movie except I am Kaathalan is technically a romcom, the comedy part is more dominant over the romance part. This, however, might be his most romantic movie so far. During the initial half, I just loved the way the glances between Ashley and Justin were used to convey their mutual attraction, and when they do get to interact with each other, the chemistry is so obvious, and we see how they grow closer while also addressing the age gap. Romantic movies that just let the main characters talk and connect are rare in Malayalam these days. Here, every interaction between Ashley and Justin feels so organic, the dialogue is so good, the emotional beats are perfect, and these two characters and their back and forth are basically the life of the movie, and that's where the writing from Girish and Kiran truly shines here. Even the writing for the texts they send each other is some of the best writing from this year in Malayalam cinema, and I'm not even exaggerating.

Nivin Pauly, when he gets to play cute, funny, or romantic, can uplift any movie even if the material he gets to work with is not great. He just needs to get enough space to do the stuff that he's REALLY good at. In this movie he gets to be cute, funny, and romantic with great material, so this is like the true comeback of the dude from Premam. Nivin Pauly smiling and blushing through a rom-com can't go wrong. That whole pre-interval part where he's being all blushy is the "yeah, the romcom goat's back" part of this movie. 

Then there's Mamitha as Ashley, which is a character that's very different from Sona or Reenu. Girish A.D. romances tend to pair an introvert with an extrovert, and here Ashley is more of the introvert. Whether it's the humor, romance, or the more dramatic moments, Mamitha has such a perfect hold over the character, this fun girl from a middle-class conservative family who's able to be herself only when she's most comfortable. The way she silently yearns over Justin in the initial half is some of the best yearning acting I've seen, and that scene where they eventually confront each other was built up to perfectly.

Now this is a film with a fairly simple plotline; there's nothing big happening here dramatically. Like, if we think about it from a "story beat A to story beat B" situation, this movie would seem like a nothingburger, but the amazing thing about BKU is that it's absolutely not a nothingburger. All the texture I mentioned earlier and the way the film handles its characters, their interactions, their dialogue, and everything adds up towards making this something real, funny, and wholesome. The first-half buildup was very beautiful, and that interval point was this movie at its peak. It did lose me a bit in the second half because while the first half focused on the main romance, the second half brings in a subplot involving Justin's brother, which starts to run in parallel. That whole subplot and the whole elaborate parody of a very popular movie towards the end felt like its own separate movie. It's not the first time a Girish movie parodied other popular films, but here it just felt like it stood out. But then the romance takes center stage again, and while it's a very simple conclusion, the acting, the dialogues, the filmmaking, and Vishnu Vijay's score bring in all the feels.

The score elevated the movie in regular intervals, especially the pre-interval sequence and the ending. There were lots of cool transitions, like that match cut at the beginning, and there was that cool montage towards the end that looked like Justin flipping through his memories like they're a book. The hopeless kozhi Glixon played by Roshan and then Suresh Krishna with his regular supply of counters were my favorites from the supporting cast.

Anyways, this is a movie that promised laughs, fun, and wholesome romance and delivers on exactly that. Impeccably cute movie.

We needed wholesome cinema back so bad.

Name: Khalifa: The Ruler
Review:
I doubt they had a full screenplay of this movie when they made and released that promo last year. Most movies never include the promo footage in the movie itself, but Khalifa is not most movies. They went to London to shoot that thing, so you better believe that they find excuses to insert that London fight scene and random shots of Rajuvettan walking stylishly through London in here. Khalifa is the kind of movie that has "making it up as we go along" written all over it. Which is okay if the results are good, but here it isn't.

Like, take the big cameo, for example, a character who, both in the promo and multiple times in the movie, was emphasized as someone so badass that the Indian government couldn't imprison him for even 30 minutes. So when it's finally revealed where he has been at the end, it feels like the punchline to a joke. Then we have Rajuvettan as Aamir Ali, who's styled impeccably and looks very fit and handsome, and then a good amount of this movie is spent on replaying the same exact shots of him walking in slow-mo through either London or Dubai or Kerala over and over again. It's like ads for Kalyan Silks' Aadi sale appearing in between the movie. Neil Nitin Mukesh, as the bad guy, gets to do a few of these fashion ads as well.

This is a so-and-so random plotline about a normal guy with a gold smuggling legacy attached to him turning into a gold smuggler out of circumstances and then fighting the other evil gold smuggler group. Of course the plotline connects itself to the real-life gold smuggling controversy during the LDF government's term in Kerala. A funny thing is, back when Empuraan was released, it got attacked by the Sangh, Prithviraj was labeled an anti-national, and then people from LDF, including the Chief Minister, supported the movie. So now, maybe to balance that out, this movie has the evil smugglers working with the LDF government, and the good smugglers are helped by the Sangh government to trap them. Or while ripping off aesthetics and the theme song from Dhurandhar, they ended up ripping off the Sangh cocksucking from that movie as well.

I appreciated that Aamir Ali's fight choreography was consistently boxing-based and was more grounded than what's usually there in Vysakh's movies. But at the same time the action just felt more bland and repetitive than being thrilling. The greatest trick Aditya Dhar pulled was convincing people that the dogshit action in Dhurandhar is the best Indian cinema has to offer. No, bro, a camera that's too close to the actors and being all shaky with janky editing isn't particularly making the action thrilling. Even Vysakh's Turbo with a far more physically restricted ikka had better action. 

KGF should take the blame for making trailer editing in Indian movies a thing, and by "trailer editing," I mean movies having sequences that are edited like trailers, not montages. The interval point of this movie is literally a trailer for this movie itself. We even hear the "Mambaram palliyile uroos" in the background when the character is not even saying it at the time. The overall writing, if there was any writing, was very bad. There's so much filler in here, like did we really need to spend that much time seeing Aamir's inconsequential romance with a clearly non-Mallu actress? Neil Nithin Mukesh at least tries to sync his lips to the Malayalam dialogue, while Malavika Sharma doesn't at all, for the one line she does get to speak. Otherwise, we literally don't see her speak at all; we never see her and Aamir hold a proper conversation. All the smuggling stuff was an inferior version of what KV Anand showed years ago in Ayan. Then there's the bad prosthetic work at the end. Jakes Bejoy's score was trying to be the Anwar soundtrack, but other than some tracks here and there, it was just LOUD. 

I hope more filmmakers don't actually believe that ripping off Dhurandhar or Animal or KGF is what a cool modern action movie is supposed to be.

Also, special shoutout to the stunt artists who played Aamir's security guards. They deserve a star just for how cool they were.

Name: The Long Walk
Review: I was thinking, damn, this is a sadder, darker, and more realistic Hunger Games situation, and then only realized at the end that this had the same director as the Hunger Games movies. Of course if an oppressive authoritarian capitalist government has a competition that exploits its citizens and broadcasts as entertainment, it's going to take all the power away from them instead of giving them weapons and combat skills. I liked how the deaths were motivated by the drama at the moment rather than delivering gore and shock every single time. But the best part is the chemistry between the lead duo, how the friendship between them forms and develops over the course of going through something horrible and traumatic together. Cooper Hoffman and David Jonsson were so good in this movie. Another standout was Mark Hamill, as a villain who never seems like a person but always like this curated authority figure with scripted lines that he wants everyone to see, reminding me of someone over here in India.

Name: Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-ups
Review:
I got the answer to a question I've had for a long time through Toxic. The Indian censor board has multiple warning cards for various scenarios; there's one for smoking, one for drinking, and one for violence against women. So what happens when there exists a scene when every single thing comes together? In Toxic there's a fight scene in a bar, with liquor and cigarettes present, where the main character is murdering and mutilating female assassins. So the answer to the question is they don't show the violence against women warning and only show the smoking and drinking one.

Toxic on the whole didn't feel like slop, though; it felt like a slopification of a pretty interesting plotline. Underneath it all, I can see this character-driven saga of a chauvinistic and violent gangster stuck in a depressing cycle of violence and trauma with the women in his life, eventually having to deal with the aftereffects of his sins. A subversion of hypermasculine power fantasies including Yash's own KGF. But no, Toxic doesn't really commit to it. Now I can't really judge which part of the script was Yash's and which part of the script was Geethu's, but the movie does seem like it's in conflict with being an anti-hero story with some substance and drama or a KGF-Animal type. I didn't really care about all the crime drama stuff going on, since it's mostly just a repeat of "X tries to kill Raya, Raya kills X, something something, weapons, casino, blah, blah, blah" with a lot of forgettable male characters. For once we have a gangster movie where the men are more thinly written than the women.

Now this is not a full-on penis movie like Animal, but it tries to be a penis movie with a penis movie protagonist while trying to flesh out the women around him. I said "trying to" and not that it's successful at it. Because the way Toxic handles its women is confusing. On one hand this is not the kind of movie where women are on the sidelines; multiple women characters are front and center here and get plenty of screentime, including Raya's sister played by Nayanthara, who practically raised him and is shown as an equal to him, just less psychotic and less horny. Even in the case of Raya's love interests, they're not really worshipping him or acting like he's superior to them, but it's inconsistent. On one hand, we'll see Kiara's character calling out Raya's disrespect and misogyny; on the other hand, she can't help being all over him. Raya is the kind of guy who'd strip naked and ask for a fuck even before he'd ask for a woman's name; he's also a remorseless murderous criminal who has a kill count that could rival a serial killer. Just that we never convincingly see why these women would choose to be with a guy who's either violent or horny or violently horny or hornily violent. But other than the few women in the main cast, a lot of the others are indeed used as objects whose sole purpose is to show Raya being a fuckboi party animal.

It's hard to judge bad dialogues in a [Malayalam] dubbed version because I don't know for sure if the original also sucks equally. The translations were very awkward at times, and towards the end the dialogues and the dubbing were so bad that everyone in the audience, including me, was laughing at scenes that were supposed to be intense and dead serious. Again, I don't know if the same scenes were as comically bad in Kannada, so for now this is just about the bad dub. There were some metaphor lines that sounded straight out of KGF, which I assumed were Yash's own contributions. I did like Yash's performance; all things considered, he plays two characters here, and it did feel like two different people. But again, this would've worked better as a grounded Gangs of Wasseypur-ish violent gangster saga than trying to be KGF and Animal as well. Yash gets to do some intense scenes especially towards the end, when we see a more broken down and vulnerable Raya, but the script he himself co-wrote is the kind that buries that intensity with silliness.

I loved the action sequence in the circus. There was all kinds of cool gunplay and hand-to-hand combat choreography there, along with some pretty solid camera work and well-executed over-the-top gore. That and the father-son fight scene are the only places where the action made me feel something, though. All the other fight scenes range from looking like an ad, like the intro scene and the bar fight with the female assassins with all the bad sexual innuendo, both of which are so unserious and goofy, or they just seem like the same kind of shooting and stabbing on loop.

The visual effects have some solid stuff at times; the clone effects on the two Yash characters and the extra work done on the younger one to make him appear a bit different from Raya were solid. But there were also lots of obvious digital backgrounds that made this movie look like a Marvel movie. Marvel aesthetics are fine for that genre, but when it's supposed to be a gritty gangster saga, it's awkward. The CGI gore also looks deliberately stylized; the gore also worked sometimes and seemed silly at other times. Ravi Barsur was just LOUD, like always. Also, how much slow-motion walking to loud music playing in the background is too much slow-motion walking to loud music playing in the background? 

I do see the potential here; the third act, when Raya finally unravels and the sins of his past start to haunt him, is the kind of deconstruction of a hypermasculine power fantasy that films like this rarely even try to attempt. But the film still hesitates to really question everything that he did, like to truly show him as pathetic or to truly show the "female gaze" of toxic masculinity that Geethu Mohandas promised. What we get is a movie that still wants to make him look cool and murder goons in slo-mo. It should've either committed to being a penis movie or a serious drama; this in-between approach just seems like a genre mix from hell. 

There are so many absurdly shitty scenes in this movie. The scene with Rukmini Vasanth with the bomb and the scene with Kiara Advani after their first date get funnier the more I think about them. I'm not doing a scene-by-scene dissection because each scene requires its own essay.

Edit: My original rating was a 2 but I'm making it a 3 just out of spite for the way incels are shitting on it and because of the potential this did have.

Name: I'm Game
Review:
Why'd DQ choose to make his homecoming be a movie where he's barely in it during the second half? The second half made it feel like this Malayalam cinema comeback is him doing his side gig while taking a break from his main gig in Telugu and Tamil cinema. That entire extended flashback in the second half was just repeating information that was already established, and we could see the reveals coming from miles away. Sometimes such flashbacks do add to the emotional core of a movie even with repeated info (Ahem... Ghajini), but here it just felt so flat, and that character just seemed more stupid than heroic. It felt like the flashback was halting the movie to stay in a limbo rather than add anything to it, other than an obvious Ather sponsorship opportunity. 

I did enjoy the first half of the movie, though—well, the last sections of the first half. DQ plays Dan John, a rich, spoiled brat who flaunts his entitlement while also being a shameless gambling addict who wants to make easy money but ends up being in debt. The kind of dude who'd tell his mom that "it's not enough" when she literally hands him over her whole life savings. An unlikable dude for all intents and purposes. Then something happens to him, which, I guess, I shouldn't say since it's a spoiler, but it's when that something does happen to him that the movie felt interesting to me. That whole unique turmoil that Dan goes to was very fun to watch; DQ was great during these sections, bringing the right amount of comical energy and also pulling off a pretty convincing physical performance too. There's even a cool fight scene that factors in this unique factor into the choreography that reminded me of Leigh Whannel's Upgrade. And later there's another unique fight scene that reminded me of one of my favorite moments from Evil Dead 2. I also liked how they try to set it up as a medical condition rather than something supernatural.

The red flags are there in the first half too, though, especially the cringey dialogues at times and the arc with Kayadu Lohar's character. But then the second half is all downhill. The extended flashback occupies the bulk of the runtime there, and then when we finally get back to Dan, he gets a very out-of-character redemption arc that didn't feel earned, but then again, how can you set up a proper redemption arc when the main character is barely in the movie after a point? This is not the same kind of scam that Rajuvettan tried to pull in Empuraan by selling it as an A10 movie when A10 is barely in the movie. Here DQ is the lead for exactly half of the movie. Still a scam regardless.

Any attempt at drama and emotional payoffs falls flat, and then, like Rdx, the movie resorts to showing violence towards women to make us hate the bad guys and want them to get beaten up. We're in big 2026, and there are still movies where women characters exist just to get beaten up and molested by the bad guys. Also, for a Malayalam movie, there's only like a handful of Malayalam actors in this cast, and the rest are all Telugu and Tamil actors. Vinay Fort even randomly disappears after a point, and his existence is not even acknowledged properly except once afterwards. Most of the dialogue is either English, Tamil, or Telugu, especially in the second half, where it's essentially a Tamil movie. Hearing Pepe speak Angamaly Tamil was one of the very few fun things about the flashback, though. Some of the lines are hilariously bad and made me laugh like the random "Cricket is an emotion" drop. 

The background score sounded very Instagrammy; I'm pretty sure one of the car chases had Phonk music from Gymbro reels playing exactly as is. Jakes Bejoy seems to be in his phoning-in era, though I did find two of the tracks in the album cool. Nahas should get better scripts to work with because he does show off solid filmmaking at times; I don't think anyone could've saved that flashback.

Anyway, I felt DQ delivered a good performance here, channeling both the absurdity and charm needed to pull off a character like this. I just wish Dan stayed the protagonist of the movie like in the first half instead of being absent for a large stretch of the movie during the second half. This Homecoming ended up feeling Far From Home, and I hope this doesn't mean that there's No Way Home. There's always hope for a Brand New Day, DQ.

Name: Tony
Review:
I love biopics that focus and detail on a specific event or a part of a subject's life more than those that tend to retell the broad strokes of their lives. Tony is about a small but very important turning point in Anthony Bourdain's life, the one that turned him from a literature student to a chef, or Tony to Anthony, so to say. And this movie stands on its own as just a great character-driven coming-of-age story even without a real-life person attached to it. Tony as a character has a well-defined character arc here; all the emotional beats work really well. The film is wholesome, charming, occasionally funny, and really well made.

Dominic Sessa carries the film really well, and he's in every scene here. Tony's growth as a person is really felt; Tony is a 19-year-old with all the immaturity, confusions, and impulsive decisions to be expected from that age, and then the same decisions draw him closer and closer to finding his thing to do in life. His social awkwardness, compulsive lying, various quirks, and eventual acceptance of a new environment and its new people were really fun to watch. I also really loved Antonio Banderas as the chef, a man who is in limbo between giving up on what he loves and holding onto some kind of a feeble hope, seeing a spark in Tony that Tony himself is unaware of. Their whole dynamic was really fun; when there was a scene where Tony and the chef were walking on the beach and bonding, it totally reminded me of Ustad Hotel. Maybe Anjali Menon wrote that movie after reading this part of Anthony Bourdain's autobiography? Parts of it obviously reminded me of the Bear as well, but with less shouting, except for the chaotic restaurant scene towards the end that was VERY Bear coded. But Tony does show cooking more like a job than as something beautiful or aesthetic. It's a very technical depiction, except a key moment where a special dish is being made. 

This movie also has a really great score and some amazing needle drops. I need to find the songs in this soundtrack ASAP.

How Anthony ended his life did add an air of sadness to this movie as it ended, though this never focuses on that part of his story and tries to be more about finding your people and your thing in life. Or maybe that's what the story about the cook and the fish that the chef says was about. 

Anyways it's delicious cinema. Aaah the privilege of being able to find your passion.

Name: Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar
Review:
I like a good practical thriller. I mean, sure, there might be logical loopholes here and there, but there's some amount of care put into the writing to connect several dots and provide a proper reasoning for every twist and turn. This movie is like a better Drishyam sequel than the actual Drishyam sequels. The whole cat-and-mouse setup between a woman who researched a true crime book and the man who actually wrote said true crime book was also interesting. 

The movie revolves around a group of police officers unwittingly becoming a part of a crime, and Vijayaraghavan plays the reputed veteran officer Harris who investigates said crime. Parvathi as Aleena is our main protagonist, a woman who is underestimated by everyone, including Harris from the very beginning but is way more cunning than she lets off. Unlike last month's scam girl power movie Thudakkam, here the female protagonist indeed properly carries the movie, and Parvathi does it really well (people were applauding at a key moment towards the end), and the fact that the men around her underestimate her because of her gender is pretty much a part of the narrative, though the movie never really preaches about it.

Vijayaraghavan as Harris was playing the kind of older Sethuramayyar type of character I expected Ikka to play at his current age. Harris has seen it all, he has done it all, he's brilliant, he has legendary instincts, and he's very well aware of it. He also carries this sense of pride with him; though he is capable of being emotional, he'd put his pride and reputation first, he isn't afraid of bending the rules, and he would think about every possibility. Like, this is a pretty powerful adversary to put up against any protagonist, and Harris is the kind of interesting character who could even get his own standalone stories. Vijayaraghavan just embodied the whole "he's the GOAT and he knows it" body language really well. "Nee ente posthakam alle vaayichullu? Ente Experience illello? "Ufff...

I also liked Sidharth Bharathan, and then Vinay Forrt got some surprisingly funny scenes in this otherwise dead serious movie. The dialogues can be a hit or miss at times, but the movie mostly flowed well for me, and even when some of the payoffs were predictable, the way they were reached was interesting enough. I really loved the soundtrack and the background score by Mujeeb Majeed as well. 

Still though, the cyber cell and the brilliant veteran investigator wouldn't think of checking a person's Google Maps location footprint first before checking for tower locations and all?!
